name: Python

beginner.content:
What is Python?

Python is a high-level, general-purpose programming language created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991. It was designed around one idea: code is read far more often than it is written, so it should read almost like plain English.

• High-level - you work with lists, dictionaries and objects, never with memory addresses or registers.
• Interpreted - you run the source file directly; there is no separate compile step you have to perform.
• Dynamically typed - variables don't declare a type; the type belongs to the value.
• Multi-paradigm - procedural, object-oriented and functional styles are all first-class.

Your First Python Program

In Java, printing one line needs a class, a main method and a compile step. In Python it is a single line - the file itself is the program.
codeExamples:
print("Hello, Python!")

# OUTPUT:
# Hello, Python!

beginner.content:
Indentation Is Syntax

Python uses indentation instead of curly braces to group statements into blocks. A colon : opens a block, and every line indented under it belongs to that block. The standard is 4 spaces per level.

Getting the indentation wrong is not a style problem - it is a SyntaxError or IndentationError.
codeExamples:
marks = 72

if marks >= 40:
    print("Passed")          # inside the if-block
    print("Well done!")      # still inside the if-block
print("Result printed")      # outside - runs every time

# OUTPUT:
# Passed
# Well done!
# Result printed

beginner.content:
Where Python Is Used

AreaPopular tools
Web backends & APIsDjango, Flask, FastAPI
Data analysisPandas, NumPy, Jupyter
Machine learning & AIscikit-learn, PyTorch, TensorFlow
Automation & scriptingos, pathlib, subprocess, Selenium
DevOps & cloudAnsible, AWS SDK (boto3)
Testingpytest, unittest

A Taste of Python

A few lines show the style: no type declarations, no semicolons, and powerful built-in collections.
codeExamples:
name = "Pankaj"
age = 28
scores = [90, 85, 78]

print(f"{name} is {age} years old")
print("Average score:", sum(scores) / len(scores))

for score in scores:
    if score >= 80:
        print(score, "is a distinction")

# OUTPUT:
# Pankaj is 28 years old
# Average score: 84.33333333333333
# 90 is a distinction
# 85 is a distinction

beginner.content:
Introduction

Python is a high-level, interpreted, dynamically typed, multi-paradigm language created by Guido van Rossum (1991). Its design goal is readability: code looks close to plain English and blocks are defined by indentation.
codeExamples:
# A complete Python program is just statements - no class, no main()
language = "Python"          # variable: no type declaration needed
version = 3.12               # a float; the type belongs to the value
print(f"Hello from {language} {version}")   # f-string formatting

# OUTPUT:
# Hello from Python 3.12

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Software teams need a language that is quick to write, easy to read months later, and has libraries for every domain. Python cuts boilerplate, so a developer spends time on the problem, not on the language ceremony.
codeExamples:
# Task: count words in a sentence.
# Java needs a class, main(), a split and a Map; Python needs 3 lines.
text = "to be or not to be"
counts = {}
for w in text.split():                       # split on whitespace
    counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1         # default 0 if the word is new
print(counts)

# OUTPUT:
# {'to': 2, 'be': 2, 'or': 1, 'not': 1}

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real systems: Instagram and Dropbox backends (Django), Netflix automation, NASA data pipelines, banks' risk scripts, and nearly every machine-learning product (PyTorch, scikit-learn).
codeExamples:
# Real-time style task: a tiny "log summary" an ops engineer would write
logs = ["INFO start", "ERROR disk full", "INFO retry", "ERROR timeout"]
errors = [line for line in logs if line.startswith("ERROR")]  # filter
print(f"{len(errors)} errors found:")
for e in errors:
    print(" -", e)

# OUTPUT:
# 2 errors found:
#  - ERROR disk full
#  - ERROR timeout

beginner.content:
Diagram

   source.py ──► Compiler ──► Bytecode (.pyc) ──► Python VM ──► Output
   (you write)  (automatic)   (cached)           (CPython)

   Paradigms:  Procedural  |  Object-Oriented  |  Functional

expert.content:
Python vs Java at a Glance

AspectPythonJava
TypingDynamic (checked at runtime), strongStatic (checked at compile time), strong
BlocksIndentationCurly braces
ExecutionSource compiled to bytecode on the fly, run by the CPython VMjavac compiles to .class bytecode, run by the JVM
Entry pointTop of the file (optionally guarded by if __name__ == "__main__")public static void main(String[] args)
MemoryReference counting + cyclic garbage collectorTracing garbage collectors (G1, ZGC...)
VerbosityConciseMore ceremony, more explicit
Raw speedSlower for CPU-heavy pure-Python loopsFaster thanks to the JIT compiler

"Interpreted" Is Only Half the Story

Python is usually called interpreted, but CPython (the standard implementation) first compiles your source into bytecode, then a virtual machine executes that bytecode - the same two-phase design as Java, just done automatically every time you run the file. Imported modules have their bytecode cached as .pyc files in __pycache__ so the compile step is skipped next time.
codeExamples:
import dis

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

dis.dis(add)   # show the bytecode CPython generated for add()

# OUTPUT (Python 3.12; exact opcodes vary by version):
#   RESUME           0
#   LOAD_FAST        0 (a)
#   LOAD_FAST        1 (b)
#   BINARY_OP        0 (+)
#   RETURN_VALUE

expert.content:
The Zen of Python

Python's design philosophy is shipped inside the language as an Easter egg. These principles explain many of its choices - for example, why there is usually one obvious way to do something.
codeExamples:
import this

# OUTPUT (first lines):
# The Zen of Python, by Tim Peters
#
# Beautiful is better than ugly.
# Explicit is better than implicit.
# Simple is better than complex.
# Complex is better than complicated.
# Flat is better than nested.
# Sparse is better than dense.
# Readability counts.
# ...

expert.content:
Python 2 vs Python 3

Python 3 (2008) deliberately broke compatibility with Python 2 to fix design mistakes. Python 2 reached end of life on 1 January 2020, so all new code should be Python 3. You will still see Python 2 syntax in old tutorials:

• print "hi" (statement) became print("hi") (function).
• 5 / 2 was 2 in Python 2; in Python 3 it is 2.5 (use // for floor division).
• Strings became Unicode by default; raw bytes got their own bytes type.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Is Python compiled or interpreted?Both: CPython compiles source to bytecode, then its virtual machine interprets that bytecode
Is Python strongly or weakly typed?Strongly typed - "1" + 1 raises TypeError instead of silently converting. It is also dynamically typed
Why does Python use indentation?To force readable, consistently structured code - the visual layout and the actual block structure can never disagree
What is CPython?The reference implementation of Python, written in C - what you get from python.org
Name some other Python implementationsPyPy (JIT-compiled, often much faster), MicroPython (microcontrollers), Jython (JVM, Python 2 only), IronPython (.NET)
What are .pyc files?Cached bytecode for imported modules, stored in __pycache__, so they don't need to be recompiled on every run

Advantages

Advantages: concise syntax, huge standard library ("batteries included"), enormous ecosystem, cross-platform, great for prototyping, strong community, excellent for data/AI and automation.
codeExamples:
# Advantage: "batteries included" - JSON, dates, math with no installs
import json, datetime, statistics
data = json.loads('{"scores": [70, 80, 90]}')      # parse JSON
print(statistics.mean(data["scores"]))             # stats built in
print(datetime.date(2024, 1, 31).strftime("%d %b %Y"))

# OUTPUT:
# 80
# 31 Jan 2024

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: slower than compiled languages for CPU-heavy loops, higher memory per object, runtime type errors only appear when the line runs, weak native mobile support.
codeExamples:
# Disadvantage: errors that a compiler would catch appear only at runtime
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

print(add(2, 3))          # fine
print(add("2", 3))        # TypeError only when this line executes

# OUTPUT:
# 5
# TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the GIL stops threads running Python bytecode in parallel (CPython), no true private members, deployment needs an interpreter or bundler, mobile/browser support is limited.
codeExamples:
# Limitation: CPU-bound threads do not run in parallel because of the GIL
import threading, time
def work(): sum(i * i for i in range(3_000_000))

t0 = time.perf_counter()
ts = [threading.Thread(target=work) for _ in range(2)]
[t.start() for t in ts]; [t.join() for t in ts]
print("2 threads ~ same time as running one after the other")

# OUTPUT:
# 2 threads ~ same time as running one after the other

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Choose Python where developer speed, ecosystem and integration matter more than raw single-thread speed. Put hot paths in C/Rust/NumPy, scale with processes or async, enforce quality with type hints + tests, and pin versions per service.

beginner.content:
What Gets Installed?

Installing Python gives you the interpreter - the program (python / python.exe) that reads and runs your .py files - plus the standard library (hundreds of ready-made modules like math, json and datetime) and the package installer pip.

Always install a current Python 3 release (3.12 or newer is a good choice). Python 2 is dead and must not be used for new work.

Installing on Windows

1. Download the installer from python.org/downloads.
2. On the first screen, tick "Add python.exe to PATH" - forgetting this is the #1 beginner problem.
3. Click Install Now.
4. Open a new Command Prompt or PowerShell window and check the version.

Windows also installs the py launcher, which lets you pick between several installed versions.
codeExamples:
# Run these in Command Prompt / PowerShell (not inside Python):
python --version
py --version
py -3.12 --version     # run a specific installed version
py --list              # list all installed versions

# OUTPUT (example):
# Python 3.12.6

beginner.content:
Installing on macOS and Linux

• macOS: use the python.org installer, or Homebrew (brew install python).
• Linux: Python 3 is usually pre-installed. Use your package manager to add a newer version or the venv module.

On macOS and Linux the command is usually python3, because python may be missing or point to an old system copy.
codeExamples:
# macOS (Homebrew)
brew install python
python3 --version

# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt update
sudo apt install python3 python3-pip python3-venv
python3 --version

beginner.content:
Checking the Interpreter from Inside Python

The sys module tells you exactly which interpreter is running your code - very useful when several versions are installed and something "works on one machine but not the other".
codeExamples:
import sys
import platform

print(sys.version)                        # full version string
print(sys.version_info >= (3, 10))        # compare versions safely
print(sys.executable)                     # path of the running interpreter
print(platform.python_implementation())   # which implementation

# OUTPUT (example, Windows):
# 3.12.6 (tags/v3.12.6:a4a2d2b, Sep  6 2024, 20:11:23) [MSC v.1940 64 bit (AMD64)]
# True
# C:\Users\student\AppData\Local\Programs\Python\Python312\python.exe
# CPython

beginner.content:
Introduction

Installing Python puts the interpreter (the python program, usually CPython) and the standard library on your machine. The interpreter reads your code, compiles it to bytecode and runs it.
codeExamples:
# Verify the installation from any terminal:
#   python --version        ->  Python 3.12.x
#   python -c "print(1+1)"  ->  2
import sys
print(sys.version_info[:3])     # which interpreter version is running this code
print(sys.executable)           # full path to the interpreter binary

# OUTPUT (example):
# (3, 12, 4)
# C:\Python312\python.exe

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Without an interpreter, .py files are just text. Different projects need different versions, so you must know what is installed and which one runs your code.
codeExamples:
# Same script, different results by version - so always check the version
import sys
if sys.version_info < (3, 10):
    print("match/case needs Python 3.10+")
else:
    print("Modern Python - match/case available")

# OUTPUT (on 3.12):
# Modern Python - match/case available

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Servers and CI pipelines install a pinned Python (e.g. 3.12) so every environment behaves identically; Docker images start with FROM python:3.12-slim.
codeExamples:
# Typical CI sanity check - fail fast if the wrong Python is used
import sys
REQUIRED = (3, 11)
assert sys.version_info >= REQUIRED, f"Need Python {REQUIRED}+, got {sys.version_info[:2]}"
print("Environment OK:", sys.platform)

# OUTPUT:
# Environment OK: win32

beginner.content:
Diagram

   python.org installer
          │
          ▼
   ┌───────────────────────────┐
   │  Python installation      │
   │  ├─ python.exe (interp.)  │
   │  ├─ Lib/  (std library)   │
   │  ├─ Scripts/ (pip, ...)   │
   │  └─ site-packages/        │
   └───────────────────────────┘
          │  added to PATH
          ▼
   terminal:  python script.py

expert.content:
How the Interpreter Runs Your Code

When you run python app.py, CPython:
1. Reads the source and tokenizes it.
2. Parses it into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST).
3. Compiles the AST to bytecode (a code object).
4. Executes the bytecode in its evaluation loop (the Python Virtual Machine).

Steps 1-3 happen in milliseconds every time you run a script. For imported modules the bytecode is cached as .pyc in __pycache__, which is why the second run of a large project starts faster.

Python Implementations

"Python" is a language specification; several programs implement it.
ImplementationWritten inUse it when
CPythonCDefault choice - maximum library compatibility
PyPyRPythonLong-running, CPU-heavy pure-Python code (JIT compiler)
MicroPythonCMicrocontrollers such as ESP32 and Raspberry Pi Pico
Jython / IronPythonJava / C#Embedding in JVM or .NET apps (Jython supports only Python 2.7)

Managing Multiple Versions

Real projects often need different Python versions side by side. Never overwrite or remove the operating system's own Python on Linux/macOS - system tools depend on it.

• Windows: the py launcher (py -3.11, py -3.12).
• macOS/Linux: pyenv installs and switches versions per project.
• uv: a fast modern tool that can download and manage Python versions as well as packages.
codeExamples:
# pyenv (macOS / Linux)
pyenv install 3.12.6
pyenv local 3.12.6        # writes .python-version for this folder
python --version

# uv (any OS)
uv python install 3.12
uv run --python 3.12 app.py

expert.content:
Common Installation Problems

SymptomCause and fix
"python is not recognized as an internal or external command"Python is not on PATH - re-run the installer and tick "Add python.exe to PATH", or use the py launcher
Typing python opens the Microsoft StoreWindows "App execution aliases" - turn off the python.exe aliases in Settings, or install from python.org
python shows 2.7 on an old Mac/LinuxUse python3
A package installed but import failspip installed it into a different interpreter - use python -m pip install ...

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does the interpreter do with a .py file?Tokenizes, parses to an AST, compiles to bytecode, then executes the bytecode in the Python VM
How do you find which Python is running your code?sys.executable for the path and sys.version / sys.version_info for the version
What is the py launcher?A Windows tool that picks an installed Python version, e.g. py -3.12 app.py
Why prefer python -m pip over pip?It guarantees pip installs into the same interpreter that python runs
CPython vs PyPy?CPython is the reference interpreter; PyPy adds a JIT compiler that can make pure-Python loops much faster but has weaker support for some C extensions

Advantages

Advantages: free and open source, installers for every OS, multiple versions can coexist, official python.org build is the reference.
codeExamples:
# Advantage: inspect the implementation and platform in code
import platform
print(platform.python_implementation())   # CPython, PyPy ...
print(platform.system())                  # Windows / Linux / Darwin

# OUTPUT:
# CPython
# Windows

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: several installs on one machine cause "which python?" confusion; system Python on Linux/macOS must not be modified; PATH mistakes are common on Windows.
codeExamples:
# Disadvantage: the "python" you typed may not be the one you expect
import shutil, sys
print("python on PATH :", shutil.which("python"))
print("running version:", sys.executable)
# If these differ, pip may install packages into the wrong interpreter.

# OUTPUT (example):
# python on PATH : C:\Users\me\AppData\Local\Microsoft\WindowsApps\python.exe
# running version: C:\Python312\python.exe

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the interpreter is large compared to compiled binaries; end users need Python or a bundled build (PyInstaller); old versions reach end-of-life and stop receiving security fixes.
codeExamples:
# Limitation: versions have an end-of-life; check what you are on
import sys
major_minor = sys.version_info[:2]
print("Running", major_minor, "- upgrade if it is past end-of-life (5 years)")

# OUTPUT:
# Running (3, 12) - upgrade if it is past end-of-life (5 years)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Never rely on the OS Python for applications. Use per-project interpreters (pyenv, uv, Docker) and pin the minor version in CI, Docker and pyproject.toml so dev, test and prod match.

beginner.content:
Why Use an IDE or Code Editor?

You can write Python in Notepad, but a proper editor gives you syntax highlighting, auto-completion, error underlining before you run, one-click run and debug, and automatic formatting. The two most popular choices are:

• VS Code - free, lightweight editor from Microsoft; Python support comes from extensions.
• PyCharm - full IDE from JetBrains built specifically for Python, with a free tier and a paid Professional tier.

Setting Up VS Code

1. Install VS Code from code.visualstudio.com.
2. Open the Extensions panel (Ctrl+Shift+X) and install Python by Microsoft. It brings Pylance (auto-complete, type checking) and the debugger with it.
3. Open your project folder with File → Open Folder.
4. Press Ctrl+Shift+P → Python: Select Interpreter and choose the Python (or virtual environment) to use.
5. Open a .py file and click the ▶ Run button in the top-right corner, or press F5 to debug.

Setting Up PyCharm

1. Download PyCharm from jetbrains.com/pycharm.
2. New Project → choose a location. PyCharm offers to create a virtual environment for you - accept it.
3. Right-click the project → New → Python File.
4. Right-click inside the file → Run (Shift+F10 runs again, Shift+F9 debugs).
5. Change the interpreter at any time under Settings → Project → Python Interpreter.

Your First Run

Create hello.py, paste the code below, and run it from the editor. The output appears in the integrated terminal / Run panel.
codeExamples:
name = input("What is your name? ")
print(f"Welcome to Python, {name}!")

# OUTPUT:
# What is your name? Sheru
# Welcome to Python, Sheru!

beginner.content:
VS Code vs PyCharm

AspectVS CodePyCharm
TypeGeneral editor + extensionsDedicated Python IDE
Startup / memoryLight and fastHeavier
Refactoring toolsGoodExcellent
Multiple languagesExcellent (JS, Java, Go...)Python-focused
Best forMixed-language projects, beginners who want one editor for everythingLarge Python codebases, Django projects

Introduction

VS Code (lightweight editor + Python extension) and PyCharm (full Python IDE) are the two most used tools to write, run and debug Python. Both detect interpreters and virtual environments.
codeExamples:
# After setup, this file runs with the green Run button / Shift+F10
# and you can set breakpoints by clicking the gutter.
def greet(name):
    message = f"Hello, {name}!"      # set a breakpoint on this line
    return message

print(greet("IDE"))

# OUTPUT:
# Hello, IDE!

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Typing in Notepad gives no auto-complete, linting, debugger or refactoring. An IDE catches mistakes as you type and lets you step through code, which is the fastest way to learn and to fix bugs.
codeExamples:
# The IDE underlines mistakes before you run the code:
def area(radius):
    return 3.14159 * radius ** 2

print(area(2))
# print(arera(2))   # IDE flags "arera" as undefined name immediately

# OUTPUT:
# 12.56636

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Teams share .vscode/settings.json or PyCharm run configs so everyone uses the same interpreter, formatter (Black/Ruff) and test runner.
codeExamples:
# Example .vscode/settings.json (JSON, shown as a Python dict here)
settings = {
    "python.defaultInterpreterPath": ".venv/Scripts/python.exe",
    "editor.formatOnSave": True,
    "python.testing.pytestEnabled": True,
}
for key, value in settings.items():
    print(f"{key} = {value}")

# OUTPUT:
# python.defaultInterpreterPath = .venv/Scripts/python.exe
# editor.formatOnSave = True
# python.testing.pytestEnabled = True

beginner.content:
Diagram

   ┌──────────── IDE / Editor ─────────────┐
   │ Editor ─ Linter ─ Formatter ─ Debugger│
   └───────┬───────────────────────┬───────┘
           │ selects               │ runs
           ▼                       ▼
     Interpreter (.venv)   ───►  your script ─► Terminal output

expert.content:
Project-Level VS Code Settings

Settings saved in .vscode/settings.json travel with the project, so every developer gets the same interpreter, formatter and linter. A common setup uses Ruff for linting and formatting on save.

Debugging with Breakpoints

Instead of sprinkling print() calls, click in the gutter to the left of a line number to set a breakpoint, then press F5 (VS Code) or Shift+F9 (PyCharm). Execution pauses on that line and you can:
• inspect every variable in the Variables panel,
• Step Over (F10) to run the next line, Step Into (F11) to enter a function call,
• evaluate any expression in the Debug Console.

VS Code stores launch options in .vscode/launch.json.

Other Tools Worth Knowing

• Jupyter Notebooks (.ipynb) - run code cell by cell with inline charts; supported in both VS Code and PyCharm. Standard for data science.
• IDLE - the tiny editor bundled with Python; fine for a first experiment.
• Google Colab - notebooks in the browser with nothing to install.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Your editor shows "Import could not be resolved" but the code runs. Why?The editor is using a different interpreter from the one where the package is installed - select the right interpreter / virtual environment
What is Pylance?Microsoft's Python language server for VS Code, giving completion, navigation and type checking
Why commit .vscode/settings.json?So the whole team shares the same formatter, linter and interpreter path
Breakpoint vs print debugging?A breakpoint pauses execution so you can inspect all state interactively without editing and re-running code

Advantages

Advantages: auto-complete, inline errors, integrated debugger and terminal, test runner, Git integration, refactor/rename across files.
codeExamples:
# Advantage: one-click refactor - rename 'calc' everywhere safely
def calc(a, b):          # F2 (VS Code) / Shift+F6 (PyCharm) renames all usages
    return a * b

print(calc(3, 4))

# OUTPUT:
# 12

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: PyCharm is heavy on RAM; VS Code needs extensions configured; beginners may confuse the IDE with Python itself, and pointing at the wrong interpreter breaks imports.
codeExamples:
# Disadvantage: wrong interpreter selected => "ModuleNotFoundError" in IDE
# even though the package is installed elsewhere.
try:
    import requests
    print("requests found")
except ModuleNotFoundError:
    print("Select the right interpreter (Ctrl+Shift+P > Python: Select Interpreter)")

# OUTPUT (if not installed in that interpreter):
# Select the right interpreter (Ctrl+Shift+P > Python: Select Interpreter)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: IDEs cannot fix design problems; debugging remote/containerised code needs extra config; PyCharm's best features (Django, DB tools) are in the paid edition.
codeExamples:
# Limitation: IDE debugger shows state, but cannot reproduce timing bugs
import threading
counter = 0
def add():
    global counter
    for _ in range(100_000):
        counter += 1          # race: stepping through hides the problem
ts = [threading.Thread(target=add) for _ in range(2)]
[t.start() for t in ts]; [t.join() for t in ts]
print("counter is not guaranteed to be 200000 in older/other builds:", counter)

# OUTPUT (varies):
# counter is not guaranteed to be 200000 in older/other builds: 200000

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Standardise the toolchain in-repo (formatter, linter, interpreter path, test config) so IDE choice is personal but results are identical. Treat IDE settings as code.

beginner.content:
Two Ways to Run Python

• Script mode - save code in a .py file and run the whole file with python filename.py.
• Interactive mode (the REPL) - type python with no file name and execute one statement at a time. REPL stands for Read-Eval-Print Loop: it reads your line, evaluates it, prints the result, and loops.

Running a Script

Save the following as greet.py, open a terminal in the same folder, and run it.
codeExamples:
# greet.py
city = "Pune"
print("Hello from", city)
print(2 + 3)

# In the terminal (Windows: python or py, macOS/Linux: python3):
python greet.py

# OUTPUT:
# Hello from Pune
# 5

beginner.content:
Using the REPL

At the >>> prompt the REPL shows the value of every expression automatically - no print() needed. A ... prompt means it is waiting for the rest of a multi-line block; press Enter on an empty line to finish it.

To leave: type exit(), or press Ctrl+Z then Enter on Windows, Ctrl+D on macOS/Linux.
codeExamples:
>>> 10 * 4
40
>>> name = "Python"
>>> name.upper()
'PYTHON'
>>> for i in range(3):
...     print(i)
...
0
1
2
>>> exit()

beginner.content:
Handy REPL Helpers

• _ holds the result of the last expression.
• help(obj) shows documentation, e.g. help(str.split).
• dir(obj) lists the attributes and methods of an object.
• type(obj) tells you what kind of object something is.
codeExamples:
>>> 15 * 3
45
>>> _ + 5
50
>>> dir("abc")[-5:]
['swapcase', 'title', 'translate', 'upper', 'zfill']
>>> type(3.5)
<class 'float'>

beginner.content:
Introduction

A .py file is run with python file.py. The REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop, started by typing python) runs one statement at a time and prints the result immediately.
codeExamples:
# Save as hello.py and run:  python hello.py
print("Running from a file")

# In the REPL (>>> prompt) you can try one line at a time:
#   >>> 2 + 3
#   5
#   >>> _ * 10        # '_' holds the last result
#   50

# OUTPUT:
# Running from a file

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Files are for programs you keep; the REPL is for quick experiments, learning a function, or checking behaviour without creating files.
codeExamples:
# Use the REPL to check a function before putting it in a program:
#   >>> help(str.split)
#   >>> "a,b,c".split(",")
#   ['a', 'b', 'c']
print("a,b,c".split(","))     # the same check, as a script line

# OUTPUT:
# ['a', 'b', 'c']

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Developers use the REPL (or IPython/Jupyter) to explore APIs and data; DevOps run scripts with python -m module or python script.py arg1 in cron jobs and CI.
codeExamples:
# Run with arguments:  python backup.py /data --verbose
import sys
print("script name:", sys.argv[0])
print("arguments  :", sys.argv[1:])     # everything after the script name

# OUTPUT (python backup.py /data --verbose):
# script name: backup.py
# arguments  : ['/data', '--verbose']

beginner.content:
Diagram

   python file.py                         python  (REPL)
        │                                      │
        ▼                                      ▼
   read whole file                    ┌─► Read a line
        │                             │      │
   compile → run → exit               │      ▼  Eval
                                      │      │  Print
                                      └──────┘  Loop

expert.content:
Command-Line Options You Will Actually Use

CommandWhat it does
python app.py arg1 arg2Run a script, passing arguments (available in sys.argv)
python -m moduleRun a module by name, e.g. python -m pip, python -m venv
python -c "code"Run a one-line program
python -i app.pyRun the script, then drop into the REPL with its variables still alive - great for debugging
python -m http.server 8000Serve the current folder over HTTP
python -m json.tool data.jsonPretty-print a JSON file

Command-Line Arguments and Exit Codes

sys.argv is a list of strings: index 0 is the script name, the rest are the arguments. sys.exit(code) ends the program with an exit status - 0 means success, anything else means failure, which shell scripts and CI pipelines rely on.
codeExamples:
# add.py
import sys

if len(sys.argv) != 3:
    print("Usage: python add.py <a> <b>")
    sys.exit(1)               # non-zero = error

a = int(sys.argv[1])
b = int(sys.argv[2])
print(a + b)

# $ python add.py 4 6
# OUTPUT:
# 10

expert.content:
The if __name__ == "__main__" Guard

When a file is run directly, Python sets its __name__ to "__main__". When the same file is imported, __name__ is the module name instead. Putting start-up code under this guard lets one file be both a runnable script and an importable module, without the script code running on import.
codeExamples:
# calc.py
def square(n):
    return n * n

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("Running calc.py directly")
    print(square(7))

# $ python calc.py
# OUTPUT:
# Running calc.py directly
# 49
#
# In another file:  from calc import square   -> prints nothing

expert.content:
Making a Script Executable (macOS/Linux)

A shebang line at the very top tells the operating system which interpreter to use, so the file can be run like any other command.
codeExamples:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
print("I run without typing python first")

# $ chmod +x tool.py
# $ ./tool.py
# OUTPUT:
# I run without typing python first

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the REPL?Read-Eval-Print Loop: the interactive prompt that executes one statement at a time and echoes expression values
What does if __name__ == "__main__" do?Runs the guarded code only when the file is executed directly, not when it is imported
Difference between python file.py and python -m pkg.module?-m locates the module through the import system (sys.path), so package-relative imports work and you don't need its file path
What type are the values in sys.argv?Always strings - convert them yourself, e.g. int(sys.argv[1])
What does python -i do?Runs the script and then opens the REPL with the script's variables still available

Advantages

Advantages: instant feedback in the REPL, no compile step for files, -m runs modules, -c runs one-liners, -i drops into the REPL after a script.
codeExamples:
# Advantage: python -c "..." for one-line tasks (no file at all)
#   python -c "import this"
# And the guard that lets a file be both runnable and importable:
def main():
    print("main logic")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT:
# main logic

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: REPL history is lost when closed; multi-line code is awkward there; running the wrong file or from the wrong folder changes relative paths and imports.
codeExamples:
# Disadvantage: relative paths depend on where you launch the script from
import os
print("current folder:", os.getcwd())
# open("data.txt") works only if data.txt is in that folder.

# OUTPUT (example):
# current folder: C:\Users\me\project

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: plain REPL lacks syntax highlighting and good history (use IPython); scripts re-compile on every run (only imported modules get .pyc cache).
codeExamples:
# Limitation: the script itself is not cached as .pyc, only imported modules
import sys
print("__main__ module has file:", sys.modules["__main__"].__file__ is not None)
# imported modules, by contrast, are cached in __pycache__

# OUTPUT:
# __main__ module has file: True

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Keep entry points thin: put logic in importable functions and call them from if __name__ == "__main__". That makes scripts testable and lets the same code run from CLI, tests and services.

beginner.content:
What is pip?

pip is Python's package installer. It downloads third-party libraries from PyPI (the Python Package Index, pypi.org - over half a million packages) and installs them so you can import them. It plays the role Maven or Gradle dependencies play in Java.
codeExamples:
python -m pip install requests          # install the latest version
python -m pip install requests==2.32.3  # install an exact version
python -m pip install --upgrade requests
python -m pip uninstall requests
python -m pip list                      # everything installed
python -m pip show requests             # details of one package

beginner.content:
Why Virtual Environments?

Without isolation, every project on your computer shares one set of installed packages. Project A needs Django 4, project B needs Django 5 - only one can be installed globally.

A virtual environment (venv) is a self-contained folder with its own Python executable and its own site-packages. Packages installed while it is active go only into that folder. Rule of thumb: one virtual environment per project.

Creating and Using a venv

venv is built into Python. The convention is to name the folder .venv inside your project.
codeExamples:
# 1. Create it (run once, in the project folder)
python -m venv .venv

# 2. Activate it
.venv\Scripts\activate          # Windows (cmd / PowerShell)
source .venv/bin/activate        # macOS / Linux

# The prompt now starts with (.venv)
# 3. Install packages - they go into .venv only
python -m pip install requests

# 4. Leave the environment
deactivate

beginner.content:
requirements.txt - Sharing Your Dependencies

The .venv folder is never committed to Git (add it to .gitignore). Instead you commit a list of packages, and anyone can rebuild an identical environment from it.
codeExamples:
# Save the exact versions currently installed
python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt

# requirements.txt now contains lines like:
# certifi==2024.8.30
# requests==2.32.3

# A teammate recreates the environment:
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

beginner.content:
Introduction

pip installs third-party packages from PyPI. A virtual environment (python -m venv .venv) is an isolated folder with its own interpreter and its own site-packages, so each project has its own dependencies.
codeExamples:
# Terminal commands (shown as comments - run them in a shell):
#   python -m venv .venv                 # create the environment
#   .venv\Scripts\activate               # Windows  (Linux/macOS: source .venv/bin/activate)
#   pip install requests                 # install into .venv only
#   pip freeze > requirements.txt        # record exact versions
import sys
print("inside venv:", sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix)

# OUTPUT (after activating):
# inside venv: True

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Project A may need Django 3, project B Django 5. Installing globally makes them fight. venvs give each project its own versions, and requirements files make setups reproducible.
codeExamples:
# Reproducible setup on a new machine:
#   python -m venv .venv && activate it
#   pip install -r requirements.txt
requirements = ["requests==2.32.3", "flask>=3.0,<4"]   # pinned vs ranged
for line in requirements:
    name = line.replace("==", " ").split()[0]
    print("will install:", line)

# OUTPUT:
# will install: requests==2.32.3
# will install: flask>=3.0,<4

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Every professional project ships requirements.txt or pyproject.toml; CI creates a fresh venv per run; Docker images run pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt.
codeExamples:
# Check what is installed in the current environment, from Python itself
from importlib.metadata import distributions
names = sorted(d.metadata["Name"] for d in distributions())
print(len(names) > 0, names[:3])

# OUTPUT (example):
# True ['pip', 'setuptools', 'wheel']

beginner.content:
Diagram

   System Python (3.12)
        │  python -m venv
        ▼
   ┌──────── .venv ─────────┐
   │ python (copy/link)     │
   │ Lib/site-packages/     │◄── pip install requests
   │   requests, urllib3 ...│
   └────────────────────────┘
   Project A uses .venv-A     Project B uses .venv-B   (isolated)

expert.content:
Why python -m pip and Not Just pip?

The bare pip command belongs to whichever Python appears first on PATH, which may not be the one that runs your code. python -m pip always installs into exactly the interpreter you name. You can verify which environment is active from inside Python.
codeExamples:
import sys

print(sys.executable)                  # interpreter in use
print(sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix)   # True only inside a virtual environment

# OUTPUT (inside an active .venv on Windows):
# D:\projects\shop\.venv\Scripts\python.exe
# True

expert.content:
Version Specifiers

SpecifierMeaning
requests==2.32.3Exactly this version
requests>=2.302.30 or newer
requests>=2.30,<3Any 2.x from 2.30 up, but not 3.0
requests~=2.32.0"Compatible release": >=2.32.0 and <2.33
requests!=2.31.0Anything except a known-bad version

"externally-managed-environment" Error

Recent Linux distributions and Homebrew Python block pip install into the system interpreter (PEP 668), because mixing pip packages with OS-managed packages can break system tools. The right fix is to use a virtual environment - not --break-system-packages and never sudo pip.

For command-line tools you want available everywhere (e.g. black, httpie), use pipx, which gives each tool its own private environment.

Editable Installs and Modern Tooling

• pip install -e . installs your own project in "editable" mode: imports point at your source folder, so code changes apply without reinstalling.
• pip freeze lists every package including indirect dependencies, which makes requirements files noisy. Tools like pip-tools, Poetry and uv separate the packages you asked for from a generated lock file of exact versions.
• uv is a very fast drop-in replacement: uv venv, uv pip install requests, or project mode with uv add requests.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem do virtual environments solve?Dependency conflicts between projects - each project gets its own isolated set of packages and versions
Should .venv be committed to Git?No - commit requirements.txt (or pyproject.toml + lock file) and recreate the environment from it
How do you check whether you are inside a venv?sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix, or look at sys.executable
What is PyPI?The Python Package Index - the public repository pip downloads packages from
Difference between == and ~= in requirements?== pins one exact version; ~= allows compatible patch/minor updates within a range
Why is sudo pip install a bad idea?It overwrites packages the operating system depends on and can break system tools

Advantages

Advantages: isolation, no admin rights needed, reproducibility, easy to delete and recreate, access to 500k+ PyPI packages.
codeExamples:
# Advantage: ask for a package's version without importing it
from importlib.metadata import version
print("pip version:", version("pip"))

# OUTPUT (example):
# pip version: 24.0

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: each venv duplicates packages (disk use), forgetting to activate installs to the wrong place, pip's resolver can be slow, and dependency conflicts still happen.
codeExamples:
# Disadvantage: forgetting to activate => packages go to the global interpreter
import sys
print("Using:", sys.prefix)
# If this prints the global Python path, 'pip install' will pollute it.

# OUTPUT (example, venv NOT active):
# Using: C:\Python312

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a venv is not a container: it shares the OS and system libraries, is tied to one interpreter version, and is not relocatable (paths are hard-coded).
codeExamples:
# Limitation: moving/copying a venv folder breaks it (absolute paths inside)
import sys, os
cfg = os.path.join(sys.prefix, "pyvenv.cfg")
print("pyvenv.cfg exists:", os.path.exists(cfg))     # records the base interpreter path

# OUTPUT (inside a venv):
# pyvenv.cfg exists: True

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Prefer lock files (pip-tools, Poetry, uv) over bare requirements for repeatable builds; separate runtime and dev dependencies; rebuild venvs in CI rather than caching blindly; use containers when OS-level libs matter.

beginner.content:
Single-Line Comments

A comment starts with # and runs to the end of the line. Python ignores it completely. Use comments to explain why code does something - the code itself already shows what it does.
codeExamples:
# Calculate the final price after GST
price = 1000
gst_rate = 0.18      # 18% GST on electronics
total = price + price * gst_rate
print(total)

# OUTPUT:
# 1180.0

beginner.content:
Multi-Line Comments

Python has no /* ... */ block comment. Put a # at the start of every line instead - every editor can do this for you with Ctrl+/.
codeExamples:
# This function is kept for backward compatibility.
# New code should call calculate_total() instead,
# which also applies discount coupons.
def old_total(price):
    return price * 1.18

beginner.content:
Docstrings

A docstring is a string literal placed as the first statement of a module, function or class. Unlike a comment, it is kept at runtime: help(), editors and documentation tools read it. Docstrings use triple double quotes.
codeExamples:
def area_of_circle(radius):
    """Return the area of a circle with the given radius."""
    return 3.14159 * radius ** 2

print(area_of_circle.__doc__)
help(area_of_circle)

# OUTPUT:
# Return the area of a circle with the given radius.
# Help on function area_of_circle in module __main__:
#
# area_of_circle(radius)
#     Return the area of a circle with the given radius.

beginner.content:
What is PEP 8?

PEP 8 is Python's official style guide (PEP = Python Enhancement Proposal). Following it makes your code look like everyone else's, so others can read it instantly. The rules you will use every day:
RuleExample
4 spaces per indent level, never tabs    return x
Variables and functions: snake_casetotal_marks, get_user()
Classes: CapWordsStudentRecord
Constants: UPPER_CASEMAX_RETRIES = 3
Spaces around operators and after commasx = a + b, f(a, b)
Max line length 79 (many teams use 88-100)Break long lines inside brackets
Two blank lines around top-level functions and classes

Before and After PEP 8

Both versions run identically - only one is pleasant to read.

Introduction

Comments start with # and are ignored by Python; docstrings ("""...""") document modules, classes and functions. PEP 8 is the official style guide: 4-space indents, snake_case names, 79-char lines.
codeExamples:
# single-line comment
def area(w, h):
    """Return the area of a rectangle.   <- docstring"""
    return w * h          # inline comment

print(area(3, 4))
print(area.__doc__)

# OUTPUT:
# 12
# Return the area of a rectangle.   <- docstring

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Code is read far more than written. Good comments explain why; PEP 8 makes every file look the same so teams read each other's code without friction.
codeExamples:
# BAD: explains what (obvious)
x = x + 1   # add one to x
# GOOD: explains why
retries = 3          # server drops 1 in 5 requests; 3 tries gives >99% success
total = 0
for attempt in range(retries):
    total += 1
print(total)

# OUTPUT:
# 3

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Companies enforce PEP 8 automatically with Black, Ruff or flake8 in pre-commit hooks and CI; docstrings feed tools like Sphinx and IDE hover help.
codeExamples:
# Naming per PEP 8
MAX_RETRIES = 5                  # constants: UPPER_SNAKE
class OrderService: pass         # classes: PascalCase
def calculate_tax(amount):       # functions/variables: snake_case
    return round(amount * 0.18, 2)
print(calculate_tax(200))

# OUTPUT:
# 36.0

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Source line:   total = price * qty   # why-comment
                  └──────code───────┘   └─ ignored by Python
   Docstring  ─►  stored in  obj.__doc__  ─►  help(), IDE, Sphinx
   PEP 8 tools:   Ruff / Black / flake8  ─►  CI gate

expert.content:
Docstring Conventions (PEP 257)

A one-line docstring is a short imperative sentence. A multi-line docstring has a summary line, a blank line, then details. Teams usually pick one layout - Google style (below) and NumPy style are the most common - so tools like Sphinx can generate documentation from them.
codeExamples:
def transfer(amount, from_account, to_account):
    """Move money between two accounts.

    Args:
        amount: Amount in rupees; must be positive.
        from_account: Account to debit.
        to_account: Account to credit.

    Returns:
        The transaction id as a string.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If amount is not positive.
    """
    if amount <= 0:
        raise ValueError("amount must be positive")
    return "TXN-001"

expert.content:
Other PEP 8 Rules Interviewers Notice

• Compare to None with is / is not, never ==.
• Test empty sequences by truthiness: if not items: rather than if len(items) == 0:.
• Imports go at the top, one per line, grouped: standard library, then third-party, then your own modules, separated by blank lines.
• Avoid from module import * - it hides where names come from.
• Use isinstance(x, int) rather than type(x) == int.
• A leading underscore (_helper) marks a name as internal.

Let Tools Enforce the Style

Nobody checks PEP 8 by eye in a real team. Formatters rewrite code automatically, linters report problems:
• Ruff - extremely fast linter and formatter (ruff check ., ruff format .).
• Black - the "uncompromising" formatter that made auto-formatting standard in Python.
• Flake8 / Pylint - older linters, still widely used.

Special comments silence a check on one line: # noqa: E501 for linters, # type: ignore for type checkers.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Comment vs docstring?Comments (#) are discarded by the compiler; docstrings are string objects stored in __doc__ and available at runtime
Does Python have multi-line comments?No - use # on each line. A bare triple-quoted string is an unused expression, not a comment, though it is sometimes used that way
What is PEP 8?The official Python style guide covering naming, indentation, whitespace, line length and imports
Naming convention for constants and classes?Constants UPPER_CASE, classes CapWords, functions and variables snake_case
Why x is None rather than x == None?None is a singleton, so identity is exact and fast; == can be overridden by a class's __eq__

Advantages

Advantages: readable, consistent, tool-checkable code; docstrings are available at runtime through help() and __doc__.
codeExamples:
# Advantage: docstrings become live documentation
def greet(name):
    """Return a greeting for name."""
    return f"Hi {name}"

help(greet)

# OUTPUT:
# Help on function greet in module __main__:
#
# greet(name)
#     Return a greeting for name.

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: comments can go stale and lie; over-commenting hides code; strict style debates waste time; there is no real multi-line comment syntax.
codeExamples:
# Disadvantage: stale comment contradicts the code
# Apply 10% discount
price = 100 * 0.8      # actually 20% - the comment is now wrong
print(price)

# OUTPUT:
# 80.0

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: PEP 8 is a guideline, not enforced by Python; comments are not checked by tests; docstrings add a little memory (stripped by python -OO).
codeExamples:
# Limitation: a triple-quoted string used as a "comment" is still a real string object
"""This is not a comment, it is an expression statement."""
def f():
    """Real docstring"""
print(f.__doc__)

# OUTPUT:
# Real docstring

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Automate style (Ruff + Black + pre-commit) so reviews focus on design. Comment decisions and constraints, put contracts in docstrings and types, and delete commented-out code (Git remembers it).

beginner.content:
What is a Variable?

A variable is a name that refers to a value. You create one simply by assigning to it with = - there is no declaration keyword and no type to write.
codeExamples:
student_name = "Pankaj"
age = 21
cgpa = 8.7
is_enrolled = True

print(student_name, age, cgpa, is_enrolled)

# OUTPUT:
# Pankaj 21 8.7 True

beginner.content:
Naming Rules

• Names may contain letters, digits and underscores, but cannot start with a digit.
• Names are case-sensitive: age, Age and AGE are three different variables.
• You cannot use keywords such as if, for, class, True as names.
• Convention (PEP 8): snake_case for variables, UPPER_CASE for constants.
codeExamples:
total_marks = 450       # valid
_count = 0              # valid
marks2 = 90             # valid
# 2marks = 90           # SyntaxError: invalid decimal literal
# class = "A"           # SyntaxError: invalid syntax

import keyword
print(len(keyword.kwlist), keyword.kwlist[:5])

# OUTPUT:
# 35 ['False', 'None', 'True', 'and', 'as']

beginner.content:
Built-in Data Types

CategoryTypeExampleMutable?
Numericint, float, complex42, 3.14, 2+3jNo
BooleanboolTrue, FalseNo
Textstr"hello"No
NothingNoneTypeNoneNo
Sequencelist, tuple, range[1, 2], (1, 2), range(5)list: yes, others: no
Mappingdict{"a": 1}Yes
Setset, frozenset{1, 2}set: yes, frozenset: no
Binarybytes, bytearrayb"hi"bytearray only

Checking a Value's Type

type() tells you the type of any value.
codeExamples:
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4]                 # list - mutable
coordinates = (10, 20)                 # tuple - immutable
person = {"name": "Sheru", "age": 24}  # dict
unique_ids = {1, 2, 2, 3}              # set - duplicates removed

print(type(numbers), type(coordinates))
print(type(person), type(unique_ids))
print(unique_ids)
print(type(None))

# OUTPUT:
# <class 'list'> <class 'tuple'>
# <class 'dict'> <class 'set'>
# {1, 2, 3}
# <class 'NoneType'>

beginner.content:
Multiple Assignment and Swapping

Python can assign several variables in one line, and swap two values without a temporary variable.
codeExamples:
x, y, z = 10, 20, 30
print(x, y, z)

a = b = c = 0          # chained assignment - all three refer to 0
print(a, b, c)

x, y = y, x            # swap
print(x, y)

# OUTPUT:
# 10 20 30
# 0 0 0
# 20 10

beginner.content:
Introduction

A variable is a name that points to an object in memory; every object has a type (int, float, str, bool, NoneType ...). You create a variable simply by assigning to it.
codeExamples:
# Names point at objects; the type lives on the object
count = 42            # int
price = 3.14          # float
name = "Abaji"         # str
active = True         # bool
nothing = None        # NoneType

for v in (count, price, name, active, nothing):
    print(f"{v!r:8} -> {type(v).__name__}")

# OUTPUT:
# 42       -> int
# 3.14     -> float
# 'Abaji'  -> str
# True     -> bool
# None     -> NoneType

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Programs must remember values (a price, a user name, a flag) while they run. Variables give those values readable names and types decide which operations are legal.
codeExamples:
# Without names the logic is unreadable; with names it documents itself
unit_price = 250
quantity = 4
discount = 0.1
total = unit_price * quantity * (1 - discount)
print("Total to pay:", total)

# OUTPUT:
# Total to pay: 900.0

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Every real program holds state in variables: shopping-cart totals, config values read from files, counters in loops, flags such as is_logged_in.
codeExamples:
# Invoice line the way a billing script would write it
price = 19.99
qty = 3
total = round(price * qty, 2)      # round to 2 decimals for money display
is_paid = False
print(f"Total: {total}  paid={is_paid}")

# OUTPUT:
# Total: 59.97  paid=False

beginner.content:
Diagram

   variable names (stack of references)       objects (heap)
   ┌──────────┐                              ┌───────────────┐
   │  count   │ ───────────────────────────► │ int   42      │
   ├──────────┤                              ├───────────────┤
   │  name    │ ───────────────────────────► │ str   "Abaji" │
   ├──────────┤                              ├───────────────┤
   │  price   │ ───────────────────────────► │ float 3.14    │
   └──────────┘                              └───────────────┘
   name  = label only              type + value live in the object

expert.content:
Variables Are Names, Not Boxes

In Java, int x = 5; puts the value 5 inside a memory slot named x. In Python, every value is an object living on the heap, and a variable is just a name bound to (pointing at) an object. Assignment never copies an object - it makes another name point at the same one.
codeExamples:
marks = [70, 80]
backup = marks          # NOT a copy - a second name for the same list

backup.append(90)
print(marks)            # changed through the other name!
print(marks is backup)  # same object?

real_copy = marks.copy()
real_copy.append(100)
print(marks)            # unaffected

# OUTPUT:
# [70, 80, 90]
# True
# [70, 80, 90]

expert.content:
The Chained-Assignment Trap

a = b = [] binds both names to one list. With immutable values like numbers this never matters, but with mutable ones it is a classic bug.
codeExamples:
row_a = row_b = []
row_a.append("x")
print(row_b)

# Correct: two separate lists
row_a, row_b = [], []
row_a.append("x")
print(row_b)

# OUTPUT:
# ['x']
# []

expert.content:
Extended Unpacking

A starred name collects "everything else" into a list. This works anywhere you unpack, including for loops.
codeExamples:
first, *middle, last = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
print(first, middle, last)

head, *tail = "python"
print(head, tail)

name, (city, pin) = ("Udgir", ("Latur", 413517))
print(name, city, pin)

# OUTPUT:
# 10 [20, 30, 40] 50
# p ['y', 't', 'h', 'o', 'n']
# Udgir Latur 413517

expert.content:
Deleting a Name

del x removes the name, not necessarily the object. The object is freed only when no names or containers refer to it any more.
codeExamples:
data = [1, 2, 3]
alias = data
del data
print(alias)       # the list is still alive through alias
# print(data)      # NameError: name 'data' is not defined

# OUTPUT:
# [1, 2, 3]

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How are variables different in Python and Java?Python variables are names bound to objects and carry no type; Java variables are typed storage locations
Does b = a copy a list?No - both names refer to the same list; use a.copy(), list(a) or a[:] for a shallow copy
What does a = b = [] create?One list with two names - mutating through either name is visible through both
Name the immutable built-in typesint, float, complex, bool, str, tuple, frozenset, bytes, NoneType
How do you swap two variables?a, b = b, a - the right side builds a tuple first, then it is unpacked
What does del x do?Removes the name x; the object is destroyed only when its reference count drops to zero

Advantages

Advantages: no declarations, multiple assignment, easy swapping, and one name can be rebound to any type.
codeExamples:
# Multiple assignment and tuple-swap with no temp variable
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a                 # swap
x = y = 0                   # chained assignment
print(a, b, x, y)

# OUTPUT:
# 2 1 0 0

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: a typo silently creates a brand-new variable instead of raising an error at definition time.
codeExamples:
# Disadvantage: misspelled name = new variable, original stays unchanged
total = 0
for n in [1, 2, 3]:
    totl = total + n        # typo: should be total = total + n
print(total)                # still 0 - silent bug

# OUTPUT:
# 0

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: Python has no real constants; UPPER_CASE is only a convention and any code can rebind the name.
codeExamples:
# Limitation: "constants" are not enforced by the language
MAX_USERS = 10
MAX_USERS = 20              # allowed - no error, no warning
print(MAX_USERS)
# Use typing.Final + a type checker (mypy) to get a static warning.

# OUTPUT:
# 20

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Treat variables as labels, not boxes: this mental model prevents aliasing bugs later. In larger code bases add type hints and a checker (mypy/pyright), use Final for constants, and prefer small scopes so a typo cannot hide among hundreds of names.

beginner.content:
What is Dynamic Typing?

In a statically typed language like Java, a variable's type is fixed when you declare it and checked by the compiler. In Python, which is dynamically typed, the value has a type but the variable does not - the same name can refer to an int now and a string later. Types are checked while the program runs.
codeExamples:
value = 10
print(value, type(value))

value = "ten"
print(value, type(value))

value = [1, 0]
print(value, type(value))

# OUTPUT:
# 10 <class 'int'>
# ten <class 'str'>
# [1, 0] <class 'list'>

beginner.content:
Java vs Python

Java (static)Python (dynamic)
int count = 5;count = 5
count = "five"; → compile errorcount = "five" → allowed
Type errors found before runningType errors found when that line runs

Dynamic but Strong

Dynamic does not mean Python mixes types carelessly. Python is strongly typed: it refuses operations that don't make sense for the types involved, instead of silently converting (as JavaScript does with "1" + 1 = "11").
codeExamples:
age = 25
message = "Age: " + str(age)    # convert explicitly
print(message)

print("Age: " + age)            # mixing str and int

# OUTPUT:
# Age: 25
# TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

beginner.content:
Duck Typing

"If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck." Python code usually doesn't care what type an object is - only whether it has the method or behaviour needed. Any object with a matching method works.

Introduction

Dynamic typing means types are checked at runtime and belong to objects, not names. The same name can point to an int now and a string later.
codeExamples:
x = 10
print(type(x))      # the object 10 is an int
x = "ten"           # rebind the same name to a str - perfectly legal
print(type(x))

# OUTPUT:
# <class 'int'>
# <class 'str'>

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

It lets one function work on many kinds of data without templates or overloads, which cuts code size and speeds up prototyping.
codeExamples:
def double(v):
    return v * 2             # works for anything that supports *

print(double(4))
print(double("ab"))
print(double([1, 2]))

# OUTPUT:
# 8
# abab
# [1, 2, 1, 2]

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Data coming from JSON, CSV or web forms has no fixed schema, so dynamic typing makes it natural to handle mixed values and duck-typed interfaces (anything with .read() is a file).
codeExamples:
# Mixed values from an API: normalise them to float
values = [1, "2", 3.5]
total = sum(float(v) for v in values)
print(total)

# OUTPUT:
# 6.5

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Static (Java)                       Dynamic (Python)
   ┌──────────────────────┐            ┌──────────────────────┐
   │ int x  = 10;         │            │ x = 10               │
   │ x = "ten";  ✗ compile│            │ x = "ten"   ✓ ok     │
   └──────────────────────┘            └──────────────────────┘
   type bound to the NAME              type bound to the OBJECT
   checked at compile time             checked when line runs

expert.content:
The Cost: Errors Surface Late

Because nothing is checked ahead of time, a type mistake in a rarely executed branch can sit in production for months and crash only when that branch finally runs. This is the main trade-off of dynamic typing - and the reason for type hints and tests.
codeExamples:
def apply_discount(price, is_member):
    if is_member:
        return price * 0.9
    return price - "10"        # bug - but only fails when is_member is False

print(apply_discount(100, True))   # works fine
print(apply_discount(100, False))  # crashes only now

# OUTPUT:
# 90.0
# TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for -: 'int' and 'str'

expert.content:
Type Hints: Static Checking, Optionally

Since Python 3.5 you can annotate types. The interpreter does not enforce them at runtime - they are read by tools such as mypy, Pyright and your editor, which then catch type bugs before the code runs. You get dynamic flexibility with static safety where you want it.
codeExamples:
def apply_discount(price: float, percent: float) -> float:
    return price * (1 - percent / 100)

print(apply_discount(500, 10))
print(apply_discount("500", 10))   # Python itself still runs this line...

# OUTPUT:
# 450.0
# TypeError: can't multiply sequence by non-int of type 'float'
#
# ...but mypy reports it without running the program:
# error: Argument 1 to "apply_discount" has incompatible type "str"; expected "float"

expert.content:
EAFP vs LBYL

Dynamic typing shapes Python's error-handling style. Instead of Look Before You Leap (checking types up front), idiomatic Python is Easier to Ask Forgiveness than Permission: just try the operation and handle the exception.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Static vs dynamic typing?Static: types belong to variables and are checked at compile time. Dynamic: types belong to values and are checked at runtime
Strong vs weak typing?Strong languages refuse implicit conversions between unrelated types (Python, Java); weak ones coerce silently (JavaScript, C in places)
Are type hints enforced?No - CPython ignores them at runtime; static checkers like mypy and Pyright use them
What is duck typing?Accepting any object that supports the required behaviour, regardless of its class
What is EAFP?Try the operation and catch the exception, rather than checking conditions first - the preferred Python style

Advantages

Advantages: less boilerplate, heterogeneous containers, duck typing and fast experimentation.
codeExamples:
items = [1, "a", None, 2.5, [1, 2]]       # one list, many types
print([type(i).__name__ for i in items])

# OUTPUT:
# ['int', 'str', 'NoneType', 'float', 'list']

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: wrong-type bugs are found only when the line runs, and some wrong types do not fail at all - they silently give a wrong answer.
codeExamples:
def area(w, h):
    return w * h

print(area(3, 4))          # 12 - intended
print(area("3", 4))        # '3333' - no error, wrong result!

# OUTPUT:
# 12
# 3333

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: type hints are documentation only; the interpreter never enforces them. Use mypy/pyright or runtime validators (pydantic) for real checks.

Architect's Notes

Dynamic typing trades early safety for speed of development. For services and libraries, add gradual typing (hints + mypy in CI) and validate data at system boundaries; keep fully dynamic style for scripts, notebooks and glue code.

beginner.content:
Three Built-in Number Types

• int - whole numbers: 7, -300, 0.
• float - numbers with a decimal point or exponent: 3.14, -0.5, 2e3.
• complex - numbers with a real and an imaginary part, written with j: 3+4j.

Python has no separate byte, short, long or double like Java - just these three.
codeExamples:
students = 60
average = 72.5
signal = 3 + 4j

print(type(students), type(average), type(signal))

# OUTPUT:
# <class 'int'> <class 'float'> <class 'complex'>

beginner.content:
Integers Never Overflow

A Java int overflows past about 2.1 billion. A Python int has arbitrary precision - it grows as large as memory allows. Underscores can be used to make big literals readable.

Other Integer Bases

Integers can be written in binary, octal or hexadecimal, and converted back to strings in those bases.
codeExamples:
print(0b1010, 0o17, 0xFF)      # binary, octal, hex literals
print(bin(10), oct(15), hex(255))
print(int("ff", 16), int("1010", 2))

# OUTPUT:
# 10 15 255
# 0b1010 0o17 0xff
# 255 10

beginner.content:
Mixing Types

When you combine an int and a float the result is a float. Division with / always returns a float, even when it divides evenly.
codeExamples:
print(5 + 2.0)
print(10 / 2)
print(10 // 3)      # floor division keeps an int
print(type(7 / 7))

# OUTPUT:
# 7.0
# 5.0
# 3
# <class 'float'>

beginner.content: Useful Built-in Functions
codeExamples:
print(abs(-7))            # absolute value
print(round(3.14159, 2))  # round to 2 decimal places
print(pow(2, 10))         # same as 2 ** 10
print(max(4, 9, 2), min(4, 9, 2))
print(divmod(17, 5))      # (quotient, remainder)

# OUTPUT:
# 7
# 3.14
# 1024
# 9 2
# (3, 2)

beginner.content:
Introduction

Python has three built-in numbers: int (unlimited size), float (64-bit IEEE 754 double) and complex (real + imaginary parts).
codeExamples:
big = 2 ** 100              # int never overflows
pi = 3.14159                # float
z = 3 + 4j                  # complex: real=3, imag=4
print(big)
print(type(pi).__name__, type(z).__name__)
print(abs(z))               # magnitude of a complex number

# OUTPUT:
# 1267650600228229401496703205376
# float complex
# 5.0

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Real programs need whole numbers (counts), decimals (measurements) and sometimes complex numbers (signals, physics), plus operators to split numbers apart.
codeExamples:
print(17 / 5)             # true division -> float
print(17 // 5)            # floor division
print(17 % 5)             # remainder
print(divmod(17, 5))      # both at once
print(2 ** 10)            # power

# OUTPUT:
# 3.4
# 3
# 2
# (3, 2)
# 1024

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Money should use Decimal, science uses float, cryptography relies on huge ints (RSA keys are 2048-bit integers), and signal processing uses complex numbers.
codeExamples:
from decimal import Decimal

print(0.1 + 0.2)                          # float surprise
print(Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2"))    # exact decimal arithmetic for money
print(round(2.675, 2))                    # float storage error: 2.67 not 2.68

# OUTPUT:
# 0.30000000000000004
# 0.3
# 2.67

beginner.content:
Diagram

   numbers.Number
   ├── int      unlimited, exact       2**100
   ├── float    64-bit, approximate    0.1 -> 0.1000000000000000055...
   ├── complex  (float, float)         3+4j
   └── (stdlib) Decimal  exact base-10 | Fraction  exact p/q

   float layout:  [1 sign][11 exponent][52 mantissa]

expert.content:
Floating-Point Is Approximate

float is a 64-bit IEEE 754 binary double - exactly Java's double. Many decimal fractions such as 0.1 cannot be represented exactly in binary, so tiny errors appear. Never compare floats with == after arithmetic; use math.isclose().
codeExamples:
import math

print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))

# OUTPUT:
# 0.30000000000000004
# False
# True

expert.content:
Decimal for Money, Fraction for Exact Ratios

For currency, use decimal.Decimal, which does exact base-10 arithmetic. Create it from a string - Decimal(0.1) would copy the float's error. fractions.Fraction keeps exact rational numbers.
codeExamples:
from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP
from fractions import Fraction

print(Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2"))
print(Decimal(0.1))                       # created from a float - error copied

price = Decimal("19.995")
print(price.quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP))

print(Fraction(1, 3) + Fraction(1, 6))

# OUTPUT:
# 0.3
# 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625
# 20.00
# 1/2

expert.content:
round() Uses Banker's Rounding

Python's round() rounds exact halves to the nearest even number, which avoids a systematic upward bias when summing many rounded values. This surprises people coming from Java's Math.round().
codeExamples:
print(round(0.5), round(1.5), round(2.5), round(3.5))
print(round(2.675, 2))   # 2.675 is really 2.67499999... in binary

# OUTPUT:
# 0 2 2 4
# 2.67

expert.content: Special Float Values and Limits
codeExamples:
import sys

inf = float("inf")
nan = float("nan")

print(inf > 10 ** 300, -inf < -10 ** 300)
print(nan == nan)              # NaN is not equal to anything, even itself
print(sys.float_info.max)
print(sys.maxsize)             # largest container index, not an int limit

# OUTPUT:
# True True
# False
# 1.7976931348623157e+308
# 9223372036854775807

expert.content: Working with complex Numbers
codeExamples:
import cmath

z = 3 + 4j
print(z.real, z.imag)
print(abs(z))                 # magnitude
print(z.conjugate())
print(1j * 1j)
print(cmath.sqrt(-1))

# OUTPUT:
# 3.0 4.0
# 5.0
# (3-4j)
# (-1+0j)
# 1j

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Can a Python int overflow?No - ints have arbitrary precision and grow as needed (floats can overflow to inf)
Why is 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3?0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation, so the stored values carry tiny errors
What should you use for money?decimal.Decimal created from strings (or integer paise/cents)
What does round(2.5) return?2 - Python rounds halves to the nearest even number
What is the type of 8 / 2?float (4.0) - true division always returns a float
Is NaN equal to itself?No - nan == nan is False; use math.isnan()

Advantages

Advantages: arbitrary-precision integers (no overflow bugs), underscores for readability, built-in complex type, rich math module.
codeExamples:
import math
print(math.factorial(25))      # exact, no overflow
print(1_000_000 + 0b101 + 0xFF)  # binary and hex literals, underscores
print(math.sqrt(16), math.pi)

# OUTPUT:
# 15511210043330985984000000
# 1000260
# 4.0 3.141592653589793

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: float cannot represent most decimals exactly, so equality tests on floats are fragile.
codeExamples:
import math
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)                  # False
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))      # True - compare with tolerance

# OUTPUT:
# False
# True

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: floats have a finite range and special values (inf, nan); ints have no limit but huge ints are slow and string conversion is capped at 4300 digits by default.
codeExamples:
import sys
print(sys.float_info.max)             # largest float
print(1e308 * 10)                     # overflows silently to inf
print(float("inf") - float("inf"))    # nan, and nan != nan
try:
    int("1" * 5000)                   # 3.11+ safety cap on digit strings
except ValueError:
    print("ValueError: too many digits")

# OUTPUT:
# 1.7976931348623157e+308
# inf
# nan
# ValueError: too many digits

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Choose the type by the correctness requirement: int for counting, Decimal for money and anything audited, float for scientific work (NumPy float64/float32 for bulk speed). Never compare floats with ==, and store money as integer cents or Decimal across service boundaries.

beginner.content:
The bool Type

bool has exactly two values: True and False - note the capital letters. Comparisons produce booleans, and if / while use them to make decisions.
codeExamples:
is_logged_in = True
marks = 35

passed = marks >= 40
print(passed, type(passed))

if is_logged_in and not passed:
    print("Please retake the exam")

# OUTPUT:
# False <class 'bool'>
# Please retake the exam

beginner.content:
Truthy and Falsy Values

Any object can be used where a boolean is expected. These values count as False ("falsy"); everything else is True ("truthy"):

• False and None
• zero of any number type: 0, 0.0, 0j
• empty containers: "", [], (), {}, set(), range(0)
codeExamples:
print(bool(0), bool(42), bool(-1))
print(bool(""), bool(" "), bool("False"))
print(bool([]), bool([0]))

cart = []
if not cart:                 # Pythonic emptiness check
    print("Your cart is empty")

# OUTPUT:
# False True True
# False True True
# False True
# Your cart is empty

beginner.content:
What is None?

None represents "no value" or "nothing here yet" - similar to Java's null. It is the only value of type NoneType. A function without a return statement returns None.
codeExamples:
middle_name = None

def greet(name):
    print("Hello", name)      # no return statement

result = greet("Sheru")
print(result)
print(type(None))

# OUTPUT:
# Hello Sheru
# None
# <class 'NoneType'>

beginner.content:
Checking for None

Always test for None with is / is not. There is only one None object in the whole program, so an identity check is exact.
codeExamples:
discount = None

if discount is None:
    print("No discount applied")

discount = 0
if discount is not None:
    print("Discount is", discount)

# OUTPUT:
# No discount applied
# Discount is 0

beginner.content:
Introduction

bool has two values, True and False, and is a subclass of int (True == 1). None is the single object of type NoneType and means "no value".
codeExamples:
print(isinstance(True, int))   # bool is an int subclass
print(True + True)              # 2
print(type(None).__name__)
print(None is None)

# OUTPUT:
# True
# 2
# NoneType
# True

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Conditions need yes/no answers, and programs need a way to say "nothing here yet" that is different from 0 or an empty string. Python also treats many values as truthy or falsy inside if.
codeExamples:
for v in [0, "", [], None, "a", 1]:
    print(repr(v), bool(v))

# OUTPUT:
# 0 False
# '' False
# [] False
# None False
# 'a' True
# 1 True

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

None is the standard marker for "not found", "not set" and the safe default for mutable arguments; booleans drive every validation and feature flag.
codeExamples:
def add_item(item, bag=None):
    if bag is None:            # fresh list each call; avoids shared-default bug
        bag = []
    bag.append(item)
    return bag

print(add_item(1))
print(add_item(2))

# OUTPUT:
# [1]
# [2]

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Falsy values                     Truthy values
   ┌───────────────────────┐        ┌────────────────────────┐
   │ False  None           │        │ True                   │
   │ 0  0.0  0j            │        │ any non-zero number    │
   │ ""  []  ()  {}  set() │        │ any non-empty container│
   └───────────┬───────────┘        └────────────┬───────────┘
               └──────────► if x: ◄──────────────┘
   test "missing" with  x is None   (not  not x)

expert.content:
bool Is a Subclass of int

For historical reasons True and False are the integers 1 and 0 in disguise. This is handy for counting, but it also means a bool passes an isinstance(x, int) check.
codeExamples:
print(issubclass(bool, int))
print(True + True, True * 10)
print(isinstance(True, int))

results = [True, False, True, True]
print(sum(results), "passed")      # counting with sum()

# OUTPUT:
# True
# 2 10
# True
# 3 passed

expert.content:
The "if not x" Trap with 0 and None

if not value treats None, 0 and "" the same. When 0 or an empty string is a valid value, test for None explicitly.

Customising Truthiness

bool(obj) calls the object's __bool__() method; if that is missing it falls back to __len__() (zero length = False); if both are missing the object is always True.

Why is None and Not == None

== calls __eq__, which any class can override - even to claim it equals None. is compares identity and cannot be fooled. It is also slightly faster and is what PEP 8 requires.
codeExamples:
class Weird:
    def __eq__(self, other):
        return True              # claims to equal everything

w = Weird()
print(w == None)
print(w is None)

# OUTPUT:
# True
# False

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
List the falsy values in PythonFalse, None, numeric zeros (0, 0.0, 0j, Decimal(0)...), and empty containers ("", [], (), {}, set(), range(0))
What does bool("False") return?True - any non-empty string is truthy
What is True + True?2, because bool is a subclass of int
What does a function return without a return statement?None
Why use is None?None is a singleton; identity is exact and cannot be overridden by __eq__
How is truthiness of an object decided?__bool__() if defined, else __len__() != 0, else True

Advantages

Advantages: truthiness removes noisy comparisons, and or/and short-circuit to give compact defaults.
codeExamples:
name = ""
display = name or "guest"          # empty string is falsy -> default used
items = []
if not items:
    print("cart is empty")
print(display)

# OUTPUT:
# cart is empty
# guest

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: truthiness can't tell 0 or "" apart from "missing", causing subtle bugs.
codeExamples:
timeout = 0                    # user really wants 0 (no waiting)
bad = timeout or 30            # bug: 0 is falsy, becomes 30
good = 30 if timeout is None else timeout
print(bad, good)

# OUTPUT:
# 30 0

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: None supports no operations, and bool cannot be subclassed (it only ever has two instances).

Architect's Notes

Use is None for absence, plain truthiness for emptiness, and never == True. In APIs prefer Optional[T] hints and avoid returning None for errors that callers must handle; raise or return a result object instead.

beginner.content:
Creating Strings

A string is a sequence of Unicode characters. You can use single quotes, double quotes, or triple quotes - there is no separate char type; a single character is just a string of length 1.
codeExamples: first = 'Python' second = "Python" print(first == second) quote = "It's easy" # double quotes let you use ' inside html = 'Home' # single quotes let you use " inside letter = "A" print(type(letter), len(letter)) # OUTPUT: # True # 1

beginner.content:
Multi-line Strings

Triple quotes (""" or ''') let a string span several lines, keeping the line breaks.
codeExamples:
address = """DHIPAN Software Technologies
Udgir, Latur
Maharashtra"""

print(address)

# OUTPUT:
# DHIPAN Software Technologies
# Udgir, Latur
# Maharashtra

beginner.content:
Joining and Repeating

+ concatenates strings and * repeats them. To join a string with a number, convert the number first, or use an f-string.
codeExamples:
first_name = "Sheru"
last_name = "Patil"
full_name = first_name + " " + last_name
print(full_name)

print("-" * 20)

age = 22
print(full_name + " is " + str(age))
print(f"{full_name} is {age}")

# OUTPUT:
# Sheru Patil
# --------------------
# Sheru Patil is 22
# Sheru Patil is 22

beginner.content: Length, Membership and Looping
codeExamples:
course = "JavaSchoolLab"

print(len(course))
print("School" in course)
print("python" not in course)

for ch in "abc":
    print(ch)

# OUTPUT:
# 13
# True
# True
# a
# b
# c

beginner.content:
Strings Are Immutable

You can read individual characters, but you cannot change a string in place. Every "modification" builds a brand-new string.
codeExamples:
word = "java"
# word[0] = "J"       # TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment

word = "J" + word[1:]   # build a new string instead
print(word)
print(word.upper())     # methods also return new strings
print(word)             # the original is unchanged

# OUTPUT:
# Java
# JAVA
# Java

beginner.content:
Introduction

A str is an immutable sequence of Unicode characters. Create with single, double or triple quotes.
