print(r"\d+\.\d+")                  # appears exactly as typed

# OUTPUT:
# é A α
# \d+\.\d+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: a raw string cannot end with a single backslash, so paths ending in a slash need a workaround.
codeExamples:
# r"C:\Users\" is a SyntaxError (the last \" escapes the quote)
path = r"C:\Users" + "\\"          # concatenate a normal "\\" instead
print(path + "data.txt")

# OUTPUT:
# C:\Users\data.txt

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: raw means no escapes at all, so you cannot write a newline or tab in it; r"\n" is two characters.
codeExamples:
s = r"line1\nline2"
print(len(r"\n"), s)                 # backslash and n, not a newline
print(s.replace("\\n", "\n"))         # convert on purpose when needed

# OUTPUT:
# 2 line1\nline2
# line1
# line2

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Prefer pathlib.Path over hand-built Windows path strings, and use raw strings (or re.VERBOSE with triple-quoted raw strings) for every regex. Treat escape handling as a boundary concern: never build strings for SQL or shells by hand, use parameterised APIs.

beginner.content:
f-strings

An f-string (formatted string literal, Python 3.6+) starts with f before the quote. Anything inside { } is evaluated as Python code and inserted into the text. It is the modern, preferred way to build strings.
codeExamples:
name = "Sheru"
marks = 87
total = 100

print(f"{name} scored {marks} out of {total}")
print(f"Percentage: {marks / total * 100}%")
print(f"Uppercase: {name.upper()}")

# OUTPUT:
# Sheru scored 87 out of 100
# Percentage: 87.0%
# Uppercase: SHERU

beginner.content:
Format Specifiers

After a colon inside the braces you can control how a value is displayed: {value:spec}.
SpecExampleResult
.2ff"{3.14159:.2f}"3.14
,f"{1234567:,}"1,234,567
.1%f"{0.256:.1%}"25.6%
05df"{42:05d}"00042
>8f"{'hi':>8}"      hi
b, xf"{10:b}", f"{255:x}"1010, ff
codeExamples:
price = 1499.5
gst = 0.18

print(f"Price: {price:.2f}")
print(f"GST: {gst:.0%}")
print(f"Total: {price * (1 + gst):,.2f}")
print(f"Invoice #{7:04d}")

# OUTPUT:
# Price: 1499.50
# GST: 18%
# Total: 1,769.41
# Invoice #0007

beginner.content:
Older Styles: format() and %

You will meet two older styles in existing code. Both still work, but prefer f-strings in new code.
codeExamples:
name, age = "Pankaj", 28

print("{} is {} years old".format(name, age))
print("{0} likes {1}; {0} codes daily".format(name, "Python"))
print("{n} is {a}".format(n=name, a=age))

print("%s is %d years old" % (name, age))     # printf style, like C/Java
print("Pi is about %.2f" % 3.14159)

# OUTPUT:
# Pankaj is 28 years old
# Pankaj likes Python; Pankaj codes daily
# Pankaj is 28
# Pankaj is 28 years old
# Pi is about 3.14

beginner.content:
Introduction

An f-string (f"...") embeds expressions in braces and formats them with a mini-language after a colon. Older styles are str.format() and the % operator.
codeExamples:
name, age = "Ada", 36
print(f"{name} is {age}, next year {age + 1}")
print(f"{name!r}")                 # repr
print(f"{age=}")                   # self-documenting (3.8+)
print("{} / {}".format(name, age), "%s-%d" % (name, age))

# OUTPUT:
# Ada is 36, next year 37
# 'Ada'
# age=36
# Ada / 36 Ada-36

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Output must look right: fixed decimals, thousands separators, percentages, zero padding. Doing that by hand is clumsy.

Real-Time Use

Report lines with aligned columns.
codeExamples:
items = [("Pen", 10, 1.5), ("Notebook", 3, 45.25)]
for name, qty, price in items:
    print(f"{name:<10}{qty:>5}{price:>9.2f}")

# OUTPUT:
# Pen          10     1.50
# Notebook      3    45.25

beginner.content:
Diagram

   f"{price:>9.2f}"
       │    │││ │└─ type  f = fixed point
       │    │││ └── precision .2
       │    ││└──── width 9
       │    │└───── align  > right
       │    └────── ':' starts the format spec
       └─────────── expression (any Python)

expert.content:
The Full Format Spec Mini-Language

The general form is {value:[[fill]align][sign][#][0][width][,][.precision][type]}.

Self-Documenting Expressions and Conversions

{expr=} (Python 3.8+) prints the expression text and its value - perfect for quick debugging. !r, !s and !a apply repr(), str() or ascii() before formatting.
codeExamples:
user = "sheru"
balance = 2500.756

print(f"{user=}")
print(f"{balance=:.2f}")
print(f"{len(user) * 2 = }")
print(f"Name: {user!r}")

# OUTPUT:
# user='sheru'
# balance=2500.76
# len(user) * 2 = 10
# Name: 'sheru'

expert.content:
Nested Fields, Dates and Literal Braces

The spec itself can contain { } fields for dynamic widths. Objects such as datetime define their own specs. To print a literal brace, double it: {{ and }}.
codeExamples:
from datetime import datetime

width, prec = 10, 3
print(f"[{3.14159:{width}.{prec}f}]")

when = datetime(2026, 10, 4, 18, 30)
print(f"{when:%d %b %Y, %I:%M %p}")

key = "id"
print(f"{{ {key}: 7 }}")

# OUTPUT:
# [     3.142]
# 04 Oct 2026, 06:30 PM
# { id: 7 }

expert.content:
When Not to Use f-strings

• Logging: pass arguments separately - logger.info("User %s logged in", user). The message is only formatted if that log level is enabled, and log tools can group messages by template.
• SQL: never build queries with f-strings - that is SQL injection. Use parameterised queries: cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", (user_id,)).
• Templates supplied at runtime (e.g. from a config file): use str.format() or string.Template; f-strings are fixed in source code.
codeExamples:
from string import Template

template = "Dear $name, your order $order has shipped."   # e.g. loaded from a file
print(Template(template).substitute(name="Pankaj", order="#1042"))
print("Hi {name}".format_map({"name": "Sheru"}))

# OUTPUT:
# Dear Pankaj, your order #1042 has shipped.
# Hi Sheru

expert.content:
The % Tuple Pitfall

With % formatting, a tuple on the right is always unpacked into the placeholders - so formatting a single tuple value needs wrapping. f-strings don't have this problem.
codeExamples:
point = (3, 4)
print("Point: %s" % (point,))      # wrapped in a 1-tuple
print(f"Point: {point}")
print("Point: %s" % point)

# OUTPUT:
# Point: (3, 4)
# Point: (3, 4)
# TypeError: not all arguments converted during string formatting

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Which formatting style should you use?f-strings for normal code - fastest and most readable; format() for runtime templates; % mainly for logging calls
How do you print a float with 2 decimals and thousands separators?f"{x:,.2f}"
What does f"{x=}" do?Prints the expression and its value, e.g. x=42 (Python 3.8+)
How do you include a literal brace in an f-string?Double it: {{ or }}
Why not build SQL with f-strings?It allows SQL injection - use parameterised queries instead
When is an f-string evaluated?At runtime, each time the line executes - it is an expression, not a constant

Advantages

Advantages: fastest and most readable form; supports nested specs and date formats.
codeExamples:
from datetime import date
pi, width = 3.14159, 8
print(f"[{pi:{width}.3f}]")                  # width taken from a variable
print(f"{date(2024, 3, 5):%d/%m/%Y}")

# OUTPUT:
# [   3.142]
# 05/03/2024

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: an f-string is evaluated on the spot, so it cannot be a reusable template stored in a file or database; use str.format for that.
codeExamples:
template = "Hi {name}, you owe {amt:.2f}"      # could come from a config file
print(template.format(name="Bo", amt=12.5))

# OUTPUT:
# Hi Bo, you owe 12.50

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: f-strings always format eagerly (wasteful in logging), and str.format with untrusted templates can leak object attributes.
codeExamples:
import logging
class Noisy:
    def __str__(self):
        print("__str__ called")
        return "N"

log = logging.getLogger("demo")        # level WARNING: debug is disabled
n = Noisy()
log.debug(f"{n}")                      # formats BEFORE the logger decides to drop it
log.debug("%s", n)                     # lazy: never formatted
print("{0.__class__.__name__}".format(5))   # templates can reach attributes

# OUTPUT:
# __str__ called
# int

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use f-strings everywhere for readability, but pass lazy arguments to logging, use parameterised queries for SQL, and never let users supply format templates. For i18n use gettext with named placeholders so translators can reorder them.

beginner.content:
Text vs Bytes

Computers store and send bytes (numbers 0-255). Humans read text (characters). Python 3 keeps the two strictly separate:

• str - a sequence of Unicode characters. This is what you work with in your program.
• bytes - a sequence of raw bytes, written b"...". This is what goes into files and across networks.

Encoding turns text into bytes; decoding turns bytes back into text. The rules for doing so are called an encoding - almost always UTF-8.

Unicode Code Points

Unicode gives every character in every language a unique number called a code point. ord() gives the code point of a character; chr() gives the character for a code point.
codeExamples:
print(ord("A"), ord("a"), ord("₹"), ord("अ"))
print(chr(65), chr(8377), chr(2309))
print(hex(ord("₹")))

# OUTPUT:
# 65 97 8377 2309
# A ₹ अ
# 0x20b9

beginner.content: encode() and decode()
codeExamples:
text = "Price: ₹500"

data = text.encode("utf-8")         # str -> bytes
print(data)
print(type(data), len(text), len(data))

back = data.decode("utf-8")         # bytes -> str
print(back, back == text)

# OUTPUT:
# b'Price: \xe2\x82\xb9500'
# <class 'bytes'> 11 13
# Price: ₹500 True

beginner.content:
Always Specify the Encoding for Files

When opening text files, pass encoding="utf-8". Otherwise Python uses the operating system's default, which on Windows has historically not been UTF-8 - a file that reads fine on Linux can then crash or show garbled text on Windows.
codeExamples:
with open("greeting.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("नमस्ते, Python!")

with open("greeting.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read())

# OUTPUT:
# नमस्ते, Python!

beginner.content:
Introduction

Unicode gives every character a number (code point). Encoding (UTF-8 is standard) turns text (str) into bytes; decoding turns bytes back into str.
codeExamples:
s = "héllo"
b = s.encode("utf-8")
print(len(s), len(b))              # 5 characters, 6 bytes
print(b)
print(b.decode("utf-8") == s)

# OUTPUT:
# 5 6
# b'h\xc3\xa9llo'
# True

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Files, sockets and databases only store bytes. You must pick an encoding at the boundary or text will be corrupted.
codeExamples:
print(ord("A"), chr(8364))        # code point <-> character
print("€".encode("utf-8"))

# OUTPUT:
# 65 €
# b'\xe2\x82\xac'

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Mojibake (garbled text) is what you see when bytes are decoded with the wrong encoding; it is a daily real-world bug.
codeExamples:
data = "naïve café".encode("utf-8")
print(data.decode("latin-1"))      # wrong codec
print(data.decode("utf-8"))        # right codec

# OUTPUT:
# naÃ¯ve cafÃ©
# naïve café

beginner.content:
Diagram

   str (code points)           bytes (on disk / network)
   ┌─────────────────┐ encode ┌──────────────────────┐
   │ "héllo"         │ ─────► │ 68 c3 a9 6c 6c       │
   │ 5 characters    │ ◄───── │ 6 bytes (UTF-8)      │
   └─────────────────┘ decode └──────────────────────┘
   rule: decode on input, work in str, encode on output

expert.content:
How UTF-8 Works

UTF-8 is a variable-length encoding: ASCII characters take 1 byte (so plain English files are identical in ASCII and UTF-8), while other characters take 2 to 4 bytes. That is why len(text) (characters) and len(text.encode()) (bytes) can differ.
codeExamples:
for ch in ["A", "é", "₹", "😀"]:
    encoded = ch.encode("utf-8")
    print(ch, f"U+{ord(ch):04X}", len(encoded), "bytes", encoded)

# OUTPUT:
# A U+0041 1 bytes b'A'
# é U+00E9 2 bytes b'\xc3\xa9'
# ₹ U+20B9 3 bytes b'\xe2\x82\xb9'
# 😀 U+1F600 4 bytes b'\xf0\x9f\x98\x80'

expert.content:
Decode Errors and Error Handlers

Decoding bytes with the wrong encoding raises UnicodeDecodeError - or worse, silently produces garbage ("mojibake"). The errors argument controls what happens with bad bytes.
codeExamples:
data = "café".encode("utf-8")

print(data.decode("latin-1"))                    # wrong encoding: mojibake
print(b"caf\xe9".decode("utf-8", errors="replace"))
print(b"caf\xe9".decode("utf-8", errors="ignore"))
print("₹ price".encode("ascii", errors="replace"))
print(b"caf\xe9".decode("utf-8"))

# OUTPUT:
# cafÃ©
# caf�
# caf
# b'? price'
# UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xe9 in position 3: unexpected end of data

expert.content:
One Visible Character, Several Code Points

"é" can be stored as one code point (U+00E9) or as "e" followed by a combining accent (U+0301). They look identical but compare unequal. Normalise text with unicodedata.normalize() before comparing or storing user input.
codeExamples:
import unicodedata

a = "caf\u00e9"          # precomposed é
b = "cafe\u0301"         # e + combining acute accent

print(a, b, a == b, len(a), len(b))

na = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", a)
nb = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", b)
print(na == nb, len(nb))
print(unicodedata.name("₹"))

# OUTPUT:
# café café False 4 5
# True 4
# RUPEE SIGN

expert.content:
The "Unicode Sandwich"

The rule professional Python code follows:
1. Decode bytes to str as early as possible (when reading files, network data, database results).
2. Work only with str inside your program.
3. Encode to bytes as late as possible (when writing or sending).

Mixing str and bytes is a TypeError in Python 3, which forces you to be explicit.
codeExamples:
print(b"abc" == "abc")
print(b"abc" + "def")

# OUTPUT:
# False
# TypeError: can't concat str to bytes

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
str vs bytes?str holds Unicode text; bytes holds raw 8-bit values. Convert with encode() and decode()
What is UTF-8?A variable-length (1-4 byte) Unicode encoding, backward-compatible with ASCII - the default for the web and Python source files
Why can len(s) != len(s.encode())?len counts code points; non-ASCII characters need several bytes in UTF-8
What causes UnicodeDecodeError?Decoding bytes with an encoding that doesn't match how they were written
Why always pass encoding to open()?The default depends on the operating system, so files may be read differently on Windows and Linux
What is Unicode normalisation?Converting equivalent sequences (e.g. é vs e + accent) to one canonical form so they compare equal

Advantages

Advantages: one model for every language and emoji; Python 3 strings are Unicode by default.
codeExamples:
s = "你好"
print(len(s), len(s.encode("utf-8")))
print(s.encode("utf-8"))
print("👍".encode("utf-8"))

# OUTPUT:
# 2 6
# b'\xe4\xbd\xa0\xe5\xa5\xbd'
# b'\xf0\x9f\x91\x8d'

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: encoding or decoding with an incompatible codec raises errors; you can choose to replace or ignore, but data is lost.

Limitations

Limitations: the same visible text can have several code point sequences, so equality and len can disagree with what users see. Normalise first.
codeExamples:
import unicodedata
a = "\u00e9"            # one code point
b = "e\u0301"           # e + combining acute accent
print(a == b, len(a), len(b))
print(unicodedata.normalize("NFC", b) == a)

# OUTPUT:
# False 1 2
# True

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Adopt the Unicode sandwich: decode at the input boundary, keep str inside, encode at the output boundary, always passing encoding="utf-8" explicitly to open(). Normalise (NFC) before comparing or indexing user text, and never silently use errors="ignore" on data you care about.

beginner.content:
print() - Showing Output

print() writes values to the screen. Give it several values separated by commas and it puts a space between them and a newline at the end.
codeExamples:
print("Hello")
print("Marks:", 87, "Grade:", "A")
print()                       # just a blank line
print(10 + 5)

# OUTPUT:
# Hello
# Marks: 87 Grade: A
#
# 15

beginner.content:
sep and end

• sep - what goes between the values (default: a space).
• end - what goes after the last value (default: a newline "\n").
codeExamples:
print("2026", "10", "04", sep="-")
print("a", "b", "c", sep="")

print("Loading", end="")
print("...", end=" ")
print("done")

for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i, end=" ")
print()

# OUTPUT:
# 2026-10-04
# abc
# Loading... done
# 1 2 3 4 5

beginner.content:
input() - Reading from the Keyboard

input(prompt) shows the prompt, waits for the user to type a line and press Enter, and returns what they typed as a string (without the newline).
codeExamples:
name = input("Enter your name: ")
print("Welcome,", name)

# OUTPUT:
# Enter your name: Dheeraj
# Welcome, Dheeraj

beginner.content:
Reading Numbers

Because input() always returns a string, convert it with int() or float() before doing maths. Forgetting this is the most common beginner bug.
codeExamples:
a = input("First number: ")
b = input("Second number: ")
print("Wrong:", a + b)                 # string concatenation!

a = int(a)
b = int(b)
print("Right:", a + b)

# OUTPUT:
# First number: 10
# Second number: 20
# Wrong: 1020
# Right: 30

beginner.content:
Reading Several Values on One Line

Split the line, then convert each part.
codeExamples:
x, y = input("Enter two numbers: ").split()
x, y = int(x), int(y)
print("Sum:", x + y)

marks = list(map(int, input("Enter marks: ").split()))
print("Average:", sum(marks) / len(marks))

# OUTPUT:
# Enter two numbers: 4 9
# Sum: 13
# Enter marks: 70 80 90
# Average: 80.0

beginner.content:
Introduction

input(prompt) reads one line from the keyboard and returns it as a str; print(...) writes values to the screen, separated by sep and finished with end.
codeExamples:
name = input("Name: ")          # program pauses until Enter
print("Hi", name)
print("a", "b", "c", sep="-", end="!\n")

# OUTPUT (example, user typed Abaji):
# Name: Abaji
# Hi Abaji
# a-b-c!

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Programs need to take data from a user and show results. Because input always returns text, convert before calculating.
codeExamples:
age = int(input("Age: "))       # str -> int
print("Next year you will be", age + 1)

# OUTPUT (example, user typed 25):
# Age: 25
# Next year you will be 26

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Console tools validate input in a loop until it is usable.
codeExamples:
while True:
    raw = input("Enter a number: ")
    try:
        n = float(raw)
        break
    except ValueError:
        print("Not a number, try again")
print(f"Square: {n * n}")

# OUTPUT (example, user typed abc then 4):
# Enter a number: abc
# Not a number, try again
# Enter a number: 4
# Square: 16.0

beginner.content:
Diagram

   keyboard ──► stdin ──► input("Q: ") ──► str ──► int()/float() ──► logic
                                                                      │
   screen ◄── stdout ◄── print(a, b, sep=" ", end="
") ◄─────────────┘

expert.content:
Validating Input in a Loop

Real programs must survive bad input. Keep asking until the value is valid, and strip surrounding whitespace.
codeExamples:
def ask_age():
    while True:
        text = input("Age: ").strip()
        try:
            age = int(text)
        except ValueError:
            print("Please enter a whole number.")
            continue
        if 0 < age < 120:
            return age
        print("Age must be between 1 and 119.")

age = ask_age()
print("Saved age", age)

# OUTPUT:
# Age: twenty
# Please enter a whole number.
# Age: 200
# Age must be between 1 and 119.
# Age: 21
# Saved age 21

expert.content:
print() Arguments: file and flush

The full signature is print(*objects, sep=" ", end="\n", file=sys.stdout, flush=False).
• file - send output somewhere else, such as sys.stderr or an open file.
• flush=True - push the text out immediately. Output to a terminal is line-buffered, so text without a newline may not appear right away - important for progress indicators.
codeExamples:
import sys
import time

print("Something went wrong", file=sys.stderr)

with open("log.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print("written to a file", file=f)

for pct in (0, 50, 100):
    print(f"\rProgress: {pct}%", end="", flush=True)
    time.sleep(0.5)
print()

# OUTPUT (the progress line updates in place):
# Something went wrong
# Progress: 100%

expert.content:
Unpacking into print()

print(*items) spreads a list into separate arguments, which is a neat way to print a list without brackets.
codeExamples:
scores = [90, 85, 78]
print(scores)
print(*scores)
print(*scores, sep=", ")
print(*"abc", sep="|")

# OUTPUT:
# [90, 85, 78]
# 90 85 78
# 90, 85, 78
# a|b|c

expert.content:
Handling End of Input

If input ends - the user presses Ctrl+D (macOS/Linux) or Ctrl+Z then Enter (Windows), or input is piped from a file that runs out - input() raises EOFError. Ctrl+C raises KeyboardInterrupt. Handle both for a clean exit.

Never eval() User Input

Old tutorials sometimes use eval(input()) to read numbers or lists. eval runs any Python expression, so a user could type __import__("os").system("...") and execute commands. Convert explicitly, or use ast.literal_eval() for Python literals.
codeExamples:
import ast

text = "[1, 2, 3]"                    # imagine this came from input()
values = ast.literal_eval(text)        # only literals allowed - safe
print(values, type(values))

# OUTPUT:
# [1, 2, 3] <class 'list'>

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What type does input() return?Always str - convert it with int(), float() and so on
How do you print without a newline?print(x, end="")
What do sep and end do?sep is placed between values, end is placed after the last one
How do you print to stderr?print(msg, file=sys.stderr)
Why might print output appear late?Output is buffered; use flush=True or end with a newline
Why is eval(input()) dangerous?It executes arbitrary code typed by the user
What does input() raise at end of input?EOFError

Advantages

Advantages: print accepts many arguments, converts them to text and has sep, end, file, flush.
codeExamples:
print(1, 2, 3, sep=", ")
for i in range(3):
    print(i, end=" ")              # stay on the same line
print()
print(*["x", "y", "z"])           # unpack a list into arguments

# OUTPUT:
# 1, 2, 3
# 0 1 2
# x y z

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: input blocks the program, always returns str, and raises EOFError when there is no stdin (cron jobs, pipes, tests).

Limitations

Limitations: it is strictly line-based and echoes what is typed (use getpass for passwords). Tests can feed it a fake stdin.
codeExamples:
import io, sys
sys.stdin = io.StringIO("anaji\nsecret\n")   # fake keyboard
user = input()                               # one line at a time, newline removed
pwd = input()
print(user, pwd)
sys.stdin = sys.__stdin__                    # restore

# OUTPUT:
# anaji secret

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Interactive input is for scripts and teaching. Real tools take arguments (argparse/typer), config files or environment variables so they can be automated and tested; wrap any unavoidable input() in a function so tests can inject values.

beginner.content:
Why Format Output?

Raw print() output is fine for debugging, but reports, receipts and tables need aligned columns, a fixed number of decimal places and separators. f-string format specifiers handle almost all of this.

Aligning Columns

< aligns left, > aligns right and ^ centres, inside a given width. Align text to the left and numbers to the right.
codeExamples:
items = [("Notebook", 3, 45.0), ("Pen", 10, 12.5), ("Geometry Box", 1, 150.0)]

print(f"{'Item':<15}{'Qty':>5}{'Price':>10}")
print("-" * 30)
for name, qty, price in items:
    print(f"{name:<15}{qty:>5}{price:>10.2f}")

# OUTPUT:
# Item             Qty     Price
# ------------------------------
# Notebook           3     45.00
# Pen               10     12.50
# Geometry Box       1    150.00

beginner.content: Numbers: Decimals, Separators and Percentages
codeExamples:
revenue = 1234567.891
growth = 0.0725

print(f"Revenue: {revenue:,.2f}")
print(f"Growth: {growth:.1%}")
print(f"Rounded: {revenue:.0f}")
print(f"Roll no: {7:03d}")

# OUTPUT:
# Revenue: 1,234,567.89
# Growth: 7.2%
# Rounded: 1234568
# Roll no: 007

beginner.content: A Complete Receipt
codeExamples:
cart = {"Python Book": 599.0, "USB Cable": 149.5, "Mouse": 450.0}
gst_rate = 0.18

width = 32
print("JavaSchoolLab Store".center(width))
print("=" * width)
subtotal = 0
for item, price in cart.items():
    print(f"{item:<22}{price:>10.2f}")
    subtotal += price
gst = subtotal * gst_rate
print("-" * width)
print(f"{'Subtotal':<22}{subtotal:>10.2f}")
print(f"{'GST (18%)':<22}{gst:>10.2f}")
print(f"{'TOTAL':<22}{subtotal + gst:>10.2f}")

# OUTPUT:
#       JavaSchoolLab Store
# ================================
# Python Book               599.00
# USB Cable                 149.50
# Mouse                     450.00
# --------------------------------
# Subtotal                 1198.50
# GST (18%)                 215.73
# TOTAL                    1414.23

beginner.content:
Introduction

Formatting output means controlling width, alignment, precision and separators so results are easy to read. Tools: format specs in f-strings, str.ljust/rjust/center, and print arguments.
codeExamples:
print(f"{'Name':<10}|{'Qty':^5}|{'Price':>8}")
print("-" * 25)
print("abc".ljust(6, "."), "abc".rjust(6, "."), "abc".center(7, "*"))

# OUTPUT:
# Name      | Qty |   Price
# -------------------------
# abc... ...abc **abc**

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Raw numbers like 1234567.891 or 0.256 are hard to read; users expect separators, fixed decimals and percentages.

Real-Time Use

A receipt or report printer lines up columns and totals.
codeExamples:
rows = [("Tea", 2, 1.5), ("Cake", 1, 3.25)]
total = 0
for n, q, p in rows:
    print(f"{n:<8}{q:>3} x {p:>6.2f} = {q * p:>7.2f}")
    total += q * p
print(f"TOTAL: {total:.2f}")

# OUTPUT:
# Tea       2 x   1.50 =    3.00
# Cake      1 x   3.25 =    3.25
# TOTAL: 6.25

beginner.content:
Diagram

   {value : [fill][align][sign][#][0][width][,][.prec][type]}

   f"{42:*^9}"   fill=*  align=^ (center)  width=9   ->  ***42****
   f"{3.14159:8.2f}"          width=8  .2f             ->  '    3.14'
   align:  <  left    >  right    ^  center    =  after sign

expert.content:
Dynamic Column Widths

Hard-coded widths break when the data changes. Compute the width from the data and pass it into the spec with a nested field.
codeExamples:
students = {"Pankaj": 91.5, "Sheru": 78.25, "Dheeraj Kumar": 88.0}

w = max(len(name) for name in students) + 2
for name, score in students.items():
    print(f"{name:<{w}}{score:>6.1f}")

# OUTPUT:
# Pankaj           91.5
# Sheru            78.2
# Dheeraj Kumar    88.0

expert.content:
pprint for Nested Data

print() puts a large dict or list on one long line. pprint wraps and indents nested structures so they are readable.
codeExamples:
from pprint import pprint

config = {
    "database": {"host": "localhost", "port": 3306, "user": "admin"},
    "features": ["login", "quiz", "certificates", "leaderboard"],
    "debug": False,
}
pprint(config, width=50, sort_dicts=False)

# OUTPUT:
# {'database': {'host': 'localhost',
#               'port': 3306,
#               'user': 'admin'},
#  'features': ['login',
#               'quiz',
#               'certificates',
#               'leaderboard'],
#  'debug': False}

expert.content:
Wrapping Long Text and Pretty JSON

textwrap wraps paragraphs to a width; json.dumps(indent=...) pretty-prints data for APIs and logs.
codeExamples:
import json
import textwrap

para = "Python is a high-level language that emphasises readability and lets you express ideas in fewer lines of code."
print(textwrap.fill(para, width=40))
print(textwrap.shorten(para, width=40, placeholder="..."))

print(json.dumps({"name": "Sheru", "skills": ["Python", "SQL"]}, indent=2))

# OUTPUT:
# Python is a high-level language that
# emphasises readability and lets you
# express ideas in fewer lines of code.
# Python is a high-level language that...
# {
#   "name": "Sheru",
#   "skills": [
#     "Python",
#     "SQL"
#   ]
# }

expert.content:
Locale-Aware and Indian Number Formatting

The , spec always groups digits in thousands (1,234,567). Indian formatting groups lakhs and crores (12,34,567). Python has no built-in spec for that, so either use the locale module with an Indian locale installed, a library such as Babel, or a small helper.
codeExamples:
def indian_format(n):
    s = str(int(n))
    if len(s) <= 3:
        return s
    head, tail = s[:-3], s[-3:]
    groups = []
    while len(head) > 2:
        groups.insert(0, head[-2:])
        head = head[:-2]
    if head:
        groups.insert(0, head)
    return ",".join(groups) + "," + tail

print(f"{1234567:,}")
print(indian_format(1234567))
print(indian_format(150000000))

# OUTPUT:
# 1,234,567
# 12,34,567
# 15,00,00,000

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How do you right-align a number in 10 characters with 2 decimals?f"{x:>10.2f}"
How do you use a variable width?Nest it: f"{text:<{width}}"
How do you print nested dicts readably?pprint.pprint(), or json.dumps(data, indent=2) for JSON-compatible data
How do you wrap long text?textwrap.fill(text, width)
Why does f"{78.25:.1f}" give 78.2?Formatting rounds half to even on the exact binary value; 78.25 is exactly representable, so the tie goes to the even digit 2

Advantages

Advantages: a compact mini-language covers number bases, signs, grouping and alignment in one place.
codeExamples:
n = 255
print(f"{n:b} {n:o} {n:X} {n:+d}")
print(f"{42:*^9}")                # fill character with centering

# OUTPUT:
# 11111111 377 FF +255
# ***42****

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: width is a minimum, not a maximum, and double-width (CJK) characters break column alignment.
codeExamples:
print(f"{'abcdefgh':<4}|")       # not truncated
print(f"{'abcdefgh':.3}|")        # precision truncates strings
print(f"{'你好':<6}|")             # padded by characters, drawn wider on screen

# OUTPUT:
# abcdefgh|
# abc|
# 你好    |

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a spec must match the type, and there is no built-in table or wrapping support.
codeExamples:
try:
    print(f"{'abc':d}")
except ValueError as e:
    print("ValueError:", e)

import textwrap
print(textwrap.fill("Python makes text wrapping easy", width=16))

# OUTPUT:
# ValueError: Unknown format code 'd' for object of type 'str'
# Python makes
# text wrapping
# easy

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use format specs for logs and quick reports; for real tables use tabulate/rich, for money use Decimal with locale or babel, and for user-facing text use i18n libraries since separators and decimal marks differ per locale. Machine-readable output should be JSON or CSV, never pretty-printed text.

beginner.content:
The Three Standard Streams

Every program starts with three open streams, available as file-like objects in the sys module:
StreamPurposeUsed byJava equivalent
sys.stdinStandard inputinput()System.in
sys.stdoutStandard outputprint()System.out
sys.stderrError / diagnostic outputTracebacks, warningsSystem.err

Writing with sys.stdout

sys.stdout.write() writes exactly the string you give it - no automatic spaces and no newline. It accepts only strings.
codeExamples:
import sys

sys.stdout.write("Hello")
sys.stdout.write(" World\n")
sys.stdout.write(str(42) + "\n")       # convert numbers yourself

sys.stderr.write("Warning: low disk space\n")

# OUTPUT:
# Hello World
# 42
# Warning: low disk space

beginner.content:
Reading with sys.stdin

sys.stdin.readline() reads one line including its trailing newline, so strip it. Unlike input() it shows no prompt.
codeExamples:
import sys

print("Enter your city:")
city = sys.stdin.readline().strip()
print("You live in", city)

# OUTPUT:
# Enter your city:
# Pune
# You live in Pune

beginner.content:
Reading Every Line

sys.stdin can be looped over like a file. This is how command-line tools process piped data.
codeExamples:
# count_words.py
import sys

total = 0
for line in sys.stdin:
    total += len(line.split())
print("Words:", total)

# $ type notes.txt | python count_words.py      (Windows)
# $ cat notes.txt | python count_words.py       (macOS / Linux)
# OUTPUT:
# Words: 128

beginner.content:
Introduction

sys.stdin and sys.stdout are the file-like objects behind input() and print(). You can read from, write to, or replace them.
codeExamples:
import sys
n = sys.stdout.write("hi\n")      # no automatic newline, returns characters written
print(n)
print(sys.stdout.encoding)

# OUTPUT (encoding varies):
# hi
# 3
# utf-8

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Command-line programs are chained with pipes (cat data | python tool.py), so they must read stdin and write stdout instead of asking questions.
codeExamples:
import sys, io
sys.stdin = io.StringIO("3\n10 20 30\n")      # simulate piped input
n = int(sys.stdin.readline())
nums = list(map(int, sys.stdin.readline().split()))
print(n, sum(nums))
sys.stdin = sys.__stdin__

# OUTPUT:
# 3 60

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Filters (grep-like tools) stream over stdin line by line without loading everything into memory.
codeExamples:
import sys, io
from collections import Counter
sys.stdin = io.StringIO("to be\nor not to be\n")
counts = Counter(w for line in sys.stdin for w in line.split())
print(counts.most_common(2))
sys.stdin = sys.__stdin__

# OUTPUT:
# [('to', 2), ('be', 2)]

beginner.content:
Diagram

   shell:  cat in.txt | python tool.py > out.txt 2> err.txt

   in.txt ──► sys.stdin ──► [ tool.py ] ──► sys.stdout ──► out.txt
                                │
                                └─────────► sys.stderr ──► err.txt
   fd 0 = stdin    fd 1 = stdout    fd 2 = stderr

expert.content:
Fast Input for Competitive Programming

input() carries overhead on every call. When reading hundreds of thousands of lines, bind sys.stdin.readline once, or read everything at once with sys.stdin.buffer.read() and split.
codeExamples:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline          # common competitive-programming idiom

n = int(input())
nums = list(map(int, input().split()))
print(sum(nums))

# Even faster: read all tokens at once
# data = sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()
# n, nums = int(data[0]), list(map(int, data[1:]))

# Input:
# 5
# 1 2 3 4 5
# OUTPUT:
# 15

expert.content:
Why stdout and stderr Are Separate

Shells can redirect them independently. Normal results go to stdout so they can be piped into another program, while errors go to stderr so they still reach the user (or a log) without corrupting the data stream.
codeExamples:
# report.py
import sys

print("id,name")                     # data -> stdout
print("1,Pankaj")
print("skipped 3 bad rows", file=sys.stderr)   # diagnostics -> stderr

# $ python report.py > out.csv          -> out.csv gets only the CSV,
#                                          the warning still shows on screen
# $ python report.py 2> errors.log      -> warning goes to errors.log
# $ python report.py > out.csv 2>&1     -> both into out.csv

expert.content:
Redirecting Output Inside Python

contextlib.redirect_stdout temporarily points sys.stdout at another file-like object - useful for capturing output from code you can't change, or in tests.
codeExamples:
import io
from contextlib import redirect_stdout

def noisy():
    print("lots of output")
    return 7

buffer = io.StringIO()
with redirect_stdout(buffer):
    result = noisy()

print("captured:", repr(buffer.getvalue()))
print("result:", result)

# OUTPUT:
# captured: 'lots of output\n'
# result: 7

expert.content:
Text Layer vs Binary Layer, and Encoding

sys.stdout is a text stream that encodes str to bytes; sys.stdout.buffer is the underlying binary stream. If printing non-ASCII text fails with UnicodeEncodeError on an older Windows console or when output is redirected, reconfigure the encoding or set the environment variable PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8.
codeExamples:
import sys

print(sys.stdout.encoding)
sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")      # Python 3.7+
print("₹ नमस्ते")

sys.stdout.buffer.write(b"raw bytes\n")
sys.stdout.flush()
print(sys.stdin.isatty())      # False when input is piped in

# OUTPUT (typical):
# utf-8
# ₹ नमस्ते
# raw bytes
# True

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
print() vs sys.stdout.write()?print converts values to str, adds separators and a newline; write takes one string and outputs it exactly, returning the number of characters written
input() vs sys.stdin.readline()?input shows a prompt and strips the newline; readline keeps the newline and is faster for bulk input
Why write errors to stderr?So they are not mixed into data that is redirected or piped from stdout
How do you capture printed output in Python?contextlib.redirect_stdout with an io.StringIO, or the capsys fixture in pytest
How do you detect piped input?sys.stdin.isatty() is False when input does not come from a terminal

Advantages

Advantages: redirection lets you capture or reroute output without changing the code that prints (great for tests).
codeExamples:
import io
from contextlib import redirect_stdout

buf = io.StringIO()
with redirect_stdout(buf):
    print("captured")
print(repr(buf.getvalue()))

# OUTPUT:
# 'captured\n'

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: write only accepts str, and output is buffered when piped, so ordering with stderr or a crash can surprise you; use flush=True.
codeExamples:
import sys
try:
    sys.stdout.write(42)
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)
print("progress...", end="", flush=True)    # show now, even if piped
print(" done")

# OUTPUT:
# TypeError: write() argument must be str, not int
# progress... done

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: reads are blocking with no timeout, and readline keeps the newline and returns an empty string at end of input.
codeExamples:
import sys, io
sys.stdin = io.StringIO("a\nb\n")
print([sys.stdin.readline() for _ in range(3)])
sys.stdin = sys.__stdin__

# OUTPUT:
# ['a\n', 'b\n', '']

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Write tools as pure functions that take and return data, with a thin main() that wires them to stdin/stdout/argv; this keeps them testable and composable in pipelines. Send diagnostics to stderr, data to stdout, and for high-volume reading iterate over the file object or use sys.stdin.buffer for binary data.

beginner.content:
What is Control Flow?

By default Python runs statements top to bottom, one after another. Control flow statements change that order. Every program is built from three basic structures:

• Sequence - statements run in order.
• Selection - choose which block runs: if, elif, else, match.
• Iteration - repeat a block: for, while.

break, continue and pass fine-tune how loops and blocks behave.

Control Flow Statements at a Glance

StatementPurposeJava equivalent
if / elif / elseRun a block only when a condition is trueif / else if / else
match / caseChoose a branch by matching a value's shape (3.10+)switch
forRepeat once per item of a sequence or iterableenhanced for (for (T x : items))
whileRepeat while a condition stays truewhile
breakLeave the loop immediatelybreak
continueSkip to the next iterationcontinue
passDo nothing (placeholder)empty block {}

Selection and Iteration Together

Python uses a colon : plus indentation for every block - there are no braces and no parentheses are needed around conditions.
codeExamples:
age = 20

if age < 13:
    category = "child"
elif age < 20:
    category = "teenager"
else:
    category = "adult"

print(category)

# Looping over a list directly - no index counter needed
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
for fruit in fruits:
    print(fruit)

# OUTPUT:
# adult
# apple
# banana
# cherry

beginner.content:
A Small Complete Program

Sequence, selection and iteration combined: count how many students passed.
codeExamples:
marks = [72, 35, 88, 40, 19]
passed = 0

for m in marks:
    if m >= 40:
        passed += 1
        print(m, "-> pass")
    else:
        print(m, "-> fail")

print(f"{passed} of {len(marks)} students passed")

# OUTPUT:
# 72 -> pass
# 35 -> fail
# 88 -> pass
# 40 -> pass
# 19 -> fail
# 3 of 5 students passed

beginner.content:
Introduction

Control flow decides which statements run, in what order, and how many times. Python gives you three tools: branching (if/elif/else, match), looping (for, while) and jumping (break, continue, return). Blocks are marked by indentation.
codeExamples:
# Sequence -> branch -> loop: the three shapes of every program
temperature = 31                      # 1. sequence: runs top to bottom
if temperature > 30:                  # 2. branch: choose ONE path
    print("hot day")
else:
    print("pleasant day")
for hour in range(3):                 # 3. loop: repeat a block
    print("hour", hour)

# OUTPUT:
# hot day
# hour 0
# hour 1
# hour 2

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Without control flow a program is a fixed list of steps that can never react to data. Decisions and repetition let one program handle any input, any number of records, and any error situation.

Real-Time Use

Every real system uses it: web servers route by URL, payment code branches on status, ETL jobs loop over millions of rows, retry logic loops until success or a limit.
codeExamples:
# Real-time style: retry an unreliable call at most 3 times
attempts = 0
responses = ["timeout", "timeout", "ok"]     # simulated server replies
while attempts < 3:
    reply = responses[attempts]
    attempts += 1
    if reply == "ok":
        print(f"success after {attempts} attempts")
        break
    print("retrying...", reply)
else:
    print("gave up")                         # runs only if no break happened

# OUTPUT:
# retrying... timeout
# retrying... timeout
# success after 3 attempts

beginner.content:
Diagram

            ┌───────────┐
            │  start    │
            └─────┬─────┘
                  ▼
            ┌───────────┐  False   ┌───────────┐
        ┌──►│ condition ├─────────►│  skip /   │
        │   └─────┬─────┘          │  else     │
        │         │ True           └─────┬─────┘
        │         ▼                      │
        │   ┌───────────┐                │
        │   │  body     │                │
        │   └─────┬─────┘                │
        └─────────┘ (loops only)         ▼
                                    next statement

expert.content:
Features Java Doesn't Have

• Loop else - a for or while can have an else block that runs only if the loop finished without break.
• Conditional expression - x if condition else y, Python's version of the ternary operator.
• Comprehensions - build a list from a loop and a condition in one expression.
• Structural pattern matching - match can destructure lists, dicts and objects, far beyond a classic switch.
codeExamples:
numbers = [3, 7, 11, 15]

for n in numbers:
    if n % 2 == 0:
        print("Found an even number:", n)
        break
else:
    print("No even numbers")

status = "adult" if 20 >= 18 else "minor"
evens_squared = [n * n for n in range(10) if n % 2 == 0]
print(status, evens_squared)

# OUTPUT:
# No even numbers
# adult [0, 4, 16, 36, 64]

expert.content:
Exceptions Are Control Flow Too

try / except also redirects execution. Idiomatic Python often prefers trying an operation and handling failure (EAFP) over checking every condition in advance with if.

Prefer Flat Over Nested

"Flat is better than nested" (the Zen of Python). Deeply indented control flow is hard to read. Guard clauses, continue, helper functions and lookup tables keep code flat - later topics in this module show each technique.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What are the three basic control structures?Sequence, selection (if/match) and iteration (for/while)
Does Python have a switch statement?Since 3.10 it has match/case; before that, if/elif chains or dictionary dispatch were used
Does Python have a do-while loop?No - use while True: with a break at the end
When does a loop's else block run?When the loop ends normally, i.e. without hitting break
How are blocks defined?By a colon and consistent indentation, not braces

Advantages

Advantages: readable (indentation = structure), for iterates over any iterable directly, loop else and chained comparisons remove helper flags, and there are very few keywords to learn.
codeExamples:
# Advantage: chained comparison and direct iteration read like English
age = 25
if 18 <= age < 60:                    # no "age >= 18 and age < 60" needed
    print("working age")
for name in ["Abaji", "Raoji"]:         # no index variable needed
    print("hello", name)

# OUTPUT:
# working age
# hello Abaji
# hello Raoji

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: indentation errors change meaning silently, there is no do-while or classic C-style for(;;), and deep nesting becomes hard to read.
codeExamples:
# Disadvantage: one wrongly indented line changes the logic, with no error
total = 0
for n in range(1, 4):
    total += n
print("inside-loop print?", total)      # at loop level: prints once, after the loop

total = 0
for n in range(1, 4):
    total += n
    print("running total", total)       # indented: prints every pass

# OUTPUT:
# inside-loop print? 6
# running total 1
# running total 3
# running total 6

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: Python has no goto and no labelled break, so leaving two nested loops at once needs a function, flag or exception; loops are also slower than vectorised or built-in alternatives.

Architect's Notes

Keep functions flat: prefer guard clauses (early return) over deep nesting, and replace long if-chains with dict dispatch or match. When logic must exit several loops, extract it into a function and return. Do not hand-write loops where a built-in (sum, any, comprehension) states the intent directly.

beginner.content:
The if Statement

if runs its block only when the condition is true. Write the condition, then a colon, then the indented block. Parentheses around the condition are not needed.
codeExamples:
temperature = 38

if temperature > 35:
    print("It's a hot day")
    print("Drink plenty of water")

print("Weather check done")

# OUTPUT:
# It's a hot day
# Drink plenty of water
# Weather check done

beginner.content:
if ... else

else provides the block that runs when the condition is false. Exactly one of the two blocks always runs.
codeExamples:
number = 7

if number % 2 == 0:
    print(number, "is even")
else:
    print(number, "is odd")

# OUTPUT:
# 7 is odd

beginner.content:
if ... elif ... else

elif ("else if") checks another condition when the previous ones were false. Python tests the conditions top to bottom and runs only the first block whose condition is true; the rest are skipped.

Combining Conditions

Use and, or and not to build larger conditions, and chained comparisons for ranges.
codeExamples:
age = 22
has_licence = True

if age >= 18 and has_licence:
    print("You can drive")

hour = 14
if 9 <= hour < 17:
    print("Office is open")

day = "Sunday"
if day == "Saturday" or day == "Sunday":
    print("Weekend!")

# OUTPUT:
# You can drive
# Office is open
# Weekend!

beginner.content:
Truthiness in Conditions

Any value can be a condition. Empty strings, empty collections, 0 and None count as false; everything else is true.
codeExamples:
name = input("Your name: ").strip()

if name:
    print("Hello,", name)
else:
    print("You didn't enter a name")

# OUTPUT:
# Your name:
# You didn't enter a name

beginner.content:
Introduction

if runs a block when its condition is truthy; elif tests further conditions in order; else is the fallback. Only the first matching branch runs. Python also has a one-line conditional expression: a if cond else b.
codeExamples:
score = 72
if score >= 90:
    grade = "A"
elif score >= 75:
    grade = "B"
elif score >= 60:
    grade = "C"                    # first True branch wins
else:
    grade = "F"
print(grade)
print("pass" if score >= 40 else "fail")   # conditional expression

# OUTPUT:
# C
# pass

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Programs must react to data: valid or invalid input, logged in or not, stock available or not. if is the basic decision tool, and truthiness (empty = False) keeps checks short.
codeExamples:
# Truthiness: empty containers, 0, None and "" are False
items = []
if not items:                      # shorter than len(items) == 0
    print("cart is empty")
name = ""
print("name given" if name else "name missing")

# OUTPUT:
# cart is empty
# name missing

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Used for input validation, permission checks, feature flags, pricing rules and status handling in APIs.

Diagram

   value ──► if A? ──True──► block A ──┐
               │False                  │
               ▼                       │
            elif B? ──True──► block B ─┤
               │False                  │
               ▼                       │
             else ──────────► block C ─┤
                                       ▼
                               continue after

expert.content:
Order Matters in elif Chains

Because only the first true branch runs, put the most specific conditions first. A broad condition placed early "swallows" the cases after it.
codeExamples:
marks = 95

# Wrong order - the A+ branch can never run
if marks >= 40:
    print("Pass")
elif marks >= 90:
    print("A+")

# Right order
if marks >= 90:
    print("A+")
elif marks >= 40:
    print("Pass")

# OUTPUT:
# Pass
# A+

expert.content:
The Conditional Expression (Ternary)

value_if_true if condition else value_if_false is an expression, so it can be used inside assignments, function arguments and f-strings. Keep it for simple choices - nested ternaries quickly become unreadable.
codeExamples:
stock = 0
label = "In stock" if stock > 0 else "Out of stock"
print(label)

n = -5
print(f"{n} is {'positive' if n > 0 else 'zero' if n == 0 else 'negative'}")

# OUTPUT:
# Out of stock
# -5 is negative

expert.content:
Replacing Long if/elif Chains with a Dictionary

When each branch just maps a key to a value or an action, a dictionary lookup is shorter, faster and easier to extend. For ranges of numbers, the bisect module can replace a ladder of comparisons.
codeExamples:
import bisect

day_type = {"Saturday": "weekend", "Sunday": "weekend"}
print(day_type.get("Monday", "weekday"))

def grade(marks):
    cutoffs = [40, 60, 75, 90]
    grades = ["F", "C", "B", "A", "A+"]
    return grades[bisect.bisect_right(cutoffs, marks)]

print([grade(m) for m in (35, 40, 74, 75, 90, 100)])

# OUTPUT:
# weekday
# ['F', 'C', 'B', 'A', 'A+', 'A+']

expert.content:
Common Mistakes

MistakeProblemFix
if x = 5:SyntaxError - = is assignmentif x == 5:
if day == "Sat" or "Sun":Always true - "Sun" alone is a truthy stringif day in ("Sat", "Sun"):
if x == True:Redundant and not PEP 8if x:
if len(items) > 0:Works, but not idiomaticif items:
if x == None:Can be fooled by __eq__if x is None:
Missing colon or inconsistent indentationSyntaxError / IndentationErrorColon after the condition; 4 spaces
codeExamples:
day = "Monday"

if day == "Saturday" or "Sunday":      # bug
    print("Weekend (wrong!)")

if day in ("Saturday", "Sunday"):       # correct
    print("Weekend")
else:
    print("Weekday")

# OUTPUT:
# Weekend (wrong!)
# Weekday

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How many elif branches can run?At most one - the first whose condition is true
What is Python's ternary operator?a if condition else b
Why is if x == "a" or "b": always true?It parses as (x == "a") or "b", and the non-empty string "b" is truthy
Is else required?No - if and elif blocks can stand without it
How can you replace a long if/elif chain?With a dictionary lookup, match/case, or bisect for numeric ranges

Advantages

Advantages: evaluates lazily with and/or short-circuiting, accepts any object via truthiness, and chained comparisons keep range tests readable.
codeExamples:
# Advantage: short-circuit protects against errors
user = None
if user and user["active"]:        # user["active"] never evaluated when user is None
    print("active user")
else:
    print("no active user")

# OUTPUT:
# no active user

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: long elif ladders are hard to maintain; truthiness hides intent (0 and None both fail); a single = instead of == is a SyntaxError (good) but is vs == confusion is not.
codeExamples:
# Disadvantage: truthiness treats 0 like "missing"
discount = 0                       # a valid value: zero percent
if discount:
    print("has discount")
else:
    print("treated as no discount (0 is falsy)")
if discount is not None:           # explicit check expresses the real intent
    print("discount provided:", discount)

# OUTPUT:
# treated as no discount (0 is falsy)
# discount provided: 0

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the condition is evaluated every time (no compiled jump table); a conditional expression cannot hold statements; there is no assignment inside a condition except the walrus operator :=.
codeExamples:
# Limitation: conditional expressions hold values only, not statements
n = 7
label = "odd" if n % 2 else "even"
print(label)
# "print('x') if n else pass" is a SyntaxError - use a normal if block

# Walrus assigns inside the condition (3.8+)
if (size := len("python")) > 5:
    print("long word of", size)

# OUTPUT:
# odd
# long word of 6

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Order conditions from most specific or most common to least, and keep each branch short. If a ladder maps a value to an action, use a dict of functions or match; if branches multiply with each new feature, the design usually wants polymorphism or a strategy table instead.

beginner.content:
What is a Nested Condition?

A nested condition is an if statement inside another if (or elif / else) block. The inner condition is only checked when the outer one is true. Each level is indented 4 more spaces.
Example: Largest of Three Numbers

Example: Leap Year

A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, except century years, which must also be divisible by 400.

Flattening with and / or

Many nested conditions can be written as a single condition. The leap-year rule becomes one line.

Introduction

A nested condition is an if inside another if. The inner test is only reached when the outer test passed. Equivalent flat forms use and or early returns.

Why Do We Need This?

Real rules depend on several factors in layers (is the user logged in, then is the role admin, then is the resource owned). Nesting expresses dependent checks.

Real-Time Use

Authorization, form validation, order workflows and game rules all layer conditions. Developers flatten them with guard clauses for readability.
codeExamples:
# Flattened with guard clauses (same logic, no pyramid)
def checkout(cart, paid, address):
    if not cart:
        return "empty cart"
    if not paid:
        return "payment pending"
    if not address:
        return "address missing"
    return "order placed"

print(checkout(["pen"], True, ""))
print(checkout(["pen"], True, "Pune"))

# OUTPUT:
# address missing
# order placed

beginner.content:
Diagram

   if logged_in? ──No──────────────► deny
        │Yes
        ▼
   if is_admin? ──Yes──────────────► allow
        │No
        ▼
   if is_owner? ──Yes──► allow
        │No
        ▼
       deny

expert.content:
The Arrow Anti-Pattern

Deep nesting pushes the important code far to the right ("arrow code") and makes it hard to see which else belongs to which if. A good rule: if you are more than two or three levels deep, restructure.

Guard Clauses: Fail Fast, Return Early

Check each failure case first and return immediately. The "happy path" then sits at the lowest indentation level, and every rule reads as one line.

continue as a Guard Inside Loops

The same idea works in loops: skip the items you don't want with continue instead of wrapping the real work in another if.

Decision Tables

When the outcome depends on a combination of several conditions, a lookup table keyed by a tuple of conditions can replace a whole tree of nested ifs.
codeExamples:
# (is_member, order_over_1000) -> discount
DISCOUNTS = {
    (True, True): 0.20,
    (True, False): 0.10,
    (False, True): 0.05,
    (False, False): 0.0,
}

def discount(is_member, total):
    return DISCOUNTS[(is_member, total > 1000)]

print(discount(True, 1500), discount(False, 500))

# OUTPUT:
# 0.2 0.0

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a guard clause?An early return (or continue) that handles an invalid case first, so the main logic isn't nested
How do you reduce nesting?Combine conditions with and/or, use guard clauses, extract functions, or use lookup tables
Write the leap-year condition in one liney % 4 == 0 and (y % 100 != 0 or y % 400 == 0)
Which if does an else belong to?The if at the same indentation level - Python has no "dangling else" ambiguity

Advantages

Advantages: mirrors dependent rules directly, avoids repeating the outer test, and lets the inner check use values proven valid by the outer one.
codeExamples:
# Advantage: inner check is safe because the outer one passed
data = {"items": [3, 4]}
if "items" in data:
    if data["items"]:              # safe: key is known to exist
        print("first:", data["items"][0])

# OUTPUT:
# first: 3

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: deep nesting (the "arrow anti-pattern") hurts readability, is harder to test, and the else of an inner if is easy to attach to the wrong level.

Limitations

Limitations: Python has no hard nesting limit for ifs, but the parser caps indentation depth (about 100 levels) and readers cap far sooner; there is no switch fall-through to flatten the structure.
codeExamples:
# Limitation: combining with 'and' is flat but loses separate messages
age, has_id = 17, True
if age >= 18 and has_id:
    print("allowed")
else:
    print("denied")       # cannot tell WHICH rule failed without extra tests

# OUTPUT:
# denied

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Prefer guard clauses and small predicate functions (is_owner(user, post)) so each rule has a name and a unit test. More than about three levels of nesting is a design smell: extract functions, or model the rules as a data-driven table.

beginner.content:
The for Loop

Python's for loop goes through the items of any iterable - a list, string, tuple, dictionary, file, and more - one at a time. It works like Java's enhanced for loop (for (String s : list)); there is no C-style for (i = 0; i < n; i++).
codeExamples:
languages = ["Java", "Python", "SQL"]
for lang in languages:
    print("I am learning", lang)

for ch in "Hi!":
    print(ch)

# OUTPUT:
# I am learning Java
# I am learning Python
# I am learning SQL
# H
# i
# !

beginner.content:
range() - Looping a Number of Times

range() produces a sequence of integers:
CallProduces
range(5)0, 1, 2, 3, 4
range(2, 6)2, 3, 4, 5
range(1, 10, 3)1, 4, 7
range(10, 0, -2)10, 8, 6, 4, 2
Like slicing, the stop value is not included.
codeExamples:
for i in range(3):
    print("Hello", i)

for n in range(10, 0, -2):
    print(n, end=" ")
print()

# OUTPUT:
# Hello 0
# Hello 1
# Hello 2
# 10 8 6 4 2

beginner.content:
Accumulating Results

A loop often builds up a total, a count or a new list.
codeExamples:
prices = [120, 45, 300, 80]

total = 0
expensive = []
for p in prices:
    total += p
    if p > 100:
        expensive.append(p)

print("Total:", total)
print("Expensive items:", expensive)

n = 5
factorial = 1
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    factorial *= i
print(f"{n}! = {factorial}")

# OUTPUT:
# Total: 545
# Expensive items: [120, 300]
# 5! = 120

beginner.content:
enumerate() - Index and Value Together

When you need the position too, use enumerate() instead of range(len(...)).
codeExamples:
students = ["Pankaj", "Sheru", "Dheeraj"]

for rank, name in enumerate(students, start=1):
    print(rank, name)

# OUTPUT:
# 1 Pankaj
# 2 Sheru
# 3 Dheeraj

beginner.content:
Looping over Dictionaries and Pairs

dict.items() gives key-value pairs; zip() walks several sequences in step.
codeExamples:
stock = {"pen": 10, "book": 4}
for item, qty in stock.items():
    print(f"{item}: {qty}")

names = ["Abaji", "Raoji"]
marks = [91, 84]
for name, mark in zip(names, marks):
    print(name, "scored", mark)

# OUTPUT:
# pen: 10
# book: 4
# Abaji scored 91
# Raoji scored 84

beginner.content:
Introduction

for walks over any iterable (list, string, dict, file, generator). range(start, stop, step) produces integers lazily: stop is excluded.
codeExamples:
for ch in "abc":                 # strings are iterable
    print(ch, end=" ")
print()
print(list(range(5)))              # 0..4
print(list(range(2, 10, 3)))       # start, stop, step
print(list(range(5, 0, -2)))       # counting down

# OUTPUT:
# a b c
# [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
# [2, 5, 8]
# [5, 3, 1]

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Repeating work over a collection or a fixed count is the most common task in programming. Python's for avoids manual counters and index errors.
codeExamples:
prices = [120, 80, 45]
total = 0
for p in prices:                   # no index, no length arithmetic
    total += p
print("total:", total)
for i, p in enumerate(prices, start=1):   # when you also need a position
    print(i, p)

# OUTPUT:
# total: 245
# 1 120
# 2 80
# 3 45

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Processing files line by line, rows from a database, items in a shopping cart, pages of an API, and batches of a dataset all use for.
codeExamples:
# Real-time: process records in batches of 3
records = list(range(1, 9))
BATCH = 3
for start in range(0, len(records), BATCH):
    batch = records[start:start + BATCH]
    print("processing", batch)

# OUTPUT:
# processing [1, 2, 3]
# processing [4, 5, 6]
# processing [7, 8]

beginner.content:
Diagram

   iterable ──► iter() ──► iterator
                              │
              ┌───────────────┘
              ▼
        ┌─► next() ──► value ──► loop body ─┐
        │      │                            │
        └──────┼────────────────────────────┘
               ▼ StopIteration
            loop ends (else block runs)

expert.content:
range Is a Lazy Sequence

range does not build a list in memory - it computes values on demand, so range(10**12) costs the same memory as range(5). It still supports len(), indexing, slicing and a fast O(1) in test.
codeExamples:
import sys

r = range(0, 100, 7)
print(len(r), r[3], r[-1], 49 in r, 50 in r)
print(r[2:5])
print(sys.getsizeof(range(10**12)), sys.getsizeof(list(range(1000))))

# OUTPUT (sizes in bytes, 64-bit CPython):
# 15 21 98 True False
# range(14, 35, 7)
# 48 8056

expert.content:
Don't Modify a List While Looping over It

Removing items shifts the remaining ones left, so the loop skips the element right after each removal. Loop over a copy, or better, build a new list.
codeExamples:
nums = [1, 2, 2, 3]
for n in nums:
    if n == 2:
        nums.remove(n)
print(nums)                         # one 2 survived!

nums = [1, 2, 2, 3]
nums = [n for n in nums if n != 2]  # build a new list instead
print(nums)

# OUTPUT:
# [1, 2, 3]
# [1, 3]

expert.content:
Pythonic Looping Toolkit

Instead ofWrite
for i in range(len(items)): items[i]for item in items:
a manual counterfor i, item in enumerate(items):
indexing two lists by ifor a, b in zip(xs, ys):
range(len(x) - 1, -1, -1)for item in reversed(x):
sorting a copy firstfor item in sorted(x):
a loop that only sums / testssum(...), any(...), all(...)
codeExamples:
marks = [72, 35, 88]
print(sum(marks), any(m < 40 for m in marks), all(m >= 30 for m in marks))

for m in reversed(marks):
    print(m, end=" ")
print()

# zip stops at the shortest input; strict=True (3.10+) raises instead
print(list(zip([1, 2, 3], ["a", "b"])))

# OUTPUT:
# 195 True True
# 88 35 72
# [(1, 'a'), (2, 'b')]

expert.content:
The Loop Variable Outlives the Loop

Unlike Java, a for loop does not create its own scope. The loop variable still exists after the loop, holding the last value - and doesn't exist at all if the loop never ran.
codeExamples:
for i in range(3):
    pass
print(i)

for j in []:
    pass
print(j)

# OUTPUT:
# 2
# NameError: name 'j' is not defined

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What can a for loop iterate over?Any iterable: sequences, dicts, sets, files, generators and objects implementing __iter__
Is the stop value of range() included?No - range(1, 5) gives 1, 2, 3, 4
Does range() create a list?No - it is a lazy, immutable sequence object with O(1) memory
How do you get the index while looping?enumerate(iterable, start=0)
Why not remove items from a list while iterating over it?Indices shift and elements get skipped; iterate over a copy or build a new list
What does zip() do with unequal lengths?Stops at the shortest; use itertools.zip_longest or strict=True

Advantages

Advantages: range uses constant memory (it is lazy), supports len(), indexing and in; loops work with any iterable; for...else detects "no break".
codeExamples:
# Advantage: range is lazy - a billion numbers cost almost nothing
big = range(1_000_000_000)
print(len(big), big[10], 999_999_999 in big)   # O(1) operations
import sys
print(sys.getsizeof(big))                      # small, fixed size

# OUTPUT:
# 1000000000 10 True
# 48

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: modifying a list while looping over it skips items; Python loops are slower than C; a loop variable leaks outside the loop.
codeExamples:
# Disadvantage: removing while iterating skips elements
nums = [1, 2, 2, 3]
for n in nums:
    if n == 2:
        nums.remove(n)
print(nums)                        # one 2 survived!
for i in range(2):
    pass
print("leaked loop variable:", i)

# OUTPUT:
# [1, 2, 3]
# leaked loop variable: 1

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: range accepts integers only (use numpy.arange or a generator for floats), step cannot be 0, and a one-shot iterator (generator) can be looped only once.

Architect's Notes

Iterate over items, not indexes; reach for enumerate, zip and comprehensions. For million-row or CPU-bound work move the loop into NumPy/pandas or a compiled library, and for huge streams use generators to keep memory flat.

beginner.content:
The while Loop

A while loop repeats its block as long as its condition is true. The condition is checked before every iteration. Use while when you don't know in advance how many times to loop; use for when you are going through a known collection or count.
codeExamples:
count = 1

while count <= 5:
    print("Count is", count)
    count += 1              # without this the loop never ends

print("Loop finished")

# OUTPUT:
# Count is 1
# Count is 2
# Count is 3
# Count is 4
# Count is 5
# Loop finished

beginner.content:
Example: Sum of Digits

A classic case where the number of iterations depends on the data.
codeExamples:
number = 90817
total = 0

while number > 0:
    digit = number % 10      # last digit
    total += digit
    number //= 10            # drop the last digit

print("Sum of digits:", total)

# OUTPUT:
# Sum of digits: 25

beginner.content: Looping Until the Input Is Valid
codeExamples:
password = input("Set a password: ")

while len(password) < 8:
    print("Too short - use at least 8 characters.")
    password = input("Set a password: ")

print("Password saved.")

# OUTPUT:
# Set a password: abc
# Too short - use at least 8 characters.
# Set a password: python123
# Password saved.

beginner.content:
while True with break

Python has no do-while loop. The standard replacement is an infinite while True: loop that exits with break - the body always runs at least once.
codeExamples:
while True:
    command = input("Enter command (help/quit): ").strip().lower()
    if command == "quit":
        print("Bye!")
        break
    elif command == "help":
        print("Available: help, quit")
    else:
        print("Unknown command")

# OUTPUT:
# Enter command (help/quit): list
# Unknown command
# Enter command (help/quit): help
# Available: help, quit
# Enter command (help/quit): quit
# Bye!

beginner.content:
Infinite Loops

If the condition never becomes false, the loop runs forever. Press Ctrl+C in the terminal to stop it - Python raises KeyboardInterrupt. Always make sure something inside the loop moves it toward ending.
codeExamples:
n = 10
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    # forgot n -= 1  -> prints 10 forever

beginner.content:
Introduction

while repeats a block as long as its condition stays true. Use it when the number of repetitions is not known in advance. An optional else runs when the condition becomes false without a break.
codeExamples:
count = 3
while count > 0:
    print("countdown", count)
    count -= 1                     # must change state or the loop never ends
else:
    print("liftoff")

# OUTPUT:
# countdown 3
# countdown 2
# countdown 1
# liftoff

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Some repetition depends on a runtime event (user types a valid value, server answers, queue empties), not on a count. for cannot express that cleanly; while can.
codeExamples:
# Collatz sequence: length is unknown up front
n, steps = 6, 0
while n != 1:
    n = n // 2 if n % 2 == 0 else 3 * n + 1
    steps += 1
print("steps to reach 1:", steps)

# OUTPUT:
# steps to reach 1: 8

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Event loops, menu programs, polling a job until it is finished, reading from sockets, and game main loops are all while loops.
codeExamples:
# Real-time: poll a job until done (simulated)
statuses = iter(["queued", "running", "running", "done"])
status = next(statuses)
while status != "done":
    print("status:", status)
    status = next(statuses)        # in real code: call API, then sleep
print("job finished")

# OUTPUT:
# status: queued
# status: running
# status: running
# job finished

beginner.content:
Diagram

         ┌──────────────────┐
   ┌────►│ condition true?  │
   │     └───┬──────────┬───┘
   │     Yes │          │ No
   │         ▼          ▼
   │   ┌───────────┐  else block
   │   │ body      │      │
   │   │ (update!) │      ▼
   │   └─────┬─────┘   after loop
   └─────────┘

expert.content:
while ... else

The else block runs when the condition becomes false - but not if the loop exited through break. It answers the question "did the search finish without finding anything?"
codeExamples:
def first_divisor(n):
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            print(n, "is divisible by", d)
            break
        d += 1
    else:
        print(n, "is prime")

first_divisor(91)
first_divisor(97)

# OUTPUT:
# 91 is divisible by 7
# 97 is prime

expert.content:
The Walrus Operator in Loop Conditions

:= lets you read a value and test it in the same condition, removing the duplicated "read before the loop, read again at the end" pattern.
codeExamples:
# Without walrus - input() appears twice
line = input("> ")
while line != "done":
    print("Got", line)
    line = input("> ")

# With walrus
while (line := input("> ")) != "done":
    print("Got", line)

# Reading a file in fixed-size chunks
# with open("big.bin", "rb") as f:
#     while chunk := f.read(4096):
#         process(chunk)

expert.content:
Prefer for When You Can

A while loop that manages its own counter is easy to get wrong (off-by-one errors, forgotten increments). If you are counting or walking a collection, for is safer and clearer.
codeExamples:
items = ["a", "b", "c"]

# Error-prone
i = 0
while i < len(items):
    print(items[i])
    i += 1

# Clear and safe
for item in items:
    print(item)

expert.content:
Retrying with a Limit

Real systems retry flaky operations - but never forever. Combine a counter with while ... else or a for over range, and wait longer between attempts (exponential backoff).
codeExamples:
import random
import time

def unreliable_call():
    return random.random() > 0.6      # succeeds about 40% of the time

attempt = 0
delay = 0.1
while attempt < 5:
    attempt += 1
    if unreliable_call():
        print(f"Succeeded on attempt {attempt}")
        break
    print(f"Attempt {attempt} failed, retrying in {delay:.1f}s")
    time.sleep(delay)
    delay *= 2
else:
    print("Giving up after 5 attempts")

# OUTPUT (varies - random):
# Attempt 1 failed, retrying in 0.1s
# Succeeded on attempt 2

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
for vs while?for iterates over a known iterable; while repeats until a condition becomes false, when the number of iterations isn't known
How do you write a do-while in Python?while True: with the body first and a break when the exit condition holds
When does while-else run its else block?When the condition becomes false; it is skipped if the loop ended with break
How do you stop an infinite loop?Ctrl+C raises KeyboardInterrupt
How do you sum the digits of a number?Loop while n > 0, adding n % 10 and doing n //= 10

Advantages

Advantages: expresses condition-driven repetition directly; while True plus break gives a clean "loop and a half" (replacement for do-while).
codeExamples:
# Advantage: do-while pattern with while True + break
values = iter([-7, -2, 5])
while True:
    v = next(values)
    if v > 0:
        print("accepted", v)
        break                      # exit when valid
    print("rejected", v)

# OUTPUT:
# rejected -7
# rejected -2
# accepted 5

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: easy to write an infinite loop by forgetting to update the condition; state bookkeeping is manual; harder to read than a for when a collection exists.
codeExamples:
# Disadvantage: forgot to update i => infinite loop. Guard with a limit.
i, guard = 0, 0
while i < 3:
    guard += 1
    if guard > 5:                  # safety net for demonstration
        print("would loop forever: i never changes, i =", i)
        break

# OUTPUT:
# would loop forever: i never changes, i = 0

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: floating-point conditions may never become exactly equal, and a blocking while freezes the program (use threads, asyncio or sleeps with timeouts).
codeExamples:
# Limitation: float accumulation never hits exactly 1.0
x, loops = 0.0, 0
while loops < 10:                  # a "while x != 1.0" test would never be reliable
    x += 0.1
    loops += 1
print(loops, x)
print("exactly 1.0?", x == 1.0)
print("close enough?", abs(x - 1.0) < 1e-9)   # use a tolerance instead

# OUTPUT:
# 10 0.9999999999999999
# exactly 1.0? False
# close enough? True

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Every while needs a clear termination argument: a changing variable, a timeout, or a max-attempts cap. In services prefer bounded loops with backoff and deadlines; for concurrency-heavy waits use asyncio or event callbacks rather than busy polling.

beginner.content:
Three Small Keywords

KeywordWhat it does
breakExits the loop immediately - remaining iterations are skipped
continueSkips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the next one
passDoes nothing at all - a placeholder where Python requires a statement
break - Stop When You've Found It
codeExamples:
balances = [1200, 540, -300, 800, -50]

for b in balances:
    if b < 0:
        print("First negative balance:", b)
        break
    print("Checked", b)

# OUTPUT:
# Checked 1200
# Checked 540
# First negative balance: -300

beginner.content: continue - Skip This One
codeExamples:
for n in range(1, 11):
    if n % 3 == 0:
        continue            # skip multiples of 3
    print(n, end=" ")
print()

lines = ["apple", "", "  ", "mango"]
for line in lines:
    if not line.strip():
        continue            # skip blank lines
    print("Processing", line)

# OUTPUT:
# 1 2 4 5 7 8 10
# Processing apple
# Processing mango

beginner.content:
pass - "Nothing Here Yet"

Python does not allow an empty block. pass fills the gap while you are sketching code you will write later.

pass vs continue

They are easy to confuse. pass does nothing and execution carries on to the next line; continue jumps straight to the next iteration.
codeExamples:
for n in range(4):
    if n == 2:
        pass
    print("with pass:", n)

for n in range(4):
    if n == 2:
        continue
    print("with continue:", n)

# OUTPUT:
# with pass: 0
# with pass: 1
# with pass: 2
# with pass: 3
# with continue: 0
# with continue: 1
# with continue: 3

beginner.content:
Introduction

break leaves the nearest loop immediately; continue skips to the next iteration; pass does nothing and is a placeholder where a statement is required.

Why Do We Need This?

Loops often need exceptions to the normal path: stop when found, skip invalid items, or reserve space for code written later. These keywords avoid deep nesting and extra flags.

Real-Time Use

Parsers skip comment lines with continue, search routines break on first match, and class skeletons or abstract stubs use pass in early design.

Diagram

   for item in data:
        │
        ├── bad item?  ──► continue ──┐ (next item)
        │                             │
        ├── found?     ──► break ──────────► after loop
        │                             │
        └── process(item)             │
              └─────────◄─────────────┘

expert.content:
break Only Leaves the Innermost Loop

Python has no labelled break outer; like Java. A break inside a nested loop ends only that inner loop. See the Nested Loops topic for the standard ways to exit several loops at once.

The continue Trap in while Loops

In a while loop you update the counter yourself. If continue runs before the update, the counter never changes and the loop runs forever.
codeExamples:
# BUG - infinite loop when i reaches 2
# i = 0
# while i < 5:
#     if i == 2:
#         continue
#     print(i)
#     i += 1

# Fix: update first, then decide
i = 0
while i < 5:
    i += 1
    if i == 3:
        continue
    print(i, end=" ")
print()

# OUTPUT:
# 1 2 4 5

expert.content:
break and the Loop else Clause

A loop's else block runs only when no break happened. This replaces the "found" flag variable you would need in Java.

Don't Silence Errors with pass

except: pass hides every error, including bugs and KeyboardInterrupt, making problems impossible to diagnose. Catch the specific exception you expect. When ignoring it really is correct, contextlib.suppress states the intent clearly.
codeExamples:
import os
from contextlib import suppress

# Bad
try:
    os.remove("temp.txt")
except:
    pass

# Good - only the expected error is ignored
with suppress(FileNotFoundError):
    os.remove("temp.txt")

expert.content:
pass, Ellipsis and Docstrings

Any statement satisfies Python's "block can't be empty" rule. ... (Ellipsis) is common in type stubs and abstract methods, and a docstring alone is a perfectly good body.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
break vs continue?break ends the whole loop; continue ends only the current iteration
pass vs continue?pass does nothing and execution continues on the next line; continue jumps to the next iteration
Does break exit all nested loops?No, only the innermost loop containing it
Why is except: pass bad?It swallows every exception, including real bugs and Ctrl+C
Is a loop's else run after break?No - only when the loop completes without break

Advantages

Advantages: flatten logic (guard-style continue), save work by exiting early, and let you stub code that is not ready yet.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: overuse creates "jumpy" logic that is hard to follow; continue in a while before the update statement causes infinite loops.
codeExamples:
# Disadvantage: continue skipped the increment => never ends (capped here)
i, guard = 0, 0
while i < 5 and guard < 4:
    guard += 1
    if i == 2:
        continue                   # i is never incremented again
    i += 1
print("stuck at i =", i)

# OUTPUT:
# stuck at i = 2

expert.content:
Limitations
