Variables vanish when the program ends. Files let data survive, be shared between programs, and be larger than memory.
codeExamples:
# Data written now can be read by a completely different run
with open("notes.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("remember me")
with open("notes.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:     # default mode is "r"
    print(f.read())

# OUTPUT:
# remember me

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Logs, configuration, exports, uploads, caches and data-science inputs are all files opened every day.
codeExamples:
# Typical log appender: "a" adds to the end, never erases
import datetime
with open("app.log", "a", encoding="utf-8") as log:
    log.write("started\n")
with open("app.log", encoding="utf-8") as log:
    print(len(log.readlines()) >= 1)

# OUTPUT:
# True

beginner.content:
Diagram

   your code --open("a.txt","w")--> Python file object --buffer--> OS --> disk
        ^                                |
        +-------- read()/write() --------+      close() flushes buffer, frees handle

expert.content:
What a File Object Really Is

In text mode, open() returns an io.TextIOWrapper: a layer that decodes bytes to str, sitting on top of a buffered binary stream, which sits on top of the raw operating-system file. Binary mode skips the text layer.
codeExamples:
f = open("notes.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8")
print(type(f))
print(f.name, f.mode, f.encoding, f.closed)
print(type(f.buffer))              # the binary layer underneath
f.close()
print(f.closed)

g = open("notes.txt", "rb")
print(type(g))
g.close()

# OUTPUT:
# <class '_io.TextIOWrapper'>
# notes.txt w utf-8 False
# <class '_io.BufferedWriter'>
# True
# <class '_io.BufferedReader'>

expert.content:
Buffering and flush()

Writes go into an in-memory buffer first and reach the disk in larger blocks, which is much faster. Until the buffer is flushed (by flush(), close() or the buffer filling up), other readers may not see the data - and if the program crashes, it is lost.
codeExamples:
f = open("buf.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8")
f.write("data")

with open("buf.txt", encoding="utf-8") as reader:
    print(repr(reader.read()))      # still in f's buffer

f.flush()                            # push it to the OS
with open("buf.txt", encoding="utf-8") as reader:
    print(repr(reader.read()))
f.close()

# OUTPUT:
# ''
# 'data'

expert.content:
The newline Parameter

In text mode Python uses universal newlines: when reading, (Windows) and are converted to ; when writing, is converted to the platform's line ending. newline="" turns translation off - required by the csv module - and newline=" " forces Unix endings on every platform.
codeExamples:
with open("unix.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="\n") as f:
    f.write("a\nb\n")

with open("unix.txt", "rb") as f:
    print(f.read())                  # exactly what is on disk

# OUTPUT:
# b'a\nb\n'

expert.content:
Opening Files Next to Your Script

Relative paths depend on where Python was started, so a script that works from its own folder can fail when run from elsewhere (an IDE, a scheduler, another directory). Build paths from the script's location instead.
codeExamples:
from pathlib import Path

BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent     # folder containing this script
config_path = BASE_DIR / "config.txt"

config_path.write_text("debug=true", encoding="utf-8")
print(config_path.name, config_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

# OUTPUT:
# config.txt debug=true

expert.content:
Why Closing Matters

• Each open file uses an operating-system file handle, and processes have a limit (often 1024 on Linux). Leaking handles in a loop eventually raises OSError: [Errno 24] Too many open files.
• Unflushed writes may be lost.
• On Windows, an open file usually can't be deleted or renamed by other programs.

CPython often closes files when the object is garbage-collected, but that is an implementation detail - always close explicitly, ideally with the with statement (next topics).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
"w" vs "a" vs "x"?"w" erases or creates; "a" keeps content and writes at the end; "x" creates only if the file doesn't exist
Why pass encoding="utf-8"?The default encoding depends on the platform (e.g. cp1252 on many Windows systems), so files may be read differently elsewhere
What does open() return in text mode?An io.TextIOWrapper wrapping a buffered binary stream
What is a relative path relative to?The current working directory (os.getcwd()), not the script's folder
How do you write a Windows path safely?A raw string r"C:\data\f.txt", doubled backslashes, forward slashes, or pathlib
Why must files be closed?To flush buffered data and free the OS file handle

Advantages

Advantages: one simple API for text and binary, buffered for speed, the x mode gives atomic "create only if absent".
codeExamples:
import os
with open("once.txt", "x") as f:       # fails if the file already exists
    f.write("first")
try:
    open("once.txt", "x")
except FileExistsError:
    print("refused to overwrite")
os.remove("once.txt")

# OUTPUT:
# refused to overwrite

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: mode w destroys existing content instantly, forgetting close() leaks handles, and the default encoding depends on the OS.
codeExamples:
with open("keep.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("important data")
with open("keep.txt", "w") as f:       # opened for write: content erased immediately
    pass
print(repr(open("keep.txt").read()))

# OUTPUT:
# ''

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a missing file or directory raises FileNotFoundError, permissions can raise PermissionError, and OS limits on open handles exist.

Architect's Notes

Always pass encoding explicitly (utf-8) for portable behaviour and prefer pathlib for paths. For crash-safe updates write to a temp file then os.replace() it over the original instead of truncating in place.

beginner.content:
Writing Text

write(text) writes a string and returns the number of characters written. It does not add a newline - include \n yourself. Opening with "w" creates the file or erases an existing one.
codeExamples:
with open("students.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    count = f.write("Abaji\n")
    f.write("Raoji\n")
    f.write("Kanhoji\n")

print(count)

with open("students.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read())

# OUTPUT:
# 6
# Abaji
# Raoji
# Kanhoji
#

beginner.content:
Three Ways to Read

MethodReturns
read()The whole file as one string
readline()The next line, including its \n; "" at the end of the file
readlines()A list of all lines, each with its \n
codeExamples:
with open("students.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("Abaji\nRaoji\nKanhoji\n")

with open("students.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(repr(f.read()))

with open("students.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(repr(f.readline()))
    print(repr(f.readline()))

with open("students.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.readlines())

# OUTPUT:
# 'Abaji\nRaoji\nKanhoji\n'
# 'Abaji\n'
# 'Raoji\n'
# ['Abaji\n', 'Raoji\n', 'Kanhoji\n']

beginner.content:
Looping Over Lines - the Best Way

A file object is iterable: for line in f reads one line at a time, so it works even for files larger than your memory. Each line still ends with \n; remove it with rstrip("\n") (or strip() to also remove spaces).
codeExamples:
with open("marks.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("Abaji,91\nRaoji,78\nKanhoji,85\n")

total = 0
with open("marks.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        name, mark = line.rstrip("\n").split(",")
        total += int(mark)
        print(f"{name:<8}{mark}")
print("Total:", total)

# OUTPUT:
# Abaji   91
# Raoji   78
# Kanhoji 85
# Total: 254

beginner.content:
Appending

Mode "a" keeps the existing content and adds new text at the end - ideal for logs. Mode "w" would wipe the file first.
codeExamples:
with open("log.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("started\n")

with open("log.txt", "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("user logged in\n")

with open("log.txt", "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("user logged out\n")

with open("log.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read(), end="")

with open("log.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:   # "w" truncates
    f.write("fresh start\n")

with open("log.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read(), end="")

# OUTPUT:
# started
# user logged in
# user logged out
# fresh start

beginner.content:
writelines() and print(file=...)

writelines() writes every string from a list (or any iterable) - again without adding newlines. print(..., file=f) writes like print does, with spaces and a newline.
codeExamples:
items = ["pen", "book", "bag"]

with open("items.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.writelines(items)                          # no separators!
    f.write("\n")
    f.writelines(item + "\n" for item in items)   # add them yourself
    print("total", len(items), "items", file=f)

with open("items.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read(), end="")

# OUTPUT:
# penbookbag
# pen
# book
# bag
# total 3 items

beginner.content:
Introduction

Reading: read() (whole), readline() (one line), readlines() (list). Writing: write(), writelines(). Appending uses mode a.
codeExamples:
with open("poem.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("line one\n")
    f.writelines(["line two\n", "line three\n"])   # no newlines added for you
with open("poem.txt", "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("line four\n")                           # appended at the end

with open("poem.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.readline().strip())     # first line only
    print(f.read().count("\n"))     # remaining lines

# OUTPUT:
# line one
# 3

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Different tasks need different read styles: a tiny config can be slurped, a 20 GB log must be streamed line by line.
codeExamples:
# Iterating a file reads lazily - constant memory
count = 0
with open("poem.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:                  # one line at a time
        count += 1
print("lines:", count)

# OUTPUT:
# lines: 4

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Log scanning, CSV-less data dumps, report generation and appending audit records are classic uses.
codeExamples:
# Find error lines in a log without loading it all
with open("big.log", "w") as f:
    f.write("INFO a\nERROR b\nINFO c\nERROR d\n")
with open("big.log") as f:
    errors = [ln.rstrip() for ln in f if "ERROR" in ln]
print(errors)

# OUTPUT:
# ['ERROR b', 'ERROR d']

beginner.content:
Diagram

   mode  read  write  truncate  create  pointer starts
    r     yes   no     no        no      start
    w     no    yes    YES       yes     start
    a     no    yes    no        yes     END
    r+    yes   yes    no        no      start

expert.content:
Reading Huge Files in Chunks

read() loads the whole file into memory. For very large files (or files without line breaks), read a fixed number of characters (or bytes in binary mode) at a time. read() returns an empty string at the end, which ends the walrus loop.
codeExamples:
with open("big.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("abcdefghij")

with open("big.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    while chunk := f.read(4):
        print(repr(chunk))

# OUTPUT:
# 'abcd'
# 'efgh'
# 'ij'

expert.content:
seek() and tell()

tell() returns the current position and seek(pos) moves to it. In binary mode the position is a byte offset. In text mode it is an opaque number - only seek to 0 or to a value previously returned by tell(), because multi-byte characters and newline translation make "character position" ambiguous.
codeExamples:
with open("letters.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("ABCDEFGHIJ")

with open("letters.txt", "rb") as f:
    f.seek(3)
    print(f.read(4), f.tell())
    f.seek(0)                  # back to the start
    print(f.read(2))

# OUTPUT:
# b'DEFG' 7
# b'AB'

expert.content:
Counting Lines, Words and Characters

A small wc clone that streams the file line by line.
codeExamples:
with open("poem.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("Twinkle twinkle little star\nHow I wonder\nwhat you are\n")

lines = words = chars = 0
with open("poem.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        lines += 1
        words += len(line.split())
        chars += len(line)
print(lines, words, chars)

# OUTPUT:
# 3 10 54

expert.content:
Filtering a Log File

Reading one file and writing the interesting lines to another - streamed, so the log can be any size.
codeExamples:
with open("app.log", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("INFO start\nERROR disk full\nINFO retry\nERROR timeout\n")

with open("app.log", encoding="utf-8") as src, \
     open("errors.log", "w", encoding="utf-8") as dst:
    for line_no, line in enumerate(src, start=1):
        if "ERROR" in line:
            dst.write(f"{line_no}: {line}")

with open("errors.log", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read(), end="")

# OUTPUT:
# 2: ERROR disk full
# 4: ERROR timeout

expert.content:
Writing Atomically

If a program crashes halfway through open("data.txt", "w"), the file is left truncated or half-written. The safe pattern: write a temporary file in the same folder, then os.replace() it over the original - a rename that is atomic on the same file system, so readers see either the old file or the new one, never a broken one.
codeExamples:
import os
import tempfile

def write_atomic(path, text):
    folder = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(path))
    fd, tmp_path = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=folder)
    try:
        with os.fdopen(fd, "w", encoding="utf-8") as tmp:
            tmp.write(text)
        os.replace(tmp_path, path)          # atomic swap
    except BaseException:
        os.remove(tmp_path)
        raise

write_atomic("settings.txt", "theme=dark\n")
with open("settings.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read(), end="")

# OUTPUT:
# theme=dark

expert.content:
r+ Mode Pitfalls

"r+" opens for reading and writing without erasing. Writes overwrite characters at the current position rather than inserting, and after a read() the position is at the end, so the next write appends. To change the middle of a text file, it is usually simpler to read it, modify the string, and write it back.
codeExamples:
with open("greet.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("Hello World")

with open("greet.txt", "r+", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("Jello")                 # overwrites the first 5 characters
with open("greet.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read())

with open("greet.txt", "r+", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.read()                         # now at the end
    f.write("!")                     # so this appends
with open("greet.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read())

# OUTPUT:
# Jello World
# Jello World!

expert.content:
Shortcuts and the Java Equivalents

TaskPythonJava
Whole file as textPath(p).read_text(encoding="utf-8")Files.readString(path)

Write textPath(p).write_text(s, encoding="utf-8")Files.writeString(path, s)

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
read() vs readline() vs readlines()?Whole file as a string; the next line; a list of all lines
How do you read a huge file efficiently?Iterate over the file object line by line, or read fixed-size chunks
Does write() add a newline?No - and neither does writelines(); print(..., file=f) does
What does readline() return at the end of the file?An empty string ""
"w" vs "a"?"w" truncates the file first; "a" adds to the end
How do you avoid a half-written file after a crash?Write to a temporary file, then os.replace() it over the original

Advantages

Advantages: seek()/tell() allow random access; iteration is memory-friendly.
codeExamples:
with open("poem.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.seek(5)                       # jump to char offset 5
    print(f.read(3))                # 'one'
    print(f.tell())                 # position after reading
    f.seek(0)                       # rewind
    print(f.readline().strip())

# OUTPUT:
# one
# 8
# line one

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: read() on a huge file can exhaust memory; write does not add newlines; text mode translates line endings.
codeExamples:
with open("nl.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("a")
    f.write("b")                    # no newline added
    f.write("c\n")
print(open("nl.txt").read().strip())

# OUTPUT:
# abc

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a file opened with r cannot be written and vice versa; reading text after an exhausted read returns an empty string.
codeExamples:
with open("poem.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.read()
    print(repr(f.read()))           # already at end of file
    try:
        f.write("x")
    except Exception as e:
        print(type(e).__name__, e)

# OUTPUT:
# ''
# UnsupportedOperation not writable

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Stream, never slurp, anything whose size you do not control; for appends from several processes use one writer or OS-level locking, since interleaved writes can corrupt lines. Use logging, not manual files, for application logs.

beginner.content:
The Problem with Manual close()

Calling close() yourself works only if execution reaches that line. If an exception happens in between, close() is skipped and the file stays open.
codeExamples:
f = open("data.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8")
try:
    f.write("line 1\n")
    result = 10 / 0                 # something goes wrong
    f.close()                       # never reached
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("error!")

print("closed?", f.closed)

# OUTPUT:
# error!
# closed? False

beginner.content:
with Closes the File for You

with open(...) as f: opens the file, runs the indented block, and always closes the file when the block ends - normally, through return, or because of an exception. This is the standard way to work with files in Python.
codeExamples:
with open("data.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("hello\n")
    print("inside, closed?", f.closed)

print("after, closed?", f.closed)

# OUTPUT:
# inside, closed? False
# after, closed? True

beginner.content: Even When an Exception Happens
codeExamples:
try:
    with open("data.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write("partial\n")
        raise ValueError("bad data")
except ValueError as error:
    print("caught:", error)

print("closed?", f.closed)

with open("data.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read(), end="")             # the write was flushed on close

# OUTPUT:
# caught: bad data
# closed? True
# partial

beginner.content:
Several Files in One with

Separate the files with commas. A common pattern is reading one file and writing a transformed copy to another.
codeExamples:
with open("names.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("abaji\nraoji\nkanhoji\n")

with open("names.txt", encoding="utf-8") as src, open("upper.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as dst:
    for line in src:
        dst.write(line.upper())

with open("upper.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read(), end="")

# OUTPUT:
# ABAJI
# RAOJI
# KANHOJI

beginner.content:
Long with Statements (Python 3.10+)

Since Python 3.10 you can wrap the context managers in parentheses and put each on its own line.
codeExamples:
with open("names.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("abaji\nraoji\nkanhoji\n")

with (
    open("names.txt", encoding="utf-8") as src,
    open("copy.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as dst,
):
    dst.write(src.read())

with open("copy.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(len(f.readlines()), "lines copied")

# OUTPUT:
# 3 lines copied

beginner.content:
Introduction

with opens a context manager and guarantees its cleanup. For files that means the file is closed when the block ends, even if an error happens inside.
codeExamples:
with open("w.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("data")
    print("inside, closed?", f.closed)
print("after,  closed?", f.closed)

# OUTPUT:
# inside, closed? False
# after,  closed? True

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Manual open/close forgets the close on an early return or exception, leaking handles and losing unflushed data.

Real-Time Use

Used for files, locks, DB transactions, temporary directories and timers. You can open several at once, e.g. copying a file.
codeExamples:
with open("src.txt", "w") as s:
    s.write("copy me")
with open("src.txt") as s, open("dst.txt", "w") as d:    # two managers, one with
    d.write(s.read())
print(open("dst.txt").read())

# OUTPUT:
# copy me

beginner.content:
Diagram

   with open(...) as f:
        |
        +--> __enter__()  -> returns f
        |    ... your block ... (error or not)
        +--> __exit__()   -> f.close()   (always)

expert.content:
What with Does Under the Hood

The object after with is a context manager. Python calls its __enter__() method at the start (its return value is bound by as) and its __exit__() method at the end, passing details of any exception. A file's __exit__ closes it. Writing your own context managers is covered in the Context Managers module.
codeExamples:
f = open("data.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8")
print(f.__enter__() is f)        # files return themselves from __enter__
f.__exit__(None, None, None)     # what with calls when the block ends
print(f.closed)

# OUTPUT:
# True
# True

expert.content:
The try/finally Equivalent

A with block over a file behaves like this try/finally - just shorter, and impossible to get wrong.
codeExamples:
# with open("data.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
#     content = f.read()

with open("data.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("hello")

f = open("data.txt", encoding="utf-8")
try:
    content = f.read()
finally:
    f.close()                    # runs whether or not an exception occurred

print(content, f.closed)

# OUTPUT:
# hello True

expert.content:
Compared with Java try-with-resources

JavaPython
Syntaxtry (var r = new BufferedReader(...)) { ... }with open(...) as f: ...
ProtocolImplements AutoCloseable.close()Implements __enter__ / __exit__
Can see the exception?No - close() gets no exception detailsYes - __exit__ receives it and may even suppress it
Multiple resourcesSeparated by ;, closed in reverse orderSeparated by ,, closed in reverse order

Not Just Files

Many standard-library objects are context managers. Each one defines what "clean up" means for it.
codeExamples:
import threading
import tempfile
import zipfile

lock = threading.Lock()
with lock:                                   # acquired, then always released
    print("locked?", lock.locked())
print("locked?", lock.locked())

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:   # deleted afterwards
    path = tmp + "/report.zip"
    with zipfile.ZipFile(path, "w") as zf:   # zip archive finalised on exit
        zf.writestr("hello.txt", "hi")
    with zipfile.ZipFile(path) as zf:
        print(zf.namelist())

# OUTPUT:
# locked? True
# locked? False
# ['hello.txt']

expert.content:
Gotcha: sqlite3 Connections Don't Close

Using a sqlite3 connection in with manages a transaction: it commits if the block succeeds and rolls back if it raises. It does not close the connection. Close it yourself, or wrap it in contextlib.closing().
codeExamples:
import sqlite3
from contextlib import closing

with closing(sqlite3.connect(":memory:")) as conn:   # closes at the end
    with conn:                                        # commits / rolls back
        conn.execute("CREATE TABLE t (x INTEGER)")
        conn.execute("INSERT INTO t VALUES (42)")
    print(conn.execute("SELECT x FROM t").fetchone())

# OUTPUT:
# (42,)

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why use with for files?The file is closed automatically when the block ends, even if an exception is raised
What methods make an object usable in with?__enter__ and __exit__ - the context manager protocol
What is the try/finally equivalent?Open, then try: use the file, finally: close it
How do you open two files in one with?Separate them with commas; since 3.10 they can be grouped in parentheses over several lines
Is the variable from as usable after the block?Yes, the name still exists, but the file is closed - reading it raises ValueError
Does with sqlite3.connect(...) close the connection?No - it only commits or rolls back the transaction

Advantages

Advantages: short, exception-safe, and you can write your own context manager with a class or contextlib.
codeExamples:
from contextlib import contextmanager
@contextmanager
def announce(name):
    print("enter", name)
    try:
        yield name
    finally:
        print("exit", name)

with announce("job") as j:
    print("working on", j)

# OUTPUT:
# enter job
# working on job
# exit job

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the variable stays alive after the block (just closed), and a context manager that swallows exceptions in __exit__ can hide errors.
codeExamples:
from contextlib import suppress
with suppress(ZeroDivisionError):      # swallows on purpose
    1 / 0
    print("never printed")
print("continued silently")

# OUTPUT:
# continued silently

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: using a file after the block raises ValueError, and the protocol only works for objects that implement __enter__ and __exit__.

Architect's Notes

Make every resource with an acquire/release lifecycle a context manager, and use contextlib.ExitStack when the number of resources is dynamic. Keep with blocks short so resources are held for the minimum time.

beginner.content:
Two Ways to Open a File

Text mode ("r", "w")Binary mode ("rb", "wb")
Reads/writesstrbytes
EncodingDecodes/encodes with encoding=None - raw bytes
Line endingsTranslated (\r\n ↔ \n)Untouched
Use for.txt, .csv, .json, .py, .htmlImages, PDFs, zip, audio, any non-text data
In Java terms: text mode is like a Reader/Writer, binary mode like an InputStream/OutputStream.

Same File, Two Views

Reading the same file in text mode gives characters; in binary mode it gives the bytes actually stored on disk. "é" takes two bytes in UTF-8.
codeExamples:
with open("cafe.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="\n") as f:
    f.write("café\n")

with open("cafe.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    text = f.read()
with open("cafe.txt", "rb") as f:
    raw = f.read()

print(repr(text), type(text).__name__, len(text))
print(raw, type(raw).__name__, len(raw))
print(raw.decode("utf-8") == text)

# OUTPUT:
# 'café\n' str 5
# b'caf\xc3\xa9\n' bytes 6
# True

beginner.content:
Writing Bytes

In binary mode you must write bytes, not str - encode text first.
codeExamples:
with open("data.bin", "wb") as f:
    f.write(b"\x00\x01\x02")
    f.write("OK".encode("utf-8"))

with open("data.bin", "rb") as f:
    print(f.read())

with open("data.bin", "wb") as f:
    f.write("text")

# OUTPUT:
# b'\x00\x01\x02OK'
# TypeError: a bytes-like object is required, not 'str'

beginner.content:
Newline Translation

Text mode converts line endings for you; binary mode shows what is really in the file. Here the file is written with Windows line endings on purpose.
codeExamples:
with open("lines.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="\r\n") as f:
    f.write("line1\nline2\n")

with open("lines.txt", "rb") as f:
    print(f.read())                          # what is on disk

with open("lines.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(repr(f.read()))                    # translated back to \n

# OUTPUT:
# b'line1\r\nline2\r\n'
# 'line1\nline2\n'

beginner.content:
Copying Any File in Chunks

Binary mode can copy anything - an image, a PDF, a zip - byte for byte. Reading fixed-size chunks keeps memory use small even for huge files.
codeExamples:
with open("photo.bin", "wb") as f:          # stand-in for an image
    f.write(bytes(range(256)) * 4)           # 1024 bytes

with open("photo.bin", "rb") as src, open("photo_copy.bin", "wb") as dst:
    while chunk := src.read(100):            # 100 bytes at a time
        dst.write(chunk)

with open("photo.bin", "rb") as a, open("photo_copy.bin", "rb") as b:
    original, copy = a.read(), b.read()
print(len(original), len(copy), original == copy)

# OUTPUT:
# 1024 1024 True

beginner.content:
Reading a File Signature

Many binary formats start with fixed "magic bytes" that identify the type, whatever the file extension says. A PNG image always starts with b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n"; a PDF starts with b"%PDF"; a zip with b"PK".
codeExamples:
PNG_SIGNATURE = b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n"

with open("fake.png", "wb") as f:
    f.write(PNG_SIGNATURE + b"...image data...")

def file_type(path):
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        head = f.read(8)
    if head == PNG_SIGNATURE:
        return "PNG image"
    if head.startswith(b"%PDF"):
        return "PDF document"
    if head.startswith(b"PK"):
        return "ZIP archive"
    return "unknown"

print(file_type("fake.png"))

# OUTPUT:
# PNG image

beginner.content:
Introduction

Text mode (r/w) works with str and decodes/encodes bytes using an encoding. Binary mode (rb/wb) works with raw bytes and no translation.
codeExamples:
text = "café"                     # 4 characters
with open("t.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write(text)
with open("t.txt", "rb") as f:
    raw = f.read()
print(raw, len(text), len(raw))

# OUTPUT:
# b'caf\xc3\xa9' 4 5

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Images, PDFs, zips and executables are not text; decoding them as text corrupts or fails. Text files need the right encoding to show international characters.
codeExamples:
png_header = bytes([0x89, 0x50, 0x4E, 0x47])
with open("img.bin", "wb") as f:
    f.write(png_header)
with open("img.bin", "rb") as f:
    data = f.read()
print(data[1:4].decode("ascii"), list(data))

# OUTPUT:
# PNG [137, 80, 78, 71]

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

File uploads, downloads, image processing, protocol messages and copying any file safely (chunked) all use binary mode.
codeExamples:
# Chunked binary copy: works for any file type and size
with open("src.bin", "wb") as f:
    f.write(bytes(range(256)) * 4)
with open("src.bin", "rb") as s, open("dst.bin", "wb") as d:
    while chunk := s.read(300):          # 300 bytes at a time
        d.write(chunk)
print(open("src.bin", "rb").read() == open("dst.bin", "rb").read())

# OUTPUT:
# True

beginner.content:
Diagram

   str  --encode(utf-8)-->  bytes  ---> disk
   str  <--decode(utf-8)--  bytes  <--- disk
   text mode : Python does encode/decode + newline translation
   binary    : you get / give raw bytes, nothing is changed

expert.content:
Why Binary Mode for Non-Text Files

Opening an image in text mode makes Python try to decode its bytes as text, which usually fails - and even when it doesn't, newline translation corrupts the data on write. Rule: if the file isn't human-readable text, use "rb" / "wb". (See Unicode, Encoding & Decoding for the str/bytes relationship.)
codeExamples:
with open("image.bin", "wb") as f:
    f.write(b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n\xff\xd8")

with open("image.bin", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.read()

# OUTPUT:
# UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0x89 in position 0: invalid start byte

expert.content:
bytearray: Mutable Bytes

bytes is immutable like str. bytearray is its mutable twin - useful when building or patching binary data in place. Indexing either one gives integers 0-255.
codeExamples:
data = b"hello"
print(data[0], data[:2])

buf = bytearray(b"hello")
buf[0] = ord("H")             # change one byte
buf.extend(b"!")
print(buf, bytes(buf))

# OUTPUT:
# 104 b'he'
# bytearray(b'Hello!') b'Hello!'

expert.content:
struct: Reading and Writing Binary Records

Binary formats store numbers as fixed-size byte groups. struct.pack turns Python values into bytes according to a format string and struct.unpack reverses it. Here < means little-endian, H a 2-byte unsigned int and I a 4-byte unsigned int.
codeExamples:
import struct

FORMAT = "<HHI"                         # item id, quantity, price in paise
record = struct.pack(FORMAT, 7, 3, 1500)
print(record, struct.calcsize(FORMAT))

with open("orders.bin", "wb") as f:
    f.write(record)

with open("orders.bin", "rb") as f:
    item_id, qty, price = struct.unpack(FORMAT, f.read(struct.calcsize(FORMAT)))
print(item_id, qty, price)

# OUTPUT:
# b'\x07\x00\x03\x00\xdc\x05\x00\x00' 8
# 7 3 1500

expert.content:
base64: Bytes Inside Text

JSON, e-mail and HTML can only carry text. Base64 encodes arbitrary bytes using 64 safe ASCII characters (about 33% larger), so binary data such as a small image can travel inside a text format.
codeExamples:
import base64

raw = b"Hi!"
encoded = base64.b64encode(raw)
print(encoded, encoded.decode("ascii"))
print(base64.b64decode(encoded) == raw)
print(base64.b64encode(b"Python"))

# OUTPUT:
# b'SGkh' SGkh
# True
# b'UHl0aG9u'

expert.content:
Copying and Measuring Files

For real copies use shutil, which handles buffering for you (copy2 also preserves timestamps). File sizes on disk are in bytes, which for text depends on the encoding.
codeExamples:
import os
import shutil
from pathlib import Path

with open("hello.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("नमस्ते")                      # 6 characters

shutil.copyfile("hello.txt", "hello_copy.txt")

print(len("नमस्ते"))
print(os.path.getsize("hello.txt"))
print(Path("hello_copy.txt").stat().st_size)

# OUTPUT:
# 6
# 18
# 18

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Text mode vs binary mode?Text mode reads/writes str, applying an encoding and newline translation; binary mode reads/writes raw bytes unchanged
Which mode for images or PDFs?Binary - "rb" / "wb"
What does f.read() return in "rb" mode?A bytes object
bytes vs bytearray?bytes is immutable; bytearray is mutable
How do you parse fixed-layout binary records?With the struct module (pack / unpack with a format string)
Why can len(text) differ from the file size?The file stores encoded bytes; in UTF-8 non-ASCII characters take 2-4 bytes

Advantages

Advantages: text mode handles encodings and newlines for you; binary mode is exact and fastest, with seek by byte.
codeExamples:
# Binary mode: byte-exact random access
with open("src.bin", "rb") as f:
    f.seek(250)
    print(list(f.read(4)))

# OUTPUT:
# [250, 251, 252, 253]

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: text mode on the wrong encoding raises UnicodeDecodeError or shows mojibake; binary needs manual decode.
codeExamples:
with open("latin.txt", "wb") as f:
    f.write("café".encode("latin-1"))     # byte 0xe9
try:
    open("latin.txt", encoding="utf-8").read()
except UnicodeDecodeError as e:
    print("UnicodeDecodeError:", e.reason)

# OUTPUT:
# UnicodeDecodeError: invalid continuation byte

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: binary files cannot be iterated by meaningful "lines", text-mode seek offsets are opaque, and writing str to a binary file is a TypeError.
codeExamples:
try:
    with open("x.bin", "wb") as f:
        f.write("text")
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)

# OUTPUT:
# TypeError: a bytes-like object is required, not 'str'

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Decide the encoding at the system boundary (UTF-8 everywhere) and keep str internally and bytes only at I/O edges. For large binary data consider memoryview, mmap, or streaming APIs instead of reading whole files.

beginner.content:
What is a CSV File?

CSV (Comma-Separated Values) is a plain-text table: one line per row, values separated by commas, usually with a header row first. Excel, Google Sheets, databases and almost every tool can import and export it.

Python's built-in csv module reads and writes CSV correctly - including the tricky cases such as values that themselves contain commas or quotes.

Rule: always open CSV files with newline="" (the csv module handles line endings itself) and encoding="utf-8".

Writing with csv.writer

writerow() writes one row (a list of values); writerows() writes many. Numbers are converted to text automatically.
codeExamples:
import csv

rows = [
    ["name", "city", "marks"],
    ["Abaji", "Pune", 91],
    ["Raoji", "Latur", 78],
]

with open("students.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerows(rows)

with open("students.csv", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read(), end="")

# OUTPUT:
# name,city,marks
# Abaji,Pune,91
# Raoji,Latur,78

beginner.content:
Reading with csv.reader

Each row comes back as a list of strings - even numbers. Convert them yourself before doing arithmetic.
codeExamples:
import csv

with open("students.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    csv.writer(f).writerows([["name", "city", "marks"], ["Abaji", "Pune", 91], ["Raoji", "Latur", 78]])

with open("students.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    reader = csv.reader(f)
    header = next(reader)                # first row = column names
    print(header)
    for row in reader:
        print(row, "-> marks + 5 =", int(row[2]) + 5)

# OUTPUT:
# ['name', 'city', 'marks']
# ['Abaji', 'Pune', '91'] -> marks + 5 = 96
# ['Raoji', 'Latur', '78'] -> marks + 5 = 83

beginner.content:
DictWriter and DictReader

Working with column names instead of positions is clearer and survives column reordering. DictReader uses the header row as keys automatically.
codeExamples:
import csv

students = [
    {"name": "Abaji", "marks": 91},
    {"name": "Raoji", "marks": 78},
]

with open("marks.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=["name", "marks"])
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerows(students)

with open("marks.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        print(row["name"], int(row["marks"]), row)

# OUTPUT:
# Abaji 91 {'name': 'Abaji', 'marks': '91'}
# Raoji 78 {'name': 'Raoji', 'marks': '78'}

beginner.content:
Why Not Just split(",")?

A value containing a comma is wrapped in quotes in a real CSV file. split(",") breaks it apart; the csv module understands the quoting.
codeExamples:
import csv

with open("address.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    csv.writer(f).writerow(["Abaji", "Pune, MH", 91])

with open("address.csv", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    line = f.read().strip()
print(line)
print(line.split(","))                   # wrong: 4 pieces

with open("address.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(next(csv.reader(f)))           # right: 3 values

# OUTPUT:
# Abaji,"Pune, MH",91
# ['Abaji', '"Pune', ' MH"', '91']
# ['Abaji', 'Pune, MH', '91']

beginner.content: A Small Report: Total Marks per Student
codeExamples:
import csv

data = """name,subject,marks
Abaji,Maths,91
Raoji,Maths,78
Abaji,Physics,85
Raoji,Physics,66
"""
with open("results.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write(data)

totals = {}
with open("results.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        totals[row["name"]] = totals.get(row["name"], 0) + int(row["marks"])

for name, total in totals.items():
    print(f"{name:<6}{total:>4}")

# OUTPUT:
# Abaji  176
# Raoji  144

beginner.content:
Introduction

CSV (comma-separated values) stores tables as text lines. The csv module reads and writes them correctly, handling quotes and embedded commas.
codeExamples:
import csv
with open("people.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:   # newline="" is required
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["name", "age"])
    w.writerow(["Abaji", 30])
    w.writerow(["Li, Wei", 25])        # comma inside a value is quoted
print(open("people.csv", encoding="utf-8").read())

# OUTPUT:
# name,age
# Abaji,30
# "Li, Wei",25

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Splitting on "," by hand breaks on quoted commas and line breaks inside fields. The module follows the real CSV rules.
codeExamples:
line = '"Li, Wei",25'
print("naive :", line.split(","))
import csv
print("csv   :", next(csv.reader([line])))

# OUTPUT:
# naive : ['"Li', ' Wei"', '25']
# csv   : ['Li, Wei', '25']

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Spreadsheet exports, bank statements, data-science inputs and database dumps move as CSV. DictReader gives each row as a dict.
codeExamples:
import csv
with open("people.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        print(row["name"], int(row["age"]) + 1)

# OUTPUT:
# Abaji 31
# Li, Wei 26

beginner.content:
Diagram

   header : name , age
   row 1  : Abaji , 30          reader --> ['Abaji','30']
   row 2  : "Li, Wei" , 25     DictReader --> {'name':'Li, Wei','age':'25'}
   (rows are streamed one at a time from the file)

expert.content:
Delimiters and Quoting Options

• delimiter="\t" reads and writes tab-separated files (TSV); ";" is common in European Excel exports.
• quoting=csv.QUOTE_ALL quotes every field; csv.QUOTE_NONNUMERIC quotes text fields only - and when used for reading, converts every unquoted field to float.
codeExamples:
import csv

with open("data.tsv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f, delimiter="\t")
    writer.writerow(["name", "city"])
    writer.writerow(["Abaji", "Pune, MH"])     # comma is not special in a TSV

with open("data.tsv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for row in csv.reader(f, delimiter="\t"):
        print(row)

# OUTPUT:
# ['name', 'city']
# ['Abaji', 'Pune, MH']

import csv

with open("q.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    csv.writer(f, quoting=csv.QUOTE_NONNUMERIC).writerow(["Abaji", 91, 8.5])

with open("q.csv", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read(), end="")

with open("q.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(next(csv.reader(f, quoting=csv.QUOTE_NONNUMERIC)))

# OUTPUT:
# "Abaji",91,8.5
# ['Abaji', 91.0, 8.5]

expert.content:
Surviving Bad Rows

Real files contain blanks and typos. Convert each row inside try/except, report the problem with a line number, and keep going instead of crashing on row 40,000.
codeExamples:
import csv

data = """name,marks
Abaji,91
Raoji,
Kanhoji,abc
Moropant,85
"""
with open("raw.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write(data)

total = 0
with open("raw.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line_no, row in enumerate(csv.DictReader(f), start=2):   # line 1 is the header
        try:
            total += int(row["marks"])
        except ValueError:
            print(f"line {line_no}: skipping bad marks {row['marks']!r}")

print("total:", total)

# OUTPUT:
# line 3: skipping bad marks ''
# line 4: skipping bad marks 'abc'
# total: 176

expert.content:
Excel and the BOM: utf-8-sig

Excel saves "CSV UTF-8" files with an invisible byte order mark (BOM) at the start. Read with plain utf-8 and the BOM sticks to the first header, so row["name"] mysteriously fails. The utf-8-sig encoding strips it when reading - and adds it when writing, so Excel shows non-English text correctly.
codeExamples:
import csv

with open("excel.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
    csv.writer(f).writerow(["name", "marks"])

with open("excel.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(next(csv.reader(f)))

with open("excel.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
    print(next(csv.reader(f)))

# OUTPUT:
# ['\ufeffname', 'marks']
# ['name', 'marks']

expert.content:
Large Files and Appending

csv.reader reads one row at a time, so a multi-gigabyte file is processed with constant memory - as long as you don't call list() on the reader. To add rows to an existing file, open it in append mode "a".
codeExamples:
import csv

with open("log.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    csv.writer(f).writerow(["time", "event"])

for time, event in [("10:00", "login"), ("10:05", "logout")]:
    with open("log.csv", "a", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        csv.writer(f).writerow([time, event])

with open("log.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    row_count = sum(1 for _ in csv.reader(f))   # streams - never loads the whole file
print(row_count)

# OUTPUT:
# 3

expert.content:
For Analysis, Reach for pandas

The csv module is ideal for streaming and simple transformations. For grouping, filtering and statistics, the third-party pandas library loads a CSV into a DataFrame in one line (covered in the Data Science module).
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("results.csv")          # the file from the report example
print(df.groupby("name")["marks"].sum())

# OUTPUT:
# name
# Abaji    176
# Raoji    144
# Name: marks, dtype: int64

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why open CSV files with newline=""?The csv module handles line endings itself; without it, extra blank lines appear on Windows and quoted newlines can be misread
What type are values from csv.reader?Always strings - convert numbers with int() or float()
reader vs DictReader?reader gives each row as a list; DictReader gives a dict keyed by the header row
Why not parse CSV with split(",")?Quoted fields can contain commas, quotes and newlines; the csv module handles the quoting rules
How do you read a CSV saved by Excel?Use encoding="utf-8-sig" to strip the byte order mark
How do you process a huge CSV?Iterate the reader row by row (streaming) instead of loading everything into a list

Advantages

Advantages: human readable, universal, streams row by row, works with Excel; DictWriter keeps columns by name.
codeExamples:
import csv, io
buf = io.StringIO()
w = csv.DictWriter(buf, fieldnames=["id", "city"])
w.writeheader()
w.writerow({"id": 1, "city": "Pune"})
print(buf.getvalue().strip().splitlines())

# OUTPUT:
# ['id,city', '1,Pune']

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: no types (everything is a string), no schema, and dialect differences (semicolon, tab) cause surprises.
codeExamples:
import csv, io
rows = list(csv.reader(io.StringIO("a,b\n1,2")))
print(rows, type(rows[1][0]).__name__)       # numbers come back as str
print(list(csv.reader(io.StringIO("a;b"), delimiter=";")))

# OUTPUT:
# [['a', 'b'], ['1', '2']] str
# [['a', 'b']]

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: no nesting, no random update (rewrite the file), no concurrency control, and huge files are slow compared with binary columnar formats.
codeExamples:
import csv, io
buf = io.StringIO()
csv.writer(buf).writerow(["tags", ["a", "b"]])     # nested list is just str()-ed
print(buf.getvalue().strip())

# OUTPUT:
# tags,"['a', 'b']"

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use CSV for interchange, not as a database. For analytics prefer Parquet/Arrow or pandas with explicit dtypes; for relational updates use SQLite. Always open with newline="" and an explicit encoding, and validate/convert types on load.

beginner.content:
What is JSON?

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the standard text format for structured data - web APIs, configuration files, NoSQL databases. It looks almost exactly like Python dicts and lists, and the built-in json module converts between the two.
JSONPython
object {"a": 1}dict
array [1, 2]list
string "text"str
number 7 / 7.5int / float
true / falseTrue / False
nullNone

Saving Data: json.dump

json.dump(data, file, indent=2) writes the data as nicely indented JSON. Note how True becomes true and None becomes null.
codeExamples:
import json

settings = {
    "theme": "dark",
    "font_size": 14,
    "autosave": True,
    "recent_files": ["notes.txt", "todo.md"],
    "proxy": None,
}

with open("settings.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump(settings, f, indent=2)

with open("settings.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read())

# OUTPUT:
# {
#   "theme": "dark",
#   "font_size": 14,
#   "autosave": true,
#   "recent_files": [
#     "notes.txt",
#     "todo.md"
#   ],
#   "proxy": null
# }

beginner.content:
Loading Data: json.load

json.load(file) reads the file back into Python objects - a full round trip.
codeExamples:
import json

settings = {"theme": "dark", "font_size": 14, "autosave": True, "proxy": None}
with open("settings.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump(settings, f, indent=2)

with open("settings.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    loaded = json.load(f)

print(loaded)
print(loaded == settings, type(loaded["autosave"]), loaded["proxy"])

# OUTPUT:
# {'theme': 'dark', 'font_size': 14, 'autosave': True, 'proxy': None}
# True <class 'bool'> None

beginner.content:
Updating a JSON File

JSON files can't be edited in place. The pattern is always: load the whole file, change the Python objects, dump everything back.
codeExamples:
import json

with open("settings.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump({"theme": "light", "font_size": 14}, f)

with open("settings.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:     # 1. load
    settings = json.load(f)

settings["theme"] = "dark"                              # 2. change
settings["font_size"] += 2

with open("settings.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:  # 3. dump
    json.dump(settings, f)

with open("settings.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read())

# OUTPUT:
# {"theme": "dark", "font_size": 16}

beginner.content:
A Load-or-Create Helper

The first time an app runs there is no settings file yet. Fall back to defaults when the file is missing.

Introduction

JSON is a text format for nested data (objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, null). json.dump/load work with files, dumps/loads with strings.
codeExamples:
import json
data = {"name": "Abaji", "skills": ["py", "sql"], "active": True, "boss": None}
with open("p.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump(data, f, indent=2)
with open("p.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    back = json.load(f)
print(back == data, back["skills"][0])

# OUTPUT:
# True py

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Programs in different languages need a shared, readable way to exchange structured data - REST APIs and config files use JSON.
codeExamples:
import json
text = json.dumps({"id": 1, "tags": ["a", "b"]})
print(text)                    # a plain string, ready to send over a network
print(json.loads(text)["tags"])

# OUTPUT:
# {"id": 1, "tags": ["a", "b"]}
# ['a', 'b']

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Settings files (package.json style), API request/response bodies, NoSQL documents and log events (JSON lines).
codeExamples:
import json
# JSON Lines: one record per line, appendable and streamable
with open("events.jsonl", "w") as f:
    for e in ({"t": 1, "ok": True}, {"t": 2, "ok": False}):
        f.write(json.dumps(e) + "\n")
with open("events.jsonl") as f:
    print([json.loads(line)["ok"] for line in f])

# OUTPUT:
# [True, False]

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Python object --json.dump(obj, f)--> text file {"k": ...}
   dict  -> object      list/tuple -> array     str -> string
   int/float -> number  True/False -> true/false   None -> null
   Python object <--json.load(f)-- text file

expert.content:
A Round Trip Is Not Always Lossless

JSON has fewer types than Python. Tuples become lists, and because JSON object keys must be strings, non-string keys become strings.
codeExamples:
import json

data = {"point": (3, 4), 1: "one", "ok": True}

text = json.dumps(data)
print(text)

back = json.loads(text)
print(back)
print(back == data)

# OUTPUT:
# {"point": [3, 4], "1": "one", "ok": true}
# {'point': [3, 4], '1': 'one', 'ok': True}
# False

expert.content:
Objects JSON Can't Represent

Dates, sets, Decimals and your own classes are not JSON types, so dump raises TypeError. Pass a default= function that converts them into something JSON understands.
codeExamples:
import json
from datetime import datetime

json.dumps({"created": datetime(2026, 10, 4)})

# OUTPUT:
# TypeError: Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable

expert.content:
Non-English Text: ensure_ascii=False

By default json escapes every non-ASCII character as \uXXXX. That is valid JSON, but unreadable. ensure_ascii=False keeps the real characters - remember encoding="utf-8" when writing the file.

sort_keys and Compact Output

sort_keys=True makes output stable (useful for diffs and tests). separators=(",", ":") removes spaces for the smallest possible payload.

JSON Lines for Logs and Big Data

A single JSON document must be loaded completely. JSON Lines (.jsonl) stores one JSON object per line: you can append new records cheaply and read them back one at a time.
codeExamples:
import json

events = [
    {"user": "abaji", "action": "login"},
    {"user": "raoji", "action": "buy", "amount": 499},
]

with open("events.jsonl", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for event in events:
        f.write(json.dumps(event) + "\n")

with open("events.jsonl", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:                        # one record at a time
        event = json.loads(line)
        print(event["user"], event["action"], event.get("amount", "-"))

# OUTPUT:
# abaji login -
# raoji buy 499

expert.content:
Handling Corrupt Files

A half-written or hand-edited file raises json.JSONDecodeError (a subclass of ValueError), which tells you exactly where parsing failed. Note that trailing commas are not allowed in JSON.

Compared with Java

TaskJava (Jackson)Python
Object to JSON textmapper.writeValueAsString(obj)json.dumps(obj)
Write to a filemapper.writeValue(file, obj)json.dump(obj, f)
Read from a filemapper.readValue(file, Settings.class)json.load(f) - gives dicts/lists
Library neededJackson or Gson (third-party)Built in

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
dump vs dumps, load vs loads?dump/load work with files; dumps/loads work with strings ("s" for string)
What happens to a tuple in a JSON round trip?It comes back as a list
Why does {1: "a"} come back as {"1": "a"}?JSON object keys must be strings
How do you serialise a datetime?Pass default= a function that returns e.g. obj.isoformat()
How do you keep Hindi or ₹ readable in output?ensure_ascii=False and write the file with UTF-8 encoding
What is JSON Lines?One JSON object per line - appendable and streamable, common for logs

Advantages

Advantages: readable, language neutral, safe to load (no code execution), pretty-printable and sortable.
codeExamples:
import json
print(json.dumps({"b": 1, "a": [1, 2]}, indent=2, sort_keys=True))

# OUTPUT:
# {
#   "a": [
#     1,
#     2
#   ],
#   "b": 1
# }

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: no comments, no date/set/bytes types, and text is larger than binary formats.
codeExamples:
import json, datetime
try:
    json.dumps({"when": datetime.date(2024, 1, 31)})
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)

# OUTPUT:
# TypeError: Object of type date is not JSON serializable

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: dict keys become strings, tuples become lists, NaN is non-standard, and very large numbers or precision may differ between languages. Use default= for custom types.

Architect's Notes

Prefer JSON for interchange and configuration; version your schema and validate input (jsonschema, pydantic). Do not use it for large analytics or when you need exact round-trip of Python types - choose a schema-based binary format (Protobuf, Avro) there.

beginner.content:
What is Pickle?

Pickling converts (almost) any Python object - dicts, lists, sets, tuples, your own class instances - into a stream of bytes that can be saved to a file and turned back into an equal object later (unpickling). It is Python's equivalent of Java's Serializable + ObjectOutputStream.

Unlike JSON, pickle keeps Python types exactly: a set stays a set, a tuple stays a tuple. Pickle files are binary, so open them with "wb" and "rb".
Saving and Loading
codeExamples:
import pickle

data = {
    "name": "Abaji",
    "marks": [91, 85],
    "skills": {"python", "sql"},
    "point": (3, 4),
}

with open("data.pkl", "wb") as f:        # binary write
    pickle.dump(data, f)

with open("data.pkl", "rb") as f:        # binary read
    loaded = pickle.load(f)

print(loaded == data, type(loaded["skills"]), loaded["point"])
print(sorted(loaded["skills"]))

# OUTPUT:
# True <class 'set'> (3, 4)
# ['python', 'sql']

beginner.content:
Pickling Your Own Objects

Instances of your classes work too - attributes are saved and restored, and methods are available again after loading.
codeExamples:
import pickle

class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, marks):
        self.name = name
        self.marks = marks

    def average(self):
        return sum(self.marks) / len(self.marks)

s = Student("Raoji", [78, 66, 90])

with open("student.pkl", "wb") as f:
    pickle.dump(s, f)

with open("student.pkl", "rb") as f:
    restored = pickle.load(f)

print(restored.name, restored.average())
print(restored is s)                     # an equal copy, not the same object

# OUTPUT:
# Raoji 78.0
# False

beginner.content:
dumps and loads: Bytes in Memory

pickle.dumps() returns the bytes instead of writing a file, and pickle.loads() turns bytes back into an object - handy for caches and for sending objects between processes.
codeExamples:
import pickle

blob = pickle.dumps(["pen", "book", 3])
print(type(blob))
print(pickle.loads(blob))

# Several objects can be stored in one file, one after another
with open("many.pkl", "wb") as f:
    pickle.dump("first", f)
    pickle.dump({"second": 2}, f)

with open("many.pkl", "rb") as f:
    print(pickle.load(f), pickle.load(f))

# OUTPUT:
# <class 'bytes'>
# ['pen', 'book', 3]
# first {'second': 2}

beginner.content:
The Class Must Exist When Loading

A pickle stores the name of the class (module + class name) and the attribute values - not the class's code. The program that unpickles must be able to import the same class; otherwise loading fails.
codeExamples:
# save.py defined class Student and pickled an instance into student.pkl.
# load.py (no Student class defined or imported):
import pickle

with open("student.pkl", "rb") as f:
    s = pickle.load(f)

# OUTPUT:
# AttributeError: Can't get attribute 'Student' on <module '__main__' ...>
#
# Fix: put Student in its own module (e.g. models.py) and import it in both programs.

beginner.content:
Introduction

pickle serialises almost any Python object (even custom class instances) to bytes and restores it later. Use pickle.dump/load with binary files.
codeExamples:
import pickle
obj = {"nums": {1, 2, 3}, "t": (1, 2), "name": "x"}      # set and tuple preserved
with open("o.pkl", "wb") as f:
    pickle.dump(obj, f)
with open("o.pkl", "rb") as f:
    back = pickle.load(f)
print(back == obj, type(back["nums"]).__name__)

# OUTPUT:
# True set

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

JSON cannot hold sets, tuples, class instances or cyclic structures. Pickle saves Python-specific state exactly, which is handy for caching and sending objects between processes.
codeExamples:
import pickle
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y): self.x, self.y = x, y
p = pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(Point(3, 4)))
print(type(p).__name__, p.x, p.y)

# OUTPUT:
# Point 3 4

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Caching expensive results (trained ML models, computed tables), and multiprocessing, which pickles arguments to send them to worker processes.
codeExamples:
import pickle, os
cache = "result.pkl"
if os.path.exists(cache):
    result = pickle.load(open(cache, "rb"))
else:
    result = sum(i * i for i in range(1000))     # pretend this is slow
    pickle.dump(result, open(cache, "wb"))
print(result)

# OUTPUT:
# 332833500

beginner.content:
Diagram

   object --pickle.dump--> bytes (.pkl) --pickle.load--> object
   WARNING: load = executes code described by the bytes
   trusted file only  | for strangers use JSON / signed data

expert.content:
Security: Never Unpickle Untrusted Data

Unpickling is not just reading data - a pickle can instruct Python to call functions while it rebuilds objects (this is how the __reduce__ protocol works). A maliciously crafted pickle can therefore run arbitrary code on your machine the moment you call pickle.load.

• Only unpickle data you created and stored somewhere attackers cannot modify.
• Never accept pickles from users, uploads, network requests or downloaded files.
• For data exchange, use JSON (or another data-only format). If you must verify stored pickles, sign them with hmac and check the signature before loading.

Pickle vs JSON

AspectpickleJSON
FormatBinaryHuman-readable text
LanguagesPython onlyEvery language
TypesAlmost any Python object: sets, tuples, class instances, nested referencesdict, list, str, number, bool, null
Safe with untrusted input?No - can execute codeYes - only data
Long-term storageFragile - breaks if classes are renamed or movedStable
Typical useCaches, saving intermediate Python results, multiprocessingAPIs, config files, data exchange

Protocols

The pickle format has versions called protocols. Newer protocols are faster and more compact; older ones can be read by older Pythons. pickle.dump(obj, f, protocol=pickle.HIGHEST_PROTOCOL) picks the newest the running Python supports.
codeExamples:
import pickle

print(pickle.HIGHEST_PROTOCOL, pickle.DEFAULT_PROTOCOL)

data = list(range(1000))
small = pickle.dumps(data, protocol=pickle.HIGHEST_PROTOCOL)
print(pickle.loads(small) == data)

# OUTPUT (Python 3.12):
# 5 4
# True

expert.content:
What Can't Be Pickled

Objects tied to the running process or to code that can't be found by name: lambdas and nested functions, open files, sockets, database connections, locks and threads. Pickling them raises an error (a PicklingError, AttributeError or TypeError, depending on the object).
codeExamples:
import pickle
import threading

f = open("temp.bin", "wb")
candidates = [lambda x: x * 2, f, threading.Lock()]

for obj in candidates:
    try:
        pickle.dumps(obj)
    except Exception as error:
        print(type(obj).__name__, "-> cannot pickle:", type(error).__name__)

f.close()

# OUTPUT (Python 3.12):
# function -> cannot pickle: PicklingError
# BufferedWriter -> cannot pickle: TypeError
# lock -> cannot pickle: TypeError

expert.content:
Customising with __getstate__ and __setstate__

When an object holds something unpicklable (a lock, a connection), leave it out of the saved state with __getstate__ and recreate it after loading with __setstate__.
codeExamples:
import pickle
import threading

class Cache:
    def __init__(self):
        self.data = {}
        self.lock = threading.Lock()          # cannot be pickled

    def __getstate__(self):
        state = self.__dict__.copy()
        del state["lock"]                     # save everything except the lock
        return state

    def __setstate__(self, state):
        self.__dict__.update(state)
        self.lock = threading.Lock()          # recreate it after loading

cache = Cache()
cache.data["pi"] = 3.14

copy = pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(cache))
print(copy.data, type(copy.lock).__name__)

# OUTPUT:
# {'pi': 3.14} lock

expert.content:
Alternatives Built on Pickle

• shelve (standard library) - a persistent, dict-like store on disk; values are pickled for you.
• joblib (third-party) - efficient for large NumPy arrays; the usual way to save scikit-learn models.
• json - when the data must be readable, portable or received from others.
codeExamples:
import shelve

with shelve.open("store") as db:
    db["abaji"] = {"marks": [91, 85], "skills": {"python"}}

with shelve.open("store") as db:          # later, even in another run
    print(db["abaji"]["marks"], "abaji" in db)

# OUTPUT:
# [91, 85] True

expert.content:
Compared with Java Serialization

AspectJavaPython pickle
Opt-inClass must implement SerializableMost objects work automatically
Skip a fieldtransient__getstate__ / __setstate__
Write / readObjectOutputStream / ObjectInputStreampickle.dump / pickle.load
SecurityDeserialization of untrusted data is dangerousSame - never unpickle untrusted data

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is pickling?Serialising a Python object into bytes (unpickling rebuilds it)
Why open pickle files with "wb"/"rb"?Pickle data is binary, not text
Is it safe to unpickle data from a user?No - a crafted pickle can execute arbitrary code during loading
Pickle vs JSON?Pickle supports almost any Python object but is Python-only and unsafe for untrusted input; JSON is text, portable and safe but supports only basic types
Why can't a lambda be pickled?Functions are pickled by importable name, and a lambda has no name to look up
How do you exclude an attribute from pickling?Implement __getstate__ (and __setstate__ to restore it)

Advantages

Advantages: handles almost any object, shared references and cycles, fast, and one line to use.
codeExamples:
import pickle
a = [1, 2]
data = pickle.loads(pickle.dumps([a, a]))
print(data[0] is data[1])       # shared reference preserved

# OUTPUT:
# True

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: Python-only, not human readable, and version sensitive. Most important: unpickling untrusted data can run arbitrary code.

Limitations

Limitations: lambdas, open files, sockets and generators cannot be pickled, and the class definition must be importable when loading.
codeExamples:
import pickle
try:
    pickle.dumps(lambda x: x)
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)

# OUTPUT:
# PicklingError

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use pickle only for trusted, short-lived, same-version Python data (caches, IPC). For storage or network exchange choose JSON, MessagePack or Protobuf; for models use safe formats (safetensors, ONNX) or HMAC-sign the pickle. Never unpickle anything from an untrusted source.

beginner.content:
What is a Module?

A module is simply a file of Python code - any .py file is a module, and its name is the file name without .py. Python also ships with hundreds of ready-made modules (the standard library: math, random, json, datetime...), and you can install more with pip.

import makes another module's functions, classes and variables available in your file - like Java's import java.util.List;, except that Python imports are ordinary statements that run when the line executes.

import module

import math gives you a single name, math. Everything inside is reached with a dot. This keeps it obvious where each name comes from.
codeExamples:
import math

print(math.sqrt(49))
print(math.pi)
print(math.ceil(4.2), math.floor(4.8))

# OUTPUT:
# 7.0
# 3.141592653589793
# 5 4

beginner.content:
from module import name

from math import sqrt, pi copies just those names into your file, so you can use them without the math. prefix. Import several names by separating them with commas, or wrap a long list in parentheses.
codeExamples:
from math import sqrt, pi
from datetime import (
    date,
    timedelta,
)

print(sqrt(81), round(pi, 2))
print(date(2026, 10, 4) + timedelta(days=30))

# OUTPUT:
# 9.0 3.14
# 2026-11-03

beginner.content:
Avoid from module import *

from math import * dumps every public name of the module into your file. It is discouraged because:
• you can no longer see where a name came from;
• it can silently overwrite your own names or names from another module;
• tools and readers can't tell which names exist.

A module can limit what * exports with an __all__ list (see Creating Modules).
codeExamples:
pow = "my power setting"
from math import *              # math also has a pow()

print(pow)                      # our variable was replaced!

# OUTPUT:
# <built-in function pow>

beginner.content: When an Import Fails
codeExamples:
import xyz

# OUTPUT:
# ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'xyz'

from math import squareroot

# OUTPUT (the part in brackets shows where math lives and varies):
# ImportError: cannot import name 'squareroot' from 'math' (...)

beginner.content:
Where to Put Imports (PEP 8)

Imports go at the top of the file, one module per line, in three groups separated by a blank line:
1. standard library
2. third-party packages (installed with pip)
3. your own project's modules
codeExamples:
# standard library
import json
import os
from datetime import date

# third-party
import requests

# this project
from shop.cart import Cart
from shop.utils import format_price

beginner.content:
Introduction

import m loads module m and binds the name m; you use m.name. from m import name copies a specific name into your namespace.
codeExamples:
import math                       # whole module: use math.sqrt
from math import pi, floor         # specific names: use directly
print(math.sqrt(16), pi, floor(2.7))

# OUTPUT:
# 4.0 3.141592653589793 2

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Nobody writes everything from scratch. Imports reuse the standard library, third-party packages and your own files, and keep code organised.
codeExamples:
# Without import you would re-implement everything
from statistics import mean, median
scores = [70, 80, 90, 100]
print(mean(scores), median(scores))

# OUTPUT:
# 85 85.0

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Every real script starts with imports: web frameworks, data libraries, logging, file and date handling.
codeExamples:
# Typical script header
import os
import sys
from datetime import date
from pathlib import Path

print(isinstance(os.getcwd(), str), sys.version_info.major, date(2024, 3, 1).year, Path("a/b.txt").suffix)

# OUTPUT:
# True 3 2024 .txt

beginner.content:
Diagram

   import m
      |  1. look in sys.modules (cache) --found--> bind name m
      |  2. search sys.path for m.py / package
      |  3. compile + execute module body once
      +--4. store in sys.modules, bind name
   from m import x  ==> same, then bind only x

expert.content:
What import Actually Does

The first time a module is imported, Python:
1. finds it (searching sys.path),
2. loads it - compiling to bytecode, cached in __pycache__,
3. executes the whole file from top to bottom, creating its functions and variables,
4. caches the module object in sys.modules.

Every later import of the same module just returns the cached object - the file is not run again.
codeExamples:
# helper.py
print("helper.py is running")

def greet():
    return "hi"

# main.py
import sys
import helper
import helper                   # already cached - nothing printed
from helper import greet        # still the same cached module

print(greet())
print("helper" in sys.modules)

# OUTPUT (python main.py):
# helper.py is running
# hi
# True

expert.content:
from-import Copies the Binding

from config import debug creates a new name debug in your module that points at the object config.debug pointed at at import time. If config later rebinds its variable, your copy doesn't follow. Use import config and read config.debug when a value can change.
codeExamples:
# config.py
debug = False

def enable_debug():
    global debug
    debug = True

# main.py
import config
from config import debug, enable_debug

enable_debug()
print(debug)            # the copy made at import time
print(config.debug)     # always looked up on the module

# OUTPUT:
# False
# True

expert.content:
Circular Imports

If a.py imports b.py while b.py imports a.py, one of them is used while it is only partially initialised - its later definitions don't exist yet.
codeExamples:
# a.py
from b import helper_b

def helper_a():
    return "A"

# b.py
from a import helper_a

def helper_b():
    return "B"

# main.py
import a

# OUTPUT (the path in brackets varies):
# ImportError: cannot import name 'helper_a' from partially initialized module 'a' (most likely due to a circular import) (...)

expert.content:
Fixing Circular Imports

• Best: move the shared code into a third module that both import - circular imports usually signal tangled responsibilities.
• Import the module, not the name (import a, then call a.helper_a() inside a function) - the attribute is looked up only when the function runs, after both modules finished loading.
• Move the import inside the function that needs it (a local import).
codeExamples:
# b.py - fixed
import a                     # module object only; nothing looked up yet

def helper_b():
    return "B uses " + a.helper_a()   # resolved at call time

expert.content:
Local (Lazy) Imports

An import inside a function runs only when the function is called. This speeds up start-up when a heavy module is rarely needed, and breaks import cycles. After the first call the module comes from sys.modules, so repeated calls are cheap.
codeExamples:
def export_report(rows):
    import csv                  # only loaded if a report is exported
    import io
    buffer = io.StringIO()
    csv.writer(buffer).writerows(rows)
    return buffer.getvalue()

print(export_report([["id", "name"], [1, "Abaji"]]), end="")

# OUTPUT:
# id,name
# 1,Abaji

expert.content:
Dynamic Imports with importlib

When the module name is only known at runtime (plugins, configurable back-ends), importlib.import_module(name) imports it from a string. importlib.reload(module) re-executes a module's code, but objects created earlier - names copied with from ... import, instances of old classes - keep pointing at the old versions, so reload is a REPL convenience, not a deployment tool.
codeExamples:
import importlib

for name in ["math", "statistics"]:
    module = importlib.import_module(name)
    print(module.__name__, "loaded")

stats = importlib.import_module("statistics")
print(stats.mean([2, 4, 9]))

# OUTPUT:
# math loaded
# statistics loaded
# 5

expert.content:
Python import vs Java import

AspectJavaPython
When it happensCompile time - only a naming shortcutRuntime - executes the module the first time
Needed to use a class?No - the fully qualified name always worksYes - a module must be imported before use
UnitClasses and packagesModules (files) and packages (folders)
Wildcardimport java.util.*;from x import * (discouraged)

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
import x vs from x import y?The first binds the module name and you write x.y; the second binds y directly in your namespace
Is a module's code run every time it is imported?No - only on the first import; later imports return the object cached in sys.modules
Why avoid from x import *?It hides where names come from and can silently overwrite existing names
ModuleNotFoundError vs ImportError?ModuleNotFoundError (a subclass) means the module itself wasn't found; ImportError also covers a missing name inside a module
How do you fix a circular import?Move shared code to a third module, import the module instead of names, or import inside a function
How do you import a module whose name is in a string?importlib.import_module(name)

Advantages

Advantages: a module is imported only once and cached in sys.modules, so repeated imports are cheap.
codeExamples:
import sys
import json
import json                                  # second import: no reload
print("json" in sys.modules, sys.modules["json"] is json)

# OUTPUT:
# True True

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: from m import * pollutes the namespace and name clashes silently overwrite earlier names.
codeExamples:
from math import *
print(sqrt(9))
sqrt = "oops"                                # you just shadowed math.sqrt
try:
    print(sqrt(9))
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)

# OUTPUT:
# 3.0
# TypeError: 'str' object is not callable

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: circular imports (a imports b, b imports a) fail with partially initialised modules, and from m import name binds a copy of the reference, so later changes in m are not seen.
codeExamples:
import types, sys
cfg = types.ModuleType("cfg"); cfg.level = 1
sys.modules["cfg"] = cfg                     # a stand-in module
from cfg import level                        # copies the value 1
cfg.level = 2
print(level, cfg.level)                      # level did not follow

# OUTPUT:
# 1 2

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Import at the top of the file, one module per line, grouped stdlib / third-party / local (PEP 8). Avoid star imports. Break import cycles by moving shared code to a third module or importing inside the function; heavy imports can be lazy to cut start-up time (CLI tools).

beginner.content:
What is an Import Alias?

as gives an imported module or name a different local name:

• import module as short
• from module import name as other

Aliases shorten long names you type constantly and resolve clashes between two names that would otherwise collide. Java has no equivalent - you would have to write the fully qualified class name.
codeExamples:
import statistics as stats
from datetime import datetime as dt

print(stats.mean([70, 80, 90]))
print(dt(2026, 10, 4).strftime("%d %b %Y"))

# OUTPUT:
# 80
# 04 Oct 2026

beginner.content:
Community-Standard Aliases

Some aliases are so universal that every tutorial, answer and codebase uses them. Use exactly these - readers expect them.
ImportLibrary
import numpy as npNumPy - arrays and numerical computing
import pandas as pdpandas - data tables (DataFrames)
import matplotlib.pyplot as pltMatplotlib - charts
import seaborn as snsSeaborn - statistical charts
import tensorflow as tfTensorFlow - machine learning
codeExamples:
import numpy as np            # pip install numpy

marks = np.array([72, 88, 95])
print(marks.mean(), marks.max())

# OUTPUT:
# 85.0 95

beginner.content:
Resolving Name Clashes

math.sqrt works on real numbers, cmath.sqrt on complex numbers. Importing both as sqrt would make the second silently replace the first. Aliases keep both.
codeExamples:
from math import sqrt
from cmath import sqrt as complex_sqrt

print(sqrt(16))
print(complex_sqrt(-16))
print(sqrt(-16))

# OUTPUT:
# 4.0
# 4j
# ValueError: math domain error

beginner.content:
Shortening Deep Package Paths

Some modules live deep inside packages. An alias saves you from repeating the full path.
codeExamples:
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

root = ET.fromstring("<course><name>Python</name></course>")
print(root.find("name").text)

# OUTPUT:
# Python

beginner.content:
Introduction

as gives an import a shorter or different local name: import numpy as np, from math import sqrt as root.
codeExamples:
import datetime as dt
from math import sqrt as root
print(dt.date(2024, 5, 17).isoformat(), root(25))

# OUTPUT:
# 2024-05-17 5.0

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Long module names are tedious to type, and two modules may export the same name. Aliases solve both.
codeExamples:
from json import loads as json_loads
from ast import literal_eval as py_eval      # both could be called "loads"/"eval"
print(json_loads("[1, 2]"), py_eval("(1, 2)"))

# OUTPUT:
# [1, 2] (1, 2)

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Community conventions: np, pd, plt, tf. Also used to choose an implementation by availability.

Diagram

   import numpy as np
       real module object  <---- name "np" (your namespace)
   sys.modules["numpy"]    <---- same object, still cached under its real name

expert.content:
When NOT to Alias

An alias is a new name every reader must learn. Only use one when it is a community standard, fixes a clash, or shortens a genuinely long path. import os as o or import json as j save two keystrokes and cost readability.
codeExamples:
# Unhelpful - nobody expects these
import json as j
import random as rnd

# Fine - standard or clarifying
import numpy as np
from cmath import sqrt as complex_sqrt

expert.content:
An Alias Doesn't Rename the Module

as only changes the name in your file. The module object is the same one stored in sys.modules under its real name.
codeExamples:
import sys
import json as j

print(j.__name__)
print(j is sys.modules["json"])
print("json" in dir())          # the real name was not bound here

# OUTPUT:
# json
# True
# False

expert.content:
import a.b.c as c Binds Only c

A plain import xml.etree.ElementTree binds the top-level name xml, and you must write the full dotted path every time. With as, only the alias is bound - the top-level package name is not.
codeExamples:
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

print(ET.__name__)
print("ET" in dir(), "xml" in dir())

# OUTPUT:
# xml.etree.ElementTree
# True False

expert.content:
Optional Fast Implementations

Aliasing inside try/except ImportError lets the rest of the code use one name whether or not an optional, faster package is installed - as long as both offer the functions you call.
codeExamples:
try:
    import ujson as json        # faster, if installed
except ImportError:
    import json                 # standard library fallback
