# ['name', 'city', 'marks']
# ['Abaji', 'Pune', '91']
# ['Raoji', 'Latur', '78']
# [['a', 'b'], ['c', 'd']]

beginner.content:
Why Not Just split(",")?

Real CSV values can contain commas, quotes and even newlines, protected by double quotes. split breaks them; the csv module handles them correctly.
codeExamples:
import csv

line = 'Abaji,"Pune, MH",91'

print(line.split(","))
print(next(csv.reader([line])))

# OUTPUT:
# ['Abaji', '"Pune', ' MH"', '91']
# ['Abaji', 'Pune, MH', '91']

beginner.content:
DictReader and Writing CSV

csv.DictReader uses the header row as keys. csv.writer quotes values only where needed. By default it ends each row with \r\n, as the CSV standard specifies.
codeExamples:
import csv
import io

text = "name,marks\nAbaji,91\nRaoji,78\n"
for row in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(text)):
    print(row["name"], int(row["marks"]) + 5)

out = io.StringIO()
writer = csv.writer(out)
writer.writerow(["name", "city"])
writer.writerow(["Abaji", "Pune, MH"])
print(repr(out.getvalue()))

# OUTPUT:
# Abaji 96
# Raoji 83
# 'name,city\r\nAbaji,"Pune, MH"\r\n'

beginner.content:
Introduction

The json module converts between Python objects and JSON text; the csv module reads and writes delimited tables. Both work on file objects or in-memory text.
codeExamples:
import json, csv, io
print(json.dumps({"a": [1, 2], "ok": True}))
rows = list(csv.reader(io.StringIO("id,name\n1,Ann\n2,Baji\n")))
print(rows)

# OUTPUT:
# {"a": [1, 2], "ok": true}
# [['id', 'name'], ['1', 'Ann'], ['2', 'Baji']]

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Programs exchange data with APIs (JSON) and spreadsheets (CSV). Parsing by hand with split or regex breaks on quotes, nesting and escapes.
codeExamples:
import json
raw = '{"name": "Lee, \\"Jr\\"", "n": 1}'      # escaped quotes + comma inside a value
print(raw)
print(json.loads(raw)["name"])                # parsed correctly, no manual splitting

# OUTPUT:
# {"name": "Lee, \"Jr\"", "n": 1}
# Lee, "Jr"

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Convert a CSV report to JSON for an API - a daily ETL chore.
codeExamples:
import csv, io, json
text = "id,score\n1,90\n2,75\n"
data = [{"id": int(r["id"]), "score": int(r["score"])} for r in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(text))]
print(json.dumps(data))

# OUTPUT:
# [{"id": 1, "score": 90}, {"id": 2, "score": 75}]

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Python objects <--json.dumps/loads--> text (JSON)
   list of rows   <--csv.writer/reader--> text (CSV, one record per line)
   file object / StringIO is the pipe in both cases

expert.content:
Serialising Custom Types

json.dumps knows only dicts, lists, strings, numbers, booleans and None. For anything else, pass a default= function that converts unknown objects, or subclass json.JSONEncoder.

Decoding into Objects and Exact Money

object_hook is called for every decoded JSON object, so you can turn dicts into objects with attribute access. parse_float=Decimal keeps prices exact instead of converting them to binary floats.
codeExamples:
import json
from decimal import Decimal
from types import SimpleNamespace

text = '{"name": "Abaji", "address": {"city": "Pune"}, "balance": 1999.99}'

user = json.loads(text, object_hook=lambda d: SimpleNamespace(**d))
print(user.name, user.address.city)

exact = json.loads(text, parse_float=Decimal)
print(exact["balance"], type(exact["balance"]))

# OUTPUT:
# Abaji Pune
# 1999.99 <class 'decimal.Decimal'>

expert.content:
Handling Invalid JSON

Bad input raises json.JSONDecodeError (a subclass of ValueError) with the line and column of the problem. A frequent cause is Python-style text: single quotes, True, or a trailing comma.
codeExamples:
import json

bad = "{'name': 'Abaji'}"            # single quotes are not valid JSON

try:
    json.loads(bad)
except json.JSONDecodeError as error:
    print("Invalid JSON:", error)

# OUTPUT:
# Invalid JSON: Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes: line 1 column 2 (char 1)

expert.content:
Command-Line JSON and Large Files

• python -m json.tool data.json validates and pretty-prints a JSON file - handy for inspecting API responses.
• json.load reads the whole document into memory. For very large data, use JSON Lines (one JSON object per line, .jsonl) and process it line by line, or a streaming parser such as the third-party ijson.
codeExamples:
import io
import json

log = io.StringIO('{"user": "abaji", "ms": 120}\n{"user": "raoji", "ms": 340}\n')

total = 0
for line in log:                    # one small object at a time
    record = json.loads(line)
    total += record["ms"]
print(total)

# $ python -m json.tool response.json     (pretty-prints, or reports the error)

# OUTPUT:
# 460

expert.content:
csv Dialects, Delimiters and Quoting

A dialect bundles formatting rules: "excel" (the default, comma-separated) and "excel-tab" (tab-separated). Individual options such as delimiter and quoting override them. csv.Sniffer can guess the format of unknown text.
ConstantQuotes
csv.QUOTE_MINIMALOnly fields that need it (default)
csv.QUOTE_ALLEvery field
csv.QUOTE_NONNUMERICAll non-numeric fields (readers then convert unquoted fields to float)
csv.QUOTE_NONENever - needs an escapechar for special characters
codeExamples:
import csv
import io

row = ["Abaji", 91]

for quoting in (csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL, csv.QUOTE_ALL, csv.QUOTE_NONNUMERIC):
    out = io.StringIO()
    csv.writer(out, quoting=quoting).writerow(row)
    print(repr(out.getvalue()))

out = io.StringIO()
csv.writer(out, dialect="excel-tab").writerow(row)
print(repr(out.getvalue()))

print(list(csv.reader(["Abaji;91"], delimiter=";")))
print(repr(csv.Sniffer().sniff("a;b;c\n1;2;3\n").delimiter))

# OUTPUT:
# 'Abaji,91\r\n'
# '"Abaji","91"\r\n'
# '"Abaji",91\r\n'
# 'Abaji\t91\r\n'
# [['Abaji', '91']]
# ';'

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
dumps vs dump, loads vs load?The -s versions work with strings; the others read from or write to file objects
What does JSON null become in Python?None (and true/false become True/False)
Why does {1: "a"} come back as {"1": "a"}?JSON object keys are always strings
How do you serialise a datetime or Decimal?Pass default= (e.g. str) or a custom JSONEncoder subclass via cls=
Why use the csv module instead of split(",")?It handles quoted fields containing commas, quotes and newlines
What type are values read by csv.reader?Always strings - convert them yourself
How do you process a huge JSON data set?Use JSON Lines and parse one line at a time, or a streaming parser

Advantages

Advantages: in the standard library, streaming for CSV, configurable (indent, sort_keys, dialects, quoting).
codeExamples:
import csv, io
buf = io.StringIO()
csv.writer(buf, quoting=csv.QUOTE_ALL).writerow(["a", 1, "x,y"])
print(buf.getvalue().strip())

# OUTPUT:
# "a","1","x,y"

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: malformed JSON raises JSONDecodeError; CSV gives only strings so you must convert and validate each value.
codeExamples:
import json
try:
    json.loads("{bad json}")
except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
    print("JSONDecodeError:", e.msg, "at char", e.pos)

# OUTPUT:
# JSONDecodeError: Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes at char 1

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: json loads the whole document into memory (use JSON Lines or ijson for huge data), and neither module understands schemas or enforces types.
codeExamples:
import json
big = json.loads(json.dumps(list(range(5))))   # whole structure lives in RAM at once
print(big, json.loads("1e400"))                # huge numbers become inf as float

# OUTPUT:
# [0, 1, 2, 3, 4] inf

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

For production pipelines validate at the boundary (pydantic or jsonschema), stream big files, and prefer typed columnar formats for analytics. Pin an explicit encoding and newline policy; never hand-roll CSV or JSON parsing.

beginner.content:
What Is the re Module?

re provides regular expressions - patterns that describe text, such as "one or more digits" or "a word followed by @". This topic is a tour of the module's functions; the Regular Expressions module later covers pattern syntax in depth.

A handful of tokens is enough for the examples here:
TokenMatches
\d / \w / \sA digit / a word character (letter, digit, _) / whitespace
.Any character except a newline
+ / * / ?One or more / zero or more / zero or one of the previous item
{n}Exactly n of the previous item
[abc] / [0-9]One character from the set / range
^ / $Start / end of the string

Always Use Raw Strings for Patterns

Regex patterns are full of backslashes. In a normal string Python processes escapes first - "\b" becomes a backspace character instead of the regex "word boundary". Prefixing the pattern with r passes the backslashes through untouched.
codeExamples:
import re

text = "cat scat category"

print(re.findall("\bcat\b", text))      # "\b" is a backspace here
print(re.findall(r"\bcat\b", text))     # raw string: word boundary

# OUTPUT:
# []
# ['cat']

beginner.content:
search, match and fullmatch

All three return a match object on success and None otherwise - they differ in where the pattern may match.
FunctionPattern must match...
re.search(p, s)Anywhere in the string (first occurrence)
re.match(p, s)At the start of the string
re.fullmatch(p, s)The whole string - ideal for validation
codeExamples:
import re

text = "Order 42 shipped"

print(re.search(r"\d+", text))
print(re.match(r"\d+", text))            # text doesn't start with a digit
print(re.match(r"\d+", "42 orders"))

print(re.fullmatch(r"\d{6}", "411001"))
print(re.fullmatch(r"\d{6}", "4110011"))  # 7 digits - not a full match

# OUTPUT:
# <re.Match object; span=(6, 8), match='42'>
# None
# <re.Match object; span=(0, 2), match='42'>
# <re.Match object; span=(0, 6), match='411001'>
# None

beginner.content:
Working with a Match Object

group() returns the matched text; start(), end() and span() give its position. Always check for None before using it.
codeExamples:
import re

m = re.search(r"\d+", "Order 42 shipped")
if m:
    print(m.group(), m.start(), m.end(), m.span())

m = re.search(r"\d+", "no numbers here")
print(m)
if m is None:
    print("not found")

# OUTPUT:
# 42 6 8 (6, 8)
# None
# not found

beginner.content:
findall and finditer - Every Match

findall returns a list of matched strings. finditer yields match objects one at a time, so you also get positions.
codeExamples:
import re

bill = "Rs 250 for 3 pens and 12 pencils"

print(re.findall(r"\d+", bill))
print(sum(int(n) for n in re.findall(r"\d+", bill)))

for m in re.finditer(r"\d+", bill):
    print(m.group(), m.span())

# OUTPUT:
# ['250', '3', '12']
# 265
# 250 (3, 6)
# 3 (11, 12)
# 12 (22, 24)

beginner.content:
sub and split

re.sub replaces every match; re.split splits wherever the pattern matches - unlike str.split, it can use several different separators at once.
codeExamples:
import re

print(re.sub(r"\s+", " ", "too    many     spaces"))
print(re.sub(r"\d", "X", "Card 4321-8765"))

print(re.split(r"[,;\s]+", "pen, book;bag  ink"))

# OUTPUT:
# too many spaces
# Card XXXX-XXXX
# ['pen', 'book', 'bag', 'ink']

beginner.content:
Validating an Indian PIN Code with re.compile

A PIN code has 6 digits and does not start with 0. re.compile turns the pattern into a reusable object with the same methods.
codeExamples:
import re

PIN = re.compile(r"[1-9]\d{5}")

for code in ["411001", "011001", "41100", "4110a1"]:
    print(code, bool(PIN.fullmatch(code)))

# OUTPUT:
# 411001 True
# 011001 False
# 41100 False
# 4110a1 False

beginner.content:
Introduction

Regular expressions describe text patterns. re offers search, match, fullmatch, findall, sub and split. Use raw strings (r"...") for patterns.
codeExamples:
import re
text = "Order 66 shipped on 2024-05-17"
print(re.findall(r"\d+", text))
m = re.search(r"(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})", text)
print(m.group(0), m.groups())

# OUTPUT:
# ['66', '2024', '05', '17']
# 2024-05-17 ('2024', '05', '17')

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Validating and extracting from messy text (emails, phones, logs) with plain string methods needs many fragile lines; one pattern does it declaratively.
codeExamples:
import re
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"[\w.]+@\w+\.\w+", "ann.k@example.com")))
print(re.sub(r"\s+", " ", "too    many\n spaces"))

# OUTPUT:
# True
# too many spaces

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Log parsing, input validation, scraping, search-and-replace in tools and tokenizers. Named groups make results readable.
codeExamples:
import re
line = "2024-05-17 ERROR disk full"
m = re.match(r"(?P<date>\S+) (?P<level>[A-Z]+) (?P<msg>.*)", line)
print(m["level"], "|", m["msg"])
pat = re.compile(r"ERROR")                     # compile once, reuse in loops
print(bool(pat.search(line)))

# OUTPUT:
# ERROR | disk full
# True

beginner.content:
Diagram

   pattern  r"(d{4})-(d{2})"      text "on 2024-05"
        compile --> matcher --scan--> Match object
                                      .group(1) -> '2024'   .span() -> (3, 10)
   no match --> None   (always check before .group)

expert.content:
Flags

Flags change how a pattern is interpreted. Combine them with |.
FlagEffect
re.IGNORECASE / re.ICase-insensitive matching
re.MULTILINE / re.M^ and $ match at every line, not just the whole string
re.DOTALL / re.S. also matches newlines
re.VERBOSE / re.XWhitespace is ignored and # starts a comment - for readable patterns
codeExamples:
import re

print(re.findall(r"python", "Python PYTHON python", re.IGNORECASE))

text = "id: 1\nname: Abaji\nid: 2"
print(re.findall(r"^id: (\d+)", text))
print(re.findall(r"^id: (\d+)", text, re.MULTILINE))

# OUTPUT:
# ['Python', 'PYTHON', 'python']
# ['1']
# ['1', '2']

expert.content: Readable Patterns with re.VERBOSE
codeExamples:
import re

MOBILE = re.compile(r"""
    ^
    (?:\+91[-\s]?)?     # optional country code
    [6-9]\d{9}          # 10 digits, starting with 6-9
    $
""", re.VERBOSE)

for number in ["+91 9876543210", "9876543210", "12345"]:
    print(number, bool(MOBILE.match(number)))

# OUTPUT:
# +91 9876543210 True
# 9876543210 True
# 12345 False

expert.content:
Groups and Named Groups

Parentheses capture part of a match. (?P<name>...) gives a group a name. Note that when a pattern contains groups, findall returns the groups rather than the whole match.
codeExamples:
import re

m = re.search(r"(?P<day>\d{2})-(?P<month>\d{2})-(?P<year>\d{4})", "Due on 15-08-2026")
print(m.group(0), m.group(1), m.group("year"))
print(m.groupdict())

emails = "abaji@gmail.com, raoji@yahoo.com"
print(re.findall(r"(\w+)@(\w+)\.com", emails))

# OUTPUT:
# 15-08-2026 15 2026
# {'day': '15', 'month': '08', 'year': '2026'}
# [('abaji', 'gmail'), ('raoji', 'yahoo')]

expert.content:
Smarter Replacements

The replacement can refer to groups (\1, \g<name>) or be a function that receives each match object and returns the replacement text.
codeExamples:
import re

print(re.sub(r"(\d{2})-(\d{2})-(\d{4})", r"\3-\2-\1", "Exam on 15-08-2026"))

def double(m):
    return str(int(m.group()) * 2)

print(re.sub(r"\d+", double, "3 pens, 10 books"))

# OUTPUT:
# Exam on 2026-08-15
# 6 pens, 20 books

expert.content:
Is re.compile() Faster?

The module-level functions (re.search(pattern, ...)) compile the pattern and keep it in an internal cache, so calling them in a loop does not recompile every time. The main reasons to compile are readability - a named pattern constant such as PIN or MOBILE - and passing the pattern around as an object.

When NOT to Use Regex

• Simple text checks - "@" in s, s.startswith("http"), s.split(","), s.replace("-", "") are clearer and faster.
• Structured formats - parse JSON with json, CSV with csv, HTML with html.parser or BeautifulSoup, URLs with urllib.parse. Regex cannot reliably handle nesting.
• Catastrophic backtracking - nested quantifiers such as (a+)+$ can take exponential time on input like "aaaa...aab", freezing a server (a "ReDoS" attack). Keep patterns simple, anchor them, avoid nested repetition, and limit input length. Python 3.11 added atomic groups (?>...) and possessive quantifiers a++ to prevent this.

Java Comparison

JavaPython
Pattern.compile("\\d+")re.compile(r"\d+") - raw string, no doubled backslashes
matcher.find()re.search() / re.finditer()
matcher.matches()re.fullmatch()
matcher.lookingAt()re.match()
str.replaceAll(regex, rep)re.sub(pattern, rep, s)
str.split(regex)re.split(pattern, s) (str.split in Python is literal)

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
re.search vs re.match vs re.fullmatch?search finds a match anywhere; match only at the start; fullmatch requires the entire string to match
Why use raw strings for patterns?So Python doesn't interpret backslash escapes (like \b) before the regex engine sees them
findall vs finditer?findall returns a list of strings (or group tuples); finditer lazily yields match objects with positions
What does findall return when the pattern has groups?The captured groups, not the whole match
Is re.compile required for performance?Rarely - the module caches compiled patterns; compile mainly for readability and reuse
What is catastrophic backtracking?Exponential matching time caused by nested quantifiers on near-matching input; avoid nested repetition

Advantages

Advantages: very compact, powerful (groups, lookahead, flags), and fast C implementation.
codeExamples:
import re
print(re.sub(r"(\w+)@(\w+)", r"\2 at \1", "ann@site"))   # back-references in replacement
print(re.split(r"[,;]\s*", "a, b;c"))

# OUTPUT:
# site at ann
# ['a', 'b', 'c']

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: hard to read and maintain; greedy matching surprises beginners.
codeExamples: import re html = "boldit" print(re.findall(r"<.+>", html)) # greedy: swallows everything print(re.findall(r"<.+?>", html)) # non-greedy: tag by tag # OUTPUT: # ['boldit'] # ['', '', '', '']

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: cannot parse nested or recursive structures (HTML, balanced brackets); some patterns backtrack catastrophically and can freeze a service (ReDoS).
codeExamples:
import re
print(re.fullmatch(r"\(\w*\)", "((a))"))       # nesting depth is beyond a regular language

import time
t = time.perf_counter()
re.match(r"(a+)+$", "a" * 22 + "b")            # exponential backtracking
print("slow:", time.perf_counter() - t > 0.01) # grows 2x per extra "a"

# OUTPUT (example):
# None
# slow: True

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use regex for flat, well-bounded text patterns; use real parsers (json, html.parser, lark) for structured grammars. Compile patterns once, anchor them, avoid nested quantifiers, set timeouts or use the third-party re2 engine for untrusted input. Add verbose (re.X) comments to complex patterns.

beginner.content:
Specialised Containers

The collections module adds container types for jobs the built-in list, dict, set and tuple handle clumsily.
TypeWhat it isTypical use
CounterA dict that counts thingsWord frequencies, votes, stock levels
defaultdictA dict that creates missing values automaticallyGrouping, counting, building graphs
dequeA double-ended queue, fast at both endsQueues, BFS, "last N items"
namedtupleA tuple with named fieldsLightweight read-only records
OrderedDictA dict with order-aware extrasLRU caches, reordering keys
ChainMapSeveral dicts searched as oneLayered settings
UserDict, UserList, UserStringBase classes for custom containersSafely customising dict/list behaviour

Counter

A Counter maps each item to how many times it occurs. Missing items count as 0 instead of raising KeyError.
codeExamples:
from collections import Counter

letters = Counter("mississippi")
print(letters)
print(letters.most_common(2))
print(letters["s"], letters["z"])          # missing -> 0

# OUTPUT:
# Counter({'i': 4, 's': 4, 'p': 2, 'm': 1})
# [('i', 4), ('s', 4)]
# 4 0

from collections import Counter

stock = Counter(pen=3, book=1)
sold = Counter(pen=1, book=2)

print(stock + sold)                  # add counts
print(stock - sold)                  # subtract, dropping zero/negative results

stock.update(["pen", "bag"])         # count more items
print(stock)
print(list(Counter(a=2, b=1).elements()))

# OUTPUT:
# Counter({'pen': 4, 'book': 3})
# Counter({'pen': 2})
# Counter({'pen': 4, 'book': 1, 'bag': 1})
# ['a', 'a', 'b']

beginner.content:
defaultdict

defaultdict(factory) calls factory() to create a value the first time a missing key is accessed: list gives [], int gives 0, set gives set().
codeExamples:
from collections import defaultdict

words = ["apple", "avocado", "banana", "blueberry", "cherry"]
by_letter = defaultdict(list)
for w in words:
    by_letter[w[0]].append(w)          # no "if key not in" check needed
print(dict(by_letter))

counts = defaultdict(int)
for ch in "hello":
    counts[ch] += 1
print(dict(counts))

tags = defaultdict(set)
tags["post1"].add("python")
tags["post1"].add("python")             # sets ignore duplicates
tags["post2"].add("java")
print({post: sorted(t) for post, t in tags.items()})

# OUTPUT:
# {'a': ['apple', 'avocado'], 'b': ['banana', 'blueberry'], 'c': ['cherry']}
# {'h': 1, 'e': 1, 'l': 2, 'o': 1}
# {'post1': ['python'], 'post2': ['java']}

beginner.content:
deque

A deque ("deck") adds and removes items at both ends in O(1). With maxlen it keeps only the newest items - old ones fall off the other end automatically.
codeExamples:
from collections import deque

q = deque([1, 2, 3])
q.append(4)
q.appendleft(0)
print(q)
print(q.pop(), q.popleft())
print(q)

q.rotate(1)                   # move the last item to the front
print(q)

recent = deque(maxlen=3)
for page in ["home", "cart", "pay", "done"]:
    recent.append(page)
print(recent)

# OUTPUT:
# deque([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])
# 4 0
# deque([1, 2, 3])
# deque([3, 1, 2])
# deque(['cart', 'pay', 'done'], maxlen=3)

beginner.content:
namedtuple

A tuple whose fields also have names - covered fully in Tuples.
codeExamples:
from collections import namedtuple

Point = namedtuple("Point", "x y")
p = Point(2, 3)
print(p, p.x + p.y, p[0])

# OUTPUT:
# Point(x=2, y=3) 5 2

beginner.content:
Introduction

collections offers specialised containers: Counter, defaultdict, deque, namedtuple, OrderedDict, ChainMap.
codeExamples:
from collections import Counter, defaultdict, deque, namedtuple
print(Counter("banana").most_common(2))
groups = defaultdict(list)
for w in ["apple", "avocado", "bean"]:
    groups[w[0]].append(w)
print(dict(groups))
P = namedtuple("P", "x y")
print(P(1, 2), deque([1, 2, 3], maxlen=2))

# OUTPUT:
# [('a', 3), ('n', 2)]
# {'a': ['apple', 'avocado'], 'b': ['bean']}
# P(x=1, y=2) deque([2, 3], maxlen=2)

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Built-in list/dict need extra code for counting, grouping, queues and lightweight records; these types do it right and faster.
codeExamples:
# Plain dict needs a check on every first insert; defaultdict does not
plain = {}
for ch in "aab":
    if ch not in plain: plain[ch] = 0
    plain[ch] += 1
from collections import Counter
print(plain, Counter("aab"))

# OUTPUT:
# {'a': 2, 'b': 1} Counter({'a': 2, 'b': 1})

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Word frequencies, sliding windows (deque), BFS queues, grouping DB rows, immutable records, and layered config lookups (ChainMap).
codeExamples:
from collections import deque, ChainMap
window = deque(maxlen=3)
for x in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]:
    window.append(x)                  # oldest item drops automatically
print(list(window), sum(window) / len(window))
cfg = ChainMap({"debug": True}, {"debug": False, "port": 80})
print(cfg["debug"], cfg["port"])      # first mapping wins

# OUTPUT:
# [3, 4, 5] 4.0
# True 80

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Counter      : item -> count        defaultdict : missing key -> factory()
   deque        : [<-O(1)- items -O(1)->]   namedtuple : tuple with names
   ChainMap     : lookup layers  m1 -> m2 -> m3 (first hit wins)

expert.content:
OrderedDict Today

Plain dicts keep insertion order since Python 3.7, so OrderedDict is no longer needed just for ordering. It still has extras a dict lacks:
• move_to_end(key, last=True) - move a key to either end in O(1).
• popitem(last=False) - remove the oldest entry (FIFO).
• Equality between two OrderedDicts is order-sensitive (comparison with a plain dict is not).
codeExamples:
from collections import OrderedDict

od = OrderedDict(a=1, b=2, c=3)
od.move_to_end("a")
print(list(od))
od.move_to_end("c", last=False)
print(list(od))
print(od.popitem(last=False))

print(OrderedDict(a=1, b=2) == OrderedDict(b=2, a=1))
print(dict(a=1, b=2) == dict(b=2, a=1))
print(OrderedDict(a=1, b=2) == dict(b=2, a=1))

# OUTPUT:
# ['b', 'c', 'a']
# ['c', 'b', 'a']
# ('c', 3)
# False
# True
# True

expert.content:
An LRU Cache Sketch

A Least-Recently-Used cache keeps the newest entries and evicts the one untouched for longest. move_to_end marks an entry as recently used; popitem(last=False) evicts the oldest. (For caching function results, functools.lru_cache already does this for you.)
codeExamples:
from collections import OrderedDict

class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.data = OrderedDict()

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.data:
            return None
        self.data.move_to_end(key)           # mark as recently used
        return self.data[key]

    def put(self, key, value):
        self.data[key] = value
        self.data.move_to_end(key)
        if len(self.data) > self.capacity:
            self.data.popitem(last=False)    # evict the least recently used

cache = LRUCache(2)
cache.put("a", 1)
cache.put("b", 2)
cache.get("a")                               # "a" is now the most recent
cache.put("c", 3)                            # evicts "b"
print(list(cache.data), cache.get("b"))

# OUTPUT:
# ['a', 'c'] None

expert.content:
Subclass UserDict, Not dict

The built-in dict is implemented in C, and methods like update() and the constructor do not call your overridden __setitem__. UserDict is written in Python on top of MutableMapping, so every write goes through your method. (ChainMap, the other mapping in this module, is covered in Dictionary Unpacking.)

collections.abc for Type Checks

collections.abc defines abstract base classes such as Iterable, Sequence, MutableSequence and Mapping. Check against these to accept any suitable container, not only one concrete class.
codeExamples:
from collections import UserDict
from collections.abc import Mapping, MutableSequence, Iterable

print(isinstance({}, Mapping), isinstance(UserDict(), Mapping))
print(isinstance([], MutableSequence), isinstance((), MutableSequence))
print(isinstance("abc", Iterable), isinstance(42, Iterable))

# OUTPUT:
# True True
# True False
# True False

expert.content:
Complexity: deque vs list

Operationlistdeque
Add/remove at the endO(1)O(1)
Add/remove at the frontO(n) - insert(0, x), pop(0)O(1) - appendleft, popleft
Index in the middleO(1)O(n)
SlicingSupportedNot supported
Use a list for random access, a deque for queues.

Java Equivalents

PythonJava
dequeArrayDeque
defaultdict(list)map.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(x)
Countermap.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum) or Collectors.groupingBy(..., counting())
OrderedDict / LRULinkedHashMap with access order and removeEldestEntry
namedtupleA record

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How do you count word frequencies?Counter(words), then most_common(n) for the top n
defaultdict vs dict.get / setdefault?defaultdict creates the missing value automatically on access; get only reads with a fallback; setdefault inserts on a per-call basis
Why use deque for a queue?popleft/appendleft are O(1); list.pop(0) and insert(0, x) are O(n)
Is OrderedDict still useful?Yes for move_to_end, popitem(last=False) and order-sensitive equality - e.g. LRU caches
Why subclass UserDict instead of dict?dict's C methods (update, constructor) skip overridden __setitem__; UserDict routes every write through it
What does deque(maxlen=3) do?Keeps only the 3 most recent items; older items are discarded automatically

Advantages

Advantages: deque appends/pops at both ends in O(1) (list pop(0) is O(n)), Counter supports arithmetic, namedtuple gives readable fields.
codeExamples:
from collections import Counter
a, b = Counter("aab"), Counter("abc")
print(a + b)
print(a - b)

# OUTPUT:
# Counter({'a': 3, 'b': 2, 'c': 1})
# Counter({'a': 1})

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: defaultdict silently creates keys on read; deque has no slicing and slow middle access.
codeExamples:
from collections import defaultdict, deque
d = defaultdict(int)
_ = d["typo"]                          # a read inserted a key!
print(dict(d))
try:
    deque([1, 2, 3])[0:2]
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)

# OUTPUT:
# {'typo': 0}
# TypeError: sequence index must be integer, not 'slice'

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: namedtuple fields are immutable (use dataclass for mutable records), and none of these containers is thread-safe for compound operations.
codeExamples:
from collections import namedtuple
P = namedtuple("P", "x y")
p = P(1, 2)
try:
    p.x = 9
except AttributeError as e:
    print("AttributeError: cannot assign to a namedtuple field")
print(p._replace(x=9))                 # make a modified copy instead

# OUTPUT:
# AttributeError: cannot assign to a namedtuple field
# P(x=9, y=2)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Choose the container that states your intent: Counter for tallies, deque for queues/windows, dataclass over namedtuple when you need defaults, methods or mutability. For concurrency use queue.Queue; for large numeric data use NumPy or pandas.

beginner.content:
Two Toolboxes

• itertools - fast, memory-efficient building blocks for looping: infinite counters, combinations, grouping, slicing iterators.
• functools - tools for working with functions: caching, pre-filling arguments, reducing, generating comparison methods.

Every itertools function returns a lazy iterator, so the examples wrap results in list() to show them.

Infinite Iterators: count, cycle, repeat

These never stop on their own. Always limit them - with islice, zip with a finite iterable, or a break.
codeExamples:
from itertools import count, cycle, repeat, islice

print(list(islice(count(10, 5), 4)))       # 10, 15, 20, ...
print(list(islice(cycle("AB"), 5)))        # A, B, A, B, ...
print(list(repeat("x", 3)))                # repeat can also be finite
print(list(zip(["r1", "r2", "r3"], cycle(["odd", "even"]))))

# OUTPUT:
# [10, 15, 20, 25]
# ['A', 'B', 'A', 'B', 'A']
# ['x', 'x', 'x']
# [('r1', 'odd'), ('r2', 'even'), ('r3', 'odd')]

beginner.content:
Slicing and Joining Iterators: islice, chain

Iterators can't be sliced with [a:b]; islice(it, start, stop, step) does it lazily. chain walks several iterables one after another.
codeExamples:
from itertools import islice, chain

print(list(islice(range(100), 2, 10, 3)))
print(list(chain([1, 2], "ab", (3,))))
print(list(chain.from_iterable([[1, 2], [3], [4, 5]])))   # flatten one level

# OUTPUT:
# [2, 5, 8]
# [1, 2, 'a', 'b', 3]
# [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

beginner.content:
Combinatorics

FunctionOrder matters?Repeats allowed?
product(it, repeat=n)YesYes
permutations(it, r)YesNo
combinations(it, r)NoNo
combinations_with_replacement(it, r)NoYes
codeExamples:
from itertools import product, permutations, combinations, combinations_with_replacement

join = lambda tuples: ["".join(t) for t in tuples]

print(join(product("ab", repeat=2)))
print(join(permutations("abc", 2)))
print(join(combinations("abc", 2)))
print(join(combinations_with_replacement("abc", 2)))

# OUTPUT:
# ['aa', 'ab', 'ba', 'bb']
# ['ab', 'ac', 'ba', 'bc', 'ca', 'cb']
# ['ab', 'ac', 'bc']
# ['aa', 'ab', 'ac', 'bb', 'bc', 'cc']

beginner.content: groupby, accumulate, takewhile, dropwhile, batched
codeExamples:
import operator
from itertools import groupby, accumulate, takewhile, dropwhile, batched

# groupby groups CONSECUTIVE equal keys - here: run-length encoding
print([(ch, len(list(g))) for ch, g in groupby("aaabccdd")])

print(list(accumulate([1, 2, 3, 4], operator.mul)))      # running product

print(list(takewhile(lambda x: x < 5, [1, 3, 6, 2])))    # stop at the first failure
print(list(dropwhile(lambda x: x < 5, [1, 3, 6, 2])))    # skip until the first failure

print(list(batched("ABCDEFG", 3)))                        # Python 3.12+

# OUTPUT:
# [('a', 3), ('b', 1), ('c', 2), ('d', 2)]
# [1, 2, 6, 24]
# [1, 3]
# [6, 2]
# [('A', 'B', 'C'), ('D', 'E', 'F'), ('G',)]

beginner.content:
functools: reduce, partial, cache

reduce and partial were covered in the Functions module; lru_cache / cache remember a function's results so repeated calls with the same arguments are instant. (functools.wraps is explained in the Decorators module.)
codeExamples:
from functools import reduce, partial, lru_cache

print(reduce(lambda a, b: a * b, [1, 2, 3, 4]))

round2 = partial(round, ndigits=2)
print(round2(3.14159))

@lru_cache(maxsize=128)
def fib(n):
    return n if n < 2 else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

print(fib(30))
print(fib.cache_info())

# OUTPUT:
# 24
# 3.14
# 832040
# CacheInfo(hits=28, misses=31, maxsize=128, currsize=31)

beginner.content:
cached_property and total_ordering

• @cached_property computes an attribute on first access and stores it on the instance.
• @total_ordering fills in <=, > and >= when you define __eq__ and one of the ordering methods.

Introduction

itertools builds fast, memory-friendly iterators (chain, islice, product, permutations, groupby, accumulate). functools has higher-order tools (reduce, partial, lru_cache, wraps).
codeExamples:
from itertools import chain, islice, count, product, accumulate
from functools import reduce, partial
print(list(chain([1, 2], "ab")), list(islice(count(10), 3)))
print(list(product("ab", [1, 2])))
print(list(accumulate([1, 2, 3, 4])), reduce(lambda a, b: a * b, [1, 2, 3, 4]))
double = partial(pow, 2)               # pow(2, x)
print(double(5))

# OUTPUT:
# [1, 2, 'a', 'b'] [10, 11, 12]
# [('a', 1), ('a', 2), ('b', 1), ('b', 2)]
# [1, 3, 6, 10] 24
# 32

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Nested loops, manual counters and repeated expensive calls clutter code and waste time. These tools replace them with tested building blocks and caching.

Real-Time Use

Batching records, sliding combinations, test-case generation (product), caching API/DB lookups, pre-filled callbacks (partial), and decorators that keep metadata (wraps).

Diagram

   source --> chain --> filter/islice --> accumulate --> consumer
   (each stage lazy: one item flows through at a time, no big lists)
   lru_cache: call(args) --hit--> stored result
                         --miss--> compute, store, return

expert.content:
Laziness: Huge or Infinite Inputs, Tiny Memory

itertools objects produce one item at a time, so their memory use doesn't depend on how many items they could produce. product(range(10_000), repeat=3) describes a trillion tuples, yet it only stores its inputs - the results are generated as you ask for them.
codeExamples:
import sys
from itertools import product, islice

combos = product(range(10_000), repeat=3)          # 10**12 tuples - not built
print(list(islice(combos, 3)))
print(sys.getsizeof(combos) < 1_000)

# OUTPUT:
# [(0, 0, 0), (0, 0, 1), (0, 0, 2)]
# True

expert.content:
The groupby Pitfall: Sort First

groupby starts a new group every time the key changes. Unsorted input produces several groups for the same key. Sort by the same key first (or use a defaultdict(list) when order doesn't matter).
codeExamples:
from itertools import groupby

words = ["apple", "avocado", "banana", "apricot"]
first = lambda w: w[0]

for letter, group in groupby(words, key=first):
    print(letter, list(group))

print("--- sorted ---")
for letter, group in groupby(sorted(words, key=first), key=first):
    print(letter, list(group))

# OUTPUT:
# a ['apple', 'avocado']
# b ['banana']
# a ['apricot']
# --- sorted ---
# a ['apple', 'avocado', 'apricot']
# b ['banana']

expert.content:
lru_cache in Practice

• maxsize bounds memory: least-recently-used entries are evicted. maxsize=None (or @cache, 3.9+) never evicts.
• cache_info() shows hits and misses; cache_clear() empties it.
• Arguments must be hashable - they become dictionary keys.
• Only cache pure functions: a cached result never notices that the outside world changed.
• On methods, the cache holds a reference to self, keeping instances alive as long as the cache lives.
codeExamples:
from functools import cache

@cache
def total(items):
    return sum(items)

print(total((1, 2, 3)))        # tuples are hashable
total.cache_clear()
print(total.cache_info().currsize)
total([1, 2, 3])

# OUTPUT:
# 6
# 0
# TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'

expert.content:
cached_property vs property

@property@cached_property
ComputedOn every accessOnce, on first access
Reflects later data changesYesNo - until you del obj.attr
Stored whereNowhereIn the instance's __dict__
Works with __slots__YesNo - needs an instance __dict__
Use forCheap or changing valuesExpensive values of data that doesn't change

singledispatch: Overloading by Type

Python has no method overloading, but @singledispatch picks an implementation based on the type of the first argument, registered with type annotations.

Itertools Recipes

The official itertools documentation ends with a list of "recipes" - small functions built from these tools, such as take, flatten and sliding_window. Several became built-ins (pairwise in 3.10, batched in 3.12), and the third-party more-itertools package ships the rest ready-made.
codeExamples:
from itertools import islice, chain
from collections import deque

def take(n, iterable):
    return list(islice(iterable, n))

def sliding_window(iterable, n):
    it = iter(iterable)
    window = deque(islice(it, n - 1), maxlen=n)
    for x in it:
        window.append(x)
        yield tuple(window)

flatten = chain.from_iterable

print(take(3, "abcdef"))
print(list(sliding_window([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 3)))
print(list(flatten([[1], [2, 3]])))

# OUTPUT:
# ['a', 'b', 'c']
# [(1, 2, 3), (2, 3, 4), (3, 4, 5)]
# [1, 2, 3]

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
permutations vs combinations?permutations count different orders as different results; combinations don't
Why does groupby give duplicate groups?It only groups consecutive equal keys - sort the input by the key first
How do you take the first n items of an iterator?list(islice(it, n))
What does lru_cache need from arguments?They must be hashable; results are cached per unique argument combination
cached_property vs property?cached_property computes once and stores the value on the instance; property recomputes on every access
What does total_ordering do?Generates the remaining comparison methods from __eq__ and one of __lt__/__le__/__gt__/__ge__

Advantages

Advantages: lazy (constant memory), implemented in C, expressive pipelines; infinite streams are fine.
codeExamples:
from itertools import count, islice
squares = (n * n for n in count(1))    # infinite, lazy
print(list(islice(squares, 5)))

# OUTPUT:
# [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: groupby only groups adjacent equal keys, permutations/product explode combinatorially, and heavy chaining hurts readability.
codeExamples:
from itertools import groupby, permutations
print([(k, len(list(g))) for k, g in groupby("aabaa")])    # unsorted input
print(len(list(permutations(range(8)))))                   # 8! results

# OUTPUT:
# [('a', 2), ('b', 1), ('a', 2)]
# 40320

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: iterators are single-use; lru_cache needs hashable arguments, keeps references alive (memory), and caches stale results for impure functions.

Architect's Notes

Use itertools for streaming pipelines and functools.cache for pure, hashable-argument functions; bound the cache (maxsize) and never cache functions with side effects. When a chain gets hard to read, a named generator function is clearer than five nested iterator calls.

beginner.content:
Paths as Objects

pathlib (Python 3.4+) represents file-system paths as Path objects instead of plain strings. You join paths with the / operator, ask a path for its name or extension, and read or write files directly from it. It handles Windows \ and macOS/Linux / separators for you - it plays the role of java.nio.file.Path and Files in Java.
codeExamples:
from pathlib import Path

report = Path("data") / "2024" / "sales.csv"
print(report.as_posix())         # forward slashes on every OS
print(type(report).__name__)     # WindowsPath on Windows, PosixPath elsewhere

print(Path.cwd())                # current working directory
print(Path.home())               # your home folder

# OUTPUT (the last three lines depend on your machine - e.g.):
# data/2024/sales.csv
# WindowsPath
# C:\Users\abaji\projects\shop
# C:\Users\abaji

beginner.content:
Parts of a Path

These attributes only look at the text of the path - the file doesn't need to exist. PurePosixPath is used here so the output is identical on every operating system.
codeExamples:
from pathlib import PurePosixPath

p = PurePosixPath("/home/abaji/reports/sales.2024.csv")

print(p.name)           # final component
print(p.stem)           # name without the last suffix
print(p.suffix)         # last extension
print(p.suffixes)       # all extensions
print(p.parent)         # containing folder
print(p.parents[1])     # two levels up
print(p.parts)
print(p.with_suffix(".xlsx").name)
print(p.with_name("summary.txt"))

# OUTPUT:
# sales.2024.csv
# sales.2024
# .csv
# ['.2024', '.csv']
# /home/abaji/reports
# /home/abaji
# ('/', 'home', 'abaji', 'reports', 'sales.2024.csv')
# sales.2024.xlsx
# /home/abaji/reports/summary.txt

beginner.content:
Reading and Writing Files

write_text/read_text open, write/read and close the file in one call - always pass encoding="utf-8". write_bytes/read_bytes do the same for binary data. The examples work inside a temporary folder that is deleted automatically afterwards.
codeExamples:
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    notes = Path(tmp) / "notes.txt"
    print(notes.exists())

    notes.write_text("line 1\nline 2\n", encoding="utf-8")
    print(notes.exists(), notes.is_file(), notes.is_dir())
    print(notes.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines())

    data = Path(tmp) / "data.bin"
    data.write_bytes(bytes([0, 255, 16]))
    print(data.read_bytes())

# OUTPUT:
# False
# True True False
# ['line 1', 'line 2']
# b'\x00\xff\x10'

beginner.content:
Folders: mkdir, iterdir, glob

mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) creates a folder and any missing parents, and doesn't complain if it already exists. iterdir() lists a folder; glob() matches a pattern in one folder and rglob() searches recursively. Their order isn't guaranteed, so sort the results.
codeExamples:
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    project = Path(tmp) / "project"
    (project / "src" / "utils").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    (project / "README.md").write_text("# Demo", encoding="utf-8")
    (project / "src" / "app.py").write_text("print(1)", encoding="utf-8")
    (project / "src" / "utils" / "helpers.py").write_text("", encoding="utf-8")

    print(sorted(p.name for p in project.iterdir()))
    print(sorted(p.name for p in (project / "src").glob("*.py")))
    print(sorted(p.relative_to(project).as_posix() for p in project.rglob("*.py")))

# OUTPUT:
# ['README.md', 'src']
# ['app.py']
# ['src/app.py', 'src/utils/helpers.py']

beginner.content:
Renaming and Deleting

rename() returns the new Path (3.8+). unlink() deletes a file; rmdir() deletes an empty folder.
codeExamples:
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    draft = Path(tmp) / "draft.txt"
    draft.write_text("v1", encoding="utf-8")

    final = draft.rename(draft.with_name("final.txt"))
    print(draft.exists(), final.name)

    final.unlink()
    print(final.exists())

    empty = Path(tmp) / "empty"
    empty.mkdir()
    empty.rmdir()
    print(empty.exists())

# OUTPUT:
# False final.txt
# False
# False

beginner.content:
Introduction

pathlib.Path represents file system paths as objects. The / operator joins parts, and methods like read_text, exists, glob replace many os/os.path calls.
codeExamples:
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("reports") / "2024" / "may.txt"       # join with /
p.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
p.write_text("sales: 10\n", encoding="utf-8")
print(p.name, p.stem, p.suffix, p.exists())
print(p.read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip())

# OUTPUT:
# may.txt may .txt True
# sales: 10

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

String paths need the right separator, careful splitting and several modules (os, os.path, glob, shutil). pathlib gathers it in one readable, cross-platform API.
codeExamples:
from pathlib import PurePosixPath
q = PurePosixPath("/data/images/photo.final.png")
print(q.parent, q.with_suffix(".jpg").name, q.parts)

# OUTPUT:
# /data/images photo.final.jpg ('/', 'data', 'images', 'photo.final.png')

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Finding files, building output paths, batch renaming, locating the script's own folder via Path(__file__).parent.
codeExamples:
from pathlib import Path
for n in ("a.py", "b.py", "c.txt"):
    Path("proj").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    (Path("proj") / n).touch()
print(sorted(f.name for f in Path("proj").glob("*.py")))
print(sorted(f.name for f in Path("proj").iterdir()))

# OUTPUT:
# ['a.py', 'b.py']
# ['a.py', 'b.py', 'c.txt']

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Path("proj") / "a.py"  --->  proj/a.py   (object, not string)
        .parent  .name  .stem  .suffix  .parts
        .exists() .is_file() .glob("*.py") .read_text() .write_text()
   Pure* : only string logic     Path : also touches the file system

expert.content:
pathlib vs os.path

Older code uses string functions from os and os.path. Both still work; pathlib is the modern, more readable choice.
Taskos / os.pathpathlib
Joinos.path.join(a, b)Path(a) / b
File nameos.path.basename(p)p.name
Folderos.path.dirname(p)p.parent
Extensionos.path.splitext(p)[1]p.suffix
Exists?os.path.exists(p)p.exists()
Make foldersos.makedirs(p, exist_ok=True)p.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
List a folderos.listdir(p)p.iterdir()
Find filesglob.glob("**/*.py", recursive=True)p.rglob("*.py")
Read a fileopen(p).read()p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
Most standard-library functions (open, shutil, os) accept Path objects directly.

Pure Paths vs Concrete Paths

• Pure paths (PurePath, PurePosixPath, PureWindowsPath) only manipulate text - no file-system access. You can parse a Windows path on Linux and vice versa.
• Concrete paths (Path) add file-system methods. Path(...) automatically creates a WindowsPath or PosixPath for the current OS.
codeExamples:
from pathlib import PureWindowsPath, PurePosixPath

w = PureWindowsPath(r"C:\Users\Abaji\report.docx")
print(w.drive, w.name, w.suffix)
print(w.parent)
print(w.as_posix())

print(PurePosixPath("/srv/app") / "static" / "site.css")
print(PureWindowsPath("C:/data") == PureWindowsPath("c:\\DATA"))   # Windows paths are case-insensitive

# OUTPUT:
# C: report.docx .docx
# C:\Users\Abaji
# C:/Users/Abaji/report.docx
# /srv/app/static/site.css
# True

expert.content:
Absolute Paths, resolve() and relative_to()

• absolute() prefixes the current directory; resolve() also follows symbolic links and removes .. parts.
• relative_to(base) gives the path relative to a base folder (and raises ValueError if it isn't inside it); is_relative_to() (3.9+) checks first.
codeExamples:
from pathlib import Path, PurePosixPath

print(Path("reports/../data/sales.csv").resolve())

css = PurePosixPath("/srv/app/static/css/site.css")
print(css.relative_to("/srv/app"))
print(css.is_relative_to("/srv/app"), css.is_relative_to("/etc"))

# OUTPUT (first line depends on your current folder - e.g.):
# /home/abaji/project/data/sales.csv
# static/css/site.css
# True False

expert.content:
Files Next to Your Script: Path(__file__).parent

Relative paths like Path("config.json") are resolved against the current working directory - wherever the user launched Python from, not where the script lives. To load a file shipped alongside your code, build the path from __file__.
codeExamples:
from pathlib import Path

BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
CONFIG = BASE_DIR / "config.json"

print(CONFIG.name, CONFIG.parent == BASE_DIR)

# OUTPUT:
# config.json True
# CONFIG is now correct no matter which folder you run the script from

expert.content:
File Metadata with stat()

stat() returns size, timestamps and permissions.
codeExamples:
import tempfile
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    f = Path(tmp) / "hello.txt"
    f.write_text("hello", encoding="utf-8")
    info = f.stat()
    print(info.st_size, "bytes")
    print(datetime.fromtimestamp(info.st_mtime))

# OUTPUT (the timestamp is when you run it - e.g.):
# 5 bytes
# 2026-10-04 18:30:12.345678

expert.content:
Whole Folders: shutil

pathlib works on single files and empty folders. For copying, moving and deleting trees, use shutil, which accepts Path objects: copy2, copytree, move, rmtree. Be careful - rmtree deletes everything inside, with no recycle bin.
codeExamples:
import shutil
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    src = Path(tmp) / "src"
    (src / "sub").mkdir(parents=True)
    (src / "sub" / "a.txt").write_text("A", encoding="utf-8")

    backup = shutil.copytree(src, Path(tmp) / "backup")
    print(sorted(p.relative_to(backup).as_posix() for p in backup.rglob("*")))

    shutil.rmtree(src)
    print(src.exists(), backup.exists())

# OUTPUT:
# ['sub', 'sub/a.txt']
# False True

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why prefer pathlib over os.path?Paths are objects with readable methods and the / operator; separators are handled per OS
stem vs suffix vs name?For "report.csv": name "report.csv", stem "report", suffix ".csv"
How do you create nested folders safely?p.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
How do you find all .py files recursively?Path(".").rglob("*.py")
PurePath vs Path?PurePath only manipulates the path text; Path adds file-system operations
How do you open a file located next to the script?Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "file.txt"
How do you delete a non-empty folder?shutil.rmtree(path) - rmdir() only removes empty folders

Advantages

Advantages: readable, object oriented, works on Windows and POSIX, supports rglob recursion, stat, rename and unlink.
codeExamples:
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("proj/a.py")
p.rename("proj/z.py")
print(Path("proj/z.py").exists(), Path("proj/a.py").exists())
print(sorted(x.name for x in Path("proj").rglob("*.py")))

# OUTPUT:
# True False
# ['b.py', 'z.py']

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: a Path is not a str, so older APIs may need str(p); read/write helpers load whole files; there is no built-in recursive copy (use shutil).
codeExamples:
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("proj/b.py")
print(isinstance(p, str), str(p).replace("\\", "/"))
print("proj/" + p.name)                 # string + Path would be a TypeError

# OUTPUT:
# False proj/b.py
# proj/b.py

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a path object does not check existence by itself; Windows and POSIX paths follow different rules (case, drive letters), so pure-path classes differ.
codeExamples:
from pathlib import Path, PureWindowsPath, PurePosixPath
print(PureWindowsPath("C:/Data/a.TXT") == PureWindowsPath("c:/data/a.txt"))   # case-insensitive
print(PurePosixPath("/Data/a.TXT") == PurePosixPath("/data/a.txt"))
try:
    Path("missing.txt").read_text()
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("FileNotFoundError: path objects do not guarantee existence")

# OUTPUT:
# True
# False
# FileNotFoundError: path objects do not guarantee existence

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use pathlib as the default path type in new code and accept os.PathLike in APIs (os.fspath). Do not rely on case sensitivity or separators; for large file I/O stream with open() rather than read_text(), and use shutil for trees and tempfile for scratch space.

beginner.content:
Running Other Programs

The subprocess module starts external programs - git, a compiler, another Python script - waits for them, and collects their output and exit code. It is Python's counterpart of Java's ProcessBuilder.

The main function is subprocess.run([program, arg1, arg2, ...]). Pass the command as a list: the first item is the program, each further item is one argument.

The examples run Python itself (sys.executable) as the child program, so they work the same on Windows, macOS and Linux.

Capturing Output

capture_output=True collects what the program prints; text=True decodes it from bytes into strings. The result object holds returncode, stdout and stderr.
codeExamples:
import subprocess
import sys

result = subprocess.run(
    [sys.executable, "-c", "print('Hello from a child process')"],
    capture_output=True,
    text=True,
)

print(result.returncode)            # 0 means success
print(result.stdout.strip())
print(repr(result.stderr))

# OUTPUT:
# 0
# Hello from a child process
# ''

beginner.content:
Exit Codes and Errors

By convention a program exits with 0 on success and a non-zero code on failure. run() doesn't raise on failure by default - check returncode, or pass check=True to get a CalledProcessError.
codeExamples:
import subprocess
import sys

failing = [sys.executable, "-c", "import sys; print('oops', file=sys.stderr); sys.exit(3)"]

result = subprocess.run(failing, capture_output=True, text=True)
print(result.returncode, result.stderr.strip())

try:
    subprocess.run(failing, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
except subprocess.CalledProcessError as error:
    print("Failed with exit code", error.returncode)

# OUTPUT:
# 3 oops
# Failed with exit code 3

beginner.content:
Timeouts

timeout=seconds stops waiting: the child is killed and TimeoutExpired is raised. Always set one when calling programs that might hang.
codeExamples:
import subprocess
import sys

try:
    subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", "import time; time.sleep(5)"], timeout=1)
except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
    print("Took too long - the child process was killed")

# OUTPUT:
# Took too long - the child process was killed

beginner.content:
Running Real Tools

Any installed program works the same way. Shell built-ins such as dir (Windows) are not programs, so they need the shell - prefer Python equivalents like pathlib instead.
codeExamples:
import subprocess

result = subprocess.run(["git", "--version"], capture_output=True, text=True)
print(result.stdout.strip())

# OUTPUT (depends on your installed version - e.g.):
# git version 2.46.0

beginner.content:
Introduction

subprocess starts other programs from Python. subprocess.run runs a command, waits, and returns a CompletedProcess with return code and captured output.
codeExamples:
import subprocess, sys
res = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", "print('hi from child')"],
                     capture_output=True, text=True)
print(res.returncode, repr(res.stdout))

# OUTPUT:
# 0 'hi from child\n'

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Some jobs are best done by existing tools (git, ffmpeg, compilers, shell scripts). Scripts need to start them, pass input, read results and detect failure reliably.
codeExamples:
import subprocess, sys
res = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", "import sys; print(sys.stdin.read().upper())"],
                     input="pipe me", capture_output=True, text=True)
print(res.stdout.strip())

# OUTPUT:
# PIPE ME

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Build and deploy scripts, CI steps, calling git or Docker, media conversion, and running untrusted work in a separate process with a timeout.
codeExamples:
import subprocess, sys
try:
    subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", "import sys; sys.exit(3)"], check=True)
except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
    print("failed with code", e.returncode)

# OUTPUT:
# failed with code 3

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Python parent --run([...])--> OS creates child process
        stdin  ---- input= ---->  child
        stdout <--- captured ---  child       returncode: 0 ok / non-zero fail
        timeout / check=True turn hangs and failures into exceptions

expert.content:
Why shell=True Is Dangerous

With shell=True the command is a single string interpreted by the system shell (cmd.exe or /bin/sh). If any part comes from a user, characters like ;, &&, | or $( ) can smuggle in extra commands - shell injection. With a list and no shell, each item is passed as exactly one argument and nothing is interpreted. If you truly need a shell, quote untrusted parts with shlex.quote (POSIX shells).
codeExamples:
import shlex

filename = "report.txt; rm -rf ~"          # imagine this came from a user

# DANGEROUS - the shell sees TWO commands:
#   subprocess.run(f"cat {filename}", shell=True)
# SAFE - the whole string is ONE argument to cat:
#   subprocess.run(["cat", filename])

print(shlex.quote(filename))
print(shlex.split("git commit -m 'first commit'"))

# OUTPUT:
# 'report.txt; rm -rf ~'
# ['git', 'commit', '-m', 'first commit']

expert.content:
Sending Input, Environment and Working Directory

• input= writes data to the child's standard input.
• env= replaces the child's environment variables - start from a copy of os.environ, or the child loses PATH and other essentials.
• cwd= runs the child in another folder.
codeExamples:
import os
import subprocess
import sys

result = subprocess.run(
    [sys.executable, "-c", "import sys; print(sys.stdin.read().upper())"],
    input="hello\nworld",
    capture_output=True,
    text=True,
)
print(result.stdout, end="")

env = {**os.environ, "APP_MODE": "test"}
result = subprocess.run(
    [sys.executable, "-c", "import os; print(os.environ['APP_MODE'])"],
    env=env,
    capture_output=True,
    text=True,
)
print(result.stdout.strip())

# OUTPUT:
# HELLO
# WORLD
# test

expert.content:
Popen: Streaming Long-Running Processes

run() waits for the program to finish before returning. Popen starts it and returns immediately, so you can read its output line by line while it runs - useful for build tools, servers and progress logs.
codeExamples:
import subprocess
import sys

cmd = [sys.executable, "-u", "-c", "for i in range(3): print('step', i)"]

with subprocess.Popen(cmd, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, text=True) as proc:
    for line in proc.stdout:              # arrives as the child prints it
        print("got:", line.rstrip())

print("exit code", proc.returncode)

# OUTPUT:
# got: step 0
# got: step 1
# got: step 2
# exit code 0

expert.content:
Avoid os.system

os.system("command") is the old way: it always goes through the shell (injection risk), can't capture output, and returns a platform-dependent status value. subprocess.run replaces it - and os.popen - in all new code.

Compared with Java's ProcessBuilder

TaskJavaPython
Build the commandnew ProcessBuilder("git", "status")["git", "status"]
Run and waitpb.start().waitFor()subprocess.run(cmd)
Read outputprocess.getInputStream()capture_output=True → result.stdout
Working directorypb.directory(dir)cwd=dir
Environmentpb.environment().put(k, v)env={**os.environ, k: v}
TimeoutwaitFor(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)timeout=5

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How do you run a command and capture its output?subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
Why pass the command as a list?Each item becomes exactly one argument with no shell parsing, which prevents injection and quoting bugs
What does check=True do?Raises CalledProcessError if the exit code is non-zero
How do you stop a hung process?Pass timeout=; the child is killed and TimeoutExpired is raised
run() vs Popen?run waits for completion and returns the result; Popen returns immediately so you can interact with or stream from the process
Why is os.system discouraged?It always uses the shell, can't capture output and gives a platform-dependent status

Advantages

Advantages: full control over args, environment, working directory, pipes and timeouts; a list of arguments avoids shell parsing (and injection).
codeExamples:
import subprocess, sys
user_input = "x; echo HACKED"                 # hostile text stays ONE argument
res = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", "import sys; print(sys.argv[1])", user_input],
                     capture_output=True, text=True)
print(res.stdout.strip())

# OUTPUT:
# x; echo HACKED

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: shell=True with user data is a security hole, commands differ per OS, and output capture of very large results uses memory.
codeExamples:
import subprocess
# shell=True hands the string to the shell, which interprets ; | && and so on
# (shown for a POSIX shell such as bash; Windows cmd.exe behaves differently)
res = subprocess.run("echo one; echo two", shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True)
print(res.stdout.split())                     # the shell ran TWO commands

# OUTPUT:
# ['one', 'two']

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a missing program raises FileNotFoundError, a hanging child blocks forever unless you set timeout, and the child cannot share Python objects (only bytes/text).

Architect's Notes

Always pass an argument list, set timeout and check=True, and use sys.executable for Python children. Prefer a library API over shelling out when one exists (better errors, portability). For many parallel workers use multiprocessing or concurrent.futures, and treat any shell=True as a security review item.

beginner.content:
Classes and Objects

A class is a blueprint that describes what data an object holds (attributes) and what it can do (methods). An object (or instance) is one concrete thing built from that blueprint. One Student class can produce thousands of student objects, each with its own name and marks.
codeExamples:
class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, marks):
        self.name = name          # attributes - data stored on each object
        self.marks = marks

    def has_passed(self):         # method - behaviour
        return self.marks >= 40


s1 = Student("Pankaj", 85)        # two separate objects
s2 = Student("Sheru", 32)

print(s1.name, s1.has_passed())
print(s2.name, s2.has_passed())
print(type(s1))

# OUTPUT:
# Pankaj True
# Sheru False
# <class '__main__.Student'>

beginner.content:
The Four Pillars at a Glance

PillarIdeaIn Python
EncapsulationBundle data with the methods that use it; hide internalsClasses, plus naming conventions (_internal, __private)
InheritanceA class reuses and extends another classclass Child(Parent): - multiple parents allowed
PolymorphismOne interface, many implementationsMethod overriding and duck typing
AbstractionExpose what an object does, not howAbstract base classes (abc) and protocols
Each pillar has its own topic in this module.

A Complete Small Class

A bank account keeps its balance and the rules for changing it in one place. Callers use the methods instead of editing the balance directly.

Everything Is an Object

In Python, numbers, strings, functions, modules and even classes are objects - each has a type and can have attributes and methods. Java has primitives (int, double) that are not objects; Python does not.
codeExamples:
print(type(42), (42).bit_length())
print(type("hi"), "hi".upper())
print(type(len))
print(type(int))                 # a class is itself an object, of type 'type'
print(isinstance(42, object), isinstance(len, object))

# OUTPUT:
# <class 'int'> 6
# <class 'str'> HI
# <class 'builtin_function_or_method'>
# <class 'type'>
# True True

beginner.content:
Introduction

OOP models a program as objects: bundles of data (attributes) and behaviour (methods) created from a blueprint called a class. In Python everything is already an object - ints, strings, functions - and class lets you define your own types.
codeExamples:
# A class is a blueprint; each call creates a new object (instance)
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name):         # runs when Dog("...") is called
        self.name = name              # data stored on the object

    def speak(self):                  # behaviour that uses the object's data
        return f"{self.name} says Woof"

d = Dog("Rex")                        # create an instance
print(d.speak())
print(type(d).__name__)               # the class this object came from

# OUTPUT:
# Rex says Woof
# Dog

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Without classes, data and the functions that work on it drift apart (a dict here, ten loose functions there). A class keeps state and the rules that protect it in one place, so large programs stay understandable.
codeExamples:
# Procedural: data and logic are separate; nothing stops bad usage
acct = {"balance": 100}
def deposit(a, amt): a["balance"] += amt

# OOP: state + behaviour travel together
class Account:
    def __init__(self, balance):
        self.balance = balance
    def deposit(self, amt):
        self.balance += amt

a = Account(100)
a.deposit(50)
print(a.balance)

# OUTPUT:
# 150

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real systems: Django/SQLAlchemy models (one class per table), GUI widgets, game entities, HTTP clients and every framework you plug into by subclassing.

Diagram

   class Dog  (blueprint)
   ┌──────────────────────────┐
   │ attrs:   name            │
   │ methods: speak()         │
   └────────────┬─────────────┘
                │ Dog("Rex")      Dog("Fido")
        ┌───────┴────────┐     ┌──────┴─────────┐
        │ obj 1          │     │ obj 2          │
        │ name = "Rex"   │     │ name = "Fido"  │
        └────────────────┘     └────────────────┘

expert.content:
How Python OOP Differs from Java

FeatureJavaPython
Access controlprivate/protected/public enforced by the compilerConventions only: _name (internal), __name (name-mangled)
Method overloadingSeveral methods with the same nameNo - the last def wins; use default and variable arguments
TypingNominal: must implement the interfaceDuck typing: any object with the right methods works
InheritanceSingle class inheritance + interfacesMultiple inheritance, resolved by the MRO
Classes at runtimeMostly fixed after compilationClasses are objects; attributes can be added to objects and classes at runtime
thisImplicitself is an explicit first parameter
FieldsDeclared in the class bodyUsually created by assignment in __init__

Duck Typing in Action

No shared base class or interface is needed - Python only cares that the object has the method being called.

Objects Are Open by Default

A normal Python object stores its attributes in a dictionary, so new attributes can be attached at runtime - even to a class. It is flexible, but a typo silently creates a new attribute instead of failing. Later topics show __slots__, @property and dataclasses for tighter control.

Modern Shortcut: dataclasses

For classes that mainly hold data, @dataclass writes __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ for you - similar to Java records or Lombok.
codeExamples:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Product:
    name: str
    price: float
    qty: int = 1

pen = Product("Pen", 12.5, 4)
print(pen)
print(pen == Product("Pen", 12.5, 4))

# OUTPUT:
# Product(name='Pen', price=12.5, qty=4)
# True

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Class vs object?A class is the blueprint; an object is an instance created from it with its own data
What are the four pillars of OOP?Encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and abstraction
Does Python have private members?Not enforced - _name is a convention, __name triggers name mangling
Does Python support method overloading?No - use default arguments, *args/**kwargs or functools.singledispatch
What is duck typing?Using any object that provides the needed methods, regardless of its class
Is a class an object in Python?Yes - classes are instances of type

Advantages

Advantages: reuse through inheritance, clear modelling of real-world things, state kept next to its rules, easy extension (add a new class, leave old code alone).
codeExamples:
# Reuse: Cat gets describe() for free from Animal
class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
    def describe(self):
        return f"I am {self.name}"

class Cat(Animal):          # inherits everything from Animal
    pass

print(Cat("Tom").describe())

# OUTPUT:
# I am Tom

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: easy to over-engineer. A class with one method and no state is just a function with extra ceremony; deep hierarchies are hard to follow.
codeExamples:
# Over-engineered: a class used as a function
class Adder:
    def __init__(self, a, b):
        self.a, self.b = a, b
    def run(self):
        return self.a + self.b

def add(a, b):              # the simple version does the same job
    return a + b

print(Adder(2, 3).run(), add(2, 3))

# OUTPUT:
# 5 5

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: Python has no truly private members; encapsulation is by convention. Anyone can read or overwrite an object's attributes.

Architect's Notes

Use classes when you have state that must obey invariants or several interchangeable behaviours. Prefer plain functions, dataclasses and composition for simple data and one-off logic; Python is multi-paradigm, so do not force everything into a hierarchy.

beginner.content:
Instance Attributes

An instance attribute is a variable that belongs to one object. It is created by assigning to self.name, usually in __init__. Each object has its own copy - changing one object never changes another. They play the role of Java's instance fields, but are not declared in advance.
codeExamples:
class Course:
    def __init__(self, title, fee):
        self.title = title
        self.fee = fee

java = Course("Core Java", 4999)
python = Course("Python", 3999)

python.fee = 2999                 # change one object only
print(java.title, java.fee)
print(python.title, python.fee)

# OUTPUT:
# Core Java 4999
# Python 2999

beginner.content:
Methods and self

A method is a function defined inside a class. Its first parameter, by convention named self, receives the object the method was called on - so the method can read and change that object's attributes.

Missing Attributes

Reading an attribute that doesn't exist raises AttributeError.
codeExamples:
class Course:
    def __init__(self, title):
        self.title = title

c = Course("Python")
print(c.title)
print(c.duration)

# OUTPUT:
# Python
# AttributeError: 'Course' object has no attribute 'duration'

beginner.content:
Attributes Can Be Added Later - But Shouldn't Be

Python lets you attach a new attribute to an object at any time. It works, but only that one object gets it, and readers of the class can't see it exists. Create every attribute in __init__ (use None if there is no value yet).
codeExamples:
class Course:
    def __init__(self, title):
        self.title = title
        self.mentor = None          # declared up front, even if unknown

a = Course("Python")
b = Course("Java")
a.discount = 10                 # only a has this

print(a.discount)
print(hasattr(b, "discount"))

# OUTPUT:
# 10
# False

beginner.content:
__dict__ and the Attribute Functions

An object's attributes live in a dictionary, obj.__dict__. The built-ins getattr, setattr, hasattr and delattr work with attribute names given as strings - handy when the name comes from data.
codeExamples:
class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, city):
        self.name = name
        self.city = city

s = Student("Abaji", "Pune")
print(s.__dict__)

field = "city"
print(getattr(s, field))
setattr(s, "marks", 91)
print(hasattr(s, "marks"), getattr(s, "email", "not set"))
delattr(s, "city")
print(s.__dict__)

# OUTPUT:
# {'name': 'Abaji', 'city': 'Pune'}
# Pune
# True not set
# {'name': 'Abaji', 'marks': 91}

beginner.content:
Introduction

Attributes are variables attached to a class or an object; methods are functions defined in a class that receive the instance as the first argument (self).
codeExamples:
class Car:
    wheels = 4                         # class attribute: shared by all cars

    def __init__(self, color):
        self.color = color             # instance attribute: one per car

    def describe(self):                # method
        return f"{self.color} car with {self.wheels} wheels"

c = Car("red")
print(c.describe())

# OUTPUT:
# red car with 4 wheels

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Objects must hold state and expose operations. Python also lets you read and write attributes by name at runtime, which frameworks use for configuration and serialization.
codeExamples:
class Settings:
    pass

s = Settings()
setattr(s, "debug", True)              # same as s.debug = True, name is a string
print(getattr(s, "debug"))             # read by name
print(getattr(s, "port", 8080))        # default when missing
print(hasattr(s, "host"))

# OUTPUT:
# True
# 8080
# False

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Serializers, ORMs and form libraries loop over an object's attributes. vars(obj) exposes them as a dict, ready for JSON.

Diagram

   obj.color ──► look in obj.__dict__ ──found──► value
                       │ not found
                       ▼
                 look in Class.__dict__ ──found──► value / bound method
                       │ not found
                       ▼
                 look in parent classes (MRO) ──► else AttributeError

expert.content:
obj.method() Is Class.method(obj)

When you look up a method on an instance, Python returns a bound method: the function with the instance already filled in as self. Calling obj.method(x) is exactly Class.method(obj, x). That is why self must be written explicitly in the definition - it really is just the first argument.
codeExamples:
class Greeter:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def greet(self, other):
        return f"{self.name} greets {other}"

g = Greeter("Abaji")
print(g.greet("Raoji"))
print(Greeter.greet(g, "Raoji"))      # identical call

bound = g.greet                      # a bound method object
print(bound("Kanhoji"))
print(bound.__self__ is g, bound.__func__ is Greeter.greet)

# OUTPUT:
# Abaji greets Raoji
# Abaji greets Raoji
# Abaji greets Kanhoji
# True True

expert.content:
Attribute Lookup Order

For obj.x, Python checks the instance (obj.__dict__) first, then the class, then the base classes in MRO order (a simplification - data descriptors such as properties take priority, covered later). Methods are found on the class, which is why every instance shares one copy of each method.
codeExamples:
class Base:
    level = "base"

class Child(Base):
    kind = "child-class"

c = Child()
print(c.level, c.kind)       # found on Base and Child
c.kind = "instance"          # instance attribute now shadows the class one
print(c.kind, Child.kind)
print("greet" in c.__dict__, "kind" in c.__dict__)

# OUTPUT:
# base child-class
# instance child-class
# False True

expert.content:
Preview: __slots__

Declaring __slots__ replaces the per-instance __dict__ with fixed storage for the listed names. Objects use less memory and typos fail loudly instead of creating new attributes. It is covered in depth in the Advanced Python module.
codeExamples:
class Point:
    __slots__ = ("x", "y")

    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

p = Point(1, 2)
p.x = 10
print(p.x, hasattr(p, "__dict__"))
p.z = 3

# OUTPUT:
# 10 False
# AttributeError: 'Point' object has no attribute 'z'

expert.content:
Methods vs Attributes: Forgetting the Parentheses

obj.method without () is the bound method object itself, which is always truthy - a classic bug in conditions.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Where are instance attributes stored?In the object's __dict__ (unless the class uses __slots__)
What is self?The instance the method is called on, passed automatically as the first argument
What does obj.method(x) translate to?type(obj).method(obj, x) - via a bound method
How do you read an attribute whose name is in a string?getattr(obj, name, default)
In what order is an attribute looked up?Instance, then class, then base classes along the MRO (data descriptors first)
Why not add attributes outside __init__?Objects end up with different shapes, the class no longer documents its data, and typos go unnoticed

Advantages

Advantages: attributes can be added, inspected and removed dynamically; methods are bound to the object automatically.
codeExamples:
class Box: pass
b = Box()
b.size = 10                            # add an attribute on the fly
print(b.size)
del b.size                             # remove it again
print(hasattr(b, "size"))

# OUTPUT:
# 10
# False

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: a typo silently creates a brand new attribute instead of raising an error.

Limitations

Limitations: every instance carries a __dict__ (memory cost). __slots__ removes it and blocks unknown attributes, but gives up flexibility.

Architect's Notes

Attribute lookup (instance, then class, then bases) is the engine behind everything in Python OOP. Use __slots__ for millions of small objects, dataclasses for plain data, and properties when an attribute needs validation; do not scatter dynamic setattr through business code.

beginner.content:
__init__: Setting Up a New Object

__init__ runs automatically every time you create an object with ClassName(...). It receives the arguments you passed and stores them as attributes. It plays the role of a Java constructor - strictly it is an initialiser: the object already exists when __init__ runs, it just fills it in.
codeExamples:
class Employee:
    def __init__(self, name, salary):
        print("__init__ running for", name)
        self.name = name
        self.salary = salary

e = Employee("Raoji", 45000)
print(e.name, e.salary)

# OUTPUT:
# __init__ running for Raoji
# Raoji 45000

beginner.content:
What Is self?

self is the object being created or used. In Java the current object is available implicitly as this; Python makes it an explicit first parameter of every instance method. You never pass it yourself - Python does.

• self.name = name - the left side is an attribute of the object, the right side is the local parameter.
• Forgetting self. creates a local variable that disappears when __init__ ends.

Default Values Instead of Constructor Overloading

Java often provides several constructors. Python has only one __init__; default parameter values cover the same cases.
codeExamples:
class Ticket:
    def __init__(self, passenger, seat="any", meal="veg"):
        self.passenger = passenger
        self.seat = seat
        self.meal = meal

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.passenger} | {self.seat} | {self.meal}"

print(Ticket("Abaji"))
print(Ticket("Raoji", "12A"))
print(Ticket("Kanhoji", meal="jain"))

# OUTPUT:
# Abaji   | any | veg
# Raoji   | 12A | veg
# Kanhoji | any | jain

beginner.content:
Validating in __init__

The initialiser is the right place to reject bad data, so an invalid object can never exist.
codeExamples:
class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, marks):
        if not name.strip():
            raise ValueError("name is required")
        if not 0 <= marks <= 100:
            raise ValueError(f"marks must be 0-100, got {marks}")
        self.name = name.strip()
        self.marks = marks

s = Student("Abaji", 91)
print(s.name, s.marks)
Student("Raoji", 120)

# OUTPUT:
# Abaji 91
# ValueError: marks must be 0-100, got 120

beginner.content:
Calling the Wrong Number of Arguments

The error counts only the arguments you pass - self is supplied automatically.
codeExamples:
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

Point(1)

# OUTPUT:
# TypeError: Point.__init__() missing 1 required positional argument: 'y'

beginner.content:
Introduction
