The constructor hook is __init__: Python calls it on a freshly created object to set its initial state. self is that object, passed automatically as the first argument; the name is a convention, not a keyword.
codeExamples:
class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, grade):
        self.name = name               # self = the new object
        self.grade = grade

    def whoami(self):
        return self                    # self is just the object itself

s = Student("Ann", 10)
print(s.name, s.grade)
print(s.whoami() is s)

# OUTPUT:
# Ann 10
# True

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Without a constructor every object starts empty and callers must remember to fill each field. __init__ guarantees a valid starting state, with defaults.
codeExamples:
class Server:
    def __init__(self, host="localhost", port=8000, tags=None):
        self.host = host
        self.port = port
        self.tags = tags if tags is not None else []   # never use [] as default!

a, b = Server(), Server("example.com", 443)
a.tags.append("dev")
print(a.host, a.port, a.tags)
print(b.host, b.port, b.tags)

# OUTPUT:
# localhost 8000 ['dev']
# example.com 443 []

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Alternative constructors via @classmethod build objects from other formats (CSV rows, JSON, environment).

Diagram

   Student("Ann", 10)
        │
        ▼
   ┌───────────────────┐   1. __new__(cls)        -> allocate empty object
   │ type.__call__     │   2. __init__(self, ...) -> fill it with state
   └───────────────────┘   3. return the object
        │
        ▼
   s ──► { name: "Ann", grade: 10 }

expert.content:
How an Object Is Created

ClassName(args) does two steps:
1. __new__(cls, ...) creates the empty object (inherited from object; you rarely override it).
2. __init__(self, ...) initialises it, if __new__ returned an instance of the class.

Override __new__ only for special cases: subclassing immutable types like int/str/tuple, caching instances, or singletons.

__new__ for Immutable Types

An immutable object's value must be set when it is created, so subclasses of str, int or tuple customise __new__, not __init__.

__init__ Must Return None

__init__ cannot return the object or any other value - Python raises TypeError if it does.

Alternative Constructors with @classmethod

Instead of overloaded constructors, Python uses named factory methods decorated with @classmethod - like dict.fromkeys or datetime.fromisoformat. Class and static methods have their own topic; here is the pattern.

Keep __init__ Simple

• Assign every attribute in __init__ so the object's shape is clear.
• Avoid slow work (network calls, file reads) - pass dependencies in or use a factory method.
• Don't call methods that subclasses may override before all attributes are set.
• For plain data holders, let @dataclass generate __init__ and add checks in __post_init__.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Is __init__ a constructor?It is an initialiser - __new__ creates the object, __init__ sets it up
Why is self explicit in Python?A method is a plain function; self is just its first argument, filled in when called through an instance
How do you get multiple constructors?Default arguments, or alternative constructors with @classmethod
When would you override __new__?Subclassing immutable types, instance caching or singletons
What may __init__ return?Only None - anything else raises TypeError
Is self a keyword?No - it is a convention, but always follow it

Advantages

Advantages: a single place to validate input and enforce invariants so no invalid object can exist.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: there is only one __init__ per class; defining it twice silently replaces the first (no overloading).

Limitations

Limitations: __init__ initialises, it does not create: the object already exists (made by __new__), and __init__ must return None.

Architect's Notes

Keep __init__ cheap and side-effect free (no network or file work) so objects are easy to test; inject dependencies through parameters. Prefer classmethod factories over many optional arguments, and use __new__ only for immutable subclasses or singletons.

beginner.content:
What is Encapsulation?

Encapsulation means keeping an object's data together with the methods that work on it, and letting outside code use the object through those methods rather than poking at its internals. The object can then enforce its own rules - a balance never goes negative, marks stay between 0 and 100.

Java enforces this with private fields and getters/setters. Python has no access modifiers; it relies on naming conventions instead.

Three Levels by Convention

NameMeaningEnforced?
balancePublic - part of the API-
_balanceInternal - "please don't use this from outside" (like protected)No, convention only
__balanceName-mangled - renamed to _ClassName__balanceMakes accidental access harder, not impossible
Protecting Data Through Methods

Double Underscore: Name Mangling

An attribute named __pin inside class Account is stored as _Account__pin. The plain name doesn't work from outside the class.
codeExamples:
class Account:
    def __init__(self, pin):
        self.__pin = pin

    def check_pin(self, pin):
        return pin == self.__pin          # inside the class the short name works

acc = Account("4321")
print(acc.check_pin("4321"))
print(acc.__dict__)
print(acc._Account__pin)                  # still reachable - not real security
print(acc.__pin)

# OUTPUT:
# True
# {'_Account__pin': '4321'}
# 4321
# AttributeError: 'Account' object has no attribute '__pin'

beginner.content:
"We Are All Consenting Adults"

Python's philosophy is to trust developers: a leading underscore clearly says "internal", and anyone who uses it anyway accepts the risk that it may change. This keeps the language simple and makes debugging and testing easier. Expose behaviour (methods like deposit) rather than raw data, and the convention works well in practice.

Introduction

Encapsulation means bundling data with the methods that operate on it and controlling outside access. Python relies on conventions: _name means "internal", __name triggers name mangling.
codeExamples:
class Account:
    def __init__(self):
        self.owner = "Ann"             # public
        self._balance = 100            # protected by convention
        self.__pin = 1234              # name-mangled to _Account__pin

a = Account()
print(a.owner, a._balance)
try:
    print(a.__pin)
except AttributeError:
    print("no attribute __pin")
print(a._Account__pin)                 # still reachable, just renamed

# OUTPUT:
# Ann 100
# no attribute __pin
# 1234

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

If anyone can write balance = -500, invariants break. Routing changes through methods lets the class refuse invalid states.

Real-Time Use

Libraries expose a small public API and hide internals so they can change them later. Anything starting with an underscore is "do not depend on this".

Diagram

   outside code
        │  only the public door
        ▼
   ┌─────────────────────────────┐
   │ Wallet                      │
   │  public:  spend() money     │
   │  ┌───────────────────────┐  │
   │  │ _money  (internal)    │  │
   │  └───────────────────────┘  │
   └─────────────────────────────┘

expert.content:
What Name Mangling Is Really For

Mangling exists to avoid name clashes in subclasses, not to hide data. If a parent and a child both use __id, each gets its own mangled attribute, so the child can't accidentally overwrite the parent's internal state.

Properties Instead of Getters and Setters

Java code starts with private fields plus getX()/setX() "just in case". Python starts with a public attribute; if validation is needed later, @property turns attribute access into method calls without changing callers. It has its own topic - here is the idea, including a read-only attribute.

Immutable Objects

The strongest encapsulation is data that can't change. @dataclass(frozen=True) blocks assignment after creation (and makes instances hashable). "Changes" create a new object with dataclasses.replace.
codeExamples:
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace, FrozenInstanceError

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Money:
    amount: int
    currency: str = "INR"

price = Money(500)
try:
    price.amount = 0
except FrozenInstanceError:
    print("cannot modify a frozen object")

discounted = replace(price, amount=450)
print(price, discounted)

# OUTPUT:
# cannot modify a frozen object
# Money(amount=500, currency='INR') Money(amount=450, currency='INR')

expert.content:
Don't Leak Mutable Internals

Returning an internal list lets callers modify the object behind its back. Return a copy or a tuple.

Python vs Java

JavaPython
public fieldPlain attribute
protected_name (convention)
private__name (mangling) or _name
Getter/setter methods@property when needed
final fieldRead-only property, frozen dataclass, typing.Final hint

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Does Python have private variables?No enforced ones - _x is a convention, __x is name-mangled to _Class__x
What is name mangling for?Avoiding accidental attribute clashes between a class and its subclasses
Should you write getters and setters?Not by default - use public attributes and switch to @property when logic is needed
How do you make a read-only attribute?A @property without a setter, or a frozen dataclass
What does "consenting adults" mean?Python trusts developers to respect underscore conventions instead of enforcing access rules

Advantages

Advantages: you can change the internal representation without breaking users of the class.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: writing Java-style getters/setters for every field is verbose; in Python a plain public attribute is usually better until you need logic (then use a property).
codeExamples:
class Verbose:                      # un-Pythonic
    def __init__(self): self._x = 0
    def get_x(self): return self._x
    def set_x(self, v): self._x = v

class Simple:                       # Pythonic
    def __init__(self): self.x = 0

v, s = Verbose(), Simple()
v.set_x(5); s.x = 5
print(v.get_x(), s.x)

# OUTPUT:
# 5 5

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: nothing is truly private. Name mangling only renames; a determined caller can still change the value.
codeExamples:
class Account:
    def __init__(self):
        self.__pin = 1234

a = Account()
a._Account__pin = 0                    # bypasses the "private" attribute
print(a._Account__pin)
print([k for k in vars(a)])

# OUTPUT:
# 0
# ['_Account__pin']

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Python's philosophy is "we are all consenting adults": document the public API, prefix internals with an underscore and validate in methods or properties. Reserve __mangling for avoiding name clashes in subclasses, not for security; real security needs process or service boundaries.

beginner.content:
What is Inheritance?

Inheritance lets a new class (the child or subclass) reuse the attributes and methods of an existing class (the parent or base class), then add or change what it needs. It models an "is-a" relationship: a Car is a Vehicle. Python writes the parent in parentheses where Java writes extends.
codeExamples:
class Vehicle:
    def __init__(self, brand):
        self.brand = brand

    def start(self):
        return f"{self.brand} is starting"

class Car(Vehicle):              # Java: class Car extends Vehicle
    pass

c = Car("Tata")
print(c.start())                 # inherited method
print(c.brand)                   # inherited attribute

# OUTPUT:
# Tata is starting
# Tata

beginner.content:
Extending the Parent

A child can add new methods and attributes. To keep the parent's set-up, call its __init__ with super().__init__(...) (the super() topic covers it in detail).
codeExamples:
class Vehicle:
    def __init__(self, brand):
        self.brand = brand

    def start(self):
        return f"{self.brand} is starting"

class Car(Vehicle):
    def __init__(self, brand, seats):
        super().__init__(brand)          # let Vehicle set brand
        self.seats = seats               # Car's own attribute

    def describe(self):                  # new method
        return f"{self.brand} car with {self.seats} seats"

c = Car("Mahindra", 7)
print(c.start())
print(c.describe())

# OUTPUT:
# Mahindra is starting
# Mahindra car with 7 seats

beginner.content:
Overriding a Method

Defining a method with the same name in the child replaces the parent's version for child objects (the Method Overriding topic goes deeper).

isinstance() and issubclass()

A child object is also an instance of every parent class. Every class ultimately inherits from object, just as every Java class extends Object.
codeExamples:
class Animal:
    pass

class Dog(Animal):
    pass

d = Dog()
print(isinstance(d, Dog), isinstance(d, Animal), isinstance(d, object))
print(issubclass(Dog, Animal), issubclass(Animal, Dog))
print(Dog.__bases__, Animal.__bases__)

# OUTPUT:
# True True True
# True False
# (<class '__main__.Animal'>,) (<class 'object'>,)

beginner.content:
Introduction

Inheritance lets a child class reuse and extend a parent class, forming an "is-a" relationship: a Dog is an Animal.
codeExamples:
class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
    def eat(self):
        return f"{self.name} eats"

class Dog(Animal):                     # Dog inherits from Animal
    def bark(self):
        return f"{self.name} barks"

d = Dog("Rex")
print(d.eat())
print(d.bark())
print(isinstance(d, Animal), issubclass(Dog, Animal))

# OUTPUT:
# Rex eats
# Rex barks
# True True

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Copy-pasting shared code into many classes means fixing each bug many times. Inheritance puts shared behaviour in one place.

Real-Time Use

Exception hierarchies are the most common real use: catch one base class to handle a whole family of errors.
codeExamples:
class AppError(Exception): pass
class NotFound(AppError): pass
class Forbidden(AppError): pass

def handler(kind):
    if kind == "nf": raise NotFound("page missing")
    raise Forbidden("no access")

for k in ("nf", "fb"):
    try:
        handler(k)
    except AppError as e:                  # one except catches both children
        print(type(e).__name__, "->", e)

# OUTPUT:
# NotFound -> page missing
# Forbidden -> no access

beginner.content:
Diagram

          ┌──────────┐
          │ Animal   │  eat()
          └────┬─────┘
        ┌──────┴───────┐
   ┌────┴─────┐   ┌────┴─────┐
   │ Dog      │   │ Cat      │
   │ bark()   │   │ meow()   │
   └──────────┘   └──────────┘
   child ──is-a──► parent

expert.content:
Inheritance vs Composition

Inheritance means "is-a"; composition means "has-a" - an object holds other objects and delegates to them. Composition is usually more flexible: parts can be swapped, and you don't inherit methods you don't want. Prefer it unless the child truly is a specialised kind of the parent.

Signs of a Bad Hierarchy

• Deep chains (5+ levels): behaviour is scattered and hard to trace.
• Refused bequest: a child overrides a parent method just to raise an error, because it isn't really that kind of thing.
• Inheritance only to reuse code, with no real is-a relationship - use composition or a helper function.
• Fragile base class: a small change in the parent silently breaks children.

Inheriting from Built-in Types

You can subclass list, dict or str, but the built-ins are implemented in C and their methods don't call each other through your overrides. Overriding __setitem__ on a dict subclass is ignored by update() and the constructor. collections.UserDict / UserList are written in Python and respect overrides.

Python vs Java Inheritance

AspectJavaPython
Syntaxclass B extends Aclass B(A):
Multiple inheritanceClasses: no (interfaces: yes)Yes - class C(A, B):, ordered by the MRO
Root classObjectobject
Preventing inheritancefinal classNo keyword; typing.final is a hint for type checkers
Parent constructorsuper(...) must be firstsuper().__init__(...) - optional, anywhere, but usually first
Overriding check@Overridetyping.override (3.12+), for type checkers
Multiple inheritance and method resolution order have their own topic.

Forgetting to Call the Parent __init__

If the child defines __init__ and doesn't call super().__init__(), the parent's attributes are never created - an AttributeError appears later, far from the cause.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How do you inherit in Python?Put the parent class in parentheses: class Child(Parent):
Does Python support multiple inheritance?Yes - the MRO (C3 linearisation) decides lookup order
What does every class inherit from?object
Inheritance vs composition?Inheritance models is-a and shares implementation; composition models has-a and delegates - usually more flexible
Why subclass UserDict instead of dict?dict's C methods (update, constructor) bypass overridden methods; UserDict respects them
What happens if a child __init__ doesn't call super().__init__()?The parent's initialisation is skipped, so its attributes are missing

Advantages

Advantages: code reuse, a natural type hierarchy and polymorphism (a child can be used wherever a parent is expected).
codeExamples:
class Shape:
    def area(self): return 0
class Square(Shape):
    def __init__(self, s): self.s = s
    def area(self): return self.s ** 2

shapes = [Shape(), Square(3)]
print([s.area() for s in shapes])

# OUTPUT:
# [0, 9]

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: tight coupling. A child inherits everything, including methods that break its rules (the fragile base class problem).
codeExamples:
class Stack(list):                    # "is-a list" - but too much exposed
    def push(self, x): self.append(x)

s = Stack()
s.push(1); s.push(2)
s.insert(0, 9)                         # list method breaks stack discipline
print(s)
print(s.pop())

# OUTPUT:
# [9, 1, 2]
# 2

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: some built-in types cannot be subclassed, and a class can only extend what is designed to be extended.
codeExamples:
try:
    class MyBool(bool):                # bool is final
        pass
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)

# OUTPUT:
# TypeError: type 'bool' is not an acceptable base type

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Favour composition ("has-a") over inheritance when you only want to reuse code; inherit only for a genuine is-a relationship and keep hierarchies shallow (2-3 levels). Wrapping a list inside a Stack class is safer than subclassing list.

beginner.content:
What is Polymorphism?

Polymorphism ("many forms") means one interface, many behaviours: code calls the same method on different objects, and each object responds in its own way. The caller doesn't need to know the exact class.

Polymorphism Through Inheritance

As in Java, subclasses override a method of a common base class, and code written against the base class works with every subclass.

Duck Typing: No Common Base Class Needed

Java needs a shared interface or superclass before two classes can be used interchangeably. Python only needs the method to exist: "if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck".

Built-in Polymorphism

You have been using polymorphism all along: len(), + and for work on many different types.
codeExamples:
print(len("hello"), len([1, 2, 3]), len({"a": 1}))
print(1 + 2, "ab" + "cd", [1] + [2])

for item in ("x", "y"):
    print(item, end=" ")
for ch in "hi":
    print(ch, end=" ")
print()

# OUTPUT:
# 5 3 1
# 3 abcd [1, 2]
# x y h i

beginner.content:
Introduction

Polymorphism ("many forms") means different classes respond to the same method call in their own way. Python uses duck typing: if it has the method, it works; no common parent required.
codeExamples:
class Circle:
    def __init__(self, r): self.r = r
    def area(self): return 3.14 * self.r * self.r

class Rect:
    def __init__(self, w, h): self.w, self.h = w, h
    def area(self): return self.w * self.h

for shape in (Circle(2), Rect(2, 3)):      # same call, different behaviour
    print(type(shape).__name__, shape.area())

# OUTPUT:
# Circle 12.56
# Rect 6

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Without polymorphism, code fills up with if type == ... chains that must be edited for every new type.
codeExamples:
class Email:
    def send(self, msg): return f"email: {msg}"
class Sms:
    def send(self, msg): return f"sms: {msg}"

def notify(channel, msg):                  # knows nothing about concrete types
    return channel.send(msg)

print(notify(Email(), "hi"))
print(notify(Sms(), "hi"))

# OUTPUT:
# email: hi
# sms: hi

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Built-ins are polymorphic: len, + and for work on many types. Payment, storage and logging backends are swapped the same way.
codeExamples:
print(len("abc"), len([1, 2]), len({"a": 1}))   # len works on many types
print(1 + 2, "a" + "b", [1] + [2])             # + means different things

# OUTPUT:
# 3 2 1
# 3 ab [1, 2]

beginner.content:
Diagram

   shape.area()
        │
        ├──► Circle.area()  -> pi*r*r
        ├──► Rect.area()    -> w*h
        └──► Tri.area()     -> b*h/2
   one call site, many implementations

expert.content:
No Method Overloading

Java resolves overloads at compile time by parameter types. Python has no overloading: a second def with the same name replaces the first. Use default values, *args, or functools.singledispatch (dispatch on the type of the first argument).

Operator Overloading Is Polymorphism Too

Defining special methods such as __add__, __eq__ or __len__ lets your objects respond to operators and built-ins. The Python Data Model module covers this in depth.

Making Duck Typing Checkable: Protocols

Duck typing is checked only at runtime - a missing method fails when it is called. typing.Protocol (see Interfaces using Protocols) describes the required methods so tools like mypy can check them before running, still without inheritance.

Java vs Python Polymorphism

AspectJavaPython
Compile-time (overloading)Yes - chosen by parameter typesNo - use defaults, *args or singledispatch
Runtime (overriding)Yes - virtual methodsYes - every method is "virtual"
Requirement to be interchangeableCommon interface/superclassJust the right methods (duck typing)
Operator overloadingNot for user classesYes, via special methods
When errors appearCompile timeRuntime (or with a type checker)

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is polymorphism?The ability to call the same method on different objects and get type-specific behaviour
Does Python support method overloading?No - the last definition wins; use default arguments, *args or functools.singledispatch
What is duck typing?Using an object by the methods it has, not by its class or base class
Are Python methods virtual?Yes - the method is looked up on the actual object's class at call time
Give examples of built-in polymorphismlen() on str/list/dict, + on numbers/strings/lists, iteration over any iterable

Advantages

Advantages: add a new type without touching existing code (open/closed principle); simpler call sites.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: duck typing is checked only at runtime; a missing method fails when that line runs.

Limitations

Limitations: Python has no method overloading by argument type. Use functools.singledispatch for type-based dispatch.

Architect's Notes

Depend on behaviour (a method contract), not on concrete classes. Document the contract with a Protocol or ABC so static checkers catch mismatches that duck typing would only reveal at runtime.

beginner.content:
What is Abstraction?

Abstraction means exposing what an object does through a simple interface while hiding how it does it. You drive a car with a steering wheel and pedals without knowing how the engine works. In code, callers use a few clear methods; the messy details stay inside.

Designing a Simple API

The caller only needs pay(amount). Validation, fees and talking to the bank are hidden behind it - and can change without affecting callers.

Abstraction at Every Level

LevelWhat it hidesExample
FunctionA sequence of stepscalculate_gst(amount)
ClassData plus the rules for changing itaccount.withdraw(500)
ModuleA whole featurejson.dumps(data)
Package / libraryA subsystemrequests.get(url)
codeExamples:
import json

# You never see how json builds the string - just call the abstraction
print(json.dumps({"course": "Python", "modules": 40}))
print(sorted([3, 1, 2]))          # which sorting algorithm? you don't need to know

# OUTPUT:
# {"course": "Python", "modules": 40}
# [1, 2, 3]

beginner.content:
Abstraction vs Encapsulation

They work together but are not the same: abstraction is about the design of a simple interface; encapsulation (its own topic) is about protecting the internal data behind that interface.

Introduction

Abstraction exposes what an object does and hides how. Callers use a simple interface while complicated steps stay inside.
codeExamples:
class Coffee:
    def make(self):                        # one simple public method
        self._boil(); self._brew()
        return "coffee ready"
    def _boil(self): pass                  # hidden detail
    def _brew(self): pass                  # hidden detail

print(Coffee().make())

# OUTPUT:
# coffee ready

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Complexity overwhelms. If every caller had to know the ten steps of charging a card, any change would ripple everywhere.
codeExamples:
class PaymentGateway:
    def charge(self, amount):              # callers see only this
        token = self._tokenize()
        self._call_bank(token, amount)
        return f"charged {amount}"
    def _tokenize(self): return "tok_123"
    def _call_bank(self, token, amount): pass

print(PaymentGateway().charge(25))

# OUTPUT:
# charged 25

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Database drivers, file objects and HTTP clients all present one small interface (read, write, get) over very different internals.
codeExamples:
import io
for f in (io.StringIO("hello"), io.BytesIO(b"hello")):
    print(f.read())                        # same call, different internals

# OUTPUT:
# hello
# b'hello'

beginner.content:
Diagram

   caller ──► ┌──────────────────────┐
              │ public interface     │  charge(amount)
              ├──────────────────────┤
              │ hidden: tokenize()   │
              │         call_bank()  │
              │         log()        │
              └──────────────────────┘

expert.content:
A Base Class as a Contract

A base class can define the operations every implementation must provide. The simplest version raises NotImplementedError - but that is only detected when the method is called. An incomplete subclass can still be created.
codeExamples:
class Storage:
    def save(self, key, data):
        raise NotImplementedError("subclasses must implement save()")

class DiskStorage(Storage):
    pass                                  # forgot to implement save()

s = DiskStorage()                         # no error yet!
print("created", type(s).__name__)
s.save("a", 1)

# OUTPUT:
# created DiskStorage
# NotImplementedError: subclasses must implement save()

expert.content:
Enforcing It with an Abstract Base Class

With abc.ABC and @abstractmethod, Python refuses to create an object of a class that hasn't implemented every abstract method - the error appears early, like Java's compile-time check. The Abstract Classes & ABC topic covers this fully.

Leaky Abstractions

An abstraction "leaks" when callers must know about the hidden details to use it correctly - for example a method that returns a raw database row, or raises a low-level KeyError from an internal dict. Good abstractions return domain values and raise domain exceptions.

Java vs Python

JavaPython
abstract classA class inheriting ABC with @abstractmethods
interfaceAn ABC with only abstract methods, or a typing.Protocol
private helpersNames starting with _ (by convention)
Missing implementation caught at compile timeCaught when instantiating (ABC) or calling (NotImplementedError)

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is abstraction?Exposing a simple interface for what an object does while hiding how it does it
Abstraction vs encapsulation?Abstraction designs the simple interface; encapsulation protects the internal state behind it
NotImplementedError vs @abstractmethod?NotImplementedError fails only when the method is called; an ABC refuses to instantiate an incomplete subclass
How is abstraction achieved in Python?Functions, classes with small public APIs, modules, ABCs and Protocols
What is a leaky abstraction?One that forces callers to know its internal details, e.g. by returning raw internal data or low-level exceptions

Advantages

Advantages: less coupling, implementations can be replaced, easier testing with fakes.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: abstractions can leak or add needless indirection (layers that only forward calls).
codeExamples:
class Wrapper:                           # adds nothing, only forwards
    def __init__(self, inner): self.inner = inner
    def run(self): return self.inner.run()

class Real:
    def run(self): return "done"

print(Wrapper(Real()).run())               # one extra hop for no benefit

# OUTPUT:
# done

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: without abc, Python does not force subclasses to implement the abstract part; the error appears only when the method is called.

Architect's Notes

Good abstractions are small and stable; create one only when you have two real implementations or a real need to isolate change. Enforce them with ABCs or Protocols, and avoid speculative layers that make the code harder to follow.

beginner.content:
Two Kinds of Variables in a Class

• An instance variable belongs to one object. It is usually created in __init__ with self.name = ..., and every object has its own copy.
• A class variable is defined directly in the class body. There is one copy, shared by all objects - like a static field in Java.
codeExamples:
class Student:
    school = "DHIPAN Academy"          # class variable - shared

    def __init__(self, name, marks):
        self.name = name                # instance variables - per object
        self.marks = marks

a = Student("Abaji", 91)
b = Student("Raoji", 78)

print(a.name, a.marks, a.school)
print(b.name, b.marks, b.school)
print(Student.school)                   # read it through the class too

# OUTPUT:
# Abaji 91 DHIPAN Academy
# Raoji 78 DHIPAN Academy
# DHIPAN Academy

beginner.content:
Changing a Class Variable Affects Everyone

Assign through the class name to change the shared value.
codeExamples:
class Student:
    school = "DHIPAN Academy"

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

a = Student("Abaji")
b = Student("Raoji")

Student.school = "DHIPAN Institute"     # change it once, on the class
print(a.school, "|", b.school)

# OUTPUT:
# DHIPAN Institute | DHIPAN Institute

beginner.content:
Counting Instances

A class variable is the natural place for data about the class as a whole, such as how many objects have been created.
codeExamples:
class Order:
    count = 0                           # shared counter

    def __init__(self, item):
        Order.count += 1                # update via the class
        self.order_no = Order.count     # each order gets its own number
        self.item = item

o1 = Order("pen")
o2 = Order("book")
o3 = Order("bag")
print(Order.count, o1.order_no, o3.order_no)

# OUTPUT:
# 3 1 3

beginner.content:
Constants on the Class

Values that are the same for every object and never change - limits, rates, defaults - are written as UPPER_CASE class variables.
codeExamples:
class SavingsAccount:
    INTEREST_RATE = 0.04
    MIN_BALANCE = 1000

    def __init__(self, balance):
        self.balance = balance

    def yearly_interest(self):
        return self.balance * self.INTEREST_RATE

acc = SavingsAccount(50000)
print(acc.yearly_interest(), SavingsAccount.MIN_BALANCE)

# OUTPUT:
# 2000.0 1000

beginner.content:
Introduction

Class variables live on the class and are shared by every instance. Instance variables live on each object (set via self) and belong to it alone.
codeExamples:
class Dog:
    species = "Canis"                  # class variable (shared)
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name               # instance variable (per object)

a, b = Dog("Rex"), Dog("Fido")
print(a.species, b.species, a.name, b.name)
Dog.species = "Canis lupus"            # change once, all see it
print(a.species, b.species)

# OUTPUT:
# Canis Canis Rex Fido
# Canis lupus Canis lupus

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Some data is naturally per-object (a name), other data is naturally global to the type (a counter, a constant, a registry). Each needs a home.
codeExamples:
class User:
    count = 0                          # how many users exist
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        User.count += 1                # update the CLASS variable explicitly

User("a"); User("b"); User("c")
print(User.count)

# OUTPUT:
# 3

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Class variables hold constants, default config, counters and plugin registries.
codeExamples:
class Plugin:
    registry = []                      # shared list of all plugins
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        Plugin.registry.append(name)

Plugin("csv"); Plugin("json")
print(Plugin.registry)

# OUTPUT:
# ['csv', 'json']

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Dog class  ─────────────  species = "Canis"   (shared)
      ▲            ▲
      │            │
   ┌──┴────┐   ┌───┴───┐
   │ a     │   │ b     │
   │ name  │   │ name  │   (separate copies)
   └───────┘   └───────┘
   lookup: instance first, then class

expert.content:
The Shadowing Trap

Reading self.count finds the class variable if the object has no attribute of that name. But assigning self.count = ... (including self.count += 1) always creates an instance attribute that hides the class one - the class variable is not changed.
codeExamples:
class Visitor:
    count = 0

    def __init__(self):
        self.count += 1                 # BUG: reads 0 from the class, writes to the instance

v1 = Visitor()
v2 = Visitor()
print(Visitor.count, v1.count, v2.count)

# OUTPUT:
# 0 1 1

expert.content:
The Mutable Class Variable Trap

A list or dict defined as a class variable is one object shared by every instance. Mutating it through one object changes it for all of them. Create mutable per-object data in __init__.
codeExamples:
class Cart:
    items = []                          # BUG: one list for every cart

    def add(self, item):
        self.items.append(item)         # mutates the shared list

c1 = Cart()
c2 = Cart()
c1.add("pen")
print(c2.items)

class FixedCart:
    def __init__(self):
        self.items = []                 # a new list per cart

    def add(self, item):
        self.items.append(item)

f1 = FixedCart()
f2 = FixedCart()
f1.add("pen")
print(f1.items, f2.items)

# OUTPUT:
# ['pen']
# ['pen'] []

expert.content:
Attribute Lookup Order and __dict__

obj.attr is looked up in this order: the object's own __dict__, then its class, then the base classes (following the MRO). Instance variables live in the object's __dict__; class variables live in the class's __dict__.
codeExamples:
class Student:
    school = "DHIPAN"

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

s = Student("Abaji")
print(s.__dict__)                       # only instance data
print("school" in Student.__dict__, "school" in s.__dict__)

s.school = "Other"                      # creates an instance attribute
print(s.__dict__)
print(s.school, Student.school)

del s.school                            # remove it: the class value shows again
print(s.school)

# OUTPUT:
# {'name': 'Abaji'}
# True False
# {'name': 'Abaji', 'school': 'Other'}
# Other DHIPAN
# DHIPAN

expert.content:
Java static Fields vs Python Class Variables

AspectJavaPython
Declarationstatic int count;count = 0 in the class body
Instance fieldsDeclared in the class bodyCreated by assigning self.x (usually in __init__)
Writing obj.count = 5Changes the static field (with a warning)Creates an instance attribute that shadows it
Constantsstatic finalUPPER_CASE by convention (not enforced)

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Instance vs class variable?An instance variable belongs to one object; a class variable is defined in the class body and shared by all objects
Why does self.count += 1 not update a class counter?Assignment through self creates an instance attribute; update it via ClassName.count
Why is items = [] as a class variable dangerous?The single list is shared by every instance, so one object's changes appear in all
In what order are attributes looked up?Instance __dict__, then the class, then base classes in MRO order
What is the Java equivalent of a class variable?A static field

Advantages

Advantages: shared data is stored once, saving memory, and constants are changed in one place.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: a mutable class variable is shared by all instances, a classic bug.
codeExamples:
class Cart:
    items = []                         # BUG: one list for every cart
    def add(self, x): self.items.append(x)

a, b = Cart(), Cart()
a.add("apple")
print(b.items)                         # b sees a's apple!

# OUTPUT:
# ['apple']

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: assigning through an instance does not change the class variable; it creates a new instance attribute that shadows it.
codeExamples:
class Counter:
    n = 0

a = Counter()
a.n = 5                                # creates instance attribute, class untouched
print(a.n, Counter.n)
print("n" in vars(a))

# OUTPUT:
# 5 0
# True

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Treat class variables as constants or explicitly managed shared state. Never use mutable class-level defaults; create them in __init__ or use dataclasses.field(default_factory=...). Shared mutable state also makes concurrent code and tests harder.

beginner.content:
Three Kinds of Methods

KindDecoratorFirst parameterCan useTypical use
Instance methodnoneself (the object)Instance and class dataMost methods - work on one object
Class method@classmethodcls (the class)Class dataAlternative constructors, class-wide settings
Static method@staticmethodnoneOnly its argumentsHelper functions that belong with the class
All Three in One Class
codeExamples:
class Temperature:
    unit = "Celsius"                    # class variable

    def __init__(self, degrees):
        self.degrees = degrees

    def describe(self):                 # instance method
        return f"{self.degrees} {self.unit}"

    @classmethod
    def set_unit(cls, unit):            # class method
        cls.unit = unit

    @staticmethod
    def c_to_f(c):                      # static method
        return c * 9 / 5 + 32

t = Temperature(37)
print(t.describe())
print(Temperature.c_to_f(37))
Temperature.set_unit("deg C")
print(t.describe())

# OUTPUT:
# 37 Celsius
# 98.6
# 37 deg C

beginner.content:
Class Methods as Alternative Constructors

Python has only one __init__ (no constructor overloading). A @classmethod gives you extra, clearly named ways to create objects - like Java's static factory methods (LocalDate.of(...), LocalDate.parse(...)).

Static Methods as Helpers

A static method receives no self or cls. Use it for a utility that is logically part of the class but doesn't need any object or class data.

Which One Should I Use?

• Needs the object's data (self.x)? → instance method.
• Needs the class (to create objects or change class-wide data)? → class method.
• Needs neither? → static method - or simply a function in the module.

Introduction

Python has three method kinds. An instance method gets self (the object), a class method (@classmethod) gets cls (the class), and a static method (@staticmethod) gets neither - it is a plain function namespaced inside the class.
codeExamples:
class Pizza:
    base = "dough"

    def __init__(self, toppings):
        self.toppings = toppings

    def describe(self):                  # instance method: needs the object
        return f"{self.base} + {self.toppings}"

    @classmethod
    def margherita(cls):                 # class method: gets the class
        return cls(["tomato", "mozzarella"])

    @staticmethod
    def is_valid(topping):               # static method: no self, no cls
        return topping != "pineapple"

p = Pizza.margherita()
print(p.describe())
print(Pizza.is_valid("pineapple"))

# OUTPUT:
# dough + ['tomato', 'mozzarella']
# False

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Different jobs need different access: per-object data, class-wide data/factories, or just a related helper. Choosing the right kind keeps intent obvious and makes subclassing work.

Real-Time Use

Class methods as factories (dict.fromkeys, datetime.fromtimestamp), static methods for validators/utilities grouped with the class.
codeExamples:
from datetime import date

print(date.fromisoformat("2024-03-05"))   # classmethod factory in the stdlib
print(dict.fromkeys(["a", "b"], 0))       # another one

# OUTPUT:
# 2024-03-05
# {'a': 0, 'b': 0}

beginner.content:
Diagram

   obj.method()      ──► method(obj, ...)       self = the instance
   Class.cmethod()   ──► cmethod(Class, ...)    cls  = the class
   Class.smethod()   ──► smethod(...)           nothing injected

           instance data │ class data │ no data
   instance    yes       │    yes     │
   class        -        │    yes     │
   static       -        │     -      │  utility

expert.content:
How Binding Works

When you access a method through an object, Python creates a bound method that inserts the object as the first argument. obj.method(x) is really Class.method(obj, x). A class method binds the class instead; a static method binds nothing.
codeExamples:
class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.value = 0

    def increment(self, step=1):
        self.value += step
        return self.value

c = Counter()
print(c.increment())
print(Counter.increment(c, 5))      # the same call, written explicitly
Counter.increment()

# OUTPUT:
# 1
# 6
# TypeError: Counter.increment() missing 1 required positional argument: 'self'

expert.content:
Class Methods and Inheritance

cls is the class the method was called on - including a subclass. So a factory written with cls(...) automatically returns subclass objects. A static method, or a hard-coded class name, would not.

Static Method or Module Function?

Unlike Java, Python doesn't force every function into a class. A plain module-level function is often the better choice for a helper that doesn't relate to one class. Use a static method when the helper clearly belongs to the class's concept (so it's found with the class, and subclasses can override it).

Java vs Python

JavaPython
Instance method, implicit thisInstance method, explicit self parameter
static method@staticmethod (or a module function)
No direct equivalent@classmethod - receives the class, works with subclasses
Constructor overloadingOne __init__ plus classmethod factories

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
@classmethod vs @staticmethod?A class method receives the class as cls and can create instances or change class state; a static method receives nothing automatically
What is an alternative constructor?A classmethod such as Date.from_string() that builds an object from different input
Why use cls(...) instead of the class name in a factory?So subclasses calling it get instances of the subclass
What does obj.method(x) translate to?type(obj).method(obj, x) - the object is passed as self
When is a module function better than a static method?When the helper isn't really part of the class's concept

Advantages

Advantages: class methods respect inheritance: cls is the subclass that was called, so factories build the right type.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: confusing for beginners, and a static method is just a function: many are better placed at module level.
codeExamples:
class MathUtil:
    @staticmethod
    def double(x): return x * 2         # needs nothing from the class

def double(x): return x * 2             # simpler, same result

print(MathUtil.double(4), double(4))

# OUTPUT:
# 8 8

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a class method cannot see instance data, and a static method cannot see anything of the class unless you name it explicitly.

Architect's Notes

Use classmethods for alternative constructors and for state shared by the class, instance methods for behaviour on data, and avoid staticmethods when a module-level function is clearer. Classmethod factories scale better than constructors with many optional flags.

beginner.content:
Java-Style Getters and Setters Aren't Pythonic

In Java, fields are private and you write getBalance() / setBalance() "just in case" you need logic later. In Python you start with a plain public attribute. If you later need logic, you turn it into a property - and callers keep writing obj.balance, unchanged.

@property: A Method Read Like an Attribute

@property turns a method into a computed attribute: you access it without parentheses, and its value is calculated each time.
codeExamples:
class Rectangle:
    def __init__(self, width, height):
        self.width = width
        self.height = height

    @property
    def area(self):
        return self.width * self.height

r = Rectangle(3, 4)
print(r.area)                 # no ()
r.width = 10
print(r.area)                 # always up to date

# OUTPUT:
# 12
# 40

beginner.content:
Setters with Validation

Add @name.setter to run code when the attribute is assigned. The value is stored in a "private" attribute with a leading underscore.

Read-Only Properties

A property with no setter can be read but not assigned.

Deleters

@name.deleter runs on del obj.name - rarely needed, but useful for clearing cached or sensitive data.

Introduction

@property turns a method into an attribute-style accessor. Callers write obj.age while your code can run validation or computation behind it. @x.setter defines how assignment works.

Why Do We Need This?

You start with a plain public attribute. Later you need validation. A property lets you add it without changing a single caller, unlike Java where getters would have been needed from day one.

Real-Time Use

ORMs and validators use properties for derived fields (full_name), read-only ids and lazy loading.

Diagram

   p.age = 5                          print(p.age)
      │                                    │
      ▼                                    ▼
   ┌───────────────┐                ┌───────────────┐
   │ age.setter    │ validate       │ age getter    │
   └──────┬────────┘                └──────┬────────┘
          ▼                                ▼
       self._age  (stored)  ◄────────── self._age

expert.content:
Upgrading an Attribute Without Breaking Callers

This is the real reason Python doesn't need defensive getters/setters: the access syntax is the same for a plain attribute and a property. You can add validation years later, and every obj.price = ... in the codebase automatically goes through it.

cached_property for Expensive Values

A property recomputes on every access. functools.cached_property computes once per object and then stores the result in the instance - good for expensive values that don't change.

Keep Properties Cheap

Readers assume obj.x is fast and has no side effects. If something is slow (a database query, a network call) or changes state, make it a method with a verb name (fetch_orders()) so the cost is visible at the call site. Name properties as nouns or adjectives (area, is_empty).

Under the Hood: property Is a Descriptor

@property is shorthand for creating a property object - a descriptor with __get__, __set__ and __delete__ methods - stored on the class. That is why it lives on the class but intercepts access on instances. The Advanced Python module covers descriptors in depth.
codeExamples:
class Rectangle:
    def __init__(self, w, h):
        self.w = w
        self.h = h

    def _get_area(self):
        return self.w * self.h

    area = property(_get_area)       # the same as using @property

r = Rectangle(2, 5)
print(r.area, type(Rectangle.__dict__["area"]).__name__)

# OUTPUT:
# 10 property

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why don't Python classes need getX/setX methods?A plain attribute can later become a property without changing how callers access it
What does @property do?Turns a method into an attribute-style accessor computed on each access
How do you make an attribute read-only?Define a property without a setter; assignment raises AttributeError
Where does a property store its value?Usually in an underscore attribute such as self._marks
property vs cached_property?property recomputes every access; cached_property computes once per instance and caches the result
What is a property under the hood?A descriptor object stored on the class

Advantages

Advantages: a stable public API, validation, derived values, and cached computation via functools.cached_property.
codeExamples:
from functools import cached_property

class Report:
    @cached_property
    def data(self):
        print("computing once...")
        return [1, 2, 3]

r1 = Report()
print(r1.data)
print(r1.data)                           # cached: no recomputation

# OUTPUT:
# computing once...
# [1, 2, 3]
# [1, 2, 3]

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: a property looks like cheap attribute access but can hide slow or failing code; debugging surprises follow.
codeExamples:
import time

class Slow:
    @property
    def value(self):
        time.sleep(0.2)                  # looks innocent: obj.value
        return 42

s = Slow()
t = time.perf_counter()
s.value
print("took >0.1s:", time.perf_counter() - t > 0.1)

# OUTPUT:
# took >0.1s: True

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: properties are defined per class, not per instance, and are not visible in vars(obj); they need the underscore backing field.

Architect's Notes

Start with plain attributes and introduce properties only when you need validation, computation or to deprecate an old name. Keep getters fast and side-effect free; if an operation is expensive or can fail in unexpected ways, make it an explicit method.

beginner.content:
What is Method Overriding?

When a child class defines a method with the same name as a method in its parent, the child's version overrides the parent's. Calls on a child object use the child's method - even calls made from code inside the parent class. This is how one interface gets different behaviour per class (runtime polymorphism), exactly as in Java.

Replacing vs Extending

An override can replace the parent's behaviour completely, or extend it by calling the parent version with super() and adding to the result.
codeExplanations: describe() is defined only in Employee, but inside it self.annual_pay() is looked up on the actual object. For the Manager object that finds Manager.annual_pay, which first calls the parent's version through super() (60000 * 12 = 720000) and then adds the 50000 bonus. This is the same dynamic dispatch Java uses for non-static, non-final methods.

beginner.content:
Overriding Methods Inherited from object

Every class inherits from object, which supplies default __str__, __repr__ and __eq__. The default string shows a memory address and the default equality compares identity - override them to give your objects meaningful behaviour, like toString() and equals() in Java.
codeExamples:
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

p = Point(1, 2)
print(p)
print(p == Point(1, 2))

# OUTPUT (the address varies):
# <__main__.Point object at 0x...>
# False

beginner.content:
Introduction

Overriding means a subclass defines a method with the same name as one in its parent, replacing it for objects of the subclass.

Why Do We Need This?

A parent provides a sensible default; children need their own behaviour. Overriding lets them specialise without changing the parent or the calling code.

Real-Time Use

Frameworks are built on it: you subclass and override hooks like setUp in unittest, get in a Django view, or run in threading.Thread.
codeExamples:
import threading

class Worker(threading.Thread):
    def run(self):                       # override the hook Thread calls
        print("working in", self.name)

w = Worker(name="T1")
w.start(); w.join()

# OUTPUT:
# working in T1

beginner.content:
Diagram

   obj = Dog()
   obj.speak()
       │
       ▼
   Dog     defines speak()?  yes ──► run Dog.speak
       │ no
       ▼
   Animal  defines speak()?  yes ──► run Animal.speak

expert.content:
No @Override - but typing.override (3.12+)

Java's @Override makes the compiler reject a method that doesn't actually override anything - catching typos. Python has no such check at runtime: a misspelled method is simply a new method. Python 3.12 added typing.override; it does nothing at runtime except mark the function, but type checkers such as mypy and Pyright report an error when a marked method has no matching parent method.

Overriding vs Overloading

OverridingOverloading
MeaningChild redefines a parent method with the same nameSeveral methods with the same name but different parameters
JavaSupported (@Override)Supported, resolved at compile time
PythonSupportedNot supported - a later def replaces the earlier one; use default arguments, *args or functools.singledispatchmethod
typing.overload exists, but only describes alternative signatures to type checkers - it does not create real overloads.

Keep Overrides Compatible (Liskov Substitution)

Code written for the parent must keep working with any child. An override that changes the parameters - or raises errors the parent never did - breaks every caller that treats the objects uniformly.
codeExplanations: The loop is written against the Shape interface: area() with no arguments. Square changed that contract by requiring a unit, so the very first polymorphic call on a Square fails. Keep the same parameters in overrides; if a child needs extra options, make them optional (e.g. unit="sq cm") so the parent-style call still works.

expert.content:
Overriding Class Attributes

Overriding isn't limited to methods. A child can redefine a class attribute, and inherited methods that read it through self pick up the child's value - a light-weight way to customise behaviour without rewriting methods.

Java vs Python Overriding Rules

RuleJavaPython
Check that a method really overrides@Override, enforced by the compiler@typing.override, enforced only by type checkers
Prevent overridingfinal method@typing.final - again only for type checkers
Static/class methodsStatic methods are hidden, not overriddenClass methods and static methods can be overridden like any attribute
Access levelCannot reduce visibilityNo access modifiers
Calling the parent versionsuper.method()super().method()

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is method overriding?A child class redefining a method inherited from its parent; calls on child objects use the child's version
How do you call the parent's version from an override?super().method_name(...)
Does Python support method overloading?No - the last definition wins; use default or variable arguments instead
What is Python's equivalent of @Override?typing.override (3.12+), checked by static type checkers, not at runtime
Which object methods are commonly overridden?__str__, __repr__, __eq__ (with __hash__), and comparison methods
Why keep an override's signature compatible?So code written against the parent works with every child (Liskov Substitution Principle)

Advantages

Advantages: customise behaviour while reusing the rest; combined with super() you extend rather than replace.
codeExamples:
class Base:
    def greet(self): return "Hello"
class Polite(Base):
    def greet(self): return super().greet() + ", sir"   # extend parent result

print(Polite().greet())

# OUTPUT:
# Hello, sir

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: Python does not check signatures, so an override with different parameters compiles fine and fails at the call.

Limitations

Limitations: there is no @Override/final check in the language; typos create new methods instead of overriding. Type checkers offer typing.override (3.12+).
codeExamples:
class Base:
    def save(self): return "base save"
class Child(Base):
    def sav(self): return "child save"   # typo: not an override!

print(Child().save())                    # still the parent's

# OUTPUT:
# base save

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Obey the Liskov substitution principle: an override must accept what the parent accepts and honour its promises. Prefer the template-method pattern (parent calls small overridable hooks) over overriding big methods, and use typing.override plus a type checker to catch typos.

beginner.content:
Inheriting from Several Classes

Java allows a class to extend only one class (plus any number of interfaces). Python allows a class to inherit from several classes at once - list them in the parentheses. The child gets the attributes and methods of all of them.

Mixins: Small Reusable Pieces of Behaviour

The most common, safest use of multiple inheritance is the mixin: a small class that adds one capability and isn't meant to be used on its own. A main class "mixes in" the abilities it needs. By convention mixin names end in Mixin.

The Diamond Problem

When two parents share a grandparent and both define the same method, which version does the child get? This shape is called the diamond:
A
B(A)C(A)
D(B, C)
Python answers it with the Method Resolution Order (MRO): a single, fixed list of classes that Python searches, left to right, to find an attribute.
codeExplanations: D has no hello() of its own, so Python walks the MRO: D, then B - which has hello(), so B's version is used. The MRO lists B before C because D was declared as D(B, C): parents are searched in the order you write them. A, the shared grandparent, appears only once and only after both B and C, and object, the root of every class, is always last.

beginner.content:
Seeing the MRO

ClassName.__mro__ (a tuple) and ClassName.mro() (a list) both show the order. help(ClassName) prints it as well, under "Method resolution order".

Introduction

Python lets a class inherit from several parents. The MRO (Method Resolution Order, computed by the C3 algorithm) is the single linear order in which Python searches the classes for an attribute.
codeExamples:
class A:
    def who(self): return "A"
class B(A):
    def who(self): return "B"
class C(A):
    def who(self): return "C"
class D(B, C):                           # diamond: D -> B -> C -> A
    pass

print(D().who())
print([k.__name__ for k in D.__mro__])

# OUTPUT:
# B
# ['D', 'B', 'C', 'A', 'object']

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Sometimes behaviour is orthogonal (logging, JSON serialisation, timestamps). Mixins combine such capabilities without a deep tree.

Real-Time Use

Django class-based views (LoginRequiredMixin, ListView), socketserver (ThreadingMixIn) and DRF all use mixins.
codeExamples:
import socketserver
print([c.__name__ for c in socketserver.ThreadingTCPServer.__mro__][:3])

# OUTPUT:
# ['ThreadingTCPServer', 'ThreadingMixIn', 'TCPServer']

beginner.content:
Diagram

         A
        /        B   C        D.__mro__ = [D, B, C, A, object]
         /          search left to right, each class once
         D(B, C)

expert.content:
How the MRO Is Computed: C3 Linearisation

Python (since 2.3) builds the MRO with the C3 algorithm, which guarantees three properties:
• a class always comes before its parents;
• parents keep the left-to-right order in which they were listed;
• the order is monotonic - a class's MRO is consistent with the MROs of its parents.

The rule: L[C] = C + merge(L[P1], ..., L[Pn], [P1, ..., Pn]). "merge" repeatedly takes the first head of a list that does not appear in the tail (any position except the first) of another list. For the diamond above:
L[D] = D + merge([B, A, object], [C, A, object], [B, C])
• take B (not in any tail) → merge([A, object], [C, A, object], [C])
• A is in the tail of [C, A, object], so skip it; take C → merge([A, object], [A, object])
• take A, then object → D, B, C, A, object
codeExamples:
class A: pass
class B: pass
class C: pass
class D: pass
class E: pass
class K1(A, B, C): pass
class K2(D, B, E): pass
class K3(D, A): pass
class Z(K1, K2, K3): pass

print([cls.__name__ for cls in Z.mro()])

# OUTPUT:
# ['Z', 'K1', 'K2', 'K3', 'D', 'A', 'B', 'C', 'E', 'object']

expert.content:
Inconsistent Hierarchies Are Rejected

If no order can satisfy the C3 rules, Python refuses to create the class. Here Z(X, Y) asks for X before Y, but Y is a subclass of X and must come before it.

Cooperative Multiple Inheritance Needs super() Everywhere

With multiple inheritance, "the next class" after a given class depends on the object's MRO, not on that class's own parent. If every class calls super(), each method in the chain runs exactly once, in MRO order. If one class calls its parent directly, the chain breaks or a shared base runs twice. The super() topic traces this step by step.
codeExplanations: App's MRO is App, Cache, Database, Base, object. Inside Cache.setup, super() means "the class after Cache in the MRO of this object", which is Database - not Base, even though Cache's only parent is Base. That is why every setup runs once and Base, shared by both branches, runs only at the end.

expert.content:
Python vs Java

JavaPython
Inherit implementation fromOne class onlyAny number of classes
Multiple "types"Many interfacesMany base classes, ABCs or Protocols
Diamond conflictsDefault methods from two interfaces must be resolved explicitly by overridingResolved automatically by the MRO
Typical reuse toolInterfaces with default methods, compositionMixins, composition
Guidance: keep multiple inheritance to mixins that add independent behaviour. For anything more complex, composition (holding an object instead of inheriting from it) is usually clearer.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Does Python support multiple inheritance?Yes - a class can list several base classes
What is the MRO?The Method Resolution Order: the ordered list of classes Python searches for an attribute, available as __mro__ or mro()
Which algorithm computes it?C3 linearisation: children before parents, parents in declaration order, consistent with the parents' MROs
How does Python solve the diamond problem?The shared base appears once in the MRO, after all its subclasses; with super() each method runs once
What is a mixin?A small class that adds one reusable capability to other classes through multiple inheritance
When does class creation fail because of the MRO?When the requested base order contradicts the hierarchy, e.g. class Z(X, Y) where Y subclasses X

Advantages

Advantages: combine independent capabilities, avoid code duplication, and the C3 order is deterministic (and calling each parent once with super() is possible).
codeExamples:
class Walk:
    def move(self): return "walk"
class Swim:
    def swim(self): return "swim"
class Duck(Walk, Swim): pass

d = Duck()
print(d.move(), d.swim())

# OUTPUT:
# walk swim

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: hard to reason about; the winning method depends on parent order, so changing the order changes behaviour.
codeExamples:
class A:
    def hi(self): return "A"
class B:
    def hi(self): return "B"
class X(A, B): pass
class Y(B, A): pass

print(X().hi(), Y().hi())               # parent order matters

# OUTPUT:
# A B

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: some orders are impossible; C3 refuses to build an inconsistent hierarchy.
codeExamples:
class A: pass
class B(A): pass
try:
    class C(A, B):                       # A before its own child B: impossible
        pass
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", str(e)[:40])

# OUTPUT:
# TypeError: Cannot create a consistent method resolu

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Keep multiple inheritance to small, stateless mixins that cooperate through super(). If you need diamonds with state, prefer composition. Always print Class.__mro__ when debugging surprising method selection.

beginner.content:
What Does super() Do?

super() gives you access to methods of the parent class from inside a child class. Its most common job is calling the parent's __init__ so the parent can set up its own attributes - just like super(...) as the first line of a Java constructor. Python does not call the parent constructor automatically.

Forgetting to Call the Parent __init__

If the child defines its own __init__ and never calls the parent's, the parent's attributes are simply never created.

Calling Other Parent Methods

super() works for any method, not just __init__. Use it to extend a parent method instead of copying its code.

super() vs Parent.__init__(self)

You can also call the parent explicitly by name: Vehicle.__init__(self, brand, 4). It works for simple single inheritance, but:
• it hard-codes the parent's name - rename or re-parent the class and every call must change;
• with multiple inheritance it can run a shared base class twice (see the Expert tab).

In Python 3, write super().method(...) with no arguments. The old two-argument form super(Car, self) still works and is mainly seen in Python 2 era code.

Introduction

super() returns a proxy that finds the next class in the MRO after the current one, so you can call the parent's version of a method (most often __init__).

Why Do We Need This?

If a child overrides __init__ and forgets the parent's, the parent's attributes never get created.

Real-Time Use

Extending a built-in or framework class while keeping its behaviour: log then delegate.

Diagram

   D.__mro__ = D -> B -> C -> A -> object

   D.run() ──super()──► B.run() ──super()──► C.run() ──super()──► A.run()
   "next in line", not "my parent"

expert.content:
super() Follows the MRO, Not "the Parent"

super() returns a proxy that searches the Method Resolution Order of the current object, starting just after the class in which the call is written. With single inheritance that is the parent. With multiple inheritance it may be a sibling class.
codeExamples:
class Base:
    def __init__(self):
        print("Base.__init__")

class Left(Base):
    def __init__(self):
        print("Left start")
        super().__init__()
        print("Left end")

class Right(Base):
    def __init__(self):
        print("Right start")
        super().__init__()
        print("Right end")

class Child(Left, Right):
    def __init__(self):
        print("Child start")
        super().__init__()
        print("Child end")

print([c.__name__ for c in Child.__mro__])
Child()

# OUTPUT:
# ['Child', 'Left', 'Right', 'Base', 'object']
# Child start
# Left start
# Right start
# Base.__init__
# Right end
# Left end
# Child end
codeExplanations: Left's own parent is Base, yet the super().__init__() inside Left calls Right.__init__, because Right is the next class after Left in Child's MRO. Each __init__ runs exactly once and Base, shared by both branches, runs only once at the very end of the chain. The "end" lines print in reverse as each call returns.

expert.content:
What Goes Wrong with Explicit Parent Calls

The same diamond written with Parent.__init__(self) calls runs Base.__init__ twice - a real bug if it opens a connection, registers the object or resets state.

Cooperative Arguments with **kwargs

In a cooperative hierarchy each class doesn't know who comes next in the MRO, so it can't know that class's parameters. The pattern: each __init__ takes the keyword arguments it needs, and passes the rest on with **kwargs. By the time the chain reaches object.__init__, nothing is left over.
codeExplanations: Product's MRO is Product, Named, Priced, object. Named.__init__ receives name="Pen" plus price=10 in kwargs, and forwards price=10 to the next class, Priced, which uses it and forwards an empty kwargs to object.__init__. Always pass these arguments by keyword - positional arguments can't be routed safely through a chain whose order depends on the final class.

expert.content:
super() in Class Methods

Inside a @classmethod, super() calls the parent's class method while keeping cls bound to the class that was actually used - so alternative constructors keep returning the right subclass.

How Zero-Argument super() Works

super() with no arguments is shorthand for super(CurrentClass, first_argument). The compiler gives every method that uses super (or __class__) a hidden __class__ cell pointing at the class where the method was defined; at runtime super() reads that cell plus the method's first argument (self or cls). Consequences:
• it only works inside a function defined in a class body;
• a method copied onto a different class still uses the class where it was written.

Java vs Python

JavaPython
Parent constructor callsuper(args), must be the first statement; inserted automatically if omittedsuper().__init__(args), anywhere in __init__; never automatic
Parent method callsuper.method()super().method()
What "super" refers toAlways the direct superclassThe next class in the object's MRO

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Does Python call the parent's __init__ automatically?No - only if the child doesn't define __init__; otherwise call super().__init__(...) yourself
super() vs Parent.__init__(self)?super() follows the MRO and runs each class once in a diamond; explicit calls hard-code the parent and can run a base twice
Does super() always mean the parent class?No - it means the next class after the current one in the object's MRO, which may be a sibling
Why pass **kwargs in cooperative __init__ methods?Each class takes its own arguments and forwards the rest, because it can't know which class comes next
How does zero-argument super() know the class?Through a hidden __class__ cell created by the compiler, plus the method's first argument

Advantages

Advantages: no hard-coded parent name (rename-safe) and it makes cooperative multiple inheritance work: every class in the MRO runs once.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: in multiple inheritance super() may not call the class you expect (it follows the MRO, not "the parent"), and all classes must accept compatible arguments.

Limitations

Limitations: zero-argument super() only works inside a method defined in a class body (it relies on __class__ and the first argument).

Architect's Notes

Always call super().__init__(...) in cooperative hierarchies and accept **kwargs in mixins so the chain can pass unknown arguments along. If the plumbing gets ugly, that is a signal to use composition instead of deep inheritance.

beginner.content:
What is an Abstract Class?

An abstract class defines a common interface for a family of classes but is incomplete itself: some methods are declared without a real implementation, and every concrete subclass must provide them. You can't create objects of the abstract class directly.

Python has no abstract keyword. Instead, inherit from abc.ABC and mark methods with the @abstractmethod decorator.

You Can't Instantiate an Abstract Class

The check happens when an object is created. A subclass that doesn't implement every abstract method is still abstract and can't be instantiated either.

Concrete Methods in an Abstract Class

An abstract class can also contain normal methods that use the abstract ones. Subclasses get them for free - this is the template method pattern: the base class fixes the overall algorithm, subclasses fill in the steps.

Abstract Properties

Stack @property on top of @abstractmethod to require subclasses to provide a property.

Introduction

An abstract base class (from the abc module) declares methods that subclasses must implement. Python refuses to instantiate a class that still has unimplemented @abstractmethods.

Why Do We Need This?

A plain base class with NotImplementedError fails late (when the method is called). ABC fails early (when the object is created), so the bug is found at startup.

Real-Time Use

Frameworks define ABCs for plugin systems; the standard library uses them in collections.abc (Mapping, Sequence, Iterable).
codeExamples:
from collections.abc import Sequence, Iterable

print(isinstance([1, 2], Sequence), isinstance("ab", Sequence))
print(isinstance(5, Iterable))

# OUTPUT:
# True True
# False

beginner.content:
Diagram

   ┌──────────────────────────┐
   │ Shape (ABC)              │
   │  @abstractmethod area()  │   cannot be instantiated
   └────────────┬─────────────┘
         ┌──────┴───────┐
   ┌─────┴─────┐  ┌─────┴─────┐
   │ Square    │  │ Circle    │   must implement area()
   │ area() ok │  │ area() ok │
   └───────────┘  └───────────┘

expert.content:
Abstract Methods Can Have a Body

Unlike Java, a Python abstract method may contain real code. Subclasses must still override it, but they can call the base version with super() to reuse a default part.

collections.abc: Implement a Little, Get a Lot

The standard library's abstract base classes give you mixin methods for free. Subclass collections.abc.Sequence, implement just __getitem__ and __len__, and you also get in, iteration, reversed(), index() and count().

Virtual Subclasses with register()

SomeABC.register(OtherClass) declares that an existing class counts as a subclass for isinstance/issubclass checks, without changing it - handy for third-party classes you can't modify. Python does not verify that the registered class actually implements the abstract methods, and it inherits none of the ABC's methods.
codeExamples:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Exporter(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def export(self, data): ...

class LegacyCsvWriter:                 # existing class, not ours to change
    def export(self, data):
        return ",".join(data)

Exporter.register(LegacyCsvWriter)

w = LegacyCsvWriter()
print(isinstance(w, Exporter), issubclass(LegacyCsvWriter, Exporter))
print(w.export(["a", "b"]))

# OUTPUT:
# True True
# a,b

expert.content:
ABC vs Protocol

ABCProtocol (see next topic)
RelationshipNominal - a class must inherit from (or register with) the ABCStructural - any class with matching methods qualifies
EnforcedAt runtime, when instantiatingBy static type checkers (runtime only with @runtime_checkable)
Shared codeYes - concrete and mixin methods are inheritedUsually just the interface
Best forClass families you control, template methodsDescribing what a function needs from its arguments, third-party types

Java Abstract Classes vs Python ABCs

JavaPython
Declarationabstract class Shapeclass Shape(ABC)
Abstract methodabstract double area(); - no body allowed@abstractmethod def area(self) - body allowed
When the error appearsCompile timeRuntime, when you try to create an object
Multiple abstract basesOnly one abstract class (plus interfaces)Any number

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How do you create an abstract class in Python?Inherit from abc.ABC (or use metaclass=ABCMeta) and decorate methods with @abstractmethod
When is the "can't instantiate" error raised?At runtime, when creating an instance of a class that still has unimplemented abstract methods
Can an abstract method have an implementation?Yes - subclasses must still override it but may call it via super()
What does ABC.register() do?Makes a class a virtual subclass for isinstance/issubclass checks without inheritance or verification
What do you get from subclassing collections.abc.Sequence?Free mixin methods - __contains__, __iter__, __reversed__, index and count - once you implement __getitem__ and __len__
Is a class with @abstractmethod but without ABC abstract?No - the check only works when the metaclass is ABCMeta (inheriting from ABC provides it)

Advantages

Advantages: an enforced contract, mixin methods that build on abstract ones, and isinstance checks against the interface.
codeExamples:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Exporter(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def body(self): ...
    def export(self):                    # concrete method built on the abstract one
        return "<<" + self.body() + ">>"

class Csv(Exporter):
    def body(self): return "a,b"

print(Csv().export())

# OUTPUT:
# <<a,b>>

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: more ceremony and stronger inheritance coupling; every implementer must subclass explicitly.
codeExamples:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Speaker(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def speak(self): ...

class Robot:                             # has speak() but is NOT a Speaker
    def speak(self): return "beep"

print(isinstance(Robot(), Speaker))      # False, even though it quacks

# OUTPUT:
# False

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: enforcement happens only at instantiation, never on the class itself, and only for the abstract names (not their signatures).

Architect's Notes

Use an ABC when you control the implementers and want shared concrete code plus early failure. When you only need a structural contract for third-party or duck-typed objects, prefer a Protocol; ABCs create a nominal hierarchy that is harder to evolve.

beginner.content:
Interfaces in Python

In Java, a class satisfies an interface only if it declares implements Drawable - this is nominal typing (based on names). Python traditionally relies on duck typing: any object with a draw() method can be drawn, no declaration needed.

typing.Protocol (Python 3.8+) lets you write that duck-typed interface down so editors and type checkers can verify it. This is structural typing, often called "static duck typing": a class matches the protocol because of its structure (its methods), not because it inherits from anything.

Defining and Using a Protocol

A protocol is a class that inherits from Protocol and lists method signatures, usually with ... as the body. Classes that match it never mention it.

Who Checks It?

Protocols are checked by static type checkers such as mypy and Pyright (and by your editor), before the program runs. At runtime, Python itself doesn't check type hints - a wrong argument fails only when the missing method is actually called.
codeExamples:
from typing import Protocol

class Drawable(Protocol):
    def draw(self) -> str: ...

def render(item: Drawable) -> None:
    print("Rendering", item.draw())

render(42)

# OUTPUT (running the program):
# AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'draw'
#
# mypy reports the problem without running anything:
# error: Argument 1 to "render" has incompatible type "int"; expected "Drawable"

beginner.content:
A Practical Example: Anything That Can Send a Message

The checkout code depends only on the protocol, so new notifiers - or test doubles - can be added without touching it or inheriting from a shared base.
codeExamples:
from typing import Protocol

class Notifier(Protocol):
    def send(self, to: str, message: str) -> bool: ...

class EmailNotifier:
    def send(self, to: str, message: str) -> bool:
        print(f"Email to {to}: {message}")
        return True

class FakeNotifier:                       # for tests
    def __init__(self):
        self.sent = []

    def send(self, to: str, message: str) -> bool:
        self.sent.append((to, message))
        return True

def place_order(customer: str, notifier: Notifier) -> None:
    notifier.send(customer, "Order confirmed")

place_order("abaji@mail.com", EmailNotifier())
fake = FakeNotifier()
place_order("raoji@mail.com", fake)
print(fake.sent)

# OUTPUT:
# Email to abaji@mail.com: Order confirmed
# [('raoji@mail.com', 'Order confirmed')]

beginner.content:
Introduction

A Protocol (typing.Protocol, Python 3.8+) describes an interface by its shape: any class with the right methods satisfies it, with no inheritance. This is structural typing, "static duck typing".

Why Do We Need This?
