The problem: A form that only says "invalid password" frustrates users. A single combined regex cannot say which requirement was missed.

Why we need it:
  • Learn the one pattern per rule design: simple patterns, clear messages.
  • Practise re.search with classes and quantifiers.
  • Understand why composition rules are not the same as password strength.

Complete Example: missing_rules() lists what is wrong

A complete, runnable program. Save it in a file and run it with python.
codeExamples:
import re

RULES = {
    "at least 8 characters": r".{8,}",
    "a lowercase letter":    r"[a-z]",
    "an uppercase letter":   r"[A-Z]",
    "a digit":               r"\d",
    "a special character":   r"[^\w\s]",
}


def missing_rules(password):
    return [rule for rule, pattern in RULES.items() if not re.search(pattern, password)]


def main():
    for password in ["Passw0rd!", "password", "SHORT1!", "Str0ng#Pass"]:
        missing = missing_rules(password)
        message = "OK" if not missing else "needs " + ", ".join(missing)
        print(password, "->", message)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT:
# Passw0rd! -> OK
# password -> needs an uppercase letter, a digit, a special character
# SHORT1! -> needs at least 8 characters, a lowercase letter
# Str0ng#Pass -> OK
codeExplanations: The list comprehension keeps only the rules whose pattern is NOT found. An empty list means every rule passed. Because dictionaries keep insertion order, messages always appear in the same order as the rules.

beginner.content:
The Goal

Check a password against common rules: at least 8 characters, one lowercase letter, one uppercase letter, one digit and one special character. A single clear pattern for each rule is easier to write, and easier to explain to the user, than one giant regex.

Step 1: One Pattern per Rule

Keep the rules in a dictionary of message: pattern. re.search() checks that each pattern appears somewhere in the password, and the function returns the list of rules that failed - perfect for showing helpful error messages.
codeExamples:
import re

RULES = {
    "at least 8 characters": r".{8,}",
    "a lowercase letter":    r"[a-z]",
    "an uppercase letter":   r"[A-Z]",
    "a digit":               r"\d",
    "a special character":   r"[^\w\s]",
}

def check_password(password):
    return [rule for rule, pattern in RULES.items()
            if not re.search(pattern, password)]

print(check_password("Passw0rd!"))
print(check_password("abc"))

# OUTPUT:
# []
# ['at least 8 characters', 'an uppercase letter', 'a digit', 'a special character']
codeExplanations: The list comprehension keeps only the rules whose pattern is NOT found in the password. An empty list means every rule passed. [^\w\s] means "not a letter, digit, underscore or whitespace", which is a practical definition of a special character.

beginner.content:
Step 2: A Friendly Validator

Wrap the check so it tells the user exactly what to fix.
codeExamples:
import re

RULES = {
    "at least 8 characters": r".{8,}",
    "a lowercase letter":    r"[a-z]",
    "an uppercase letter":   r"[A-Z]",
    "a digit":               r"\d",
    "a special character":   r"[^\w\s]",
}

def validate(password):
    missing = [rule for rule, pattern in RULES.items()
               if not re.search(pattern, password)]
    if missing:
        return "Password needs: " + ", ".join(missing)
    return "Password accepted"

print(validate("password"))
print(validate("Str0ng#Pass"))

# OUTPUT:
# Password needs: an uppercase letter, a digit, a special character
# Password accepted

beginner.content:
Introduction

This project checks password strength with lookaheads: at least 8 characters, an uppercase letter, a lowercase letter, a digit and a symbol. Each lookahead tests one rule from the start of the string.
codeExamples:
import re
STRONG = re.compile(r"""
    ^(?=.*[a-z])          # a lowercase letter
     (?=.*[A-Z])          # an uppercase letter
     (?=.*\d)             # a digit
     (?=.*[^\w\s])        # a symbol
     .{8,}$               # length 8+
""", re.VERBOSE)

for p in ["Passw0rd!", "password", "SHORT1!a", "NoDigits!!"]:
    print(f"{p:12} {bool(STRONG.match(p))}")

# OUTPUT:
# Passw0rd!    True
# password     False
# SHORT1!a     True
# NoDigits!!   False

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Weak passwords are the top cause of account takeover. A policy check at signup blocks the worst choices, and telling the user exactly which rule failed improves the experience.
codeExamples:
import re
RULES = {
    "8+ characters":  r".{8,}",
    "an uppercase":   r"[A-Z]",
    "a lowercase":    r"[a-z]",
    "a digit":        r"\d",
    "a symbol":       r"[^\w\s]",
}
def check(pw):
    return [name for name, pat in RULES.items() if not re.search(pat, pw)]

print(check("abc"))
print(check("Str0ng!pass"))

# OUTPUT:
# ['8+ characters', 'an uppercase', 'a digit', 'a symbol']
# []

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Signup and reset-password forms, admin tools and onboarding scripts. Modern guidance (NIST) prefers length and a breached-password check over complex character rules.
codeExamples:
import re
def strength(pw):
    score = sum(bool(re.search(p, pw)) for p in [r"[a-z]", r"[A-Z]", r"\d", r"[^\w\s]"])
    score += len(pw) >= 12
    return ["weak", "weak", "fair", "good", "strong", "excellent"][score]

print(strength("abc"), strength("Abcdef1!"), strength("Abcdef1!ghijk"))

# OUTPUT:
# weak good excellent

beginner.content:
Diagram

   password ─► ┌ (?=.*[a-z]) ┐
               │ (?=.*[A-Z]) │  all lookaheads start at position 0,
               │ (?=.*\d)    │  none consume text; every one must pass
               │ (?=.*\W)    │
               └ .{8,}       ┘ ─► ALLOW / DENY (+ which rule failed)

expert.content:
The Single-Pattern Version With Lookaheads

All rules can be combined into one pattern by stacking lookaheads at the start (each checks one rule without consuming text), followed by the character set that is actually allowed. It is compact, but when it fails you cannot say which rule failed - the multi-pattern version above is friendlier.
codeExamples:
import re

PASSWORD = re.compile(r"""
    (?=.*[a-z])        # a lowercase letter
    (?=.*[A-Z])        # an uppercase letter
    (?=.*\d)           # a digit
    (?=.*[^\w\s])      # a special character
    \S{8,}             # 8+ characters, no whitespace at all
""", re.VERBOSE)

for p in ["Passw0rd!", "password1!", "Short1!", "Has Space1!", "Str0ng#Pass"]:
    print(p, "->", bool(PASSWORD.fullmatch(p)))

# OUTPUT:
# Passw0rd! -> True
# password1! -> False
# Short1! -> False
# Has Space1! -> False
# Str0ng#Pass -> True

expert.content:
Rejecting Repeats With a Backreference

A backreference can ban weak patterns such as the same character three times in a row. (.)\1{2,} means "any character, followed by that same character at least two more times".
codeExamples:
import re

def has_repeats(password):
    return re.search(r"(.)\1{2,}", password) is not None

print(has_repeats("Passsw0rd!"))
print(has_repeats("Passw0rd!"))

# OUTPUT:
# True
# False

expert.content:
What Regex Cannot Do - and What to Do Instead

  • Strength is not composition: "Password1!" satisfies every rule above and is still a terrible password. Current guidance (NIST SP 800-63B) favours length and blocking known-breached or common passwords over forced character mixes.
  • Never store the password itself. Store a salted, slow hash (bcrypt, scrypt or argon2) - not a plain regex-checked string, and not a fast hash like MD5.
  • Generating passwords: use the secrets module, not random.
codeExamples:
import hashlib, os

password = "Str0ng#Pass"
salt = os.urandom(16)

digest = hashlib.scrypt(password.encode(), salt=salt, n=2**14, r=8, p=1)
print(len(salt), len(digest))        # store both: salt and digest

# OUTPUT:
# 16 64

expert.content:
Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
User sees exactly which rules failed"Password1!" passes every rule yet is weak
Adding or changing a rule is one dictionary entryComposition rules push users to predictable patterns
Each pattern is trivial and easy to testDoes not check breached or common-password lists
Can reuse the same rules on server and in documentationNever replaces secure hashing (argon2, bcrypt, scrypt)

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How do lookaheads help with password rules?Each lookahead checks one rule at the start position without consuming text, so all rules are ANDed
Why prefer one pattern per rule?You can report exactly which rules failed, and each pattern stays simple
Is a password that passes all rules strong?Not necessarily - length and unpredictability matter more than composition
How should passwords be stored?As a salted hash from a slow algorithm (bcrypt, scrypt, argon2) - never plain text
Which module generates secure random values?secrets, not random

Advantages

Advantages: a declarative policy; each rule is independent; re.VERBOSE with comments documents the policy in the code itself.
codeExamples:
import re
common = re.compile(r"(password|qwerty|123456)", re.I)
print(bool(common.search("MyPassword9")))        # reject common substrings

# OUTPUT:
# True

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: composition rules push users to predictable choices such as Password1!, which passes the regex yet is trivially guessable.
codeExamples:
import re
STRONG = re.compile(r"^(?=.*[a-z])(?=.*[A-Z])(?=.*\d)(?=.*[^\w\s]).{8,}$")
print(bool(STRONG.match("Password1!")))          # passes, but terrible

# OUTPUT:
# True

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: regex cannot measure entropy or check breach lists, and the dot does not match newline, so a password containing one is handled differently unless you use re.S.
codeExamples:
import re
P = re.compile(r"^(?=.*\d).{8,}$")
print(bool(P.match("abc\ndef12345")))        # . stops at the newline: lookahead fails
print(bool(re.compile(r"^(?=.*\d).{8,}$", re.S).match("abc\ndef12345")))

# OUTPUT:
# False
# True

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Follow NIST 800-63B: minimum length, check against breached lists (HIBP k-anonymity API), no forced composition, allow passphrases and password managers. Hash with Argon2 or bcrypt; never log or store the raw password. Regex is a UX hint, not the security.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Application logs are text lines with a regular layout. In this project a regex with named groups turns each line into a record (time, level, module, message). From records you can count levels, find errors and build reports. Lines that do not match are counted and skipped instead of crashing the parser.
Figure: from raw text to a summary

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: A server writes thousands of log lines a minute. Reading them by eye does not scale; split() breaks when messages contain spaces or brackets.

Why we need it:
  • Convert unstructured text into structured data.
  • Summarise logs: counts per level, errors per module.
  • Practise robust parsing: skip bad lines, stay memory-friendly with generators.

Complete Example: Counting levels and reporting errors

A complete, runnable program. Save it in a file and run it with python.
codeExamples:
import re
from collections import Counter

LOG = re.compile(
    r"(?P<time>\d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}) (?P<level>[A-Z]+) \[(?P<module>\w+)\] (?P<message>.*)"
)

LINES = [
    "14:32:10 INFO [auth] User abaji logged in",
    "14:32:15 ERROR [db] Connection timeout",
    "garbage line",
    "14:33:01 WARNING [auth] Login failed for raoji",
    "14:35:42 ERROR [auth] Invalid token",
]


def main():
    levels = Counter()
    skipped = 0

    for line in LINES:
        match = LOG.fullmatch(line)
        if match is None:
            skipped += 1
            continue
        levels[match["level"]] += 1
        if match["level"] == "ERROR":
            print("ERROR in", match["module"], "->", match["message"])

    print(dict(levels))
    print("skipped:", skipped)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT:
# ERROR in db -> Connection timeout
# ERROR in auth -> Invalid token
# {'INFO': 1, 'ERROR': 2, 'WARNING': 1}
# skipped: 1
codeExplanations: fullmatch() returns None for the malformed line, which we count and skip. Named groups give readable access (match["level"]). Counter keeps insertion order, so the summary shows INFO first, then ERROR, then WARNING.

beginner.content:
The Goal

Application logs are lines of text with a regular layout. Using a regex with named groups you can turn each line into a dictionary of fields (timestamp, level, module, message), then count and filter them. Our log format: 
2026-10-05 14:32:10 ERROR [db] Connection timeout after 30s
Step 1: Parse One Line
codeExamples:
import re

LOG = re.compile(
    r"(?P<time>\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2} \d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}) "
    r"(?P<level>[A-Z]+) "
    r"\[(?P<module>\w+)\] "
    r"(?P<message>.*)"
)

line = "2026-10-05 14:32:10 ERROR [db] Connection timeout after 30s"
m = LOG.fullmatch(line)

print(m.groupdict())

# OUTPUT:
# {'time': '2026-10-05 14:32:10', 'level': 'ERROR', 'module': 'db', 'message': 'Connection timeout after 30s'}
codeExplanations: The pattern is split over several adjacent raw strings that Python joins into one. \[ and \] match literal square brackets. (?P<message>.*) takes whatever remains of the line. groupdict() returns every named group as a dictionary - one parsed record.

beginner.content:
Step 2: Parse Many Lines and Count Levels

Loop over the lines, skip any that do not match (match returns None), and count levels with collections.Counter.
codeExamples:
import re
from collections import Counter

LOG = re.compile(
    r"(?P<time>\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2} \d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}) "
    r"(?P<level>[A-Z]+) \[(?P<module>\w+)\] (?P<message>.*)"
)

lines = """2026-10-05 14:32:10 INFO [auth] User abaji logged in
2026-10-05 14:32:15 ERROR [db] Connection timeout after 30s
this line is malformed
2026-10-05 14:33:01 WARNING [auth] Login failed for user=raoji ip=10.0.0.5
2026-10-05 14:35:42 ERROR [auth] Invalid token""".splitlines()

counts = Counter()
skipped = 0
for line in lines:
    m = LOG.fullmatch(line)
    if m:
        counts[m["level"]] += 1
    else:
        skipped += 1

print(dict(counts))
print("skipped:", skipped)

# OUTPUT:
# {'INFO': 1, 'ERROR': 2, 'WARNING': 1}
# skipped: 1

beginner.content:
Introduction

This project parses log lines into structured records using a compiled regex with named groups: timestamp, level, module and message. The result is a list of dicts you can filter and count.
codeExamples:
import re
LINE = re.compile(r"(?P<ts>\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2} \d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}) "
                  r"\[(?P<level>[A-Z]+)\] (?P<module>[\w.]+): (?P<msg>.*)")

line = "2024-03-15 10:21:05 [ERROR] db.conn: timeout after 30s"
print(LINE.match(line).groupdict())

# OUTPUT:
# {'ts': '2024-03-15 10:21:05', 'level': 'ERROR', 'module': 'db.conn', 'msg': 'timeout after 30s'}

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Raw logs are text; to answer questions (how many errors per module?) you need fields. Regex turns each line into data without a heavy tool.
codeExamples:
import re
from collections import Counter
LINE = re.compile(r"\[(?P<level>[A-Z]+)\] (?P<module>[\w.]+):")
logs = ["[INFO] app: start", "[ERROR] db: fail", "[ERROR] db: fail again", "[WARN] app: slow"]
levels = Counter(m["level"] for m in map(LINE.search, logs))
print(levels)

# OUTPUT:
# Counter({'ERROR': 2, 'INFO': 1, 'WARN': 1})

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Incident triage, audit reports, alert rules, access-log analysis (IP, status, bytes) and converting legacy logs to JSON for tools like ELK.
codeExamples:
import re, json
ACCESS = re.compile(r'(?P<ip>[\d.]+) - - \[(?P<time>[^\]]+)\] "(?P<method>\w+) (?P<path>\S+) [^"]*" (?P<status>\d{3}) (?P<size>\d+)')
line = '10.0.0.5 - - [15/Mar/2024:10:21:05 +0000] "GET /api/users HTTP/1.1" 200 512'
rec = ACCESS.match(line).groupdict()
rec["status"], rec["size"] = int(rec["status"]), int(rec["size"])
print(json.dumps(rec))

# OUTPUT:
# {"ip": "10.0.0.5", "time": "15/Mar/2024:10:21:05 +0000", "method": "GET", "path": "/api/users", "status": 200, "size": 512}

beginner.content:
Diagram

   log file ─► line ─► compiled regex (named groups) ─► dict
      │                    │ no match                      │
      │                    └──► count / dead-letter file   ▼
      └─ read lazily ◄──────────────────────── filter ─► aggregate ─► report

expert.content:
Extracting key=value Pairs From the Message

Many log messages carry structured data as key=value pairs. A second, small regex pulls them out of the free-text message into a dictionary.
codeExamples:
import re

message = "Login failed for user=raoji ip=10.0.0.5 attempts=3"

fields = dict(re.findall(r"(\w+)=(\S+)", message))
print(fields)

# OUTPUT:
# {'user': 'raoji', 'ip': '10.0.0.5', 'attempts': '3'}

expert.content:
Streaming a Large File With a Generator

Log files can be gigabytes. Do not call read() or readlines(). Iterate the file object (one line at a time) inside a generator, so memory use stays constant, and convert the timestamp to a real datetime so you can filter by time.
codeExamples:
import re
from datetime import datetime

LOG = re.compile(
    r"(?P<time>\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2} \d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}) "
    r"(?P<level>[A-Z]+) \[(?P<module>\w+)\] (?P<message>.*)"
)

def parse_log(path):
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:                         # lazy: one line at a time
            m = LOG.fullmatch(line.rstrip("\n"))
            if m:
                record = m.groupdict()
                record["time"] = datetime.strptime(record["time"], "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
                yield record

errors = (r for r in parse_log("app.log") if r["level"] == "ERROR")
for record in errors:
    print(record["time"], record["module"], record["message"])

expert.content:
A Web-Server Access Log

The same technique parses the Common Log Format used by Apache and Nginx. Note [^\]]+ (anything except a closing bracket) for the timestamp and [^"]* for the rest of the quoted request.
codeExamples:
import re

ACCESS = re.compile(
    r'(?P<ip>\S+) \S+ \S+ \[(?P<time>[^\]]+)\] '
    r'"(?P<method>[A-Z]+) (?P<path>\S+) [^"]*" '
    r'(?P<status>\d{3}) (?P<size>\d+|-)'
)

line = '127.0.0.1 - - [05/Oct/2026:14:32:10 +0530] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 1043'
print(ACCESS.match(line).groupdict())

# OUTPUT:
# {'ip': '127.0.0.1', 'time': '05/Oct/2026:14:32:10 +0530', 'method': 'GET', 'path': '/index.html', 'status': '200', 'size': '1043'}

expert.content:
Design Notes

  • Be strict, but never crash: real logs contain malformed lines and multi-line stack traces. Count or collect lines that do not match instead of raising.
  • Anchor patterns and prefer specific classes (\d{4}, [A-Z]+) over .* to keep matching fast.
  • Prefer structured logging (JSON lines) for new systems: json.loads is faster and safer than regex. Parse text logs only when you cannot change the producer.

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Works on any text logs without changing the applicationFragile: a change in log format breaks the pattern
Named groups produce readable, self-documenting codeMulti-line records (stack traces) need extra handling
Generators can stream gigabyte files with constant memorySlower than parsing JSON logs
Easy to extend: add fields, filters, time windowsStructured (JSON) logging avoids parsing altogether

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why named groups for a log parser?groupdict() converts a line directly into a record with readable field names
How do you process a multi-GB log file?Iterate the file lazily inside a generator; never read the whole file into memory
How do you handle lines that do not match?Check for None, then skip or count them - do not let the parser crash
Why [^\]]+ for the timestamp?It matches everything up to the closing bracket and cannot run past it, unlike a greedy .*
Is regex the best log format solution?No - structured (JSON) logging avoids parsing altogether

Advantages

Advantages: fast to write, streams line by line with constant memory, and named groups make the schema self-documenting.
codeExamples:
import re, io
LINE = re.compile(r"\[(?P<level>[A-Z]+)\] (?P<msg>.*)")
stream = io.StringIO("[INFO] a\n[ERROR] b\n[ERROR] c\n")
errors = (m["msg"] for m in map(LINE.match, stream) if m and m["level"] == "ERROR")
print(list(errors))

# OUTPUT:
# ['b', 'c']

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: any format drift (new field, different timestamp) makes lines stop matching, and those lines vanish silently unless you count the misses.
codeExamples:
import re
LINE = re.compile(r"\[(?P<level>[A-Z]+)\] (?P<msg>.*)")
lines = ["[INFO] ok", "garbage line", "[ERROR] bad"]
parsed, skipped = [], 0
for l in lines:
    m = LINE.match(l)
    if m: parsed.append(m.groupdict())
    else: skipped += 1
print(len(parsed), "parsed,", skipped, "skipped")

# OUTPUT:
# 2 parsed, 1 skipped

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: multi-line entries (stack traces) need extra logic to join continuation lines, and regex is slow on very large volumes compared with structured logging.
codeExamples:
import re
START = re.compile(r"^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2} ")
raw = ["2024-03-15 ERROR boom", "  Traceback ...", "  KeyError: x", "2024-03-15 INFO ok"]
entries = []
for line in raw:
    if START.match(line): entries.append(line)
    else: entries[-1] += " | " + line.strip()      # join continuation lines
print(entries)

# OUTPUT:
# ['2024-03-15 ERROR boom | Traceback ... | KeyError: x', '2024-03-15 INFO ok']

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Prefer structured logging (JSON) at the source so no parsing is needed. When parsing is unavoidable, compile once, stream lazily, count unmatched lines, version your patterns, and use a log pipeline (Logstash grok, Vector) for production volume.

beginner.content:
What Are Type Hints?

Python is dynamically typed, but since Python 3.5 you can annotate code with the types you expect. These type hints document intent for humans, power editor auto-completion, and let tools like mypy and Pyright catch type bugs before the program runs.

Unlike Java, the interpreter does not enforce them - they are optional metadata.

Annotating Function Parameters and Return Values

Write name: type for each parameter and -> type before the colon for the return value.
codeExamples:
def greet(name: str, times: int = 1) -> str:
    return ("Hello, " + name + "! ") * times

def log(message: str) -> None:        # returns nothing
    print("LOG:", message)

print(greet("Abaji", 2))
log("started")

# OUTPUT:
# Hello, Abaji! Hello, Abaji!
# LOG: started

beginner.content:
Annotating Variables

Use name: type = value. Most of the time you don't need it - tools infer the type from the value - but it helps for empty containers and values that start as None.
codeExamples:
count: int = 0
price: float = 99.5
city: str = "Pune"
active: bool = True
scores: list[int] = []          # without the hint, tools can't tell what goes inside

print(count, price, city, active, scores)

# OUTPUT:
# 0 99.5 Pune True []

beginner.content:
Hints Are Not Checked at Runtime

Python runs code with wrong types exactly as it would without hints. The error, if any, only appears when an operation actually fails.
codeExamples:
def double(n: int) -> int:
    return n * 2

print(double(21))
print(double("ab"))         # wrong type - Python runs it anyway

# OUTPUT:
# 42
# abab

beginner.content:
Checking with mypy

Install a type checker and run it over your files. It reads the hints and reports mistakes without executing the code.
codeExamples:
# shop.py
def total(price: float, qty: int) -> float:
    return price * qty

total(99.5, "3")

# $ pip install mypy
# $ mypy shop.py
# mypy reports (wording may vary by version):
# shop.py:4: error: Argument 2 to "total" has incompatible type "str"; expected "int"  [arg-type]
# Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 1 source file)

beginner.content:
Python vs Java Typing

JavaPython with hints
Declarationint count = 0;count: int = 0
Method signatureString greet(String name)def greet(name: str) -> str:
No return valuevoid-> None
Who checksThe compiler - alwaysAn external tool (mypy, Pyright, your IDE) - optional
At runtimeTypes enforcedHints ignored

Introduction

Type hints annotate what types variables, parameters and return values are meant to hold: x: int = 5 and def f(a: int) -> str:. Python itself does not enforce them; tools such as mypy, pyright and IDEs check them.
codeExamples:
def greet(name: str, times: int = 1) -> str:
    return ("Hello, " + name + "! ") * times

age: int = 30                 # variable annotation
print(greet("Ann", 2))
print(greet.__annotations__)

# OUTPUT:
# Hello, Ann! Hello, Ann!
# {'name': <class 'str'>, 'times': <class 'int'>, 'return': <class 'str'>}

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

In a dynamic language, a function's expected inputs live only in the author's head. Annotations document them in code, enable auto-complete and catch mismatches before the program runs.
codeExamples:
def double(n: int) -> int:
    return n * 2

# A checker (mypy) flags the next line BEFORE running:
#   error: Argument 1 to "double" has incompatible type "str"; expected "int"
print(double("ab"))        # Python runs it anyway: str * 2 works

# OUTPUT:
# abab

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Large codebases, public libraries and APIs (FastAPI, Pydantic and dataclasses read annotations at runtime), and CI pipelines that run mypy or pyright as a gate.
codeExamples:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class User:
    id: int
    name: str
    active: bool = True       # annotations define the fields

print(User(1, "Ann"))

# OUTPUT:
# User(id=1, name='Ann', active=True)

beginner.content:
Diagram

   source ──► Python runs it (ignores hints)
      │
      └──► mypy / pyright / IDE ──► reports: wrong type passed, missing return
   hints are read by:  type checkers | IDEs | Pydantic | FastAPI | dataclasses

expert.content:
Where Hints Are Stored: __annotations__

Annotations are evaluated and stored in an __annotations__ dict on the function (and on the module or class for variable annotations). Libraries such as dataclasses, Pydantic and FastAPI read them at runtime to generate code, validation and API docs. typing.get_type_hints() is the robust way to read them.

An Annotation Alone Creates No Variable

x: int without a value only records the type; the name is not bound. Reading it is still a NameError.
codeExamples:
total: int          # annotation only
print(__annotations__)
print(total)

# OUTPUT:
# {'total': <class 'int'>}
# NameError: name 'total' is not defined

expert.content:
Gradual Typing and Any

You don't have to annotate a whole project at once. Unannotated functions are treated as returning and accepting Any, which mypy never complains about. Any is compatible with every type in both directions - an escape hatch that also switches checking off, so use it sparingly. Prefer object when you mean "any value, but I won't assume anything about it".

Return Types Catch Missing Returns

A declared return type lets the checker spot paths that forget to return - a bug Python itself turns into a silent None.
codeExamples:
def grade(marks: int) -> str:
    if marks >= 40:
        return "pass"
    # forgot the fail case

print(grade(30))

# OUTPUT:
# None
#
# mypy reports (wording may vary by version):
# error: Missing return statement  [return]

expert.content:
Forward References and Postponed Evaluation

A class can't be named in its own body before it exists. Quote the annotation ("Node"), or add from __future__ import annotations so annotations are stored as strings and not evaluated at definition time. Since 3.11, typing.Self expresses "an instance of this class".
codeExamples:
from __future__ import annotations

class Node:
    def __init__(self, value: int, next: Node | None = None) -> None:
        self.value = value
        self.next = next

head = Node(1, Node(2))
print(head.next.value)
print(Node.__init__.__annotations__["next"])

# OUTPUT:
# 2
# Node | None

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Does Python enforce type hints?No - CPython ignores them at runtime; tools like mypy, Pyright and IDEs check them
Where are annotations stored?In __annotations__ on functions, classes and modules; read them with typing.get_type_hints()
How do you annotate a function that returns nothing?-> None
Any vs object?Any disables checking in both directions; object accepts anything but only allows operations every object supports
What is gradual typing?Adding hints incrementally - unannotated code is treated as Any, so typed and untyped code coexist
Why use hints if they aren't enforced?Earlier bug detection, better editor completion, self-documenting code, and runtime use by frameworks like FastAPI and Pydantic

Advantages

Advantages: self-documenting signatures, better IDE help, early bug detection, safer refactoring, and gradual adoption: annotate only what you want.
codeExamples:
import inspect
def area(w: float, h: float = 1.0) -> float:
    return w * h

print(inspect.signature(area))        # tools read the same metadata

# OUTPUT:
# (w: float, h: float = 1.0) -> float

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: extra typing effort, more verbose signatures, and a false sense of safety because wrong values still run at runtime.
codeExamples:
def square(n: int) -> int:
    return n * n

print(square(2.5))          # annotation is a promise, not a check

# OUTPUT:
# 6.25

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: annotations do not enforce anything and do not change speed; they only describe intent. Variables annotated without a value are not even created.

Architect's Notes

Adopt types incrementally: public APIs first, then core domain code, with mypy --strict on new modules. Types are documentation that is verified; they do not replace tests or runtime validation of external input (use Pydantic at boundaries).

beginner.content:
Saying What's Inside a Collection

list alone says "some list". Square brackets say what it contains - like Java generics (List<Integer>). Since Python 3.9 the built-in types can be used directly.
HintMeaningJava equivalent
list[int]A list of intsList<Integer>
set[str]A set of stringsSet<String>
dict[str, float]str keys, float valuesMap<String, Double>
tuple[str, int]Exactly two items: a str then an intA record / pair class
tuple[int, ...]Any number of intsint[] (read-only)
Using Them

Fixed-Length vs Variable-Length Tuples

A tuple hint lists the type of each position. To mean "a tuple of any length, all the same type", add ....
codeExamples:
student: tuple[str, int, float] = ("Abaji", 21, 8.7)    # exactly 3 items
rgb: tuple[int, int, int] = (255, 128, 0)
marks: tuple[int, ...] = (70, 85, 90, 65)               # any number of ints

print(student[0], rgb, len(marks))

# OUTPUT:
# Abaji (255, 128, 0) 4

beginner.content:
Nested Types

Types nest just like the data does.
codeExamples:
class_marks: dict[str, list[int]] = {
    "Abaji": [91, 85],
    "Raoji": [72, 68],
}
matrix: list[list[float]] = [[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]
edges: list[tuple[str, str]] = [("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]

print(class_marks["Abaji"][1], matrix[1][0], edges[0])

# OUTPUT:
# 85 3.0 ('A', 'B')

beginner.content: What the Checker Catches
codeExamples:
scores: list[int] = [70, 80]
scores.append("ninety")

ages: dict[str, int] = {"Abaji": 21}
ages[42] = "Raoji"

# The code runs (lists and dicts accept anything), but:
# mypy reports (wording may vary by version):
# error: Argument 1 to "append" of "list" has incompatible type "str"; expected "int"  [arg-type]
# error: Invalid index type "int" for "dict[str, int]"; expected type "str"  [index]
# error: Incompatible types in assignment (expression has type "str", target has type "int")  [assignment]

beginner.content:
Introduction

Annotate containers with their element types using the built-in generics (Python 3.9+): list[int], dict[str, float], tuple[int, str] (fixed shape), tuple[int, ...] (any length), set[str].
codeExamples:
prices: dict[str, float] = {"apple": 1.2, "pear": 0.8}
ids: list[int] = [1, 2, 3]
point: tuple[float, float] = (1.5, 2.5)        # exactly two floats
vals: tuple[int, ...] = (1, 2, 3, 4)           # any number of ints
print(prices, ids, point, vals)

# OUTPUT:
# {'apple': 1.2, 'pear': 0.8} [1, 2, 3] (1.5, 2.5) (1, 2, 3, 4)

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

A bare list says nothing about what is inside. Element types let a checker flag list_of_ints.append("x") and give the IDE enough information to complete methods on items.

Real-Time Use

Function signatures for data processing, configuration dictionaries, JSON-like structures and return types of repository or service methods.

Diagram

   list[int]            homogeneous, any length      [1, 2, 3]
   tuple[int, str]      fixed positions and types    (1, "a")
   tuple[int, ...]      homogeneous, any length      (1, 2, 3, 4)
   dict[str, float]     key type -> value type       {"a": 1.0}
   Sequence / Mapping   read-only abstract types (prefer for parameters)

expert.content:
Older Code: typing.List, typing.Dict...

Before Python 3.9 you had to import capitalised aliases from typing. They still work but are deprecated - use the built-in names in new code.
Old (3.5-3.8)Modern (3.9+)
from typing import List → List[int]list[int]
Dict[str, int]dict[str, int]
Tuple[int, str]tuple[int, str]
Set[str]set[str]

Accept General, Return Specific

For parameters, ask only for what the function actually uses. A function that just loops over its input should take Iterable[int], so callers can pass a list, tuple, set, range or generator. For return values, be specific (list[int]) so callers know exactly what they get. These abstract types live in collections.abc - the same idea as declaring a Java parameter as Collection<T> instead of ArrayList<T>.
TypePromises
Iterable[T]Can be looped over
Sequence[T]Plus len() and indexing (list, tuple, str, range) - read-only
Mapping[K, V]Read-only dict-like access
MutableSequence[T] / MutableMapping[K, V]Also allows modification

Why list[int] Isn't list[float] (Invariance)

A list[int] is not accepted where list[float] is expected, because the function could append a float into your list of ints. Read-only types such as Sequence[float] are covariant and accept it - another reason to use the abstract types for parameters. Java generics behave the same way (List<Integer> is not a List<Number>).

Generic Aliases at Runtime

list[int] creates a types.GenericAlias object. Calling it still builds a plain list - the element type is not stored or checked - and isinstance refuses parameterised generics.
codeExamples:
alias = list[int]
print(alias, type(alias))
print(alias("abc"))                 # no checking: still just list("abc")
print(isinstance([1, 2], list))
print(isinstance([1, 2], list[int]))

# OUTPUT:
# list[int] <class 'types.GenericAlias'>
# ['a', 'b', 'c']
# True
# TypeError: isinstance() argument 2 cannot be a parameterized generic

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How do you hint a list of strings?list[str] (3.9+); typing.List[str] in older code
tuple[int, str] vs tuple[int, ...]?The first is exactly two items (int then str); the second is any number of ints
Why use Iterable or Sequence for parameters?They accept any suitable container (list, tuple, generator...), making the function more reusable
Is list[int] compatible with list[float]?No - list is invariant because it is mutable; Sequence[float] accepts it
Are element types checked at runtime?No - list[int]("abc") happily builds a list of strings

Advantages

Advantages: precise contracts, checker catches wrong element types, and read-only abstractions (Sequence, Mapping) accept more inputs.
codeExamples:
from collections.abc import Sequence, Mapping

def head(items: Sequence[int]) -> int:      # accepts list, tuple, range ...
    return items[0]

def keys(m: Mapping[str, int]) -> list[str]:
    return sorted(m)

print(head([7, 8]), head((9, 1)), head(range(3, 6)), keys({"b": 1, "a": 2}))

# OUTPUT:
# 7 9 3 ['a', 'b']

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: verbose for deep structures, and list is invariant: a list[int] is not accepted where list[float] is expected.
codeExamples:
def avg(xs: list[float]) -> float:
    return sum(xs) / len(xs)

ints: list[int] = [1, 2, 3]
print(avg(ints))      # runs fine; mypy rejects it: list is invariant
                      # fix: use Sequence[float] (covariant) in the signature

# OUTPUT:
# 2.0

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: generics are erased at runtime: list[int] does not check contents, isinstance(x, list[int]) is an error, and a tuple's fixed shape is not enforced by Python.
codeExamples:
x: list[int] = ["not", "ints"]      # runs without complaint
print(x)
try:
    isinstance(x, list[int])
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)

# OUTPUT:
# ['not', 'ints']
# TypeError: isinstance() argument 2 cannot be a parameterized generic

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Accept the most general abstract type (Iterable, Sequence, Mapping) in parameters and return the most specific concrete one. Use tuple for records only when positions are obvious, otherwise a dataclass or NamedTuple.

beginner.content:
A Value of One Type or Another: Union

When a value may be one of several types, list them with | (Python 3.10+). Older code writes Union[int, str] from typing - they mean the same thing.
codeExamples:
def to_text(value: int | float | str) -> str:
    return str(value)

print(to_text(5), to_text(2.5), to_text("hi"))

# Older equivalent:
# from typing import Union
# def to_text(value: Union[int, float, str]) -> str: ...

# OUTPUT:
# 5 2.5 hi

beginner.content:
Maybe None: Optional

A very common case is "a value, or None". Write str | None, or the older Optional[str] - which is just shorthand for Union[str, None]. It is Python's version of Java's nullable reference or Optional<String>.

Narrowing: Check Before You Use

With str | None, the checker won't let you call string methods until you have ruled out None. An if value is None check (or isinstance) narrows the type inside each branch.
codeExamples:
def shout(name: str | None) -> str:
    return name.upper()                    # might be None!

def shout_safe(name: str | None) -> str:
    if name is None:
        return "ANONYMOUS"
    return name.upper()                    # here name is known to be str

print(shout_safe("abaji"), shout_safe(None))

# mypy reports for shout() (wording may vary by version):
# error: Item "None" of "str | None" has no attribute "upper"  [union-attr]
#
# OUTPUT:
# ABAJI ANONYMOUS

def describe(value: int | str) -> str:
    if isinstance(value, int):
        return f"number {value + 1}"       # value is int here
    return f"text {value.upper()}"         # value is str here

print(describe(41), describe("ok"))

# OUTPUT:
# number 42 text OK

beginner.content:
Introduction

Union[int, str] (or int | str in 3.10+) means "one of these types". Optional[int] is exactly int | None: the value may be missing.
codeExamples:
from typing import Optional

def find(name: str, users: dict[str, int]) -> Optional[int]:    # int | None
    return users.get(name)

def show(v: int | str) -> str:           # 3.10+ union syntax
    return f"value={v}"

print(find("ann", {"ann": 1}), find("baji", {"ann": 1}))
print(show(5), show("x"))

# OUTPUT:
# 1 None
# value=5 value=x

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Real functions sometimes return nothing (lookup misses) or accept several input forms. Stating this explicitly forces callers to handle None, preventing the most common runtime error: AttributeError: 'NoneType'.

Real-Time Use

Database lookups, optional config values, function arguments with defaults of None, API fields that may be absent, and parsers returning either a value or an error type.

Diagram

   Optional[int]  ==  int | None
                 ┌── int ──► use as int
   value ────────┤
                 └── None ─► must be handled   (if v is None: ...)
   narrowing:  if v is not None:  # checker treats v as int here

expert.content:
"Optional" Does Not Mean "Optional Argument"

Optional[X] only means the value may be None. Whether the caller can omit the argument depends on having a default value. The two ideas are independent.
codeExamples:
def a(note: str | None):            # may be None, but must be passed
    return note

def b(note: str = "none"):           # may be omitted, but never None
    return note

def c(note: str | None = None):      # may be omitted AND may be None
    return note

print(a(None), b(), c())
a()

# OUTPUT:
# None none None
# TypeError: a() missing 1 required positional argument: 'note'

expert.content:
The Two Spellings Are Equivalent

Optional[int], Union[int, None] and int | None all describe the same type, and the checker treats them identically. Prefer X | None in code that targets Python 3.10 or newer; it reads more naturally and needs no import.
codeExamples:
from typing import Optional, Union

print(Optional[int])
print(Union[int, None])
print(int | None)
print(type(int | None))

# OUTPUT:
# typing.Optional[int]
# typing.Optional[int]
# int | None
# <class 'types.UnionType'>

expert.content:
Return None or Raise?

A -> X | None return type forces every caller to handle None. That is right when "not found" is a normal outcome (searching, dict.get). When the absence means something went wrong, raise an exception and keep the return type plain - the checker then doesn't make every caller add None checks.
codeExamples:
def find_user(user_id: int) -> str | None:     # "not found" is normal
    return {1: "Abaji"}.get(user_id)

def load_user(user_id: int) -> str:             # absence is an error
    users = {1: "Abaji"}
    if user_id not in users:
        raise KeyError(f"no user {user_id}")
    return users[user_id]

print(find_user(5))
print(load_user(1))
load_user(5)

# OUTPUT:
# None
# Abaji
# KeyError: 'no user 5'

expert.content:
Other Narrowing Tools

• Early return / guard clause - after if x is None: return, the rest of the function sees X.
• assert - assert x is not None narrows for the checker (but is removed with python -O, so don't rely on it for real validation).
• Truthiness - if name: also narrows, but treats "" like None.
• Custom type guards - typing.TypeGuard / TypeIs (3.13) let your own boolean functions narrow types.
codeExamples:
def first_word(text: str | None) -> str:
    if not text:
        return ""
    return text.split()[0]                 # text is str here

print(repr(first_word(None)), repr(first_word("")), first_word("hello world"))

# OUTPUT:
# '' '' hello

expert.content:
Unions Are Checked by Tools, Not by Python

At runtime nothing stops a wrong type; a union only helps the checker. If you must validate input from outside (JSON, forms), check with isinstance - which accepts X | Y unions directly since 3.10 - or use a validation library such as Pydantic.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does Optional[str] mean?str or None - exactly the same as Union[str, None] and str | None
Does Optional make an argument optional to pass?No - only a default value does; Optional only allows None as a value
What is type narrowing?The checker refining a union inside a branch after an is None or isinstance check
Union vs |?Same meaning; the | syntax needs Python 3.10+ (or from __future__ import annotations inside annotations)
When should a function return None instead of raising?When absence is a normal, expected result; raise when it indicates an error

Advantages

Advantages: makes absence visible in the signature; type narrowing with isinstance or is None keeps code safe; unions model sum types.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: every caller must handle None, which spreads checks through the code, and big unions force many isinstance branches.

Limitations

Limitations: Optional[int] means "may be None", not "argument may be omitted"; a parameter still needs a default to be optional. X | Y syntax needs Python 3.10+ at runtime (use from __future__ import annotations for older).
codeExamples:
from typing import Optional
def f(x: Optional[int]):          # no default: x is still REQUIRED
    return x

try:
    f()
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)

# OUTPUT:
# TypeError: f() missing 1 required positional argument: 'x'

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Avoid returning None for errors in core logic: raise exceptions, or use a result type, or the null-object pattern. Reserve Optional for genuine absence, and keep unions small; if you branch on type often, consider polymorphism or a tagged union.

beginner.content:
Literal: Only These Exact Values

Sometimes a parameter is a str, but only a few specific strings make sense - a file mode, a sort direction, a log level. Literal[...] lists the allowed values so the checker can reject typos.
codeExamples:
from typing import Literal

def open_report(path: str, mode: Literal["r", "w"]) -> str:
    return f"opening {path} in mode {mode}"

def sort_marks(marks: list[int], order: Literal["asc", "desc"] = "asc") -> list[int]:
    return sorted(marks, reverse=(order == "desc"))

print(open_report("report.txt", "r"))
print(sort_marks([70, 90, 80], "desc"))
print(open_report("report.txt", "x"))     # runs - but the checker flags it

# mypy reports (wording may vary by version):
# error: Argument 2 to "open_report" has incompatible type "Literal['x']"; expected "Literal['r', 'w']"  [arg-type]
#
# OUTPUT:
# opening report.txt in mode r
# [90, 80, 70]
# opening report.txt in mode x

beginner.content:
Final: A Constant That Must Not Be Reassigned

Python has no final keyword like Java. The UPPER_CASE naming convention signals a constant; Final makes the checker enforce it.
codeExamples:
from typing import Final

MAX_RETRIES: Final = 3
GST_RATE: Final[float] = 0.18

MAX_RETRIES = 5          # Python allows it at runtime...
print(MAX_RETRIES)

# mypy reports (wording may vary by version):
# error: Cannot assign to final name "MAX_RETRIES"  [misc]
#
# OUTPUT:
# 5

beginner.content:
Literal vs Final vs Java

PythonPurposeJava
Literal["asc", "desc"]Restrict a value to a fixed setAn enum
X: Final = 3Never reassign this namestatic final int X = 3;
@final on a classNo subclassesfinal class
@final on a methodNo overridingfinal method
In every case Python's version is checked only by tools - the interpreter never blocks it.

Introduction

Literal["a", "b"] restricts a value to specific constants. Final marks a name as a constant that must not be reassigned. Both are checked by type checkers, not by Python at runtime.
codeExamples:
from typing import Literal, Final

Mode = Literal["r", "w", "a"]
MAX_USERS: Final = 100

def open_file(path: str, mode: Mode) -> str:
    return f"{path} opened with {mode}"

print(open_file("x.txt", "w"))
print(MAX_USERS)

# OUTPUT:
# x.txt opened with w
# 100

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

A plain str accepts typos like "wirte". Literal limits input to the allowed values, and Final stops accidental changes to configuration constants.
codeExamples:
from typing import Literal
Direction = Literal["up", "down"]

def move(d: Direction) -> int:
    return 1 if d == "up" else -1

print(move("up"))
# move("left")   # checker: Argument 1 has incompatible type "Literal['left']"
print(move("left"))   # Python does not stop it at runtime

# OUTPUT:
# 1
# -1

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Function options (modes, log levels, HTTP methods), state names in state machines, discriminated unions, and constants such as limits, versions and defaults.
codeExamples:
from typing import Literal, get_args
Level = Literal["debug", "info", "error"]

def log(level: Level, msg: str) -> str:
    return f"[{level.upper()}] {msg}"

print(log("info", "started"))
print(get_args(Level))            # allowed values are available at runtime

# OUTPUT:
# [INFO] started
# ('debug', 'info', 'error')

beginner.content:
Diagram

   x: str                 any string at all
   x: Literal["r","w"]    only these exact values  ──► typo caught by checker
   LIMIT: Final = 10      checker: no reassignment   (runtime: not enforced)
   Enum                   runtime-enforced set of named constants

expert.content:
@final Classes and Methods

typing.final marks a class that must not be subclassed, or a method that must not be overridden. At runtime the decorator does almost nothing (since 3.11 it sets a __final__ attribute where it can).

Final Is About the Name, Not the Object

Final stops rebinding, not mutation - exactly like Java's final reference. A Final list can still be appended to. For truly immutable constants, use a tuple or frozenset.
codeExamples:
from typing import Final

ALLOWED_ROLES: Final = ["admin", "editor"]
ALLOWED_ROLES.append("hacker")          # mutation is allowed (by Python and mypy)
print(ALLOWED_ROLES)

SAFE_ROLES: Final = ("admin", "editor")  # immutable value as well as final name
print("hacker" in SAFE_ROLES)

# OUTPUT:
# ['admin', 'editor', 'hacker']
# False

expert.content:
Literal vs Enum

Both restrict a value to a fixed set. Literal keeps plain strings (easy for JSON and configuration, nothing to import at call sites). An Enum is a real runtime type: values are validated when converted, it can carry methods, and it is iterable. Choose an enum when the set of values is a concept of its own in your program.
codeExamples:
from enum import Enum
from typing import Literal, get_args

Direction = Literal["asc", "desc"]
print(get_args(Direction))

class Order(Enum):
    ASC = "asc"
    DESC = "desc"

print(Order("desc"), [o.value for o in Order])
Order("sideways")

# OUTPUT:
# ('asc', 'desc')
# Order.DESC ['asc', 'desc']
# ValueError: 'sideways' is not a valid Order

expert.content:
Literal Values Are Not Checked at Runtime

Like every hint, Literal is ignored by Python. When the value comes from outside (user input, an API), validate it yourself - get_args() lets you reuse the same list of allowed values.
codeExamples:
from typing import Literal, get_args

Level = Literal["debug", "info", "error"]

def set_level(level: str) -> Level:
    if level not in get_args(Level):
        raise ValueError(f"invalid level: {level!r}")
    return level            # type: ignore[return-value]  (checker can't see the narrowing)

print(set_level("info"))
set_level("loud")

# OUTPUT:
# info
# ValueError: invalid level: 'loud'

expert.content:
LiteralString (3.11+)

typing.LiteralString accepts only strings written as literals in the source code (or built from them), not strings that came from user input. Database and shell libraries use it to let checkers flag SQL or command injection: a query built from a literal passes, a query built with an f-string from user data is rejected by the checker.
codeExamples:
from typing import LiteralString

def run_query(sql: LiteralString) -> str:
    return f"executing: {sql}"

print(run_query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"))   # literal - accepted

user_input = input("id: ")
run_query(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = {user_input}")   # flagged by the checker

# mypy / Pyright report that a plain "str" is not a "LiteralString"
# (support and wording vary by tool and version)

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does Literal["r", "w"] mean?The value must be exactly "r" or "w" - checked by type checkers only
Does Final make a constant immutable?No - it forbids rebinding the name; the object itself can still be mutated
How do you prevent subclassing in Python?Decorate the class with typing.final - enforced by type checkers, not at runtime
Literal vs Enum?Literal restricts plain values for the checker; Enum is a runtime type with validation and methods
How do you read the values of a Literal at runtime?typing.get_args(MyLiteral)
What is LiteralString for?Letting checkers flag injection by accepting only strings built from source-code literals

Advantages

Advantages: precise, self-documenting APIs; IDE auto-completes the allowed values; checkers verify exhaustive if/match over a Literal.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: values must be written literally, so variables of type str are rejected, and long lists of choices belong in an Enum instead.
codeExamples:
from enum import Enum
class Color(Enum):          # better than Literal for many reusable choices
    RED = "red"
    GREEN = "green"

print(Color("red"), [c.value for c in Color])

# OUTPUT:
# Color.RED ['red', 'green']

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: Final is not enforced at runtime (only by checkers), and a Final list or dict can still be mutated; Literal does not check values at runtime either.
codeExamples:
from typing import Final
LIMIT: Final = 10
LIMIT = 99                    # checker error; Python allows it
ITEMS: Final = [1, 2]
ITEMS.append(3)               # Final does not make it immutable
print(LIMIT, ITEMS)

# OUTPUT:
# 99 [1, 2, 3]

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use Literal for small closed sets at API boundaries and Enum when values need behaviour or runtime validation. Combine Final with immutable types (tuple, frozenset, MappingProxyType) if you truly need immutability.

beginner.content:
Dictionaries with a Known Shape

A lot of real data arrives as dictionaries with a fixed set of keys: JSON from an API, a row from a database, a config file. dict[str, object] says nothing useful about it. A TypedDict describes each key and the type of its value, so editors can autocomplete keys and type checkers (mypy, Pyright) can catch typos and wrong types.

In Java you would write a class or a record for this. A TypedDict describes the data without changing it: at runtime the object is still an ordinary dict.
codeExamples:
from typing import TypedDict

class Student(TypedDict):
    name: str
    age: int
    marks: list[int]

s: Student = {"name": "Abaji", "age": 21, "marks": [80, 90]}

print(s["name"], sum(s["marks"]))
print(type(s))

# OUTPUT:
# Abaji 170
# <class 'dict'>

beginner.content:
What the Type Checker Catches

Python itself runs every line below. A type checker reports the mistakes before the program runs - exactly the kind of bug that otherwise surfaces as a KeyError deep inside a web request.
codeExamples:
from typing import TypedDict

class Student(TypedDict):
    name: str
    age: int
    marks: list[int]

a: Student = {"name": "Raoji", "age": 22}                    # missing "marks"
b: Student = {"name": "Kanhoji", "age": "22", "marks": []}    # age is a str
print(a["nmae"])                                            # typo in the key

# mypy reports (wording may vary by version):
# error: Missing key "marks" for TypedDict "Student"
# error: Incompatible types (expression has type "str", TypedDict item "age" has type "int")
# error: TypedDict "Student" has no key "nmae"

beginner.content:
Optional Keys: total=False

By default every key is required. total=False makes all keys of that class optional - useful for "settings that may or may not be present". Read optional keys with .get().
codeExamples:
from typing import TypedDict

class Options(TypedDict, total=False):
    debug: bool
    port: int

defaults: Options = {}
custom: Options = {"port": 8080}

print(custom.get("port", 80), custom.get("debug", False))
print(sorted(Options.__optional_keys__))

# OUTPUT:
# 8080 False
# ['debug', 'port']

beginner.content:
Mixing Required and Optional: Required / NotRequired

Since Python 3.11, NotRequired[...] marks a single key as optional (and Required[...] does the reverse inside a total=False class).
codeExamples:
from typing import NotRequired, TypedDict

class User(TypedDict):
    id: int
    email: str
    phone: NotRequired[str]          # may be missing

u1: User = {"id": 1, "email": "abaji@example.com"}
u2: User = {"id": 2, "email": "raoji@example.com", "phone": "98765 43210"}

print(sorted(User.__required_keys__), sorted(User.__optional_keys__))
print(u1.get("phone", "not given"), u2.get("phone"))

# OUTPUT:
# ['email', 'id'] ['phone']
# not given 98765 43210

beginner.content:
Introduction

TypedDict describes the exact keys and value types of a dictionary. At runtime it is still a plain dict; type checkers verify the keys and types.
codeExamples:
from typing import TypedDict

class Movie(TypedDict):
    title: str
    year: int

m: Movie = {"title": "Dune", "year": 2021}
print(m["title"], type(m).__name__)

# OUTPUT:
# Dune dict

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

JSON payloads and configs are dicts, and a plain dict[str, Any] hides which keys exist. TypedDict gives fields names and types without changing the data format, and without defining a class instance.
codeExamples:
from typing import TypedDict

class User(TypedDict):
    id: int
    name: str

def label(u: User) -> str:
    return f"#{u['id']} {u['name']}"       # checker verifies these keys exist

print(label({"id": 7, "name": "Ann"}))

# OUTPUT:
# #7 Ann

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Typed JSON responses from APIs, config dictionaries, rows from database drivers and kwargs bundles (Unpack[...]).
codeExamples:
import json
from typing import TypedDict, NotRequired

class Address(TypedDict):
    city: str
    zip: NotRequired[str]                  # optional key (3.11+)

class Customer(TypedDict):
    name: str
    address: Address

c: Customer = json.loads('{"name": "Ann", "address": {"city": "Pune"}}')
print(c["address"]["city"], c["address"].get("zip", "n/a"))

# OUTPUT:
# Pune n/a

beginner.content:
Diagram

   JSON text ──json.loads──► dict (plain)  ──annotated as──► Movie(TypedDict)
                                                  │
                      type checker verifies:  keys exist, value types match
   runtime:  still just a dict  (no validation, no cost)

expert.content:
At Runtime It Is Only a dict

A TypedDict performs no validation. Calling the class just builds a plain dict, and isinstance checks are not allowed, because there is no real class behind the data.
codeExamples:
from typing import TypedDict

class Student(TypedDict):
    name: str
    age: int

s = Student(name="Raoji", age="not a number")    # accepted at runtime
print(s, type(s))

try:
    isinstance(s, Student)
except TypeError as error:
    print("TypeError:", error)

# OUTPUT:
# {'name': 'Raoji', 'age': 'not a number'} <class 'dict'>
# TypeError: TypedDict does not support instance and class checks

expert.content:
Typing JSON from an API

json.loads() returns Any, so the checker trusts whatever you assign it to. A TypedDict then documents the expected shape for the rest of the code - but it does not prove the data really has that shape. When the data comes from outside your program, validate it (by hand, or with a library such as pydantic) at the boundary.
codeExamples:
import json
from typing import TypedDict

class Order(TypedDict):
    id: int
    total: float
    items: list[str]

def parse_order(text: str) -> Order:
    data = json.loads(text)
    if not isinstance(data.get("id"), int):
        raise ValueError("order id must be an int")
    return data

order = parse_order('{"id": 7, "total": 499.0, "items": ["pen", "book"]}')
print(order["id"], len(order["items"]))

# OUTPUT:
# 7 2

expert.content:
The Functional Syntax

Keys that are not valid Python identifiers (hyphens, keywords such as class) can't be written as class attributes. The functional form accepts any string keys.
codeExamples:
from typing import TypedDict

Headers = TypedDict("Headers", {"content-type": str, "x-request-id": str})

h: Headers = {"content-type": "application/json", "x-request-id": "abc123"}
print(h["content-type"])

# OUTPUT:
# application/json

expert.content:
TypedDict vs dataclass vs NamedTuple

AspectTypedDictdataclassNamedTuple
Runtime objectPlain dictInstance of your classA tuple subclass
Accessd["name"]obj.namet.name or t[0]
MutableYesYes (unless frozen=True)No
Methods / validationNoYes (__post_init__)Methods, no validation
JSON round tripDirect - it already is a dictNeeds conversion (asdict)Needs conversion (_asdict)
Best forDescribing existing dict data (JSON, kwargs)Your own domain objectsSmall immutable records

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a TypedDict?A type hint describing a dict with specific keys and value types, checked by static type checkers
What type is a TypedDict value at runtime?A plain dict - there is no validation and isinstance checks raise TypeError
How do you make keys optional?total=False for the whole class, or NotRequired[...] per key (3.11+)
TypedDict vs dataclass?TypedDict types existing dict-shaped data; a dataclass creates a real class with attributes and methods
Does annotating JSON with a TypedDict validate it?No - it only informs the type checker; validate external data explicitly or with a library such as pydantic

Advantages

Advantages: zero runtime cost, works directly with json, supports required and optional keys, inheritance, and nesting.
codeExamples:
from typing import TypedDict

class Base(TypedDict):
    id: int
class Item(Base, total=False):             # extra keys optional
    note: str

i: Item = {"id": 1}
print(i, Item.__required_keys__, Item.__optional_keys__)

# OUTPUT:
# {'id': 1} frozenset({'id'}) frozenset({'note'})

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: no validation at runtime and no methods or defaults; wrong data passes silently, and values are accessed with ["key"] rather than attributes.
codeExamples:
from typing import TypedDict
class Movie(TypedDict):
    title: str
    year: int

bad: Movie = {"title": 123}          # wrong type and missing key; no runtime error
print(bad)

# OUTPUT:
# {'title': 123}

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: isinstance(x, Movie) is not allowed, structural typing means any dict with those keys matches, and keys must be strings that are valid as identifiers (unless using the functional syntax).

Architect's Notes

Use TypedDict to type data you do not own (JSON, third-party dicts) and dataclasses or Pydantic models for domain objects and validated input. When a payload crosses a trust boundary, validate it at runtime; the hint alone proves nothing.

beginner.content:
Typing a Function That Takes a Function

Functions are values in Python, so parameters often receive functions: callbacks, key functions, strategies. Callable[[ArgType1, ArgType2], ReturnType] describes such a parameter - the list holds the argument types, the last item is the return type.

Import it from collections.abc (preferred since Python 3.9; typing.Callable also works). It plays the role of Java's functional interfaces such as BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer>.

Common Shapes

HintMeaningJava equivalent
Callable[[], None]No arguments, returns nothingRunnable
Callable[[str], int]Takes a str, returns an intFunction<String, Integer>
Callable[[int], bool]A test on an intPredicate<Integer>
Callable[[], float]Produces a valueSupplier<Double>
Callable[..., str]Any arguments, returns a str-

Callbacks and Strategies

A dictionary of strategy functions is a common Python replacement for a Java strategy interface with several implementing classes.

What the Type Checker Catches

Passing a function with the wrong signature runs into trouble at runtime only when it is called. The type checker reports it immediately.
codeExamples:
from collections.abc import Callable

def run_twice(task: Callable[[], None]) -> None:
    task()
    task()

def greet(name: str) -> None:
    print("Hello", name)

run_twice(greet)

# mypy reports (wording may vary by version):
# error: Argument 1 to "run_twice" has incompatible type "Callable[[str], None]"; expected "Callable[[], None]"
#
# At runtime:
# TypeError: greet() missing 1 required positional argument: 'name'

beginner.content:
Introduction

Callable[[ArgTypes], ReturnType] annotates anything callable: functions, lambdas, methods, classes. Callable[[int, int], int] is "takes two ints, returns an int". Callable[..., T] accepts any arguments.
codeExamples:
from collections.abc import Callable

def apply(fn: Callable[[int, int], int], a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return fn(a, b)

print(apply(lambda x, y: x + y, 2, 3))
print(apply(max, 7, 4))

# OUTPUT:
# 5
# 7

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Passing functions around is common (callbacks, key functions, strategies). Without a Callable hint the signature says nothing about what shape the function must have, so wrong callbacks fail only at runtime.
codeExamples:
from collections.abc import Callable

def run_twice(task: Callable[[], str]) -> list[str]:
    return [task(), task()]

print(run_twice(lambda: "ping"))
# run_twice(len)   # checker: len needs 1 argument, Callable[[], str] gives none

# OUTPUT:
# ['ping', 'ping']

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Event handlers, retry and cache decorators, dispatch tables, dependency injection, middleware chains and sort keys.

Diagram

   Callable[[int, str], bool]
             └─params──┘  └return┘
   accepts:  def f(a: int, b: str) -> bool     lambda a, b: True
             SomeClass.method (bound)          class with __call__
   Callable[..., Any]  = "any callable at all"

expert.content:
Callable[..., T] - When Arguments Don't Matter

The ellipsis means "any parameters". It is useful for helpers that only care about the result, such as a timing or retry wrapper - but it switches off argument checking, so prefer a precise signature when you know it.
codeExamples:
import time
from collections.abc import Callable

def timed(func: Callable[..., int], *args: object) -> int:
    start = time.perf_counter()
    result = func(*args)
    print(f"{func.__name__} took {time.perf_counter() - start:.4f}s")
    return result

print(timed(sum, [1, 2, 3]))

# OUTPUT (time varies - e.g.):
# sum took 0.0000s
# 6

expert.content:
ParamSpec: Decorators That Keep the Signature

A decorator typed as Callable[..., Any] loses the wrapped function's parameter types, so every call to the decorated function goes unchecked. ParamSpec captures the whole parameter list and passes it through, and a TypeVar carries the return type. Python 3.12 adds a shorter syntax: def logged[**P, R](func: Callable[P, R]) -> Callable[P, R].
codeExamples:
import functools
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import ParamSpec, TypeVar

P = ParamSpec("P")
R = TypeVar("R")

def logged(func: Callable[P, R]) -> Callable[P, R]:
    @functools.wraps(func)
    def wrapper(*args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> R:
        print("calling", func.__name__)
        return func(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper

@logged
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a + b

print(add(2, 3))
add("2", 3)        # caught by the checker thanks to ParamSpec

# OUTPUT:
# calling add
# 5
# calling add
# TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
#
# mypy reports (wording may vary by version):
# error: Argument 1 to "add" has incompatible type "str"; expected "int"

expert.content:
Callback Protocols for Complex Signatures

Callable[[...], ...] can only express positional parameters. Keyword-only parameters, default values, overloads or *args need a callback protocol: a Protocol with a __call__ method. Any function with a matching signature satisfies it.

Hints Are Not Runtime Checks

Callable annotations are ignored when the program runs. To check at runtime that something can be called, use callable(obj) - which is also true for classes and objects with __call__.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How do you type a parameter that takes a function?Callable[[ArgTypes...], ReturnType] from collections.abc
What does Callable[..., int] mean?A callable with any parameters that returns an int
Why use ParamSpec?So a decorator's wrapper keeps the wrapped function's exact parameter types for the type checker
When is Callable not enough?For keyword-only arguments, defaults or overloads - use a Protocol with __call__
Python equivalent of Java's Function/Predicate/Supplier?Callable[[T], R], Callable[[T], bool], Callable[[], T]

Advantages

Advantages: documents callback contracts, enables checking of arguments and return values, and works with generics to type higher-order functions and decorators.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: it cannot express keyword-only or named arguments, optional parameters or overloads; for those you need a Protocol with __call__.

Limitations

Limitations: nothing is checked at runtime; a Callable is only a promise. Decorators that preserve the wrapped signature need ParamSpec.

Architect's Notes

Use Callable for simple callbacks and a Protocol with __call__ when parameter names, keywords or defaults matter. In decorators use ParamSpec + TypeVar so wrapped signatures remain visible to tooling.

beginner.content:
The Problem: Losing the Type

A function that returns the first item of a list works for lists of anything. Typing it with Any (or object) loses information: the checker no longer knows that first([1, 2]) is an int. A type variable links the input type to the output type - exactly what Java's <T> T first(List<T> items) does.
codeExamples:
from typing import TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")

def first(items: list[T]) -> T:
    return items[0]

n = first([10, 20, 30])          # checker knows: int
s = first(["a", "b"])            # checker knows: str
print(n + 1, s.upper())

# OUTPUT:
# 11 A

beginner.content:
Python 3.12 Syntax (PEP 695)

Python 3.12 lets you declare type parameters in square brackets, just like Java's angle brackets - no separate TypeVar line needed. Both styles mean the same thing; use the new one on 3.12+.
codeExamples:
def first[T](items: list[T]) -> T:
    return items[0]

def swap[A, B](pair: tuple[A, B]) -> tuple[B, A]:
    return pair[1], pair[0]

print(first([3.5, 1.0]))
print(swap(("id", 7)))

# OUTPUT:
# 3.5
# (7, 'id')

beginner.content:
A Generic Class: Stack[T]

A generic class is parameterised by a type, so Stack[int] and Stack[str] are checked separately - like Stack<Integer> in Java. The classic spelling inherits from Generic[T]; Python 3.12 allows class Stack[T]:.

Introduction

A TypeVar is a placeholder type that links input and output types: def first(xs: list[T]) -> T means "returns the same type that the list holds". Generic[T] (or the 3.12 syntax class Box[T]) makes a class parameterised over a type.
codeExamples:
from typing import TypeVar, Generic

T = TypeVar("T")

def first(items: list[T]) -> T:
    return items[0]

class Box(Generic[T]):
    def __init__(self, item: T) -> None:
        self.item = item
    def get(self) -> T:
        return self.item

print(first([10, 20]), first(["a", "b"]))
print(Box("hello").get(), Box(3.5).get())

# OUTPUT:
# 10 a
# hello 3.5

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Without generics you must choose between Any (no checking) and a separate function per type. A TypeVar keeps one implementation while the checker still knows exactly what comes out.
codeExamples:
from typing import TypeVar
T = TypeVar("T")

def pick(a: T, b: T, flag: bool) -> T:
    return a if flag else b

x = pick(1, 2, True)             # checker infers int
y = pick("a", "b", False)        # checker infers str
print(x, y)

# OUTPUT:
# 1 a

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Typed containers (Stack, Repository, Cache, Result), utility functions (first, chunk, merge), and framework base classes such as Repository[User].

Diagram

   def first(xs: list[T]) -> T
                  │         ▲
        list[int] ─┘         └─ checker binds T = int  ──► returns int
        list[str] ──────────────────────────  T = str  ──► returns str
   Box[T] : one class definition, many checked specialisations (erased at runtime)

expert.content:
Bounded Type Variables

TypeVar("A", bound=Animal) means "any subclass of Animal" - the equivalent of Java's <A extends Animal>. Unlike a plain Animal parameter, the function returns the same subtype it received. In 3.12 syntax: def loudest[A: Animal](...).

Constrained Type Variables

TypeVar("N", int, float) (3.12: [N: (int, float)]) means "exactly one of these types". Both arguments must then be the same type, and the result has that type too.
codeExamples:
def add_all[N: (int, float)](a: N, b: N) -> N:
    return a + b

print(add_all(2, 3))
print(add_all(1.5, 2.5))
add_all("a", "b")

# OUTPUT:
# 5
# 4.0
#
# mypy reports (wording may vary by version) for the last line:
# error: Value of type variable "N" of "add_all" cannot be "str"

expert.content:
Variance: Why list[int] Is Not a list[float]

Lists are invariant: a function taking list[float] could append a float to your list[int], so the checker refuses. Read-only types such as Sequence are covariant and accept the narrower type - the same reasoning as Java's List<? extends Number>.
codeExamples:
from collections.abc import Sequence

def total_list(values: list[float]) -> float:
    return sum(values)

def total_seq(values: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return sum(values)

ints: list[int] = [1, 2, 3]
print(total_seq(ints))       # fine
print(total_list(ints))      # runs, but the checker objects

# OUTPUT:
# 6
# 6
#
# mypy reports (wording may vary by version):
# error: Argument 1 to "total_list" has incompatible type "list[int]"; expected "list[float]"

expert.content:
Python Generics vs Java Generics

ConceptJavaPython
Generic method<T> T first(List<T> xs)def first[T](xs: list[T]) -> T
Generic classclass Stack<T>class Stack[T]:
Upper bound<T extends Animal>[T: Animal] / bound=Animal
Who checksThe compiler - code won't compileExternal tools (mypy, Pyright) - the interpreter ignores hints
Wrong type at runtimePrevented at compile timeRuns unless a tool stops it

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a TypeVar for?To link types across a signature, e.g. the return type equals the element type of the argument
Bound vs constrained TypeVar?Bound accepts any subtype of one type; constrained accepts exactly one of a listed set of types
What does PEP 695 add?Python 3.12 syntax for type parameters: def f[T](...), class C[T]:, [T: Bound]
Why is list invariant?Because it is mutable - accepting list[int] as list[float] would allow inserting floats into an int list
Are generics enforced at runtime?No - they are hints for type checkers; Stack[int]() happily stores a str at runtime

Advantages

Advantages: reusable and type-safe at once; bounds and constraints restrict allowed types; the call site gets precise inference.
codeExamples:
from typing import TypeVar

Number = TypeVar("Number", int, float)            # constrained: only int or float
def add(a: Number, b: Number) -> Number:
    return a + b

class HasLen:
    def __len__(self): return 3
S = TypeVar("S", bound=HasLen)                    # bound: must be a HasLen (or subclass)
def longest(a: S, b: S) -> S:
    return a if len(a) >= len(b) else b

print(add(1, 2), add(1.5, 2.5), type(longest(HasLen(), HasLen())).__name__)

# OUTPUT:
# 3 4.0 HasLen

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: variance (covariant, contravariant, invariant) is hard to learn, and generic signatures can become hard to read.
codeExamples:
from typing import TypeVar, Generic

T_co = TypeVar("T_co", covariant=True)       # read-only containers can be covariant
class ReadOnlyBox(Generic[T_co]):
    def __init__(self, item: T_co) -> None:
        self._item = item
    def get(self) -> T_co:
        return self._item

b: ReadOnlyBox[float] = ReadOnlyBox[int](5)  # OK because covariant (a list[int] -> list[float] is not)
print(b.get())

# OUTPUT:
# 5

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: type arguments are erased at runtime (Box[int] and Box[str] are the same class), and you cannot create instances of T or check isinstance(x, T).
codeExamples:
from typing import TypeVar, Generic
T = TypeVar("T")
class Box(Generic[T]):
    pass

print(type(Box[int]()) is type(Box[str]()))
try:
    isinstance(1, T)
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)

# OUTPUT:
# True
# TypeError: isinstance() arg 2 must be a type, a tuple of types, or a union

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use generics for containers and algorithms where input and output types are linked; do not over-generalise business code. Prefer Protocol bounds to nominal ones, and learn variance before writing public generic libraries. In 3.12+ prefer the new def f[T](x: T) syntax.

beginner.content:
Static Duck Typing

Python code usually relies on duck typing: "if it has a close() method, I can close it". typing.Protocol lets the type checker understand that idea. A protocol lists the methods (and attributes) a type must have; any class that has them matches - no inheritance or implements needed. This is called structural typing.

Java interfaces are nominal: a class satisfies Closeable only if it declares implements Closeable. (The OOP module's Interfaces with Protocols topic introduces the idea; this topic covers the typing side in more depth.)

What the Checker Enforces

A class that lacks a required method, or has it with an incompatible signature, is rejected by the type checker. The interpreter still runs the code until the missing method is actually called.

Protocols You Already Use

The standard library defines many protocols. Prefer them over concrete types in parameters so callers can pass any suitable object.
ProtocolRequiresSatisfied by
collections.abc.Iterable[T]__iter__list, tuple, set, dict, str, generators, files
collections.abc.Sized__len__Anything that works with len()
collections.abc.Sequence[T]Indexing and len()list, tuple, str, range
typing.SupportsInt / SupportsAbs__int__ / __abs__Numbers and custom numeric types

Introduction

A Protocol defines a type by its shape (methods and attributes) instead of its inheritance. Any class with the right methods satisfies it, with no base class: this is static "duck typing".
codeExamples:
from typing import Protocol

class Speaker(Protocol):
    def speak(self) -> str: ...

class Dog:                         # does NOT inherit Speaker
    def speak(self) -> str: return "Woof"
class Robot:
    def speak(self) -> str: return "Beep"

def announce(s: Speaker) -> None:
    print(s.speak())

announce(Dog()); announce(Robot())

# OUTPUT:
# Woof
# Beep

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Inheritance couples classes to a base you may not control (third-party code). A Protocol lets your function accept anything that behaves correctly while a checker still verifies the methods exist.
codeExamples:
from typing import Protocol

class Closeable(Protocol):
    def close(self) -> None: ...

def shutdown(*resources: Closeable) -> None:
    for r_ in resources:
        r_.close()

import io
shutdown(io.StringIO(), io.BytesIO())      # stdlib classes match without inheriting
print("closed all")

# OUTPUT:
# closed all

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Dependency injection and test doubles, plug-in interfaces, repository and gateway abstractions in clean architecture, and typing for libraries that accept "file-like" objects.

Diagram

   nominal (ABC):    class Dog(Animal)    ──► must inherit
   structural:       class Dog:           ──► has speak() -> str ✓
                                              │
   Protocol Speaker { speak() -> str } ◄──────┘ matches by SHAPE
   checker: "Dog is a Speaker"  (no base class, no registration)

expert.content:
Generic Protocols

A protocol can have type parameters, describing families such as "something with a get() that returns a T". With the Python 3.12 syntax the checker infers the variance; with the older TypeVar style, a type variable used only in return positions must be declared covariant.
codeExamples:
# Before Python 3.12
from typing import Protocol, TypeVar

T_co = TypeVar("T_co", covariant=True)

class Source(Protocol[T_co]):
    def get(self) -> T_co: ...

expert.content:
Callback Protocols

A protocol with only a __call__ method describes a function signature in full detail - keyword-only parameters, defaults, names - things Callable[[...], ...] can't express. Plain functions match it structurally.
codeExamples:
from typing import Protocol

class Validator(Protocol):
