codeExplanations: UserService never knows which repository it gets. With FakeRepo the test checks only the service logic and runs instantly; with SqliteRepo it also exercises real SQL and the table schema. The label is padded to 11 characters, so the colons line up.

beginner.content:
Two Different Questions

  • A unit test asks: "Does this one piece of code work, on its own?" It tests a single function or class with its dependencies replaced by simple stand-ins. It is fast (milliseconds) and needs no network, files or database.
  • An integration test asks: "Do these pieces work together?" It wires real components together - your code with a real database, a real file system, a real HTTP stack - and checks the combined behaviour. It is slower, but catches problems unit tests cannot: wrong SQL, bad configuration, mismatched data formats.

A Service to Test

The service gets its repository passed in (dependency injection). That small design choice is what lets us test it both ways.

The Unit Test: A Fake Repository

No database - just a tiny in-memory fake. We are testing only UserService's own logic.

The Integration Test: A Real Database

Now the same service runs against a real SQL repository (an in-memory SQLite database). If the SQL, the table or the column mapping were wrong, only this test would catch it.
codeExamples:
import sqlite3

class SqliteRepo:
    def __init__(self, conn):
        self.conn = conn

    def find(self, user_id):
        row = self.conn.execute(
            "SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = ?", (user_id,)
        ).fetchone()
        return {"name": row[0]} if row else None

conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
conn.execute("CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)")
conn.execute("INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 'Abaji')")

service = UserService(SqliteRepo(conn))

print(service.greet(1))
print(service.greet(2))

# OUTPUT:
# Hello, Abaji!
# Hello, guest!

beginner.content:
Side by Side

AspectUnit testIntegration test
ScopeOne function or classSeveral components together
DependenciesFaked or mockedReal (DB, files, services)
SpeedMillisecondsSeconds
Failure tells youExactly which unit is wrongSomething in the chain is wrong
QuantityMany (hundreds or thousands)Fewer

Introduction

A unit test checks one small piece (a function or class) in isolation, with dependencies faked. An integration test checks that several real pieces work together (code + database, service + service). End-to-end tests drive the whole system.
codeExamples:
# Unit: pure logic, nothing external
def total(prices): return sum(prices)

def test_unit_total():
    assert total([1, 2, 3]) == 6

# Integration: real sqlite database + our code together
import sqlite3
def save_and_count(rows):
    con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    con.execute("create table t(x int)")
    con.executemany("insert into t values (?)", [(r,) for r in rows])
    return con.execute("select count(*) from t").fetchone()[0]

def test_integration_db():
    assert save_and_count([1, 2, 3]) == 3

test_unit_total(); test_integration_db()
print("both pass")

# OUTPUT:
# both pass

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Unit tests alone cannot prove the parts fit together; integration tests alone are slow and make failures hard to localise. You need both, in the right proportion.
codeExamples:
# Each unit is correct, yet the combination is wrong:
def to_cents(amount):  return int(amount * 100)       # unit test passes
def fmt(cents):        return f"{cents / 10:.2f}"     # BUG: should be / 100

def test_to_cents():   assert to_cents(1.5) == 150
def test_fmt():        assert fmt(150) == "15.00"     # test encoded the bug

print(fmt(to_cents(1.5)))          # integration view shows 15.00, not 1.50

# OUTPUT:
# 15.00

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

The test pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests (DB, queue, HTTP API with a test client), very few end-to-end UI tests. Integration tests often use Docker/testcontainers.
codeExamples:
# Typical layering with markers (pytest.ini registers them)
import pytest

@pytest.mark.unit
def test_price_rule(): assert round(10 * 0.9, 2) == 9.0

@pytest.mark.integration
def test_repo_roundtrip():
    import sqlite3
    con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    con.execute("create table u(name text)")
    con.execute("insert into u values ('a')")
    assert con.execute("select name from u").fetchall() == [("a",)]

# CI: pytest -m unit   (every commit)   |   pytest -m integration (nightly / PR)
print("layers defined")

# OUTPUT:
# layers defined

beginner.content:
Diagram

          /          few      End-to-end  (slow, brittle, high confidence)
         /          /----        some     Integration (real DB / HTTP / queue)
       /            /--------      many     Unit        (fast, isolated, mocked edges)

expert.content:
The Testing Pyramid

Aim for a pyramid: a wide base of fast unit tests, a smaller middle layer of integration tests, and a thin top of slow end-to-end (E2E) tests that drive the whole system like a user (a browser, a real API call). 
        /\
       /E2E\         few  - slow, brittle, high confidence
      /------\
     /integra-\       some - real DB / HTTP boundaries
    /  tion    \
   /------------\
  /  unit tests  \    many - fast, precise, cheap
 /________________\
Inverting it (the "ice-cream cone": mostly E2E, few unit tests) gives a slow, flaky suite where a failure rarely points at the cause.

Test Doubles: Dummy, Stub, Fake, Mock, Spy

"Mock" is used loosely, but there are distinct kinds of stand-ins:
DoubleWhat it does
DummyFills a parameter; never actually used
StubReturns canned answers (return_value)
FakeA simple working implementation (the in-memory repo above)
MockA stand-in that verifies it was called correctly
SpyWraps the real object and records calls
Prefer fakes and stubs (check outcomes) over strict mocks (check interactions); they survive refactoring better.

An Integration Test With Real Setup and Teardown

Integration tests need real resources prepared and cleaned up. A pytest fixture gives each test a fresh in-memory database; marking the test lets you run slow tests separately.
codeExamples:
import sqlite3
import pytest

@pytest.fixture
def db():
    conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    conn.execute("CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)")
    yield conn
    conn.close()

@pytest.mark.integration
def test_round_trip(db):
    db.execute("INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 'Abaji')")
    service = UserService(SqliteRepo(db))
    assert service.greet(1) == "Hello, Abaji!"
    assert service.greet(99) == "Hello, guest!"

# Run only the fast tests:        pytest -m "not integration"
# Run only integration tests:     pytest -m integration

# OUTPUT:
# ... 1 passed in 0.01s

expert.content:
Real Dependencies in CI

SQLite is convenient, but if production uses PostgreSQL, tests against SQLite can pass while real queries fail (different SQL dialects and types). For high-fidelity integration tests run the real engine in a throw-away container using Docker Compose or the testcontainers package, and run migrations as part of test setup. Also useful: contract tests (verify your code and a service agree on request/response shapes) and freezing time/randomness to keep tests deterministic.

Flaky Tests

A flaky test passes and fails with no code change. Common causes: reliance on the clock or random values, shared state between tests, test-order dependence, real network calls, and sleeping instead of waiting for a condition. A flaky suite teaches people to ignore red builds, so fix or quarantine flaky tests immediately. Running with pytest-randomly exposes order dependence.

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Unit tests: milliseconds, pinpoint the failing functionUnit tests with fakes can pass while the real system is broken
Integration tests: catch wiring, SQL and config bugsIntegration tests are slower and need set-up and clean-up
Dependency injection makes both styles possibleA failing integration test does not say which part is wrong
The pyramid keeps the suite fast and affordableFakes must be kept in sync with the real component

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Unit vs integration test?Unit tests one piece in isolation with fakes; integration tests several real components working together
What is the testing pyramid?Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few end-to-end tests
How does dependency injection help testing?You can pass in a fake or a real dependency without changing the code under test
Fake vs mock?A fake is a working lightweight implementation; a mock records and verifies calls
What causes flaky tests?Time, randomness, shared state, ordering, real network, and sleeps instead of explicit waits

Advantages

Advantages: unit tests are fast (ms) and pinpoint failures; integration tests catch wiring, SQL, serialization and config bugs that mocks hide.
codeExamples:
import time

t = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(1000):
    assert (2 + 2) == 4            # 1000 unit checks
print("1000 unit asserts took under 50 ms:", time.perf_counter() - t < 0.05)

# OUTPUT:
# 1000 unit asserts took under 50 ms: True

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: unit tests with heavy mocking test the mock, not reality; integration tests are slower, need environments, and are flakier (timeouts, ports, shared data).
codeExamples:
from unittest.mock import Mock

repo = Mock()
repo.find.return_value = {"id": 1}      # the real DB would return a tuple/Row

def service(repo):
    return repo.find(1)["id"]

print(service(repo))     # green unit test, but real repo returns Row objects
                         # that may not support ["id"] at all

# OUTPUT:
# 1

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: neither kind proves performance, concurrency or real-world data quirks; the unit/integration boundary is fuzzy, and teams argue about definitions rather than value.
codeExamples:
# A race that no single-threaded unit test shows:
import threading
n = 0
def inc():
    global n
    for _ in range(100_000):
        n += 1                       # read-modify-write is not atomic
ts = [threading.Thread(target=inc) for _ in range(4)]
[t.start() for t in ts]; [t.join() for t in ts]
print(n <= 400_000)                  # may be lower on some versions/runs

# OUTPUT (varies):
# True

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Shape the suite as a pyramid, but test where the risk is: a thin CRUD service may deserve mostly integration tests, while a pricing engine deserves dense unit tests. Mock only what you do not own, keep integration tests hermetic (containers, ephemeral databases) and add a few contract tests between services.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Test-Driven Development (TDD) reverses the usual order: you write a failing test first (red), write just enough code to make it pass (green), then clean up the code while the tests stay green (refactor). You repeat this in tiny steps. The tests drive the design, and you always have a safety net. The cycle is the same in Java with JUnit.
Figure: the red-green-refactor cycle

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: When tests are written last, they are often skipped under deadline pressure, they are shaped by the code that already exists, and big untested "clean-ups" break behaviour without anyone noticing.

Why we need it:
  • Design code from the caller's point of view before implementing it.
  • Build a safety net so refactoring is safe.
  • Work in small steps: always one failing test to fix.
  • Guarantee that every behaviour has at least one test.

Complete Example: The finished slugify() and its test cases

This is the end state of three TDD cycles: each row in CASES began as one failing test. The tiny runner at the bottom stands in for pytest so the program runs with plain Python.
codeExamples:
import re

CASES = [
    ("Hello World", "hello-world"),               # cycle 1
    ("  Hello,   World! ", "hello-world"),        # cycle 2: punctuation
    ("", ""),                                     # cycle 3: empty input
    ("Python 3.12 Rocks", "python-3-12-rocks"),   # cycle 4: digits
]


def slugify(text):
    text = re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "-", text.lower())
    return text.strip("-")


def run_tests():
    passed = 0
    for given, expected in CASES:
        actual = slugify(given)
        status = "PASS" if actual == expected else "FAIL"
        passed += actual == expected
        print(status, repr(given), "->", repr(actual))
    return passed


def main():
    passed = run_tests()
    print(passed, "of", len(CASES), "passed")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT:
# PASS 'Hello World' -> 'hello-world'
# PASS '  Hello,   World! ' -> 'hello-world'
# PASS '' -> ''
# PASS 'Python 3.12 Rocks' -> 'python-3-12-rocks'
# 4 of 4 passed
codeExplanations: The first version of slugify() was just text.lower().replace(" ", "-") - the simplest code that passed cycle 1. Cycle 2 failed on punctuation, which forced the regular expression (the refactor). Because the old cases stay in the list, every rewrite is checked against all earlier behaviour.

beginner.content:
Tests First

Test-Driven Development (TDD) reverses the usual order: you write a failing test first, then just enough code to make it pass, then clean up. The tests drive the design, and you always have a safety net. It works in a short repeating loop:
StepColourWhat you do
1RedWrite one small test for behaviour that does not exist yet. Run it - it must fail.
2GreenWrite the simplest code that makes the test pass.
3RefactorImprove the code's structure while keeping all tests green.

Worked Example: slugify()

We want a function that turns a title into a URL slug: "Hello World" becomes "hello-world". Red: write the test and a stub that fails.
codeExamples:
# slugs.py
def slugify(text):
    return ""

# test_slugs.py
from slugs import slugify

def test_lowercases_and_joins_words_with_hyphens():
    assert slugify("Hello World") == "hello-world"

# OUTPUT of pytest (shortened):
# E   AssertionError: assert '' == 'hello-world'
# FAILED test_slugs.py::test_lowercases_and_joins_words_with_hyphens

beginner.content:
Green: The Simplest Thing That Passes

Don't solve problems you don't have a test for yet.

Next Cycle: Add a Harder Test, Then Refactor

Real titles contain punctuation and extra spaces. Add a failing test, then generalise the code with a regular expression. Because the first test still exists, you know the refactor kept the old behaviour.
codeExamples:
# test_slugs.py (added)
def test_removes_punctuation_and_extra_spaces():
    assert slugify("  Hello,   World! ") == "hello-world"

def test_empty_string():
    assert slugify("") == ""

# slugs.py (refactored - all three tests pass)
import re

def slugify(text):
    text = re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "-", text.lower())
    return text.strip("-")

print(slugify("Hello World"))
print(slugify("  Hello,   World! "))
print(repr(slugify("")))

# OUTPUT:
# hello-world
# hello-world
# ''

beginner.content:
Introduction

TDD is a workflow: write a failing test first (Red), write the least code to pass it (Green), then clean the code while tests stay green (Refactor). Repeat in small steps.
codeExamples:
# RED: test written first; fizzbuzz does not exist yet -> NameError (fails)
def test_three():  assert fizzbuzz(3) == "Fizz"

# GREEN: the simplest thing that passes
def fizzbuzz(n):
    return "Fizz"

test_three()
print("green")

# OUTPUT:
# green

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Writing the test first forces you to define behaviour and design an easy-to-use API before coding, prevents untested code, and gives a safety net for refactoring.
codeExamples:
# Next test triangulates the behaviour -> forces a real implementation
def fizzbuzz(n):
    if n % 15 == 0: return "FizzBuzz"     # refactor step: ordering matters
    if n % 3 == 0:  return "Fizz"
    if n % 5 == 0:  return "Buzz"
    return str(n)

for n, want in [(1, "1"), (3, "Fizz"), (5, "Buzz"), (15, "FizzBuzz")]:
    assert fizzbuzz(n) == want
print("all green")

# OUTPUT:
# all green

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Used for business logic, parsers, bug fixes (write a test that reproduces the bug first, then fix) and legacy refactors. The bug-first habit alone prevents regressions.
codeExamples:
# Bug report: "empty cart crashes". Step 1: reproduce as a failing test.
def average(xs):
    return sum(xs) / len(xs) if xs else 0.0    # Step 2: fix

def test_empty_cart():
    assert average([]) == 0.0                  # regression test stays forever

test_empty_cart()
print("regression guarded")

# OUTPUT:
# regression guarded

beginner.content:
Diagram

   ┌────────┐  write failing test   ┌────────┐  minimal code   ┌──────────┐
   │  RED   │ ────────────────────► │ GREEN  │ ──────────────► │ REFACTOR │
   └────────┘                       └────────┘                 └────┬─────┘
        ▲                                                          │
        └────────────── next behaviour ────────────────────────────┘

expert.content:
Rules of the Game

  • Take small steps. Each test adds one new behaviour; a cycle lasts minutes, not hours.
  • See it fail for the right reason. A test that has never failed might not test anything. Check the failure message matches what you expect.
  • Never refactor on red. Get to green first; then change structure with tests protecting you.
  • Test behaviour, not implementation. Assert on inputs and outputs, not on private methods or call order, so refactoring does not break tests.
  • Name tests as specifications: test_withdraw_more_than_balance_raises reads like a requirement.

Triangulation

A first test can be satisfied by a hard-coded answer. A second example forces generalisation: you "triangulate" the real rule from several cases. Parametrized tests make this cheap.

Chicago (Classic) vs London (Mockist) Style

AspectChicago / classicistLondon / mockist
DirectionInside-out: build core logic firstOutside-in: start from the outer layer
CollaboratorsUse real objects where cheapMock collaborators to design interfaces
VerifiesState / resultsInteractions (calls made)
RiskSlower to find the right designTests coupled to implementation
Most teams mix both. Related practices: ping-pong pairing (one writes a failing test, the other makes it pass) and BDD (writing tests in business language, e.g. pytest-bdd).

When TDD Works Well - and When It Doesn't

  • Great for: business logic, parsers, algorithms, bug fixes (write a test that reproduces the bug first, then fix it).
  • Awkward for: exploratory code where you don't yet know what you want, UI layout, and glue code. Spike a prototype first, then rewrite test-first.
  • Legacy code without tests: write characterization tests that pin down what the code does today, then refactor safely.
  • Common pitfalls: writing too many tests before any code, testing private details, and skipping the refactor step so the code stays messy.

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Every behaviour is backed by a test from day oneSlower at the start: needs discipline and practice
Refactoring is safe: tests show immediately what brokePoorly chosen tests lock in a bad design
Code ends up simpler and easier to callHard to apply to UI, exploratory or unclear requirements
Small steps make debugging trivialPassing tests do not prove the tests themselves are right

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the TDD cycle?Red (failing test), Green (minimal code to pass), Refactor (clean up with tests green)
Why must you see the test fail first?It proves the test can fail, and that it fails for the intended reason
What are the benefits?A regression safety net, simpler testable design, and living documentation of behaviour
How would you fix a bug using TDD?Write a failing test that reproduces it, fix the code, keep the test as a regression guard
Does TDD guarantee good design?No - it encourages testable design, but you still need to refactor and think about structure

Advantages

Advantages: high coverage naturally, small focused designs, fast feedback, living documentation, and confidence to refactor.
codeExamples:
# Tests double as examples of how the API is meant to be used
def test_usage_example():
    cart = {"apple": 2, "pear": 1}
    assert sum(cart.values()) == 3

test_usage_example()
print("spec as code")

# OUTPUT:
# spec as code

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: slower at first, needs discipline and skill, tests can be brittle if they assert implementation details, and it fits poorly for exploratory or UI-heavy work.
codeExamples:
# Brittle test: asserts HOW, not WHAT
from unittest.mock import Mock
sorter = Mock()
def run(data, sorter): return sorter.quicksort(data)
run([3, 1], sorter)
sorter.quicksort.assert_called_once()    # switching to mergesort breaks this test

print("test knows too much about the implementation")

# OUTPUT:
# test knows too much about the implementation

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: tests prove only what you thought to check; TDD does not replace design, integration, performance or security testing, and you cannot test-drive what you cannot specify.
codeExamples:
def is_prime(n):
    return n > 1 and all(n % i for i in range(2, n))

# Test-driven, all green...
assert is_prime(2) and not is_prime(4) and is_prime(7)
# ...yet this implementation is O(n) per call and hopeless for big numbers.
# No unit test asked about performance.
print("green but slow for large n")

# OUTPUT:
# green but slow for large n

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Apply TDD most strictly to domain logic with stable contracts; use spike-then-test for exploratory code. Test behaviour through public interfaces so refactors do not break tests, and pair TDD with CI and code review. It is a design technique first, a coverage technique second.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Code coverage measures how much of your code actually ran while the tests ran. A line that never ran cannot have been checked, so coverage is excellent at finding untested code. In Python the standard tool is coverage.py, usually through pytest --cov; the Java counterpart is JaCoCo. The demo below builds a tiny line tracker with sys.settrace to show what such tools do underneath.
Figure: coverage shows what ran; it cannot show that results were checked

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: A green test run says nothing about what was not tested. Whole branches (error handling, rare inputs) may never execute and you would not know.

Why we need it:
  • Find untested lines and branches quickly.
  • Turn "what did I forget?" into a concrete to-do list of line numbers.
  • Set a quality gate in CI (for example fail below 80 percent).
  • Spot dead code that no test or caller ever reaches.

Complete Example: A tiny line-coverage tracker

Real tools (coverage.py) work the same way: they trace which lines execute. Line numbers are printed relative to the def line so the output does not depend on where the code is saved. Works on CPython 3.12.
codeExplanations: classify has five body lines (offsets 1 to 5). Calling it with 5 runs only the two if-tests and the final return, so offsets 2 and 4 (the two early returns) are missed: 3 of 5 is 60 percent. Adding -1 and then 0 as inputs, which is exactly what new tests would do, drives coverage to 100 percent.

beginner.content:
What is Code Coverage?

Code coverage measures how much of your code was executed while the tests ran. If a line never ran, no test can possibly have checked it. Coverage is therefore good at finding untested code. The standard tool is coverage.py, used directly or through the pytest-cov plugin (JaCoCo is the Java equivalent). 
pip install pytest pytest-cov

pytest --cov=mypkg                   # measure the package "mypkg"
pytest --cov=mypkg --cov-report=term-missing   # also list missed line numbers
pytest --cov=mypkg --cov-report=html           # browsable report in htmlcov/

Reading a Report

For each file the report shows statements, how many were missed, the percentage, and (with term-missing) the exact missed line numbers - your to-do list of untested code.
codeExamples:
# shop.py
def price_with_tax(price, tax_rate):
    if price < 0:
        raise ValueError("price cannot be negative")
    return price * (1 + tax_rate)

# test_shop.py
import pytest
from shop import price_with_tax

def test_price_with_tax():
    assert price_with_tax(100, 0.18) == pytest.approx(118)

# pytest --cov=shop --cov-report=term-missing
#
# OUTPUT (shortened; the exact layout varies by version):
# Name      Stmts   Miss  Cover   Missing
# -----------------------------------------
# shop.py       4      1    75%   3
#
# Line 3 (the raise) never ran: no test passes a negative price.
codeExplanations: The test only covers the normal path. The report points at the missing line: the error case is untested. Adding a test with pytest.raises(ValueError) for a negative price would raise coverage to 100% and, more importantly, check that the error behaviour works.

beginner.content:
What Number Should You Aim For?

There is no magic number. Many teams use 80-90% as a sensible gate. Coverage is a guide to what you forgot, not a score to maximise: 100% coverage can still hide bugs, and chasing the last few percent often produces pointless tests.

Introduction

Code coverage measures which lines (and optionally branches) of your code executed while the tests ran. In Python use coverage.py or pytest-cov.

Why Do We Need This?

Coverage shows untested code: the places where a change can break silently. It turns "do we test enough?" into a number and a list of missing lines.
codeExamples:
# Missing branch: the else path of a conditional expression
def sign(n):
    return "pos" if n > 0 else "non-pos"

def test_sign():
    assert sign(5) == "pos"

# Line coverage says 100% (one line). Branch coverage (--cov-branch) says 50%
# because the false branch never ran.

# OUTPUT (example, --cov-branch):
# Stmts Miss Branch BrPart Cover
#     2    0      2      1   75%

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

CI gates enforce a floor (--cov-fail-under=85), PR bots show coverage deltas, and reports in HTML highlight red lines. Exclude boilerplate with # pragma: no cover.
codeExamples:
# pyproject.toml settings, shown as text so the snippet is runnable
config = """
[tool.coverage.run]
branch = true
source = ["mypkg"]

[tool.coverage.report]
fail_under = 85
exclude_lines = ["pragma: no cover", "if __name__ == .__main__.:"]
"""
print(config.splitlines()[1])

# OUTPUT:
# [tool.coverage.run]

beginner.content:
Diagram

   tests run ──► tracer records executed lines/branches ──► .coverage data
                                                                │
                      report (term / html / xml) ◄──────────────┘
                      Stmts  Miss  Branch  Cover  Missing lines

expert.content:
Line Coverage vs Branch Coverage

Line coverage only asks "did this line run?". Branch coverage asks "did both outcomes of every decision happen?". An if with no else can show 100% line coverage while its "condition is false" path was never tested. Turn branch coverage on: --cov-branch or branch = true in the config.
codeExamples:
def apply_discount(price, is_member):
    if is_member:
        price = price - 10
    return price

def test_member_discount():
    assert apply_discount(100, True) == 90

# Line coverage: 100%  (every line ran)
# Branch coverage: the path "is_member is False" never ran
#
# pytest --cov=. --cov-branch --cov-report=term-missing
#
# OUTPUT (shortened):
# Name    Stmts  Miss Branch BrPart  Cover   Missing
# ---------------------------------------------------
# d.py        4     0      2      1    83%   2->4
#
# "2->4" means: the jump from line 2 (the if) to line 4 (skipping the body)
# was never taken.

expert.content:
Configuration, Exclusions and Gates

Put settings in pyproject.toml so every run measures the same way. Use # pragma: no cover sparingly, for code that genuinely cannot be tested (a __main__ guard, defensive branches). fail_under makes the build fail when coverage drops.
codeExamples:
# pyproject.toml
[tool.coverage.run]
branch = true
source = ["mypkg"]
omit = ["*/tests/*", "*/migrations/*"]

[tool.coverage.report]
fail_under = 85
show_missing = true
exclude_also = [
    "if __name__ == .__main__.:",
    "raise NotImplementedError",
]

# In code, for one-off exclusions:
def debug_dump(obj):  # pragma: no cover
    print(obj)

expert.content:
Coverage Is Not Quality

Coverage only proves code ran, not that its result was checked. This test earns full coverage and verifies nothing:

Mutation Testing: Testing Your Tests

Mutation testing (mutmut, cosmic-ray) automatically makes small changes to your code (turn - into +, > into >=) and re-runs the tests. If the tests still pass, that "mutant" survived: your tests don't really check that behaviour. It measures the strength of assertions, which coverage cannot. It is slow, so run it on critical modules or in a nightly job.

Using Coverage in CI and Reviews

  • Fail the build on coverage dropping (fail_under) or require coverage of changed lines only (e.g. diff-cover, Codecov patch coverage) so old untested code doesn't block new work.
  • Measure subprocess and multi-process code with concurrency settings; combine reports from parallel runs with coverage combine.
  • Read the HTML report when deciding what to test next: red lines show exactly what no test touches.

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Points to exact untested lines (--cov-report=term-missing)Executed is not verified: a test with no asserts still counts
Cheap to add in CI as a quality gate100 percent coverage can still hide bugs
Branch coverage reveals untested decisionsChasing the number encourages low-value tests
HTML reports make gaps easy to browseTracing slows the test run a little

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does code coverage measure?The percentage of code executed during the test run
Line vs branch coverage?Line: did each line run. Branch: did both outcomes of each decision run
Does 100% coverage mean no bugs?No - it shows code ran, not that results were asserted; tests with no assertions still count
What is mutation testing?Automatically changing code to see whether the tests notice; surviving mutants reveal weak tests
How do you enforce a minimum?fail_under in coverage config, or --cov-fail-under=85 with pytest-cov

Advantages

Advantages: cheap to collect, finds dead and untested code, branch mode catches skipped paths, integrates with every CI, supports combining parallel runs.
codeExamples:
# Programmatic use of coverage.py (pip install coverage)
import coverage

cov = coverage.Coverage()
cov.start()
sum(i for i in range(10))          # code measured while running
cov.stop()
print("measuring works:", cov.get_data() is not None)

# OUTPUT:
# measuring works: True

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: chasing 100% invites weak tests, adds 10-50% runtime overhead, and a high number gives false confidence.
codeExamples:
def divide(a, b):
    return a / b

def test_divide():
    divide(10, 2)            # executes the line, asserts NOTHING

test_divide()
print("100% line coverage, zero verification")

# OUTPUT:
# 100% line coverage, zero verification

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: coverage cannot tell if assertions are meaningful, does not measure data-dependent bugs or concurrency, and misses subprocess code unless configured (parallel mode).
codeExamples:
def risky(x):
    return 100 / x            # bug only for x == 0

def test_risky():
    assert risky(5) == 20     # line is 100% covered, but the ZeroDivisionError
                              # input was never tried
test_risky()
print("covered but still buggy for x=0")

# OUTPUT:
# covered but still buggy for x=0

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use coverage as a negative signal (what is surely untested), not a target. Set a modest floor with branch coverage and require coverage on changed lines in PRs rather than a global 100%. Combine with mutation testing (mutmut) for a real measure of test strength on critical modules.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Print debugging means adding temporary print() calls to see what a program is really doing: which values variables hold, which branch ran, how many times a loop repeated. It needs no tools and works everywhere. Python adds two helpers: the f-string trick f"{x=}" (prints the expression and its value) and repr() (shows hidden detail such as quotes and spaces). In Java the same job is done with System.out.println before you reach for jdb or an IDE debugger.
Figure: print debugging narrows the bug to the first place where a value goes wrong

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: A program gives a wrong answer but no error. Reading the code again and again does not reveal which variable holds an unexpected value at which moment.

Why we need it:
  • Make the program's hidden state visible at chosen points.
  • Narrow down a bug: the last correct print and the first wrong print bracket the faulty line.
  • Debug quickly with no setup - useful in scripts, servers and notebooks.
  • Learn the habit that leads to logging and real debuggers later.

Complete Example: A reusable debug() helper and the f"{x=}" trick

Debug lines go to stderr so they never mix with real output; here both appear in the terminal in program order.
codeExamples:
import sys

DEBUG = True


def debug(label, value):
    if DEBUG:
        print(f"[DEBUG] {label} = {value!r}", file=sys.stderr)


def parse_prices(text):
    prices = []
    for part in text.split(","):
        debug("part", part)
        prices.append(float(part.strip()))
    return prices


def average(prices):
    debug("count", len(prices))
    return sum(prices) / len(prices)


def main():
    raw = "10, 20.5 ,30"
    prices = parse_prices(raw)
    print(f"{prices=}")
    print(f"{round(average(prices), 2)=}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT:
# [DEBUG] part = '10'
# [DEBUG] part = ' 20.5 '
# [DEBUG] part = '30'
# prices=[10.0, 20.5, 30.0]
# [DEBUG] count = 3
# round(average(prices), 2)=20.17
codeExplanations: The !r in the f-string applies repr(), so the debug lines show quotes and the stray spaces in ' 20.5 '. The f"{prices=}" form prints the source text of the expression, an equals sign and the value. The DEBUG constant lets you switch all debug output off in one place instead of deleting prints. The average is 60.5 / 3 = 20.1666..., rounded to 20.17.

beginner.content:
The Simplest Debugger

When code does something unexpected, the quickest first step is to look at the values. Adding print() calls to show variables at key points is called print debugging. It needs no tools, works everywhere, and is how most programmers start. The aim is always the same: find the first place where reality differs from what you expected.

Label Your Output: the f"{x=}" Trick

A bare print(total) prints a number with no clue what it is. Python 3.8+ has a shortcut: f"{x=}" prints the expression and its value.
codeExamples:
x = 42
name = "Abaji"
items = [1, 2, 3]

print(f"{x=}, {name=}")
print(f"{len(items)=}, {x * 2=}")

# OUTPUT:
# x=42, name='Abaji'
# len(items)=3, x * 2=84
codeExplanations: The "=" after an expression inside an f-string prints the source text of the expression, an equals sign, and the repr() of its value. Note name='Abaji' shows quotes - a string value is easy to tell apart from a number.

beginner.content:
Use repr() to See What Is Really There

print() shows the friendly str() form, which hides whitespace and type. repr() shows the precise form, exposing the usual culprits: stray spaces, newlines, or a string where you expected a number.
codeExamples:
value = "5"
line = "  hello\n"

print(value, 5)                 # look the same
print(repr(value), repr(5))     # clearly different types
print(line)
print(repr(line))

# OUTPUT:
# 5 5
# '5' 5
#   hello
#
# '  hello\n'

beginner.content:
Narrowing Down a Bug

Print the inputs and the intermediate results of the suspect function. Here the crash is a symptom; the printout reveals the cause: an empty list.
codeExamples:
def average(numbers):
    total = sum(numbers)
    print(f"DEBUG {total=} {len(numbers)=}")
    return total / len(numbers)

print(average([]))

# OUTPUT:
# DEBUG total=0 len(numbers)=0
# Traceback (most recent call last):
#   ...
# ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

beginner.content:
Introduction

print debugging means inserting print() calls to see variable values and which branches run. It is the fastest first tool because it needs no setup.
codeExamples:
def average(nums):
    total = sum(nums)
    print("DEBUG total =", total, "count =", len(nums))   # inspect state
    return total / len(nums)

print(average([4, 6, 8]))

# OUTPUT:
# DEBUG total = 18 count = 3
# 6.0

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

When a result is wrong you must see what the program actually did, not what you believe it did. Printing intermediate values narrows the search to the line where reality and expectation diverge.
codeExamples:
def discount(price, pct):
    result = price - price * pct       # BUG: pct is 10, not 0.10
    print(f"{price=} {pct=} {result=}")  # f"{x=}" prints name and value
    return result

discount(200, 10)

# OUTPUT:
# price=200 pct=10 result=-1800

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Quick checks in scripts, notebooks and CI logs. Better habits: repr() via !r to reveal hidden whitespace, file=sys.stderr to keep stdout clean, and pprint for nested data.
codeExamples:
import sys
from pprint import pprint

name = "Abaji "                       # trailing space is invisible with plain print
print(f"name={name!r}")              # repr shows quotes and spaces
print("diagnostic", file=sys.stderr) # separate stream from real output
pprint({"user": {"id": 1, "tags": ["a", "b"]}}, width=30)

# OUTPUT (stdout):
# name='Abaji '
# {'user': {'id': 1,
#           'tags': ['a', 'b']}}

beginner.content:
Diagram

   suspect code ──► insert print() ──► run ──► read output
        ▲                                         │
        └────── narrow down, move prints ◄────────┘
   finished? remove prints / switch to logging

expert.content:
Send Debug Output to stderr and Flush It

Debug prints mixed into normal output corrupt programs whose stdout is parsed or piped. Print diagnostics to stderr with file=sys.stderr. stdout is buffered when redirected, so output can appear late or be lost in a crash - flush=True forces it out immediately.
codeExamples:
import sys

def debug(*args):
    print("DEBUG:", *args, file=sys.stderr, flush=True)

result = 6 * 7
debug("computed", result)
print(result)                       # real output stays clean

# Run:  python app.py > out.txt
# out.txt contains only:   42
# The terminal still shows: DEBUG: computed 42

expert.content:
Pretty-Printing and Tracing Calls

pprint formats nested data readably. A small decorator can print every call's arguments and return value, which is invaluable for recursive functions, without editing the function's body.

A Systematic Approach

Print debugging works best as a method, not a scatter-gun:
  1. Reproduce the bug reliably, with the smallest input that triggers it.
  2. Form a hypothesis ("the list is empty by the time we reach line 12").
  3. Print to test the hypothesis - one or two prints, not twenty.
  4. Bisect: print halfway through the code path. If the value is already wrong, the bug is in the first half; otherwise the second.
  5. Fix, then remove every debug print (search for "DEBUG").
traceback.print_stack() prints how the code got to this line, answering "who called this function with that argument?".

When to Stop Using print()

SituationBetter tool
You need to inspect many variables or explore interactivelyThe debugger: breakpoint() / pdb / IDE
The message should stay in the code and be switchablelogging (levels, handlers, timestamps)
Crash in productionLogs plus the stack trace (logger.exception)
Expected behaviour you want to keep checkingAn automated test with assert
Leaving stray prints in committed code is a smell: they clutter output, can leak sensitive data, and slow hot loops. Linters such as ruff (rule T20) flag them.

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Zero setup: works in any editor, server or scriptNeeds code edits and a re-run for every new question
f"{x=}" labels the value automatically (3.8+)Easy to forget a print and ship it to production
Output survives in logs and CI where no debugger can attachCannot pause, step or change values while running
Easy to show a whole execution history, not just one momentLarge outputs become noise; no levels or filtering

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does f"{x=}" do?Prints the expression text and its repr value, e.g. x=42 (Python 3.8+)
Why use repr() when debugging?It reveals exact content - quotes, whitespace, escape characters, types - that str() hides
Why print debug output to stderr?It keeps stdout clean for real output and piping
Why flush=True?Redirected stdout is buffered; flushing ensures the output appears before a crash
Print vs logging vs debugger?Print: quick and temporary. Logging: permanent, leveled and configurable. Debugger: interactive inspection and stepping

Advantages

Advantages: zero setup, works everywhere (servers, containers, notebooks), shows the actual runtime flow, and needs no tool knowledge.
codeExamples:
def collatz(n):
    steps = 0
    while n != 1:
        n = n // 2 if n % 2 == 0 else 3 * n + 1
        steps += 1
        print(f"  step {steps}: n={n}")
    return steps

print("steps:", collatz(6))

# OUTPUT:
#   step 1: n=3
#   step 2: n=10
#   step 3: n=5
#   step 4: n=16
#   step 5: n=8
#   step 6: n=4
#   step 7: n=2
#   step 8: n=1
# steps: 8

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: you must edit code and re-run, forgotten prints reach production, output floods for loops, and there is no level/timestamp control. Use logging for anything permanent.
codeExamples:
import io, contextlib

buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buf):
    print("debug leftover")           # a stray print corrupts program output
    print('{"ok": true}')             # intended JSON response

print(repr(buf.getvalue()))           # consumer now gets invalid JSON

# OUTPUT:
# 'debug leftover\n{"ok": true}\n'

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: printing changes timing (hides race conditions), buffering can reorder output relative to stderr, it cannot pause or change state, and printing big objects can itself be slow or trigger side effects in __repr__.
codeExamples:
import sys
print("to stdout")                    # buffered when piped
print("to stderr", file=sys.stderr)   # unbuffered
sys.stdout.flush()                    # fix: flush or run python -u

# When piped to a file, stderr text can appear BEFORE earlier stdout text.

# OUTPUT (order may differ when redirected):
# to stdout
# to stderr

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Treat print as a scratchpad, never as a diagnostic strategy for services: use structured logging with levels and correlation ids, and add a linter rule (flake8 T201) to block stray prints. For hard-to-reproduce bugs prefer a debugger, tracing or a failing test.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A traceback (stack trace) is the list of function calls that were active when an exception was raised. Python prints it oldest call first and the exception type and message last, so you read it from the bottom up. Each frame shows the file, the line number, the function name and the source line. Java prints the same idea as Exception in thread "main" ... followed by at lines, but with the newest call first. The traceback module lets a program inspect the same frames.
Figure: frames run oldest to newest; the last line names the exception

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: Beginners see ten lines of red text, panic, and copy the whole thing into a search engine. They miss that the answer is in the last line and the failing line number.

Why we need it:
  • Find what failed (last line), where (last frame) and how we got there (frames above).
  • Fix errors in minutes instead of guessing.
  • Understand that the reported line is where the error was detected, not always where the mistake is.
  • Log or report tracebacks from your own code with the traceback module.

Complete Example: Walking the frames of a traceback

Instead of letting the program crash, we catch the error and print the same information a traceback contains.
codeExplanations: traceback.extract_tb() turns the traceback object into a list of frame summaries, oldest first, just like the printed traceback. The last frame is where the exception was raised, so its name and source line answer "where". The list starts at main because that is the function whose try block caught the error.

beginner.content:
What is a Traceback?

When an exception is not handled, Python stops and prints a traceback (also called a stack trace): the chain of function calls that led to the error. It looks intimidating, but it is the most useful debugging information you will get - it tells you what went wrong, where, and how the program got there.

Read It From the Bottom Up

Save this as app.py and run it:
codeExamples:
def parse_age(text):
    return int(text)

def read_user(record):
    return parse_age(record["age"])

def main():
    print(read_user({"age": "abc"}))

main()

# OUTPUT (Python 3.11+ also underlines the failing part with ^^^^ markers):
# Traceback (most recent call last):
#   File "app.py", line 10, in <module>
#     main()
#   File "app.py", line 8, in main
#     print(read_user({"age": "abc"}))
#   File "app.py", line 5, in read_user
#     return parse_age(record["age"])
#   File "app.py", line 2, in parse_age
#     return int(text)
# ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'
codeExplanations: The last line is the answer to "what": the exception type (ValueError) and its message. The frame just above it is where the exception was raised: line 2 in parse_age. Frames above that show who called whom, oldest first - the program started at line 10, called main, which called read_user, which called parse_age.

beginner.content:
A Three-Step Reading Routine

  1. Last line: the exception type and message. Often this alone explains the bug.
  2. The last frame(s) in your code: the file, line number and the source line that failed.
  3. Work upward only if you need to know how bad data got there: who passed "abc" to parse_age?
The bug is not always on the line the traceback points to: the line shows where the error was detected. Here the real mistake is that bad input reached parse_age.

Common Exceptions and Their Usual Causes

ExceptionTypical cause
NameErrorVariable used before assignment, or a typo in a name
TypeErrorWrong type: "5" + 5, calling None, wrong number of arguments
ValueErrorRight type, bad value: int("abc")
KeyErrorMissing dictionary key (the key is in the message)
IndexErrorList index out of range
AttributeErrorObject has no such attribute - often a value that is None
ImportError / ModuleNotFoundErrorPackage not installed in this virtual environment, or wrong module name
ZeroDivisionErrorDivision or modulo by zero
FileNotFoundErrorWrong path or wrong working directory
IndentationError / SyntaxErrorCode could not be parsed - fix before it can run

Introduction

A traceback lists the chain of calls that led to an exception, oldest call first and the failing line last, followed by the exception type and message. Read it from the bottom up.
codeExamples:
def c(): return 1 / 0
def b(): return c()
def a(): return b()

try:
    a()
except ZeroDivisionError:
    import traceback
    traceback.print_exc()

# OUTPUT (abridged):
# Traceback (most recent call last):
#   File "x.py", line 6, in <module>
#     a()
#   File "x.py", line 3, in a
#     def a(): return b()
#   File "x.py", line 2, in b
#     def b(): return c()
#   File "x.py", line 1, in c
#     def c(): return 1 / 0
# ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Most debugging time is wasted guessing. The traceback already tells you the exception type, the exact file and line, and the path taken, so reading it well finds many bugs in seconds.
codeExamples:
data = {"name": "Abaji"}
try:
    print(data["age"])
except KeyError as e:
    print("type   :", type(e).__name__)
    print("missing:", e)          # message names the missing key
    print("line   :", e.__traceback__.tb_lineno)

# OUTPUT:
# type   : KeyError
# missing: 'age'
# line   : 3

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Production logs contain tracebacks; on-call engineers triage by the last frame in your code, not the library frames. Chained exceptions (raise ... from) show the root cause.

Diagram

   Traceback (most recent call last):       oldest call (entry point)
     File "app.py", line 20, in main        │
       run()                                ▼
     File "app.py", line 12, in run         calls go down
       parse(x)                             │
     File "app.py", line  5, in parse       ▼
       return int(s)                        failing line  <-- start here
   ValueError: invalid literal for int()    exception type + message (last line)

expert.content:
Chained Exceptions

Sometimes you see two tracebacks joined by a sentence. That means one exception happened while another was being handled (or was raised deliberately from it). Read the first block as the root cause and the last as the consequence.
  • "During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred" - an accident: a new error inside an except block.
  • "The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception" - deliberate: raise NewError(...) from original.

The traceback Module: Capture and Inspect Traces

You can use tracebacks from code, not only read them on screen. traceback.format_exc() returns the text of the exception currently being handled (ideal for logs), and traceback.extract_tb() turns it into structured frames.
codeExamples:
import traceback

def a():
    b()

def b():
    return 1 / 0

try:
    a()
except ZeroDivisionError as error:
    text = traceback.format_exc()
    print(text.splitlines()[-1])

    for frame in traceback.extract_tb(error.__traceback__):
        print(frame.name)

# OUTPUT:
# ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
# <module>
# a
# b

expert.content:
Never Throw the Trace Away

The worst debugging experience is a program that hides its errors. Avoid:
  • except: pass or except Exception: pass - silently swallows every bug, including ones you did not anticipate.
  • raise NewError("failed") inside except without from - loses the clear cause link.
  • print(error) alone - gives the message but no location. Use logging.exception("...") inside an except block to log message and traceback.
Use a bare raise to re-raise the current exception unchanged after logging or cleanup: the original traceback is preserved.
codeExamples:
import logging

logging.basicConfig(format="%(levelname)s: %(message)s")

def risky():
    return {}["missing"]

try:
    risky()
except KeyError:
    logging.exception("risky() failed")     # message + full traceback

# OUTPUT (shortened):
# ERROR: risky() failed
# Traceback (most recent call last):
#   ...
# KeyError: 'missing'

expert.content:
Tracebacks in Unusual Places

  • Threads: an unhandled exception in a thread prints its traceback but does not stop the main program. Install threading.excepthook to log such failures.
  • Whole program: sys.excepthook is called for any uncaught exception - the place to log a crash before exit.
  • asyncio: an exception inside a task that is never awaited is reported only when the task is garbage-collected ("Task exception was never retrieved"). Always await or gather your tasks.
  • Python 3.11+: tracebacks include ^^^^ markers pointing at the exact sub-expression, and ExceptionGroup shows several errors at once with nested traces.
  • Run with python -X dev to enable extra runtime checks and warnings while debugging.

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Shows the exact file, line and call path of a failureShows where the error was detected, not always its cause
The last line alone often explains the bugLong chains (frameworks, chained exceptions) are noisy
Available for free on every unhandled exceptionOrder differs from Java (oldest first, not newest first)
traceback module lets you log or format it yourselfSays nothing about variable values at the time

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
In which order do you read a traceback?Last line first (type and message), then the last frames in your own code; work upward to see the call chain
Which end of the trace is the most recent call?The bottom - "most recent call last"
What does "The above exception was the direct cause..." mean?The new exception was raised with raise ... from; the first one is the root cause
How do you log a traceback?logging.exception(...) inside the except block, or logger.error(..., exc_info=True)
Is the bug always on the line shown?No - that is where it was detected; the cause may be earlier, such as bad data passed in

Advantages

Advantages: exact location, full call path, exception type plus message, and since Python 3.11 precise ^^^^ markers show which sub-expression failed.
codeExamples:
import traceback, sys

def f(d): return d["a"]["b"]       # which lookup failed?

try:
    f({"a": {}})
except KeyError:
    tb = traceback.extract_tb(sys.exc_info()[2])[-1]
    print(tb.name, tb.lineno, repr(tb.line))

# OUTPUT:
# f 3 'def f(d): return d["a"]["b"]'

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: long recursive or framework tracebacks are noisy, the failing line may only be a symptom of earlier bad data, and swallowed exceptions leave no trace at all.

Limitations

Limitations: a traceback shows where the error surfaced, not where wrong data was created; async/thread tracebacks lose the originating caller, and local variable values are not included by default.
codeExamples:
import traceback

def f():
    x = 41
    raise ValueError("bad")

try:
    f()
except ValueError as e:
    te = traceback.TracebackException.from_exception(e, capture_locals=True)
    print(any("x = 41" in line for line in te.format()))   # locals need opt-in

# OUTPUT:
# True

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Log tracebacks with logger.exception so they land in your aggregator with context, never swallow broad exceptions, and use raise ... from to preserve causality. Add error-tracking (Sentry) that captures local variables for production-only failures.

beginner.content:
Introduction

pdb is Python's built-in interactive debugger. Calling the built-in breakpoint() pauses the program and opens a (Pdb) prompt where you can print variables, step line by line and continue. Running python -m pdb script.py does the same without editing the code, and post-mortem debugging inspects the state at the moment of a crash. It is the command-line counterpart of jdb or the IDE debugger you use in Java.
Figure: breakpoint() stops execution; you decide when it continues

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: With print debugging you must guess which variables to print, edit the code and re-run for every new question. Intermittent or long-running programs make that very slow.

Why we need it:
  • Pause at any line and inspect every variable.
  • Step through code (n, s, r) to watch the control flow.
  • Inspect a crash post-mortem: the locals of the failing frame.
  • Debug on servers and over SSH where no IDE is available.

Complete Example: Inspecting the failing frame, like pdb.post_mortem()

pdb itself is interactive, so this program reads the same data pdb shows after a crash: the failing function, its local variables and its line number.
codeExplanations: Each traceback entry links to the frame object of a function call. Following tb_next to the last entry reaches the frame where the error occurred, and f_locals holds its variables: values is the empty list and total is 0, which explains the division by zero. pdb.post_mortem() builds exactly this view for you.

beginner.content:
Pause the Program and Look Around

A debugger lets you stop a running program at a chosen line (a breakpoint) and then inspect variables and step through the code one line at a time. Python ships with pdb, a command-line debugger. Since Python 3.7 you start it by simply calling the built-in breakpoint().
codeExamples:
def total_price(items):
    total = 0
    for name, price in items:
        breakpoint()                  # program pauses here
        total += price
    return total

print(total_price([("pen", 10), ("book", 250)]))

# SESSION (what you see and type; (Pdb) is the debugger prompt):
# > app.py(5)total_price()
# -> total += price
# (Pdb) p name, price
# ('pen', 10)
# (Pdb) n
# > app.py(3)total_price()
# -> for name, price in items:
# (Pdb) c
# > app.py(5)total_price()
# -> total += price
# (Pdb) p total
# 10
# (Pdb) c
# 260
codeExplanations: breakpoint() stops before line 5 runs. "p name, price" prints values, "n" executes one line and moves to the next, and "c" continues until the next breakpoint - which is hit again on the next loop iteration. "p total" shows 10 because the first item was already added. The final "c" lets the program finish and print 260.

beginner.content:
The Essential Commands

CommandMeaning
n (next)Run the current line; stay in this function (steps over calls)
s (step)Step into a function call on the current line
c (continue)Run until the next breakpoint or the end
r (return)Run until the current function returns
p expr / pp exprPrint / pretty-print an expression
l / llList source around the current line / the whole function
w (where)Show the call stack
u / dMove up / down one frame in the stack
q (quit)Stop debugging and exit the program
hHelp; h n explains one command
Pressing Enter alone repeats the previous command. You can also type any Python statement at the prompt (use ! in front if it clashes with a command name, e.g. !n = 5).

Starting the Debugger Without Editing Code

You do not have to add breakpoint(). Run the whole script under the debugger, and after a crash inspect the state at the moment of failure (a post-mortem).
codeExamples:
# Start at the first line:
#   python -m pdb app.py
#
# Run, and drop into pdb only if an uncaught exception occurs:
#   python -m pdb -c continue app.py
#
# Run normally, then open an interactive prompt after a crash:
#   python -i app.py
#   >>> import pdb; pdb.pm()        # post-mortem of the last exception

def divide(a, b):
    return a / b

print(divide(10, 0))

# With "python -m pdb -c continue app.py" the crash opens pdb at the failing line:
# ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
# > app.py(2)divide()
# -> return a / b
# (Pdb) p a, b
# (10, 0)

beginner.content:
Introduction

pdb is Python's built-in interactive debugger. Calling breakpoint() (3.7+) pauses the program at that line and gives a prompt where you can inspect and step through code.
codeExamples:
def total(prices):
    s = 0
    for p in prices:
        breakpoint()          # program stops here; type commands at (Pdb)
        s += p
    return s

# (Pdb) p p        -> print the variable
# (Pdb) n          -> next line
# (Pdb) c          -> continue
# Disable all breakpoints: set PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0
print("function defined, not called")

# OUTPUT:
# function defined, not called

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Printing guesses is slow. A debugger lets you stop at the exact moment, look at every variable, evaluate expressions and move line by line, without editing code for each question.
codeExamples:
# Post-mortem: debug AFTER a crash with  python -m pdb script.py
# or from code:
import pdb, sys

def crash():
    return {}["missing"]

try:
    crash()
except KeyError:
    tb = sys.exc_info()[2]
    # pdb.post_mortem(tb)    # would open (Pdb) in the crashed frame
    print("frame variables available at:", tb.tb_next.tb_frame.f_code.co_name)

# OUTPUT:
# frame variables available at: crash

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Common commands: l list source, n next, s step into, r return, b 42 set breakpoint, w where (stack), u/d up/down frames, !expr run code. IDEs (VS Code, PyCharm) wrap the same idea.
codeExamples:
# Scripted pdb session (stdin simulated) so it runs without a human
import pdb, io, sys

def f(x):
    y = x * 2
    return y

cmds = io.StringIO("p x\nn\np y\nc\n")
dbg = pdb.Pdb(stdin=cmds, stdout=sys.stdout)
dbg.use_rawinput = False
dbg.runcall(f, 21)

# OUTPUT (abridged):
# > <string>(4)f()
# (Pdb) 21
# (Pdb) > ...(5)f()
# (Pdb) 42

beginner.content:
Diagram

   program running ──► breakpoint() ──► (Pdb) prompt
                                          │  p var   inspect
                                          │  n / s   step over / into
                                          │  w / u   stack navigation
                                          └─ c ──► program resumes

expert.content:
Conditional Breakpoints and Breakpoint Management

Stopping on every iteration of a 10,000-item loop is hopeless. Set a breakpoint with a condition so it fires only for the interesting case, and manage breakpoints by number.
CommandEffect
b 12Breakpoint at line 12 of the current file
b app.py:12, price > 100Breakpoint that fires only when the condition is true
b total_priceBreakpoint at a function's first line
bList all breakpoints with hit counts
disable 1 / enable 1 / cl 1Disable, re-enable, clear breakpoint 1
tbreak 12Temporary breakpoint, removed after the first hit
until 20Continue until line 20 is reached (skips loop iterations)
codeExamples:
def process(orders):
    for order in orders:
        total = sum(order["prices"])
        order["total"] = total
    return orders

# Stop only for the suspicious order:
#   (Pdb) b app.py:3, total > 1000
#   Breakpoint 1 at app.py:3
#   (Pdb) c
#
# Or in code, with a plain if:
def process_v2(orders):
    for order in orders:
        total = sum(order["prices"])
        if total > 1000:
            breakpoint()
        order["total"] = total

expert.content:
Inspecting Anything: Stack Frames and Live Objects

Use w to see the call stack and u/d to move between frames - each frame has its own local variables, so you can ask "what was the caller's value?". display expr re-prints an expression after every step, and interact opens a full Python REPL with the current locals. 
(Pdb) w                      # the call stack
  app.py(10)<module>()
  app.py(8)main()
> app.py(2)parse_age()
(Pdb) u                      # move to the caller's frame
(Pdb) p record               # that frame's variables
{'age': 'abc'}
(Pdb) d
(Pdb) display text           # show 'text' after every command
(Pdb) interact               # full Python prompt; Ctrl-D to return

Configuring breakpoint()

breakpoint() is a hook, not hard-wired to pdb. The environment variable PYTHONBREAKPOINT controls what it calls:
  • PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0 - every breakpoint() is ignored (a safe default for production and CI).
  • PYTHONBREAKPOINT=ipdb.set_trace - use ipdb (tab completion, colours) after pip install ipdb.
  • PYTHONBREAKPOINT=pudb.set_trace - a full-screen terminal debugger.
Still, a forgotten breakpoint() that reaches production will freeze a service waiting for input. Lint for it (ruff rule T100) and set PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0 on servers.

IDE Debuggers and Remote Debugging

VS Code and PyCharm provide the same ideas with a graphical interface: click the gutter to set a breakpoint, then use Step Over (n), Step Into (s), Step Out (r), Continue (c), a Variables panel, a Watch list, and the Call Stack panel. Useful extras:
  • Conditional breakpoints and hit counts - fire on the 500th iteration.
  • Logpoints - print a message when a line is reached without editing code or stopping.
  • Exception breakpoints - stop automatically when a given exception is raised, even if it is later caught.
  • Remote debugging with debugpy to attach to a program in a container or on a server.
codeExamples:
# Attach an IDE to a running script (pip install debugpy)
import debugpy

debugpy.listen(("0.0.0.0", 5678))
print("Waiting for debugger to attach...")
debugpy.wait_for_client()          # blocks until VS Code connects
debugpy.breakpoint()               # optional: stop here once attached

expert.content:
Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Built in: nothing to install, works over SSH and in containersText-only interface is slower than a graphical IDE debugger
Inspect and even change variables while the program is pausedNeeds a terminal: awkward in GUI apps and background services
Post-mortem mode shows the state at the crashForgotten breakpoint() calls freeze programs in production
breakpoint() can be switched off with PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0Command names (n, s, c) must be learned

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How do you start the debugger from code?breakpoint() (Python 3.7+); older code uses import pdb; pdb.set_trace()
n vs s?n steps over a call; s steps into the called function
What is post-mortem debugging?Inspecting the program state after an uncaught exception: python -m pdb script.py or pdb.pm()
How do you stop only when a condition is true?Conditional breakpoint: b file.py:12, price > 100
How can you disable all breakpoints without editing code?Set PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0

Advantages

Advantages: built-in, works over SSH and in containers, inspect and change live state, conditional breakpoints (b 10, x > 5), post-mortem on crashes.
codeExamples:
import pdb
# Conditional breakpoint logic, shown as the equivalent plain code:
for i in range(5):
    if i == 3:
        # breakpoint()     # would stop only when i == 3
        print("would pause at i =", i)

# OUTPUT:
# would pause at i = 3

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: command-line UX is terse, awkward for async/multi-thread programs, and a forgotten breakpoint() hangs a server waiting for input.
codeExamples:
import os
# Safe guard: let operations disable debugger stops in production images
os.environ["PYTHONBREAKPOINT"] = "0"       # breakpoint() becomes a no-op
breakpoint()
print("continued without stopping")

# OUTPUT:
# continued without stopping

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: it freezes the process (not suitable for latency-sensitive prod), needs a terminal, cannot step back in time, and optimised or C-extension code cannot be stepped into.
codeExamples:
import pdb, sys
# pdb cannot step inside C functions:
# (Pdb) s on  sum([1,2,3])   executes sum as ONE step - you never see its inside.
print(sum.__module__ if hasattr(sum, "__module__") else "builtin")

# OUTPUT:
# builtins

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use pdb (or remote debuggers like debugpy) for local and staging investigation; in production prefer logging, tracing and core-dump style post-mortems that do not stop the process. Remove breakpoints in CI via a pre-commit check and set PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0 in production images.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The standard logging module records what a program does as messages with a severity level: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR and CRITICAL. A logger has a threshold level and silently drops anything below it, so one program can be verbose in development and quiet in production without code changes. It is the Python counterpart of Java's SLF4J / Log4j, and the level names are almost the same.
Figure: a logger passes messages at or above its level

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: print() output cannot be switched off, filtered or sent elsewhere. Production code is flooded with debug text, or you delete the prints and lose the information when a bug appears.

Why we need it:
  • Separate routine detail from real problems using levels.
  • Change verbosity by configuration, not by editing code.
  • Add context (logger name, level, time) to every message automatically.
  • Use the same API in libraries and applications.

Complete Example: Five levels, two thresholds

The same five messages are emitted twice: first with the logger at WARNING, then at DEBUG. Output goes to stdout.
codeExamples:
import logging
import sys

FORMAT = "%(levelname)-8s %(name)s: %(message)s"


def build_logger(level):
    handler = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)
    handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter(FORMAT))
    logger = logging.getLogger("shop")
    logger.setLevel(level)
    logger.addHandler(handler)
    return logger


def emit_all(logger):
    logger.debug("cache miss for item %d", 7)
    logger.info("order %s created", "A-101")
    logger.warning("low stock: %d left", 3)
    logger.error("payment failed")
    logger.critical("database down")


def main():
    logger = build_logger(logging.WARNING)
    print("--- level WARNING ---")
    emit_all(logger)

    logger.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)
    print("--- level DEBUG ---")
    emit_all(logger)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT:
# --- level WARNING ---
# WARNING  shop: low stock: 3 left
# ERROR    shop: payment failed
# CRITICAL shop: database down
# --- level DEBUG ---
# DEBUG    shop: cache miss for item 7
# INFO     shop: order A-101 created
# WARNING  shop: low stock: 3 left
# ERROR    shop: payment failed
# CRITICAL shop: database down
codeExplanations: %(levelname)-8s pads the level name to 8 characters so the columns line up. The handler itself has no level, so the logger's threshold decides what passes: WARNING lets three messages through, DEBUG lets all five. Arguments such as %d are formatted only when a message is actually emitted.

beginner.content:
Why logging Instead of print()?

print() is fine for a quick look, but real applications need more. The standard logging module gives you:
  • Severity levels - separate routine detail from real problems.
  • Switchable output - show everything while developing, only warnings in production, without editing code.
  • Context - timestamps, module name, line number, thread, and tracebacks added automatically.
  • Destinations - console, files, email, network - decided by configuration, not by each call.
It is Python's equivalent of Java's SLF4J / Log4j.

The Five Levels

A logger only emits messages at or above its configured level. The default level is WARNING, which is why info() messages seem to vanish until you configure logging.
LevelNumberUse for
DEBUG10Detailed diagnostics for developers
INFO20Normal events: started, request served, job finished
WARNING30Something unexpected, but the program carries on (disk nearly full)
ERROR40A failure: an operation could not be completed
CRITICAL50The whole program may not be able to continue

Your First Logger

basicConfig() sets up a console handler once. getLogger(name) returns a named logger; each call logs at one level.
codeExamples:
import logging

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(levelname)s:%(name)s:%(message)s",
)
log = logging.getLogger("shop")

log.debug("hidden - below INFO")
log.info("started")
log.warning("low stock: %d items", 3)
log.error("payment failed")

# OUTPUT (written to stderr):
# INFO:shop:started
# WARNING:shop:low stock: 3 items
# ERROR:shop:payment failed
codeExplanations: The level INFO lets INFO and above through, so the debug line is dropped. The format string describes each line: level name, logger name, message. Notice the message uses %d with a separate argument rather than formatting the string first - the logging module does the formatting only if the message is actually emitted.

beginner.content:
Logging Exceptions

Inside an except block, log.exception() logs at ERROR level and appends the full traceback. It is the right way to record a caught failure.
codeExamples:
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s:%(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("calc")

def divide(a, b):
    try:
        return a / b
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        log.exception("could not divide %s by %s", a, b)
        return None

print(divide(10, 0))

# OUTPUT (shortened):
# ERROR:could not divide 10 by 0
# Traceback (most recent call last):
#   ...
# ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
# None

beginner.content:
Introduction

The logging module records events with a severity level: DEBUG (10), INFO (20), WARNING (30), ERROR (40), CRITICAL (50). Only records at or above the logger's level are emitted.
codeExamples:
import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format="%(levelname)s:%(name)s:%(message)s")

log = logging.getLogger("app")
log.debug("detail for developers")
log.info("service started")
log.warning("disk 85% full")
log.error("payment failed")

# OUTPUT (stderr):
# DEBUG:app:detail for developers
# INFO:app:service started
# WARNING:app:disk 85% full
# ERROR:app:payment failed

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

print has no severity, timestamp, destination or on/off switch. Logging lets you keep diagnostics in the code permanently and turn verbosity up or down by configuration without editing source.
codeExamples:
import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING, format="%(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("svc")

log.debug("hidden")             # below WARNING -> dropped
log.info("hidden too")
log.warning("shown")

# OUTPUT:
# WARNING shown

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Services use INFO for business events, WARNING for recoverable oddities, ERROR for failed operations, and logger.exception inside except to attach the traceback. Use lazy %s arguments.
codeExamples:
import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("orders")

order_id = 42
log.info("processing order %s", order_id)    # formatted only if emitted (lazy)
try:
    1 / 0
except ZeroDivisionError:
    log.exception("order %s failed", order_id)  # ERROR + traceback

# OUTPUT (abridged):
# INFO processing order 42
# ERROR order 42 failed
# Traceback (most recent call last): ...
# ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

beginner.content:
Diagram

   logger.info("msg") ──► logger level check ──► Handler(s) ──► Formatter ──► destination
        │                    (>= INFO ?)        (own level)    (template)    console/file
        └── hierarchy:  root ─► app ─► app.db   (child propagates to parent handlers)

expert.content:
One Logger per Module: getLogger(__name__)

Loggers form a hierarchy by dotted name: "app.db" is a child of "app", which is a child of the root logger. A child with no level of its own inherits its parent's level, and its records propagate upward to the parents' handlers. Creating log = logging.getLogger(__name__) at the top of each module mirrors your package structure automatically, so you can tune verbosity per package.
codeExamples:
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING,
                    format="%(name)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")

logging.getLogger("app").setLevel(logging.DEBUG)

logging.getLogger("app.db").debug("query ran")     # inherits DEBUG from "app"
logging.getLogger("other").debug("never shown")    # inherits WARNING from root
logging.getLogger("other").warning("shown")

# OUTPUT:
# app.db DEBUG query ran
# other WARNING shown

expert.content:
Lazy Formatting: Pass Arguments, Do Not Build the String

log.debug("value=%s", obj) defers formatting until the record is actually emitted. log.debug(f"value={obj}") formats every time, even when DEBUG is off - wasted work in hot paths, and an expensive __str__ may run for nothing. For costly argument computation guard with log.isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG).
codeExamples:
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
log = logging.getLogger("demo")

class Costly:
    def __str__(self):
        print("formatting!")
        return "costly"

log.debug("value=%s", Costly())        # DEBUG is off: __str__ never runs
log.debug(f"value={Costly()}")         # the f-string calls __str__ immediately

if log.isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG):
    log.debug("expensive: %s", sum(range(10_000_000)))

# OUTPUT:
# formatting!

expert.content:
Rules for Libraries vs Applications

  • Applications configure logging once, at startup (basicConfig or dictConfig) in the entry-point module.
  • Libraries only call getLogger(__name__) and log. They must never call basicConfig or add real handlers - that is the application's decision. A library may add a NullHandler to its top-level logger to avoid "no handlers" noise.
  • Don't log in module-level code that runs on import, before configuration exists.
  • Don't call logging.info() (module-level functions use the root logger) from library code; use a named logger.
codeExamples:
# mylib/__init__.py
import logging
logging.getLogger(__name__).addHandler(logging.NullHandler())

# mylib/client.py
import logging
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)         # "mylib.client"

def fetch(url):
    log.debug("fetching %s", url)
    ...

expert.content:
Useful Extras: exc_info, extra and stack_info

OptionEffect
exc_info=TrueAttach the current exception's traceback to any level (log.warning("retrying", exc_info=True))
stack_info=TrueAttach the current call stack (no exception needed)
extra={"user_id": 7}Add custom fields to the record, usable as %(user_id)s in a formatter
log.setLevel(...)Change a logger's threshold at runtime
logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL)Silence everything, e.g. during tests
Security: never log passwords, tokens, card numbers or other personal data. Logs are copied to many systems and kept for a long time.
codeExamples:
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO,
                    format="%(levelname)s [user=%(user_id)s] %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("audit")

log.info("profile updated", extra={"user_id": 7})

# OUTPUT:
# INFO [user=7] profile updated

expert.content:
Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Levels let you filter noise without touching call sitesDefault level is WARNING: info() seems to vanish
Verbosity is a configuration choice per environmentMore setup than a simple print()
Lazy % formatting avoids wasted workEasy to log secrets or personal data by accident
Standard library: same API in every Python projectLevel choice is subjective; teams need conventions

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What are the logging levels, in order?DEBUG (10), INFO (20), WARNING (30), ERROR (40), CRITICAL (50)
What is the default level and why does it matter?WARNING - so debug and info messages are dropped until you configure a lower level
Why getLogger(__name__)?Names follow the module hierarchy, so you can set levels per package and see where each message came from
Why log.info("x=%s", x) instead of an f-string?Formatting is deferred until the message will actually be emitted
How do you log an exception with its traceback?log.exception("msg") inside the except block, or exc_info=True
Should a library configure logging?No - only the application configures handlers; a library just uses a named logger (and a NullHandler)

Advantages

Advantages: levels, hierarchical loggers (app.db inherits from app), per-module control, lazy formatting, thread-safe, and the library standard so third-party code logs through it.
codeExamples:
import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(name)s %(message)s")

logging.getLogger("app.db").setLevel(logging.DEBUG)       # noisy only for db
logging.getLogger("app.db").debug("query ran")
logging.getLogger("app.web").debug("request")             # dropped (parent INFO)
logging.getLogger("app.web").info("GET /")

# OUTPUT:
# app.db query ran
# app.web GET /

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: configuration is verbose and has gotchas (basicConfig only works once, handlers duplicate), and the %-style API feels dated.
codeExamples:
import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="first %(message)s")
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format="second %(message)s")  # IGNORED
logging.info("hello")
