print(child.parent())

# OUTPUT:
# True
# Parent freed
# None

expert.content:
Hidden Cycles

Some cycles are not obvious:
  • Bound methods and lambdas stored on self: self.cb = self.on_event or self.cb = lambda: self.x make self refer to itself through the callback.
  • Exceptions: an exception holds its traceback, the traceback holds each frame, and a frame's locals may hold the exception. This is why Python deletes the name in except ... as e at the end of the block. Storing e in a longer-lived variable recreates the cycle and keeps every local in the failing frames alive.
  • Closures: a function that refers to itself through a free variable (a recursive inner function).
codeExamples:
import gc

class Widget:
    def __init__(self):
        self.callback = self.on_click      # self -> bound method -> self

    def on_click(self):
        pass

w = Widget()
print(w.callback.__self__ is w)           # the cycle: w -> callback -> w

del w
print(gc.collect() > 0)                    # only the cycle collector frees it

# OUTPUT:
# True
# True

expert.content:
Finding Cycles

gc.set_debug(gc.DEBUG_SAVEALL) makes the collector keep every object it finds unreachable in the list gc.garbage instead of freeing it, so you can inspect what was in a cycle.
codeExamples:
import gc

class Node:
    pass

gc.collect()
gc.set_debug(gc.DEBUG_SAVEALL)

a = Node()
a.me = a                      # an object referring to itself
del a
gc.collect()

found = [o for o in gc.garbage if isinstance(o, Node)]
print(len(found))

gc.set_debug(0)               # restore normal behaviour
gc.garbage.clear()

# OUTPUT:
# 1

expert.content:
Cycles and __del__

Before Python 3.4, an object with a __del__ method that was part of a cycle could never be collected and ended up in gc.garbage forever (a real leak). PEP 442 fixed this: the collector now safely finalizes such objects. gc.garbage is nowadays only for rare uncollectable objects (typically from C extensions). Design guidance:
  • Prefer ownership trees: parents own children, children hold weak references upward.
  • Don't rely on prompt cleanup of objects in cycles - use with blocks for resources.
  • Don't call gc.collect() habitually to "fix" memory: if memory keeps growing, find what still holds references (gc.get_referrers, tracemalloc).

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Cycles let you model real structures: trees, graphs, parent linksMemory is held longer than needed
The collector eventually reclaims them automatically__del__ and resource release are delayed
Weak back-links remove the cycle but keep navigationCycles are invisible in the code until you look for them
Detectable with gc.collect() and gc.get_referrers()Weak links add code and may return None

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a reference cycle?Objects that reference each other (or themselves), so their counts never reach zero
Who frees a cycle?The cyclic garbage collector (gc module), not reference counting
How can you avoid cycles in a parent/child design?Make the back-reference (child to parent) a weakref
Why does Python delete e after an except block?To avoid the cycle exception -> traceback -> frame -> e
Can objects with __del__ in a cycle be collected?Yes since Python 3.4 (PEP 442); before that they leaked into gc.garbage

Advantages

Advantages: cycles make natural data structures possible (graphs, trees with parent links), and Python handles them for you through the GC.
codeExamples:
import gc
class G:
    def __init__(self): self.me = self    # self-cycle
for _ in range(1000):
    G()                                   # all become garbage immediately
print("freed:", gc.collect() >= 1000)

# OUTPUT:
# freed: True

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: cyclic garbage lingers until the next collection, raising peak memory, and __del__ on cyclic objects makes finalisation order unpredictable.

Limitations

Limitations: the GC only finds unreachable cycles; a cycle reachable from a global stays forever, and C extensions that do not support GC tracking can leak cycles.
codeExamples:
import gc
registry = []
class Node:
    def __init__(self): self.me = self; registry.append(self)

Node()
print(gc.collect())              # 0 collected: registry still reaches it
print(len(registry))

# OUTPUT:
# 0
# 1

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Break cycles by design: use weakref (or a weak parent pointer) for back references, avoid __del__, and expose explicit close/dispose methods or context managers. Monitor with gc.set_debug(gc.DEBUG_SAVEALL) in tests to assert that important objects do not form uncollected cycles.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A normal reference owns its target: while it exists, the object stays alive. A weak reference lets you observe an object without owning it. When the last normal reference disappears, the object is freed and the weak reference becomes empty (calling it returns None). The weakref module also offers WeakValueDictionary and weakref.finalize for cleanup callbacks. Java provides the same idea through java.lang.ref.WeakReference and WeakHashMap.
Figure: only the strong name keeps the object alive; deleting it empties the weak side

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: A cache that stores objects in a normal dictionary keeps every one of them alive forever, so it only grows. A child holding its parent normally creates a cycle.

Why we need it:
  • Build caches that never keep unused objects alive.
  • Create back-references without reference cycles.
  • Register observers that do not prevent their own cleanup.
  • Run a callback when an object dies (weakref.finalize).

Complete Example: weakref.ref, WeakValueDictionary and finalize

A complete, runnable program. Save it in a file and run it with python.
codeExamples:
import weakref


class Image:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name


def main():
    cache = weakref.WeakValueDictionary()
    img = Image("logo.png")
    cache["logo"] = img                        # weak: does not own img
    ref = weakref.ref(img)
    weakref.finalize(img, print, "image finalized")

    print("entries in cache:", len(cache))
    print("ref gives object:", ref() is img)

    del img                                    # the last strong reference
    print("after del:", len(cache), ref())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT:
# entries in cache: 1
# ref gives object: True
# image finalized
# after del: 0 None
codeExplanations: The cache and the ref both point to the image weakly, so the only owner is the name img. When img is deleted, the object is freed at once: the finalize callback prints its message, the cache entry disappears and ref() returns None. Note that only instances of your own classes can be weakly referenced; plain int, str, list and dict cannot.

beginner.content:
A Reference That Does Not Keep the Object Alive

A normal reference keeps its target alive. A weak reference lets you look at an object without owning it: if every normal reference disappears, the object is freed and the weak reference simply becomes empty. Calling a weakref.ref object returns the target while it is alive, and None afterwards.
codeExamples:
import weakref

class Data:
    pass

d = Data()
r = weakref.ref(d)

print(r() is d)          # alive: calling r gives the object back
del d                    # last normal reference gone, so the object is freed
print(r())

# OUTPUT:
# True
# None

beginner.content:
Why Would You Want That?

  • Caches that should not prevent unused entries from being freed.
  • Back-references (child to parent) that would otherwise create reference cycles.
  • Observers/listeners that must not keep a dead object alive just because it subscribed.
  • Cleanup callbacks that run when an object disappears.
Java has the same idea: WeakReference and WeakHashMap.

WeakValueDictionary: A Self-Cleaning Cache

It maps keys to objects weakly: when an object is no longer used anywhere else, its entry vanishes automatically.
codeExamples:
import weakref

class Image:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

cache = weakref.WeakValueDictionary()

img = Image("logo.png")
cache["logo"] = img
print(len(cache))

del img                  # nothing else holds the image
print(len(cache))

# OUTPUT:
# 1
# 0
codeExplanations: A normal dict would keep the Image alive forever, so the cache would only ever grow. With WeakValueDictionary the cache holds the image only as long as some other part of the program still uses it - exactly the semantics of a cache of "things that are in use".

beginner.content:
Not Everything Can Be Weakly Referenced

Instances of your own classes can. Built-in int, str, tuple, list and dict cannot (subclasses of list and dict can).
codeExamples:
import weakref

try:
    weakref.ref([1, 2, 3])
except TypeError as error:
    print("TypeError:", error)

class MyList(list):
    pass

print(weakref.ref(MyList()) is not None)

# OUTPUT:
# TypeError: cannot create weak reference to 'list' object
# True

beginner.content:
Introduction

A weak reference points to an object without increasing its reference count. When the last strong reference disappears the object is freed and the weak reference returns None.
codeExamples:
import weakref

class Img:
    pass

img = Img()
w = weakref.ref(img)           # weak: does not keep img alive
print(w() is img)              # call it to get the object (or None)

del img                        # last strong reference gone
print(w())                     # object was freed

# OUTPUT:
# True
# None

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Caches, registries and observer lists hold objects only to be helpful; if they hold them strongly they cause memory leaks. Weak references let those structures never extend an object's life.
codeExamples:
import weakref

class User:
    def __init__(self, n): self.n = n

cache = weakref.WeakValueDictionary()
u = User("abaji")
cache["abaji"] = u
print(len(cache))              # 1
del u
print(len(cache))              # entry vanished automatically

# OUTPUT:
# 1
# 0

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Used in: object caches (WeakValueDictionary), per-object metadata (WeakKeyDictionary), observer/event systems (WeakSet, WeakMethod), parent back-pointers in trees, and weakref.finalize for cleanup.
codeExamples:
import weakref

class Conn:
    pass

c = Conn()
weakref.finalize(c, print, "connection cleaned up")   # runs when c is freed
print("working")
del c

# OUTPUT:
# working
# connection cleaned up

beginner.content:
Diagram

   strong ref ──► ┌──────────┐ ◄·· weak ref (no count)
   refcount = 1   │  Object  │
                  └──────────┘
   del strong ──► refcount = 0 ──► freed ──► weak() returns None

expert.content:
weakref.finalize: Safe Cleanup When an Object Dies

weakref.finalize(obj, func, *args) registers a function to run once, when obj is garbage-collected (or at interpreter exit). Unlike __del__ it works reliably even for objects in cycles, never resurrects the object, and cannot be forgotten by a subclass.
codeExamples:
import weakref

class TempFile:
    def __init__(self, path):
        self.path = path

f = TempFile("/tmp/data.bin")
weakref.finalize(f, print, "cleaning up /tmp/data.bin")

print("using the file")
del f                              # triggers the callback

# OUTPUT:
# using the file
# cleaning up /tmp/data.bin

expert.content:
proxy and WeakMethod

weakref.proxy(obj) behaves like the object itself (no need to call it) but raises ReferenceError once the object is gone. Bound methods need WeakMethod: a plain weakref.ref(obj.method) dies immediately because the bound-method object is temporary. This is the foundation of safe observer / event systems.

__slots__ and __weakref__

A class that defines __slots__ has no per-instance dictionary - and also no __weakref__ slot unless you ask for one. Add "__weakref__" to the slots to allow weak references to its instances.

Pitfalls and Related Types

  • Always check the result. r() can be None at any moment; grab it into a local variable and test it before use (obj = r(); if obj is not None: ...) so it cannot vanish between the check and the use.
  • Timing differs between implementations. CPython frees at once when the count hits zero; PyPy collects later, so code must not assume instant disappearance.
  • WeakKeyDictionary keys objects weakly (store extra data about objects you do not own); WeakSet holds a set of objects weakly (e.g., a registry of live instances).
  • Callbacks run at odd times (during garbage collection); keep them short and never raise.
  • Don't weakly reference things nobody else owns: weakref.ref(Data()) is dead before the next line.
codeExamples:
import weakref

class Data:
    pass

r = weakref.ref(Data())          # the temporary object has no other owner
print(r())

instances = weakref.WeakSet()
a = Data()
instances.add(a)
print(len(instances))
del a
print(len(instances))

# OUTPUT:
# None
# 1
# 0

expert.content:
Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Caches clean themselves up automaticallyTarget may vanish at any moment, so always check for None
Breaks reference cycles without losing the linkBuilt-in int, str, list, dict are not supported
Observers cannot keep dead objects aliveBehaviour depends on CPython's immediate freeing
finalize gives a reliable cleanup hookExtra complexity compared with a plain reference

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a weak reference?A reference that does not increase the refcount; the target can be freed and the reference then returns None
Give two uses.Caches that should not retain objects, and back-references that avoid reference cycles
Why can't you weakly reference a list or int?Built-in types do not provide the weakref slot; subclasses and user classes can
Why use WeakMethod?A bound method object is temporary, so a plain weakref to it would die immediately
weakref.finalize vs __del__?finalize is reliable for cycles, runs once, and is registered separately from the class

Advantages

Advantages: breaks cycles without leaks, automatic self-cleaning caches, no explicit unregister calls, and finalize is more reliable than __del__.
codeExamples:
import weakref

class Parent:
    def __init__(self): self.kids = []
class Child:
    def __init__(self, p):
        self.parent = weakref.ref(p)    # weak back pointer: no cycle
        p.kids.append(self)

p = Parent(); c = Child(p)
print(c.parent() is p)

# OUTPUT:
# True

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: you must always check for None before use, behaviour depends on refcounting timing, and debugging "why did it vanish" can be confusing.
codeExamples:
import weakref

class A: pass
a = A()
w = weakref.ref(a)
a = None                        # rebinding also drops the object
obj = w()
print(obj)
# obj.attr   would raise AttributeError: 'NoneType' ...

# OUTPUT:
# None

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: not every type supports weak references: int, str, list, dict, tuples cannot be weakly referenced (subclasses can), and classes using __slots__ need a __weakref__ slot.
codeExamples:
import weakref

try:
    weakref.ref([1, 2])
except TypeError as e:
    print(e)

class Slotted:
    __slots__ = ("x",)                       # no __weakref__ -> not weak-referenceable
class SlottedOK:
    __slots__ = ("x", "__weakref__")
weakref.ref(SlottedOK())
print("slot with __weakref__ works")

# OUTPUT:
# cannot create weak reference to 'list' object
# slot with __weakref__ works

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Prefer weak references for caches that must not pin memory and for child-to-parent links, but use bounded strong caches (functools.lru_cache) when you need predictable hit rates, since weak entries disappear as soon as callers drop them. Never rely on weakref callbacks for critical cleanup ordering; use context managers.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Python objects carry overhead: a reference count, a type pointer and the data itself. So an int that needs 4 bytes in C or Java takes about 28 bytes in CPython. Small objects are served by a fast internal allocator (pymalloc) that carves memory from larger arenas divided into pools and blocks. Containers such as lists over-allocate spare room so that append is cheap on average. sys.getsizeof() reports an object's own size, but only shallowly.
Figure: small objects come from pools; lists keep spare capacity

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: Programs that store millions of small values use far more RAM than the raw data suggests, and developers cannot tell where it goes without understanding the per-object cost.

Why we need it:
  • Estimate memory use before building large data structures.
  • Understand why append is amortized O(1) (over-allocation).
  • Know that getsizeof excludes the objects a container refers to.
  • Decide when to switch to compact types (array, NumPy, generators).

Complete Example: Shallow size, deep size and list growth

Exact byte counts vary by Python version, so the program compares sizes instead of printing them.
codeExamples:
import sys

ITEMS = 1000
APPENDS = 100


def deep_size(numbers):
    shallow = sys.getsizeof(numbers)
    return shallow + sum(sys.getsizeof(n) for n in numbers)


def count_resizes(appends):
    items = []
    last = sys.getsizeof(items)
    resizes = 0
    for i in range(appends):
        items.append(i)
        size = sys.getsizeof(items)
        if size != last:                 # the list grew its buffer
            resizes += 1
            last = size
    return resizes


def main():
    numbers = list(range(ITEMS))
    print("int bigger than 8 bytes:", sys.getsizeof(1) > 8)
    print("big int bigger than small:", sys.getsizeof(10 ** 100) > sys.getsizeof(1))
    print("empty smaller than full:", sys.getsizeof([]) < sys.getsizeof(numbers))
    print("deep bigger than shallow:", deep_size(numbers) > sys.getsizeof(numbers))
    print("resizes fewer than appends:", count_resizes(APPENDS) < APPENDS)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT:
# int bigger than 8 bytes: True
# big int bigger than small: True
# empty smaller than full: True
# deep bigger than shallow: True
# resizes fewer than appends: True
codeExplanations: Every int is an object bigger than a bare 8-byte pointer, and larger numbers need more digits. getsizeof(numbers) counts only the list's pointer array; adding the size of each int shows the real footprint. Over-allocation means the buffer grows only a handful of times during 100 appends.

beginner.content:
Objects Take More Space Than You Think

In C an int is 4 bytes. In Python an int is a full object with a reference count, a type pointer and its digits, so even 1 takes roughly 28 bytes on a 64-bit build. sys.getsizeof(obj) reports the size of the object itself.
codeExamples:
import sys

print(sys.getsizeof(1))
print(sys.getsizeof(1.0))
print(sys.getsizeof("a"))
print(sys.getsizeof([]))
print(sys.getsizeof({}))

# OUTPUT (typical values for 64-bit Python 3.12; they vary by version):
# 28
# 24
# 42
# 56
# 64

beginner.content:
getsizeof Is Shallow

It counts only the container itself - not the objects it refers to. A list of a million numbers is much bigger than getsizeof suggests, because each number is its own object.
codeExamples:
import sys

numbers = list(range(1000))
print(sys.getsizeof(numbers))                       # just the list's pointer array
print(sum(sys.getsizeof(n) for n in numbers) > sys.getsizeof(numbers))

# OUTPUT (the first number varies by version):
# 8056
# True

beginner.content:
Lists Over-Allocate

Growing a list one item at a time would mean copying it on every append. Instead Python reserves extra room, so most appends are free and occasionally the size jumps. That is why append is "amortized O(1)".
codeExamples:
import sys

items = []
last = sys.getsizeof(items)
changes = 0

for i in range(100):
    items.append(i)
    size = sys.getsizeof(items)
    if size != last:
        changes += 1
        last = size

print(changes < 20)           # far fewer resizes than appends

# OUTPUT:
# True

beginner.content:
Introduction

CPython allocates memory in layers: the OS gives big arenas, pymalloc splits them into pools and blocks for small objects (up to 512 bytes), and larger requests go to the C malloc. Python code itself never calls malloc.
codeExamples:
import sys

print(sys.getsizeof(0))        # int object
print(sys.getsizeof(""))       # empty str
print(sys.getsizeof([]))       # empty list
print(sys.getsizeof({}))       # empty dict

# OUTPUT (64-bit CPython 3.12):
# 28
# 41
# 56
# 64

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Every object carries a header (reference count and type pointer) and containers over-allocate to make appends cheap. Knowing this lets you estimate memory and avoid surprising out-of-memory failures.
codeExamples:
import sys

lst = []
last = sys.getsizeof(lst)
for i in range(20):
    lst.append(i)
    size = sys.getsizeof(lst)
    if size != last:
        print(f"len={len(lst):2d} size grew to {size}")   # over-allocation steps
        last = size

# OUTPUT (3.12):
# len= 1 size grew to 88
# len= 5 size grew to 120
# len= 9 size grew to 184
# len=17 size grew to 256

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Use tracemalloc to find which lines allocate the most, sys.getsizeof for one object, and __slots__ / array / NumPy to shrink millions of objects.
codeExamples:
import tracemalloc

tracemalloc.start()
data = [str(i) * 10 for i in range(50_000)]        # allocation burst
snap = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
top = snap.statistics("lineno")[0]
print("biggest allocator is line", top.traceback[0].lineno)
print("size over 1 MB:", top.size > 1_000_000)

# OUTPUT (example):
# biggest allocator is line 5
# size over 1 MB: True

beginner.content:
Diagram

   OS memory
     │ mmap
     ▼
   ┌─ Arena (1 MiB) ───────────────────────────────┐
   │ ┌─ Pool (16 KiB, one size class) ─┐  ┌─ Pool ─┐│
   │ │ block │ block │ block │ ...     │  │  ...   ││
   │ └─────────────────────────────────┘  └────────┘│
   └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   objects > 512 bytes  ──►  C malloc directly

expert.content:
pymalloc: Python's Small-Object Allocator

Calling the operating system's malloc for every tiny object would be slow and fragment memory. CPython therefore layers its own allocator, pymalloc, for objects of 512 bytes or less:
LevelWhat it is
ArenaA large chunk requested from the OS (1 MiB on 3.10+; 256 KiB before)
PoolA slice of an arena (16 KiB on 3.10+) dedicated to one block size class
BlockA fixed-size slot in a pool holding one object (size classes in steps of 16 bytes on 64-bit)
Allocating takes the next free block from a pool of the right size class; freeing puts the block back on that pool's free list - very fast, and no per-object malloc overhead. Anything larger than 512 bytes goes straight to the system malloc.

Why the Process Size Doesn't Always Shrink

An arena is returned to the OS only when every block in it is free. A few long-lived objects scattered across arenas can pin them all, so after freeing a million objects the process may still hold most of its memory (it is reused by later allocations, but the OS shows it as used). This is fragmentation, and a common cause of "my Python process never gives memory back". Mitigations: allocate big short-lived data in a separate process (a worker that exits), keep long-lived and short-lived objects apart, use compact structures (array, numpy, __slots__), or process data in chunks and streams.
codeExamples:
import sys

class Plain:
    def __init__(self):
        self.a = 1
        self.b = 2

class Slotted:
    __slots__ = ("a", "b")
    def __init__(self):
        self.a = 1
        self.b = 2

print(hasattr(Plain(), "__dict__"))       # each instance carries a dict
print(hasattr(Slotted(), "__dict__"))     # no per-instance dict

# OUTPUT:
# True
# False
codeExplanations: A normal instance stores its attributes in a per-instance dictionary, which costs memory. __slots__ replaces it with a small fixed array of attribute slots, which can cut memory per instance substantially when you create millions of small objects. The trade-off: you cannot add arbitrary new attributes.

expert.content:
Free Lists and Reuse

CPython keeps small free lists of recently freed objects of hot types (floats, tuples of small sizes, lists, dicts, frames) and reuses them for the next allocation instead of going through the allocator. This is why a newly created list often reuses the address of one that was just freed - the cause of some surprising id() results (see the last topic of this module).

Measuring: tracemalloc and sys._debugmallocstats

tracemalloc records where memory is allocated, so you can see the current and peak usage and find the lines responsible for growth. sys._debugmallocstats() dumps pymalloc's arenas, pools and size classes to stderr.
codeExamples:
import tracemalloc

tracemalloc.start()

data = [str(i) for i in range(100_000)]

current, peak = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()
print(current > 1_000_000, peak >= current)

snapshot = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
top = snapshot.statistics("lineno")[0]
print(top.size > 1_000_000)           # the comprehension line is the top allocator

tracemalloc.stop()

# OUTPUT:
# True True
# True

expert.content:
Configuring the Allocator

  • PYTHONMALLOC=debug adds guard bytes around blocks to detect buffer overruns in C extensions.
  • PYTHONMALLOC=malloc bypasses pymalloc so tools like Valgrind and AddressSanitizer can see every allocation.
  • Free-threaded builds of Python 3.13+ use mimalloc instead of pymalloc, because pymalloc relies on the GIL.
  • Choose compact structures deliberately: array.array('i', ...) stores raw 4-byte ints (about 8x smaller than a list of int objects), bytes/bytearray for binary data, generators instead of lists for streams, and numpy arrays for numeric work.
codeExamples:
import sys
from array import array

as_list = list(range(100_000))
as_array = array("i", range(100_000))

list_total = sys.getsizeof(as_list) + sum(sys.getsizeof(n) for n in as_list)
print(sys.getsizeof(as_array) < list_total / 5)

# OUTPUT:
# True

expert.content:
Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
pymalloc makes small-object allocation fastEach object has header overhead (about 28 bytes for an int)
Over-allocation gives amortized O(1) appendLists reserve spare capacity that may go unused
Memory is managed automatically: no manual malloc/freegetsizeof is shallow and misleads on containers
sys.getsizeof and tracemalloc help measure usageMemory is not always returned to the operating system

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does a Python int take about 28 bytes?It is a full heap object: reference count, type pointer, size and digit storage
What does sys.getsizeof not include?The size of the objects a container refers to (it is shallow)
What is pymalloc?CPython's allocator for objects of 512 bytes or less, organised into arenas, pools and blocks
Why might memory not return to the OS after freeing objects?Arenas are released only when completely empty; fragmentation keeps them pinned
How do you find what is using memory?tracemalloc snapshots, or gc.get_objects() counts by type
How does __slots__ save memory?It removes the per-instance __dict__, storing attributes in fixed slots

Advantages

Advantages: pymalloc makes small allocations very fast and reduces fragmentation, memory is freed automatically, and the tooling (tracemalloc, gc, sys) is built in.
codeExamples:
class Plain:
    def __init__(self): self.a = 1; self.b = 2
class Slim:
    __slots__ = ("a", "b")                       # no per-instance dict
    def __init__(self): self.a = 1; self.b = 2

import sys
print(sys.getsizeof(Plain().__dict__) > 0, hasattr(Slim(), "__dict__"))

# OUTPUT:
# True False

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: higher per-object overhead than C or Java primitives, memory fragmentation can keep arenas allocated, and a big list of ints costs far more than raw numbers.
codeExamples:
import sys, array

nums = list(range(1000))
raw = array.array("i", range(1000))
list_cost = sys.getsizeof(nums) + sum(sys.getsizeof(n) for n in nums)
print("list of ints ~", list_cost, "bytes")
print("array('i')   ~", sys.getsizeof(raw), "bytes")

# OUTPUT (3.12, approx):
# list of ints ~ 36000 bytes
# array('i')   ~ 4064 bytes

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: getsizeof is shallow (excludes referenced objects), freed memory is often not returned to the OS, and a process footprint may not shrink after releasing data.
codeExamples:
import sys
inner = [bytearray(1000) for _ in range(10)]
outer = [inner]
print(sys.getsizeof(outer))            # only the outer list's own pointers
print(sys.getsizeof(inner[0]))         # each inner is separate

# Deep size needs recursion or pympler.asizeof.

# OUTPUT:
# 64
# 1057

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

For memory-heavy workloads choose the data layout first: arrays, NumPy, Arrow, __slots__ or dataclasses(slots=True), generators for streaming. Profile with tracemalloc in staging, recycle worker processes to cap fragmentation (max_requests), and use memory limits in containers so leaks fail fast.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Creating a new object costs time and memory, so CPython creates one and shares it for values used everywhere. Sharing is safe only because these objects are immutable. The main cases are the small-integer cache (-5 to 256), the singletons None, True, False and the empty tuple, and string interning (sys.intern). Java has the same ideas: the Integer cache (-128 to 127) and the String pool with String.intern(). In both languages these are implementation details, so always compare values with ==, not is.
Figure: what CPython shares automatically (an implementation detail)

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: Programs that use the same small numbers and names millions of times would waste memory and time allocating identical objects again and again.

Why we need it:
  • Save memory and allocation time for very common immutable values.
  • Make identity checks cheap: x is None is always correct.
  • Make dictionary key lookups faster with interned strings.
  • Avoid the bug of using is where == is meant.

Complete Example: Which values are shared (CPython 3.12)

Values are built at run time (with int() and join()) so compile-time constant merging does not hide the caches. The results are CPython-specific.
codeExamples:
import sys


def make_int(text):
    return int(text)


def make_text(parts):
    return "".join(parts)


def main():
    print("int 256 shared:", make_int("256") is make_int("256"))
    print("int 257 shared:", make_int("257") is make_int("257"))
    print("int 257 equal:", make_int("257") == make_int("257"))
    print("None shared:", None is None)
    print("empty tuple shared:", tuple() is tuple())
    print("two lists shared:", [] is [])

    first = make_text(["py", "thon"])
    second = make_text(["py", "thon"])
    print("runtime strings shared:", first is second)

    first = sys.intern(first)
    second = sys.intern(second)
    print("after intern shared:", first is second)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT:
# int 256 shared: True
# int 257 shared: False
# int 257 equal: True
# None shared: True
# empty tuple shared: True
# two lists shared: False
# runtime strings shared: False
# after intern shared: True
codeExplanations: 256 is inside the small-integer cache so both calls return one object; 257 is outside, so two distinct but equal objects are created ("is" False, "==" True). None and the empty tuple are single instances; lists are mutable and never shared. Strings built at run time are separate objects until sys.intern() maps both to one stored copy.

beginner.content:
Sharing Instead of Copying

Creating a fresh object costs time and memory. For values that are used constantly, CPython creates one object and shares it. Because the shared objects are immutable, sharing is safe: nobody can change the value behind your back. Two mechanisms matter: the small-integer cache and string interning. Both are CPython implementation details, not language guarantees.

The Small-Integer Cache

CPython pre-creates the integers from -5 to 256. Every use of those values refers to the same object. Larger integers are created fresh each time they are computed.
codeExamples:
a = int("256")
b = int("256")
print(a is b)              # inside the cache: one shared object

c = int("257")
d = int("257")
print(c is d)              # outside the cache: two separate objects
print(c == d)              # but equal in value

# OUTPUT:
# True
# False
# True
codeExplanations: int("256") is used instead of a plain literal so the numbers are created at run time. (Two literals of the same value in one block of code share a single constant object, which hides the cache.) is compares identity, == compares value, and the output shows they can differ for equal numbers.

beginner.content:
Singletons: None, True and False

There is exactly one None, one True and one False in a program. That is why x is None is the correct test and always safe. The empty tuple is also a single shared object.
codeExamples:
x = None
y = None
print(x is y)

a = tuple()
b = tuple()
print(a is b)

l1 = []
l2 = []
print(l1 is l2)            # mutable objects are never shared

# OUTPUT:
# True
# True
# False

beginner.content:
String Interning

Interning stores one copy of a string and reuses it. CPython automatically interns strings that look like identifiers (letters, digits, underscore) when they appear in source code. Strings built at run time are usually not interned, even if equal.
codeExamples:
import sys

a = "".join(["py", "thon"])        # built at run time
b = "".join(["py", "thon"])
print(a == b, a is b)

a = sys.intern(a)                  # explicitly intern both
b = sys.intern(b)
print(a is b)

# OUTPUT:
# True False
# True

beginner.content:
Introduction

Interning reuses a single object for equal immutable values. CPython caches small integers (-5 to 256), interns identifier-like strings, and shares empty tuples and the singletons None, True, False.
codeExamples:
a = 256; b = 256
print(a is b)              # True: cached small int

x = int("1000"); y = int("1000")
print(x is y)              # False: separate objects created at runtime

import sys
s1 = sys.intern("hello world!")
s2 = sys.intern("hello world!")
print(s1 is s2)            # explicit interning

# OUTPUT:
# True
# False
# True

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Programs create huge numbers of tiny values. Reusing one shared immutable object saves memory and makes identity comparison a fast pointer check.
codeExamples:
import sys

words = ["status_ok"] * 3
print(words[0] is words[1])               # same object three times

dyn1 = "".join(["sta", "tus ok"])         # built at runtime, not interned
dyn2 = "".join(["sta", "tus ok"])
print(dyn1 == dyn2, dyn1 is dyn2)

# OUTPUT:
# True
# True False

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Dictionary keys and attribute names are interned so lookups compare pointers first. Large parsers call sys.intern on repeated tokens to cut memory. Compiler constant folding also merges identical literals in one code object.
codeExamples:
import sys

rows = [f"user{i % 3}" for i in range(9)]            # 9 strings, 3 distinct
print(len({id(s) for s in rows}))                    # 9 separate objects

rows = [sys.intern(s) for s in rows]                 # collapse duplicates
print(len({id(s) for s in rows}))                    # 3 objects

# OUTPUT:
# 9
# 3

beginner.content:
Diagram

   int cache:  -5 ... 256   ──► one object per value (preallocated)
   a = 100 ─┐
   b = 100 ─┴──► [ int 100 ]        a is b -> True
   c = 1000 ───► [ int 1000 ]       d = 1000 ───► [ int 1000 ]  (c is d may be False)
   interned strings:  "name" "id" "status"  ──► intern table (dict)

expert.content:
Why Interning Exists

Python looks names up in dictionaries constantly: every attribute access, global, and keyword argument is a string key. If equal keys are the same object, a dictionary can first compare pointers (one machine instruction) before falling back to comparing characters, and the hash is already cached. Interning therefore speeds up attribute lookup and saves memory for the many identical names in a program.

Compile-Time Merging of Constants

The compiler merges identical constants within one code object, so two equal literals in the same function or module often are the same object - even outside the small-int range. This is why the outcome of is on literals depends on how and where the code was compiled. It is also why Python 3.8+ emits a SyntaxWarning for x is 256 or x is "text".
codeExamples:
def same(a, b):
    return a is b

print(same(int("1000"), int("1000")))   # created at run time: two objects
print(same(1000, 1000))                 # two literals in one code object: merged

# OUTPUT (CPython):
# False
# True

expert.content:
What Else Is Cached or Reused?

ObjectBehaviour in CPython
Integers -5 to 256Pre-created singletons
None, True, False, Ellipsis, NotImplementedLanguage-level singletons
Empty tuple, empty string, single Latin-1 charactersShared singletons
Identifier-like string constants, attribute and variable namesInterned automatically
Floats, lists, dicts, sets, instancesNever cached by value (but recycled through internal free lists)
Immortal objects (3.12+)The above singletons never change their reference count

Using sys.intern Deliberately

When a program holds millions of repeated strings (log levels, country codes, column names parsed from a file) interning them can cut memory and make equality checks cheaper. Interned strings are tracked in an internal table (and, since 3.12, freed when no longer used, unless they are immortal). Only intern values that really repeat - interning unique data wastes time.
codeExamples:
import sys

raw = ["IN", "US", "IN", "UK", "IN", "US"] * 1000
parsed = ["".join(list(code)) for code in raw]       # equal strings, separate objects

print(len({id(s) for s in parsed}) > 3)              # many distinct objects

interned = [sys.intern(s) for s in parsed]
print(len({id(s) for s in interned}))                # one object per distinct value

# OUTPUT:
# True
# 3

expert.content:
Explicit Caching Is Different

Interning and the small-int cache are automatic and invisible. For your own expensive results use explicit caching - functools.lru_cache / functools.cache - which returns the same result object for repeated arguments.
codeExamples:
from functools import lru_cache

@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def build_table(n):
    print("building")
    return tuple(range(n))

a = build_table(5)
b = build_table(5)
print(a is b)
print(build_table.cache_info().hits)

# OUTPUT:
# building
# True
# 1

expert.content:
Rules to Remember

  • Never use is to compare numbers or strings. Use ==. Use is only for singletons: None, True, False and for real identity checks.
  • The range -5..256 is an implementation detail that has changed before and may change again; PyPy, Jython and others behave differently.
  • Caching works only for immutable values. Mutable objects are never shared automatically.
  • Don't use interning for security-sensitive comparisons or to "optimize" without measuring.

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Saves memory for frequently used valuesBehaviour is an implementation detail and may change between versions
Avoids repeated allocation: faster programsMakes is look like it works for values, causing hidden bugs
Safe because the shared objects are immutableInterning costs a dictionary lookup per call
sys.intern speeds up comparing many repeated stringsInterned strings may stay in memory longer than needed

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Which integers are cached in CPython?-5 to 256 inclusive
What is string interning?Keeping a single shared copy of equal strings so they can be compared by identity and take less memory
How do you intern a string manually?sys.intern(s)
Why is x is 1000 unreliable?Whether two equal numbers are the same object depends on caching and compilation, not on the language rules
Why is it safe to share cached objects?They are immutable, so no one can modify them

Advantages

Advantages: lower memory, faster equality and dict lookup (identity shortcut), and fewer allocations for small ints and singletons.
codeExamples:
import timeit
n1 = "a" * 50; n2 = "a" * 50
same = n1
print(timeit.timeit(lambda: same == n1, number=200_000) >= 0)
# == checks identity first: the same object compares without scanning characters

# OUTPUT:
# True

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: interning behaviour is inconsistent across contexts, so code that uses is on strings or ints works sometimes and fails other times; interned strings may live forever.
codeExamples:
a = "hello_world"
b = "hello_world"
print(a is b)            # True: both literals share one constant here

c = "hello world"
d = "hello world"
print(c == d)            # always compare with ==, never rely on identity

# OUTPUT (typical CPython):
# True
# True

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the cache ranges and rules are implementation details that change between versions (3.12 immortalises many), only immutable types are safe to share, and sys.intern accepts only exact str.
codeExamples:
import sys
try:
    sys.intern(b"bytes")
except TypeError as e:
    print("only str:", e)

print(() is ())               # empty tuple singleton (CPython detail)

# OUTPUT:
# only str: intern() argument must be str, not bytes
# True

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Never use is for numeric or string equality; reserve it for None and sentinel objects. Use sys.intern deliberately for million-row string columns, but prefer categorical encodings (pandas category, enums) for large cardinality-bounded data. Do not depend on cache boundaries when writing portable code.

topics.name: Why Does Python Sometimes Reuse the Same Object?

beginner.content:
Introduction

"Why does Python sometimes reuse the same object?" The honest answer has several parts. CPython shares immutable values that are used everywhere (small integers, None, interned strings), the compiler merges equal constants, some functions return their argument unchanged when copying is pointless (tuple(t), str(s)), and freed memory is recycled for new objects. Java learners will recognise the Integer cache and the String pool. Reuse is a performance optimisation, never a promise.
Figure: sharing is only safe for immutable values

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: The same-looking code gives True for one pair of values and False for another, which makes is seem random and unreliable.

Why we need it:
  • Give a complete interview answer instead of "small integers are cached".
  • Know which objects are safe to share (immutable) and which never are (mutable).
  • Learn why is is for identity (None) and == is for values.
  • Avoid writing code that depends on CPython implementation details.

Complete Example: Reuse and non-reuse side by side (CPython 3.12)

Every value is created at run time so the results do not come from compile-time constants. Results are CPython-specific.
codeExamples:
def make_int(text):
    return int(text)


def report(label, value):
    print(label, "->", value)


def main():
    small = make_int("100")
    report("small int cached", small is make_int("100"))

    big = make_int("1000")
    report("big int cached", big is make_int("1000"))

    numbers = tuple([1, 2, 3])
    report("tuple(t) is t", tuple(numbers) is numbers)

    text = "".join(["a", "b", "c"])
    report("str(s) is s", str(text) is text)

    items = [1, 2, 3]
    report("list(l) is l", list(items) is items)
    report("list(l) == l", list(items) == items)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT:
# small int cached -> True
# big int cached -> False
# tuple(t) is t -> True
# str(s) is s -> True
# list(l) is l -> False
# list(l) == l -> True
codeExplanations: 100 lies in the small-integer cache, 1000 does not. Passing an exact tuple or str to tuple() or str() returns the very same object because copying an immutable value is pointless, but list() must copy since lists are mutable. Every pair is equal in value; only identity differs. The takeaway: use == for values and is only for None.

beginner.content:
The Interview Question

"Why does Python sometimes reuse the same object?"
This is a classic expert-level question because the honest answer has several parts. Python reuses objects for performance and memory reasons, but only in specific situations and only where it is safe. A complete answer names the situations, explains why it is safe, and warns that you must not depend on it.

The Surprise

The same-looking code can behave differently depending on the type and on how the values were created:
codeExamples:
a = int("100")
b = int("100")
print(a is b)             # True: 100 is in the small-integer cache

x = int("1000")
y = int("1000")
print(x is y)             # False: created separately

s1 = "hello"
s2 = "hello"
print(s1 is s2)           # True: identifier-like constant, interned

l1 = [1, 2]
l2 = [1, 2]
print(l1 is l2)           # False: mutable objects are never shared

# OUTPUT:
# True
# False
# True
# False

beginner.content:
The Short Answer

  1. Immutable values are safe to share, so CPython caches the common ones: small integers (-5 to 256), None/True/False, the empty tuple, single characters.
  2. Strings are interned: identifier-like strings in source code (and names) are stored once.
  3. The compiler merges equal constants within the same code object.
  4. Freed memory is recycled, so a new object can receive the same address (id) as an old, dead one.
  5. Some functions return the argument itself when copying would be pointless (tuple(t), str(s)).
Mutable objects (lists, dicts, sets) are never shared automatically, because modifying one would change every user.

expert.content:
Reason 1: Immutable Singletons and Caches

Covered in detail in the previous topic: the small-int cache, the singleton constants and interned strings. In Python 3.12+ these are also immortal, so even their reference counts never change.

Reason 2: The Same Address Is Reused After an Object Dies

id() returns an address, and an address is only unique among objects alive at the same time. Once an object is freed its memory can be handed to the next object of that size - often immediately. This produces the confusing result below: two different lists seem to have the same identity.
codeExamples:
# The first list is freed as soon as id() returns, before the second one is made.
print(id([1, 2]) == id([3, 4]))

# Keep both alive at once and the identities must differ.
first = [1, 2]
second = [3, 4]
print(id(first) == id(second))

# OUTPUT (CPython; the first line is typically True but is not guaranteed):
# True
# False
codeExplanations: In the first line the temporary list [1, 2] is destroyed right after id() is evaluated, so its memory (via a free list) is the natural place for [3, 4]. In the second case both lists exist together and cannot share an address. Moral: never compare id() values of objects that are not both alive.

expert.content:
Reason 3: Copy Operations That Return the Original

For immutable objects a "copy" would be indistinguishable from the original, so CPython returns the original and saves the allocation. Mutable objects always get a real copy.
codeExamples:
t = (1, 2, 3)
print(tuple(t) is t)       # immutable: no copy needed
print(t[:] is t)           # full slice of a tuple returns the same tuple

s = "abc"
print(str(s) is s)

l = [1, 2, 3]
print(list(l) is l)        # mutable: a real copy is required
print(l[:] is l)

# OUTPUT:
# True
# True
# True
# False
# False

expert.content:
Reason 4: Constant Folding and Merging

The compiler evaluates constant expressions ahead of time and stores each distinct constant once per code object. You can see them in co_consts.
codeExamples:
def f():
    a = 1000
    b = 1000          # same constant, stored once
    c = 2 * 500       # folded at compile time into 1000
    return a is b, a is c

print(f())
print(f.__code__.co_consts)

# OUTPUT (CPython 3.12; the constants tuple differs a little between versions):
# (True, True)
# (None, 1000)

expert.content:
How to Write Correct Code Regardless

DoDon't
Compare values with ==Use is on numbers, strings or tuples
Use is None / is not NoneWrite == None
Treat id() as meaningful only while the object livesStore ids to "remember" objects (use weak references or the objects)
Copy mutable objects explicitly (list(x), copy.deepcopy)Assume assignment copies
Assume nothing about cachingDepend on -5..256 or on interning in program logic
Different implementations make different choices: PyPy compares small ints by value and has no -5..256 rule at all, so code that relies on CPython's caching is not portable.

A Model Interview Answer

"Python reuses objects when it is both safe and cheap. Immutable values such as small integers, None, True/False, the empty tuple and identifier-like strings are cached or interned in CPython, so all uses share one object. The compiler also merges equal constants within a code object, and operations like tuple(t) return the original because a copy would be identical. Separately, CPython recycles memory, so a new object can get the address of a freed one, which makes id() look equal for unrelated objects. None of this is guaranteed by the language, so I compare values with == and use is only for singletons like None."

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Less memory used for common immutable valuesReuse rules vary by type, version and implementation
Fewer allocations make programs fasterTempts developers to misuse is for equality
Identity test is None is cheap and reliableResults differ between a script, the REPL and PyPy
Immutability makes sharing safe in every threadRecycled addresses make id() comparisons confusing

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why do two equal small ints share an object?CPython pre-creates -5..256 and reuses them; safe because ints are immutable
Why can id([1]) == id([2]) be True?The first list is freed before the second is created, so the address is reused
Why does tuple(t) is t hold but list(l) is l not?Immutable objects need no copy; mutable ones must be duplicated
Is this behaviour part of the Python language?No, it is a CPython implementation detail that may differ or change
When is is the right operator?For singletons (None, True, False) and genuine identity tests

beginner.content:
Introduction

"Python" is a language; CPython is the C program that actually runs it - the python you download from python.org. It first compiles your source to bytecode, then a virtual machine (the PVM) interprets that bytecode instruction by instruction. This is the same two-step idea as Java, where javac produces .class bytecode and the JVM runs it - except CPython performs the compile step automatically on every run.
Figure: CPython pipeline: javac-like front end, JVM-like evaluation loop

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: Without knowing what the interpreter does, behaviour such as "syntax errors appear before any output", "imports create __pycache__" or "Python is slow in tight loops" looks like random magic.

Why we need it:
  • Understand that Python is compiled to bytecode and then interpreted, not "just interpreted".
  • Know which parts are the language and which are CPython implementation details (bytecode, GIL, reference counting).
  • Reason about performance, start-up time and error timing from the pipeline stages.
  • Map familiar Java ideas (javac, bytecode, JVM) onto their Python counterparts.

Complete Example: Walking one line through the CPython pipeline

The standard library exposes each stage. This program takes one statement from source text to a running result.
codeExplanations: tokenize splits the text into names, numbers and operators (we filter out NEWLINE and ENDMARKER tokens). ast.parse builds the tree whose first statement is an Assign node. compile() turns the tree into a code object, and exec() hands it to the evaluation loop, which creates the name total in the namespace dictionary.

beginner.content:
Python the Language vs Python the Program

"Python" is a language specification. To run Python code you need an implementation - a program that reads your code and executes it. The reference implementation, and the one you almost certainly use, is CPython: written in C, maintained by the Python core developers, and what you download from python.org. When you type python app.py, the python executable is the CPython interpreter.

Is Python Interpreted or Compiled?

Both. CPython first compiles your source code into a compact, low-level form called bytecode, then a virtual machine (the Python Virtual Machine, PVM) interprets that bytecode one instruction at a time. 
source code (.py)
      |  tokenizer + parser
      v
syntax tree (AST)
      |  compiler
      v
bytecode (code objects)    <-- cached in __pycache__/*.pyc
      |  evaluation loop (the PVM)
      v
program runs
Java follows a similar plan: javac produces .class bytecode, and the JVM runs it. The difference is that Python does the compile step automatically and invisibly every time you run or import code, and CPython has no JIT compiler in normal builds.
Which Python Am I Running?
codeExamples:
import platform
import sys

print(platform.python_implementation())
print(sys.implementation.name)
print(sys.version_info >= (3, 8))
print(sys.executable.endswith(("python", "python.exe", "python3")))

# OUTPUT (on CPython):
# CPython
# cpython
# True
# True
codeExplanations: platform.python_implementation() and sys.implementation.name tell you which implementation is running. sys.version_info is a tuple that can be compared with another tuple to test for a minimum version. sys.executable is the path of the interpreter program itself.

beginner.content:
Other Implementations

ImplementationWritten in / runs onNotable for
CPythonCThe reference; best library compatibility
PyPyRPython (Python subset)A JIT compiler; often several times faster on pure-Python code
JythonJava / JVMUse Java classes from Python (lags behind current Python versions)
IronPython.NETIntegration with .NET libraries
MicroPythonCTiny; runs on microcontrollers
GraalPyGraalVMPython on the JVM with GraalVM's JIT
Behaviour that is not part of the language rules (object identity quirks, memory management) can differ between them.

Introduction

CPython is the reference implementation of Python, written in C. The word "Python" usually means CPython: it compiles your source to bytecode and executes it on a stack-based virtual machine (the eval loop).
codeExamples:
import sys, platform

print(platform.python_implementation())      # which implementation runs this
print(sys.implementation.name)               # 'cpython'
print(sys.version_info[:2])

# OUTPUT (example):
# CPython
# cpython
# (3, 12)

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

The language is a specification; you need an implementation to run it. Knowing the interpreter explains performance (GIL, bytecode loop), memory model (refcounting) and why some behaviour is "CPython detail".
codeExamples:
# Same code, different engines: CPython, PyPy (JIT), Jython (JVM), MicroPython (embedded)
import sys
impl = sys.implementation.name
print("running on", impl)
print("has refcounts:", hasattr(sys, "getrefcount"))

# OUTPUT (CPython):
# running on cpython
# has refcounts: True

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Servers and CI run CPython; data-heavy code relies on its C API (NumPy, pandas); PyPy speeds long-running pure-Python loops; MicroPython targets microcontrollers; Cython and mypyc compile Python-like code to C extensions.
codeExamples:
import sys, sysconfig

print("C compiler used to build:", "GCC" in sys.version or "MSC" in sys.version
      or "Clang" in sys.version)
print("GIL build:", sysconfig.get_config_var("Py_GIL_DISABLED") in (None, 0))

# OUTPUT (typical):
# C compiler used to build: True
# GIL build: True

beginner.content:
Diagram

   source.py ─► Tokenizer ─► Parser ─► AST ─► Compiler ─► Bytecode (code object)
                                                                │
                                              ┌─────────────────▼───────────┐
                                              │  Eval loop (virtual machine) │
                                              │  stack, frames, refcounting  │
                                              └─────────────────┬───────────┘
                                                                ▼
                                                  C runtime / OS calls

expert.content:
What Is Inside the CPython Source

Knowing the layout of the source repository makes the rest of this module concrete:
Directory / fileContents
Parser/Tokenizer and the PEG parser (since 3.9; the grammar is in Grammar/python.gram)
Python/compile.c, symtable.cSymbol-table analysis and bytecode generation
Python/bytecodes.c, ceval.cThe bytecode definitions and the evaluation loop
Objects/Built-in types: listobject.c, dictobject.c, longobject.c...
Modules/, Lib/C-accelerated modules and the pure-Python standard library
Include/The C API used by extension modules (NumPy, etc.)

Everything Is a PyObject

At the C level every Python value begins with the same header: a reference count and a pointer to its type (PyObject). A type object contains function pointers for behaviour (tp_repr, tp_hash, tp_call...). That uniform layout is what lets the evaluation loop treat an integer, a list and a function identically, and what dunder methods like __add__ plug into.
codeExamples:
import sys

x = 42
print(type(x), type(type(x)))        # a type is also an object
print(sys.getsizeof(x))              # header + the integer's digits
print(isinstance(int, object))       # even classes are PyObjects

# OUTPUT (64-bit CPython 3.12):
# <class 'int'> <class 'type'>
# 28
# True

expert.content:
The Evaluation Loop and Modern Speed-ups

ceval.c contains a big loop that fetches the next bytecode instruction and runs the matching C code, using a stack for operands (the PVM is a stack machine). Recent releases made it much faster:
  • 3.11 - the specializing adaptive interpreter (PEP 659): hot instructions rewrite themselves for the types they actually see (for example BINARY_OP becomes BINARY_OP_ADD_INT), and cheaper "zero-cost" exception handling. Often 10-60% faster.
  • 3.12: immortal objects (PEP 683), per-interpreter GIL groundwork, inlined comprehensions (PEP 709).
  • 3.13: an experimental JIT (copy-and-patch, off by default) and an experimental free-threaded build without the GIL (PEP 703).
  • Later releases continue this direction; check the "What's New" page of your version.

Useful Interpreter Flags

Flag / variableEffect
python -m dis file.pyDisassemble a script's bytecode
python -X importtime -c "import json"Print the time each import took (startup profiling)
python -X devDevelopment mode: extra runtime checks and warnings
python -O / -OORemove assert statements (and docstrings with -OO)
python -B or PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1Do not write .pyc files
python -IIsolated mode: ignore environment variables and the user site-packages
python -c "code" / -m moduleRun a one-liner / a module as a script

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Reference implementation: every library and tutorial targets itNo JIT in standard builds: slower than the JVM on hot loops
Compile step is automatic - no separate build toolGlobal Interpreter Lock limits CPU-bound threads (changing in free-threaded builds)
Simple C core: easy to embed and extend with C modulesBytecode is an implementation detail and changes between versions
Bytecode is portable across operating systemsCompile cost is paid on every run unless .pyc caching applies

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is CPython?The reference implementation of Python, written in C
Is Python interpreted or compiled?Both: source is compiled to bytecode, which the virtual machine interprets
What is the PVM?The Python Virtual Machine - the stack-based evaluation loop that executes bytecode
CPython vs PyPy?PyPy is another implementation with a JIT, usually faster for pure-Python code but less compatible with C extensions
What is the specializing adaptive interpreter?A 3.11+ optimisation where bytecode instructions specialise themselves to the observed operand types

Advantages

Advantages: most compatible implementation, all C extensions work, best ecosystem and tooling, and a clear, readable C code base.
codeExamples:
import math
print(type(math.sqrt))        # built-in function implemented in C
print(math.sqrt.__module__)

# OUTPUT:
# <class 'builtin_function_or_method'>
# math

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: no JIT by default (an experimental one arrived in 3.13), interpretation overhead per bytecode, and the GIL limits multi-threaded CPU work.
codeExamples:
import time
t = time.perf_counter()
total = 0
for i in range(3_000_000):
    total += i                # every iteration runs several bytecodes
print(total, "in", round(time.perf_counter() - t, 2), "s (about 0.1-0.3 s)")

# OUTPUT (varies):
# 4499998500000 in 0.15 s (about 0.1-0.3 s)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: behaviour like refcount timing, int caching and dict ordering of internals is implementation-specific; portability to PyPy/others is not guaranteed for C-extension heavy code.
codeExamples:
import sys
# Code that assumes CPython internals breaks elsewhere:
if hasattr(sys, "_getframe"):
    print("frame access available (CPython/PyPy), but not guaranteed by the spec")

# OUTPUT:
# frame access available (CPython/PyPy), but not guaranteed by the spec

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Pick the runtime to match the workload: CPython for compatibility, PyPy for long-running pure-Python CPU work, free-threaded 3.13+ builds for threaded CPU scaling once your dependencies support it. Do not write code that depends on CPython internals unless it is isolated behind an interface.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Before running anything, CPython compiles the whole source in stages: tokenizing, parsing into an AST, symbol-table analysis and code generation. The result is a code object holding bytecode. The built-in compile() performs these stages for you. In Java, javac does the same job ahead of time and writes a .class file; Python does it in memory at run or import time.
Figure: compile() runs all stages; syntax errors stop it before anything executes

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: If you think Python runs each line as it reads it, you cannot explain why a syntax error at the bottom of a file stops the program before the first print, or why a NameError only appears when the bad line runs.

Why we need it:
  • Separate compile-time problems (syntax errors) from run-time problems (NameError, TypeError).
  • Use compile(), exec() and eval() to build tools such as REPLs, calculators and plug-in loaders.
  • Understand compile-time optimisations such as constant folding.
  • Know where a code object comes from before studying bytecode and frames.

Complete Example: Compile time versus run time

This program compiles good and broken source, shows that nothing runs at compile time, and proves a NameError only appears at run time.
codeExplanations: The broken source has a valid print() first, yet compile() rejects the whole text, so nothing executes. A reference to an undefined name is perfectly valid syntax, so it compiles and fails only when eval() runs it. The compiler also folds 2 * 3 into the constant 6 before the program runs.

beginner.content:
Python Compiles Before It Runs

Before a single line of your program executes, CPython reads the whole file and compiles it to bytecode. This is why a syntax error anywhere in a file stops the program immediately - even in code that would never have been reached - while a runtime error (like a NameError) only shows up when that line actually runs.
codeExamples:
print("this never prints")

if False:
    x = (1 +      # incomplete expression, in code that would never run

# OUTPUT:
#   File "app.py", line 4
#     x = (1 +
#         ^
# SyntaxError: '(' was never closed
#
# The first print() did NOT run: the whole file failed to compile.

beginner.content:
The Stages

  1. Tokenizing - split the text into tokens: names, numbers, operators, keywords, indentation.
  2. Parsing - check the tokens follow the grammar and build an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST). Since Python 3.9 this uses a PEG parser.
  3. Symbol-table analysis - decide for each name whether it is local, global or a closure variable.
  4. Code generation - walk the AST and emit bytecode, plus optimisations (constant folding, removing dead code).
  5. The result is a code object that the interpreter can execute.

Doing It Yourself With compile()

The built-in compile(source, filename, mode) runs the stages and returns a code object. You can then run it with exec() (statements) or eval() (an expression). The mode is "exec", "eval" or "single".
codeExamples:
code = compile("x = 1 + 2", "<string>", "exec")

print(type(code).__name__)
print(3 in code.co_consts)       # 1 + 2 was folded into 3 at compile time

namespace = {}
exec(code, namespace)            # run the statements
print(namespace["x"])

expr = compile("6 * 7", "<string>", "eval")
print(eval(expr))

# OUTPUT:
# code
# True
# 3
# 42
codeExplanations: The compiler does not emit an addition for 1 + 2; it computes the constant 3 once, so the running program does no arithmetic at all. exec() runs the compiled statements inside the dictionary we passed, which is how the variable x ends up there. eval() compiles in "eval" mode and returns the expression's value.

beginner.content: Syntax Errors Come From the Compiler
codeExamples:
try:
    compile("x = ", "<string>", "exec")
except SyntaxError as error:
    print(type(error).__name__)
    print(error.msg)

# OUTPUT:
# SyntaxError
# invalid syntax

beginner.content:
Introduction

Before running, CPython compiles source code into bytecode: a compact instruction list for its virtual machine. The built-in compile() exposes this step and returns a code object.
codeExamples:
code = compile("x = 2 + 3\nprint(x)", "<demo>", "exec")
print(type(code).__name__)
exec(code)                      # run the compiled code

# OUTPUT:
# code
# 5

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Interpreting text line by line would be slow. Compiling once into bytecode lets the VM run simple, fast instructions and allows optimisations such as constant folding to happen up front.
codeExamples:
import dis
src = "y = 60 * 60 * 24"
dis.dis(compile(src, "<s>", "exec"))     # the multiplication is gone: folded

# OUTPUT (3.12, abridged):
#   1   RESUME        0
#       LOAD_CONST    0 (86400)
#       STORE_NAME    0 (y)
#       RETURN_CONST  1 (None)

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Compilation happens at import time and for exec/eval. Frameworks compile templates and expressions; syntax errors surface here, before any line of the module runs.

Diagram

   "x = 1 + 2"
        │ tokenize
        ▼
   NAME  =  NUMBER  +  NUMBER
        │ parse
        ▼
      AST ─► symbol table ─► optimise (fold 1+2 -> 3)
        │ codegen
        ▼
   Bytecode:  LOAD_CONST 3 ; STORE_NAME x

expert.content:
Seeing the Tokens

The tokenize module exposes the first stage. Every token has a type, the text, and its position - the raw material for syntax highlighters and code formatters.
codeExamples:
import io
import tokenize

source = "x = 1 + 2"
tokens = tokenize.generate_tokens(io.StringIO(source).readline)

for token in tokens:
    print(tokenize.tok_name[token.type], repr(token.string))

# OUTPUT (Python 3.12):
# NAME 'x'
# OP '='
# NUMBER '1'
# OP '+'
# NUMBER '2'
# NEWLINE ''
# ENDMARKER ''

expert.content:
Definition Time vs Execution Time

Compiling a function does not run it, and does not even create the function. The compiler turns the body into a nested code object stored as a constant of the enclosing code. The def statement, executed later at run time, builds the function object from that code object.
codeExamples:
source = "def f():\n    return 1\n"

code = compile(source, "<string>", "exec")      # compiles; defines nothing
namespace = {}
print("f" in namespace)

exec(code, namespace)                           # the def statement runs now
print("f" in namespace)
print(namespace["f"]())

# OUTPUT:
# False
# True
# 1

expert.content:
Compile-Time Optimisations

CPython's compiler performs only safe, simple optimisations:
  • Constant folding: 60 * 60 * 24 becomes 86400; "ab" + "cd" becomes "abcd".
  • Dead-code removal: the body of if False: or while 0: is dropped.
  • Constant containers: x in [1, 2, 3] is compiled to test against a constant tuple (or frozenset).
  • -O flag: removes assert statements and code guarded by if __debug__:. -OO also strips docstrings.
Don't count on any more than this: Python is dynamic, so the compiler cannot assume that len is the built-in or that a + b is addition.
codeExamples:
def seconds_per_day():
    return 60 * 60 * 24

print(seconds_per_day.__code__.co_consts)

def unreachable():
    if False:
        return "never"
    return "always"

print("never" in unreachable.__code__.co_consts)

# OUTPUT (CPython 3.12):
# (None, 86400)
# False

expert.content:
compile() Flags and Producing an AST Instead

compile() can stop after parsing and give you the AST (ast.PyCF_ONLY_AST), accept an AST object as input, or turn on __future__ features. Tools like pytest use this to rewrite the AST of your test modules (that is how a plain assert can report detailed values).
codeExamples:
import ast

tree = compile("a + b", "<string>", "eval", flags=ast.PyCF_ONLY_AST)
print(type(tree).__name__)

code = compile(tree, "<ast>", "eval")        # AST -> code object
print(eval(code, {"a": 2, "b": 3}))

# OUTPUT:
# Expression
# 5

expert.content:
Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Syntax errors are caught for the whole file before it runsName and type errors are still found only at run time
Optimisations like constant folding come for freeCompilation cost is repeated for every uncached run
compile() lets programs build and run code dynamicallyexec()/eval() on untrusted text is a serious security risk
Same code object can be run many times without re-parsingFewer compile-time guarantees than javac's static type checking

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
When does Python compile your code?Every time a module is run or imported (unless a valid cached .pyc exists), before any of it executes
Why does a syntax error stop the whole program?The entire file is compiled first; a parse failure prevents any code from running
What are the compilation stages?Tokenize, parse to AST, symbol-table analysis, generate and optimise bytecode into a code object
What does compile() return?A code object that can be run with exec or eval
What does the -O flag do?Strips assert statements and __debug__ blocks

Advantages

Advantages: faster than re-parsing, early syntax checks, compile modes (exec, eval, single), and flags such as optimize levels.
codeExamples:
print(eval(compile("3 * 7", "<e>", "eval")))        # expression mode
code = compile("a = 1", "<x>", "exec", optimize=0)
ns = {}
exec(code, ns)
print(ns["a"])

# OUTPUT:
# 21
# 1

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: compile time adds startup cost for large modules, bytecode is version specific, and dynamic exec of strings is a security and debugging risk.
codeExamples:
import time
src = "\n".join(f"v{i} = {i} * 2" for i in range(20000))
t = time.perf_counter()
compile(src, "<big>", "exec")
print("compile of 20k lines took ms:", round((time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000) > 0)

# OUTPUT (varies):
# compile of 20k lines took ms: True

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the compiler only understands syntax, not types (type errors appear at runtime), and compiled code objects are tied to the interpreter version that made them.
codeExamples:
import sys
code = compile("1 + 1", "<v>", "eval")
print(sys.version_info[:2], "magic number is tied to this version")
print(sys.implementation.cache_tag)     # e.g. cpython-312

# OUTPUT (example):
# (3, 12) magic number is tied to this version
# cpython-312

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Compilation costs are paid once per module per interpreter version, so ship pre-compiled .pyc (compileall) in containers to speed cold starts. Avoid eval/exec of untrusted strings; if you must, use ast.literal_eval or a restricted DSL.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A .pyc file is the compiled bytecode of a module, stored in a __pycache__ folder so the next import can skip compilation. Its name carries the interpreter version, for example mod.cpython-312.pyc. The file starts with a 16-byte header (magic number, flags, timestamp or hash, source size) followed by a marshal-serialised code object. It is similar in spirit to a Java .class file, but it is a disposable cache, not a deliverable.
Figure: layout of a .pyc file (Python 3.7+): 16-byte header, then the code object

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: Without a cache, every import would re-tokenize, re-parse and re-compile the source, making start-up of large programs noticeably slower - and you would not understand the mysterious __pycache__ folders.

Why we need it:
  • Speed up start-up by reusing compiled bytecode when the source is unchanged.
  • Keep caches for several Python versions side by side via the cache tag.
  • Decide what to commit (never __pycache__) and what is safe to delete.
  • Understand how Python detects stale caches (timestamp or hash in the header).

Complete Example: Create a .pyc, read its header, run it

The program compiles a tiny module in a temporary folder, inspects the resulting .pyc file and executes the cached code object.
codeExamples:
import importlib.util
import marshal
import os
import py_compile
import tempfile

HEADER_SIZE = 16                      # magic + flags + mtime/hash + size (3.7+)
SOURCE = "GREETING = 'hello from cache'\n"


def build_pyc(folder):
    source_path = os.path.join(folder, "mod.py")
    with open(source_path, "w") as handle:
        handle.write(SOURCE)
    return py_compile.compile(source_path)


def read_bytes(path):
    with open(path, "rb") as handle:
        return handle.read()


def main():
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
        pyc_path = build_pyc(folder)
        print(os.path.basename(os.path.dirname(pyc_path)))
        print(pyc_path.endswith(".pyc"))

        data = read_bytes(pyc_path)
        print(data[:4] == importlib.util.MAGIC_NUMBER)

        code = marshal.loads(data[HEADER_SIZE:])
        print(code.co_name)

        namespace = {}
        exec(code, namespace)
        print(namespace["GREETING"])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT:
# __pycache__
# True
# True
# <module>
# hello from cache
codeExplanations: py_compile writes the .pyc into a __pycache__ folder beside the source. The first four bytes equal importlib.util.MAGIC_NUMBER, which changes with the Python version. Skipping the 16-byte header, marshal.loads rebuilds the module's code object (named <module>), and exec() runs it without ever reading the source again.

beginner.content:
What is the __pycache__ Folder?

After you import a module, a folder named __pycache__ appears beside it, holding files like helpers.cpython-312.pyc. A .pyc file is the compiled bytecode of that module, saved so Python can skip the compile step next time. It is a cache: delete it and Python simply regenerates it. 
myproject/
  main.py                      <- the script you run: NOT cached
  helpers.py
  __pycache__/
    helpers.cpython-312.pyc    <- bytecode of helpers.py for CPython 3.12
The file name shows the Python version (cpython-312 = CPython 3.12), so different versions keep separate caches side by side.

Faster Start-Up, Not Faster Code

A .pyc saves only the compilation time when a module is loaded. Once loaded, the code runs exactly as fast as it would without the cache. That is why the script you run directly (main.py) is not cached: it is loaded only once, so caching it would not help.
Finding the Cache Path
codeExamples:
import importlib.util
import sys

print(sys.implementation.cache_tag)
path = importlib.util.cache_from_source("helpers.py")
print(path.replace("\\", "/"))

# OUTPUT (CPython 3.12):
# cpython-312
# __pycache__/helpers.cpython-312.pyc
codeExplanations: cache_from_source() applies the standard naming rule: a __pycache__ folder next to the source, and the interpreter's cache tag inserted before the .pyc extension. The replace() call only makes the Windows backslash path print like the others.

beginner.content:
Should You Commit It?

  • No - add __pycache__/ and *.pyc to .gitignore. They are generated, machine- and version-specific files.
  • It is always safe to delete them.
  • To stop Python writing them (for example in a read-only container) run with python -B or set PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1.

Introduction

When a module is imported, CPython saves its compiled bytecode into a .pyc file inside __pycache__/, named with the interpreter tag, for example mod.cpython-312.pyc. Next time it loads the .pyc instead of recompiling.
codeExamples:
import py_compile, tempfile, os

d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
src = os.path.join(d, "mod.py")
open(src, "w").write("print('hi')\n")
pyc = py_compile.compile(src)             # writes into __pycache__
print(os.path.relpath(pyc, d))

# OUTPUT (3.12):
# __pycache__\mod.cpython-312.pyc

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Parsing and compiling large modules on every start wastes time. Caching bytecode makes repeated imports, scripts, and CLI tools start faster.
codeExamples:
import importlib.util, sys
print(importlib.util.cache_from_source("pkg/util.py"))
print(sys.dont_write_bytecode)             # True if caching is disabled

# OUTPUT (3.12, POSIX paths shown):
# pkg/__pycache__/util.cpython-312.pyc
# False

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

The header stores a magic number, flags and either the source mtime and size or a hash. If the source changes the .pyc is regenerated. Docker images often run python -m compileall at build; the main script itself is never cached.
codeExamples:
import importlib.util, struct, py_compile, tempfile, os

d = tempfile.mkdtemp(); p = os.path.join(d, "m.py")
open(p, "w").write("x = 1\n")
pyc = py_compile.compile(p)
head = open(pyc, "rb").read(16)
magic = head[:4]
print(magic == importlib.util.MAGIC_NUMBER)        # version check
flags = struct.unpack("<I", head[4:8])[0]
print("flags:", flags)                              # 0 = timestamp based

# OUTPUT:
# True
# flags: 0

beginner.content:
Diagram

   import mod
      │
      ├─ __pycache__/mod.cpython-312.pyc exists and is fresh?
      │        yes ─► marshal.load ─► code object ─► execute
      └─ no  ─► compile mod.py ─► write .pyc ─► execute
   .pyc layout:  [magic 4B][flags 4B][mtime 4B][size 4B][marshalled code]

expert.content:
Anatomy of a .pyc File

Since Python 3.7 a .pyc has a 16-byte header followed by a marshalled code object (the compiled module, serialized with the marshal module):
BytesMeaning
0-3Magic number - identifies the bytecode version; changes in every minor Python release
4-7Flags - say whether validation uses timestamp or hash (PEP 552)
8-15Source file modification time + size, or a hash of the source
16 onwardThe marshalled code object
codeExamples:
import importlib.util
import marshal
import os
import py_compile
import tempfile

folder = tempfile.mkdtemp()
source = os.path.join(folder, "hello.py")
with open(source, "w") as f:
    f.write("print('hello from a .pyc')\n")

pyc_path = py_compile.compile(source, cfile=os.path.join(folder, "hello.pyc"))
