with open(pyc_path, "rb") as f:
    header = f.read(16)
    code = marshal.load(f)

print(header[:4] == importlib.util.MAGIC_NUMBER)
print(len(header))
exec(code)

# OUTPUT:
# True
# 16
# hello from a .pyc

expert.content:
How Python Decides the Cache Is Stale

On every import Python compares the header with the source file:
  • Timestamp-based (default): the recorded modification time and size must match the .py file. Edit the file and the cache is ignored and rewritten.
  • Hash-based (PEP 552): the header holds a hash of the source. Checked hash pycs re-hash the source on import; unchecked hash pycs are trusted without checking, which gives reproducible builds (identical output for identical input) - useful for packaging and deployment.
  • If the magic number differs (a different Python version) the file is ignored.
codeExamples:
import py_compile

py_compile.compile(
    "helpers.py",
    invalidation_mode=py_compile.PycInvalidationMode.CHECKED_HASH,
)

# Or pre-compile a whole tree (what installers like pip do):
#   python -m compileall src/
#   python -m compileall --invalidation-mode checked-hash src/

expert.content:
Controlling Where Bytecode Is Written

SettingEffect
python -B, PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1, sys.dont_write_bytecodeDon't write .pyc files
PYTHONPYCACHEPREFIX=/tmp/pycache (3.8+)Write all caches under one separate directory tree instead of beside the sources
python -m compileallPre-compile everything now (faster first start-up in containers)
module.__cached__The path of the .pyc a loaded module used
In Docker, a common pattern is PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 for development images (no clutter in mounted volumes) and an explicit compileall step in production images (no compile work on cold start).

Myths and Pitfalls

  • A .pyc is not "protected" code. Bytecode is easily disassembled (dis) and often decompiled back to near-original source. Shipping only .pyc files is obscurity, not security.
  • Bytecode is not portable between versions. A 3.11 .pyc will not run on 3.12 (different magic number and instruction set). It is portable across operating systems for the same version.
  • Stale caches after clock problems: timestamp validation can be fooled if files are restored with misleading mtimes; hash-based pycs avoid this.
  • Read-only installs: if Python cannot write the cache it silently runs without it - correct but slower to start.
  • Source-less distribution: a .pyc placed directly next to (not inside) the missing .py can still be imported; zipapp bundles also use this machinery.

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Faster start-up: the compile step is skipped on later importsDoes not make running code faster, only loading it
Versioned file names let several Pythons share one source treeNot portable between Python versions
Automatic: stale caches are detected and regeneratedClutters the folder tree and must be git-ignored
Safe to delete at any timeShipping only .pyc files is weak protection for source code

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a .pyc file?Cached compiled bytecode of a module, stored in __pycache__
Does it make the program run faster?No - only the loading of imported modules (it skips recompiling)
Why isn't the main script cached?It is loaded once, so caching would give no benefit
How does Python know a .pyc is outdated?By the source's modification time and size stored in the header, or by a source hash for hash-based pycs; the magic number must also match the version
Is it safe to delete __pycache__?Yes - it is regenerated on the next import

Advantages

Advantages: faster imports, automatic invalidation, read-only deployments can ship pre-built .pyc, and unchecked hash-based .pyc give reproducible builds.
codeExamples:
import py_compile, tempfile, os
p = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "r.py")
open(p, "w").write("v = 7\n")
out = py_compile.compile(p, invalidation_mode=py_compile.PycInvalidationMode.CHECKED_HASH)
print(os.path.exists(out))                         # hash-based, reproducible

# OUTPUT:
# True

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: stale or orphaned files clutter repositories (add __pycache__/ to .gitignore), read-only file systems cannot write them, and they speed up loading only, not execution.
codeExamples:
import time
# .pyc does NOT make the loop faster, only module loading:
t = time.perf_counter()
sum(i for i in range(1_000_000))
print("runtime speed unchanged by pyc:", time.perf_counter() - t > 0)

# OUTPUT:
# runtime speed unchanged by pyc: True

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the format is not portable across Python versions, it is not a secure or obfuscated form (bytecode decompiles easily), and the top-level script is always recompiled.
codeExamples:
import marshal, py_compile, tempfile, os
p = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "s.py")
open(p, "w").write("secret = 'password123'\n")
pyc = py_compile.compile(p)
code = marshal.loads(open(pyc, "rb").read()[16:])    # skip the 16-byte header
print(code.co_consts)       # strings are visible: pyc is not protection

# OUTPUT:
# ('password123', None)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Pre-compile in the build stage (compileall, optionally with unchecked-hash for immutable images) and set PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 plus a read-only file system at runtime. Never treat .pyc as a way to protect secrets or IP; use compiled extensions or server-side logic instead.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Bytecode is the list of tiny instructions the Python Virtual Machine executes. It is stack based: instructions push values onto an operand stack and others pop them to compute. The dis module disassembles it, much like javap -c does for a Java .class file. Bytecode is a CPython implementation detail: opcodes are renamed, added and merged between versions.
Figure: a + b on the stack machine (3.13 may fuse the two loads into one instruction)

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: Without looking at bytecode, performance questions ("is this faster than that?") are guesses, and you cannot see what the interpreter really does for a simple expression like a + b.

Why we need it:
  • See exactly which instructions a function compiles to and how the operand stack is used.
  • Compare two ways of writing code by looking at what each really does.
  • Debug surprising behaviour (global vs local lookups, default arguments).
  • Learn the Python counterpart of reading javap -c output.

Complete Example: Asking questions of the bytecode

Instead of printing the full disassembly (which differs between versions), the program queries stable facts about it.
codeExamples:
import dis


def add(a, b):
    return a + b


def shout(text):
    return print(text.upper())


def has_op(func, prefix):
    return any(ins.opname.startswith(prefix)
               for ins in dis.get_instructions(func))


def main():
    # Prefixes are used because 3.13 fuses LOAD_FAST pairs
    # and 3.12+ may use RETURN_CONST in other functions.
    print("add loads locals:   ", has_op(add, "LOAD_FAST"))
    print("add uses BINARY_OP: ", has_op(add, "BINARY_OP"))
    print("add returns:        ", has_op(add, "RETURN"))
    print("add uses a global:  ", has_op(add, "LOAD_GLOBAL"))
    print("shout uses a global:", has_op(shout, "LOAD_GLOBAL"))

    effect = dis.stack_effect(dis.opmap["BINARY_OP"], 0)
    print("BINARY_OP stack effect:", effect)
    print("has raw bytes:", len(add.__code__.co_code) > 0)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT (Python 3.11 - 3.13):
# add loads locals:    True
# add uses BINARY_OP:  True
# add returns:         True
# add uses a global:   False
# shout uses a global: True
# BINARY_OP stack effect: -1
# has raw bytes: True
codeExplanations: dis.get_instructions yields one object per instruction, so we can ask whether an opcode family appears. add reads only locals (LOAD_FAST), so it has no LOAD_GLOBAL, while shout looks up the built-in print through a global lookup. BINARY_OP pops two values and pushes one, a net stack change of -1.

beginner.content:
What is Bytecode?

Bytecode is the list of simple instructions the Python Virtual Machine actually executes. Each instruction is tiny: load a variable, add two values, jump, call a function. The VM is stack-based: instructions push values onto an operand stack and other instructions pop them off and compute. The standard dis (disassembler) module prints bytecode in readable form. Note: bytecode is an implementation detail of CPython. Instruction names and numbers change between versions; the examples below are from Python 3.12.
Your First Disassembly
codeExamples:
import dis

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

dis.dis(add)

# OUTPUT (Python 3.12):
#   1           0 RESUME                   0
#
#   2           2 LOAD_FAST                0 (a)
#               4 LOAD_FAST                1 (b)
#               6 BINARY_OP                0 (+)
#              10 RETURN_VALUE
codeExplanations: Reading it as a stack machine: LOAD_FAST a pushes a; LOAD_FAST b pushes b; BINARY_OP (+) pops both, adds them and pushes the result; RETURN_VALUE pops the result and returns it. The numbers at the left are the line numbers and byte offsets. "FAST" means a fast local variable, stored in an array and addressed by index. RESUME is a no-op marker at the start of a function.

beginner.content:
Reading the Columns

ColumnMeaning
First number (e.g. 2)Source line the instruction came from
Second number (e.g. 4)Byte offset of the instruction
LOAD_FASTThe opcode name
1The raw argument (an index into a table)
(b)The argument resolved to something readable
>>Marks a jump target (shown in code with branches and loops)

Instructions as Data

dis.get_instructions() returns the instructions as objects, so you can analyse code programmatically.
codeExamples:
import dis

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

for instruction in dis.get_instructions(add):
    print(instruction.opname, repr(instruction.argrepr))

# OUTPUT (Python 3.12):
# RESUME ''
# LOAD_FAST 'a'
# LOAD_FAST 'b'
# BINARY_OP '+'
# RETURN_VALUE ''

beginner.content:
Introduction

Bytecode is the low-level instruction set of the CPython VM. The dis module disassembles functions into readable instructions like LOAD_FAST, BINARY_OP, RETURN_VALUE.
codeExamples:
import dis

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

dis.dis(add)

# OUTPUT (3.12):
#   1           0 RESUME                   0
#   2           2 LOAD_FAST                0 (a)
#               4 LOAD_FAST                1 (b)
#               6 BINARY_OP                0 (+)
#              10 RETURN_VALUE

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Reading bytecode shows what Python really does, explains performance differences between two ways of writing the same thing, and helps debug closures, comprehensions and scoping.
codeExamples:
import dis

def f(): return [i * 2 for i in range(3)]
def g():
    out = []
    for i in range(3): out.append(i * 2)
    return out

def count(fn): return sum(1 for _ in dis.get_instructions(fn))
print("comprehension instructions:", count(f) > 0)
print("loop instructions         :", count(g) > count(f) )

# OUTPUT (3.12):
# comprehension instructions: True
# loop instructions         : True

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Profiling micro-optimisations, understanding the stack machine, security tools that analyse bytecode, debuggers and coverage tools (which hook line events), and learning why a, b = b, a needs no temporary.
codeExamples:
import dis
def swap(a, b):
    a, b = b, a
    return a, b
ops = [i.opname for i in dis.get_instructions(swap)]
print("SWAP" in ops or "ROT_TWO" in ops)     # 3.11+ uses SWAP, older ROT_TWO

# OUTPUT:
# True

beginner.content:
Diagram

   def add(a, b): return a + b

   VM operand stack
   ┌────────┐ LOAD_FAST a    ┌────────┐ LOAD_FAST b    ┌────────┐ BINARY_OP +  ┌────────┐
   │        │ ─────────────► │   a    │ ─────────────► │   b    │ ───────────► │ a + b  │
   └────────┘                └────────┘                │   a    │              └────────┘
                                                       └────────┘  RETURN_VALUE

expert.content:
Branches and Loops

Control flow compiles to jump instructions. Disassembling an if shows how a condition becomes a test followed by a conditional jump.
codeExamples:
import dis

def sign(n):
    if n < 0:
        return "negative"
    return "non-negative"

dis.dis(sign)

# OUTPUT (Python 3.12, simplified: offsets and jump targets are left out):
#   2           RESUME
#
#   3           LOAD_FAST                0 (n)
#               LOAD_CONST               1 (0)
#               COMPARE_OP               2 (<)
#               POP_JUMP_IF_FALSE        (jump over the next line)
#
#   4           RETURN_CONST             2 ('negative')
#
#   5     >>    RETURN_CONST             3 ('non-negative')
codeExplanations: n < 0 is evaluated onto the stack, then POP_JUMP_IF_FALSE jumps over the first return when the condition is false. RETURN_CONST (3.12) returns a constant directly. The exact instruction names and the way jump targets are labelled change with the version - the structure test-then-jump does not.

expert.content:
Why Local Variables Are Faster Than Globals

Bytecode shows why performance advice holds. A local is read with LOAD_FAST, an array index. A global or built-in needs LOAD_GLOBAL, a dictionary lookup (with a cache in modern versions). A hot loop that calls a global function repeatedly can be sped up by binding it to a local first.

Specialization: Bytecode That Rewrites Itself

Since 3.11, after a function has run a few times, generic instructions are replaced by specialised versions tuned to the types seen (BINARY_OP becomes BINARY_OP_ADD_INT, LOAD_ATTR becomes LOAD_ATTR_INSTANCE_VALUE...). The adaptive=True option of dis shows the warmed-up form. Because of this, microbenchmarks measured on cold code can mislead.
codeExamples:
import dis

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

for _ in range(1000):          # warm the function up with ints
    add(1, 2)

dis.dis(add, adaptive=True)    # look for BINARY_OP_ADD_INT in the output

expert.content:
Code You Can Learn From the Disassembly

  • Chained comparison: a < b < c evaluates b only once (it uses a stack COPY).
  • Membership against a literal: x in (1, 2, 3) uses one constant tuple; no list is built on each call.
  • f-strings: compile to direct formatting instructions, which is why they beat % and .format in speed.
  • Comprehensions: before 3.12 each comprehension had its own function (and frame); 3.12 inlines them.
  • try/except: since 3.11 costs nothing when no exception occurs: an exception table replaces setup instructions.
codeExamples:
import dis

def f(x):
    return x in (1, 2, 3)

constants = f.__code__.co_consts
print((1, 2, 3) in constants)

names = [i.opname for i in dis.get_instructions(f)]
print("BUILD_LIST" in names, "BUILD_TUPLE" in names)

# OUTPUT:
# True
# False False

expert.content:
Practical Uses of dis

  • Settling "which is faster?" arguments by seeing what is really executed (then confirm with timeit).
  • Understanding surprising behaviour such as why x += 1 on a global needs a global declaration, or what a decorator really does.
  • Tooling: coverage tools, debuggers and profilers hook into line and instruction events; bytecode-rewriting libraries instrument or optimise code.
  • Never depend on bytecode in production logic. It changes every release; code that inspects opcodes will break.
Command line: python -m dis script.py disassembles a whole file; dis.show_code(func) prints a summary of the code object.

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Shows exactly what the interpreter executesOpcodes change between Python versions
Stack model is tiny and easy to reason aboutReading raw output takes practice
dis is built in - no extra toolsBytecode speed does not map simply to wall-clock time
Useful for settling micro-optimisation arguments with evidenceNot a stable interface to build tools on

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is Python bytecode?The low-level instruction set the PVM executes, produced by compiling source code
What kind of machine executes it?A stack machine: instructions push and pop operands on an evaluation stack
How do you inspect bytecode?dis.dis(function) or python -m dis file.py
LOAD_FAST vs LOAD_GLOBAL?Fast locals are an array index; globals/builtins are dictionary lookups - locals are faster
Is bytecode stable across versions?No - opcodes change in nearly every release; it is a CPython implementation detail

Advantages

Advantages: a tangible view of execution, stable enough for tooling, dis.Bytecode and get_instructions give structured access, and show_caches/adaptive reveal 3.11+ specialisation.
codeExamples:
import dis
def f(x): return x + 1
for ins in dis.get_instructions(f):
    if ins.opname == "BINARY_OP":
        print(ins.opname, ins.argrepr, "at offset", ins.offset)

# OUTPUT (3.12):
# BINARY_OP + at offset 6

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: opcodes change between versions (even minor ones), output is noisy for beginners, and bytecode length is not a reliable measure of speed.
codeExamples:
import dis, io, contextlib
def f(a): return -a
buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buf): dis.dis(f)
print("UNARY_NEGATIVE" in buf.getvalue())     # opcode names/numbers differ by version

# OUTPUT (3.12):
# True

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: dis shows only the generic instructions, not the specialised ones the adaptive interpreter swaps in at runtime (use adaptive=True after warm-up), and nothing about C-level cost of each opcode.
codeExamples:
import dis
def f(x): return x + 1
for _ in range(100): f(1)                      # warm up the adaptive interpreter
dis.dis(f, adaptive=True)                      # shows e.g. BINARY_OP_ADD_INT

# OUTPUT (3.12, abridged):
#   2  RESUME
#      LOAD_FAST   0 (x)
#      LOAD_CONST  1 (1)
#      BINARY_OP_ADD_INT 0 (+)
#      RETURN_VALUE

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use dis for learning, verifying optimisations and writing tooling, but never ship logic that depends on specific opcodes. For performance work measure with timeit and profilers first; bytecode inspection explains results rather than predicting them.

beginner.content:
Introduction

An Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) is the tree that the parser builds from your source, with each node standing for a construct such as an assignment or an addition. The ast module lets Python programs read, analyse and rewrite that tree before it is compiled. Java offers a similar view through the compiler tree API and annotation processors; in Python the tree is a plain, easy-to-use part of the standard library.
Figure: AST of: total = price * qty + tax (the multiplication sits deeper, so it runs first)

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: Analysing code with string searches or regular expressions breaks on comments, strings and formatting, so tools like linters or code generators cannot trust it.

Why we need it:
  • Analyse code structurally: find every function, import or call reliably.
  • Build linters, formatters, checkers and code-generation tools.
  • Transform code safely by editing the tree and recompiling it.
  • Evaluate literals safely with ast.literal_eval() instead of eval().

Complete Example: Read and rewrite code with ast

The program collects variable names with a visitor, then rewrites every addition into a subtraction using a transformer.
codeExplanations: The visitor skips total because it has a Store context and records the names that are only read, in tree order. The transformer replaces each Add operator node with Sub, so 10 + 5 compiles as 10 - 5. literal_eval safely turns a list literal into a real list without running arbitrary code.

beginner.content:
What is an AST?

An Abstract Syntax Tree is a tree that represents the structure of your code. The parser turns text such as x = 1 + 2 * 3 into nested nodes - an assignment whose value is an addition whose right side is a multiplication. "Abstract" means irrelevant details (whitespace, parentheses, comments) are dropped and only meaning remains. The AST is what the compiler consumes to produce bytecode, and the ast module lets your code read and change it.

Parsing and Dumping a Tree

ast.parse() returns the tree; ast.dump(tree, indent=2) prints it in readable form.
codeExamples:
import ast

tree = ast.parse("x = 1 + 2 * 3")
print(ast.dump(tree.body[0], indent=2))

# OUTPUT (Python 3.9+; newer versions may omit empty fields):
# Assign(
#   targets=[
#     Name(id='x', ctx=Store())],
#   value=BinOp(
#     left=Constant(value=1),
#     op=Add(),
#     right=BinOp(
#       left=Constant(value=2),
#       op=Mult(),
#       right=Constant(value=3))))
codeExplanations: The tree shows operator precedence: 2 * 3 is nested deeper than the addition, so it is evaluated first. The target x is a Name node with a Store context (it is being assigned), while names being read have a Load context. tree.body is the list of statements in the module.

beginner.content:
Common Node Types

NodeRepresents
ModuleThe whole file; its body is a list of statements
FunctionDef, ClassDefA def or class statement
Assign, Return, If, ForStatements
Name, Constant, AttributeA variable, a literal value, obj.attr
BinOp, Compare, BoolOpArithmetic, comparisons, and/or
CallA function call

Finding Things With NodeVisitor

Subclass ast.NodeVisitor and define visit_<NodeName> methods. The visitor walks the tree and calls yours for each matching node. Here we list every function call with its line number - the seed of a linter.
codeExamples:
import ast

source = """def greet(name):
    print("Hello", name)

def main():
    greet("Abaji")
    greet("Raoji")
"""

class CallFinder(ast.NodeVisitor):
    def visit_Call(self, node):
        if isinstance(node.func, ast.Name):
            print(node.func.id, "on line", node.lineno)
        self.generic_visit(node)          # keep walking into children

CallFinder().visit(ast.parse(source))

# OUTPUT:
# print on line 2
# greet on line 5
# greet on line 6

beginner.content:
Introduction

An AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) is the tree form of source code that the parser produces. The ast module lets Python code parse, inspect, transform and compile that tree.
codeExamples:
import ast

tree = ast.parse("x = 1 + 2")
print(ast.dump(tree.body[0].value))

# OUTPUT:
# BinOp(left=Constant(value=1), op=Add(), right=Constant(value=2))

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Text is hard to analyse reliably (regex breaks on nested syntax), but a tree is exact. Linters, formatters, type checkers and refactoring tools all work on ASTs.
codeExamples:
import ast

src = "def f(a, b): return a + b\ndef g(): pass\nclass C: pass"
tree = ast.parse(src)
funcs = [n.name for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.FunctionDef)]
print(funcs, [n.name for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.ClassDef)])

# OUTPUT:
# ['f', 'g'] ['C']

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Used by pytest (assert rewriting), flake8/ruff plugins, black, mypy, code generators and safe expression evaluation via ast.literal_eval. NodeVisitor and NodeTransformer implement custom checks and rewrites.
codeExamples:
import ast

class NoPrint(ast.NodeVisitor):                 # a tiny linter
    def visit_Call(self, node):
        if isinstance(node.func, ast.Name) and node.func.id == "print":
            print(f"line {node.lineno}: avoid print()")
        self.generic_visit(node)

NoPrint().visit(ast.parse("x = 1\nprint(x)\nprint('hi')"))

# OUTPUT:
# line 2: avoid print()
# line 3: avoid print()

beginner.content:
Diagram

   "total = price * 2"
              │ ast.parse
              ▼
          Assign
          ├─ targets: Name(total, Store)
          └─ value:   BinOp
                      ├─ left : Name(price, Load)
                      ├─ op   : Mult
                      └─ right: Constant(2)

expert.content:
Changing Code: NodeTransformer

A NodeTransformer can replace nodes. After modifying a tree, call ast.fix_missing_locations (new nodes lack line numbers), then compile and run it. ast.unparse (3.9+) converts a tree back to source.
codeExamples:
import ast

class AddToMul(ast.NodeTransformer):
    def visit_BinOp(self, node):
        self.generic_visit(node)                # transform children first
        if isinstance(node.op, ast.Add):
            node.op = ast.Mult()
        return node

tree = ast.parse("2 + 3", mode="eval")
tree = ast.fix_missing_locations(AddToMul().visit(tree))

print(ast.unparse(tree))
print(eval(compile(tree, "<ast>", "eval")))

# OUTPUT:
# 2 * 3
# 6

expert.content:
ast.literal_eval: Safe Evaluation of Literals

eval() runs any code, so passing it untrusted text is a security hole. ast.literal_eval() parses the text and accepts only Python literals (numbers, strings, lists, dicts, tuples, sets, booleans, None) - never calls or names.
codeExamples:
import ast

print(ast.literal_eval("[1, 2, {'a': (3, 4)}]"))

try:
    ast.literal_eval("__import__('os').getcwd()")
except ValueError:
    print("rejected: not a literal")

# OUTPUT:
# [1, 2, {'a': (3, 4)}]
# rejected: not a literal

expert.content:
Building a Tiny Linter

ast.walk(tree) yields every node, which is enough for simple checks. This one flags print() calls left in code and functions without a docstring - using only the standard library.
codeExamples:
import ast

source = '''def documented():
    """Does something."""
    return 1

def undocumented():
    print("debug")
    return 2
'''

tree = ast.parse(source)

for node in ast.walk(tree):
    if isinstance(node, ast.FunctionDef) and ast.get_docstring(node) is None:
        print(f"line {node.lineno}: function '{node.name}' has no docstring")
    if (isinstance(node, ast.Call) and isinstance(node.func, ast.Name)
            and node.func.id == "print"):
        print(f"line {node.lineno}: print() call left in code")

# OUTPUT:
# line 5: function 'undocumented' has no docstring
# line 6: print() call left in code

expert.content:
Where the AST Is Used in the Real World

  • Linters and checkers: pyflakes (inside flake8), pylint, bandit (security rules) analyse the AST.
  • pytest rewrites the AST of test modules so that a plain assert a == b reports the values of a and b.
  • Code generation and macros: libraries that transform Python (dataclass-like generators, numba-style JITs, DSLs) inspect function ASTs.
  • Formatters and refactoring tools: Black parses code and checks the AST is equivalent after formatting; LibCST keeps comments and whitespace, which the plain AST cannot.
  • Documentation generators read function signatures and docstrings without importing (running) the code - safer for untrusted code.

Limits and Gotchas

  • Comments and formatting are lost. ast.unparse produces valid but re-formatted code. For round-trip editing use LibCST.
  • The tree changes between versions. New syntax adds nodes (Match in 3.10, TypeAlias in 3.12) and some nodes change (Constant replaced Num/Str in 3.8). Test your tool on each supported version.
  • Positions: nodes carry lineno, col_offset, end_lineno, end_col_offset - use them for precise error reporting.
  • Mind the context: forgetting fix_missing_locations after building nodes leads to confusing "missing lineno" compile errors.
  • Parsing is not executing. ast.parse is safe on untrusted code; compile/exec/eval of the result is not.

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Exact structural view of code, immune to formattingNode classes and fields change between Python versions
Visitor and Transformer classes make walking easyComments and exact formatting are lost in the tree
Enables linters, refactoring tools and code generatorsHand-built trees need correct line numbers (fix_missing_locations)
literal_eval gives a safe alternative to evalVerbose compared with a simple text search for small jobs

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is an AST?A tree of nodes representing the structure of the source code, produced by the parser and consumed by the compiler
How do you get one in Python?ast.parse(source); show it with ast.dump(tree, indent=2)
NodeVisitor vs NodeTransformer?A visitor only reads the tree; a transformer returns replacement nodes to modify it
Why prefer ast.literal_eval to eval?It accepts only literals, so untrusted input cannot run code
Name a tool that relies on the AST.flake8/pyflakes, pylint, bandit, Black, and pytest's assertion rewriting

Advantages

Advantages: precise structural understanding, safe literal parsing, ability to rewrite code programmatically, and positions (lineno, col_offset) on nodes.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: node classes change between Python versions (for example Num to Constant), trees are verbose, and ast drops comments and formatting.
codeExamples:
import ast
tree = ast.parse("x = 1  # a comment\n")
print("comment" in ast.dump(tree))           # comments do not exist in the AST

# OUTPUT:
# False

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: parsing validates syntax only (no name resolution or types), unparse output is normalised (ast.unparse), and very deep expressions can hit recursion limits.
codeExamples:
import ast
tree = ast.parse("x   =   (1+2)")
print(ast.unparse(tree))                    # formatting is lost and regenerated

# OUTPUT:
# x = 1 + 2

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Build tooling on ast (or libcst when comments and formatting must survive), not on regular expressions. Pin tests to the Python versions you support because node shapes evolve, and never use eval where ast.literal_eval or a small parser will do.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Every time a code block runs (a module, a function call, a class body), CPython creates a frame: the working record of that execution. It points to the code object, the local variables, the globals and the calling frame (f_back). The chain of frames is the call stack, exactly like JVM stack frames, and it is what a traceback prints. The inspect module lets you walk it.
Figure: the call stack: newest frame on top, each linked to its caller

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: Without the frame model it is hard to explain why recursive calls do not overwrite each other's variables, how tracebacks are produced, or how a logger knows which function called it.

Why we need it:
  • Understand the call stack and why each call has independent local variables.
  • Read tracebacks and RecursionError messages with confidence.
  • Build tools that need the caller's context: loggers, debuggers, test helpers.
  • See how globals, locals and the code object fit together at run time.

Complete Example: Walking the call stack with f_back

The program lists the active function names, counts the extra frames recursion creates, and checks a frame's globals.
codeExplanations: call_chain starts at its caller's frame and follows f_back until None, collecting each frame's function name. The name <module> is the top-level frame. recurse(3) creates four live frames (n = 3, 2, 1, 0) at the deepest point, each with its own n, which is why the count differs by 4. The frame of main shares the module's global namespace.

beginner.content:
Code Blocks

Python programs are built from code blocks - pieces of code executed as a unit. The block types are: a module, a function body, a class body, and strings run by exec() / eval(). Each time a block runs, CPython creates a frame: the working area for that execution.

What a Frame Holds

A frame is the runtime record of one running block. It holds:
PartPurposeAttribute
CodeThe code object being executedf_code
Local variablesNames local to this callf_locals
Globals / builtinsThe module namespace and built-insf_globals, f_builtins
Current lineWhere execution is nowf_lineno
CallerThe frame that called this onef_back
Value stackOperand stack for bytecode (internal)-
Calling a function creates a new frame on top of the caller's; returning destroys it. Together the chain of frames is the call stack you see in a traceback.

Walking the Call Stack

Each frame points to its caller through f_back, so you can walk from the current frame to the program's start.
codeExplanations: inspect.currentframe() returns the frame of the function that called it (inner). Following f_back gives the caller (outer) and finally the module-level frame, whose name is <module>. This is exactly the information a traceback prints, reversed.

beginner.content:
A Class Body Runs Immediately

A function body runs when the function is called, but a class body runs right away, once, when the class is defined - in its own frame.
codeExamples:
class Config:
    print("running the class body")
    debug = True
    level = 3 * 2

print("class defined")
print(Config.level)

# OUTPUT:
# running the class body
# class defined
# 6

beginner.content:
Introduction

Each function call creates a frame: the execution context holding the code object, local variables, the operand stack and the current instruction. Frames form a call stack; return or an exception pops the frame.
codeExamples:
import sys

def inner():
    f = sys._getframe()
    print("in", f.f_code.co_name, "called from", f.f_back.f_code.co_name)

def outer():
    inner()

outer()

# OUTPUT:
# in inner called from outer

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Frames explain scoping (locals vs globals vs builtins), recursion limits, tracebacks (a list of frames), generators that pause and resume, and how debuggers show variables.
codeExamples:
import inspect

def f(x):
    y = x * 2
    frame = inspect.currentframe()
    print(frame.f_locals)                  # snapshot of local names
    print(frame.f_lineno, frame.f_code.co_name)

f(5)

# OUTPUT:
# {'x': 5, 'y': 10, 'frame': <frame ...>}
# 5 f

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Debuggers, profilers (sys.setprofile), coverage tools (sys.settrace) and loggers (findCaller) all walk frames. Generators and coroutines keep a frame alive between resumptions.
codeExamples:
import sys

calls = []
def tracer(frame, event, arg):
    if event == "call":
        calls.append(frame.f_code.co_name)
    return None

def a(): b()
def b(): pass

sys.settrace(tracer); a(); sys.settrace(None)
print(calls)

# OUTPUT:
# ['a', 'b']

beginner.content:
Diagram

   call stack (grows down)             one frame
   ┌────────────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────────────┐
   │ <module>               │         │ f_code    -> code object │
   ├────────────────────────┤         │ f_locals  -> {x: 5}      │
   │ outer()                │         │ f_globals -> module dict │
   ├────────────────────────┤         │ f_back    -> caller      │
   │ inner()   (running)    │ ◄────── │ value stack, f_lasti     │
   └────────────────────────┘         └──────────────────────────┘

expert.content:
Names Are Resolved by Scope, Decided at Compile Time

Name lookup follows LEGB: Local, Enclosing function, Global, Built-in. Which scope a name belongs to is decided by the compiler for each function: if the function assigns to a name anywhere, that name is local throughout the function. This explains a classic error.
codeExplanations: Because of the assignment x = 5, the compiler marks x as a local variable of f for the whole function. The print(x) therefore looks for a local that has no value yet, instead of falling back to the global x. Adding "global x" or removing the assignment fixes it.

expert.content:
Generators Suspend Their Frames

A normal call destroys its frame on return. A generator keeps its frame alive between yields, with all locals and the current position preserved, and resumes it on the next next(). That is what makes generators and async coroutines possible.
codeExamples:
import inspect

def counter():
    n = 0
    while True:
        n += 1
        yield n

g = counter()
print(inspect.getgeneratorstate(g))
next(g)
next(g)
print(inspect.getgeneratorstate(g))
print(g.gi_frame.f_locals)           # the suspended frame's local variables

# OUTPUT:
# GEN_CREATED
# GEN_SUSPENDED
# {'n': 2}

expert.content:
Hooking Into Execution: sys.settrace

The interpreter can report events - a function call, a new line, a return, an exception - to a callback. Debuggers, coverage tools and profilers are built on this (sys.settrace, sys.setprofile, and the lower-overhead sys.monitoring in 3.12+).
codeExamples:
import sys

def tracer(frame, event, arg):
    if event == "call":
        print("call", frame.f_code.co_name)
    return None                      # no per-line tracing inside the call

def a():
    b()

def b():
    pass

sys.settrace(tracer)
a()
sys.settrace(None)

# OUTPUT:
# call a
# call b

expert.content:
How Frames Are Implemented (CPython 3.11+)

  • Frames used to be heap objects created on every call, which was a major cost. Since 3.11 they live in a contiguous per-thread data stack and are cheap to push and pop.
  • A full Python frame object (what sys._getframe() returns) is created lazily, only when something like a traceback or debugger asks for it.
  • Python-to-Python calls no longer use the C stack, so deep recursion is limited by the recursion limit rather than a C stack overflow.
  • Exceptions are found through a static exception table in the code object ("zero-cost" try); the interpreter unwinds frames until it finds a handler.
  • Each thread has its own stack of frames; the GIL decides which thread runs the evaluation loop.

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Each call has isolated locals, so recursion just worksDeep recursion hits the recursion limit (default 1000)
Frames give precise tracebacks for debuggingFrame objects add memory and call overhead
inspect makes the stack available to toolsFrame attributes differ between Python versions
Simple linked-list model, easy to reason aboutInspecting frames at run time is slow and easy to misuse

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a frame?The runtime record of one executing code block: its code, local and global namespaces, current position and a link to the caller
What are the kinds of code block?Module, function body, class body, and exec/eval strings
When does a class body run?Immediately, once, when the class statement executes
Why does print(x); x = 5 in a function raise UnboundLocalError?Assignment makes x local for the whole function at compile time
How are generators different from normal calls?Their frame survives between yields, preserving locals and position

Advantages

Advantages: a uniform model for all calls, introspection of the live program, and cheap suspension for generators and async code.
codeExamples:
def counter():
    n = 0
    while True:
        n += 1
        yield n            # frame (and local n) is suspended, not destroyed

c = counter()
print(next(c), next(c), c.gi_frame.f_locals["n"])

# OUTPUT:
# 1 2 2

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: each call has setup cost (Python function calls are slower than in compiled languages), frames hold references that delay garbage collection, and deep recursion is bounded.
codeExamples:
import timeit
def f(): pass
print(timeit.timeit(f, number=1_000_000) > 0)    # about 30-50 ns per call (varies)

# OUTPUT:
# True

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: frame objects are CPython internals (f_locals semantics changed in 3.13), accessing them is slow, and tail-call elimination does not exist so recursion depth is limited.

Architect's Notes

Do not build business logic on frame inspection; keep it to debuggers, loggers and test tooling. Convert deep recursion to loops or explicit stacks, and remember that stored tracebacks and generators keep frames, and all their locals, alive.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A code object is the immutable result of compiling a function body: bytecode, constants, variable names and more. A function object is created when def runs and wraps a code object together with defaults, globals and closure cells. Many function objects can share one code object. If you know Java, think of the code object as the compiled method body and the function object as a reference to it bound to its environment.
Figure: one code object can back many function objects

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: Treating "function" as one single thing hides how closures, default values and dynamic function creation work, and why two functions made by a factory can share the same compiled code.

Why we need it:
  • Separate what to run (code object) from what it runs with (function object).
  • Inspect a function's parameters, local names and free variables via co_* attributes.
  • Understand closures: shared code, separate captured values.
  • Build or modify functions dynamically with code.replace().

Complete Example: One code object, many functions

A closure factory creates two functions. The program shows they share code but not captured values, and inspects the code object.
codeExamples:
def make_adder(n):
    def add(x):
        return x + n
    return add


def describe(code):
    print(code.co_name, code.co_argcount, code.co_varnames, code.co_freevars)


def is_immutable(code):
    try:
        code.co_name = "other"
    except AttributeError:
        return True
    return False


def main():
    add_two = make_adder(2)
    add_ten = make_adder(10)

    print("same code object:", add_two.__code__ is add_ten.__code__)
    print("same function:   ", add_two is add_ten)
    print(add_two(5), add_ten(5))
    print("captured:", add_two.__closure__[0].cell_contents)

    describe(add_two.__code__)
    print("immutable:", is_immutable(add_two.__code__))
    print(add_two.__code__.replace(co_name="renamed").co_name)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT:
# same code object: True
# same function:    False
# 7 15
# captured: 2
# add 1 ('x',) ('n',)
# immutable: True
# renamed
codeExplanations: The inner def add is compiled once, so both functions point at the same code object, yet each call to make_adder builds a new function object with its own closure cell (n = 2 or n = 10). co_freevars lists the captured name n, separate from the local names in co_varnames. The code object is read-only, but replace() returns a modified copy.

beginner.content:
Function = Code + Context

When Python compiles a function body it produces a code object: an immutable bundle holding the bytecode and the information needed to run it. A function object is created later, when the def statement runs, and wraps a code object together with its runtime context (the module's globals, default values, closure cells, name, docstring). One code object can back many function objects - for example every function a factory returns.
Code object (__code__)Function object
Compiled once, immutableCreated each time def executes
Bytecode, constants, variable namesCode + globals + defaults + closure
Knows nothing about defaults or the moduleCallable

Inspecting a Code Object

Every function exposes its code object as __code__, with attributes starting co_.
codeExamples:
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    message = greeting + ", " + name
    return message

code = greet.__code__

print(code.co_name)
print(code.co_argcount)
print(code.co_varnames)
print(code.co_filename.endswith(".py"))

# OUTPUT:
# greet
# 2
# ('name', 'greeting', 'message')
# True
codeExplanations: co_argcount is the number of positional parameters; co_varnames lists the local variable names, parameters first, then other locals in order of first assignment. The default value "Hello" is not in the code object - it belongs to the function object (greet.__defaults__).

beginner.content:
The Most Useful Attributes

AttributeHolds
co_nameThe function name
co_argcount, co_kwonlyargcountNumber of positional and keyword-only parameters
co_varnamesNames of local variables (including parameters)
co_namesGlobal names and attribute names the code refers to
co_constsConstants used by the code (and nested code objects)
co_codeThe raw bytecode, as bytes
co_freevars, co_cellvarsClosure variables used from / provided to other functions
co_firstlineno, co_filenameWhere the function was defined
co_flagsBit flags: generator? uses *args? ...
codeExamples:
def show(items):
    print(len(items))

print(show.__code__.co_names)       # the global names it looks up
print(show.__code__.co_varnames)    # its locals

# OUTPUT:
# ('print', 'len')
# ('items',)

beginner.content:
Introduction

A code object is the immutable result of compiling a block: it holds the bytecode, constants, names and argument info. A function object wraps a code object plus its globals and defaults, reachable through f.__code__.
codeExamples:
def greet(name, greeting="Hi"):
    msg = f"{greeting}, {name}"
    return msg

c = greet.__code__
print(c.co_name, c.co_argcount)
print(c.co_varnames)
print(c.co_consts)

# OUTPUT (3.12):
# greet 2
# ('name', 'greeting', 'msg')
# (None, ', ')

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

It separates what to run (the code) from where it runs (the function and frame). That lets one code object serve many closures and lets tools inspect any function without running it.
codeExamples:
def make(n):
    def add(x): return x + n          # closure
    return add

a, b = make(1), make(100)
print(a.__code__ is b.__code__)       # same code object
print(a.__closure__[0].cell_contents, b.__closure__[0].cell_contents)

# OUTPUT:
# True
# 1 100

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Frameworks read co_varnames and co_argcount to inspect signatures (older dependency injection), profilers key statistics on co_filename and co_firstlineno, and metaprogramming can build functions with types.FunctionType and code.replace().
codeExamples:
import types

def original(): return "old"
new_code = original.__code__.replace(co_consts=(None, "patched"))
patched = types.FunctionType(new_code, globals())
print(patched())

# OUTPUT:
# patched

beginner.content:
Diagram

   function object  f                      code object (immutable)
   ┌───────────────────────┐              ┌───────────────────────────┐
   │ __code__  ────────────┼────────────► │ co_code      bytecode     │
   │ __globals__           │              │ co_consts    (None, ...)  │
   │ __defaults__          │              │ co_varnames  ('a','b')    │
   │ __closure__           │              │ co_names, co_argcount ... │
   └───────────────────────┘              └───────────────────────────┘

expert.content:
Swapping the Code Inside a Live Function

Because a function merely references its code object, you can change __code__ at run time - the function keeps its name, defaults and globals but runs different instructions. (This is how some live-reload and monkey-patching tools work. Use it in tests and tools, rarely in production code.)
codeExamples:
def hello():
    return "hello"

def goodbye():
    return "goodbye"

print(hello())
hello.__code__ = goodbye.__code__
print(hello())
print(hello.__name__)                # the function object kept its own name

# OUTPUT:
# hello
# goodbye
# hello

expert.content:
Closures: co_freevars and co_cellvars

A variable shared between an outer and an inner function is stored in a cell. The outer code object lists it in co_cellvars; the inner one lists it in co_freevars. The function object's __closure__ holds the actual cells.
codeExamples:
def outer():
    x = 10
    def inner():
        return x
    return inner

inner = outer()

print(outer.__code__.co_cellvars)
print(inner.__code__.co_freevars)
print(inner.__closure__[0].cell_contents)
print(inner.__code__.co_varnames)       # x is NOT a local of inner

# OUTPUT:
# ('x',)
# ('x',)
# 10
# ()

expert.content:
Flags and Nested Code Objects

co_flags records properties of the function. And a function body is itself a constant of the code that defines it, so code objects nest.
codeExamples:
import inspect

def gen():
    yield 1

def varargs(*args, **kwargs):
    pass

print(bool(gen.__code__.co_flags & inspect.CO_GENERATOR))
print(bool(varargs.__code__.co_flags & inspect.CO_VARARGS))
print(bool(varargs.__code__.co_flags & inspect.CO_VARKEYWORDS))

module_code = compile("def f():\n    return 1\nx = f()\n", "<string>", "exec")
nested = [c.co_name for c in module_code.co_consts if hasattr(c, "co_code")]
print(nested)

# OUTPUT:
# True
# True
# True
# ['f']

expert.content:
Building and Modifying Code Objects

Code objects are immutable, but code.replace(**changes) (3.8+) returns a modified copy, and types.FunctionType turns a code object into a callable. This is the lowest-level way to generate functions dynamically.
codeExamples:
import types

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

new_code = add.__code__.replace(co_name="plus")
plus = types.FunctionType(new_code, globals())

print(plus(2, 3))
print(plus.__name__)

# OUTPUT:
# 5
# plus

expert.content:
Debugging and Tooling Uses

  • Tracebacks and debuggers use co_filename, co_name and the line table to show where an error happened. In 3.11+, co_positions() gives line and column ranges per instruction, which powers the ^^^^ markers in modern tracebacks.
  • Coverage tools read co_lines() to learn which lines can execute.
  • Frameworks inspect co_varnames[:co_argcount] (or the nicer inspect.signature) to discover parameter names, as dependency-injection and test frameworks do.
  • Exception handling (3.11+) is stored in co_exceptiontable; the line table in co_linetable.
  • Code objects are hashable and comparable, and marshal can serialize them - exactly what a .pyc file contains.

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Compiled once and shared: saves memory and timeAttribute set differs between Python versions
Immutability makes code objects safe to share and cacheEditing code objects is advanced and easy to get wrong
Clear separation of code from runtime environmentTwo-level model (code vs function) confuses beginners
Rich co_* metadata supports debuggers and toolsNot a portable, documented format like Java class files

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Code object vs function object?A code object is immutable compiled code; a function object adds globals, defaults, closure and name around it
Where do default argument values live?On the function object (__defaults__), not in the code object
What is in co_consts?Literal constants and nested code objects (for inner functions and classes)
What are cell variables?Variables shared between a function and its inner functions; stored in cells referenced by __closure__
How do you change a code object?You can't mutate it; use code.replace(...) to get a modified copy

Advantages

Advantages: introspection of any function, cheap sharing between closures, and replace() creates modified copies safely because code objects are immutable.
codeExamples:
def f(a, b, *args, **kw): pass
c = f.__code__
print(c.co_argcount, c.co_flags & 0x04 != 0, c.co_flags & 0x08 != 0)  # *args, **kw flags

# OUTPUT:
# 2 True True

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: attributes and layout are CPython internals that change between versions (3.11 added co_qualname, exception tables), so raw manipulation is fragile.
codeExamples:
def f(): pass
print(hasattr(f.__code__, "co_qualname"))     # new in 3.11
print(hasattr(f.__code__, "co_lnotab"))       # deprecated; replaced by co_lines()

# OUTPUT (3.12):
# True
# True

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: code objects are read-only (you cannot edit bytecode in place), they cannot be pickled by the standard pickle (only marshalled), and they carry no runtime state such as variable values.
codeExamples:
import pickle
def f(): pass
try:
    pickle.dumps(f.__code__)
except TypeError as e:
    print("cannot pickle:", e)

# OUTPUT:
# cannot pickle: cannot pickle 'code' object

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Code-object manipulation belongs in debuggers, profilers and compilers, not in application logic. If you need runtime-generated behaviour, prefer closures, functools, or decorators; if you need to alter code, regenerate from an AST and recompile.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A namespace maps names to objects, usually through a dictionary: built-ins, module globals, a function's locals, a class's attributes. Before generating bytecode, the compiler builds a symbol table that decides for every name whether it is local, global or a free (closure) variable. At run time a lookup follows the LEGB order: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in. Java resolves names at compile time with block scopes; Python decides scope at compile time too, but binds names dynamically.
Figure: LEGB lookup: the first scope that has the name wins

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: Without this model, errors such as UnboundLocalError, shadowed built-ins and "why can't my inner function change this variable?" feel arbitrary.

Why we need it:
  • Predict which variable a name refers to using the LEGB rule.
  • Understand global and nonlocal and why they are needed.
  • Use globals(), vars() and symtable to inspect scopes.
  • Avoid accidentally shadowing built-ins like list or len.

Complete Example: Scopes decided by the symbol table

The standard symtable module exposes the compiler's scope decisions; the program also checks the runtime namespaces.
codeExamples:
import builtins
import symtable

SOURCE = """
count = 0

def outer():
    total = 1
    def inner():
        return total + count
    return inner
"""


def find_table(table, name):
    for child in table.get_children():
        if child.get_name() == name:
            return child
    return None


def main():
    module = symtable.symtable(SOURCE, "<demo>", "exec")
    outer = find_table(module, "outer")
    inner = find_table(outer, "inner")

    print(sorted(outer.get_identifiers()))
    print("total local in outer:", outer.lookup("total").is_local())
    print("total free in inner: ", inner.lookup("total").is_free())
    print("count global in inner:", inner.lookup("count").is_global())

    print("len in builtins:", "len" in vars(builtins))
    print("len in globals():", "len" in globals())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT:
# ['inner', 'total']
# total local in outer: True
# total free in inner:  True
# count global in inner: True
# len in builtins: True
# len in globals(): False
codeExplanations: symtable parses the source and records, per function, how each name is classified. total is assigned in outer, so it is local there, but inner only reads it, making it a free (enclosing) variable; count is never assigned in either function, so it resolves as a global. The last two lines show that len lives in the built-in namespace, not the module namespace.

beginner.content:
What is a Namespace?

A namespace is a mapping from names to objects - in practice a dictionary. Python has several, living at different times:
NamespaceContainsLives
Built-inlen, print, ValueError...Whole program
Global (module)Names defined at the top level of a fileWhile the module is loaded
EnclosingNames of an outer function, seen by an inner oneWhile the closure exists
LocalParameters and variables of one function callThat call
Class / instanceClass attributes; instance attributes in __dict__The class / the object
Lookup order is LEGB: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in. The first scope that has the name wins.

Looking at Namespaces

globals() and locals() return the current namespaces; vars(obj) returns an object's attribute dictionary.

Built-ins Can Be Shadowed

The built-in namespace is searched last, so assigning to a built-in's name in your module hides it from that point on - a classic beginner bug.
codeExamples:
import builtins

print(builtins.list is list)

list = [1, 2, 3]                    # shadows the built-in "list"
try:
    list("abc")
except TypeError as error:
    print("TypeError:", error)

del list                            # the built-in becomes visible again
print(list("abc"))

# OUTPUT:
# True
# TypeError: 'list' object is not callable
# ['a', 'b', 'c']

beginner.content:
Class Bodies Are Not Enclosing Scopes

A method cannot see class-level names without qualifying them: the class body's namespace is skipped when searching enclosing scopes.

Introduction

A namespace is a mapping from names to objects (module globals, a function's locals, a class body, builtins). The compiler builds a symbol table that decides, per name, whether it is local, global, free (closure) or cell.
codeExamples:
x = "global"

def f():
    y = "local"
    print(sorted(locals()))          # function namespace
    print("x" in globals())          # module namespace

f()
print(type(__builtins__).__name__ in ("module", "dict"))

# OUTPUT:
# ['y']
# True
# True

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Without clear namespaces, names would collide. The rules (LEGB: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in) make lookups predictable and are the reason for bugs like UnboundLocalError.

Real-Time Use

Real impact: closures with nonlocal, module-level state, class attribute resolution, name shadowing of builtins (list = []), and plug-in systems that exec code into a custom dict.
codeExamples:
def counter():
    n = 0
    def inc():
        nonlocal n          # refers to the enclosing namespace
        n += 1
        return n
    return inc

c = counter(); c(); c()
print(c())

ns = {}
exec("a = 5\nb = a * 2", ns)         # custom namespace for dynamic code
print(ns["b"])

# OUTPUT:
# 3
# 10

expert.content:
Symbol Tables: Scopes Are Decided at Compile Time

Before generating bytecode the compiler builds a symbol table for each block, classifying every name: local, global, free (from an enclosing function) or cell (shared with an inner function). The classification follows simple rules - a name that is assigned in a block is local unless declared global/nonlocal. The result decides which instruction is emitted: LOAD_FAST for locals, LOAD_GLOBAL for globals, LOAD_DEREF for closure variables, LOAD_NAME in module and class bodies. The symtable module exposes it.
codeExamples:
import symtable

source = """x = 1
def f(a):
    y = a + x
    return y
"""

table = symtable.symtable(source, "<string>", "exec")
f = table.get_children()[0]

print(table.get_type(), f.get_type(), f.get_name())
for symbol in sorted(f.get_symbols(), key=lambda s: s.get_name()):
    print(symbol.get_name(), symbol.is_parameter(), symbol.is_local(), symbol.is_global())

# OUTPUT:
# module function f
# a True True False
# x False False True
# y False True False
codeExplanations: Each row is name, is_parameter, is_local, is_global. "a" is a parameter and therefore local. "x" is only read in f and assigned nowhere in it, so it is classified as global (found later in the module namespace). "y" is assigned in f, so it is local. Because the classification is made before the program runs, UnboundLocalError exists: a name assigned anywhere in a function is local for the whole function.

expert.content:
The Dictionaries Behind the Names

A module's namespace really is a dict: module.__dict__, which is also what globals() returns. sys.modules is the dictionary of all loaded modules. An object's attributes are in obj.__dict__ (unless __slots__ is used). Function locals are special: for speed they are kept in a fixed array ("fast locals"), not a dictionary, and locals() builds a snapshot on request.
codeExamples:
import math
import sys

print(math.__dict__["pi"] == math.pi)
print(globals() is sys.modules["__main__"].__dict__)

def f():
    x = 1
    snapshot = locals()
    x = 2
    return snapshot["x"]          # a copy taken earlier, not a live view

def g():
    x = 1
    locals()["x"] = 99            # writing to the snapshot changes nothing
    return x

print(f(), g())

# OUTPUT:
# True
# True
# 1 1

expert.content:
Name Mangling and Declarations

  • global and nonlocal are compile-time declarations that change how a name is classified in a function - they are not run-time statements.
  • Private names: inside a class, an identifier of the form __name (two leading underscores, not ending in two) is mangled to _ClassName__name by the compiler, to avoid accidental clashes in subclasses.
  • Comprehensions had their own scope (an implicit function) until Python 3.12, which now inlines them (PEP 709); the loop variable still does not leak out.
codeExamples:
class Account:
    def __init__(self):
        self.__balance = 100        # stored as _Account__balance

print(Account().__dict__)

total = 0
def add(n):
    global total                    # compile-time: treat "total" as global
    total += n

add(5)
print(total)

squares = [i * i for i in range(3)]
print("i" in globals())             # the comprehension variable did not leak

# OUTPUT:
# {'_Account__balance': 100}
# 5
# False

expert.content:
exec, eval and Custom Namespaces

exec and eval run code in the namespaces you give them, which is how you sandbox (weakly!) or isolate code, and how templates and REPLs work. Remember __builtins__ is inserted into the globals dictionary if missing.
codeExamples:
namespace = {"price": 100}

exec("tax = price * 0.18\ntotal = price + tax", namespace)

print(namespace["total"])
print("tax" in globals())              # nothing leaked into our own module
print("__builtins__" in namespace)

# OUTPUT:
# 118.0
# False
# True

expert.content:
Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Simple rule (LEGB) decides every name lookupAssigning to a name makes it local for the whole function
Scopes are plain dictionaries you can inspectUnboundLocalError surprises beginners
Compile-time classification makes local access fastBuilt-ins can be shadowed silently
Closures and modules fall out of the same mechanismChanging outer variables needs global or nonlocal

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does LEGB stand for?Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in - the order in which names are looked up
What is a symbol table?Compiler data classifying each name in a block as local, global, free or cell, built before bytecode generation
Why can't a method see a class variable without self.?A class body is not an enclosing scope for the functions defined inside it
Does modifying locals() change a local variable?No - inside a function it returns a snapshot
What is name mangling?The compiler renames __x inside class C to _C__x to avoid accidental overrides

Advantages

Advantages: isolation between modules and functions, predictable LEGB lookup, introspection through vars() / dir(), and the symtable module for analysis.
codeExamples:
import symtable

src = "g = 1\ndef f(a):\n    b = a + g\n    return b\n"
top = symtable.symtable(src, "<s>", "exec")
fn = top.get_children()[0]
for s in fn.get_symbols():
    kind = "param" if s.is_parameter() else "global" if s.is_global() else "local"
    print(s.get_name(), kind)

# OUTPUT:
# a param
# b local
# g global

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: shadowing is silent, a name used for assignment anywhere in a function becomes local everywhere in it, and global lookups are slower than local ones.
codeExamples:
print = "oops"                  # shadows the builtin in this module
try:
    print("hello")
except TypeError as e:
    print("shadowed:", e)
del print                        # remove shadow -> builtin visible again
print("hello again")

# OUTPUT:
# shadowed: 'str' object is not callable
# hello again

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: class bodies do not form an enclosing scope for methods, comprehensions have their own scope (inlined in 3.12 but still isolated), and modifying locals() inside a function does not change variables.

Architect's Notes

Keep module state minimal and explicit: pass dependencies as arguments, avoid global and nonlocal for anything but tiny closures, and never shadow builtins (enable linters A001/A002). For plug-in or template systems always exec into a dedicated dict, and remember that exec is not a sandbox.

topics.name: What is the Global Interpreter Lock?

beginner.content:
Introduction

The Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) is a mutex inside CPython that lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time. Many threads can exist, but they must take turns holding the lock. The lock is released while a thread waits (sleep, network, file I/O), so waiting work still overlaps. In Java the contrast is sharp: JVM threads run truly in parallel on all cores, and you protect shared data yourself with synchronized or java.util.concurrent.
Figure: two threads take turns on the single GIL - never both running Python code at once

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: Beginners add threads to a calculation expecting it to run on every core, then find it is no faster - and have no idea why.

Why we need it:
  • Explain why threads do not speed up CPU-heavy Python code.
  • Show when threads still help: tasks that spend their time waiting.
  • Let you choose the right tool (threads, processes, asyncio) instead of guessing.
  • Remove the myth that Python is "single-threaded" - threads exist, they just take turns.

Complete Example: Threads overlap waiting

Five tasks each wait 0.3 seconds. Run one after another they need about 1.5 s; in five threads they overlap because sleep releases the GIL. Only safe boolean checks are printed because exact timings vary.
codeExamples:
import threading
import time

TASKS = 5       # number of tasks
DELAY = 0.3     # seconds each task waits


def wait_task():
    time.sleep(DELAY)                   # waiting: the GIL is released


def run_sequential():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(TASKS):
        wait_task()
    return time.perf_counter() - start


def run_threaded():
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=wait_task) for _ in range(TASKS)]
    start = time.perf_counter()
    for thread in threads:
        thread.start()
    for thread in threads:
        thread.join()                   # wait for all threads to finish
    return time.perf_counter() - start


def main():
    sequential = run_sequential()
    threaded = run_threaded()
    print("tasks:", TASKS)
    print("sequential >= 1.4 s:", sequential >= 1.4)
    print("threaded < 1.0 s:", threaded < 1.0)
    print("threads at least 2x faster:", sequential / threaded > 2)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT:
# tasks: 5
# sequential >= 1.4 s: True
# threaded < 1.0 s: True
# threads at least 2x faster: True
codeExplanations: sleep() releases the GIL, so while one thread waits the others can start their own wait. Five waits of 0.3 s overlap into roughly 0.3 s instead of 1.5 s. If the tasks were pure calculation instead, the GIL would force them to take turns and no such gain would appear.

beginner.content:
One Thread at a Time

The Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) is a mutex inside CPython that allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at any moment, even on a computer with many CPU cores. A program can have dozens of threads, but to run Python code each must first hold the GIL, so they take turns. Think of a meeting room with one microphone: many people (threads) are in the room, but only the one holding the microphone (the GIL) can speak (run Python code). Others wait until it is passed on.

What This Means in Practice

  • CPU-heavy work does not speed up with threads. Four threads doing arithmetic take about as long as one thread doing all of it, because they cannot run Python code at the same time.
  • Waiting work does speed up with threads. The GIL is released while a thread waits for a network response, a file read or time.sleep(). Other threads use that time to run.
  • Threads still exist and still interleave. The GIL does not make your program single-threaded; it only stops two threads from running Python bytecode simultaneously.

Threads Overlap Their Waiting

Five tasks that each wait half a second take 2.5 seconds one after another, but only about 0.5 seconds in five threads - the GIL is released during sleep.
codeExamples:
import threading
import time

def worker():
    time.sleep(0.5)                 # waiting: the GIL is released

start = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(5):
    worker()
sequential = time.perf_counter() - start

start = time.perf_counter()
threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker) for _ in range(5)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
threaded = time.perf_counter() - start

print(sequential >= 2.5)
print(threaded < 1.5)

# OUTPUT:
# True
# True
codeExplanations: The sequential version must take at least 5 x 0.5 = 2.5 seconds. In the threaded version all five sleeps run at the same time, so the whole thing finishes in roughly half a second. We print comparisons rather than exact times because the times vary from machine to machine.

beginner.content:
Is the GIL Part of Python?

No. The GIL is a feature of the CPython implementation, not of the Python language. Jython and IronPython have no GIL; PyPy has one. And since Python 3.13 there is an experimental CPython build without the GIL (see the last topic of this module).

Introduction

The GIL is a mutex inside CPython: only ONE thread may execute Python bytecode at any instant. Threads still exist and interleave, but they take turns. The interpreter forces a switch request every "switch interval".
codeExamples:
import sys, threading

# How often the interpreter asks the running thread to give up the GIL
print("switch interval (s):", sys.getswitchinterval())

# Threads are real OS threads, but they take turns on the interpreter
def show():
    print("running in", threading.current_thread().name)

t = threading.Thread(target=show, name="worker-1")
t.start(); t.join()

# OUTPUT:
# switch interval (s): 0.005
# running in worker-1

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

CPython manages memory with reference counts. Every object has a counter that is changed on nearly every operation. Without protection, two threads could corrupt a counter and free live memory, so a single global lock keeps the interpreter simple and safe.
codeExamples:
import sys

a = []                              # one reference: the name a
print(sys.getrefcount(a))           # +1 because the argument itself is a reference
b = a                               # second name, counter goes up
print(sys.getrefcount(a))
del b                               # counter goes down again
print(sys.getrefcount(a))

# OUTPUT:
# 2
# 3
# 2

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Every CPython web server, scraper and script you run lives under the GIL. Practical effect: threads are great for waiting (network, disk) because the GIL is released during blocking calls, but do not speed up pure-Python number crunching.

Diagram

   Thread A ──┐                 ┌──────────────┐
   Thread B ──┼──► wait for ──► │  GIL (mutex) │ ──► runs bytecode
   Thread C ──┘     the lock    └──────────────┘     (one at a time)
                                      ▲
        released on: I/O, sleep, every 5 ms (switch interval)

expert.content:
How the GIL Is Passed Around

A thread running Python code does not hold the GIL forever. Since Python 3.2 the mechanism is time-based:
  1. A waiting thread asks for the GIL and waits up to the switch interval (5 ms by default).
  2. If the running thread has not released it by then, the waiter sets a "drop request" flag.
  3. The running thread notices the flag at the next safe point in the evaluation loop (between bytecode instructions), releases the GIL, and the waiter takes it.
A thread also releases the GIL voluntarily whenever it makes a blocking call.
codeExamples:
import sys

print(sys.getswitchinterval())

sys.setswitchinterval(0.001)       # ask for a faster hand-over
print(sys.getswitchinterval())

# OUTPUT:
# 0.005
# 0.001

expert.content:
Who Releases the GIL?

Releases the GILHolds the GIL
time.sleep(), waiting on Lock, Event, Queue.getPure Python code: loops, arithmetic, function calls
Socket and file reads and writesManipulating Python objects (lists, dicts, strings)
subprocess waits, sqlite3 queriesMost operations of the built-in types
Heavy C code that opts in: NumPy kernels, zlib, hashlib on large data, many image librariesAnything in a C extension that does not release it
This is why a threaded web scraper or file downloader works well, a threaded image-processing script using NumPy can too, and a threaded pure-Python number cruncher does not.

Real Threads, Preemptive Scheduling

Python threads are real operating-system threads (pthreads or Windows threads). The OS decides which runnable thread gets a CPU; the GIL then decides which one may interpret bytecode. Because the hand-over happens at arbitrary bytecode boundaries, thread execution can be interrupted in the middle of a statement such as counter += 1 - which is why locks are still essential (the next topics show this).

Which Implementations Have a GIL?

ImplementationGIL?
CPython (standard build)Yes
CPython 3.13+ free-threaded buildNo (optional, experimental then supported - see last topic)
PyPyYes
Jython (JVM), IronPython (.NET)No - they use the host runtime's threads
Since Python 3.12 each sub-interpreter can also have its own GIL (PEP 684), the basis for running several interpreters in parallel inside one process.

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Simple, single lock: easy for the interpreter to implementCPU-bound threads cannot use more than one core
Single-threaded programs stay fast (no fine-grained locking)Java-style multi-core threading does not carry over
Waiting work (I/O, sleep) still overlaps across threadsAdding threads to calculations can even make them slower
Built-in objects are safe from corruption by simultaneous accessYour own multi-step operations still need locks

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the GIL?A mutex in CPython that lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time
Does it make multithreading useless?No - threads still help I/O-bound work because the GIL is released while waiting
How often does a thread give up the GIL?On blocking calls, or when another thread has waited for the switch interval (5 ms by default)
Is the GIL part of the Python language?No, it is a CPython implementation detail
Why do C libraries like NumPy scale across threads?They release the GIL while running their C code

Advantages

Advantages: very fast single-threaded code (no per-object locks), simple C-extension writing, many built-in operations such as list.append are effectively atomic, no data-structure corruption at interpreter level.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: CPU-bound threads do not run in parallel, so extra cores sit idle; multi-threaded CPU code can even be slower than single-threaded due to lock hand-off.
codeExamples:
import threading, time

def burn():
    n = 0
    for i in range(5_000_000):
        n += i * i

t0 = time.perf_counter(); burn(); burn()
serial = time.perf_counter() - t0

t0 = time.perf_counter()
ts = [threading.Thread(target=burn) for _ in range(2)]
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join()
threaded = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"serial {serial:.2f}s  threaded {threaded:.2f}s")

# OUTPUT (example - threaded is NOT ~2x faster):
# serial 0.85s  threaded 0.88s

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the GIL does not make your code thread-safe: x += 1 is several bytecodes and can interleave. It is a CPython detail, not part of the Python language (PyPy has one, Jython does not, free-threaded 3.13 can disable it).
codeExamples:
import sys, dis

# The GIL is an implementation detail; ask the interpreter about it (3.13+)
print("GIL enabled:", getattr(sys, "_is_gil_enabled", lambda: True)())

# x += 1 is NOT atomic: load, add, store are separate bytecodes
def inc():
    global x
    x += 1
dis.dis(inc)

# OUTPUT (example, 3.12, abridged):
# GIL enabled: True
#  LOAD_GLOBAL  x
#  LOAD_CONST   1
#  BINARY_OP    13 (+=)
#  STORE_GLOBAL x

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Treat the GIL as a scheduling fact: design I/O concurrency with threads or asyncio, CPU parallelism with processes, native extensions (NumPy, Rust) or free-threaded builds. Do not rely on "the GIL makes it safe" - it protects the interpreter, not your invariants. Avoid it as an excuse to skip locks.

beginner.content:
Introduction

CPython frees memory using reference counts: each object stores how many references point to it, and it is freed at zero. These counters change on almost every operation, so two threads updating one counter at once could lose an update and cause a crash or a leak. The GIL is the simple cure: only one thread runs Python code, so counts are always consistent. The JVM instead uses a tracing garbage collector with no per-object counters, which is why it needs no such lock.
Figure: a lost update on a reference count: two increments, the count rises by one

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: Without a global lock, every reference-count change - thousands per second - would need its own lock, making all Python code slow, or risk corrupting memory.

Why we need it:
  • Understand that the GIL protects the interpreter's memory, not your logic.
  • See why a single lock was cheaper and simpler than many small locks.
  • Know why C extensions (NumPy, drivers) could be written easily for Python.
  • Avoid the trap of thinking the GIL makes counter += 1 thread-safe.

Complete Example: What the GIL protects and what it does not

Appending to a list is one protected operation. A counter increment is several steps, so the program guards it with its own Lock, just as you would use synchronized in Java.
codeExplanations: Each of the 4 threads increments 10,000 times under the lock, giving exactly 40000. Each thread also appends 1,000 items; list.append is a single protected operation, so none are lost and the length is 4000. The lock is needed for the counter because += is several bytecodes and a thread can be switched out in the middle.

beginner.content:
The Short Answer: Reference Counting

CPython tracks memory with reference counts: every object carries a counter of how many references point to it, and it is freed when the counter reaches zero. That counter is changed constantly - every assignment, function call and list access adjusts one. If two threads change the same counter at the same moment without protection, an update can be lost, and the count becomes wrong. A count too low frees an object that is still in use (a crash); a count too high leaks memory. The GIL is the simple fix: only one thread runs Python code, so the counts are always updated safely.

The Race the GIL Prevents

Incrementing a counter is three steps - read, add one, write back. Without a lock, two threads can interleave:
StepThread AThread BCount in memory
1reads 55
2reads 55
3writes 66
4writes 66 (should be 7)
Two references were added, but the count only went up by one. Locking every reference-count change individually would be extremely slow, so CPython locks the whole interpreter instead.

Other Reasons It Was Chosen

  • Simplicity. One lock is easy to implement and to reason about. Python's threading support was added in the early 1990s, when almost all machines had a single CPU.
  • Fast single-threaded code. One lock acquisition is cheaper than thousands of small locks. Most Python programs are single-threaded, and the GIL keeps them fast.
  • Easy C extensions. Extension authors can assume only one thread touches Python objects at a time. This is a major reason Python has such a large ecosystem of C-based libraries (NumPy, database drivers, GUI toolkits).
  • Safe built-in types. A list.append or dict assignment cannot be torn in half by another thread, with no per-object locks needed.

Introduction

The GIL exists because CPython's memory manager (reference counting) is not thread-safe. One coarse lock was the cheapest way to protect the counters, the allocator and all C extensions at once.
codeExamples:
import sys

x = object()
print(sys.getrefcount(x))           # counter value (includes the call argument)
y = x; z = x
print(sys.getrefcount(x))           # every new name increments the counter
# Two threads doing y = x at the same time would race on this counter
# unless something (the GIL) serialises the increments.
