# OUTPUT:
# 2
# 4

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Without a global lock, CPython would need a fine-grained lock per object (slow, deadlock-prone) or atomic counters on every incref/decref (slow on every operation). Early Python (1990s) targeted single-core machines, and the GIL made C extensions trivially easy to write.
codeExamples:
# Illustrates the problem: a non-atomic read-modify-write.
# Simulated "refcount" shared by 2 workers, with an explicit pause to show the race.
import threading, time

count = 0
def incref():
    global count
    tmp = count                     # read
    time.sleep(0.001)               # another thread runs here
    count = tmp + 1                 # write back stale value

ts = [threading.Thread(target=incref) for _ in range(10)]
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join()
print("expected 10, got", count)

# OUTPUT (example):
# expected 10, got 1

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Because of this design, thousands of C libraries (NumPy, lxml, database drivers) assume the GIL protects their state. That huge ecosystem is the main reason it was not removed for decades.

Diagram

   Without GIL                         With GIL
   Thread A: refcnt = 5 -> 6           Thread A: [lock] 5 -> 6 [unlock]
   Thread B: refcnt = 5 -> 6   (lost)  Thread B:        [lock] 6 -> 7
   Result 6 (should be 7) -> crash     Result 7  (correct, one at a time)

expert.content:
The GIL Does Not Protect Your Code

The GIL protects the interpreter's internal data (reference counts, object headers). It does not make your own multi-step operations atomic, because a thread can lose the GIL between any two bytecode instructions. counter += 1 compiles into separate load, add and store instructions:
codeExamples:
import dis

counter = 0

def increment():
    global counter
    counter += 1

names = [i.opname for i in dis.get_instructions(increment)]
print("LOAD_GLOBAL" in names)         # read
print("BINARY_OP" in names)           # add (3.11+; INPLACE_ADD before)
print("STORE_GLOBAL" in names)        # write

# OUTPUT (Python 3.11 or newer):
# True
# True
# True
codeExplanations: Three separate instructions mean another thread can be scheduled between the read and the write, and its update then overwrites ours. The exact threshold at which this shows up depends on the Python version and timing, which is what makes this kind of bug so hard to reproduce - correct code must never rely on luck.

expert.content:
The Fix: Use a Lock for Compound Operations

Protect any read-modify-write sequence with threading.Lock. The result is then always correct, whatever the thread scheduling.
codeExamples:
import threading

counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def work():
    global counter
    for _ in range(100_000):
        with lock:
            counter += 1

threads = [threading.Thread(target=work) for _ in range(4)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

print(counter)

# OUTPUT:
# 400000

expert.content:
What Is Effectively Atomic Under the GIL

Single operations implemented in C on built-in types run to completion without interruption. That is a property of today's CPython, not a language promise - treat it as a convenience, not a design tool.
Effectively atomic (one C call)NOT atomic (several steps)
lst.append(x), lst.pop()n += 1
d[key] = value, d.get(key)d[key] += 1
x = y (simple assignment)if key not in d: d[key] = ...
queue.Queue.put/get (has its own locks)lst.append(lst[-1] + 1)

Why Not Remove It? The History

  • 1996, "free threading" patch: removing the GIL by adding fine-grained locks made single-threaded Python roughly twice as slow on the hardware of the time, so it was rejected.
  • 2007-2015, Python 3 era: improved GIL scheduling (3.2) but no removal. Experiments such as Gilectomy (2016) again lost too much single-thread speed.
  • Compatibility: thousands of C extensions assume the GIL protects them. Removing it breaks that contract.
  • 2023, PEP 703: accepted a plan for an optional GIL-free build, with techniques (biased reference counting, immortal objects, per-object locks) that keep the single-thread slowdown small. It arrived as an experimental build in 3.13 (see the last topic).

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Protects reference counts with one cheap lockBlocks parallel execution of Python code on many cores
Keeps single-threaded Python fastGives a false sense of safety for compound operations
Made writing C extensions much simplerOne lock for everything means all threads contend
Built-in types like list and dict never get corruptedHard to remove later: extensions rely on it

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does the GIL exist?CPython's reference counting is not thread-safe; one global lock is a simple, fast way to protect it (and C extensions)
Does the GIL make my code thread-safe?No - it protects the interpreter, not multi-step operations like counter += 1; you still need locks
Why not use a lock per object instead?It slowed single-threaded programs and was complex; early attempts were rejected for that reason
Name a benefit of the GIL.Fast single-threaded execution, simple C extensions, and safe built-in types
What is PEP 703?The accepted proposal for an optional free-threaded (GIL-less) CPython build

Advantages

Advantages: fast single-thread performance, simple implementation, easy C-API, deterministic memory release via refcounting (objects freed immediately when unreferenced).
codeExamples:
class Res:
    def __del__(self):
        print("freed immediately")

r1 = Res()
r1 = None                           # refcount hits 0 -> freed right now
print("after reassignment")

# OUTPUT:
# freed immediately
# after reassignment

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: parallel speedup on multi-core hardware is blocked for threads, and the lock adds latency when threads fight for it (the "convoy effect").
codeExamples:
import threading, time

# One CPU-heavy thread starves the I/O thread of GIL time slices
def cpu():
    end = time.perf_counter() + 1.0
    while time.perf_counter() < end: pass

lat = []
def ticker():
    for _ in range(5):
        t = time.perf_counter(); time.sleep(0.01)
        lat.append(time.perf_counter() - t - 0.01)

c = threading.Thread(target=cpu); k = threading.Thread(target=ticker)
c.start(); k.start(); c.join(); k.join()
print(f"max extra delay: {max(lat)*1000:.1f} ms")

# OUTPUT (example):
# max extra delay: 5.2 ms

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: only bytecode-level safety. Compound operations (check-then-act) still race, and the lock cannot be removed without breaking C extensions or slowing single-thread code (the reason PEP 703 is opt-in).
codeExamples:
import threading

balance = 100
def withdraw(n):
    global balance
    if balance >= n:                # check ...
        # a thread switch here lets another thread pass the same check
        balance -= n                # ... then act: not atomic as a pair

ts = [threading.Thread(target=withdraw, args=(80,)) for _ in range(2)]
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join()
print("balance:", balance)          # usually 20, but -60 is possible

# OUTPUT (example):
# balance: 20

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

The GIL traded parallelism for simplicity and single-thread speed, and that bargain made sense for its era. Today the trade is revisited: PEP 703 free-threaded builds use biased reference counting and per-object locks. Choose the GIL build for compatibility, and free-threaded only after verifying every native dependency.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A task is CPU-bound when the processor is the bottleneck (calculating, compressing, parsing) and I/O-bound when it mostly waits (network, disk, database). The GIL hurts only the first kind, because it is released during waiting. So the right tool depends on the kind: threads or asyncio for I/O, processes for CPU. In Java you would choose between a cached thread pool and a ForkJoinPool sized to the core count in much the same way.
Figure: the kind of work decides the right concurrency tool

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: Using threads for a heavy calculation gains nothing, and using processes for a few web requests wastes memory and start-up time. Picking blindly gives slow or bloated programs.

Why we need it:
  • Diagnose what the program is waiting for before optimising.
  • Pick threads/asyncio for I/O and multiprocessing for CPU work.
  • Predict whether adding workers will help at all.
  • Avoid the cost of the wrong concurrency model.

Complete Example: Threads for waiting, processes for calculating

The I/O part overlaps four 0.3 s waits in threads. The CPU part counts primes below 50,000 in four process chunks and checks the total against a single-process run.
codeExamples:
import time
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor, ThreadPoolExecutor

WORKERS = 4
DELAY = 0.3
LIMIT = 50_000


def fake_request(_):
    time.sleep(DELAY)                   # I/O: the GIL is released


def is_prime(n):
    if n < 2:
        return False
    divisor = 2
    while divisor * divisor <= n:
        if n % divisor == 0:
            return False
        divisor += 1
    return True


def count_primes(bounds):
    low, high = bounds
    return sum(1 for n in range(low, high) if is_prime(n))


def main():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(WORKERS) as pool:
        list(pool.map(fake_request, range(WORKERS)))
    overlapped = time.perf_counter() - start < 0.9
    print("I/O in 4 threads overlapped:", overlapped)

    step = LIMIT // WORKERS
    chunks = [(i * step, (i + 1) * step) for i in range(WORKERS)]
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(WORKERS) as pool:
        total = sum(pool.map(count_primes, chunks))
    print("CPU in 4 processes, primes below 50000:", total)
    print("same as one process:", total == count_primes((0, LIMIT)))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT:
# I/O in 4 threads overlapped: True
# CPU in 4 processes, primes below 50000: 5133
# same as one process: True
codeExplanations: Four 0.3 s waits in threads finish in about 0.3 s, well under the 0.9 s limit. The prime count is split into four ranges of 12,500 numbers, each handled by its own process with its own GIL; the four counts add up to 5133, the known number of primes below 50,000. The __main__ guard is required for process pools on Windows and macOS.

beginner.content:
What Is Your Program Waiting For?

Every slow program is slow for one of two reasons:
CPU-boundI/O-bound
The bottleneckThe processor is busy calculatingThe program is waiting for something external
ExamplesImage processing, encryption, number crunching, parsing huge data, ML trainingWeb requests, database queries, reading files, API calls, user input
CPU usage while runningHigh (near 100% of a core)Low (mostly idle)
Faster if you...Add more CPU coresOverlap the waiting
Best tool in Pythonmultiprocessing or native codethreading or asyncio
The GIL only matters for the first kind. For waiting, the GIL is released, so threads are fine.

Telling Them Apart

Compare wall-clock time with CPU time (time.process_time(), the time actually spent computing). If CPU time is close to wall time the task is CPU-bound; if it is much smaller the task spent its time waiting.
codeExamples:
import time

def calculate():
    sum(i * i for i in range(2_000_000))     # pure computation

def wait():
    time.sleep(0.5)                          # pretend network call

for task in (calculate, wait):
    wall_start = time.perf_counter()
    cpu_start = time.process_time()
    task()
    wall = time.perf_counter() - wall_start
    cpu = time.process_time() - cpu_start
    kind = "CPU-bound" if cpu > wall * 0.5 else "I/O-bound"
    print(task.__name__, kind)

# OUTPUT:
# calculate CPU-bound
# wait I/O-bound

beginner.content:
I/O-bound: Use Threads

Ten "downloads" of 0.2 seconds each would take 2 seconds in a row. With a thread pool they overlap and finish in about 0.2 seconds.
codeExamples:
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def fetch(page):
    time.sleep(0.2)                  # stands in for a network request
    return f"page {page}"

start = time.perf_counter()
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10) as pool:
    pages = list(pool.map(fetch, range(10)))
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start

print(pages[:3])
print(elapsed < 1.0)

# OUTPUT:
# ['page 0', 'page 1', 'page 2']
# True

beginner.content:
CPU-bound: Use Processes

Each process has its own interpreter and its own GIL, so processes run truly in parallel on separate cores. (The if __name__ == "__main__": guard is required with multiprocessing on Windows and macOS.)

Introduction

A CPU-bound task spends its time computing (loops, math, compression). An I/O-bound task spends its time waiting (network, disk, database). The category decides which concurrency tool works.
codeExamples:
import time

def cpu_task():                     # CPU-bound: the CPU is busy the whole time
    return sum(i * i for i in range(2_000_000))

def io_task():                      # I/O-bound: mostly waiting, CPU idle
    time.sleep(0.2)

for f in (cpu_task, io_task):
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); f()
    print(f.__name__, f"{time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f}s")

# OUTPUT (example):
# cpu_task 0.14s
# io_task 0.20s

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Picking the wrong tool wastes effort: threads help only while waiting, processes help only when computing, and each has overhead. Measuring first tells you where the time goes.
codeExamples:
import time

before = time.process_time()
time.sleep(0.3)                     # waiting: wall time grows, CPU time does not
print("sleep burned CPU:", round(time.process_time() - before, 2), "s")
before = time.process_time()
sum(i for i in range(3_000_000))    # computing: CPU time grows with wall time
print("loop burned CPU > 0.05:", time.process_time() - before > 0.05)

# OUTPUT:
# sleep burned CPU: 0.0 s
# loop burned CPU > 0.05: True

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Web scraping, API calls, DB queries and file downloads are I/O-bound (use threads or asyncio). Image resizing, ML training, video encoding, hashing and simulations are CPU-bound (use processes or native code).
codeExamples:
import concurrent.futures as cf, time

def download(url):                  # I/O-bound stand-in
    time.sleep(0.3)
    return url

urls = [f"site{i}.com" for i in range(6)]
t0 = time.perf_counter()
with cf.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=6) as pool:
    done = list(pool.map(download, urls))
print(len(done), f"pages in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f}s")

# OUTPUT (example):
# 6 pages in 0.3s

beginner.content:
Diagram

              ┌─────────────── What is the task waiting on? ───────────────┐
              │                                                            │
        the network / disk / DB                              the CPU itself
              │                                                            │
        I/O-bound ──► threads / asyncio              CPU-bound ──► multiprocessing /
                      (GIL released while waiting)                 NumPy / Rust / free-threaded

expert.content:
A Decision Guide

WorkloadToolWhy
Thousands of network connectionsasyncioOne thread, tiny memory per task, no lock bugs
A few dozen blocking calls (legacy libraries, DB drivers)ThreadPoolExecutorSimple; the GIL is released while blocked
Heavy Python computationProcessPoolExecutorSeparate GIL per process: real parallelism
Numeric arraysNumPy / pandas / SciPyLoops run in C with the GIL released and often SIMD
Hot loop of plain PythonNumba, Cython, or a Rust/C extensionCompile it, then optionally release the GIL
Mixed (download, then process)Threads/async for I/O feeding a process pool for CPUEach stage uses the right model

Mixing Models: Run Blocking or CPU Work From asyncio

An async program must never block the event loop. Push blocking calls into a thread with asyncio.to_thread(), and CPU-heavy functions into a process pool with loop.run_in_executor().
codeExamples:
import asyncio
import time
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

def blocking_io():
    time.sleep(0.2)
    return "io done"

def heavy_cpu(n):
    return sum(i * i for i in range(n))

async def main():
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    with ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool:
        io_result, cpu_result = await asyncio.gather(
            asyncio.to_thread(blocking_io),                  # a worker thread
            loop.run_in_executor(pool, heavy_cpu, 1_000_000),   # another process
        )
    print(io_result, cpu_result)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

# OUTPUT:
# io done 333332833333500000

expert.content:
Costs and Pitfalls

  • Processes are not free. Starting one costs tens of milliseconds, and arguments and results are pickled and copied between processes. For tiny tasks the overhead exceeds the gain: send big batches (chunksize in pool.map) rather than many small items.
  • Workers = cores. More CPU-bound workers than cores only adds scheduling overhead. In containers, check the real CPU limit (os.cpu_count() may report the host's cores).
  • Amdahl's law: if 20% of the work cannot be parallelised, the maximum speed-up is 5x no matter how many cores you add.
  • Too many threads hurt I/O work too: remote services, databases and file descriptors have limits. Pick a worker count from measurements, not guesses.
  • Profile first. Use cProfile to find the real hotspot - often an algorithm or a missing index fixes a "CPU-bound" problem without any parallelism.

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
A simple rule picks the right tool for the jobReal programs mix both kinds of work
Threads handle thousands of waiting tasks cheaplyProcesses cost memory and start-up time
Processes give true multi-core speed for calculationsData must be pickled between processes
Avoids wasted effort optimising the wrong thingMisjudging the kind gives no speed-up at all

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
CPU-bound vs I/O-bound?CPU-bound is limited by computation speed; I/O-bound is limited by waiting for external resources
Which one benefits from threads in CPython?I/O-bound - the GIL is released while waiting
Which tool do you use for CPU-bound work?multiprocessing / ProcessPoolExecutor (or native code that releases the GIL)
How can you tell which type a task is?Compare process_time() with wall-clock time, or watch CPU usage while it runs
How do you combine asyncio with blocking or CPU work?asyncio.to_thread or run_in_executor with a thread or process pool

Advantages

Advantages of classifying: a one-line profile tells you the right model, so I/O work scales to thousands of waits on one core and CPU work scales to the core count.
codeExamples:
import os
print("cores available:", os.cpu_count())
# Rule of thumb for worker counts:
#   CPU-bound -> os.cpu_count()          (more just adds contention)
#   I/O-bound -> many (10s-1000s)        (they spend time idle)
cpu_workers = os.cpu_count()
io_workers = min(32, (os.cpu_count() or 1) + 4)   # default used by ThreadPoolExecutor
print(cpu_workers, io_workers)

# OUTPUT (example, 8-core machine):
# cores available: 8
# 8 12

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: real tasks are mixed (download then parse), so the boundary blurs, and wrong guesses give no speedup or even a slowdown.
codeExamples:
import concurrent.futures as cf, time

def crunch(n):                      # CPU-bound given to THREADS: wrong choice
    return sum(i * i for i in range(n))

t0 = time.perf_counter()
with cf.ThreadPoolExecutor(4) as pool:
    list(pool.map(crunch, [2_000_000] * 4))
print(f"4 CPU jobs in threads: {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f}s (no better than serial)")

# OUTPUT (example):
# 4 CPU jobs in threads: 0.62s (no better than serial)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: libraries like NumPy and hashlib release the GIL during heavy C work, so some "CPU-bound" tasks DO scale with threads - you must measure, not assume.
codeExamples:
import hashlib, threading, time

blob = b"x" * 50_000_000            # 50 MB

def digest():
    hashlib.sha256(blob).hexdigest()  # releases the GIL for large buffers

t0 = time.perf_counter()
ts = [threading.Thread(target=digest) for _ in range(4)]
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join()
print(f"4 hashes in threads: {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f}s (parallel in C)")

# OUTPUT (example):
# 4 hashes in threads: 0.14s (parallel in C)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Profile before choosing (cProfile, py-spy, wall vs process_time). Mixed pipelines are best split: async or threads for the I/O stage, a process pool for the compute stage, linked by queues. Prefer vectorised or native libraries over parallelising pure-Python loops.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A thread is a flow of execution inside a process and shares its memory; a process is a separate program instance with its own memory and its own interpreter - and therefore its own GIL. Threads are light but take turns on one GIL, while processes run Python code truly in parallel at the cost of copying data between them. Java developers know the same split as threads inside one JVM versus separate JVM processes.
Figure: threads share one GIL and alternate; processes each have a GIL and run side by side

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: If you do not know that processes have separate memory, you wonder why a variable changed by a worker "does not change" in the parent, or why threads gave no CPU speed-up.

Why we need it:
  • Choose threads (shared memory, cheap) or processes (parallel, isolated).
  • Understand why each process has its own GIL.
  • Know how data must travel between processes (queues, pipes).
  • Predict what shared variables do in each model.

Complete Example: Shared memory vs separate memory

The same function appends to a list. A thread changes the parent list; a process changes only its own copy and must send the result back through a Queue.
codeExamples:
import multiprocessing
import threading

shared_log = []     # a module-level list


def record(source):
    shared_log.append(source)


def process_task(queue):
    record("process")                   # changes the child's own copy
    queue.put(list(shared_log))         # send the child's view back


def main():
    queue = multiprocessing.Queue()
    child = multiprocessing.Process(target=process_task, args=(queue,))
    child.start()
    child_view = queue.get()            # read before join to avoid a hang
    child.join()
    print("child process saw:", child_view)
    print("parent after process:", shared_log)

    worker = threading.Thread(target=record, args=("thread",))
    worker.start()
    worker.join()
    print("parent after thread:", shared_log)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT:
# child process saw: ['process']
# parent after process: []
# parent after thread: ['thread']
codeExplanations: The child process works on its own copy of shared_log, so the parent list stays empty and the child reports ['process'] through the queue. The thread shares the parent's memory, so after it finishes the parent list contains 'thread'. The __main__ guard is mandatory for multiprocessing.

beginner.content:
Two Ways to Do Things at Once

A process is a running program with its own memory and its own Python interpreter. A thread is a flow of execution inside a process; all threads of one process share the same memory.
AspectThreads (threading)Processes (multiprocessing)
MemoryShared with the other threadsSeparate - nothing shared by default
GILOne GIL shared by all threadsEach process has its own GIL
Parallel Python code on many cores?No (standard CPython)Yes
Start-up costTiny (microseconds to milliseconds)Larger (tens of milliseconds; a new interpreter)
Sharing dataJust use variables (but lock them)Must send it: queues, pipes, shared memory (pickling)
If one crashesThe whole process can dieOther processes keep running
Best forI/O-bound workCPU-bound work

Shared Memory vs Separate Memory

The same function does different things to the parent's variable depending on whether it runs in a process or a thread.
codeExamples:
import multiprocessing
import threading

counter = 0

def child():
    global counter
    counter += 1
    print("child sees", counter)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    p = multiprocessing.Process(target=child)
    p.start()
    p.join()
    print("after process", counter)      # the child changed ITS OWN copy

    t = threading.Thread(target=child)
    t.start()
    t.join()
    print("after thread", counter)       # the thread changed the SAME variable

# OUTPUT:
# child sees 1
# after process 0
# child sees 1
# after thread 1
codeExplanations: The process worked on its own copy of counter (it has separate memory), so the parent still sees 0. The thread ran inside the parent's memory, so the parent sees the change. This is the central difference: threads share data effortlessly but must protect it with locks; processes are isolated and must pass data explicitly.

beginner.content:
Passing Data Between Processes

Since memory is not shared, processes communicate through queues or pipes. Items are pickled, sent, and unpickled on the other side.
codeExamples:
from multiprocessing import Process, Queue

def producer(queue):
    for i in range(3):
        queue.put(i * i)
    queue.put(None)                    # a sentinel meaning "finished"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    queue = Queue()
    worker = Process(target=producer, args=(queue,))
    worker.start()

    while (item := queue.get()) is not None:
        print("got", item)
    worker.join()

# OUTPUT:
# got 0
# got 1
# got 4

beginner.content:
Introduction

A thread is a lightweight execution path inside one process and shares its memory. A process is an independent program instance with its own memory and its own interpreter (so its own GIL).
codeExamples:
import os, threading, multiprocessing as mp

def who(tag):
    print(tag, "pid", os.getpid() == MAIN_PID and "same as parent" or "different")

MAIN_PID = os.getpid()
if __name__ == "__main__":
    t = threading.Thread(target=who, args=("thread:",)); t.start(); t.join()
    p = mp.Process(target=who, args=("process:",)); p.start(); p.join()

# OUTPUT (on Linux/fork; Windows re-imports the module and differs slightly):
# thread: pid same as parent
# process: pid different

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Threads give cheap concurrency and easy data sharing but are limited by the GIL for CPU work. Processes give true parallelism and fault isolation but cost more memory/startup and need explicit data passing.
codeExamples:
import threading, multiprocessing as mp

counter = 0
def bump():
    global counter
    counter += 1

if __name__ == "__main__":
    t = threading.Thread(target=bump); t.start(); t.join()
    print("after thread :", counter)      # memory shared -> change visible
    p = mp.Process(target=bump); p.start(); p.join()
    print("after process:", counter)      # child changed ITS OWN copy only

# OUTPUT:
# after thread : 1
# after process: 1

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Use threads for web request handlers waiting on databases, GUI background work and polling. Use processes for batch image/video jobs, data crunching, and isolating untrusted or crash-prone code (a segfault kills only that worker).
codeExamples:
import multiprocessing as mp

def crash():
    import os; os._exit(1)          # simulate a hard crash of a worker

if __name__ == "__main__":
    p = mp.Process(target=crash); p.start(); p.join()
    print("parent still alive, child exit code:", p.exitcode)
    # a crashing THREAD (e.g. in C code) would take the whole process down

# OUTPUT:
# parent still alive, child exit code: 1

beginner.content:
Diagram

   THREADS (1 process)                 PROCESSES
  ┌──────────────────────┐      ┌─────────────┐  ┌─────────────┐
  │ shared memory + GIL  │      │ memory + GIL│  │ memory + GIL│
  │  T1   T2   T3        │      │   main      │  │   worker    │
  └──────────────────────┘      └──────┬──────┘  └──────▲──────┘
   share objects directly              └── pickle / pipe ┘

expert.content:
One API for Both: concurrent.futures

ThreadPoolExecutor and ProcessPoolExecutor have the same interface, so switching between them is a one-word change. That makes it easy to measure which model suits your workload.

Start Methods and the __main__ Guard

How a new process is created depends on the start method:
MethodHowNotes
spawnStarts a fresh interpreter and re-imports your main moduleDefault on Windows and macOS; safest; needs the if __name__ == "__main__": guard
forkCopies the running process (copy-on-write)Fast, but unsafe if the parent already has threads or open locks; being phased out as a default
forkserverA clean helper process forks workers on requestSafer than fork; the default on Linux from Python 3.14
Without the __main__ guard, a spawned child re-imports your script, which starts new processes, which re-import it... Python detects this and raises a RuntimeError.
codeExamples:
import multiprocessing

print(multiprocessing.get_start_method())      # the platform default
print(multiprocessing.cpu_count() >= 1)

# Choose explicitly (once, early, inside the __main__ guard):
#   multiprocessing.set_start_method("spawn")
# or per use:
#   ctx = multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")
#   ctx.Process(target=...)

# OUTPUT (on Windows):
# spawn
# True

expert.content:
Pickling: What Can Cross the Process Boundary

Arguments and return values are serialized with pickle. That works for numbers, strings, lists, dicts and instances of top-level classes, but not for lambdas, nested functions, open files, locks, sockets or database connections. A worker function must be defined at the module top level. Large objects are expensive to copy: pass small identifiers (file names, ids) and let each worker load its own data, or use multiprocessing.shared_memory for big arrays.
codeExamples:
import pickle

def top_level(x):
    return x + 1

print(pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(top_level))(1))   # pickled by reference to its name

try:
    pickle.dumps(lambda x: x)                      # lambdas have no importable name
except (pickle.PicklingError, AttributeError) as error:
    print("cannot pickle a lambda")

# OUTPUT:
# 2
# cannot pickle a lambda

expert.content:
Sharing State Safely

  • Threads: protect shared data with Lock, RLock, Semaphore, or avoid sharing by passing work through a thread-safe queue.Queue.
  • Processes: multiprocessing.Queue / Pipe for messages, Value / Array for small shared numbers, shared_memory for big buffers (such as NumPy arrays) without copying, and Manager for shared dicts and lists (convenient but slow, since each access is an inter-process call).
  • Prefer message passing ("share by communicating") over shared mutable state in both models; it removes most locking bugs.

Choosing: A Practical Checklist

  • Waiting on a network, disk or database: threads (or asyncio).
  • Heavy computation in pure Python: processes, with batches large enough to cover start-up and pickling cost.
  • Need isolation (untrusted or crash-prone code, memory leaks): processes. Use maxtasksperchild (in multiprocessing.Pool) or max_tasks_per_child (executor) to recycle leaky workers.
  • Many tasks that share a large read-only structure: threads (or processes created with fork before heavy writes, taking care with its risks) to avoid copying it.
  • Python 3.13+ free-threaded build: threads may now give real parallelism (see the last topic).

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Threads: tiny start-up cost and easy data sharingThreads: one GIL, so no CPU parallelism
Processes: true parallel Python on every coreProcesses: heavier start-up and more memory
Processes: a crash in one does not kill the othersThreads: shared data needs locks to stay correct
Each process has its own GIL, so no contentionProcesses: data must be pickled and copied

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Thread vs process?Threads share one process's memory and one GIL; processes have separate memory and each their own GIL
Why do processes give parallelism in Python?Each has its own interpreter and GIL, so they run on separate cores at the same time
How do processes share data?Queues, pipes, shared memory or managers - data is pickled and copied
Why the if __name__ == "__main__" guard?With spawn, children re-import the main module; without the guard they would start processes recursively
What cannot be sent to a worker process?Unpicklable objects such as lambdas, open files, locks and connections

Advantages

Advantages: threads - low overhead, shared state, millisecond startup. Processes - real multi-core speedup, memory isolation, no GIL contention between workers.
codeExamples:
import multiprocessing as mp, time

def burn(n): return sum(i * i for i in range(n))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    with mp.Pool(4) as pool:
        pool.map(burn, [3_000_000] * 4)           # 4 jobs on 4 cores
    print(f"4 CPU jobs in processes: {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f}s")

# OUTPUT (example, 4+ cores - roughly 1 job's time, not 4x):
# 4 CPU jobs in processes: 0.31s

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: threads - races, deadlocks and no CPU parallelism. Processes - memory per worker, slow startup (especially "spawn"), arguments and results must be pickled.
codeExamples:
import pickle

# Everything sent to another process is pickled; some objects cannot be
data = {"ok": [1, 2, 3]}
print(len(pickle.dumps(data)), "bytes serialised")
try:
    pickle.dumps(lambda x: x)       # lambdas / open files / locks cannot cross
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, "-", str(e)[:48])

# OUTPUT (example):
# 33 bytes serialised
# PicklingError - Can't pickle <function <lambda> at 0x000001>

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: processes cannot share ordinary objects, and there is an OS cap on both (thousands of threads, hundreds of processes before memory hurts). Start method differs by OS.
codeExamples:
import multiprocessing as mp

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # fork: Linux default (fast, copies memory); spawn: Windows/macOS default
    # (fresh interpreter, re-imports the main module - hence the __main__ guard)
    print("default start method:", mp.get_start_method())
    print("available:", mp.get_all_start_methods())

# OUTPUT (example, Windows):
# default start method: spawn
# available: ['spawn']

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Default to threads/asyncio for I/O and processes for CPU, but in production prefer a managed pool (ProcessPoolExecutor, Celery, task queues) over hand-rolled workers. Keep payloads small, avoid shared mutable state, and consider whether horizontal scaling (more containers) beats in-process parallelism.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The GIL brings real limits: CPU-bound threads do not run in parallel, threads add switching overhead, and the GIL does not make your multi-step operations atomic. CPython hands the lock over about every 5 ms (sys.getswitchinterval()), so a thread can be interrupted between any two bytecodes. Unlike Java, where more threads give more throughput on more cores, you must design around this with processes, native extensions or locks.
Figure: each limitation has a standard workaround

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: Assuming threads give a speed-up, or that the GIL makes shared data safe, leads to slow programs and rare, hard-to-reproduce data corruption.

Why we need it:
  • Know what the GIL does not give you: speed-up and atomicity.
  • Recognise the workarounds: processes, C extensions, asyncio, locks.
  • Avoid shipping code that works in tests but fails under load.
  • Judge honestly whether a threaded design is worth it.

Complete Example: Correct results, no free speed-up

Four threads compute the same sum of squares and update a shared tally under a lock. Correctness is certain; speed-up is not claimed.
codeExamples:
import sys
import threading
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

N = 1000            # sum the squares below N
WORKERS = 4
REPEATS = 5000


def sum_squares(n):
    return sum(i * i for i in range(n))


class Tally:
    def __init__(self):
        self.value = 0
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def add(self):
        with self._lock:                # += is not atomic without this
            self.value += 1


def bump(tally):
    for _ in range(REPEATS):
        tally.add()


def main():
    expected = (N - 1) * N * (2 * N - 1) // 6
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(WORKERS) as pool:
        results = list(pool.map(sum_squares, [N] * WORKERS))
    print("expected sum:", expected)
    print("all threads correct:", all(r == expected for r in results))

    tally = Tally()
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=bump, args=(tally,))
               for _ in range(WORKERS)]
    for thread in threads:
        thread.start()
    for thread in threads:
        thread.join()
    print("tally:", tally.value)
    print("switch interval:", sys.getswitchinterval())   # default value


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT:
# expected sum: 332833500
# all threads correct: True
# tally: 20000
# switch interval: 0.005
codeExplanations: The formula (N-1)*N*(2N-1)/6 gives 332,833,500 for N = 1000, and every thread returns it. The tally reaches exactly 4 x 5000 = 20000 only because of the lock. The default switch interval is 0.005 seconds (5 ms), the point at which a running thread may be asked to release the GIL.

beginner.content:
Limitation 1: No Parallel Speed-up for CPU-bound Threads

Because only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time, splitting a calculation across threads does not use more than one core. It can even be slightly slower than doing it in one thread, because the threads fight over the lock and switch back and forth. Try this benchmark yourself (times differ by machine, so none are shown here):
codeExamples:
import time
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor, ThreadPoolExecutor

def burn(n):
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        total += i * i
    return total

def timed(label, run):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    run()
    print(f"{label:<10} {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    work = [5_000_000] * 4

    timed("sequential", lambda: [burn(n) for n in work])
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(4) as pool:
        timed("threads", lambda: list(pool.map(burn, work)))
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(4) as pool:
        timed("processes", lambda: list(pool.map(burn, work)))

# TYPICAL RESULT on a 4-core machine (standard CPython):
#   sequential  ~ 1x   (the baseline)
#   threads     ~ 1x or a little slower - no speed-up
#   processes   ~ 0.3x - 0.4x of the baseline (about 3x faster)
codeExplanations: All three versions do the same four chunks of work. Threads cannot run the chunks at once because of the GIL, so they take about as long as the sequential version. Processes have a GIL each, so the four chunks run on four cores. The gain is never a perfect 4x because of process start-up and result copying.

beginner.content:
Limitation 2: It Does Not Make Your Code Thread-Safe

Many beginners think "the GIL means I don't need locks". It does not. Operations that look like one step are often several, and a thread switch can happen between them. This "check then act" example looks harmless but runs the expensive part three times:
codeExamples:
import threading
import time

cache = {}
computations = []

def get(key):
    if key not in cache:             # step 1: check
        time.sleep(0.1)              # expensive work (also widens the race window)
        computations.append(key)
        cache[key] = key.upper()     # step 2: act
    return cache[key]

threads = [threading.Thread(target=get, args=("a",)) for _ in range(3)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

print(len(computations))

# OUTPUT:
# 3
codeExplanations: All three threads checked "key not in cache" before any of them had stored the result, so each decided to compute it. Every individual dictionary operation was safe, but the sequence of steps was not atomic. Fix it with a lock around the check-and-set, or use functools.lru_cache or a dedicated per-key lock.

beginner.content:
Limitation 3: Only the Main Thread Handles Signals

Signal handlers (such as Ctrl+C turning into KeyboardInterrupt) always run in the main thread. If the main thread is blocked waiting (for example on a lock) in a way that does not wake up, the program can seem to ignore Ctrl+C. Design long-running worker threads with a shared threading.Event to tell them to stop.

Introduction

GIL limitations are the situations where the lock hurts or fails to help: CPU-bound threads, lock contention, and misunderstanding that it makes your code thread-safe. It limits parallelism, not correctness.
codeExamples:
import threading, time

def count(n):
    while n: n -= 1

N = 10_000_000
t0 = time.perf_counter(); count(N); count(N)
print(f"sequential: {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f}s")

t0 = time.perf_counter()
a = threading.Thread(target=count, args=(N,)); b = threading.Thread(target=count, args=(N,))
a.start(); b.start(); a.join(); b.join()
print(f"2 threads : {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f}s")

# OUTPUT (example):
# sequential: 0.62s
# 2 threads : 0.65s

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

You need to know these limits to avoid designing a "multi-threaded speedup" that never arrives, and to avoid shipping races that the GIL merely hides most of the time.

Real-Time Use

Real symptoms: a Flask/Django worker pool using threads maxes out ONE core while others idle; a data-processing script shows 100 percent on one CPU only. Fix by running several worker processes (gunicorn -w N).
codeExamples:
import os, time

# Quick check you can run: measure CPU use vs wall time of the process
t0, c0 = time.perf_counter(), time.process_time()
sum(i * i for i in range(3_000_000))
wall = time.perf_counter() - t0
cpu = time.process_time() - c0
print(f"cpu/wall ratio: {cpu / wall:.2f}  (max 1.0 for threaded pure Python)")

# OUTPUT (example):
# cpu/wall ratio: 1.00  (max 1.0 for threaded pure Python)

beginner.content:
Diagram

   4 threads, 4 cores, pure Python
   core1 ██░░██░░██░░      only one thread holds the GIL at a time,
   core2 ░░██░░██░░██      so total CPU use is ~1 core even though
   core3 ░░░░░░░░░░░░      threads exist on all cores' schedulers
   core4 ░░░░░░░░░░░░

expert.content:
Contention and Latency

  • GIL contention overhead. With several CPU-bound threads on a multi-core machine, threads constantly request and hand over the GIL, which adds cost. Four CPU-bound threads can be slower than one.
  • Latency of I/O threads. An I/O thread that wakes up (a packet arrived) must wait to get the GIL back. If a CPU-bound thread is running, it waits up to one switch interval (5 ms) every time, so a mixed program can show poor responsiveness for its I/O.
  • Blocking calls in C extensions. A C function that does not release the GIL (many older extensions) freezes all other Python threads while it runs.
  • Fairness. The GIL is not a fair queue; a thread can reacquire it before others get a turn, so scheduling is not predictable.

Libraries That Release the GIL (and How to Do It Yourself)

Native code can release the GIL while it does not touch Python objects, so threads then run in parallel. NumPy, SciPy, many parts of pandas, hashlib (large inputs), zlib, lzma, and Pillow do this for their heavy loops. You can use the same idea:
  • Numba: @njit(nogil=True) compiles a function and releases the GIL while it runs.
  • Cython: a with nogil: block, or cdef ... nogil functions.
  • Rust / C / C++ extensions (PyO3, pybind11, the C-API macros Py_BEGIN_ALLOW_THREADS): release the GIL around work that does not use Python objects.
  • ctypes releases the GIL while calling a C function from a shared library.
codeExamples:
import hashlib
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

blocks = [bytes([i]) * 20_000_000 for i in range(4)]     # four 20 MB blocks

def digest(block):
    return hashlib.sha256(block).hexdigest()              # large input: GIL released

with ThreadPoolExecutor(4) as pool:
    results = list(pool.map(digest, blocks))

print(len(results), all(len(r) == 64 for r in results))

# OUTPUT:
# 4 True
#
# On a multi-core machine these four hashes run in parallel threads,
# because hashlib releases the GIL for large inputs.

expert.content:
Workarounds Summary

ApproachWorks becauseCost
multiprocessing / ProcessPoolExecutorOne GIL per processPickling, memory duplication, start-up
asyncioOne thread, tasks yield during I/OOnly for I/O; code must be async
Native code (NumPy, Numba, Cython, Rust)Heavy loops leave Python and release the GILExtra tooling or a rewrite
Sub-interpreters (3.12+ internals; concurrent.interpreters in 3.14)Each interpreter has its own GIL, in one processNewer; limited object sharing; extension modules must support it
Free-threaded build (3.13t and later)There is no GILSlower single thread, extension support still maturing
Another implementation (Jython, IronPython)No GILLags behind CPython; poor C-extension support

Do Not Over-Blame the GIL

  • Most Python programs are I/O-bound, single-threaded, or already use NumPy/processes - for them the GIL costs nothing noticeable.
  • When a program is slow, profile first. A better algorithm, a database index, caching or vectorisation usually outperforms any parallel rewrite.
  • Removing the GIL does not make code correct or automatically fast: you will still need locks, and parallel code has overhead.
  • Code written for the GIL era (relying on "this operation is atomic") must be revisited for free-threaded Python, which keeps built-in types safe but not your multi-step logic.

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Limits are well understood with standard workaroundsThreads give no speed-up on CPU-bound code
Processes sidestep the GIL completelyWorkarounds add complexity and memory use
Many C libraries release the GIL during heavy workSwitching between threads has its own cost
Locks and queues make shared data safeMissing locks cause rare, hard-to-find bugs

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the main limitation of the GIL?CPU-bound Python code cannot run in parallel on multiple cores using threads
Can CPU-bound threads be slower than a single thread?Yes - contention for the GIL adds overhead
Is if key not in d: d[key] = ... safe with the GIL?No - check-then-act spans several bytecodes; use a lock
How do NumPy and similar libraries avoid the limitation?Their C code releases the GIL while working on raw data
List ways around the GIL.Processes, native extensions with nogil, asyncio for I/O, sub-interpreters, free-threaded builds

Advantages

Advantages of knowing the limits: you can choose the right escape hatch: processes, native extensions that release the GIL, subinterpreters or free-threaded builds.
codeExamples:
# Escape hatch 1: processes (own GIL each)
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

def sq(n): return sum(i * i for i in range(n))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(2) as ex:
        print(list(ex.map(sq, [10, 100, 1000])))

# OUTPUT:
# [285, 328350, 332833500]

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the workarounds cost something: process pools add pickling and memory, native code adds a build chain, and thread-based speedups are unpredictable.
codeExamples:
import time, pickle
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

def passthrough(x): return len(x)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    big = list(range(2_000_000))
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(2) as ex:
        ex.submit(passthrough, big).result()
    print(f"sending 2M ints to a worker cost {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f}s of mostly pickling")

# OUTPUT (example):
# sending 2M ints to a worker cost 0.45s of mostly pickling

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: even with the GIL, race conditions on compound operations remain, and the GIL gives no ordering guarantees between threads or fairness.

Architect's Notes

Treat "uses one core" as a capacity-planning input: scale out with processes per core. If a service is CPU-bound and latency-sensitive, move the hot loop to native code rather than adding threads. Test any thread-based design under free-threaded Python before relying on accidental GIL protection.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Free-threaded Python is an optional CPython build with the GIL turned off (PEP 703), introduced as experimental in Python 3.13, so several threads can run Python code on different cores at once - much like JVM threads. Because nothing serialises threads any more, you must protect shared data with locks, exactly as in Java. The build is a separate executable (python3.13t), and some C extensions may re-enable the GIL if they are not ready.
Figure: the GIL build serialises threads; the free-threaded build runs them in parallel

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: Python programmers wanting multi-core threads had to switch to processes and copy data between them, which is heavy for large shared structures.

Why we need it:
  • Run CPU-bound threads in parallel inside one process with shared memory.
  • Know how to detect which build your program runs on.
  • Learn that correct locking matters more, not less, without the GIL.
  • Plan for the future of Python concurrency.

Complete Example: Detecting the build and staying thread-safe

This program runs on both builds. It reports which build it is on and uses a Lock, which is required with or without the GIL. Free-threaded builds need Python 3.13 or newer.
codeExamples:
import sys
import sysconfig
import threading

THREADS = 4
REPEATS = 10_000


def gil_enabled():
    check = getattr(sys, "_is_gil_enabled", None)   # exists on 3.13+
    return True if check is None else check()


def count(state, lock):
    for _ in range(REPEATS):
        with lock:                      # needed even more without the GIL
            state["value"] += 1


def main():
    free_threaded = bool(sysconfig.get_config_var("Py_GIL_DISABLED"))
    state = {"value": 0}
    lock = threading.Lock()
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=count, args=(state, lock))
               for _ in range(THREADS)]
    for thread in threads:
        thread.start()
    for thread in threads:
        thread.join()
    print("free-threaded build:", free_threaded)
    print("GIL enabled:", gil_enabled())
    print("counter:", state["value"])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT (standard build, any version):
# free-threaded build: False
# GIL enabled: True
# counter: 40000
#
# OUTPUT (python3.13t, free-threaded; first two lines differ):
# free-threaded build: True
# GIL enabled: False
# counter: 40000
codeExplanations: Py_GIL_DISABLED is 1 only in the free-threaded build, and sys._is_gil_enabled() reports the run-time state (it can be True even in that build if an incompatible extension is loaded). The counter is 40000 on both builds because the lock makes each increment atomic; without the lock the free-threaded build would lose updates.

beginner.content:
Python Without the GIL

Free-threaded Python is a build of CPython in which the GIL is turned off, so several threads can execute Python code at the same time on different cores. It comes from PEP 703, was shipped as an experimental option in Python 3.13, and moved toward official support in later releases (PEP 779). It is optional: the normal Python you install is still the GIL build. The free-threaded build is a separate executable, usually named python3.13t (the "t" stands for threaded).
Checking Which Build You Have
codeExamples:
import sys
import sysconfig

print(sysconfig.get_config_var("Py_GIL_DISABLED"))   # 1 in a free-threaded build

if hasattr(sys, "_is_gil_enabled"):                  # Python 3.13+
    print("GIL enabled:", sys._is_gil_enabled())
else:
    print("GIL enabled: True (older Python)")

# OUTPUT with the normal build (3.13):
# 0
# GIL enabled: True
#
# OUTPUT with the free-threaded build (python3.13t):
# 1
# GIL enabled: False
codeExplanations: Py_GIL_DISABLED is a build-time setting; it is 1 only in the free-threaded build. sys._is_gil_enabled() reports the state at run time: even in a free-threaded build the GIL can be switched back on, for example when you import a C extension that does not declare itself thread-safe.

beginner.content:
Getting It

  • Windows / macOS installers from python.org: in the installer's customise step, tick the option to install the free-threaded binaries. On Windows launch it with py -3.13t.
  • uv: uv python install 3.13t, then uv venv --python 3.13t.
  • Docker: use the free-threaded images of the official Python repository (tags ending in t).
  • From source: ./configure --disable-gil.
You can switch the GIL on or off at run time with python -X gil=1 / -X gil=0 or the environment variable PYTHON_GIL=1 / 0 - handy for comparing behaviour.

Real Parallelism With Plain Threads

In a free-threaded build the CPU-bound thread example finally scales - this is the same code that gave no speed-up on the normal build.
codeExamples:
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def fib(n):
    return n if n < 2 else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

start = time.perf_counter()
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:
    results = list(pool.map(fib, [27] * 4))
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start

print(results)

# OUTPUT:
# [196418, 196418, 196418, 196418]
#
# Timing (4 cores): on python3.13 the four calls run one after another,
# so it takes about 4x one call. On python3.13t they run on four cores at
# once, so it takes about 1x - roughly a 3-4x speed-up.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Free-threaded Python (PEP 703, experimental in 3.13, "python3.13t") is a CPython build without the GIL. Threads then truly run Python bytecode in parallel on several cores.
codeExamples:
import sys, sysconfig

# Is this a free-threaded build, and is the GIL actually off right now?
print("Py_GIL_DISABLED build flag:", sysconfig.get_config_var("Py_GIL_DISABLED"))
print("GIL enabled now:", getattr(sys, "_is_gil_enabled", lambda: True)())

# OUTPUT (example, standard 3.13 build):
# Py_GIL_DISABLED build flag: 0
# GIL enabled now: True

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Multi-core CPUs are the norm, but the GIL makes pure-Python threads use one core. Removing it lets CPU-bound threaded code scale without the pickling and memory cost of processes.
codeExamples:
import threading, time

def burn(n=3_000_000):
    s = 0
    for i in range(n): s += i
    return s

t0 = time.perf_counter()
ts = [threading.Thread(target=burn) for _ in range(4)]
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join()
print(f"4 CPU threads: {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f}s")

# OUTPUT (example):
# GIL build : 4 CPU threads: 0.90s   (serialised)
# python3.13t: 4 CPU threads: 0.26s  (parallel on 4 cores)

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Early adopters: data pipelines, in-memory servers and ML preprocessing that want shared in-process state across cores. You can also pick the mode at run time with PYTHON_GIL=0 or -X gil=0 on a free-threaded build.
codeExamples:
# Shell usage (not Python code) - run a script with the GIL forced on/off:
#   python3.13t -X gil=0 app.py
#   PYTHON_GIL=1 python3.13t app.py
# Inside the script, branch on what you got:
import sys
if getattr(sys, "_is_gil_enabled", lambda: True)():
    print("GIL on: use multiprocessing for CPU work")
else:
    print("GIL off: threads can use all cores")

# OUTPUT (example, standard build):
# GIL on: use multiprocessing for CPU work

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Standard build                         Free-threaded build (3.13t)
   T1 T2 T3 T4                            T1 T2 T3 T4
     | | /                                |  |  |  |
   [  GIL  ]  -> 1 core busy             per-object locks + biased refcounts
       |                                  |  |  |  |
     bytecode                           core1 core2 core3 core4 busy

expert.content:
How Python Stays Safe Without the GIL

Removing one big lock means the interpreter's internals need other protection. PEP 703's design combines several techniques:
TechniquePurpose
Biased reference countingThe owning thread updates a cheap non-atomic count; other threads use a separate atomic count - keeps the common case fast
Immortal objectsNone, True, small ints, interned strings never change their count, so sharing them needs no synchronisation
Deferred reference countingFunctions, modules and code objects that are shared by all threads avoid count traffic
Per-object locks / critical sectionsBuilt-in containers (list, dict, set) lock themselves, so each operation is safe
mimallocA thread-friendly memory allocator replaces pymalloc, which relied on the GIL
Thread-safe garbage collectionThe cycle collector stops all threads to run (stop-the-world)

What Changes for Your Code

  • Built-in types stay memory-safe. Concurrent list.append or dict updates cannot corrupt the interpreter.
  • Your multi-step logic was never safe, but now races surface far more often. Code that "worked" because the GIL rarely switched threads at the wrong moment may start to show lost updates. Use threading.Lock, queues, or thread-safe designs.
  • Use the standard tools: with lock:, queue.Queue, threading.local, and immutable data. Avoid relying on "this operation is atomic because of the GIL".
  • Mutating a collection while another thread iterates it can raise errors or give inconsistent views; iterate over a copy, or lock.
codeExamples:
import threading

counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def work():
    global counter
    for _ in range(100_000):
        with lock:                 # required in BOTH builds for correctness
            counter += 1

threads = [threading.Thread(target=work) for _ in range(8)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

print(counter)

# OUTPUT:
# 800000

expert.content:
Extension Modules and the GIL Re-enabling Rule

A C extension compiled for the normal build assumes the GIL protects it. If you import such a module into a free-threaded interpreter, Python turns the GIL back on (and prints a RuntimeWarning), because the module is not known to be safe. Extensions declare support with the Py_mod_gil module slot (Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED), or gil_used=False in PyBind11 / PyO3 equivalents, and need wheels built for the free-threaded ABI (tag cp313t). Major libraries (NumPy, SciPy, pandas, Cython, many others) have added free-threaded builds; check the compatibility trackers before depending on one. Use -X gil=0 to force the GIL off and test, or python -W error to turn the re-enable warning into a failure in CI.

Trade-offs

BenefitCost
CPU-bound Python code scales across cores with ordinary threadsSingle-threaded code is somewhat slower than in the GIL build (the overhead started large in 3.13 and has been shrinking in later releases)
Threads share memory: no pickling, no data copyingHigher memory use per object and less mature tooling
No process start-up cost, shared cachesExtensions must be audited and rebuilt
Simpler than multiprocessing for shared dataYou must write truly thread-safe code
Exact performance figures differ between releases and benchmarks; measure your own workload on both builds.

Where Free-Threading Fits Among the Options

  • Sub-interpreters (per-interpreter GIL since 3.12, a high-level concurrent.interpreters module in 3.14) give isolated parallelism inside one process with cheaper communication than separate processes.
  • Free-threading shares everything - best when threads genuinely need to work on the same large in-memory structures (a web server's caches, in-memory analytics, ML data loaders).
  • multiprocessing remains the choice for isolation and for programs that must run on every Python version today.
  • The long-term plan from the Python steering council is gradual: make the free-threaded build supported, build ecosystem confidence, and only then consider making it the default. Standard builds with a GIL remain the norm for now.
Check the "What's New" notes and the free-threading guide of the Python version you use, since this area changes quickly.

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Real multi-core parallelism for Python threadsExperimental in 3.13; support is still maturing
Threads share memory: no pickling or copyingSome single-thread code runs a little slower
Lighter than a pool of processesNot all C extensions are compatible yet
Familiar model for developers from JavaData races become possible: locks are your job

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is free-threaded Python?A CPython build (PEP 703, from 3.13) without the GIL, allowing threads to run Python code in parallel
How do you detect it?sysconfig.get_config_var("Py_GIL_DISABLED") and sys._is_gil_enabled()
How does it keep reference counts correct?Biased reference counting, immortal and deferred-count objects, per-object locks
What happens when you import an incompatible C extension?The interpreter re-enables the GIL (with a warning) unless forced off with -X gil=0
Do you still need locks without the GIL?Yes - built-ins stay safe, but multi-step operations on shared data need locks, and races become more visible

Advantages

Advantages: real thread parallelism, shared memory without pickling, simpler architecture for CPU work that must share large state.
codeExamples:
import threading

big_table = list(range(1_000_000))          # shared read-only data: no copy per worker
results = [0] * 4

def part(i):
    chunk = big_table[i::4]
    results[i] = sum(chunk)                 # each thread writes its own slot

ts = [threading.Thread(target=part, args=(i,)) for i in range(4)]
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join()
print(sum(results))

# OUTPUT:
# 499999500000

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: single-thread code is slower (about 5-10 percent in 3.13), memory use is higher, and previously "accidentally safe" code now races for real.

Limitations

Limitations: still experimental; C extensions must declare support (otherwise the GIL is re-enabled at import), and some wheels are missing for the "t" ABI.
codeExamples:
import sys, importlib

# On a free-threaded build, importing an extension that is not marked safe
# re-enables the GIL and warns. You can check afterwards:
import json                                   # pure stdlib: safe
print("GIL enabled after import:", getattr(sys, "_is_gil_enabled", lambda: True)())

# OUTPUT (example, 3.13t with only safe modules):
# GIL enabled after import: False
# (with an unsupported extension: RuntimeWarning, then True)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Adopt free-threading selectively: benchmark single-thread regressions, audit native dependencies, and add explicit locks or immutable data around shared state. Until the ecosystem is fully ready, process pools remain the safer default for production CPU parallelism, and subinterpreters (3.12+) are another middle path.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A thread is an independent flow of execution inside one program. All threads of a process share the same memory, so they can cooperate cheaply, but each has its own call stack. In Python you create a threading.Thread with a target function, call start() to run it concurrently and join() to wait for it. This is the same life cycle as Java's Thread class (new Thread(runnable), start(), join()). Because of the GIL, threads in CPython overlap waiting (I/O, sleep) very well but do not run Python bytecode in parallel.
Figure: start() makes the worker run beside main; join() waits for it to finish

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: A single-threaded program does one thing at a time: while it waits for a slow download or a sleep, everything else is frozen, and five waits of 0.3 s cost 1.5 s in total.

Why we need it:
  • Run several waiting tasks at the same time so total time is about the longest wait, not the sum.
  • Keep a program responsive: a background thread works while the main thread continues.
  • Model naturally concurrent jobs (one thread per connection, per sensor, per file).
  • Learn the base mechanism (start, join, names) that locks, events and pools build on.

Complete Example: Five overlapping worker threads

Five threads each wait 0.3 s. Started together, the whole job takes far less than the 1.5 s a sequential loop would need.
codeExamples:
import threading
import time

WORKER_COUNT = 5
DELAY = 0.3                                 # seconds each worker "works"

results = {}


def square(n):
    time.sleep(DELAY)
    results[n] = n * n                      # each thread writes its own key


def main():
    threads = [
        threading.Thread(target=square, args=(n,), name=f"worker-{n}")
        for n in range(WORKER_COUNT)
    ]

    start = time.perf_counter()
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    print("all alive:", all(t.is_alive() for t in threads))
    for t in threads:
        t.join()
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start

    print("names:", [t.name for t in threads])
    print("results:", sorted(results.items()))
    print("overlapped:", elapsed < 1.0)     # sequential would take 1.5 s
    print("any alive:", any(t.is_alive() for t in threads))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT:
# all alive: True
# names: ['worker-0', 'worker-1', 'worker-2', 'worker-3', 'worker-4']
# results: [(0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 4), (3, 9), (4, 16)]
# overlapped: True
# any alive: False
codeExplanations: All threads are created first, then started, then joined, so the five 0.3 s sleeps overlap (about 0.3 s in total). Results are read only after join() and sorted, so the output is the same on every run. After join() no thread is alive any more.

beginner.content:
A Thread in Three Steps

A thread is an independent flow of execution inside your program. Python's threading module (like java.lang.Thread) gives you the Thread class. The pattern is always:
  1. Create it: Thread(target=function, args=(...))
  2. Start it: t.start() - the function now runs concurrently.
  3. Join it: t.join() - wait until it has finished.
Call start(), not run(): calling run() just executes the function in the current thread, with no concurrency.
codeExamples:
import threading

def greet(name, times):
    for i in range(times):
        print(f"Hello {name} {i}")

t = threading.Thread(target=greet, args=("Abaji", 2))
t.start()
t.join()
print("done")

# OUTPUT:
# Hello Abaji 0
# Hello Abaji 1
# done
codeExplanations: The worker thread runs greet("Abaji", 2). join() makes the main thread wait for it, which is why "done" is printed last. Without join(), "done" could appear first or in the middle, because the two threads run independently.

beginner.content:
Running Several Threads

Create all the threads first, start them all, then join them all. Starting and joining inside the same loop would run them one after another.

Threads Do Not Return Values

A thread's target function can return a value, but join() discards it. Hand results back through a shared structure (as above), a queue.Queue, or use ThreadPoolExecutor futures (last topic of this module), which return results directly.

Waiting, Checking and Names

join(timeout) waits at most that many seconds; is_alive() tells you if the thread is still running. Give threads a name to make logs and debugging readable.
codeExamples:
import threading
import time

t = threading.Thread(target=time.sleep, args=(0.3,), name="sleeper")
t.start()

t.join(timeout=0.05)             # give up waiting after 50 ms
print(t.name, t.is_alive())

t.join()                          # now wait for real
print(t.name, t.is_alive())

# OUTPUT:
# sleeper True
# sleeper False

beginner.content:
Introduction

A thread runs a function concurrently with the rest of your program. Create one with threading.Thread(target=func, args=...), call start() to launch it and join() to wait for it to finish.
codeExamples:
import threading

def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello from {name}")

t = threading.Thread(target=greet, args=("worker",))   # create (not running yet)
t.start()                                              # begin running
t.join()                                               # wait until it finishes
print("main done")

# OUTPUT:
# Hello from worker
# main done

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Programs often need to wait (network, disk) without freezing everything else. Threads let one task wait while another continues, so a UI stays responsive and many downloads overlap.
codeExamples:
import threading, time

def task(n):
    time.sleep(1)                   # pretend to wait on a server
    print("task", n, "done")

t0 = time.perf_counter()
ts = [threading.Thread(target=task, args=(i,)) for i in range(3)]
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join()
print(f"total {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f}s instead of 3s")

# OUTPUT (example - order of the first 3 lines varies):
# task 0 done
# task 1 done
# task 2 done
# total 1.0s instead of 3s

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: background log flushing, parallel API calls, a GUI worker that keeps the window alive, a heartbeat sender. Subclassing Thread and daemon threads are common patterns.
codeExamples:
import threading, time

class Heartbeat(threading.Thread):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(daemon=True)        # daemon: dies with the main program
        self.beats = 0
    def run(self):                           # code executed by start()
        while True:
            self.beats += 1
            time.sleep(0.1)

hb = Heartbeat(); hb.start()
time.sleep(0.45)
print("beats so far:", hb.beats)

# OUTPUT (example):
# beats so far: 5

beginner.content:
Diagram

   main thread ──► Thread(...) ──► start() ──► (runs concurrently) ──┐
        │                                                           │
        └──────────────────── join()  (wait) ◄──────────────────────┘

expert.content:
Subclassing Thread

Instead of passing a function you can subclass Thread and override run(). This is handy when the thread owns state. Prefer the target= style for simple jobs; subclass when the thread is an object with a lifecycle.

Daemon Threads

A Python program exits when all non-daemon threads have finished. A daemon thread (daemon=True, set before start()) does not keep the program alive: when only daemon threads remain they are stopped abruptly - no finally blocks, no cleanup. Use daemons only for background chores that are safe to kill (heartbeats, metrics); never for work that must complete or release resources.
codeExamples:
import threading
import time

def background():
    while True:
        time.sleep(0.1)          # runs forever

t = threading.Thread(target=background, daemon=True)
t.start()

print("daemon:", t.daemon)
print("main finished - the program exits even though t is still running")

# OUTPUT:
# daemon: True
# main finished - the program exits even though t is still running

expert.content:
Exceptions Inside Threads

An exception that escapes a thread's function does not stop the main thread. By default a traceback is printed to stderr and that thread simply ends - easy to miss. Install threading.excepthook to log or collect such failures, or catch exceptions inside the target, or use futures, which re-raise on result().
codeExamples:
import threading

def hook(args):
    print("thread failed:", args.exc_type.__name__, args.exc_value)

threading.excepthook = hook

def bad():
    raise ValueError("boom")

t = threading.Thread(target=bad)
t.start()
t.join()
print("main continues")

# OUTPUT:
# thread failed: ValueError boom
# main continues

expert.content:
Thread-Local Data, Timers and Introspection

  • threading.local() gives each thread its own private attributes - ideal for per-thread connections or request context without passing arguments around.
  • threading.Timer(seconds, func) runs a function once after a delay (cancel with .cancel()).
  • threading.current_thread(), active_count(), enumerate(), main_thread(), get_ident() let you inspect what is running.
codeExamples:
import threading
import time

local = threading.local()
seen = []

def worker(n):
    local.value = n                      # private to this thread
    time.sleep(0.05)                     # other threads set THEIR value meanwhile
    seen.append((n, local.value))

threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(n,)) for n in range(3)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
print(sorted(seen))

timer = threading.Timer(0.1, print, args=("timer fired",))
timer.start()
timer.join()

# OUTPUT:
# [(0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2)]
# timer fired

expert.content:
Common Mistakes

  • Calling the function instead of passing it: Thread(target=work()) runs work immediately in the current thread and passes its result as the target. Write target=work.
  • One-item args without the comma: args=(5) is just the number 5. Use args=(5,).
  • Late-binding lambdas: Thread(target=lambda: print(i)) in a loop captures the variable i, not its value, so every thread sees the final value. Pass the value with args.
  • Forgetting to join: the main thread may finish and read incomplete results.
  • Too many threads: each costs memory (a stack of up to several MB of address space) and scheduling time. Use a pool for large numbers of tasks.
codeExamples:
import threading

threads = [threading.Thread(target=lambda: print("late binding:", i)) for i in range(3)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

fixed = [threading.Thread(target=print, args=("fixed:", i)) for i in range(3)]
for t in fixed:
    t.start()
for t in fixed:
    t.join()

# OUTPUT (lines of the same kind appear in thread-scheduling order):
# late binding: 2
# late binding: 2
# late binding: 2
# fixed: 0
# fixed: 1
# fixed: 2

expert.content:
Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Waiting tasks overlap: total time is about the longest waitThe GIL stops CPU-bound Python code from running in parallel
Threads share memory: no copying of data between themjoin() discards the return value: results need a shared structure
Cheap to create compared with separate processesShared memory invites race conditions and deadlocks
Simple API: Thread, start(), join()Output order between threads is nondeterministic and hard to test

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
start() vs run()?start() creates a new thread that calls run(); calling run() directly just runs it in the current thread
What does join() do?Blocks the caller until that thread finishes (or the timeout expires)
What is a daemon thread?A background thread that does not keep the program alive and is killed abruptly at exit
What happens if a thread raises an exception?Only that thread ends (traceback to stderr); the main thread continues - use threading.excepthook or futures to handle it
How do you get a result out of a thread?Shared structure, queue.Queue, or a Future from ThreadPoolExecutor

Advantages

Advantages: cheap to create, share memory directly, great for waiting-heavy work, and can return control to the caller immediately.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: exceptions in a thread do not reach the caller, threads cannot be killed from outside, and shared state invites bugs.
codeExamples:
import threading

def boom():
    raise ValueError("oops")

t = threading.Thread(target=boom)
try:
    t.start(); t.join()
    print("main thinks everything is fine")   # the exception stayed in the thread
except ValueError:
    print("never caught here")

# OUTPUT (example - traceback goes to stderr):
# Exception in thread Thread-1 (boom):
# ValueError: oops
# main thinks everything is fine

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a thread cannot return a value directly (use a queue, shared variable or Future), the GIL stops CPU parallelism, and each thread costs stack memory (about 8 MB virtual on Linux).
codeExamples:
import threading

t = threading.Thread(target=lambda: 42)
t.start(); t.join()
print("target return value is lost:", getattr(t, "result", None))

# Correct way to get a result: a Future from a pool
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
with ThreadPoolExecutor(1) as ex:
    print("future result:", ex.submit(lambda: 42).result())

# OUTPUT:
# target return value is lost: None
# future result: 42

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Raw threads are a low-level tool. In production prefer ThreadPoolExecutor or asyncio for lifecycle, errors and results; name threads for debugging, set daemon deliberately, and never share mutable state without a clear owner. Do not use threads for CPU-bound Python work.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A lock (mutex) allows only one thread at a time into a protected section of code, so threads that share data cannot corrupt it. threading.Lock corresponds to a Java synchronized block or a ReentrantLock. A plain Lock cannot be taken twice by the same thread; an RLock (reentrant lock, like Java's synchronized and ReentrantLock) can, which makes it the right choice when a locked method calls another locked method of the same object. Always use with lock: so the lock is released even when an exception occurs.
Figure: green = inside the critical section, red = blocked: only one holder at any moment

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: Several threads changing the same counter or object at once can interleave their read-modify-write steps and silently lose updates.

Why we need it:
  • Guarantee mutual exclusion: one thread at a time inside a critical section.
  • Keep shared objects consistent: every update completes before the next begins.
  • Use RLock so methods of a thread-safe class can call each other without self-deadlock.
  • Release automatically with with, even if the protected code raises.

Complete Example: A thread-safe Counter with RLock

Four threads update one shared Counter. increment_twice() takes the lock and then calls increment(), which takes it again: only an RLock allows that.
codeExplanations: Each increment is a read, an add and a write; the lock makes the three steps indivisible, so no update is lost. With a plain Lock the nested call in increment_twice() would block forever, because the thread already owns the lock. The RLock counts acquisitions and frees the lock only when the outermost with block ends.

beginner.content:
Why Locks?

When several threads read and change the same data, their steps can interleave and corrupt it (the next-but-one topic, Race Conditions, shows exactly how). A lock (mutex) lets only one thread at a time enter a protected section - the Python equivalent of Java's synchronized block or ReentrantLock. A lock has two operations: acquire() (take it, or wait until it is free) and release() (give it back).

Using a Lock the Right Way: with

Always use the with statement. It acquires on entry and always releases on exit, even if an exception happens inside - so the lock can never be left locked by mistake.
codeExamples:
import threading

balance = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def deposit_many(times):
    global balance
    for _ in range(times):
        with lock:                    # only one thread inside at a time
            balance += 1

threads = [threading.Thread(target=deposit_many, args=(100_000,)) for _ in range(4)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

print(balance)

# OUTPUT:
# 400000
codeExplanations: balance += 1 is a read, an add and a write. Without the lock two threads can read the same old value and one increment is lost. With the lock each increment completes before another thread starts, so the total is always exactly 4 x 100000.

beginner.content:
Trying a Lock Without Waiting
