acquire() normally waits forever. You can instead try with blocking=False or a timeout; it returns True if you got the lock and False if not. locked() reports the current state.
codeExamples:
import threading

lock = threading.Lock()

lock.acquire()
print(lock.locked())
print(lock.acquire(blocking=False))      # already taken: do not wait
print(lock.acquire(timeout=0.1))         # wait at most 0.1 s, then give up

lock.release()
print(lock.locked())

# OUTPUT:
# True
# False
# False
# False

beginner.content:
RLock: A Lock You Can Re-enter

A normal Lock is not reentrant: if the thread that holds it tries to acquire it again, it blocks forever (a self-deadlock). An RLock remembers which thread owns it and how many times it was acquired, so the same thread can acquire it repeatedly. It is released for others only when released the same number of times.
codeExamples:
import threading

rlock = threading.RLock()

with rlock:
    with rlock:                       # fine: same thread, counted twice
        print("re-entered the RLock")

class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self._lock = threading.RLock()
        self.value = 0

    def increment(self):
        with self._lock:
            self.value += 1

    def increment_twice(self):
        with self._lock:              # holds the lock...
            self.increment()          # ...and this takes it again
            self.increment()

c = Counter()
c.increment_twice()
print(c.value)

# OUTPUT:
# re-entered the RLock
# 2

beginner.content:
Introduction

A Lock is a mutual-exclusion flag: only the thread that holds it may enter the guarded section. An RLock (re-entrant lock) can be acquired again by the SAME thread without blocking itself.
codeExamples:
import threading

lock = threading.Lock()
with lock:                                   # acquire ... release automatically
    print("inside critical section, locked:", lock.locked())
print("outside, locked:", lock.locked())

# OUTPUT:
# inside critical section, locked: True
# outside, locked: False

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Two threads updating shared data can interleave their steps and lose updates. A lock makes the read-modify-write sequence indivisible.
codeExamples:
import threading

count = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def work():
    global count
    for _ in range(100_000):
        with lock:                           # only one thread at a time
            count += 1

ts = [threading.Thread(target=work) for _ in range(4)]
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join()
print(count)

# OUTPUT:
# 400000

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Used to guard counters, caches, connection pools, files being appended and any dict updated by many threads. RLock appears in classes whose public methods call each other.
codeExamples:
import threading

class Account:
    def __init__(self):
        self.balance = 0
        self._lock = threading.RLock()       # re-entrant: methods may call each other
    def deposit(self, n):
        with self._lock:
            self.balance += n
    def deposit_twice(self, n):
        with self._lock:                     # takes the lock ...
            self.deposit(n)                  # ... and deposit takes it again: OK with RLock
            self.deposit(n)

a = Account(); a.deposit_twice(50)
print(a.balance)

# OUTPUT:
# 100

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Thread A ─► acquire ─► [ critical section ] ─► release
   Thread B ─► acquire ─► ....blocked.................─► [ critical section ]

   Lock : A holds it, A asks again  ─► DEADLOCK
   RLock: A holds it, A asks again  ─► OK (counter 1 -> 2, needs 2 releases)

expert.content:
Lock vs RLock

AspectLockRLock
Same thread acquires twiceBlocks forever (deadlock)Allowed; counted
OwnerNone - any thread can release itOnly the owning thread may release it
SpeedFaster, simplerSlightly slower (tracks owner and count)
Typical useGuard one small critical sectionClasses whose public methods call each other; recursive functions
Prefer a plain Lock and keep critical sections small and non-nested. Reach for an RLock when re-entry is genuinely part of the design.
codeExamples:
import threading

lock = threading.Lock()
lock.acquire()

helper = threading.Thread(target=lock.release)     # a DIFFERENT thread releases it
helper.start()
helper.join()
print("lock still held:", lock.locked())

rlock = threading.RLock()
try:
    rlock.release()                                 # not the owner / not acquired
except RuntimeError as error:
    print("RuntimeError:", error)

# OUTPUT:
# lock still held: False
# RuntimeError: cannot release un-acquired lock

expert.content:
Design Rules for Using Locks

  • Lock the data, not the code. Associate each lock with the data it protects (often as an attribute next to it: self._lock), and take it every time that data is touched - reads of multi-field state included.
  • Keep critical sections tiny. Compute outside the lock, then lock only to read or update shared state. Never do I/O, sleep or call unknown callbacks while holding a lock.
  • Avoid nesting locks. If you must take two, always take them in the same global order (otherwise: deadlock, see the Deadlocks topic).
  • One lock per independent resource. A single global lock is simple but serialises everything; fine-grained locks scale better but are easier to get wrong.
  • Don't use acquire()/release() pairs by hand. If code between them raises, the release is skipped. Use with (or try/finally).
  • Prefer higher-level tools where possible: queue.Queue, ThreadPoolExecutor, immutable data and thread-local storage need no locks at all.

Timeouts for Robustness

In a long-running service, waiting forever on a lock turns a bug into a hang. Using a timeout lets you log, retry, or fail loudly instead.

Notes on the Implementation

  • threading.Lock wraps a low-level lock (_thread.lock), the same primitive the GIL machinery builds on. Acquiring an uncontended lock costs about as much as a function call.
  • The GIL does not make a lock unnecessary: a thread can be switched out between any two bytecodes of x += 1.
  • There is no built-in read-write lock. For read-mostly data, snapshot immutable copies, or use a third-party read-write lock.
  • Locks are not fair: waiting threads are not guaranteed to be served in order, so starvation is possible under heavy contention.
  • In multiprocessing use multiprocessing.Lock; a threading.Lock does not synchronise separate processes. In asyncio use asyncio.Lock - never a threading lock inside a coroutine.

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Simple and reliable way to protect shared dataThreads wait while the lock is held: less concurrency
with lock: releases automatically, even on exceptionsA plain Lock self-deadlocks if re-acquired by its owner
RLock lets locked methods call each other safelyForgetting the lock in one code path leaves a race condition
Supports acquire(timeout=...) to avoid waiting foreverSeveral locks used together can cause deadlocks

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why use with lock: instead of acquire/release?It releases the lock even if an exception occurs
Lock vs RLock?RLock can be re-acquired by the thread that holds it and is owned by that thread; a Lock cannot, and re-acquiring blocks forever
When do you need an RLock?When a method that holds the lock calls another method that takes the same lock (or in recursion)
How do you avoid waiting forever?acquire(timeout=...) or acquire(blocking=False)
Does the GIL remove the need for locks?No - compound operations such as x += 1 can still be interleaved

Advantages

Advantages: simple, correct protection for shared state; with guarantees release even on exceptions; acquire(timeout=...) avoids waiting forever.
codeExamples:
import threading

lock = threading.Lock()
lock.acquire()                               # held by someone
got = lock.acquire(timeout=0.2)              # try, give up after 0.2 s
print("acquired within timeout:", got)
lock.release()

# OUTPUT:
# acquired within timeout: False

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: locks serialise code (less parallelism), forgotten release causes hangs, and a plain Lock deadlocks if the same thread takes it twice.
codeExamples:
import threading

lock = threading.Lock()
with lock:
    ok = lock.acquire(blocking=False)        # same thread, plain Lock: cannot re-enter
    print("second acquire by same thread:", ok)
# Without blocking=False this line would hang forever (self-deadlock)

# OUTPUT:
# second acquire by same thread: False

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a Lock can be released by any thread, an RLock only by its owner; locks are not fair (no ordering) and are not shared across processes.
codeExamples:
import threading

lock = threading.Lock()
lock.acquire()
t = threading.Thread(target=lock.release)    # a different thread releases it: allowed
t.start(); t.join()
print("locked after foreign release:", lock.locked())

rl = threading.RLock()
try:
    rl.release()                             # never acquired by this thread
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("RLock:", e)

# OUTPUT:
# locked after foreign release: False
# RLock: cannot release un-acquired lock

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Keep critical sections tiny, never call unknown code or do I/O while holding a lock, and prefer higher-level designs (queues, immutable data, one owning thread) over shared locks. Use RLock only when re-entry is genuinely needed; frequent need often signals tangled class design.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A semaphore is a counter of permits. acquire() takes a permit and waits when none are left; release() returns one. Unlike a lock it admits up to N threads at the same time, so it limits concurrency instead of forbidding it. Java has the same class, java.util.concurrent.Semaphore, with identical acquire() and release() methods. Use threading.BoundedSemaphore if you want an error when a thread releases more often than it acquired.
Figure: Semaphore(2): two threads run at once, the others wait for a released permit

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: Starting hundreds of threads that all use a limited resource (database connections, an API with a rate limit) overloads it and makes requests fail.

Why we need it:
  • Cap the number of threads using a limited resource (connections, licences, slots).
  • Throttle load on a server without changing the number of threads you create.
  • Let extra threads wait politely instead of failing or crashing the resource.
  • Signal between threads when started with zero permits (producer releases, consumer acquires).

Complete Example: Limiting eight workers to three at a time

All eight threads start together, but a Semaphore(3) lets only three use the "resource" at any moment. A small lock protects the shared counters.
codeExamples:
import threading
import time

LIMIT = 3                                   # permits available
WORKERS = 8
WORK_TIME = 0.1                             # seconds spent holding a permit

semaphore = threading.Semaphore(LIMIT)
guard = threading.Lock()                    # protects the counters below
state = {"active": 0, "peak": 0, "done": 0}


def use_resource():
    with semaphore:                         # take a permit, give it back on exit
        with guard:
            state["active"] += 1
            state["peak"] = max(state["peak"], state["active"])
        time.sleep(WORK_TIME)
        with guard:
            state["active"] -= 1
            state["done"] += 1


def main():
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=use_resource) for _ in range(WORKERS)]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()

    print("workers finished:", state["done"])
    print("peak concurrent: ", state["peak"])
    print("within limit:    ", state["peak"] <= LIMIT)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT:
# workers finished: 8
# peak concurrent:  3
# within limit:     True
codeExplanations: Eight threads compete for three permits, so at most three are between "with semaphore" and its end at any time; the rest wait. The peak reaches exactly 3 because all threads start within a few milliseconds while each holds a permit for 0.1 s. The guard lock is still needed: the semaphore limits how many threads are inside, it does not protect the shared counters.

beginner.content:
A Counter of Permits

A semaphore is a lock that lets up to N threads in at the same time, instead of just one. It holds a counter of available "permits":
  • acquire() takes a permit (the counter goes down). If none are left, the thread waits.
  • release() returns a permit (the counter goes up) and wakes a waiting thread.
A Lock is like a semaphore with exactly one permit. Think of a car park with N spaces: the (N+1)-th car waits at the gate until one leaves. Java has the same class: java.util.concurrent.Semaphore.

Limiting Concurrency

Six workers all want to run, but the semaphore allows only two at once. The program measures the highest number that were ever inside together.
codeExamples:
import threading
import time

semaphore = threading.Semaphore(2)       # at most 2 threads inside at once
guard = threading.Lock()
active = 0
peak = 0

def worker():
    global active, peak
    with semaphore:                       # acquire on entry, release on exit
        with guard:
            active += 1
            peak = max(peak, active)
        time.sleep(0.1)                   # pretend to use the limited resource
        with guard:
            active -= 1

threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker) for _ in range(6)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

print("peak concurrent workers:", peak)

# OUTPUT:
# peak concurrent workers: 2
codeExplanations: All six threads start at once, but only two get past "with semaphore" at any moment; the others wait. The small guard lock protects the two shared counters (active and peak), because the semaphore only limits how many threads are inside, it does not protect the data they share.

beginner.content:
Typical Uses

  • Connection pools: allow at most N database or API connections at the same time.
  • Rate and load limiting: do not hit a server with more than N parallel downloads.
  • Bounded resources: N printers, N licences, N GPU slots.
  • Signalling: a semaphore starting at 0 lets one thread tell another "an item is ready".
codeExamples:
import threading
import time

ready = threading.Semaphore(0)           # no permits yet: consumers must wait

def producer():
    time.sleep(0.1)
    print("item produced")
    ready.release()                       # hand out one permit

def consumer():
    ready.acquire()                       # blocks until the producer releases
    print("item consumed")

c = threading.Thread(target=consumer)
p = threading.Thread(target=producer)
c.start()
p.start()
c.join()
p.join()

# OUTPUT:
# item produced
# item consumed

beginner.content:
Introduction

A Semaphore is a lock with a counter: up to N threads may hold it at once. acquire() decreases the counter (blocking at 0), release() increases it.
codeExamples:
import threading

sem = threading.Semaphore(2)                 # 2 permits
sem.acquire(); sem.acquire()
print("third acquire possible:", sem.acquire(blocking=False))
sem.release()
print("after one release:", sem.acquire(blocking=False))

# OUTPUT:
# third acquire possible: False
# after one release: True

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Many resources are limited: DB connections, API rate quotas, open files. A semaphore caps how many threads use the resource at once without serialising them completely.
codeExamples:
import threading, time

sem = threading.Semaphore(3)                 # at most 3 downloads at once
active = 0; peak = 0; m = threading.Lock()

def download(i):
    global active, peak
    with sem:
        with m:
            active += 1; peak = max(peak, active)
        time.sleep(0.1)
        with m:
            active -= 1

ts = [threading.Thread(target=download, args=(i,)) for i in range(9)]
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join()
print("peak concurrent downloads:", peak)

# OUTPUT:
# peak concurrent downloads: 3

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: connection-pool limits, throttling calls to a rate-limited API, limiting parallel disk-heavy jobs, a "parking lot" of N workers.
codeExamples:
import threading, time

api_slots = threading.BoundedSemaphore(2)    # 2 concurrent API calls allowed

def call_api(n):
    with api_slots:
        print(f"call {n} started")
        time.sleep(0.05)

ts = [threading.Thread(target=call_api, args=(i,)) for i in range(4)]
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join()
print("all calls finished")

# OUTPUT (example - start order varies):
# call 0 started
# call 1 started
# call 2 started
# call 3 started
# all calls finished

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Semaphore(3)         permits: [■][■][■]
   T1 acquire ─► [■][■][ ]      T2 acquire ─► [■][ ][ ]
   T3 acquire ─► [ ][ ][ ]      T4 acquire ─► BLOCKED until someone releases

expert.content:
BoundedSemaphore: Catch Over-Release Bugs

A plain Semaphore lets you release() more times than you acquire()d, silently raising the limit above N - a bug that is hard to find later. BoundedSemaphore raises ValueError instead. Use it whenever the counter is meant to represent a fixed pool.
codeExamples:
import threading

plain = threading.Semaphore(1)
plain.release()                           # no error: the limit is now 2!
print(plain.acquire(blocking=False), plain.acquire(blocking=False))

bounded = threading.BoundedSemaphore(1)
try:
    bounded.release()                     # more releases than acquires
except ValueError as error:
    print("ValueError:", error)

# OUTPUT:
# True True
# ValueError: Semaphore released too many times

expert.content:
Non-Blocking and Timed Acquire

Like locks, semaphores support acquire(blocking=False) and acquire(timeout=...), returning whether a permit was obtained. This allows "try, or skip/shed load" designs instead of queueing without limit.
codeExamples:
import threading

slots = threading.BoundedSemaphore(2)

def try_handle(request):
    if not slots.acquire(blocking=False):
        return f"{request}: busy, try later"          # shed load
    try:
        return f"{request}: handled"
    finally:
        slots.release()

print(try_handle("req-1"))

slots.acquire()
slots.acquire()                                       # both permits taken elsewhere
print(try_handle("req-2"))

# OUTPUT:
# req-1: handled
# req-2: busy, try later

expert.content:
A Semaphore-Limited Thread Pool Queue

ThreadPoolExecutor has an unbounded internal queue: submitting a million tasks stores a million pending items in memory. A semaphore gives you back-pressure: the producer blocks when too many tasks are already outstanding.
codeExamples:
import threading
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

class BoundedExecutor:
    def __init__(self, workers, max_pending):
        self._pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=workers)
        self._slots = threading.BoundedSemaphore(max_pending)

    def submit(self, func, *args):
        self._slots.acquire()                         # blocks when the queue is full
        future = self._pool.submit(func, *args)
        future.add_done_callback(lambda _: self._slots.release())
        return future

    def shutdown(self):
        self._pool.shutdown(wait=True)

executor = BoundedExecutor(workers=2, max_pending=4)
futures = [executor.submit(pow, 2, n) for n in range(10)]
print([f.result() for f in futures])
executor.shutdown()

# OUTPUT:
# [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512]

expert.content:
Semaphore vs Other Primitives

PrimitiveMeaningUse when
Lock1 thread inside; the thread that took it releases itProtect shared data
Semaphore(n)Up to n threads inside; any thread may releaseLimit access to a resource pool
EventA flag threads wait on"Go" and "stop" signals
ConditionWait until a condition on shared state holdsProducer / consumer protocols
queue.QueueThread-safe queue (built from the above)Passing work between threads (usually the best choice)
Remember: the semaphore bounds how many threads run a section, not what they do to shared data. If the section modifies shared state, it still needs its own lock. Also note asyncio.Semaphore is a different class for coroutines and multiprocessing has multiprocessing.Semaphore for processes.

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Limits concurrency to exactly N threadsDoes not protect shared data: you still need a lock
Protects limited resources from overloadA forgotten release() permanently loses a permit
with statement releases the permit automaticallyPlain Semaphore allows extra releases; use BoundedSemaphore to catch them
Can also be used as a simple signalling toolChoosing N wrongly either wastes capacity or overloads the resource

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a semaphore?A synchronisation primitive with a counter of permits; acquire decrements (waiting at zero), release increments
Semaphore vs Lock?A lock admits one thread; a semaphore admits up to N, and any thread may release it
Why prefer BoundedSemaphore?It raises ValueError if released more than acquired, catching accounting bugs
Name a real use.Limiting concurrent connections or downloads; back-pressure on a work queue
Does a semaphore protect shared data?No - with N > 1 threads inside, shared data still needs a lock

Advantages

Advantages: controls concurrency level precisely; BoundedSemaphore detects bugs where release is called too often.
codeExamples:
import threading

b = threading.BoundedSemaphore(1)
b.acquire(); b.release()
try:
    b.release()                              # more releases than acquires: bug caught
except ValueError as e:
    print("bug detected:", e)

# OUTPUT:
# bug detected: Semaphore released too many times

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: a plain Semaphore silently allows over-release, which grows the permit count, and nothing links permits to specific threads so leaks are hard to spot.
codeExamples:
import threading

s = threading.Semaphore(1)
s.release(); s.release()                     # bug: now 3 permits exist
print([s.acquire(blocking=False) for _ in range(4)])

# OUTPUT:
# [True, True, True, False]

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: works only inside one process, gives no fairness or priority, and does not protect data by itself - with N greater than 1 it does not stop races on shared data.
codeExamples:
import threading

sem = threading.Semaphore(4)                 # lets 4 threads in at once
total = 0
def add():
    global total
    with sem:
        for _ in range(100_000):
            total += 1                       # still a race: semaphore is not a mutex here

ts = [threading.Thread(target=add) for _ in range(4)]
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join()
print("expected 400000, got", total)

# OUTPUT (example - may be exact on some runs, but not guaranteed):
# expected 400000, got 398214

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use semaphores for throttling, not for protecting data (use a Lock for that). Always release in a finally/with block. For distributed or cross-process limits you need Redis, a database or an API gateway; in async code use asyncio.Semaphore instead.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Locks keep threads out of each other's way, but often one thread must wait until another says "go". An Event is a flag that threads can wait() on until another thread calls set(). A Condition combines a lock with a waiting room: a thread waits until a condition on shared data becomes true and is woken by notify(). In Java the same ideas are wait()/notify() (or Condition.await()/signal()) and CountDownLatch for one-shot signals.
Figure: the consumer sleeps in wait() until the producer calls notify()

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: Without a signalling tool, a waiting thread must busy-loop (while not ready: pass), burning a whole CPU core and still reacting late.

Why we need it:
  • Make a thread sleep until work is available instead of polling.
  • Build producer-consumer hand-offs on shared data with Condition.
  • Broadcast one-shot signals such as "start" or "stop" with Event.
  • React immediately to a change, with zero CPU use while waiting.

Complete Example: Producer and consumer with a Condition

The consumer sleeps in wait_for() until the producer has put an item in the buffer. A sentinel value tells it to stop, and an Event reports completion.
codeExamples:
import threading
from collections import deque

ITEM_COUNT = 5
SENTINEL = None                             # marks "no more items"

buffer = deque()
condition = threading.Condition()           # a lock plus a waiting room
finished = threading.Event()
consumed = []


def put(item):
    with condition:
        buffer.append(item)
        condition.notify()                  # wake the waiting consumer


def producer():
    for n in range(1, ITEM_COUNT + 1):
        put(n * 10)
    put(SENTINEL)


def consumer():
    while True:
        with condition:
            condition.wait_for(lambda: len(buffer) > 0)
            item = buffer.popleft()
        if item is SENTINEL:
            break
        consumed.append(item)
    finished.set()                          # tell main we are done


def main():
    workers = [threading.Thread(target=consumer), threading.Thread(target=producer)]
    for t in workers:
        t.start()

    print("finished in time:", finished.wait(timeout=5))
    for t in workers:
        t.join()
    print("consumed:", consumed)
    print("buffer empty:", len(buffer) == 0)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT:
# finished in time: True
# consumed: [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
# buffer empty: True
codeExplanations: The consumer is started first and goes to sleep in wait_for() because the buffer is empty. Each put() appends under the lock and calls notify(), which wakes the consumer. With a single consumer, items are consumed in the order they were produced, so the printed list is always the same. finished.wait(timeout=5) returns True as soon as the consumer sets the event.

beginner.content:
Threads Often Need to Wait for Each Other

Locks keep threads out of each other's way. But often one thread must wait until another thread says "go": a worker waits for data, a service waits for a shutdown request. Python has two tools for this:
  • Event - a simple flag. Threads wait until it is set.
  • Condition - a lock plus a waiting room: threads wait until some condition on shared data becomes true, and are woken when another thread changes that data.
Using these is far better than busy-waiting (while not ready: pass), which burns an entire CPU core doing nothing.

Event: A Flag Threads Can Wait On

An Event starts cleared. wait() blocks until another thread calls set(). All waiting threads are released at once.
MethodDoes
set()Sets the flag; wakes every waiting thread
clear()Resets the flag to False
wait(timeout=None)Blocks until set; returns True if set, False if the timeout expired
is_set()Checks the flag without waiting
codeExamples:
import threading
import time

start = threading.Event()
finished = []

def runner(n):
    start.wait()                  # every runner waits at the starting line
    finished.append(n)

threads = [threading.Thread(target=runner, args=(n,)) for n in range(3)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()

time.sleep(0.1)
print("started so far:", len(finished))     # nobody has moved yet

start.set()                       # the starting gun
for t in threads:
    t.join()
print(sorted(finished))

print(threading.Event().wait(timeout=0.1))  # nobody sets it: times out

# OUTPUT:
# started so far: 0
# [0, 1, 2]
# False

beginner.content:
Event as a Stop Signal

A very common pattern: a background worker loops until someone sets a "stop" event. Waiting on the event instead of sleep() lets it wake immediately when asked to stop.
codeExamples:
import threading

stop = threading.Event()
ticks = 0

def worker():
    global ticks
    while not stop.is_set():
        ticks += 1
        stop.wait(0.05)           # sleeps 50 ms, but wakes at once if stop is set

t = threading.Thread(target=worker)
t.start()

stop.wait(0.3)                    # let it run for a moment
stop.set()                        # ask it to finish
t.join()

print("ticked:", ticks > 0)
print("stopped cleanly")

# OUTPUT:
# ticked: True
# stopped cleanly

beginner.content:
Introduction

An Event is a simple flag threads can wait on: wait() blocks until another thread calls set(). A Condition pairs a lock with wait/notify so threads sleep until some state becomes true.
codeExamples:
import threading, time

ready = threading.Event()

def waiter():
    print("waiting for signal...")
    ready.wait()                             # blocks until set()
    print("got the signal")

t = threading.Thread(target=waiter); t.start()
time.sleep(0.2)
ready.set()                                  # wake every waiter
t.join()

# OUTPUT:
# waiting for signal...
# got the signal

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Busy loops that poll a variable waste CPU and add latency. Events and conditions let threads sleep efficiently and wake exactly when something happens.
codeExamples:
import threading, time

stop = threading.Event()

def worker():
    n = 0
    while not stop.is_set():                 # clean shutdown flag
        n += 1
        stop.wait(0.05)                      # sleeps, but wakes at once if stop is set
    print("worker stopped after", n, "loops")

t = threading.Thread(target=worker); t.start()
time.sleep(0.3); stop.set(); t.join()

# OUTPUT (example):
# worker stopped after 7 loops

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: graceful shutdown signals, "service is ready" gates at startup, and producer-consumer buffers built with a Condition.
codeExamples:
import threading
from collections import deque

buf = deque(); cond = threading.Condition()

def consumer():
    with cond:
        while not buf:                       # ALWAYS re-check in a loop
            cond.wait()                      # releases the lock while sleeping
        print("consumed:", buf.popleft())

def producer():
    with cond:
        buf.append("job-1")
        cond.notify()                        # wake one consumer

c = threading.Thread(target=consumer); c.start()
threading.Thread(target=producer).start()
c.join()

# OUTPUT:
# consumed: job-1

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Event:                               Condition:
   thread A ── wait() ──┐               consumer: with cond: while not ready: wait()
                        ├─► blocked                                  ▲
   thread B ── set()  ──┘─► A resumes   producer: with cond: ready=True; notify() ┘

expert.content:
Condition: Wait Until the Data Is Right

A Condition combines a lock with the ability to wait and be notified. The pattern:
  1. Waiter: take the lock, then while not condition: cond.wait(). wait() releases the lock while sleeping and re-acquires it before returning.
  2. Changer: take the lock, change the shared data, then cond.notify() (or notify_all()).
Always test the condition in a while loop (or use wait_for(predicate)): a woken thread must re-check, because another thread may have consumed the item first, or the wake-up may be spurious.
codeExamples:
import threading
import time

condition = threading.Condition()
buffer = []

def consumer():
    with condition:
        condition.wait_for(lambda: len(buffer) > 0)   # sleeps until True
        item = buffer.pop(0)
    print("consumed", item)

def producer():
    time.sleep(0.1)
    with condition:
        buffer.append("data")
        condition.notify()                             # wake one waiter
    print("produced data")

c = threading.Thread(target=consumer)
p = threading.Thread(target=producer)
c.start()
p.start()
c.join()
p.join()

# OUTPUT (the two lines may swap order):
# produced data
# consumed data
codeExplanations: The consumer starts first and finds the buffer empty, so wait_for() releases the lock and sleeps. After 0.1 s the producer adds the item and calls notify(). The consumer wakes, re-acquires the lock, re-checks the predicate (now true) and removes the item. Because both sides use the same lock, the buffer is never read while half-modified.

expert.content:
A Bounded Buffer With Two Conditions

A classic producer/consumer buffer with limited capacity: producers wait when it is full, consumers wait when it is empty. (In real code use queue.Queue, which is built exactly like this - the example shows the mechanism.)
codeExamples:
import threading

class BoundedBuffer:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.items = []
        self.capacity = capacity
        lock = threading.Lock()
        self.not_full = threading.Condition(lock)     # two conditions, one lock
        self.not_empty = threading.Condition(lock)

    def put(self, item):
        with self.not_full:
            self.not_full.wait_for(lambda: len(self.items) < self.capacity)
            self.items.append(item)
            self.not_empty.notify()

    def get(self):
        with self.not_empty:
            self.not_empty.wait_for(lambda: len(self.items) > 0)
            item = self.items.pop(0)
            self.not_full.notify()
            return item

buffer = BoundedBuffer(capacity=2)
consumed = []

def producer():
    for i in range(5):
        buffer.put(i)

def consumer():
    for _ in range(5):
        consumed.append(buffer.get())

threads = [threading.Thread(target=producer), threading.Thread(target=consumer)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

print(consumed)

# OUTPUT:
# [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]

expert.content:
Barrier: Wait for Everyone

A threading.Barrier(n) makes threads wait until n of them have arrived, then releases them all together - useful for phased computations ("everyone finish phase 1 before phase 2 starts"). An optional action runs once when the barrier trips.
codeExamples:
import threading

barrier = threading.Barrier(3, action=lambda: print("all arrived"))
log = []

def worker(n):
    log.append(f"phase 1 by {n}")
    barrier.wait()                 # nobody passes until all 3 have called wait()
    log.append(f"phase 2 by {n}")

threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(n,)) for n in range(3)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

phase1 = [i for i, line in enumerate(log) if line.startswith("phase 1")]
phase2 = [i for i, line in enumerate(log) if line.startswith("phase 2")]
print(max(phase1) < min(phase2))   # every phase-1 entry comes before any phase-2 entry

# OUTPUT:
# all arrived
# True

expert.content:
Choosing the Right Tool

NeedUse
One-time "go" or "stop" signal for many threadsEvent
Wait for a condition on shared state; fine control of who is wokenCondition
Hand items from producers to consumersqueue.Queue (built on Condition; handles all the waiting for you)
All threads must reach a point togetherBarrier
Limit how many threads use a resourceSemaphore
Pitfalls: a notify() sent before anyone waits is lost (conditions have no memory - an Event's flag does); calling wait() without holding the condition's lock raises RuntimeError; use notify_all() when waiters have different predicates; always give long waits a timeout so a lost wake-up cannot hang forever.

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Waiting threads use no CPU while they sleepCondition needs its lock held around wait and notify
Instant wake-up when the state changesAlways re-check the condition (wait_for or a while loop)
Event is a very simple one-flag signalA missed set() or notify() leaves a thread waiting forever
Condition expresses "wait until this is true" cleanlyAn Event carries no data: only "happened or not"

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Event vs Condition?An Event is a simple flag; a Condition pairs a lock with wait/notify so threads can wait for arbitrary conditions on shared data
Why wait in a while loop (or use wait_for)?To re-check the condition after waking: another thread may have changed it, or the wake-up was spurious
What does wait() do with the lock?Releases it while sleeping and re-acquires it before returning
notify() vs notify_all()?Wake one waiting thread vs all waiting threads
Why not busy-wait?It wastes CPU; Event/Condition put the thread to sleep until needed

Advantages

Advantages: no polling, near-zero CPU while waiting, timeouts supported, one set() releases many threads.
codeExamples:
import threading

e = threading.Event()
print("set within 0.1s?", e.wait(timeout=0.1))   # returns False on timeout
e.set()
print("set within 0.1s?", e.wait(timeout=0.1))   # returns True immediately

# OUTPUT:
# set within 0.1s? False
# set within 0.1s? True

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: Conditions are easy to misuse: forgetting the while-loop causes lost or spurious wakeups, and notify before wait is simply lost.
codeExamples:
import threading

cond = threading.Condition()
with cond:
    cond.notify()                            # nobody is waiting: notification is lost
    got = cond.wait(timeout=0.2)             # waits and times out
print("woken by earlier notify:", got)

# OUTPUT:
# woken by earlier notify: False

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: an Event cannot carry data, a set Event stays set until clear() (races on reuse), and neither works across processes (use multiprocessing.Event).
codeExamples:
import threading

e = threading.Event()
e.set(); e.clear()                           # reset flag
print("is_set after clear:", e.is_set())
# If two waiters need separate signals, one shared Event cannot tell them apart:
# use a Queue (carries data) or one Event per waiter.

# OUTPUT:
# is_set after clear: False

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

For data hand-off prefer queue.Queue, which is a tested Condition-based design. Use Event for state flags such as shutdown, and Condition only when you must wait on a compound predicate over shared state. Always document who sets, who clears, and how timeouts are handled.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the exact timing of threads. The classic form is the lost update: two threads read the same old value, each computes a new one and each writes it back, so one update overwrites the other. Statements such as balance -= 30 or count += 1 look like one step but are several; Java programmers know the same problem with unsynchronised fields, solved by synchronized or AtomicInteger. The fix is to make the whole read-compute-write sequence atomic with a lock.
Figure: both threads read 100 before either writes: balance ends at 70, not 40

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: The program gives the right answer most of the time and a wrong one occasionally, and the failure disappears whenever you add a print or run it under a debugger.

Why we need it:
  • Recognise unsafe read-modify-write sequences on shared data.
  • Understand why such bugs are rare, silent and hard to reproduce.
  • Reproduce them on purpose with a forced pause so they can be tested.
  • Fix them by protecting the whole sequence with one lock.

Complete Example: Lost update and its lock fix

A short pause between read and write forces the bad interleaving every time, so the program shows the bug and the fix side by side.
codeExamples:
import threading
import time

START_BALANCE = 100
AMOUNT = 30
PAUSE = 0.05                                # forces the bad interleaving


class Account:
    def __init__(self, balance):
        self.balance = balance
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def withdraw_unsafe(self, amount):
        current = self.balance              # 1. read
        time.sleep(PAUSE)                   # 2. other thread reads old value now
        self.balance = current - amount     # 3. write based on the OLD value

    def withdraw_safe(self, amount):
        with self._lock:                    # whole sequence is atomic
            self.withdraw_unsafe(amount)


def run_two_withdrawals(action):
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=action, args=(AMOUNT,)) for _ in range(2)]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()


def main():
    unsafe = Account(START_BALANCE)
    run_two_withdrawals(unsafe.withdraw_unsafe)
    safe = Account(START_BALANCE)
    run_two_withdrawals(safe.withdraw_safe)

    print("expected:", START_BALANCE - 2 * AMOUNT)
    print("unsafe:  ", unsafe.balance)
    print("safe:    ", safe.balance)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT:
# expected: 40
# unsafe:   70
# safe:     40
codeExplanations: In the unsafe version both threads read 100 during the 0.05 s pause, so both write 70 and one withdrawal is lost. In the safe version the lock lets the second thread read only after the first has written, so it sees 70 and writes 40. Real race conditions have no visible sleep, which is why they appear only occasionally.

beginner.content:
What Is a Race Condition?

A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the exact timing of threads - on who "wins the race" to the shared data. The same program may give the right answer 999 times and a wrong one the 1000th, which makes these bugs notoriously hard to reproduce ("heisenbugs"). They appear whenever threads read and modify shared data without coordination.

The Classic Case: Lost Update

Updating a value is three steps: read it, compute a new one, write it back. If two threads both read before either writes, one update overwrites the other. We put a tiny sleep between read and write to make the bad timing happen every time:
codeExamples:
import threading
import time

balance = 100

def withdraw(amount):
    global balance
    current = balance            # 1. read
    time.sleep(0.01)             # (any work: a network call, a calculation...)
    balance = current - amount   # 3. write based on the OLD value

threads = [threading.Thread(target=withdraw, args=(30,)) for _ in range(2)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

print(balance)

# OUTPUT:
# 70
codeExplanations: Two withdrawals of 30 from 100 should leave 40. Both threads read 100 before either wrote, so both wrote 70: one withdrawal vanished. In real code the pause is not a visible sleep but a thread switch at an unlucky moment, so the bug appears only occasionally.

beginner.content:
The Fix: Make the Whole Sequence Atomic

Hold a lock around the entire read-modify-write sequence so no other thread can slip in between.
codeExamples:
import threading
import time

balance = 100
lock = threading.Lock()

def withdraw(amount):
    global balance
    with lock:                       # the whole read-compute-write is protected
        current = balance
        time.sleep(0.01)
        balance = current - amount

threads = [threading.Thread(target=withdraw, args=(30,)) for _ in range(2)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

print(balance)

# OUTPUT:
# 40

beginner.content:
Introduction

A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the unpredictable timing of threads. Typical case: two threads do read-modify-write on the same variable and one update is lost.

Why Do We Need This?

Races produce wrong results rarely and unpredictably: they pass tests, then fail in production. You must understand them to recognise unsafe code and know which tools fix them.
codeExamples:
import threading, time

x = 0
def slow_inc():
    global x
    tmp = x                                  # read
    time.sleep(0.01)                         # widen the window so the race is certain
    x = tmp + 1                              # write

ts = [threading.Thread(target=slow_inc) for _ in range(5)]
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join()
print("expected 5, got", x)

# OUTPUT (example):
# expected 5, got 1

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real incidents: double-spending a balance, two requests creating the same unique ID, overselling the last ticket, cache stampedes. The fix is a lock, an atomic operation, or removing shared state.
codeExamples:
import threading

stock = 1; lock = threading.Lock(); sold = []

def buy(who):
    global stock
    with lock:                               # check + act become one atomic step
        if stock > 0:
            stock -= 1
            sold.append(who)

ts = [threading.Thread(target=buy, args=(f"user{i}",)) for i in range(10)]
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join()
print("sold to", len(sold), "user(s); stock", stock)

# OUTPUT:
# sold to 1 user(s); stock 0

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Thread A: read x(0) ───────────► write x(1)
   Thread B:          read x(0) ──► write x(1)       final x = 1, expected 2
                 ^^^ both read the old value before either wrote

expert.content:
Check-Then-Act (TOCTOU)

A second very common shape: a thread checks a condition and then acts on it, but the condition changes in between ("time of check to time of use"). Even if each individual step is safe, the combination is not.
codeExamples:
import threading
import time

balance = 100

def withdraw_if_enough(amount):
    global balance
    if balance >= amount:            # check
        time.sleep(0.01)             # ...other thread checks here too...
        balance -= amount            # act

threads = [threading.Thread(target=withdraw_if_enough, args=(80,)) for _ in range(2)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

print(balance)                       # an overdraft the check was meant to prevent

# OUTPUT:
# -60

expert.content:
Lazy Initialisation and Double-Checked Locking

"Create it on first use" is check-then-act too: two threads can both see None and both create the object, breaking a singleton or doing the expensive set-up twice. A lock fixes it; the extra outer check avoids taking the lock on every call afterwards.
codeExamples:
import threading
import time

created = []
_instance = None
_lock = threading.Lock()

def get_instance():
    global _instance
    if _instance is None:                 # cheap check, no lock
        with _lock:
            if _instance is None:         # check again, now exclusively
                time.sleep(0.05)          # expensive construction
                created.append(1)
                _instance = object()
    return _instance

threads = [threading.Thread(target=get_instance) for _ in range(5)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

print("instances created:", len(created))

# OUTPUT:
# instances created: 1

expert.content:
Other Shapes of Race Conditions

  • Modifying a collection while iterating it in another thread (RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration, or silently skipped items). Iterate over a snapshot (list(d.items())) or lock both sides.
  • Compound operations on collections: d[k] += 1, if k not in d: d[k] = [], lst.append(len(lst)).
  • Shared resources outside memory: two threads writing the same file, or "check the file does not exist, then create it" (use open(path, "x"), which is atomic).
  • Publication order: a thread sees an object that another thread is still building. Finish construction before sharing the reference.
  • Data races vs race conditions: a data race is an unsynchronised access to memory; a race condition is any timing-dependent wrong result (even with every access individually synchronised, like the overdraft above).

Preventing Races: Strategies from Best to Worst

  1. Don't share. Give each thread its own data (arguments, threading.local) and combine results at the end.
  2. Share only immutable data. Tuples, frozen dataclasses, strings and numbers cannot be modified, so they cannot race.
  3. Pass messages, not memory. Hand work and results over queue.Queue; one owner thread modifies each piece of state.
  4. Lock the shared state around the whole compound operation, consistently, everywhere it is touched.
  5. Use thread-safe building blocks: queue.Queue, collections.deque for append/pop, concurrent.futures.
Relying on "it is atomic in CPython because of the GIL" is the weakest option: it is an implementation detail and breaks in free-threaded builds and other interpreters.
codeExamples:
import threading
from queue import Queue

# One thread owns the shared total; workers send it messages instead of locking.
inbox = Queue()

def worker(numbers):
    inbox.put(sum(numbers))

def accumulator(expected, result):
    total = 0
    for _ in range(expected):
        total += inbox.get()
    result.append(total)

result = []
chunks = [range(0, 100), range(100, 200), range(200, 300)]
workers = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(c,)) for c in chunks]
owner = threading.Thread(target=accumulator, args=(len(chunks), result))

owner.start()
for w in workers:
    w.start()
for w in workers:
    w.join()
owner.join()

print(result[0])

# OUTPUT:
# 44850

expert.content:
Finding Race Conditions

  • Make them likely: sys.setswitchinterval(1e-6) forces very frequent thread switches in tests, exposing races that normally hide. Add random time.sleep(0) yields in suspect code.
  • Stress tests: run the code with many threads and many iterations, repeatedly, and assert invariants (totals, uniqueness, no overdraft).
  • Code review checklist: for every shared variable, ask "which lock protects this?". If the answer is "none", or "a different lock in different places", there is a bug.
  • Tooling: ThreadSanitizer (TSan) builds of CPython and extensions detect data races; pytest-repeat or pytest -p no:randomly variations help; free-threaded Python makes races more visible, so it is also a good test bed.
codeExamples:
import sys

old = sys.getswitchinterval()
sys.setswitchinterval(1e-6)          # switch threads about every microsecond
try:
    pass                             # ...run your multi-threaded test here...
finally:
    sys.setswitchinterval(old)       # always restore

print(old)

# OUTPUT:
# 0.005

expert.content:
Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Understanding races lets you spot unsafe code during reviewRaces are intermittent and often vanish when debugging
A forced pause makes the bug repeatable in testsCode that looks correct can still be unsafe (x += 1 is not atomic)
One lock around the whole sequence fixes itLocking everything reduces concurrency and risks deadlocks
Atomic helpers (queue.Queue, locks) remove the need to reason about timingTests pass by luck: absence of failure is not proof of safety

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a race condition?A bug where the outcome depends on the relative timing of threads accessing shared state
Why is counter += 1 not thread-safe in Python?It compiles to separate read, add and write steps; a thread switch between them loses an update
What is check-then-act?Testing a condition and then acting on it with a gap between - the condition may change in the gap; make both steps atomic with a lock
Name ways to avoid races without locks.Thread-local data, immutable data, message passing with queues
How do you test for races?Stress tests, tiny switch intervals, invariant assertions, ThreadSanitizer

Advantages

Advantages of fixing them properly: three toolbox options - Lock, thread-safe structures (queue.Queue, itertools.count), or confinement (each thread owns its data).

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: races are hard to reproduce, hard to debug (print statements change timing) and can hide for years until load or a Python upgrade exposes them.
codeExamples:
import sys, threading
sys.setswitchinterval(1e-6)                  # force very frequent thread switches

n = 0
def f():
    global n
    for _ in range(50_000): n += 1

ts = [threading.Thread(target=f) for _ in range(4)]
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join()
print("expected 200000, got", n)             # stress setting makes the bug visible

# OUTPUT (example):
# expected 200000, got 143377

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: locks only help where you use them. One unguarded access path (a forgotten method) re-opens the race, and there is no built-in race detector in CPython.
codeExamples:
import threading

total = 0; lock = threading.Lock()

def safe_add():
    global total
    with lock:
        total += 1

def sloppy_add():                            # forgot the lock: the guard is useless
    global total
    total += 1

ts = ([threading.Thread(target=lambda: [safe_add() for _ in range(100000)])] +
      [threading.Thread(target=lambda: [sloppy_add() for _ in range(100000)])])
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join()
print("expected 200000, got", total)

# OUTPUT (example):
# expected 200000, got 187904

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Design out sharing first: message passing via Queue, immutable snapshots, one owner thread per resource. When sharing is unavoidable, wrap the state in a class that owns its lock so callers cannot bypass it. Stress-test with a tiny switch interval and run tools such as ThreadSanitizer on native code.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A deadlock occurs when threads wait for each other forever: thread 1 holds lock A and waits for lock B, while thread 2 holds lock B and waits for lock A. Nobody can proceed, nothing is released, and the program simply hangs with no error. The conditions are the same as in Java: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and a circular wait. Break any one of them, most simply by always acquiring locks in the same global order, and deadlock becomes impossible.
Figure: solid = holds, dashed = waits for: each thread waits for the lock the other holds

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: A program that uses more than one lock freezes at random, uses no CPU, prints nothing, and cannot be stopped except by killing it.

Why we need it:
  • Recognise the circular wait pattern behind a frozen program.
  • Prevent it by acquiring multiple locks in one consistent order.
  • Detect it safely during testing with daemon threads and join(timeout).
  • Reduce risk by holding fewer locks, for a shorter time.

Complete Example: Opposite lock order versus the same order

Two scenarios run the same worker. Opposite lock order deadlocks; the same order finishes. Daemon threads and join(timeout) keep the program from hanging.
codeExplanations: With opposite order each thread takes its first lock, sleeps, then waits forever for the lock the other holds, so both are still alive after the timeout. With the same order the second thread cannot even take lock A until the first has finished, so both complete in about 0.2 s. Daemon threads let the interpreter exit even though the deadlocked pair never ends.

beginner.content:
What Is a Deadlock?

A deadlock happens when threads wait for each other forever. Thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2; thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1. Neither can continue, so neither ever releases anything. The program does not crash or print an error - it just hangs, using no CPU. 
Thread A: holds lock_a  --- waits for --->  lock_b
Thread B: holds lock_b  --- waits for --->  lock_a      (a circular wait)
It is like two people meeting in a narrow corridor, each refusing to step back until the other does.

Creating One (Safely)

The two threads below take the same two locks in opposite order. The sleep guarantees each grabs its first lock before trying for its second. They are daemon threads and we use join(timeout), so the demo reports the deadlock instead of hanging.
codeExamples:
import threading
import time

lock_a = threading.Lock()
lock_b = threading.Lock()

def worker_1():
    with lock_a:
        time.sleep(0.1)          # make sure worker_2 has taken lock_b
        with lock_b:             # waits forever
            pass

def worker_2():
    with lock_b:
        time.sleep(0.1)
        with lock_a:             # waits forever
            pass

t1 = threading.Thread(target=worker_1, daemon=True)
t2 = threading.Thread(target=worker_2, daemon=True)
t1.start()
t2.start()

t1.join(timeout=1)
t2.join(timeout=1)
print("deadlocked:", t1.is_alive() and t2.is_alive())

# OUTPUT:
# deadlocked: True
codeExplanations: After 1 second both threads are still alive, each stuck on its second lock. Without daemon=True and the timeouts this program would never end. Because the threads are daemons the interpreter can still exit.

beginner.content:
The Fix: Always Lock in the Same Order

If every thread takes the locks in the same global order, a circular wait is impossible. A simple way is to sort the locks by a fixed key (here the object's id) before acquiring.
codeExamples:
import threading
import time
from contextlib import ExitStack

lock_a = threading.Lock()
lock_b = threading.Lock()

def acquire_in_order(*locks):
    stack = ExitStack()
    for lock in sorted(locks, key=id):        # one consistent global order
        stack.enter_context(lock)
    return stack

def worker_1():
    with acquire_in_order(lock_a, lock_b):
        time.sleep(0.1)

def worker_2():
    with acquire_in_order(lock_b, lock_a):    # written in the opposite order...
        time.sleep(0.1)                       # ...but acquired in the same order

t1 = threading.Thread(target=worker_1, daemon=True)
t2 = threading.Thread(target=worker_2, daemon=True)
t1.start()
t2.start()
t1.join(timeout=2)
t2.join(timeout=2)

print("finished:", not t1.is_alive() and not t2.is_alive())

# OUTPUT:
# finished: True

beginner.content:
Introduction

A deadlock happens when threads wait for each other forever: Thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2 while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1. Nothing progresses and no error is raised.
codeExamples:
import threading, time

a, b = threading.Lock(), threading.Lock()

def t1():
    with a:
        time.sleep(0.1)
        got = b.acquire(timeout=0.5)         # timeout used so this demo ends
        print("t1 got b:", got)
        if got: b.release()

def t2():
    with b:
        time.sleep(0.1)
        got = a.acquire(timeout=0.5)
        print("t2 got a:", got)
        if got: a.release()

x = threading.Thread(target=t1); y = threading.Thread(target=t2)
x.start(); y.start(); x.join(); y.join()

# OUTPUT (both time out; without timeout the program would hang forever):
# t1 got b: False
# t2 got a: False

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Deadlocks freeze whole services (no crash, no log). Knowing the four conditions - mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no pre-emption, circular wait - tells you which one to break.
codeExamples:
# Break "circular wait": always take locks in one global order
import threading

a, b = threading.Lock(), threading.Lock()
order = {id(a): 1, id(b): 2}

def acquire_both(x, y):
    first, second = sorted((x, y), key=lambda l: order[id(l)])
    with first:
        with second:
            return "ok"

r1, r2 = [], []
t1 = threading.Thread(target=lambda: r1.append(acquire_both(a, b)))
t2 = threading.Thread(target=lambda: r2.append(acquire_both(b, a)))   # reversed args
t1.start(); t2.start(); t1.join(); t2.join()
print(r1, r2)

# OUTPUT:
# ['ok'] ['ok']

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real cases: bank transfers locking two accounts in opposite order, a callback that takes a lock the caller already holds, and DB transactions waiting on each other's rows.

Diagram

   Thread A holds [L1] ──waits──► [L2]  held by Thread B
        ▲                                   │
        └────────── waits ◄── [L1] ◄────────┘     (circular wait)

expert.content:
The Four Conditions (Coffman)

A deadlock needs all four of these at once. Remove any one and it cannot happen:
ConditionMeaningHow to break it
Mutual exclusionA resource is held by one thread at a timeUse lock-free / immutable data or queues
Hold and waitA thread holds one lock while waiting for anotherAcquire everything at once, or release before waiting
No preemptionLocks cannot be taken awayUse timeouts and back off
Circular waitA cycle of threads each waiting for the nextImpose a global lock order (the usual fix)

Timeout and Back-Off

When a consistent order is not possible, acquire the second lock with a timeout. If it fails, release the first lock, wait a little (with random jitter), and retry. This turns a permanent hang into a recoverable delay. Beware livelock: threads that keep backing off and retrying in lock-step make no progress either - the random jitter prevents it.
codeExamples:
import random
import threading
import time

def transfer(first, second, work, attempts=10):
    for _ in range(attempts):
        with first:
            if second.acquire(timeout=0.05):
                try:
                    return work()
                finally:
                    second.release()
        time.sleep(random.uniform(0.001, 0.01))     # jitter before retrying
    raise TimeoutError("could not obtain both locks")

a, b = threading.Lock(), threading.Lock()
print(transfer(a, b, lambda: "transferred"))

# OUTPUT:
# transferred

expert.content:
Other Ways to Deadlock

  • Self-deadlock: taking a non-reentrant Lock twice in the same thread (a method calling another method that takes the same lock). Use RLock or restructure.
  • Join cycles: thread A holds a lock and calls b.join() while thread B needs that lock to finish.
  • Queue deadlock: a bounded queue.Queue where producers and consumers are the same threads and the queue is full: everyone is waiting to put, nobody is calling get.
  • Thread-pool starvation: tasks that submit sub-tasks to the same pool and wait for them. With all workers occupied by waiting parents, the children can never run.
  • Callbacks under a lock: calling user code (which may take other locks) while holding your lock.
  • Forking with threads: fork() copies locks held by other threads in a locked state, with no thread alive to release them. Another reason spawn/forkserver are safer.
codeExamples:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, TimeoutError   # 3.11+: same as the built-in

pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1)

def parent():
    child = pool.submit(lambda: "child result")
    return child.result()          # waits for a worker - but the only worker is HERE

future = pool.submit(parent)
try:
    future.result(timeout=1)
except TimeoutError:
    print("deadlock: the parent waits for a child that can never start")

pool.shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True)

# OUTPUT:
# deadlock: the parent waits for a child that can never start

expert.content:
Diagnosing a Hang

When a program freezes, you need to see where each thread is stuck:
  • faulthandler.dump_traceback_later(seconds, exit=True) prints every thread's stack after a delay and can abort - a built-in watchdog for tests and CI.
  • faulthandler.register(signal.SIGUSR1) (POSIX) dumps all stacks on demand without stopping the process.
  • py-spy dump --pid <pid> inspects a running process from outside, no code changes needed.
  • sys._current_frames() gives each thread's current frame, for building your own diagnostics.
  • Debugger: pause the program and look at the threads panel; two threads waiting in acquire on each other's locks is the signature.
codeExamples:
import faulthandler
import sys

# Watchdog: if the program is still running after 30 s, print all thread
# stacks to stderr and exit. Cancel it when the work completes normally.
faulthandler.dump_traceback_later(30, exit=True)

# ... run the code that might deadlock ...

faulthandler.cancel_dump_traceback_later()
print("finished before the watchdog fired")

# OUTPUT:
# finished before the watchdog fired

expert.content:
Design Habits That Prevent Deadlocks

  • Prefer one lock over several, unless profiling shows contention. Fewer locks means fewer orderings to get wrong.
  • Never call unknown code (callbacks, overridable methods, I/O) while holding a lock.
  • Document the lock order (e.g. "always account lock before ledger lock") and enforce it in code review.
  • Use higher-level structures: queues, thread pools and futures hide most locking.
  • Give every blocking wait a timeout in production code, and log when it expires.
  • Keep critical sections short and never block inside them.

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Knowing the four conditions shows exactly how to prevent itNo error or traceback: the program just hangs silently
A consistent lock order removes the circular waitOften appears only under rare timing, so tests miss it
acquire(timeout=...) turns a hang into a handled errorEnforcing a global lock order across a large code base is hard
Daemon threads and join(timeout) make deadlocks testableDeadlocked non-daemon threads keep the process from exiting

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a deadlock?Threads blocked forever, each waiting for a resource another holds
What four conditions are required?Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait
How do you prevent the classic two-lock deadlock?Acquire locks in a single global order everywhere
Deadlock vs livelock vs starvation?Deadlock: all blocked. Livelock: all busy but making no progress. Starvation: one thread never gets its turn
How do you debug a hung program?faulthandler stack dumps, py-spy dump, or a debugger's thread view

Advantages

Advantages of the prevention techniques: lock ordering, timeouts and a single lock for the whole operation each remove one deadlock condition cheaply.
codeExamples:
import threading, time

lock = threading.Lock()
def try_work():
    if lock.acquire(timeout=0.1):            # give up instead of waiting forever
        try: return "done"
        finally: lock.release()
    return "backed off, will retry"

lock.acquire()                               # simulate a busy lock
print(try_work())
lock.release()
print(try_work())

# OUTPUT:
# backed off, will retry
# done

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: deadlocks are silent, timing dependent, and a detector is not built in. Timeouts only convert a hang into a retry problem (livelock risk).
codeExamples:
import threading, faulthandler, time

# Diagnose a hang: dump every thread's stack after N seconds
faulthandler.dump_traceback_later(0.3, exit=False)
lock = threading.Lock()
lock.acquire()
threading.Thread(target=lambda: lock.acquire(timeout=0.5)).start()
time.sleep(0.4)
faulthandler.cancel_dump_traceback_later()

# OUTPUT (example, to stderr):
# Timeout (0:00:00.300000)!
# Thread 0x... (most recent call first): File "...", line N in <lambda>

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: you cannot forcibly kill a blocked thread, and the standard library has no deadlock detector. Recovery usually means restarting the process.
codeExamples:
import threading
lock = threading.Lock()
lock.acquire()
t = threading.Thread(target=lock.acquire, daemon=True)   # blocks forever
t.start(); t.join(timeout=0.3)
print("thread still stuck:", t.is_alive())    # no API exists to kill it
# daemon=True only lets the program exit; it does not unblock the thread

# OUTPUT:
# thread still stuck: True

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Prevent rather than detect: fixed lock ordering, one coarse lock, lock-free message passing, or timeouts with backoff. Keep lock scope small and never call external code under a lock. For databases, rely on the engine's deadlock detection and retry the transaction.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A thread pool keeps a fixed number of worker threads alive and feeds them tasks from a queue, so you do not create one thread per task. In Python this is concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor, the counterpart of Java's ExecutorService (Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n)). submit() returns a Future (like Java's Future), whose result() returns the value or re-raises the task's exception. Used in a with block, the pool waits for all tasks and shuts down cleanly.
Figure: tasks wait in a queue, a fixed set of workers runs them, futures carry the results back

Purpose / Need of This Topic

The problem: Creating a thread for every small task wastes memory and start-up time, and a thousand tasks means a thousand threads, while join() gives no return values or errors.

Why we need it:
  • Reuse a fixed number of threads for many tasks.
  • Limit concurrency with max_workers so the machine is not overloaded.
  • Get return values and exceptions back through futures.
  • Shut down cleanly with a with block instead of tracking threads by hand.

Complete Example: Eight tasks on four workers

Eight 0.2 s downloads share four workers. One task fails on purpose to show that future.result() re-raises the exception in the caller.
codeExamples:
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

WORKERS = 4
TASKS = 8
DELAY = 0.2                                 # stands in for a network request
BAD_PAGE = 7


def download(page):
    time.sleep(DELAY)
    if page == BAD_PAGE:
        raise ValueError(f"page {page} is missing")
    return f"page {page}"


def main():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=WORKERS) as pool:
        futures = [pool.submit(download, n) for n in range(TASKS)]
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start

    pages, errors = [], []
    for future in futures:
        try:
            pages.append(future.result())   # value, or re-raises the task's error
        except ValueError as error:
            errors.append(str(error))

    print("downloaded:", len(pages), "last:", pages[-1])
    print("errors:", errors)
    print("faster than sequential:", elapsed < 1.0)   # 8 x 0.2 s = 1.6 s alone


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# OUTPUT:
# downloaded: 7 last: page 6
# errors: ['page 7 is missing']
# faster than sequential: True
codeExplanations: Four workers process the eight tasks in two rounds of about 0.2 s, so the total is near 0.4 s instead of 1.6 s. Futures are read in submission order, so the pages are in order and "page 6" is the last successful one. The exception raised inside the worker thread is stored in the future and re-raised by result(), where the caller can handle it.

beginner.content:
Why a Pool?

Creating a new thread for every small task is wasteful (each thread costs memory and start-up time) and dangerous (a thousand tasks means a thousand threads). A thread pool keeps a fixed number of worker threads alive and feeds them tasks from a queue; finished workers pick up the next task. Python's standard tool is concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor - the same idea as Java's ExecutorService.

submit() and Futures

pool.submit(func, *args) schedules a call and immediately returns a Future: a placeholder for the result. future.result() waits for the task and returns its value - or re-raises its exception. Using the pool in a with block waits for all tasks and shuts it down cleanly.
codeExamples:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def square(n):
    return n * n

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) as pool:
    futures = [pool.submit(square, n) for n in range(5)]
    results = [f.result() for f in futures]      # in submission order

print(results)

# OUTPUT:
# [0, 1, 4, 9, 16]

beginner.content:
map(): The Short Version

pool.map(func, iterable) applies the function to every item and yields results in input order.
codeExamples:
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def fetch(page):
    time.sleep(0.2)                     # stands in for a network request
    return f"page {page}"

start = time.perf_counter()
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10) as pool:
    pages = list(pool.map(fetch, range(10)))
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start

print(pages[:3])
print(elapsed < 1.0)                    # ten 0.2 s tasks overlapped (2 s one by one)

# OUTPUT:
# ['page 0', 'page 1', 'page 2']
# True

beginner.content:
as_completed(): Results as They Finish

map and a list of result() calls return in input order, so one slow task delays everything behind it. as_completed(futures) yields each future as soon as it is done.
codeExamples:
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed

def task(name, delay):
    time.sleep(delay)
    return name

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) as pool:
    futures = [
        pool.submit(task, "slow", 0.3),
        pool.submit(task, "fast", 0.1),
        pool.submit(task, "medium", 0.2),
    ]
    for future in as_completed(futures):
        print(future.result())

# OUTPUT:
# fast
# medium
# slow

beginner.content:
Introduction

A thread pool keeps a fixed set of worker threads alive and feeds them tasks, instead of creating a thread per task. In Python use concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor.
codeExamples:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def square(n):
    return n * n

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:      # waits for tasks on exit
    results = list(pool.map(square, range(8)))       # results keep input order
print(results)

# OUTPUT:
# [0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49]

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Creating thousands of threads is slow and exhausts memory. A pool reuses threads, limits concurrency, and gives you Futures for results and exceptions.
codeExamples:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
import time

def job(i):
    time.sleep(0.1)
    return i

t0 = time.perf_counter()
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=5) as pool:      # 20 jobs, 5 at a time
    list(pool.map(job, range(20)))
print(f"20 jobs on 5 threads: {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f}s")   # 4 waves x 0.1

# OUTPUT (example):
# 20 jobs on 5 threads: 0.4s

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: fetching many URLs, running many DB queries, resizing files, calling blocking SDKs. as_completed lets you handle results as soon as each finishes.
codeExamples:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed
import time

def fetch(url, delay):
    time.sleep(delay)
    return f"{url} ok"

with ThreadPoolExecutor(3) as pool:
    futs = [pool.submit(fetch, "slow.com", 0.3), pool.submit(fetch, "fast.com", 0.05),
            pool.submit(fetch, "mid.com", 0.15)]
    for f in as_completed(futs):                     # fastest first
        print(f.result())

# OUTPUT:
# fast.com ok
# mid.com ok
# slow.com ok

beginner.content:
Diagram

   submit(task) ─► [ queue: t5 t4 t3 ] ─┬─► worker 1 ─┐
                                        ├─► worker 2 ─┼─► Future.result()
                                        └─► worker 3 ─┘

expert.content:
Exceptions Travel Through Futures

An exception raised in a task is stored in its Future and re-raised in the caller when you ask for the result - so errors are not silently lost like in a bare Thread. You can also inspect it with future.exception().
codeExamples:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def risky(n):
    if n == 2:
        raise ValueError(f"bad input {n}")
    return n * 10

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool:
    futures = [pool.submit(risky, n) for n in range(4)]

for future in futures:
    try:
        print(future.result())
    except ValueError as error:
        print("error:", error)

# OUTPUT:
# 0
# 10
# error: bad input 2
# 30

expert.content:
Callbacks, Timeouts and Waiting

  • future.add_done_callback(fn) calls fn(future) when the task finishes (in the worker thread, or immediately if already done).
  • future.result(timeout=2) raises TimeoutError if the task takes longer. The task keeps running - a thread cannot be killed.
  • future.cancel() cancels only a task that has not started yet.
  • wait(futures, return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED) waits for the first result, all of them, or the first exception.
codeExamples:
import time
from concurrent.futures import FIRST_COMPLETED, ThreadPoolExecutor, TimeoutError, wait

def work(name, delay):
    time.sleep(delay)
    return name

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool:
    first = pool.submit(work, "quick", 0.05)
    first.add_done_callback(lambda f: print("callback got", f.result()))
    slow = pool.submit(work, "slow", 0.5)

    done, not_done = wait([first, slow], return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED)
    print([f.result() for f in done])
    print(len(not_done))

    try:
        slow.result(timeout=0.01)           # too impatient
    except TimeoutError:
        print("timed out waiting; the task is still running")

# OUTPUT (the callback line and the next line may swap):
# callback got quick
# ['quick']
# 1
# timed out waiting; the task is still running

expert.content:
Sizing the Pool

The default is min(32, os.cpu_count() + 4) workers - a sensible choice for I/O work. Guidance:
  • I/O-bound: more workers than cores is fine; the limit is the remote service, the database or your file-descriptor budget. Measure, starting from 10-50.
  • CPU-bound: threads give no speed-up under the GIL; use ProcessPoolExecutor (or a free-threaded build).
  • Calling a rate-limited API: size the pool to the allowed concurrency, not to the number of tasks.
  • Never create a pool per task. Create it once, reuse it, and shut it down at exit.
Give threads recognisable names with thread_name_prefix so logs and stack dumps say which pool a thread belongs to, and use initializer to set up per-thread resources once (for example a database connection or HTTP session stored in a threading.local).
codeExamples:
import threading
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

local = threading.local()

def init_worker():
    local.session = f"session-for-{threading.current_thread().name}"

def job(n):
    return threading.current_thread().name, local.session

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2, thread_name_prefix="fetch",
                        initializer=init_worker) as pool:
    results = list(pool.map(job, range(6)))

print(all(name.startswith("fetch_") for name, _ in results))
print(all(session.endswith(name) for name, session in results))

# OUTPUT:
# True
# True

expert.content:
Shutdown and Back-Pressure

  • Always shut down: use with, or call shutdown(wait=True). shutdown(cancel_futures=True) (3.9+) drops tasks that have not started.
  • Unbounded queue: submit never blocks, so submitting millions of tasks fills memory with pending work. Submit in batches, or bound the queue with a semaphore (see the Semaphore topic).
  • Worker threads are non-daemon (since 3.9 they are joined at exit), so a never-ending task keeps the program from exiting.
  • Don't wait on the same pool from inside a task - it can deadlock when all workers are busy waiting (see Deadlocks).
  • Mixing with asyncio: await loop.run_in_executor(pool, func, arg) or asyncio.to_thread(func, arg) lets coroutines call blocking code without freezing the event loop.

ThreadPoolExecutor vs the Alternatives

ToolBest for
ThreadPoolExecutorModern default for blocking I/O tasks; futures and clean error handling
ProcessPoolExecutorCPU-bound tasks; same API
asyncioThousands of concurrent I/O operations
multiprocessing.pool.ThreadPoolOlder API (apply_async, imap_unordered); still works
Manual Thread + QueueLong-lived workers with custom protocols

Advantages and Disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Threads are reused: no start-up cost per taskStill limited by the GIL for CPU-bound work (use processes)
max_workers caps the number of threadsToo few workers leaves tasks queued; too many wastes memory
Futures return values and propagate exceptionsA task that never finishes blocks its worker, and the shutdown wait
with block gives clean shutdownAn unread future hides its exception until result() is called

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why use a thread pool?Reuse a bounded set of threads instead of creating one per task: lower overhead and controlled concurrency
What is a Future?A handle for a result that is not ready yet; result() waits and returns it or re-raises the task's exception
map vs as_completed?map yields in input order; as_completed yields futures in completion order
Can you cancel a running task?No - only tasks that have not started; threads cannot be killed, so design tasks to check a stop flag
When is a thread pool the wrong tool?CPU-bound work in a GIL build - use a process pool

Advantages
