Model hierarchy with trees, but keep depth in mind: balanced shapes give logarithmic height, skewed ones give linear. Prefer iterative traversal for untrusted or very deep data. If you only need ordered lookup, a sorted list with bisect or a database index is often simpler than a hand-rolled tree.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A binary search tree (BST) is a binary tree where every value in the left subtree is smaller than the node and every value in the right subtree is larger. That ordering lets you discard half the tree at each step, and an in-order walk returns the values sorted.

Why Do We Need This?

A sorted list searches fast but inserts slowly (shifting); an unsorted list inserts fast but searches slowly. A BST keeps both search and insert near O(log n) when it is balanced.

Real-Time Use

Ordered maps and sets (leaderboards, schedulers, time-series indexes, database B-trees) rely on ordered tree structures. Because of the ordering you can answer range questions such as "all prices between 25 and 65" without scanning everything.

Diagram

              50
            /    \
          30      70        rule: left < node < right
         /  \    /  \
       20   40  60   80

   search 60:  50 -> go right -> 70 -> go left -> 60  (3 steps)
   balanced: O(log n)        skewed (sorted input): O(n)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: keeps data sorted automatically, O(log n) search/insert/delete when balanced, and supports min, max, successor and range queries.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: shape depends on insertion order. Inserting already-sorted data builds a chain, so operations become O(n).

Limitations

Limitations: a plain BST has no self-balancing and no standard duplicate policy; this version silently ignores duplicates. Production code uses AVL, red-black trees, B-trees, or Python's bisect on a list instead.

Architect's Notes

Do not hand-roll a BST in production; use the database index, sortedcontainers.SortedList, or bisect over a list. If you must build one, use a self-balancing variant and iterative operations. A hash table is better when you never need ordering or ranges.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A heap is a tree stored in an array where each parent is smaller than (min-heap) or larger than (max-heap) its children, so the smallest item is always at index 0. Python's heapq module implements a min-heap on a plain list.
codeExamples:
import heapq

heap = []
for x in (5, 1, 3):
    heapq.heappush(heap, x)          # O(log n) insert
print(heapq.heappop(heap))           # O(log n): always the smallest
print(heap)                          # remaining items, still a valid heap

# OUTPUT:
# 1
# [3, 5]

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Sometimes you only need "the next most important item", not a full sort. A heap hands you the minimum in O(log n) while still accepting new items at any time, which re-sorting a list each time cannot do cheaply.
codeExamples:
import heapq

todo = []
heapq.heappush(todo, (2, "write report"))     # (priority, task): lower = more urgent
heapq.heappush(todo, (1, "fix prod bug"))
heapq.heappush(todo, (3, "lunch"))
while todo:
    prio, task = heapq.heappop(todo)
    print(prio, task)

# OUTPUT:
# 1 fix prod bug
# 2 write report
# 3 lunch

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Task schedulers, Dijkstra's shortest path, event simulations, merging sorted log files and "top K" analytics all use heaps. Here a size-3 min-heap tracks the 3 largest values of a stream using constant memory.
codeExamples:
import heapq

stream = [5, 1, 9, 3, 7, 8, 2]
top3 = []
for x in stream:
    if len(top3) < 3:
        heapq.heappush(top3, x)
    elif x > top3[0]:                      # beats the smallest of the current top 3
        heapq.heapreplace(top3, x)         # pop smallest, push x
print(sorted(top3))

# OUTPUT:
# [7, 8, 9]

beginner.content:
Diagram

   array: [ 1, 3, 2, 7, 4 ]            tree view:
   index:   0  1  2  3  4                    1          <- min at root
                                           /   \
   parent(i)  = (i - 1) // 2              3     2
   children   = 2i+1 , 2i+2              / \
                                        7   4

   push: add at end, bubble UP      pop: swap root with last, bubble DOWN

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: O(1) peek of the minimum, O(log n) push/pop, and heapify builds a heap from an existing list in O(n).
codeExamples:
import heapq

nums = [9, 4, 7, 1]
heapq.heapify(nums)              # in place, O(n)
print(nums, "min =", nums[0])

# OUTPUT:
# [1, 4, 7, 9] min = 1

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the list is only partially ordered: the root is the minimum but the rest is not sorted, so you cannot print or binary-search it directly.
codeExamples:
import heapq

heap = []
for x in (5, 4, 3, 2, 1):
    heapq.heappush(heap, x)
print(heap)                      # NOT sorted, only heap-ordered
print([heapq.heappop(heap) for _ in range(5)])   # popping everything gives sorted order

# OUTPUT:
# [1, 2, 4, 5, 3]
# [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: heapq is min-heap only (negate numbers for a max-heap), and finding or removing an arbitrary item is O(n).
codeExamples:
import heapq

nums = [3, 1, 4]
maxheap = [-x for x in nums]         # negate to simulate a max-heap
heapq.heapify(maxheap)
print(-heapq.heappop(maxheap))       # largest item

print(4 in nums)                     # membership is still a linear scan

# OUTPUT:
# 4
# True

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use a heap for priority scheduling, top-K and k-way merges; use heapq.nlargest for small K. For priority queues across threads use queue.PriorityQueue; across services use a broker with priorities. If you need decrease-key or removal, add lazy deletion (mark entries stale) or a different structure.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A trie (prefix tree) stores strings character by character; words that share a prefix share the same path of nodes. A marker on a node says "a word ends here".

Why Do We Need This?

Questions like "which words start with these letters?" are slow on a list (scan everything) and awkward on a hash set (hashing needs the full word). A trie answers prefix questions by following one path.

Real-Time Use

Search-box autocomplete, spell checkers, IP routing tables (longest prefix match), phone contact search and T9 keyboards all use tries.

Diagram

   words: car, card, cat, dog

            (root)
           /      \
          c        d
          |        |
          a        o
         / \       |
        r   t*     g*          * = end of word
        |
        d*     "car" is a word AND the prefix of "card"

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: lookup time depends only on the word length, not on how many words are stored, and shared prefixes are stored once.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: each node is a dict, so memory is heavy when words share little; a plain set of strings is far smaller.

Limitations

Limitations: it matches characters exactly, so case, accents and typos are not handled unless you normalise input first; it is also in-memory only.

Architect's Notes

Tries shine for prefix-heavy workloads on bounded vocabularies. For huge dictionaries use compressed variants (radix trees, DAWGs) or let a search engine (Elasticsearch, Redis) handle it. If you only need exact membership, a set is simpler, smaller and faster.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A graph is a set of vertices (nodes) joined by edges. Edges may be directed or undirected and may carry weights. The most common Python representation is an adjacency list: a dict mapping each node to its neighbours.
codeExamples:
graph = {                      # directed graph as an adjacency list
    "A": ["B", "C"],
    "B": ["D"],
    "C": ["D"],
    "D": [],
}
print("neighbours of A:", graph["A"])
print("vertices:", len(graph), "edges:", sum(len(v) for v in graph.values()))

# OUTPUT:
# neighbours of A: ['B', 'C']
# vertices: 4 edges: 4

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Lists and trees cannot express arbitrary relationships such as friendships, road maps or dependencies, where many nodes connect to many others and cycles are allowed. Graphs can.
codeExamples:
from collections import defaultdict

friends = defaultdict(set)
def add_friendship(a, b):          # undirected: add both directions
    friends[a].add(b)
    friends[b].add(a)

add_friendship("Ann", "Baji")
add_friendship("Baji", "Cy")
add_friendship("Ann", "Di")

# friends of friends of Ann (excluding Ann and her direct friends)
direct = friends["Ann"]
fof = set().union(*(friends[f] for f in direct)) - direct - {"Ann"}
print(sorted(direct), sorted(fof))

# OUTPUT:
# ['Baji', 'Di'] ['Cy']

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Maps and GPS, social networks, recommendation engines, dependency managers, network topologies and fraud detection are graph problems. A basic real task is counting isolated groups (connected components).
codeExamples:
edges = [(1, 2), (2, 3), (4, 5)]
nodes = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
adj = {n: [] for n in nodes}
for a, b in edges:
    adj[a].append(b)
    adj[b].append(a)

seen, components = set(), 0
for start in nodes:
    if start in seen:
        continue
    components += 1                    # new unexplored group found
    stack = [start]
    while stack:                       # DFS marks everything reachable
        n = stack.pop()
        if n in seen:
            continue
        seen.add(n)
        stack.extend(adj[n])
print("components:", components)

# OUTPUT:
# components: 3

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Directed graph                 Adjacency list
        A ----> B                 A : [B, C]
        |       |                 B : [D]
        v       v                 C : [D]
        C ----> D                 D : []

   V = 4 vertices, E = 4 edges      memory O(V + E)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: models any relationship; an adjacency list uses O(V + E) memory and lists neighbours in O(1), which suits the sparse graphs found in real life.
codeExamples:
graph = {"A": ["B", "C"], "B": ["C"], "C": []}
total_edges = sum(len(n) for n in graph.values())
print("memory is proportional to V+E:", len(graph), "+", total_edges, "=", len(graph) + total_edges)

# OUTPUT:
# memory is proportional to V+E: 3 + 3 = 6

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: an adjacency matrix needs V x V cells even when almost empty, and checking "is there an edge A-B?" in an adjacency list costs O(degree).
codeExamples:
# Same 4-node path graph: 0-1, 1-2, 2-3
V = 4
matrix = [[0] * V for _ in range(V)]
for a, b in [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3)]:
    matrix[a][b] = matrix[b][a] = 1
for row in matrix:
    print(row)
print("cells:", V * V, "but only 3 edges")

# OUTPUT:
# [0, 1, 0, 0]
# [1, 0, 1, 0]
# [0, 1, 0, 1]
# [0, 0, 1, 0]
# cells: 16 but only 3 edges

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: graphs may contain cycles, so any traversal must remember visited nodes or it loops forever. Python has no built-in graph type (use dicts, or libraries like networkx).
codeExamples:
graph = {"A": ["B"], "B": ["A"]}      # A and B point at each other (a cycle)

def walk_no_memory(start, limit=6):
    path, node = [], start
    while len(path) < limit:             # without 'limit' this would never stop
        path.append(node)
        node = graph[node][0]
    return path

print(walk_no_memory("A"))

def walk_with_visited(start):
    seen, order, stack = set(), [], [start]
    while stack:
        n = stack.pop()
        if n in seen: continue
        seen.add(n); order.append(n); stack.extend(graph[n])
    return order
print(walk_with_visited("A"))

# OUTPUT:
# ['A', 'B', 'A', 'B', 'A', 'B']
# ['A', 'B']

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Pick the representation by density: adjacency list for sparse graphs, matrix for dense ones or constant-time edge checks. For serious analytics use networkx or a graph database (Neo4j); at huge scale you need partitioned graph engines. Do not model plain hierarchies as graphs; trees are simpler.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Sorting arranges items in a defined order. Python provides sorted() (returns a new list) and list.sort() (in place), both using Timsort, a stable O(n log n) algorithm. Understanding a classic like merge sort shows how it works.
codeExamples:
def merge_sort(a):
    if len(a) <= 1:
        return a
    mid = len(a) // 2
    left, right = merge_sort(a[:mid]), merge_sort(a[mid:])    # divide
    out, i, j = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):                   # merge two sorted halves
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            out.append(left[i]); i += 1
        else:
            out.append(right[j]); j += 1
    return out + left[i:] + right[j:]

data = [5, 2, 9, 1, 7, 3]
print(merge_sort(data))
print(sorted(data) == merge_sort(data))     # same as the built-in

# OUTPUT:
# [1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 9]
# True

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Sorted data enables binary search, easy duplicate detection, readable reports and merging. Python's key= argument lets you sort by any rule without writing a comparison function.
codeExamples:
words = ["pear", "fig", "apple", "kiwi"]
print(sorted(words, key=lambda w: (len(w), w)))   # by length, then alphabetically
print(sorted(words, reverse=True))

# OUTPUT:
# ['fig', 'kiwi', 'pear', 'apple']
# ['pear', 'kiwi', 'fig', 'apple']

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Leaderboards, product listings, log timelines and payroll reports all sort records on several fields. Negating a number sorts it descending inside a tuple key.
codeExamples:
staff = [("Ann", "IT", 90), ("Baji", "HR", 70), ("Cy", "IT", 95), ("Di", "HR", 80)]
# department A-Z, then salary high-to-low
for name, dept, pay in sorted(staff, key=lambda s: (s[1], -s[2])):
    print(dept, name, pay)

# OUTPUT:
# HR Di 80
# HR Baji 70
# IT Cy 95
# IT Ann 90

beginner.content:
Diagram

   [5 2 9 1 7 3]
        |  divide
   [5 2 9]   [1 7 3]
    |            |
   [2 5 9]   [1 3 7]       sort each half
        \      /
     merge (two pointers)
   [1 2 3 5 7 9]       O(n log n), stable

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: Timsort is stable (equal items keep their original order), adaptive (fast on nearly sorted data) and worst-case O(n log n). Stability allows multi-pass sorting.
codeExamples:
rows = [("Ann", "IT"), ("Baji", "HR"), ("Cy", "IT"), ("Di", "HR")]
by_dept = sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r[1])    # Baji stays before Di, Ann before Cy
print(by_dept)

# OUTPUT:
# [('Baji', 'HR'), ('Di', 'HR'), ('Ann', 'IT'), ('Cy', 'IT')]

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: comparison sorts cannot beat O(n log n), and naive algorithms such as bubble sort are O(n^2), which collapses on large inputs.

Limitations

Limitations: items must be mutually comparable, and list.sort() returns None because it changes the list in place, a frequent source of bugs.
codeExamples:
try:
    sorted([3, "a"])
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)

nums = [3, 1, 2]
print(nums.sort())        # None! sort() works in place
print(nums)

# OUTPUT:
# TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'
# None
# [1, 2, 3]

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use the built-in sorted/sort with key= for almost everything; it is C-optimised and stable. Implement your own only to learn or for special needs (external sorting of data larger than RAM, counting sort for small integer ranges). For huge data push sorting into the database or a distributed engine.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Searching locates an item in a collection. Linear search checks each item (O(n)); binary search works on sorted data and halves the range every step (O(log n)).
codeExamples:
def binary_search(items, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(items) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if items[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if items[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1          # target must be in the right half
        else:
            hi = mid - 1          # target must be in the left half
    return -1

data = [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11]
print(binary_search(data, 7))
print(binary_search(data, 4))

# OUTPUT:
# 3
# -1

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

With a million sorted records a linear search may need a million checks, while binary search needs at most about twenty. Doubling the data adds only one extra step.
codeExamples:
import math
n = 1_000_000
print("linear worst case :", n)
print("binary worst case :", math.ceil(math.log2(n + 1)))

# OUTPUT:
# linear worst case : 1000000
# binary worst case : 20

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Database indexes, dictionary lookups, version bisecting (git bisect), and range tables such as grade boundaries or tax brackets all use binary search. The bisect module does it for you.
codeExamples:
from bisect import bisect

breakpoints = [60, 70, 80, 90]          # F < 60 <= D < 70 <= C < 80 <= B < 90 <= A
grades = "FDCBA"
scores = [59, 60, 85, 90, 100]
print("".join(grades[bisect(breakpoints, s)] for s in scores))

# OUTPUT:
# FDBAA

beginner.content:
Diagram

   find 7 in  [1 3 5 7 9 11 13]
               lo       mid        hi
   step 1:     1 3 5 [7] 9 11 13      7 == 7 -> found at index 3

   find 11:    step 1: mid = 7  < 11  -> keep right half [9 11 13]
               step 2: mid = 11 == 11 -> found
   each step discards half of the remaining range: O(log n)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: logarithmic speed, tiny memory, and bisect can keep a list sorted while inserting and find insertion points for ties.
codeExamples:
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right, insort

a = [1, 3, 3, 5]
print(bisect_left(a, 3), bisect_right(a, 3))   # first and one-past-last position of 3
insort(a, 4)                                   # insert while keeping order
print(a)

# OUTPUT:
# 1 3
# [1, 3, 3, 4, 5]

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the data must already be sorted. On unsorted data binary search silently returns a wrong answer rather than an error.
codeExamples:
def binary_search(items, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(items) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if items[mid] == target: return mid
        if items[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1
    return -1

unsorted = [5, 1, 9, 3, 7]
print(binary_search(unsorted, 3), "- but 3 really is at index", unsorted.index(3))

# OUTPUT:
# -1 - but 3 really is at index 3

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: it needs random access and is famously easy to get wrong with off-by-one boundaries. Using lo < hi instead of lo <= hi misses the last remaining candidate.
codeExamples:
def buggy(items, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(items) - 1
    while lo < hi:                       # BUG: stops before checking lo == hi
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if items[mid] == target: return mid
        if items[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1
    return -1

def correct(items, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(items) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if items[mid] == target: return mid
        if items[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1
    return -1

print(buggy([7], 7), correct([7], 7))

# OUTPUT:
# -1 0

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Sort once, search many times; if you search rarely, a linear scan or a set is cheaper than sorting. Binary search generalises to "search on the answer" for any monotonic condition (capacity planning, minimum speed). Prefer bisect over hand-written loops to avoid boundary bugs.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The two-pointer technique uses two indexes that move through a sequence (often from both ends, or one fast and one slow) to solve problems in a single pass instead of nested loops.
codeExamples:
# Sorted two-sum: one pointer at each end, move toward the middle
nums = [1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 15]
target = 15
l, r = 0, len(nums) - 1
while l < r:
    s = nums[l] + nums[r]
    if s == target:
        print("indexes", (l, r), "values", (nums[l], nums[r]))
        break
    elif s < target:
        l += 1            # need a bigger sum
    else:
        r -= 1            # need a smaller sum

# OUTPUT:
# indexes (2, 4) values (4, 11)

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Brute force compares every pair (O(n^2)). When order gives you information, two pointers reduce it to O(n) with O(1) extra memory, for example removing duplicates from a sorted array in place.
codeExamples:
nums = [1, 1, 2, 2, 3]
write = 1                              # next slot for a unique value
for read in range(1, len(nums)):       # fast pointer scans, slow pointer writes
    if nums[read] != nums[read - 1]:
        nums[write] = nums[read]
        write += 1
print(nums[:write], "length", write)

# OUTPUT:
# [1, 2, 3] length 3

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Merging two sorted streams (merge step of merge sort, merging sorted log files), checking palindromes, and partitioning data all use this pattern.
codeExamples:
a, b = [1, 4, 7], [2, 3, 9]
i = j = 0
merged = []
while i < len(a) and j < len(b):       # always take the smaller front item
    if a[i] <= b[j]:
        merged.append(a[i]); i += 1
    else:
        merged.append(b[j]); j += 1
merged += a[i:] + b[j:]                # one list is exhausted; copy the rest
print(merged)

# OUTPUT:
# [1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 9]

beginner.content:
Diagram

   sorted: [ 1   2   4   7  11  15 ]   target 15
             ^                   ^
             l                   r      1 + 15 = 16 > 15 -> r moves left
             ^               ^
             l               r          1 + 11 = 12 < 15 -> l moves right
                 ^           ^
                 l           r          2 + 11 = 13 -> l moves right
                     ^       ^
                     l       r          4 + 11 = 15 -> found

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: O(n) time, O(1) extra space, and in-place updates, such as reversing a list without making a copy.
codeExamples:
items = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
l, r = 0, len(items) - 1
while l < r:
    items[l], items[r] = items[r], items[l]    # swap the ends, move inward
    l += 1
    r -= 1
print(items)

# OUTPUT:
# [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the shrinking logic depends on order. On unsorted data the pointers discard valid pairs and the answer is wrong.
codeExamples:
nums = [4, 1, 11, 2]            # NOT sorted
target = 15
l, r, found = 0, len(nums) - 1, None
while l < r:
    s = nums[l] + nums[r]
    if s == target:
        found = (nums[l], nums[r]); break
    elif s < target: l += 1
    else: r -= 1
print(found, "- but 4 + 11 = 15 exists")

# OUTPUT:
# None - but 4 + 11 = 15 exists

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: it fits pair or sequential problems; for triples you need an outer loop, so three-sum is O(n^2) overall (still better than O(n^3)). It also needs the data sorted first, an O(n log n) cost.
codeExamples:
def three_sum(nums):
    nums.sort()
    out = []
    for i in range(len(nums) - 2):
        if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]:
            continue                            # skip duplicate anchors
        l, r = i + 1, len(nums) - 1
        while l < r:
            s = nums[i] + nums[l] + nums[r]
            if s < 0: l += 1
            elif s > 0: r -= 1
            else:
                out.append([nums[i], nums[l], nums[r]])
                l += 1
                while l < r and nums[l] == nums[l - 1]:
                    l += 1
                r -= 1
    return out

print(three_sum([-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4]))

# OUTPUT:
# [[-1, -1, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Two pointers (and sliding window) replace nested loops with a single pass whenever the data has monotonic structure. Check the precondition (sorted, or a monotonic property) explicitly; if it does not hold, a hash map is usually the right substitute at the cost of O(n) extra memory.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The sliding window technique keeps a moving range over a sequence. Instead of recomputing everything for each range, you add the element that enters the window and remove the one that leaves, so each element is handled a constant number of times.
codeExamples:
# Maximum sum of any 3 consecutive numbers
nums = [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2]
k = 3
window = sum(nums[:k])              # first window
best = window
for i in range(k, len(nums)):
    window += nums[i] - nums[i - k]   # add the new element, drop the old one
    best = max(best, window)
print(best)

# OUTPUT:
# 9

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Recomputing every window from scratch repeats the same additions again and again (O(n*k)). Sliding keeps one running value and does O(n) work in total.
codeExamples:
nums = [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2, 4, 6]
k = 3
n = len(nums)

brute_ops, brute_best = 0, 0
for i in range(n - k + 1):
    s = 0
    for j in range(i, i + k):         # re-add k numbers every time
        s += nums[j]
        brute_ops += 1
    brute_best = max(brute_best, s)

slide_ops = k
w = sum(nums[:k])
slide_best = w
for i in range(k, n):
    w += nums[i] - nums[i - k]        # one add, one subtract
    slide_ops += 1
    slide_best = max(slide_best, w)

print("brute ops:", brute_ops, " sliding ops:", slide_ops, " same answer:", brute_best == slide_best, slide_best)

# OUTPUT:
# brute ops: 18  sliding ops: 8  same answer: True 12

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Rate limiters ("max 100 requests in any 60 seconds"), moving averages in dashboards, network packet windows (TCP) and "longest substring without repeats" all use a window. The variable-size version grows on the right and shrinks on the left.
codeExamples:
def longest_unique(text):
    last = {}                          # char -> last index where seen
    start = best = 0
    for i, ch in enumerate(text):
        if ch in last and last[ch] >= start:
            start = last[ch] + 1       # shrink the window past the repeat
        last[ch] = i
        best = max(best, i - start + 1)
    return best

print(longest_unique("abcabcbb"))
print(longest_unique("pwwkew"))

# OUTPUT:
# 3
# 3

beginner.content:
Diagram

   data:  [ 2  1  5  1  3  2 ]      k = 3

   step 1 [ 2  1  5 ] 1  3  2       sum = 8
   step 2   2 [ 1  5  1 ] 3  2      sum = 8 - 2 + 1 = 7
   step 3   2  1 [ 5  1  3 ] 2      sum = 7 - 1 + 3 = 9   <- best
   step 4   2  1  5 [ 1  3  2 ]     sum = 9 - 5 + 2 = 6

   add the entering element, remove the leaving one: O(1) per step

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: turns O(n*k) into O(n), uses O(1) or O(window) memory, and works on streams where the data cannot be stored.
codeExamples:
# Moving average over a stream: only the running sum is kept
data = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
k = 3
total = sum(data[:k])
averages = [total / k]
for i in range(k, len(data)):
    total += data[i] - data[i - k]
    averages.append(total / k)
print(averages)

# OUTPUT:
# [2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 5.0]

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: it only considers contiguous ranges. If the best answer uses elements that are not adjacent, the window cannot find it.
codeExamples:
nums = [9, 1, 9]
k = 2
best_window = max(nums[i] + nums[i + 1] for i in range(len(nums) - 1))
best_pair = sorted(nums)[-1] + sorted(nums)[-2]      # any two numbers
print("best window of 2:", best_window)
print("best pair overall:", best_pair)

# OUTPUT:
# best window of 2: 10
# best pair overall: 18

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the "shrink when invalid" logic assumes the condition changes monotonically as the window grows. Edge cases such as a window larger than the data must be handled explicitly.
codeExamples:
def max_window_sum(nums, k):
    if k <= 0 or k > len(nums):
        return None                    # no valid window exists
    w = sum(nums[:k])
    best = w
    for i in range(k, len(nums)):
        w += nums[i] - nums[i - k]
        best = max(best, w)
    return best

print(max_window_sum([1, 2, 3], 5))
print(max_window_sum([1, 2, 3], 2))

# OUTPUT:
# None
# 5

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use windows for any "best contiguous range" or "last N events" problem. For time-based windows in services (rate limits, metrics), prefer proven constructs (Redis sorted sets, token buckets, a metrics library) over hand-rolled in-memory code, because per-process windows break across multiple instances.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Recursion solves a problem by calling the same function on a smaller piece until a simple base case stops it. Backtracking is recursion that tries a choice, explores further, and undoes the choice if it leads nowhere.
codeExamples:
def factorial(n):
    if n <= 1:                    # base case: stops the recursion
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)   # recursive case: smaller problem

print(factorial(5))               # 5 * 4 * 3 * 2 * 1

# OUTPUT:
# 120

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Self-similar data (nested lists, folders, trees) is awkward to loop over but trivial to describe recursively: "handle one item, then handle the rest the same way".

Real-Time Use

Backtracking solves puzzles and search problems: Sudoku, N-Queens, route and schedule planning, regular-expression matching. Here we place 4 queens on a 4x4 board so none attack each other.
codeExamples:
def solve(n):
    sols, cols = [], []              # cols[row] = column of the queen in that row
    def place(row):
        if row == n:
            sols.append(cols[:])     # all rows filled: record a solution
            return
        for c in range(n):
            safe = all(c != cc and abs(c - cc) != row - rr for rr, cc in enumerate(cols))
            if safe:
                cols.append(c)       # choose
                place(row + 1)       # explore
                cols.pop()           # un-choose (backtrack)
    place(0)
    return sols

print(len(solve(4)), "solutions:", solve(4))

# OUTPUT:
# 2 solutions: [[1, 3, 0, 2], [2, 0, 3, 1]]

beginner.content:
Diagram

   subsets([1,2])                  decision tree (include / exclude)

                           start []
                          /          \
                  take 1 [1]        skip 1 []
                  /      \          /       \
          take 2 [1,2] [1]     [2]          []
                  |      |       |           |
               record  record  record     record

   choose -> explore -> un-choose (backtrack)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: short, readable code that mirrors the problem; the choose / explore / un-choose pattern generates every combination systematically.
codeExamples:
def subsets(a):
    out, cur = [], []
    def go(i):
        if i == len(a):
            out.append(cur[:])
            return
        cur.append(a[i]); go(i + 1)      # include a[i]
        cur.pop();        go(i + 1)      # exclude a[i]
    go(0)
    return out

print(subsets([1, 2, 3]))

# OUTPUT:
# [[1, 2, 3], [1, 2], [1, 3], [1], [2, 3], [2], [3], []]

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: naive recursion can repeat work exponentially. Computing Fibonacci recursively recomputes the same values millions of times.
codeExamples:
calls = 0
def fib(n):
    global calls
    calls += 1
    return n if n < 2 else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

print("fib(20) =", fib(20), "using", calls, "calls")

# OUTPUT:
# fib(20) = 6765 using 21891 calls

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: every call uses a stack frame and CPython limits depth (default about 1000). Python does not optimise tail calls, so deep recursion must be rewritten as a loop. Backtracking itself is exponential in the worst case.

Architect's Notes

Recursion is ideal for trees and divide-and-conquer, but in Python prefer iteration or an explicit stack when depth is unbounded. Add pruning to backtracking (reject partial solutions early) and memoisation when subproblems repeat; if the state space is huge, consider constraint solvers (OR-Tools) rather than raw search.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A greedy algorithm builds a solution step by step, always taking the locally best choice and never reconsidering it. When the problem has the "greedy-choice property" this gives the optimal answer very cheaply.
codeExamples:
# Make change using the largest coin that fits, each time
coins = [25, 10, 5, 1]
amount = 41
used = []
for c in coins:                  # coins sorted from largest to smallest
    while amount >= c:
        amount -= c
        used.append(c)
print(used, "->", len(used), "coins")

# OUTPUT:
# [25, 10, 5, 1] -> 4 coins

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Exhaustive search for the best schedule or selection can be exponential. Greedy rules, such as "always pick the interval that ends first", reach the best answer after one sort.
codeExamples:
# Activity selection: attend the maximum number of non-overlapping events
events = [(1, 4), (3, 5), (0, 6), (5, 7), (8, 9), (5, 9)]
chosen, last_end = [], 0
for start, end in sorted(events, key=lambda e: e[1]):   # earliest finish first
    if start >= last_end:
        chosen.append((start, end))
        last_end = end
print(chosen)

# OUTPUT:
# [(1, 4), (5, 7), (8, 9)]

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Huffman compression, Dijkstra's shortest path, minimum spanning trees (Kruskal, Prim), CPU/job scheduling and loading cargo by value-per-weight are greedy. Fractional knapsack: take the best value-per-kilo first.
codeExamples:
items = [(60, 10), (100, 20), (120, 30)]     # (value, weight)
capacity = 50
total = 0.0
for value, weight in sorted(items, key=lambda it: it[0] / it[1], reverse=True):
    take = min(weight, capacity)                 # whole item, or the fraction that fits
    total += value * take / weight
    capacity -= take
    if capacity == 0:
        break
print(total)

# OUTPUT:
# 240.0

beginner.content:
Diagram

   amount 41, coins 25 10 5 1

   41 --take 25--> 16 --take 10--> 6 --take 5--> 1 --take 1--> 0
   best-looking choice at every step, never reconsidered

   works for: activity selection, Huffman, MST, Dijkstra
   fails for: 0/1 knapsack, coin sets like {1, 3, 4}

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: usually simple, fast (often just a sort, O(n log n)) and uses little memory. Jump Game shows a one-pass greedy check.
codeExamples:
def can_reach_end(jumps):
    farthest = 0
    for i, j in enumerate(jumps):
        if i > farthest:
            return False          # we are stuck before reaching index i
        farthest = max(farthest, i + j)
    return True

print(can_reach_end([2, 3, 1, 1, 4]))
print(can_reach_end([3, 2, 1, 0, 4]))

# OUTPUT:
# True
# False

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: greedy is not always optimal. With coin values 1, 3, 4 and amount 6, greedy picks 4+1+1 (3 coins) but 3+3 (2 coins) is better.
codeExamples:
coins = [4, 3, 1]
amount = 6
used = []
for c in coins:
    while amount >= c:
        amount -= c
        used.append(c)
print("greedy:", used, "(optimal is [3, 3])")

# OUTPUT:
# greedy: [4, 1, 1] (optimal is [3, 3])

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: it can never undo a choice, so it fails on problems that need global planning, like 0/1 knapsack. You must prove (or test) that the greedy rule is correct.

Architect's Notes

Use greedy when a proof (exchange argument) or a well-known theorem backs it; otherwise treat it as a heuristic and compare against an exact method on test data. When a greedy rule fails, dynamic programming or search is the next step. Greedy heuristics are still useful in production for "good enough, fast" decisions such as load balancing.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Dynamic programming (DP) solves a problem by breaking it into overlapping subproblems and storing each answer so it is computed only once. Top-down uses recursion plus a cache (memoization); bottom-up fills a table.

Why Do We Need This?

Many problems recompute the same subproblem exponentially often. Storing answers turns exponential time into polynomial time: fib(20) needs 21891 calls without a cache but only 21 real computations with one.
codeExamples:
memo, computed = {}, 0
def fib(n):
    global computed
    if n in memo:
        return memo[n]            # cache hit: no work
    computed += 1
    memo[n] = n if n < 2 else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
    return memo[n]

print(fib(20), "computed", computed, "times")

# OUTPUT:
# 6765 computed 21 times

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

DP powers spell correction (edit distance), diff tools (longest common subsequence), route and resource planning, text justification and change-making. Minimum coins for an amount, bottom-up:

Diagram

   fib(5) without cache            with cache (each computed once)

            fib5                         fib5
          /      \                     /      \
       fib4      fib3               fib4      fib3  <- reused!
       /  \      /  \               /  \
    fib3 fib2  fib2 fib1         fib3  fib2
    ...repeated work...           table: [0,1,1,2,3,5]

   exponential O(2^n)  ->  linear O(n) time, O(n) memory

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: always finds the optimum for problems with optimal substructure, and often lets you shrink memory by keeping only the last few table entries.
codeExamples:
# Climbing stairs (1 or 2 steps at a time): ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2)
def ways(n):
    prev, cur = 1, 1                # ways(0), ways(1)
    for _ in range(n - 1):
        prev, cur = cur, prev + cur  # O(1) memory instead of a full table
    return cur

print(ways(5))

# OUTPUT:
# 8

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: tables can be large. Longest common subsequence of two strings of length m and n needs about m*n cells.

Limitations

Limitations: it needs overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure, and top-down memoization still recurses, so very deep inputs hit the recursion limit. Bottom-up avoids that.

Architect's Notes

Before coding DP, define the state, the transition and the base case on paper. Choose top-down for clarity and sparse state spaces, bottom-up for speed and to avoid recursion limits. For huge state tables look for rolling arrays or different algorithms; and remember that business problems with fuzzy constraints often fit an optimizer or solver better than hand-written DP.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Breadth-first search (BFS) explores a graph level by level using a queue; depth-first search (DFS) follows one path as deep as possible before backing up, using a stack or recursion. Both visit every reachable node in O(V + E).

Why Do We Need This?

BFS visits nodes in order of distance, so the first time it reaches a node is along a shortest path (fewest edges). DFS is memory-light and natural for exploring everything, detecting cycles and backtracking.

Real-Time Use

BFS: shortest route in a maze or on a map without weights, "degrees of separation", web crawlers. DFS: solving puzzles, finding connected regions (flood fill), dependency resolution. Maze example: S start, E exit, # wall.
codeExamples:
from collections import deque

grid = ["S.#",
        "..#",
        "#.E"]
rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
q, dist = deque([(0, 0)]), {(0, 0): 0}
while q:
    r_, c_ = q.popleft()
    if grid[r_][c_] == "E":
        print("shortest path:", dist[(r_, c_)], "steps")
        break
    for dr, dc in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):
        nr, nc = r_ + dr, c_ + dc
        if 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols and grid[nr][nc] != "#" and (nr, nc) not in dist:
            dist[(nr, nc)] = dist[(r_, c_)] + 1
            q.append((nr, nc))

# OUTPUT:
# shortest path: 4 steps

beginner.content:
Diagram

        A                BFS (queue):  A | B C | D E F      level by level
       / \               DFS (stack):  A B D E F C          deep first
      B   C
     / \   \
    D   E---F

   BFS: shortest path in unweighted graphs, memory = widest level
   DFS: memory = deepest path, good for exhaustive search

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: both are linear in the size of the graph and easy to write. An iterative DFS with an explicit stack counts connected regions ("islands") in a grid.
codeExamples:
grid = ["11000",
        "11000",
        "00100",
        "00011"]
seen, islands = set(), 0
for r0 in range(len(grid)):
    for c0 in range(len(grid[0])):
        if grid[r0][c0] == "1" and (r0, c0) not in seen:
            islands += 1                         # a new island starts here
            stack = [(r0, c0)]
            while stack:
                r1, c1 = stack.pop()
                if (r1, c1) in seen or not (0 <= r1 < 4 and 0 <= c1 < 5) or grid[r1][c1] == "0":
                    continue
                seen.add((r1, c1))
                stack += [(r1 + 1, c1), (r1 - 1, c1), (r1, c1 + 1), (r1, c1 - 1)]
print("islands:", islands)

# OUTPUT:
# islands: 3

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: DFS does not find shortest paths; the first path it finds can be much longer than the best one.

Limitations

Limitations: BFS must hold a whole frontier in memory (huge for wide graphs), and recursive DFS is bounded by the recursion limit. Both need a visited set to survive cycles.
codeExamples:
from collections import deque

graph = {0: list(range(1, 10001))}          # a "star": one hub with 10000 neighbours
for leaf in range(1, 10001):
    graph[leaf] = []

q, seen, peak = deque([0]), {0}, 1
while q:
    n = q.popleft()
    for nb in graph[n]:
        if nb not in seen:
            seen.add(nb); q.append(nb)
    peak = max(peak, len(q))
print("peak queue size:", peak)

# OUTPUT:
# peak queue size: 10000

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Choose BFS for "fewest hops" and level-based problems, DFS for exhaustive exploration, cycle detection and topological work. Always keep a visited structure and prefer iterative versions for large graphs. For weighted edges use Dijkstra, and for graphs too large for memory use database or distributed graph engines.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The shortest path problem finds the cheapest route between nodes in a weighted graph. Dijkstra's algorithm repeatedly settles the closest unsettled node using a min-heap, and works when no edge weight is negative.

Why Do We Need This?

BFS counts edges, but real routes have costs: distance, time, price. A path with fewer edges can be far more expensive than a longer one with cheap edges.

Real-Time Use

GPS navigation, network routing (OSPF), flight and logistics planning and game pathfinding (A* is Dijkstra plus a heuristic). To report the route itself, remember each node's predecessor.

Diagram

          2         1
   Home ----> Park ----> Mall
     \                   |  \
      \_______ 4 ________/   5
                              \
   Park ----------- 8 ------> Office

   heap pops closest first:  Home(0) Park(2) Mall(3) Office(8)
   best route: Home -> Park -> Mall -> Office = 2 + 1 + 5 = 8

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: O((V + E) log V) with a heap, correct for non-negative weights, and it can stop early once the target is settled.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: negative edge weights break it, because a node is assumed final once settled. Bellman-Ford handles negatives at higher cost.

Limitations

Limitations: it needs the whole graph in memory and recomputes from the source for every query; unreachable nodes keep an infinite distance. Large road networks need A*, bidirectional search or precomputed hierarchies.

Architect's Notes

Pick the algorithm by weights and scale: BFS for unweighted, Dijkstra for non-negative, Bellman-Ford for negatives, A* when you have a good heuristic. In production, routing is usually delegated to a specialised engine (OSRM, pgRouting, a graph DB) and results are cached, because recomputing per request does not scale.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A topological sort orders the nodes of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) so every dependency comes before the things that depend on it. Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes nodes that have no remaining prerequisites.

Why Do We Need This?

Whenever tasks depend on each other (install packages, compile files, run jobs) you must run them in a valid order. Python's standard library offers graphlib.TopologicalSorter; the map below says "app needs web and db, web needs http".
codeExamples:
from graphlib import TopologicalSorter

needs = {"app": ["web", "db"], "web": ["http"]}   # node -> things it depends on
print(list(TopologicalSorter(needs).static_order()))

# OUTPUT:
# ['db', 'http', 'web', 'app']

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Build tools (make, Bazel), package managers (pip, npm), workflow engines (Airflow), spreadsheet recalculation and course planning all use it. graphlib also reveals which tasks can run in parallel.
codeExamples:
from graphlib import TopologicalSorter

pipeline = {"test": {"compile"}, "lint": {"compile"}, "deploy": {"test", "lint"}}
ts = TopologicalSorter(pipeline)
ts.prepare()
while ts.is_active():
    ready = sorted(ts.get_ready())          # these can all run at the same time
    print("run in parallel:", ready)
    ts.done(*ready)

# OUTPUT:
# run in parallel: ['compile']
# run in parallel: ['lint', 'test']
# run in parallel: ['deploy']

beginner.content:
Diagram

   math --> physics --\
     \                  >--> ml
      \---> stats ----/

   in-degree:  math 0 | physics 1 | stats 1 | ml 2
   remove math -> physics 0, stats 0 -> remove both -> ml 0 -> remove

   order: math, physics, stats, ml

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: O(V + E), and the result is easy to verify: every edge must point forward in the order.
codeExamples:
graph = {"math": ["physics", "stats"], "physics": ["ml"], "stats": ["ml"], "ml": []}
order = ["math", "physics", "stats", "ml"]
pos = {n: i for i, n in enumerate(order)}
valid = all(pos[u] < pos[v] for u in graph for v in graph[u])
print("valid ordering:", valid)

# OUTPUT:
# valid ordering: True

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: it only exists for acyclic graphs. A circular dependency makes ordering impossible and must be reported as an error.
codeExamples:
from graphlib import TopologicalSorter, CycleError

deps = {"a": ["b"], "b": ["c"], "c": ["a"]}      # a needs b needs c needs a
try:
    list(TopologicalSorter(deps).static_order())
except CycleError:
    print("CycleError: circular dependency")

# OUTPUT:
# CycleError: circular dependency

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the answer is usually not unique, and which valid order you get depends on tie-breaking. If you need a deterministic order (reproducible builds) you must choose a rule, such as using a heap for alphabetical order.

Architect's Notes

Model dependencies explicitly as a DAG and fail the build on cycles with a clear message. Use graphlib for in-process ordering; for distributed jobs use a workflow engine (Airflow, Prefect, Dagster) that adds retries, scheduling and state. Make tie-breaking deterministic when reproducibility matters.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The Singleton pattern guarantees a class has exactly one instance and gives everyone access to it. In Python you can override __new__, use a decorator, or simply use a module (modules are imported once, so they are natural singletons).
codeExamples:
class Config:
    _instance = None                       # holds the one and only object

    def __new__(cls):
        if cls._instance is None:          # first call: create it
            cls._instance = super().__new__(cls)
        return cls._instance               # later calls: return the same one

a = Config()
b = Config()
print(a is b)                              # same object?

# OUTPUT:
# True

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Some things must exist once for the whole application: configuration, a connection pool, a logger, a cache. Two copies would drift apart and cause confusing bugs.

Real-Time Use

Real systems use singletons for the logging system, application settings, a database connection pool or a metrics registry. A decorator version creates the expensive resource lazily and only once.

Diagram

   client A ---\
                \        +-------------------+
   client B ----+------> |  Singleton        |
                /        |  _instance  ----->| the ONE object
   client C ---/         |  get() / __new__  |
                         +-------------------+
   Counter() -> same object every time

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: one shared instance, lazy creation, controlled global access and savings in memory and start-up cost.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: it is hidden global state. Tests are no longer independent, because a change made in one test is still there in the next.

Limitations

Limitations: with the __new__ approach, __init__ runs again on every call and silently resets state. The naive version is also not thread-safe (two threads can both create an instance) unless you add a lock.
codeExamples:
class Counter:
    _instance = None
    def __new__(cls):
        if cls._instance is None:
            cls._instance = super().__new__(cls)
        return cls._instance
    def __init__(self):
        self.n = 0                  # runs on EVERY Counter() call

c1 = Counter()
c1.n = 5
c2 = Counter()                      # __init__ runs again and resets n
print(c1.n)

# OUTPUT:
# 0

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Treat singletons with suspicion: they are global variables in disguise. Prefer creating one object at start-up and passing it in (dependency injection), or use a module-level instance. Where a true singleton is needed (process-wide pool), make creation thread-safe and give tests a reset hook. Remember each process, worker or container has its own "single" instance.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The Factory pattern moves object creation into a dedicated function or class, so callers ask for "a circle" by name instead of choosing and constructing the concrete class themselves.
codeExamples:
import math

class Circle:
    def __init__(self, r): self.r = r
    def area(self): return math.pi * self.r ** 2

class Square:
    def __init__(self, s): self.s = s
    def area(self): return self.s ** 2

def shape_factory(kind, size):
    makers = {"circle": Circle, "square": Square}     # name -> class
    return makers[kind](size)

print(round(shape_factory("circle", 2).area(), 2))
print(shape_factory("square", 3).area())

# OUTPUT:
# 12.57
# 9

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

When the exact type depends on input, config or environment, scattering if kind == ... through the program couples every caller to every class. One factory keeps that decision in a single place.

Real-Time Use

File parsers chosen by extension, payment gateways chosen by country, database drivers chosen by URL scheme and test doubles chosen by environment are all factories. Python's own open(), logging.getLogger() and json.loads behave like factories.

Diagram

   client --- "circle", 2 ---> +-----------------+
                               |  shape_factory  |
                               |  (decides type) |
                               +--------+--------+
                      +-----------------+-----------------+
                      v                                   v
                 +----------+                        +----------+
                 |  Circle  |                        |  Square  |
                 +----------+                        +----------+
   client only knows the factory and the shared interface (area())

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: a single place to change creation logic, callers depend only on the shared interface, and a registry lets you add new types without editing the factory.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: extra indirection and string keys. A typo only fails at runtime, and a reader must look in the factory to see what is created.

Limitations

Limitations: the factory only knows what is registered. A class that is defined but never added to the table is invisible, and the declared return type is just the common base, so type checkers see less.

Architect's Notes

In Python, classes and functions are first-class values, so a dict of callables is often a complete factory; avoid Java-style class hierarchies. Use classmethod alternate constructors (from_json) when one class has several creation routes. If there are only one or two types and no variation, plain constructors are clearer.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The Abstract Factory pattern provides an interface for creating a whole family of related objects without naming their concrete classes. Swap the factory and the entire family changes together.
codeExamples:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class UIFactory(ABC):                       # the abstract factory
    @abstractmethod
    def button(self): ...
    @abstractmethod
    def label(self): ...

class LightUI(UIFactory):
    def button(self): return "[Light Button]"
    def label(self):  return "Light Label"

class DarkUI(UIFactory):
    def button(self): return "[Dark Button]"
    def label(self):  return "Dark Label"

def render(factory: UIFactory):
    print(factory.label(), factory.button())

render(LightUI())
render(DarkUI())

# OUTPUT:
# Light Label [Light Button]
# Dark Label [Dark Button]

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Objects that must work together (a dark button must sit with a dark label) break when mixed from different families. One factory per family guarantees every product it creates is compatible.

Real-Time Use

Cross-platform GUI toolkits, database layers (connection + command + transaction for one vendor), and test setups that swap real services for fake ones use Abstract Factory. The application code stays the same; only the factory changes.
codeExamples:
class RealPaymentFactory:
    def gateway(self): return "charging real card"
    def receipts(self): return "emailing real receipt"

class FakePaymentFactory:                    # used in tests and demos
    def gateway(self): return "pretend charge"
    def receipts(self): return "pretend receipt"

def checkout(factory):
    print(factory.gateway(), "+", factory.receipts())

env = "test"
checkout(FakePaymentFactory() if env == "test" else RealPaymentFactory())

# OUTPUT:
# pretend charge + pretend receipt

beginner.content:
Diagram

              +--------------------+
   client --> |  UIFactory (ABC)   |
              |  button()  label() |
              +---------+----------+
                 +------+------+
                 v             v
          +-----------+  +-----------+
          |  LightUI  |  |   DarkUI  |
          +-----+-----+  +-----+-----+
                |   creates    |
        LightButton LightLabel   DarkButton DarkLabel
   (one family per factory - never mixed)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: products from one family always match, the client is unaware of concrete classes, and swapping the whole family is a one-line change.
codeExamples:
class Light:
    def button(self): return "light-btn"
    def menu(self):   return "light-menu"
class Dark:
    def button(self): return "dark-btn"
    def menu(self):   return "dark-menu"

def app(factory):                            # app code never changes
    return factory.button() + " + " + factory.menu()

print(app(Light()))
print(app(Dark()))

# OUTPUT:
# light-btn + light-menu
# dark-btn + dark-menu

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: many classes, and adding a new kind of product (say a checkbox) means changing the abstract factory and every concrete factory.

Limitations

Limitations: the pattern adds ceremony that Python rarely needs. A mapping from family name to a tuple of classes gives the same result with far less code.
codeExamples:
class DarkButton: name = "dark button"
class DarkLabel:  name = "dark label"
class LightButton: name = "light button"
class LightLabel:  name = "light label"

FAMILIES = {"dark": (DarkButton, DarkLabel), "light": (LightButton, LightLabel)}

button_cls, label_cls = FAMILIES["dark"]
print(button_cls().name, "+", label_cls().name)

# OUTPUT:
# dark button + dark label

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use Abstract Factory when you truly have several interchangeable families that must stay consistent (vendors, platforms, environments). In Python prefer simple dicts or dependency injection of a few callables. If the number of product types is likely to grow, the pattern becomes costly because every factory must change.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The Builder pattern constructs a complex object step by step. A fluent builder returns self from each step, so calls chain, and a final build() returns the finished object.

Why Do We Need This?

A constructor with many optional parameters becomes unreadable: what do True, False, True, 10 mean? A builder names every step, so the call reads like a sentence.

Real-Time Use

Query builders (SQLAlchemy, Django ORM), HTTP request builders, test-data builders, UI form builders and document generators all use this pattern.
codeExamples:
class Query:
    def __init__(self):
        self._cols, self._table, self._where = "*", None, []
    def select(self, *cols): self._cols = ", ".join(cols); return self
    def from_(self, table):  self._table = table;           return self
    def where(self, cond):   self._where.append(cond);      return self
    def build(self):
        sql = f"SELECT {self._cols} FROM {self._table}"
        if self._where:
            sql += " WHERE " + " AND ".join(self._where)
        return sql

print(Query().select("name", "age").from_("users").where("age > 18").where("active = 1").build())

# OUTPUT:
# SELECT name, age FROM users WHERE age > 18 AND active = 1

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Director / client
        |  .size("large")
        v
   +--------------+   .add("cheese")   +--------------+
   |   Builder    | -----------------> |   Builder    |
   |  (partial)   |   .add("olives")   |  (more parts)|
   +--------------+                    +------+-------+
                                              | .build()
                                              v
                                      +---------------+
                                      |  Pizza (final)|
                                      +---------------+

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: readable construction, optional parts handled cleanly, and validation can happen in one place, at build(), before an invalid object exists.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: extra class and boilerplate. In Python, keyword arguments and dataclasses with defaults usually give the same readability with less code.
codeExamples:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Pizza:
    size: str = "medium"
    toppings: tuple = field(default_factory=tuple)

print(Pizza(size="large", toppings=("cheese", "olives")))   # no builder needed

# OUTPUT:
# Pizza(size='large', toppings=('cheese', 'olives'))

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: builders are mutable and easy to reuse by mistake. If build() hands out the builder's own list, later steps silently change objects that were already built.
codeExamples:
class Pizza:
    def __init__(self, toppings): self.toppings = toppings

class BadBuilder:
    def __init__(self): self._toppings = []
    def add(self, t): self._toppings.append(t); return self
    def build(self): return Pizza(self._toppings)    # BUG: shares the same list

b = BadBuilder().add("cheese")
p1 = b.build()
b.add("olives")                                      # meant for the next pizza...
p2 = b.build()
print(p1.toppings)                                   # ...but p1 changed too

# OUTPUT:
# ['cheese', 'olives']

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Reach for a builder when an object has many optional parts, an order of assembly, or must be validated as a whole. For simple records, use dataclasses with defaults and keyword arguments. Make build() copy mutable state, and consider returning an immutable (frozen) result.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The Strategy pattern defines a family of interchangeable algorithms and lets the caller pick one at runtime. In Python a strategy is often just a function passed as an argument.
codeExamples:
def no_discount(price):  return price
def ten_percent(price):  return price * 0.9
def flat_twenty(price):  return price - 20

def checkout(price, strategy):          # behaviour is chosen by the caller
    return strategy(price)

for s in (no_discount, ten_percent, flat_twenty):
    print(s.__name__, checkout(100, s))

# OUTPUT:
# no_discount 100
# ten_percent 90.0
# flat_twenty 80

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Without Strategy, a function grows a long if/elif chain that must be edited for every new rule. Strategy moves each rule into its own unit, so adding one never touches the others (open/closed principle).

Real-Time Use

Payment methods, sorting rules, compression formats, pricing, retry/back-off policies and authentication schemes are strategies. The class-based form suits strategies that carry their own settings.

Diagram

   +-----------+   uses   +--------------------+
   |  Context  | --------> |  Strategy (iface)  |
   |  Checkout |           |  pay(amount)       |
   +-----------+           +---------+----------+
                              +------+------+
                              v             v
                        +-----------+ +-----------+
                        |   Card    | |    UPI    |
                        +-----------+ +-----------+
   swap the strategy object -> behaviour changes, Context unchanged

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: algorithms can be swapped at runtime, tested in isolation, and added without changing existing code.
codeExamples:
class Shipping:
    def __init__(self, strategy): self.strategy = strategy
    def cost(self, kg): return self.strategy(kg)

standard = lambda kg: 5 + kg
express = lambda kg: 15 + 2 * kg

order = Shipping(standard)
print("standard:", order.cost(3))
order.strategy = express                 # swap at runtime
print("express :", order.cost(3))

# OUTPUT:
# standard: 8
# express : 21

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: callers must know which strategies exist, and every strategy must accept the same arguments. A mismatched one fails only when called.
codeExamples:
def apply(strategy, x):
    return strategy(x)                  # contract: one argument

good = lambda x: x * 2
bad = lambda x, y: x * y                # different signature

print(apply(good, 4))
try:
    apply(bad, 4)
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", type(e).__name__)

# OUTPUT:
# 8
# TypeError: TypeError

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: Python does not enforce the strategy interface by default. A typing.Protocol documents it and allows an isinstance check at runtime.

Architect's Notes

In Python prefer plain functions, lambdas or functools.partial as strategies; use classes only when a strategy has state or several methods. Select the strategy from configuration or a registry at the composition root. Do not introduce the pattern for a single, stable algorithm.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The Observer pattern lets one object (the subject) notify any number of dependents (observers) when something changes, without knowing who they are. It is the basis of event handling, signals and publish/subscribe.

Why Do We Need This?

Without it, a sensor would have to call the display, the logger and the alarm directly, and adding a new consumer means editing the sensor. Observer keeps the publisher unaware of its consumers.

Real-Time Use

GUI button clicks, Django signals, webhooks, message buses, spreadsheet recalculation and "notify me when stock arrives" features all follow it. An event bus generalises the idea to named topics.

Diagram

                      +--------------+
                      |   Subject    |
                      |  (publisher) |
                      +------+-------+
                             | notify(event)
            +----------------+----------------+
            v                v                v
      +-----------+    +-----------+    +-----------+
      | Observer1 |    | Observer2 |    | Observer3 |
      |  display  |    |  logger   |    |  alarm    |
      +-----------+    +-----------+    +-----------+

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: loose coupling, observers can be added or removed at runtime, and one event can drive many reactions.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: control flow becomes hard to follow, notification order is implicit, and one failing observer can stop the rest from running.

Limitations

Limitations: a subject that stores observers keeps them alive, causing memory leaks ("lapsed listener"). weakref.WeakMethod lets observers be garbage collected.
codeExamples:
import weakref, gc

class Listener:
    def on(self, v): pass

strong_list = []
l1 = Listener()
strong_list.append(l1.on)               # bound method keeps l1 alive
ref1 = weakref.ref(l1)
del l1; gc.collect()
print("strong ref keeps it alive:", ref1() is not None)

l2 = Listener()
weak = weakref.WeakMethod(l2.on)        # does not keep l2 alive
del l2; gc.collect()
print("weak ref allows cleanup  :", weak() is None)

# OUTPUT:
# strong ref keeps it alive: True
# weak ref allows cleanup  : True

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Observer decouples producers from consumers inside one process; when reactions must survive crashes, cross services or be retried, graduate to a durable message broker. Decide on ordering, error isolation (wrap each callback in try/except) and unsubscription up front. Avoid long synchronous chains of observers triggering observers.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The Adapter pattern wraps an object whose interface does not match what the client expects, translating calls so the two can work together without changing either. Think of a travel plug adapter.
codeExamples:
class LegacyPrinter:                       # existing class we cannot change
    def print_text(self, s):
        return f"[legacy] {s}"

class PrinterAdapter:                       # exposes the interface the client wants
    def __init__(self, legacy):
        self._legacy = legacy               # wrap (composition)
    def write(self, text):                  # new name -> old name
        return self._legacy.print_text(text)

printer = PrinterAdapter(LegacyPrinter())
print(printer.write("hi"))

# OUTPUT:
# [legacy] hi

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Real systems are glued from third-party SDKs, legacy code and generated clients whose shapes you do not control. Rewriting them is impossible or risky; an adapter keeps your core code clean and in your own vocabulary.

Real-Time Use

Payment gateways (Stripe, PayPal), cloud storage SDKs (S3, Azure Blob), and logging backends are classic adapter targets: the business code calls one pay() method, an adapter per vendor does the translation.

Diagram

   Client                Adapter                  Adaptee (legacy / vendor)
  +--------+  write()  +-----------------+  print_text()  +----------------+
  | calls  |---------->| PrinterAdapter  |--------------->| LegacyPrinter  |
  | write()|           | translates call |                | print_text()   |
  +--------+           +-----------------+                +----------------+
   knows only the       holds a reference                   never modified
   target interface     to the adaptee

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: reuse existing code unchanged, isolates third-party details in one place (single point to fix when a vendor changes), supports open/closed principle. Python's duck typing and __getattr__ delegation make adapters tiny.
codeExamples:
class Dog:
    def bark(self): return "Woof"
class Cat:
    def meow(self): return "Meow"

class Adapter:                              # generic object adapter
    def __init__(self, obj, **adapted):
        self.obj = obj
        self.__dict__.update(adapted)       # add the unified method names
    def __getattr__(self, name):            # everything else is delegated
        return getattr(self.obj, name)

d, c = Dog(), Cat()
animals = [Adapter(d, speak=d.bark), Adapter(c, speak=c.meow)]
for a in animals:
    print(a.speak())                        # uniform interface
print(animals[0].bark())                    # original API still reachable

# OUTPUT:
# Woof
# Meow
# Woof

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: an extra layer of indirection and more classes; the two interfaces rarely match perfectly, so the adapter also has to translate error conventions and data shapes, which is where bugs hide.

Limitations

Limitations: an adapter can only translate what the adaptee can actually do. Missing capabilities (transactions, streaming, delete) cannot be invented; the adapter must refuse or degrade.

Architect's Notes

Put adapters at the boundary of your system (anti-corruption layer) so vendor types never leak into the domain. Define the target interface from your needs, not the vendor's, and cover each adapter with contract tests. If you control both sides, change the interface instead of adding a layer.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The Decorator pattern adds behaviour to an object by wrapping it in another object with the same interface, instead of subclassing. Wrappers can be stacked. Python also has the @decorator syntax for functions, which applies the same idea to callables.
codeExamples:
class Coffee:
    def cost(self): return 2.0
    def desc(self): return "Coffee"

class Milk:                                 # decorator: same interface as Coffee
    def __init__(self, base): self._base = base
    def cost(self): return self._base.cost() + 0.5
    def desc(self): return self._base.desc() + " + Milk"

class Sugar:
    def __init__(self, base): self._base = base
    def cost(self): return self._base.cost() + 0.2
    def desc(self): return self._base.desc() + " + Sugar"

drink = Sugar(Milk(Coffee()))               # wrap, then wrap again
print(drink.desc(), round(drink.cost(), 2))

# OUTPUT:
# Coffee + Milk + Sugar 2.7

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Cross-cutting concerns (logging, timing, caching, auth, retries) would otherwise be copied into every function. A decorator adds them once, without touching the original code.

Real-Time Use

Web frameworks use decorators for routes and permissions (@app.route, @login_required); data code uses @lru_cache; API clients use retry decorators for flaky networks.

Diagram

   client --> [ Sugar ] --> [ Milk ] --> [ Coffee ]
               +0.2          +0.5          2.0
                |              |             |
   cost() <-----+--------------+-------------+   each layer calls inward,
   = 2.7                                         then adds its own part

   @shout over greet():   call -> wrapper -> greet() -> .upper() -> result

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: follows open/closed (extend without modifying), more flexible than inheritance because wrappers combine freely at runtime, keeps each class focused on one responsibility.
codeExamples: def bold(f): return lambda: "" + f() + "" def italic(f): return lambda: "" + f() + "" def text(): return "hi" a = bold(italic(text)) # combine in any order b = italic(bold(text)) print(a()) print(b()) # OUTPUT: # hi # hi

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: many small wrapper layers are hard to debug (long stack traces), order of stacking changes results, and a careless decorator hides the wrapped function's name, docstring and signature.

Limitations

Limitations: an object wrapper is not the same type as the wrapped object (isinstance fails), and calls the inner object makes to its own methods bypass the wrapper entirely.
codeExamples:
class Service:
    def a(self): return self.b()            # internal call to b
    def b(self): return "b"

class Logged:                               # logging wrapper
    def __init__(self, inner): self._inner = inner
    def __getattr__(self, name):
        attr = getattr(self._inner, name)
        if callable(attr):
            def wrapped(*args):
                print("call", name)
                return attr(*args)
            return wrapped
        return attr

s = Logged(Service())
print(s.a())                                # only 'a' is logged, not the inner b
print(isinstance(s, Service))               # the wrapper is not a Service

# OUTPUT:
# call a
# b
# False

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use object decorators when behaviours must combine at runtime; use function decorators for cross-cutting concerns. Always use functools.wraps, keep decorators side-effect free at import time, and be explicit about ordering (auth before cache, retry outside timeout). For heavy cross-cutting needs consider middleware pipelines instead of deep stacks.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A Facade is a simple class that offers one easy interface to a complex group of subsystems. Clients call the facade; the facade coordinates the details in the correct order.
codeExamples:
class Cpu:
    def start(self): return "CPU started"
class Memory:
    def load(self): return "RAM loaded"
class Disk:
    def read(self): return "boot sector read"

class Computer:                             # the facade
    def __init__(self):
        self._cpu, self._mem, self._disk = Cpu(), Memory(), Disk()
    def boot(self):                         # one call hides 3 subsystems and the order
        return [self._disk.read(), self._mem.load(), self._cpu.start()]

for step in Computer().boot():
    print(step)

# OUTPUT:
# boot sector read
# RAM loaded
# CPU started

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Subsystems grow complicated: many classes, strict call order, many options. Every client repeating that choreography is error-prone and couples everyone to internals.

Real-Time Use

E-commerce checkout, video converters, cloud SDK "client" objects and library entry points (for example requests.get() hides sockets, TLS, redirects and pooling) are facades.

Diagram

   Client
     |  buy("book", 20)
     v
  +-------------------------------+
  |        CheckoutFacade         |   simple API
  +--------+---------+------------+
           |         |            |
           v         v            v
     +-----------+ +---------+ +----------+
     | Inventory | | Payment | | Shipping |    complex subsystems
     +-----------+ +---------+ +----------+

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: simpler API, fewer dependencies for clients, and freedom to change or replace the subsystem internals without breaking callers.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: a facade can become a "god object" that knows everything and keeps growing; it also adds one more layer to maintain and test.
codeExamples:
class AppFacade:                            # warning sign: everything in one place
    def register(self): ...
    def login(self): ...
    def buy(self): ...
    def refund(self): ...
    def report(self): ...

public = [m for m in dir(AppFacade) if not m.startswith("_")]
print(len(public), "public methods and growing")

# OUTPUT:
# 5 public methods and growing

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a facade simplifies access but does not enforce it. Python has no real private members, so callers can still reach the subsystems directly and bypass rules.
codeExamples:
class Engine:
    def start(self): return "engine started"

class Car:                                  # facade over Engine
    def __init__(self): self._engine = Engine()
    def drive(self): return self._engine.start() + ", driving"

car = Car()
print(car.drive())
print(car._engine.start())                  # nothing stops this bypass

# OUTPUT:
# engine started, driving
# engine started

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use facades to define module boundaries (one public entry per package, details underscore-prefixed or in an internal package). Keep them thin: orchestration only, no business rules, otherwise split by use case. In services, an application-service layer is effectively a facade over the domain.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The Repository pattern hides how data is stored behind a collection-like interface (add, get, all). The rest of the application asks for objects and never sees SQL, files or HTTP.

Why Do We Need This?

If business code contains SQL, switching database, testing without a database, or caching all mean editing business logic. A repository isolates persistence so the domain stays pure.

Real-Time Use

Typical apps have one repository per aggregate (UserRepository, OrderRepository) with SQL, ORM or REST implementations behind the same interface. Here the same service runs unchanged on SQLite.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: persistence-agnostic domain, trivial fakes for unit tests, one place for queries and caching, easier migration between storage technologies.
codeExamples:
class FakeRepo:                             # test double: a plain dict
    def __init__(self): self.saved = {}
    def add(self, key, value): self.saved[key] = value

def register(repo, name):                   # business logic under test
    repo.add(name.lower(), name)

repo = FakeRepo()
register(repo, "ABAJI")
assert repo.saved == {"abaji": "ABAJI"}       # no database, runs in microseconds
print("test passed:", repo.saved)

# OUTPUT:
# test passed: {'abaji': 'ABAJI'}

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: extra layer and boilerplate, leaky abstractions (generic all() forces clients to filter in memory), and a growing zoo of find_by_x methods.
codeExamples:
ROWS = [{"id": i} for i in range(1000)]

class Repo:
    def __init__(self): self.transferred = 0
    def all(self):
        self.transferred += len(ROWS); return ROWS
    def get(self, i):
        self.transferred += 1; return ROWS[i]

slow = Repo()
hit = [row for row in slow.all() if row["id"] == 7]   # filter on the client side
print("generic all():", slow.transferred, "rows moved")

fast = Repo()
fast.get(7)                                           # query-specific method
print("get(7):", fast.transferred, "row moved")

# OUTPUT:
# generic all(): 1000 rows moved
# get(7): 1 row moved

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a repository per aggregate does not give you transactions across repositories. Without a Unit of Work, a failure between two repository calls leaves data half-updated.

Architect's Notes

Define repository interfaces in the domain layer (typing.Protocol or ABC) and implement them in infrastructure. Pair with a Unit of Work for transactions and keep queries intention-revealing. For read-heavy reporting skip repositories and query directly (CQRS read side); do not wrap an ORM session in another full abstraction without a reason.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Dependency Injection means an object receives the collaborators it needs (from outside, usually via the constructor) instead of creating them itself. It makes the code flexible and testable.

Why Do We Need This?

When a class builds its own dependencies it is welded to them: you cannot switch to SMS, and you cannot test without sending real emails.

Real-Time Use

In production you inject real clients (database, mail, HTTP); in unit tests you inject fakes that record calls. FastAPI's Depends() is dependency injection built into the framework.
codeExamples:
class FakeSender:                           # test double
    def __init__(self): self.sent = []
    def send(self, to, msg):
        self.sent.append((to, msg)); return "ok"

class Notifier:
    def __init__(self, sender): self.sender = sender
    def welcome(self, user): return self.sender.send(user, "Welcome!")

fake = FakeSender()
Notifier(fake).welcome("zed")
assert fake.sent == [("zed", "Welcome!")]   # verified without any real email
print("test passed:", fake.sent)

# OUTPUT:
# test passed: [('zed', 'Welcome!')]

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Without DI                              With DI
   +------------+   creates   +--------+   +------------+  receives  +--------+
   |  Notifier  |------------>| Email  |   |  Notifier  |<-----------| Sender |
   +------------+             +--------+   +------------+            +--------+
