    u = USERS.get(name)
    return name if u and u["password_ok"] else None

def authorize(name, action):       # permission: allowed?
    perms = {"admin": {"read", "delete"}, "viewer": {"read"}}
    return action in perms[USERS[name]["role"]]

who = authenticate("baji")
print(who, authorize(who, "read"), authorize(who, "delete"))

# OUTPUT:
# baji True False

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Confusing the two is a top vulnerability class (OWASP "Broken Access Control"). A logged-in user must still be prevented from reading another user's data.

Real-Time Use

Web APIs: 401 Unauthorized means not authenticated, 403 Forbidden means authenticated but not allowed. FastAPI uses dependencies for both; enterprises add RBAC, ABAC, and SSO.

Diagram

   request ──► [ AuthN ] ──► identity known? ──no──► 401 Unauthorized
                  │ yes
                  ▼
              [ AuthZ ] ──► allowed (role / owner / policy)? ──no──► 403 Forbidden
                  │ yes
                  ▼
              business logic

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages of separating them: change login (add MFA/SSO) without touching permission rules, centralise policies, easier audits and least privilege.
codeExamples:
# Policy as data: one place to change who can do what
POLICY = {"admin": {"users:read", "users:write"}, "support": {"users:read"}}
can = lambda role, perm: perm in POLICY.get(role, set())
print(can("support", "users:read"), can("support", "users:write"))

# OUTPUT:
# True False

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: authorization logic scattered in handlers is easy to forget on one endpoint; complex policies (per-object, per-tenant) are hard to test and reason about.
codeExamples:
# Forgotten check on a new endpoint = vulnerability
endpoints = {"/users": "checked", "/export": "FORGOT check"}
print([e for e, s in endpoints.items() if s != "checked"])

# OUTPUT:
# ['/export']

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: RBAC cannot express "owner of this record" rules alone; stateless tokens carry permissions that go stale until they expire; client-side checks are never trusted.
codeExamples:
# Token says admin; the user was demoted 1 minute ago but the token lives 15 min
token_claims = {"sub": "ada", "role": "admin", "exp_in_min": 15}
db_role_now = "viewer"
print("stale privilege:", token_claims["role"] != db_role_now)

# OUTPUT:
# stale privilege: True

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Authenticate once at the edge (gateway or middleware) and authorize at every layer that touches data, deny by default. Prefer a central policy engine (OPA, Cedar, Casbin) over ad-hoc ifs when rules grow, and always verify object ownership server-side. Use short-lived tokens plus revocation lists for sensitive actions.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A JSON Web Token is a signed string header.payload.signature (each Base64URL). The server signs claims (user id, expiry) so it can later verify them without a session lookup. Signed is not encrypted: anyone can read the payload.
codeExamples:
import base64, json, hmac, hashlib

def b64(b): return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=").decode()
header = b64(json.dumps({"alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT"}).encode())
payload = b64(json.dumps({"sub": "42", "exp": 1900000000}).encode())
sig = b64(hmac.new(b"secret", f"{header}.{payload}".encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest())
token = f"{header}.{payload}.{sig}"
print(token.count("."), "dots;", "payload readable:", json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(payload + "==")))

# OUTPUT:
# 2 dots; payload readable: {'sub': '42', 'exp': 1900000000}

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Servers with many instances would need a shared session store. A signed, self-contained token lets any instance verify identity locally, ideal for APIs and microservices.
codeExamples:
import hmac, hashlib, base64
def b64(b): return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=").decode()
def sign(msg, key): return b64(hmac.new(key, msg.encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest())

msg = "header.payload"
good = sign(msg, b"secret")
print("valid  :", hmac.compare_digest(good, sign(msg, b"secret")))     # constant-time compare
print("forged :", hmac.compare_digest(good, sign("header.TAMPERED", b"secret")))

# OUTPUT:
# valid  : True
# forged : False

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Use PyJWT: short-lived access tokens (5-15 min) plus refresh tokens, with exp, iss and aud validated. FastAPI endpoints read the Bearer token from the Authorization header.
codeExamples:
# pip install pyjwt
import jwt, time
SECRET = "change-me-32-bytes-minimum-secret!!"
token = jwt.encode({"sub": "42", "exp": time.time() + 900}, SECRET, algorithm="HS256")
claims = jwt.decode(token, SECRET, algorithms=["HS256"])     # ALWAYS pin algorithms
print(claims["sub"])

# OUTPUT:
# 42

beginner.content:
Diagram

   client                                      API server
   ┌────────┐  POST /login (user+pass)         ┌──────────────┐
   │        │ ───────────────────────────────► │ verify, sign │
   │        │ ◄─────── JWT (exp 15 min) ────── │ with key     │
   │        │                                  └──────────────┘
   │        │  GET /data  Authorization: Bearer <JWT>
   │        │ ───────────────────────────────► verify signature + exp
   └────────┘ ◄────────────── 200 / 401 ─────── (no DB lookup)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: stateless verification, scales horizontally, carries claims, standard across languages, works for cross-service auth and SSO.
codeExamples:
import jwt, time
SECRET = "change-me-32-bytes-minimum-secret!!"
t = jwt.encode({"sub": "1", "exp": time.time() - 10}, SECRET, algorithm="HS256")   # already expired
try:
    jwt.decode(t, SECRET, algorithms=["HS256"])
except jwt.ExpiredSignatureError:
    print("expired token rejected automatically")

# OUTPUT:
# expired token rejected automatically

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: cannot be revoked before expiry without extra state, payload is public, large tokens on every request, easy to misuse (alg confusion, long lifetimes, storing in localStorage).
codeExamples:
import jwt
SECRET = "change-me-32-bytes-minimum-secret!!"
forged = jwt.encode({"sub": "admin"}, "", algorithm="none")        # alg=none attack
try:
    jwt.decode(forged, SECRET, algorithms=["HS256"])               # pinned algorithms block it
except jwt.InvalidTokenError as e:
    print("rejected:", type(e).__name__)

# OUTPUT:
# rejected: InvalidAlgorithmError

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: logout/revocation needs a denylist or short expiry; HS256 shares one secret between signer and verifier (use RS256/EdDSA with a public key for many verifiers); never put secrets in claims.
codeExamples:
import base64, json
payload = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(json.dumps({"sub": "1", "ssn": "123-45-6789"}).encode()).decode()
print("anyone can decode:", json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(payload))["ssn"])

# OUTPUT:
# anyone can decode: 123-45-6789

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use JWTs for short-lived access tokens between services; for browser sessions server-side sessions in HttpOnly cookies are often simpler and revocable. Pin algorithms, validate iss/aud/exp, rotate keys with a kid header and JWKS, keep lifetimes short and use refresh-token rotation. Do not store sensitive data in claims.

beginner.content:
Introduction

OAuth 2.0 is a delegation framework: a user lets an app access their data at another service (Google, GitHub) without sharing their password. The app receives an access token with limited scopes. OpenID Connect adds identity (ID token) on top.
codeExamples:
from urllib.parse import urlencode
# Step 1 of the Authorization Code flow: send the user to the provider
params = {"response_type": "code", "client_id": "my-app", "redirect_uri": "https://app.example.com/cb",
          "scope": "openid email", "state": "r4nd0m-csrf-value", "code_challenge_method": "S256",
          "code_challenge": "E9Melhoa..."}
print("https://auth.example.com/authorize?" + urlencode(params)[:70] + "...")

# OUTPUT:
# https://auth.example.com/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=my-app&redirect_u...

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Without OAuth, third-party apps would ask for your password, gaining full, unrevocable access. OAuth gives scoped, revocable, time-limited access and enables "Sign in with Google".
codeExamples:
granted_scopes = {"email", "profile"}
def can_read_calendar(scopes): return "calendar.read" in scopes
print("calendar access:", can_read_calendar(granted_scopes))      # least privilege

# OUTPUT:
# calendar access: False

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Social login, API access between SaaS products, mobile apps (Authorization Code + PKCE), server-to-server (Client Credentials), and FastAPI's OAuth2PasswordBearer for your own tokens.

Diagram

   User        Your App (client)        Auth Server         Resource API
    │  click login   │                        │                    │
    │───────────────►│ redirect + state+PKCE  │                    │
    │◄───────────────┴───────────────────────►│ user logs in,consents
    │                │◄── redirect + code ────│                    │
    │                │── code + verifier ────►│                    │
    │                │◄── access token ───────│                    │
    │                │────── Bearer token ───────────────────────►│

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: no password sharing, scoped and revocable tokens, delegated trust, wide ecosystem and libraries (Authlib), enables SSO.
codeExamples:
import secrets, hashlib, base64
# PKCE: proves the app that started the flow is the one finishing it
verifier = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
challenge = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(hashlib.sha256(verifier.encode()).digest()).rstrip(b"=").decode()
print(len(challenge), "char challenge sent first; verifier revealed only at token exchange")

# OUTPUT:
# 43 char challenge sent first; verifier revealed only at token exchange

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: complex with many grant types and easy to implement wrongly (open redirects, missing state, token leakage), OAuth itself is not authentication without OIDC.
codeExamples:
import secrets
# state parameter blocks CSRF on the callback
sent_state = secrets.token_urlsafe(16)
received_state = "attacker-controlled"
print("callback accepted:", secrets.compare_digest(sent_state, received_state))

# OUTPUT:
# callback accepted: False

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: bearer tokens grant access to whoever holds them; depends on provider availability; implicit and password grants are deprecated; refresh tokens need secure storage.
codeExamples:
deprecated = ["implicit", "resource owner password"]
recommended = ["authorization code + PKCE", "client credentials (machines)", "device code (TVs)"]
print("use:", recommended[0], "| avoid:", deprecated)

# OUTPUT:
# use: authorization code + PKCE | avoid: ['implicit', 'resource owner password']

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Do not write your own authorization server: use a proven IdP (Keycloak, Auth0, Cognito, Entra ID) and a maintained library. Use Authorization Code + PKCE everywhere, exact-match redirect URIs, short token lifetimes, and scoped tokens per service. Add token introspection or JWT validation at resource servers.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Never store passwords, store a slow, salted hash. Hashing is one-way; a unique random salt per user defeats rainbow tables; a deliberately slow algorithm (argon2id, bcrypt, scrypt, PBKDF2) makes brute force costly.
codeExamples:
import hashlib, os
salt = os.urandom(16)
h = hashlib.scrypt(b"correct horse", salt=salt, n=2**14, r=8, p=1)   # stdlib, memory-hard
print(len(salt), len(h), "bytes | stored as salt+hash, never the password")

# OUTPUT:
# 16 32 bytes | stored as salt+hash, never the password

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Databases leak. If passwords are plaintext or fast-hashed (MD5, SHA-1), a breach exposes every account within hours because users reuse passwords across sites.
codeExamples:
import hashlib
# Fast hashes are cracked at billions per second on GPUs
print(hashlib.md5(b"password123").hexdigest())          # same input -> same hash -> lookup tables
print(hashlib.md5(b"password123").hexdigest() == hashlib.md5(b"password123").hexdigest())

# OUTPUT:
# 482c811da5d5b4bc6d497ffa98491e38
# True

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Use argon2-cffi or passlib/bcrypt in web apps; the hash string embeds algorithm, parameters and salt so you can upgrade later.
codeExamples:
# pip install argon2-cffi
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
ph = PasswordHasher()
stored = ph.hash("s3cret!")                 # includes salt + params
print(stored.startswith("$argon2id$"))
print(ph.verify(stored, "s3cret!"))         # raises on mismatch
print(ph.check_needs_rehash(stored))        # upgrade params on next login

# OUTPUT:
# True
# True
# False

beginner.content:
Diagram

   password ──► + random salt ──► argon2id(cost) ──► "$argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$salt$hash"
                                                         │ stored in DB
   login attempt ──► same params + salt ──► compare constant-time ──► OK / reject

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: breach resilience, unique hashes per user, tunable cost, parameters stored with the hash, standard libraries.
codeExamples:
import hashlib, os
pw = b"same-password"
h1 = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", pw, os.urandom(16), 600_000)
h2 = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", pw, os.urandom(16), 600_000)
print("same password, different hashes:", h1 != h2)

# OUTPUT:
# same password, different hashes: True

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: intentionally uses CPU/memory so login endpoints can be DoS targets; you cannot recover forgotten passwords (only reset); high cost needs tuning per hardware.
codeExamples:
import hashlib, os, time
t = time.perf_counter()
hashlib.scrypt(b"pw", salt=os.urandom(16), n=2**15, r=8, p=1, maxmem=64 * 1024 * 1024)
print("ms per hash is intentionally noticeable:", (time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000 > 5)

# OUTPUT (varies):
# ms per hash is intentionally noticeable: True

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a weak password stays weak even if hashed well; hashing does not stop credential stuffing or phishing; bcrypt truncates inputs at 72 bytes.
codeExamples:
import hashlib, os
common = ["123456", "password", "qwerty"]
salt = b"x" * 16
stolen = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", b"qwerty", salt, 1000)
for guess in common:                                   # dictionary attack still works on weak pw
    if hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", guess.encode(), salt, 1000) == stolen:
        print("cracked:", guess)

# OUTPUT:
# cracked: qwerty

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use argon2id with parameters tuned to roughly 100-500 ms, plus rate limiting, lockouts or CAPTCHAs, breached-password checks (HIBP k-anonymity) and MFA/passkeys. Consider delegating to an IdP so you never store passwords. Add an optional server-side pepper in an HSM/secret store, and plan for rehash-on-login upgrades.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Encryption turns readable data into ciphertext using a key. Symmetric (AES-GCM, Fernet) uses one shared key; asymmetric (RSA, ECC) uses a public/private pair. Hashing is different: one-way, no key to decrypt.
codeExamples:
# pip install cryptography
from cryptography.fernet import Fernet
key = Fernet.generate_key()                  # keep this secret
f = Fernet(key)
token = f.encrypt(b"credit card 4111")
print(token[:6], f.decrypt(token))

# OUTPUT (token varies):
# b'gAAAAA' b'credit card 4111'

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Data at rest (disks, databases, backups) and in transit must stay confidential and tamper-proof even if storage or network is compromised. Authenticated encryption provides both secrecy and integrity.
codeExamples:
from cryptography.fernet import Fernet, InvalidToken
f = Fernet(Fernet.generate_key())
t = bytearray(f.encrypt(b"balance=100"))
t[20] ^= 1                                    # attacker flips one bit
try:
    f.decrypt(bytes(t))
except InvalidToken:
    print("tampering detected")

# OUTPUT:
# tampering detected

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Field-level encryption of PII in databases, encrypting backups, envelope encryption with KMS (data key encrypts data, master key encrypts the data key), and signing/verifying with public keys.
codeExamples:
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
import os
key = AESGCM.generate_key(bit_length=256)
aes = AESGCM(key)
nonce = os.urandom(12)                        # MUST be unique per message with the same key
ct = aes.encrypt(nonce, b"patient record", b"user:42")   # 3rd arg = authenticated metadata
print(aes.decrypt(nonce, ct, b"user:42"))

# OUTPUT:
# b'patient record'

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Symmetric  (one key)            Asymmetric (key pair)
   plaintext ─[key]─► ciphertext   plaintext ─[PUBLIC key]─► ciphertext
   ciphertext ─[key]─► plaintext   ciphertext ─[PRIVATE key]─► plaintext
   fast, bulk data                 slow, key exchange + signatures

   Envelope:  KMS master key ─encrypts─► data key ─encrypts─► your data

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: confidentiality plus integrity (AEAD), fast symmetric speed, public-key crypto enables key exchange and signatures, mature audited libraries.
codeExamples:
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import ed25519
priv = ed25519.Ed25519PrivateKey.generate()
sig = priv.sign(b"release-1.0.tar.gz")
priv.public_key().verify(sig, b"release-1.0.tar.gz")      # raises if invalid
print("signature valid; anyone with the public key can verify")

# OUTPUT:
# signature valid; anyone with the public key can verify

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: key management is the hard part, mistakes (nonce reuse, ECB mode, rolling your own) destroy security, encrypted data cannot be searched or indexed directly.
codeExamples:
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
import os
aes = AESGCM(AESGCM.generate_key(256))
nonce = os.urandom(12)
c1 = aes.encrypt(nonce, b"A" * 16, None)
c2 = aes.encrypt(nonce, b"B" * 16, None)       # nonce reuse = catastrophic leak (XOR of plaintexts)
print("same nonce twice: NEVER do this ->", len(c1) == len(c2))

# OUTPUT:
# same nonce twice: NEVER do this -> True

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: encryption does not hide metadata (size, timing); the key must exist where decryption happens; quantum computers threaten RSA/ECC (post-quantum migration ahead); secrets in memory are exposed to a compromised host.
codeExamples:
# Key and data must live apart
bad = {"db": "ciphertext", "key": "same server .env"}      # attacker gets both
good = {"db": "ciphertext", "key": "KMS / HSM, access audited"}
print("separate key custody:", bad["key"] != good["key"])

# OUTPUT:
# separate key custody: True

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Do not invent crypto: use high-level libraries (cryptography, libsodium/PyNaCl), authenticated modes only (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305), unique nonces and a KMS for key custody with rotation. Encrypt at the right layer (TLS in transit, disk/DB at rest, field-level for sensitive data) and plan for key loss and recovery.

beginner.content:
Introduction

HTTPS is HTTP over TLS: the client verifies the server's certificate chain, both sides negotiate keys, and all traffic is encrypted and integrity-protected. Python's ssl module and requests/httpx use it.
codeExamples:
import ssl, socket
ctx = ssl.create_default_context()           # verifies cert chain + hostname by default
with socket.create_connection(("www.python.org", 443), timeout=5) as raw:
    with ctx.wrap_socket(raw, server_hostname="www.python.org") as tls:
        print(tls.version(), tls.getpeercert()["subject"][0][0][1][:3])

# OUTPUT (needs internet, example):
# TLSv1.3 www

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Plain HTTP exposes passwords, cookies and tokens to anyone on the network path (Wi-Fi, ISPs) and allows modification of content. HTTPS gives confidentiality, integrity and server authenticity.
codeExamples:
import requests
# Verification is ON by default; never turn it off to "fix" an error
try:
    requests.get("https://expired.badssl.com/", timeout=5)
except requests.exceptions.SSLError:
    print("certificate rejected - correct behaviour")

# OUTPUT (needs internet):
# certificate rejected - correct behaviour

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Terminate TLS at a reverse proxy or load balancer (nginx, Caddy, ALB) with automatic Let's Encrypt certificates, set HSTS, and redirect HTTP to HTTPS. Internal services use mTLS in zero-trust networks.
codeExamples:
# Security headers a proxy/app adds for HTTPS sites
headers = {"Strict-Transport-Security": "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains",
           "X-Content-Type-Options": "nosniff"}
for k, v in headers.items():
    print(f"{k}: {v}")

# OUTPUT:
# Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains
# X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

beginner.content:
Diagram

   browser                                   server
      │── ClientHello (TLS versions, ciphers) ─►│
      │◄─ ServerHello + certificate chain ─────│  verify: CA signed? hostname? expiry?
      │── key exchange (ECDHE) ───────────────►│  -> shared session key
      │◄════ encrypted HTTP request/response ═►│

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: encryption, integrity, authentication, required by browsers for HTTP/2, geolocation, service workers and Secure cookies; boosts user trust and SEO.
codeExamples:
from http.cookies import SimpleCookie
c = SimpleCookie()
c["session"] = "abc"
c["session"]["secure"] = True        # only sent over HTTPS
c["session"]["httponly"] = True      # invisible to JavaScript
c["session"]["samesite"] = "Lax"
print(c.output())

# OUTPUT:
# Set-Cookie: session=abc; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Secure

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: handshake latency and CPU (small with TLS 1.3), certificate lifecycle management (expiry outages), debugging encrypted traffic is harder.
codeExamples:
from datetime import date
expires = date(2026, 12, 1)
days_left = (expires - date(2026, 10, 5)).days
print("renew now" if days_left < 30 else f"{days_left} days left", "- automate with ACME")

# OUTPUT:
# 57 days left - automate with ACME

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: encrypts the channel only, not the server's logic (SQLi and XSS still work), metadata like hostnames/IPs stays visible, trust depends on certificate authorities.
codeExamples:
# HTTPS does not validate your inputs
url = "https://shop.example.com/search?q=' OR 1=1 --"
print("encrypted in transit, still an injectable query:", "OR 1=1" in url)

# OUTPUT:
# encrypted in transit, still an injectable query: True

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Terminate TLS 1.2+ (prefer 1.3) at the edge with automated ACME renewal, enable HSTS, disable legacy protocols, and monitor expiry. Use mTLS between services where identity matters (service mesh). Never disable verification in code; pin a private CA bundle instead for internal endpoints.

beginner.content:
Introduction

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser rule: a page from origin A may not read responses from origin B unless B opts in with Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers. An origin = scheme + host + port.
codeExamples:
from urllib.parse import urlparse
def origin(url):
    u = urlparse(url)
    return f"{u.scheme}://{u.netloc}"

print(origin("https://app.example.com/page"))
print(origin("https://app.example.com") == origin("https://api.example.com"))   # different host

# OUTPUT:
# https://app.example.com
# False

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

The same-origin policy protects users: a malicious site must not read your bank page using your cookies. But legitimate front-ends on another origin (SPA at :3000, API at :8000) need a controlled exception.

Real-Time Use

In FastAPI use CORSMiddleware with explicit origins. Non-simple requests trigger a preflight OPTIONS request that the server must answer.
codeExamples:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware

app = FastAPI()
app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["https://app.example.com"],      # never "*" with credentials
    allow_methods=["GET", "POST"],
    allow_headers=["Authorization", "Content-Type"],
    allow_credentials=True,
    max_age=600,                                    # cache preflight 10 minutes
)
print("middleware stack:", [m.cls.__name__ for m in app.user_middleware])

# OUTPUT:
# middleware stack: ['CORSMiddleware']

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Browser at https://app.example.com
        │ 1. OPTIONS /data  (preflight: Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method)
        ▼
   API https://api.example.com
        │ 2. 204 + Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
        ▼
        │ 3. real request (GET/POST) allowed ──► JS can read response
   (no matching header ──► browser hides the response from JS)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: keeps the safe default (isolation) while allowing precise, server-controlled sharing between trusted origins.
codeExamples:
# Preflight decision for PUT with a custom header
def preflight(method, headers, allowed_methods={"GET", "POST"}):
    return method in allowed_methods
print("PUT allowed:", preflight("PUT", ["X-Custom"]))

# OUTPUT:
# PUT allowed: False

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: confusing errors, extra preflight round-trips, misconfiguration (reflecting any Origin, wildcard with credentials) turns it into a vulnerability.
codeExamples:
# Dangerous: echo back whatever Origin arrives
def bad_cors(origin): return {"Access-Control-Allow-Origin": origin, "Access-Control-Allow-Credentials": "true"}
print(bad_cors("https://evil.example")["Access-Control-Allow-Origin"], "<- attacker site can read user data")

# OUTPUT:
# https://evil.example <- attacker site can read user data

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: enforced only by browsers, so curl, scripts and attackers' servers ignore it; it is not authentication and does not stop CSRF-style sends.
codeExamples:
import urllib.request
# A script is not a browser: CORS never blocks it. Protect the API with auth, not CORS.
req = urllib.request.Request("http://127.0.0.1:9/private", headers={"Origin": "https://evil.example"})
print("server must still check credentials for", req.full_url)

# OUTPUT:
# server must still check credentials for http://127.0.0.1:9/private

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Prefer a same-origin deployment (reverse proxy serving UI and API under one host) to avoid CORS entirely. Otherwise use a strict allow-list per environment, never reflect Origin, avoid wildcard with credentials, and still authenticate every request: CORS is a browser convenience control, not a server security boundary.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Cross-Site Request Forgery tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request (the browser automatically attaches cookies). The server cannot tell it from a real click unless it requires a secret the attacker cannot know.
codeExamples: # evil.example page: # The browser sends the victim's bank cookie with that request. request = {"path": "/transfer", "cookie": "session=VALID", "origin": "https://evil.example"} print("server sees valid session cookie:", request["cookie"].startswith("session")) # OUTPUT: # server sees valid session cookie: True

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

State-changing endpoints that rely only on cookies for identity are exploitable from any website the user visits. Defences make requests prove they came from your own page.
codeExamples:
import secrets, hmac
SESSION = {"csrf": secrets.token_urlsafe(16)}              # stored server-side per session
def check(form_token):
    return hmac.compare_digest(SESSION["csrf"], form_token)

print("legit form:", check(SESSION["csrf"]))
print("forged    :", check("guess"))

# OUTPUT:
# legit form: True
# forged    : False

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Server-rendered forms use per-session CSRF tokens (Django middleware, Flask-WTF). APIs use SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies and require custom headers or Bearer tokens that browsers do not auto-send.
codeExamples:
from http.cookies import SimpleCookie
c = SimpleCookie()
c["sid"] = "abc"
c["sid"]["samesite"] = "Strict"        # cookie not sent on cross-site requests
c["sid"]["httponly"] = True
c["sid"]["secure"] = True
print(c.output())

# OUTPUT:
# Set-Cookie: sid=abc; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Secure

beginner.content:
Diagram

   victim logged in to bank.example (cookie stored)
        │ visits evil.example
        ▼
   evil page auto-submits form ───► bank.example/transfer  (cookie attached!)
                                         │
        without token / SameSite ───────►│ executes transfer   (attack succeeds)
        with CSRF token / SameSite ─────►│ 403 rejected

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages of the defences: SameSite cookies are a one-line browser-enforced fix; token checks are simple and framework-supported; Origin/Referer checks add defence in depth.
codeExamples:
def origin_ok(headers, host="bank.example"):
    from urllib.parse import urlparse
    o = headers.get("Origin") or headers.get("Referer", "")
    return urlparse(o).netloc == host
print(origin_ok({"Origin": "https://bank.example"}), origin_ok({"Origin": "https://evil.example"}))

# OUTPUT:
# True False

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: tokens must be wired into every form and AJAX call; SameSite behaviour differs between browsers and "Lax" still allows top-level GET navigation; subdomain takeover can bypass.
codeExamples:
# State change on GET is exploitable even with SameSite=Lax (top-level link click)
bad = "GET /delete_account"
good = "POST /delete_account (+ CSRF token)"
print("never mutate on:", bad.split()[0], "| use:", good.split()[0])

# OUTPUT:
# never mutate on: GET | use: POST

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: CSRF defences do not stop XSS (an attacker script can read the token); APIs using only Authorization headers are naturally immune, but cookie-authenticated APIs are not.
codeExamples:
# XSS defeats CSRF tokens: injected JS reads the token from the page and uses it
page_token = "tok-123"
injected_js_can_read = True
print("CSRF protection holds under XSS:", not injected_js_can_read)

# OUTPUT:
# CSRF protection holds under XSS: False

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use SameSite=Lax or Strict plus HttpOnly Secure cookies as the baseline, add synchronizer or double-submit tokens for browser forms, and require non-simple headers for APIs. Never change state on GET. For pure token-in-header APIs (no cookie auth) CSRF is not applicable, but protect against XSS since tokens in JS are stealable.

beginner.content:
Introduction

SQL injection happens when user input is concatenated into a SQL string, letting an attacker change the query's meaning. The fix is parameterised queries: the driver sends SQL and values separately.
codeExamples:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE users(name TEXT, pw TEXT)")
db.execute("INSERT INTO users VALUES ('ada', 'x'), ('baji', 'y')")

name = "' OR '1'='1"                                    # attacker input
vulnerable = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'"
print(db.execute(vulnerable).fetchall())                # returns EVERY user

# OUTPUT:
# [('ada', 'x'), ('baji', 'y')]

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

A single injectable field can leak, modify or delete the whole database or lead to remote code execution. It remains in the OWASP Top 10 because string-built queries are still common.
codeExamples:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE users(name TEXT)")
db.execute("INSERT INTO users VALUES ('ada')")
name = "' OR '1'='1"
safe = db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", (name,)).fetchall()   # placeholder
print(safe)                                             # treated purely as data

# OUTPUT:
# []

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Use placeholders in every driver (? in sqlite3, %s in psycopg), or an ORM (SQLAlchemy) that parameterises automatically. Identifiers (table/column names) cannot be parameters: use an allow-list.

Diagram

   BAD :  "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + input + "'"
                                             └─ input becomes SQL code
   GOOD:  cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", (input,))
              │ SQL text ────────► parser (structure fixed)
              └ values  ─────────► bound as data only

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages of parameterisation: complete protection for values, driver handles quoting and types, queries can be cached and planned once, code is easier to read.
codeExamples:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE t(a INT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO t VALUES (?)", [(1,), (2,), (3,)])   # batch with params
print(db.execute("SELECT SUM(a) FROM t WHERE a > ?", (1,)).fetchone())

# OUTPUT:
# (5,)

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: dynamic queries (variable filters, IN lists) tempt developers back to string building; ORMs still allow raw SQL and unsafe text() usage.
codeExamples:
ids = [1, 2, 3]
placeholders = ",".join("?" * len(ids))                 # build the placeholders, not the values
sql = f"SELECT * FROM t WHERE id IN ({placeholders})"
print(sql)

# OUTPUT:
# SELECT * FROM t WHERE id IN (?,?,?)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: parameters protect data, not logic: an over-privileged DB account still lets a successful injection do damage; stored procedures built with dynamic SQL stay vulnerable.
codeExamples:
# Least privilege limits blast radius
grants = {"app_user": ["SELECT", "INSERT", "UPDATE"], "admin": ["ALL"]}
print("app can DROP:", "DROP" in grants["app_user"] or "ALL" in grants["app_user"])

# OUTPUT:
# app can DROP: False

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Parameterise everything, use an ORM or query builder by default, allow-list dynamic identifiers, give the app a least-privilege DB role, and add static analysis (bandit) and WAF as depth, not as the fix. Review any raw SQL in code review as a security-sensitive change.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Cross-Site Scripting is injecting attacker-controlled HTML or JavaScript into a page that other users view. The script then runs with the victim's session and can steal tokens or act as the user. Defence: output encoding, templates with auto-escape, and CSP.
codeExamples:
user_comment = '' page = f"
{user_comment}
" # unsafe: raw interpolation print(page) # OUTPUT: #

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Anywhere user text is shown (comments, profile names, search echoes) is a potential injection point. One XSS defeats cookies, CSRF tokens and authentication for that user.
codeExamples:
import html
user_comment = '<script>alert(1)</script>'
print(html.escape(user_comment))          # & < > " ' become harmless entities

# OUTPUT:
# <script>alert(1)</script>

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Jinja2 auto-escapes when autoescape=True (Flask enables it for .html); React escapes by default; the danger zones are |safe, innerHTML, dangerouslySetInnerHTML and URL attributes.
codeExamples:
from jinja2 import Environment, select_autoescape env = Environment(autoescape=select_autoescape(["html"])) tpl = env.from_string("

Hello {{ name }}

") print(tpl.render(name="x")) # OUTPUT: #

Hello <b>x</b>

beginner.content:
Diagram

   attacker ─ posts <script>…</script> ─► DB (stored)
                                            │
   victim opens page ◄── server renders ◄───┘
        │ (unescaped)             │ escape at output + CSP
        ▼                         ▼
   script runs as victim      shown as plain text
   steals session/token       nothing executes

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages of the defences: auto-escaping templates fix the common case by default; CSP blocks inline scripts even if one slips through; HttpOnly cookies hide the session from JS.
codeExamples:
csp = "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'"
headers = {"Content-Security-Policy": csp, "X-Content-Type-Options": "nosniff"}
print(headers["Content-Security-Policy"].split(";")[1].strip())

# OUTPUT:
# script-src 'self'

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: context matters (HTML body vs attribute vs JS vs URL need different encoding); rich-text features need a sanitizer; strict CSP breaks inline scripts and is hard to retrofit.
codeExamples:
import html
# html.escape is right for HTML text, but not for a javascript: URL
href = "javascript:alert(1)"
print(html.escape(href))                  # unchanged! still dangerous in <a href=...>
print("allow only http(s) schemes:", href.startswith(("http://", "https://")))

# OUTPUT:
# javascript:alert(1)
# allow only http(s) schemes: False

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: escaping on input is wrong (encode at output, per context); DOM-based XSS happens entirely client-side and server escaping cannot see it; third-party scripts widen the surface.
codeExamples: # Sanitise rich text with an allow-list library (pip install bleach / nh3) import re def strip_scripts(s): return re.sub(r"(?is)", "", s) # NOT sufficient alone! print(strip_scripts("")) # regex misses event handlers # OUTPUT: #

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Encode at output by context, rely on auto-escaping templates, ban raw HTML insertion in code review, sanitise rich text with a maintained allow-list library, set a strict CSP (nonces), HttpOnly Secure SameSite cookies, and Trusted Types for DOM sinks. Treat any use of safe/innerHTML as a security exception to justify.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Server-Side Request Forgery: an attacker makes your server fetch a URL of their choosing (webhook, image-by-URL, PDF render), reaching internal systems such as http://169.254.169.254/ (cloud metadata) that the attacker cannot reach directly.
codeExamples:
import urllib.request
def fetch_preview(url):                  # VULNERABLE: fetches anything it is told to
    return urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=3).read()

# attacker supplies: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
print("server would call its own cloud metadata service and return IAM credentials")

# OUTPUT:
# server would call its own cloud metadata service and return IAM credentials

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Servers sit inside trusted networks. Any feature that makes outbound requests from user input turns the server into a proxy into that network, exposing databases, admin panels and cloud credentials.
codeExamples:
import ipaddress, socket
def is_internal(host):
    ip = ipaddress.ip_address(socket.gethostbyname(host))
    return ip.is_private or ip.is_loopback or ip.is_link_local or ip.is_reserved
for h in ["localhost", "127.0.0.1", "169.254.169.254"]:
    print(h, is_internal(h))

# OUTPUT:
# localhost True
# 127.0.0.1 True
# 169.254.169.254 True

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Typical places: webhook testers, "import from URL", avatar fetchers, link previews, XML/PDF processors. Fix with an allow-list of domains, resolving and validating IPs, blocking redirects, and network egress rules.

Diagram

   attacker ──► "fetch http://169.254.169.254/..." ──► your API server
                                                          │ trusted network
                                                          ▼
                                    internal admin / metadata / DB (no external access)
   defence:  allow-list host ─► resolve ─► reject private IPs ─► no redirects ─► egress firewall

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages of strong controls: allow-lists are simple and effective, IMDSv2 on AWS requires a token header, and egress firewalls add a safety net regardless of app bugs.
codeExamples:
# IMDSv2 needs a PUT to get a token first - a simple GET SSRF no longer works
steps = ["PUT /latest/api/token (header X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds)",
         "GET /latest/meta-data/ with X-aws-ec2-metadata-token"]
print(len(steps), "steps; blind GET-only SSRF fails")

# OUTPUT:
# 2 steps; blind GET-only SSRF fails

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: bypasses are inventive: DNS rebinding (name resolves to a public IP at check time, internal at use time), redirects, decimal/octal IPs, IPv6, URL parser differences.
codeExamples:
import ipaddress
print(ipaddress.ip_address(int("2130706433")))          # decimal form of 127.0.0.1
# http://2130706433/ is loopback; naive string checks for "127." miss it

# OUTPUT:
# 127.0.0.1

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: validating the hostname once is not enough (TOCTOU with DNS): connect to the validated IP itself and disable redirects; blind SSRF gives no response body but can still hit internal actions.
codeExamples:
import requests
def safe_get(url):
    # validate first, then refuse redirects so a 302 cannot point inward
    return requests.get(url, timeout=3, allow_redirects=False)
print("allow_redirects=False closes the redirect bypass")

# OUTPUT:
# allow_redirects=False closes the redirect bypass

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Layer controls: avoid fetching user URLs at all when possible; otherwise route through a dedicated egress proxy with allow-lists, run it in an isolated network segment, enforce IMDSv2, and block private ranges at the firewall. Resolve once and connect to the pinned IP to defeat DNS rebinding.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Secrets (API keys, DB passwords, tokens, private keys) must stay out of source code and images. They are supplied at run time from environment variables, mounted files, or a secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, Doppler).
codeExamples:
import os
# BAD : API_KEY = "sk-live-abc123"      # committed to git forever
# GOOD: read from the environment at start-up and fail fast if missing
def need(name):
    v = os.environ.get(name)
    if not v:
        raise RuntimeError(f"missing secret: {name}")
    return v
os.environ["API_KEY"] = "demo"
print(need("API_KEY"))

# OUTPUT:
# demo

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Leaked secrets in git, logs or images are one of the most common breach causes; bots scan GitHub within seconds of a push. Rotation and least privilege limit the damage.

Real-Time Use

Local dev uses git-ignored .env files; CI uses encrypted repository secrets; production uses a managed secret store with IAM, auditing and rotation; Kubernetes mounts Secrets (encrypt etcd at rest).

Diagram

   developer laptop      CI/CD                 production
   .env (git-ignored)    encrypted secrets     Vault / AWS Secrets Manager
         │                    │                      │ IAM identity
         └────────► env vars / mounted files ◄───────┘
                            │
                         app reads at start ──► never in git, image, or logs

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: central control, audit logs, automatic rotation, per-service access policies, short-lived dynamic credentials (Vault database engine), no secret sprawl.
codeExamples:
# Short-lived credentials: leak window is minutes, not forever
import time
creds = {"user": "v-app-123", "expires": time.time() + 900}
print("ttl seconds ~", int(creds["expires"] - time.time()))

# OUTPUT (varies):
# ttl seconds ~ 899

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: extra infrastructure and a new dependency (outage = cannot start), bootstrapping problem (how does the app authenticate to the vault?), developer friction.
codeExamples:
# The "secret zero" problem: something must authenticate first
chain = ["pod identity / IAM role", "-> fetch DB password from vault", "-> connect to DB"]
print(" ".join(chain))

# OUTPUT:
# pod identity / IAM role -> fetch DB password from vault -> connect to DB

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a process that uses a secret can still leak it (logs, error pages, memory dumps); env vars are visible to the process tree; rotation requires apps to reload credentials.
codeExamples:
import logging
class Redact(logging.Filter):
    def filter(self, record):
        record.msg = str(record.msg).replace("hunter2", "***")
        return True
log = logging.getLogger("app"); log.addFilter(Redact())
logging.basicConfig(format="%(message)s")
log.warning("login failed for password=hunter2")

# OUTPUT:
# login failed for password=***

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Never commit secrets; enable push protection and scanners, rotate on any suspicion, and prefer workload identity (OIDC, IAM roles) over static keys. Use short-lived dynamic credentials, mount secrets as files rather than env vars where possible, and design the app to reload rotated values without redeploy.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Secure API design builds protections into the contract: authentication, object-level authorization, input validation, rate limiting, minimal data exposure, safe errors and auditing. The OWASP API Security Top 10 is the checklist.
codeExamples:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
class CreateUser(BaseModel):                       # validate at the boundary
    email: str = Field(pattern=r"^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[a-z]{2,}$")
    age: int = Field(ge=13, le=120)
try:
    CreateUser(email="not-an-email", age=5)
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, "-> 422 Unprocessable Entity")

# OUTPUT:
# ValidationError -> 422 Unprocessable Entity

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

APIs expose business logic directly to attackers and automation. Common failures: broken object-level authorization, excessive data exposure, no rate limit, mass assignment, verbose errors.

Real-Time Use

Real systems front APIs with a gateway (TLS, auth, quotas), use versioned routes, idempotency keys for payments, pagination caps, signed webhooks and audit logs.
codeExamples:
import time
class RateLimiter:                                  # fixed window, per key
    def __init__(self, limit, window): self.limit, self.window, self.hits = limit, window, {}
    def allow(self, key):
        now = int(time.time() // self.window)
        bucket = self.hits.setdefault(key, [now, 0])
        if bucket[0] != now: bucket[:] = [now, 0]
        bucket[1] += 1
        return bucket[1] <= self.limit
rl = RateLimiter(3, 60)
print([rl.allow("user1") for _ in range(5)])

# OUTPUT:
# [True, True, True, False, False]

beginner.content:
Diagram

   client ─TLS─► gateway ──► authN ──► rate limit ──► input validation (schema)
                                                           │
                                         object-level authZ (owner check)
                                                           │
                                       business logic ──► minimal response model
                                                           │
                          audit log + safe error format ◄──┘

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: fewer incidents, predictable behaviour for clients, easier compliance (SOC2, GDPR), schema-first validation also gives documentation and generated clients.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: more design and review effort, stricter schemas slow rapid prototyping, rate limits and auth add latency and operational complexity.
codeExamples:
# Trade-off example: sequential integer IDs leak volume and enable enumeration
import uuid
print("int id:", 1001, "-> guessable | uuid4:", uuid.uuid4().version, "-> unguessable (still check authz!)")

# OUTPUT:
# int id: 1001 -> guessable | uuid4: 4 -> unguessable (still check authz!)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: design controls cannot stop stolen valid credentials, business-logic abuse (coupon farming), or flaws in dependencies; unguessable IDs are not authorization.
codeExamples:
# Safe errors: do not leak internals to the client
def handle(exc):
    log = f"internal: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"       # keep details in server logs
    return {"error": "internal_error", "request_id": "req-7f3a"}, log
body, _ = handle(KeyError("users_table"))
print(body)

# OUTPUT:
# {'error': 'internal_error', 'request_id': 'req-7f3a'}

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Adopt secure defaults by construction: schema validation at the edge, deny-by-default authorization with centralised policy, response models that whitelist fields, quotas per identity, idempotency and audit trails. Threat-model new endpoints, run SAST/DAST and dependency audits in CI, and design for revocation, versioning and graceful deprecation.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A NumPy ndarray is a fixed-type, N-dimensional block of contiguous memory. Every element has the same dtype, so operations run in compiled C instead of the Python interpreter.
codeExamples:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])      # 1-D array from a list
m = a.reshape(2, 3)                   # same memory, viewed as 2 rows x 3 cols
print(m)
print(m.shape, m.dtype, m.ndim)       # metadata every array carries

# OUTPUT:
# [[1 2 3]
#  [4 5 6]]
# (2, 3) int64 1

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Python lists store pointers to full objects, so numeric work is slow and memory hungry. Scientific code needs a compact numeric container that supports math on whole datasets at once.
codeExamples:
import numpy as np, sys

lst = list(range(1000))
arr = np.arange(1000)
print(sys.getsizeof(lst) + sum(sys.getsizeof(x) for x in lst))  # list + int objects
print(arr.nbytes)                                               # 1000 * 8 bytes

# OUTPUT (example, CPython 64-bit):
# 36856
# 8000

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Image pixels, sensor streams, financial time series, and every ML framework's tensors are ndarrays or are interchangeable with them (PyTorch, pandas, OpenCV, scikit-learn).
codeExamples:
import numpy as np

# A tiny 2x2 "grayscale image" - brighten and clip to the 0..255 range
img = np.array([[100, 200],
                [250,  30]], dtype=np.uint8)
bright = np.clip(img.astype(int) + 60, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)
print(bright)

# OUTPUT:
# [[160 255]
#  [255  90]]

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Python list                         NumPy ndarray
   +----+   +--------+                +--------------------------------+
   | ptr|-->| int obj|                | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |  (C)   |
   | ptr|-->| int obj|                +--------------------------------+
   | ptr|-->| int obj|                  one contiguous buffer, one dtype
   +----+   +--------+                  shape=(2,3)  strides=(24,8)
   scattered objects                   -> reshape = new view, same bytes

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: 10-100x faster than loops, low memory, slicing creates cheap views, rich creation helpers (zeros, linspace, random), and a universal interchange format.
codeExamples:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(10)
view = a[2:5]          # slicing returns a VIEW - no copy, O(1)
view[0] = 99           # writing through the view changes the original
print(a)
print(np.linspace(0, 1, 5))   # 5 evenly spaced points, endpoints included

# OUTPUT:
# [ 0  1 99  3  4  5  6  7  8  9]
# [0.   0.25 0.5  0.75 1.  ]

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: one dtype per array (mixed data gets coerced), fixed size (append copies), and views can cause surprising aliasing bugs.
codeExamples:
import numpy as np

mixed = np.array([1, "two", 3.0])     # everything is coerced to one type
print(mixed, mixed.dtype)

a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.append(a, 4)                   # arrays cannot grow: this builds a NEW array
print(a, b)

# OUTPUT:
# ['1' 'two' '3.0'] <U32
# [1 2 3] [1 2 3 4]

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the whole array must fit in RAM, integers silently overflow (no automatic big ints), and no built-in missing-value for integer dtypes.
codeExamples:
import numpy as np

x = np.array([250], dtype=np.uint8)
print(x + 10)                     # wraps around at 256 - no error raised
print(np.array([1, 2]).dtype)     # an int array cannot hold NaN
# np.array([1, np.nan]) forces float64 as the only way to hold a missing value

# OUTPUT:
# [4]
# int64

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use ndarrays as the numeric core and keep data in one dtype and contiguous layout so SIMD and BLAS can help. For data larger than RAM use memory-mapped files (np.memmap), Dask or Arrow; for heterogeneous, labeled tables prefer pandas or Polars. Be explicit about dtype at API boundaries to avoid silent overflow and coercion.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Vectorization means applying an operation to a whole array without a Python loop. Broadcasting is the rule that lets arrays of different shapes combine by virtually stretching size-1 (or missing) dimensions.
codeExamples:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a * 10)            # scalar broadcast to every element
print(a + np.array([10, 20, 30]))   # element-wise on equal shapes

# OUTPUT:
# [10 20 30]
# [11 22 33]

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Python loops execute one bytecode per element. Vectorized code moves the loop into C, which is dramatically faster and also shorter and clearer.
codeExamples:
import numpy as np, timeit

a = np.arange(100_000)
loop = timeit.timeit(lambda: [x * 2 for x in a], number=5)
vec  = timeit.timeit(lambda: a * 2, number=5)
print("vectorized is faster:", vec < loop)

# OUTPUT (varies by machine; typically 50-200x):
# vectorized is faster: True

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Normalising features before ML, applying a price discount to a million rows, or computing distances between points all use broadcasting instead of loops.
codeExamples:
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[1., 200.],
              [2., 400.],
              [3., 600.]])
# Standardize each column: (3,2) - (2,) broadcasts across rows
Z = (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / X.std(axis=0)
print(Z.round(2))

# OUTPUT:
# [[-1.22 -1.22]
#  [ 0.    0.  ]
#  [ 1.22  1.22]]

beginner.content:
Diagram

   shapes aligned from the RIGHT, size-1 dims are stretched:

        X      (3, 2)          col  (3, 1)        row  (   3)
      - mean   (   2)   ok     * row(   3)  -->   (3, 3)
      ----------------
      result   (3, 2)

   (3,2) + (3,)  -> 2 vs 3  -> ValueError

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: speed, no explicit loops, outer-product-style computations without building giant tiled arrays, and code that reads like the math.
codeExamples:
import numpy as np

col = np.array([[1], [2], [3]])      # shape (3,1)
row = np.array([10, 20, 30])         # shape (3,)  -> treated as (1,3)
print(col * row)                     # (3,1)*(1,3) -> (3,3) multiplication table

# OUTPUT:
# [[10 20 30]
#  [20 40 60]
#  [30 60 90]]

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: intermediate arrays use extra memory, and silent broadcasting can hide shape bugs by producing a valid but wrong result.
codeExamples:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1, 2, 3])          # shape (3,)
b = np.array([[1], [2], [3]])    # shape (3,1) - mistakenly a column
print((a + b).shape)             # you wanted (3,) but silently got (3,3)

# OUTPUT:
# (3, 3)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: dimensions must be equal or 1 (aligned from the right); otherwise NumPy raises an error. Complex branching logic does not vectorize well.
codeExamples:
import numpy as np

try:
    np.ones((3, 2)) + np.ones(3)     # trailing dims 2 vs 3 are incompatible
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)

# OUTPUT:
# operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (3,2) (3,)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Prefer vectorized expressions for bulk numeric work, but watch memory: chained operations allocate temporaries (use out=, in-place ops, or numexpr/Numba for fused kernels). Assert shapes at function boundaries to catch accidental broadcasting. When logic is branch-heavy, use np.where or consider Numba rather than contorting the algorithm.

beginner.content:
Introduction

numpy.linalg and the @ operator give matrix multiplication, inverses, determinants, solving linear systems, eigenvalues and SVD, backed by optimized BLAS/LAPACK libraries.
codeExamples:
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
B = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]])
print(A @ B)         # matrix product (NOT element-wise)
print(A * B)         # element-wise product - a different thing
print(A.T)           # transpose

# OUTPUT:
# [[2 1]
#  [4 3]]
# [[0 2]
#  [3 0]]
# [[1 3]
#  [2 4]]

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Machine learning, graphics, physics simulation and statistics are all linear algebra. You need a fast, numerically stable implementation rather than hand-written loops.
codeExamples:
import numpy as np

# Solve  2x + y = 5,  x + 3y = 10  - use solve(), do not invert
A = np.array([[2., 1.], [1., 3.]])
b = np.array([5., 10.])
x = np.linalg.solve(A, b)
print(x)                      # x=1, y=3
print(np.allclose(A @ x, b))  # verify the solution

# OUTPUT:
# [1. 3.]
# True

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Linear regression via least squares, PCA via SVD, PageRank via eigenvectors, 3-D rotations in games and robotics.
codeExamples:
import numpy as np

# Fit y = w*x + c by least squares on perfectly linear data
x = np.array([0., 1., 2., 3.])
y = 2 * x + 1
X = np.column_stack([x, np.ones_like(x)])          # design matrix [x, 1]
w, c = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]
print(round(w, 3), round(c, 3))

# OUTPUT:
# 2.0 1.0

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Ax = b                 numpy.linalg
   +---+   +-+   +-+       solve(A,b)   -> LAPACK gesv (LU)
   | A | x |x| = |b|       lstsq        -> SVD least squares
   +---+   +-+   +-+       eig / svd    -> decompositions
      \                     |
       '--> @ (matmul) --> BLAS (OpenBLAS / MKL, multithreaded)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: multithreaded BLAS speed, one consistent API, numerically stable routines (solve, lstsq, svd), and easy batching over stacked matrices.
codeExamples:
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[4., 0.], [0., 9.]])
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eig(A)       # eigen-decomposition
print(vals)
print(np.linalg.det(A))             # 4*9
print(np.linalg.norm(np.array([3., 4.])))   # Euclidean length

# OUTPUT:
# [4. 9.]
# 36.0
# 5.0

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: floating-point error accumulates, singular or ill-conditioned matrices give unreliable results, and inv() is slower and less accurate than solve().
codeExamples:
import numpy as np

S = np.array([[1., 2.], [2., 4.]])   # rows are multiples: singular
try:
    np.linalg.inv(S)
except np.linalg.LinAlgError as e:
    print("LinAlgError:", e)
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3, np.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))

# OUTPUT:
# LinAlgError: Singular matrix
# False True

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: dense matrices only (use scipy.sparse for sparse data), everything must fit in memory, and no GPU support (use CuPy, JAX or PyTorch for that).
codeExamples:
import numpy as np

n = 100_000
# A dense n x n float64 matrix would need n*n*8 bytes:
print(n * n * 8 / 1e9, "GB")      # far beyond typical RAM - use scipy.sparse

# OUTPUT:
# 80.0 GB

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Never compute inv(A) @ b; call solve, or factorize once and reuse (scipy.linalg.lu_factor). Check conditioning (np.linalg.cond) before trusting results, and move to sparse or GPU backends when dimensions grow. For ML training use autodiff frameworks rather than hand-coded gradients.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A Series is a labeled 1-D array; a DataFrame is a table of Series sharing one row index. Columns can have different dtypes.
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name":  ["Abaji", "Ben", "Chen"],
    "score": [88, 92, 75],
})
print(df)
print(df["score"].mean())    # a column is a Series

# OUTPUT:
#    name  score
# 0  Abaji     88
# 1   Ben     92
# 2  Chen     75
# 85.0

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Real data is tabular, labeled and messy. Raw NumPy gives no column names, no mixed types and no alignment, so every analysis would need bookkeeping code.
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.Series([1, 2, 3], index=["x", "y", "z"])
b = pd.Series([10, 20, 30], index=["y", "z", "w"])
print(a + b)         # arithmetic ALIGNS on labels; missing -> NaN

# OUTPUT:
# w     NaN
# x     NaN
# y    12.0
# z    23.0
# dtype: float64

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Loading CSV/SQL/Excel/JSON, cleaning it, computing KPIs, then feeding it to charts or models is the day job of analysts and data engineers.
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd, io

csv = io.StringIO("city,sales\nPune,100\nDelhi,150\n")   # stands in for a file
df = pd.read_csv(csv)
df["sales_k"] = df["sales"] / 1000                       # new derived column
print(df)
print(df.dtypes.to_dict())

# OUTPUT:
#     city  sales  sales_k
# 0   Pune    100    0.100
# 1  Delhi    150    0.150
# {'city': dtype('O'), 'sales': dtype('int64'), 'sales_k': dtype('float64')}

beginner.content:
Diagram

   DataFrame
          columns -->   name     score    <- each column is a Series
   index  +-----------+--------+--------+
     0    |  Abaji     |   88   |   (dtypes may differ per column)
     1    |  Ben      |   92   |
     2    |  Chen     |   75   |
          +-----------+--------+
   Index labels drive alignment, joins and loc[] selection

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: expressive selection (loc/iloc), label alignment, rich I/O, built-in stats, and tight integration with NumPy, Matplotlib and scikit-learn.
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6]}, index=["r1", "r2", "r3"])
print(df.loc["r2", "b"])        # label-based
print(df.iloc[0, 1])            # position-based
print(df.describe().loc[["mean", "max"]])

# OUTPUT:
# 5
# 4
#         a    b
# mean  2.0  5.0
# max   3.0  6.0

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: high memory use (often 5-10x file size), ambiguous view-vs-copy semantics, and slow row-wise Python loops.
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"x": range(3)})
# Row loops are the slow way - prefer vectorized column math
slow = [row["x"] * 2 for _, row in df.iterrows()]
fast = df["x"] * 2
print(slow, fast.tolist())
print(df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() > 0)

# OUTPUT:
# [0, 2, 4] [0, 2, 4]
# True

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: single-machine and in-memory, mostly single-threaded, and object-dtype strings are costly. Very large data needs Polars, Dask, Spark or a database.
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series(["a", "b", None, "a"] * 1000)
print(s.dtype, s.memory_usage(deep=True) > 100_000)    # object dtype is heavy
print(s.astype("category").memory_usage(deep=True) < s.memory_usage(deep=True))

# OUTPUT:
# object True
# True

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Pandas is ideal for interactive analysis of data that fits in memory. Use categorical and nullable dtypes, avoid iterrows, and consider Parquet plus Polars/DuckDB for faster pipelines. Enable copy-on-write (pandas 2.x) to remove chained-assignment ambiguity, and do not use a DataFrame as a production data structure inside tight services.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Filtering selects rows with a boolean mask. GroupBy follows split-apply-combine: split rows by key, aggregate each group, combine the results.
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"dept": ["IT", "HR", "IT", "HR"], "pay": [50, 40, 70, 45]})
print(df[df["pay"] > 44])                 # boolean mask filter
print(df.groupby("dept")["pay"].mean())   # average pay per department

# OUTPUT:
#   dept  pay
# 0   IT   50
# 2   IT   70
# 3   HR   45
# dept
# HR    42.5
# IT    60.0
# Name: pay, dtype: float64

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Questions are rarely about all rows: "which orders failed?", "revenue per region?". Without filter and group tools you would write nested loops and dictionaries.

Real-Time Use

Sales per month, error counts per service, average session length per user cohort, top-N customers per region.
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"region": ["N", "N", "S", "S", "S"],
                   "amount": [10, 30, 5, 25, 15]})
# multiple aggregations at once with named outputs
out = df.groupby("region").agg(total=("amount", "sum"),
                               orders=("amount", "count"))
print(out)

# OUTPUT:
#         total  orders
# region
# N          40       2
# S          45       3

beginner.content:
Diagram

   df  --split by key-->  group a ---> agg ---+
        (groupby)         group b ---> agg ---+--> combine --> result
                          group c ---> agg ---+

   mask = df.pay > 44   -->  [F, T, T, ...]   -->  df[mask] keeps True rows

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: concise, readable, optimized in C/Cython, supports multiple keys, named aggregations, transforms and custom functions.
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"g": ["a", "a", "b"], "v": [1, 3, 10]})
df["share"] = df["v"] / df.groupby("g")["v"].transform("sum")   # keeps row count
print(df.query("g == 'a' and v > 1"))
print(df)

# OUTPUT:
#    g  v
# 1  a  3
#    g   v  share
# 0  a   1   0.25
# 1  a   3   0.75
# 2  b  10   1.00

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: custom Python functions inside apply are slow; chained boolean conditions need parentheses and & / | (not and/or); groupby drops NaN keys by default.
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd, numpy as np

df = pd.DataFrame({"k": ["a", np.nan, "a"], "v": [1, 2, 3]})
print(df.groupby("k")["v"].sum().to_dict())              # NaN group silently dropped
print(df.groupby("k", dropna=False)["v"].sum().to_dict())

# OUTPUT:
# {'a': 4}
# {'a': 4, nan: 2}

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the groups are computed in memory on one machine, and ordered or window-style logic (rank within group, rolling) needs specific methods rather than plain aggregation.
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"g": ["a", "a", "b", "b"], "v": [5, 9, 7, 2]})
# top-1 per group needs sort + head (or idxmax), not a plain aggregation
top = df.sort_values("v", ascending=False).groupby("g").head(1).sort_index()
print(top)

# OUTPUT:
#    g  v
# 1  a  9
# 2  b  7

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

GroupBy is the workhorse for reporting, but heavy aggregation belongs where the data lives (SQL, DuckDB, warehouse) to avoid pulling raw rows into Python. Prefer built-in aggregations and transform over apply with lambdas; use categorical keys for speed and observed=True to avoid empty groups.

beginner.content:
Introduction

merge joins two DataFrames on key columns like a SQL join. pivot/pivot_table reshapes long data into a wide grid (and melt reverses it).
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd

users  = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3], "name": ["Abaji", "Ben", "Chen"]})
orders = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 1, 3], "amt": [10, 20, 5]})
print(users.merge(orders, on="id", how="left"))    # keep every user

# OUTPUT:
#    id  name   amt
# 0   1  Abaji  10.0
# 1   1  Abaji  20.0
# 2   2   Ben   NaN
# 3   3  Chen   5.0

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Data lives in many tables (normalization) and reports need a different shape than storage. You must combine and reshape without manual lookups.
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd

long = pd.DataFrame({"month": ["Jan", "Jan", "Feb", "Feb"],
                     "prod":  ["A", "B", "A", "B"],
                     "qty":   [5, 7, 6, 8]})
wide = long.pivot(index="month", columns="prod", values="qty")
print(wide)

# OUTPUT:
# prod   A  B
# month
# Feb    6  8
# Jan    5  7

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Enriching events with customer data, building monthly-by-product dashboards, preparing wide feature matrices for ML.
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd

sales = pd.DataFrame({"reg": ["N", "N", "S"], "q": ["Q1", "Q1", "Q1"], "amt": [10, 5, 7]})
pt = pd.pivot_table(sales, index="reg", columns="q", values="amt", aggfunc="sum")
print(pt)

# OUTPUT:
# q    Q1
# reg
# N    15
# S     7

beginner.content:
Diagram

   users            orders                 merge(on="id", how="left")
   id name          id amt                 id name  amt
   1  Abaji   <--+-- 1  10           -->    1  Abaji  10
   2  Ben       +-- 1  20                  1  Abaji  20
   3  Chen      '-- 3   5                  2  Ben   NaN
                                           3  Chen   5

   long (month,prod,qty) --pivot--> wide grid  --melt--> long again

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: all join types (inner/left/right/outer), validation, indicator column, flexible aggregation in pivot_table, melt to go back to long form.
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.DataFrame({"k": [1, 2], "x": ["a", "b"]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"k": [2, 3], "y": ["B", "C"]})
print(a.merge(b, on="k", how="outer", indicator=True))

# OUTPUT:
#    k    x    y      _merge
# 0  1    a  NaN   left_only
# 1  2    b    B        both
# 2  3  NaN    C  right_only

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: duplicate keys multiply rows (many-to-many explosion), and plain pivot fails on duplicate index/column pairs.
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.DataFrame({"k": [1, 1], "x": [1, 2]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"k": [1, 1], "y": [3, 4]})
print(len(a.merge(b, on="k")))            # 2 x 2 = 4 rows, not 2
try:
    a.merge(b, on="k", validate="one_to_one")
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)

# OUTPUT:
# 4
# MergeError

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: merges build hash tables in memory, key dtype mismatches (int vs str) silently match nothing, and pivot cannot aggregate.
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.DataFrame({"k": [1, 2]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"k": ["1", "2"], "v": [9, 8]})
try:
    a.merge(b, on="k")
except ValueError as e:
    print("ValueError:", str(e)[:36])      # modern pandas refuses int-vs-str keys

# OUTPUT:
# ValueError: You are trying to merge on int64 and

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Joins are where silent data bugs breed: always pass validate=, check row counts before and after, and normalize key dtypes and whitespace. For large joins push the work to SQL/DuckDB/Polars, and keep a tidy long table as the source of truth, pivoting only for presentation.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Pandas marks missing values as NaN (floats), None or pd.NA (nullable dtypes). You detect them with isna() and treat them with dropna() or fillna().
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd, numpy as np

s = pd.Series([1.0, np.nan, 3.0, None])
print(s.isna().tolist())        # which entries are missing
print(s.sum(), s.count())       # NaN skipped by default; count excludes NaN

# OUTPUT:
# [False, True, False, True]
# 4.0 2

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Real data has gaps (sensor offline, optional form fields). Ignoring them gives wrong averages, crashes models, or biases results.
codeExamples:
import numpy as np

print(np.nan == np.nan)           # NaN is never equal to itself
print(np.mean([1, 2, np.nan]))    # NumPy propagates NaN: the whole mean is NaN

# OUTPUT:
# False
# nan

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Cleaning customer records, forward-filling time-series ticks, imputing medians before model training.
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd, numpy as np

df = pd.DataFrame({"age": [25, np.nan, 35], "city": ["Pune", None, "Delhi"]})
df["age"] = df["age"].fillna(df["age"].median())     # numeric: median
df["city"] = df["city"].fillna("Unknown")            # text: sentinel
print(df)

# OUTPUT:
#     age     city
# 0  25.0     Pune
# 1  30.0  Unknown
# 2  35.0    Delhi

beginner.content:
Diagram

   raw data --> isna() mask --> decide ----+--> dropna()      (lose rows)
   [1, ?, 3]    [F, T, F]                  +--> fillna(x)     (constant / stat)
                                           +--> ffill/interp  (time series)
                                           '--> model handles NaN (e.g. trees)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: missing-aware aggregations, and flexible strategies: drop, constant, mean/median, forward/backward fill, interpolation.
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd, numpy as np

t = pd.Series([10.0, np.nan, np.nan, 40.0])
print(t.interpolate().tolist())     # straight line between known points
print(t.ffill().tolist())           # carry the last value forward

# OUTPUT:
# [10.0, 20.0, 30.0, 40.0]
# [10.0, 10.0, 10.0, 40.0]

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: NaN forces integer columns to float, and every imputation choice injects assumptions that can bias analysis.
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd

print(pd.Series([1, 2, None]).dtype)                 # int became float64
print(pd.Series([1, 2, None], dtype="Int64").tolist())   # nullable integer fixes it

# OUTPUT:
# float64
# [1, 2, <NA>]

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a function cannot tell why data is missing (random vs systematic), and dropna can discard most of your rows if every row has some gap.
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd, numpy as np

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, np.nan, 3], "b": [np.nan, 2, 3], "c": [1, 2, np.nan]})
print(len(df.dropna()))             # any-NaN rule leaves only 0 rows here
print(len(df.dropna(thresh=2)))     # keep rows with at least 2 real values

# OUTPUT:
# 0
# 3

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Treat missingness as information: record an is_missing indicator column before imputing, fit imputers on training data only (to avoid leakage), and document the strategy. Prefer pandas nullable dtypes in new pipelines, and validate completeness at ingestion with schema checks rather than fixing it deep inside analysis code.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Matplotlib is Python's foundational plotting library. The object-oriented API creates a Figure containing one or more Axes, on which you draw lines, bars, scatters and more.
codeExamples:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")            # headless backend: render to files, no window
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()          # one figure, one axes
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 8], marker="o", label="growth")
ax.set_xlabel("step"); ax.set_ylabel("value"); ax.legend()
fig.savefig("growth.png", dpi=100)
print("saved growth.png")

# OUTPUT:
# saved growth.png

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Numbers in a table hide patterns. A chart shows trends, outliers and distributions in seconds, and reports and papers need reproducible figures.
codeExamples:
import numpy as np
data = np.array([3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 6, 20])
print("mean:", data.mean().round(2), "median:", np.median(data))
# The mean looks normal, but only a plot (boxplot/hist) reveals the outlier 20.

# OUTPUT:
# mean: 6.44 median: 5.0

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Dashboards, scientific papers, monitoring reports and ML training curves; also the base of seaborn and the pandas .plot() method.
codeExamples:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"month": ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar"], "sales": [100, 140, 120]})
ax = df.plot.bar(x="month", y="sales", legend=False)   # pandas wraps Matplotlib
ax.set_title("Monthly sales")
ax.figure.savefig("sales.png")
print(type(ax).__name__)

# OUTPUT:
# Axes

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Figure  (the canvas)
   +-------------------------------------------+
   |  Axes (a plot)            Axes            |
   |  +-----------------+     +-------------+  |
   |  | line / bar /    |     | scatter     |  |
   |  | hist artists    |     | + ticks     |  |
   |  +-----------------+     +-------------+  |
   +-------------------------------------------+
        |
        v  savefig -> PNG (raster) | SVG / PDF (vector)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: total control over every element, publication-quality vector output (SVG/PDF), huge chart variety, and works in notebooks, scripts and servers.
codeExamples:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6, 2))   # side-by-side panels
a1.hist([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3], bins=3)
a2.scatter([1, 2, 3], [3, 1, 2])
fig.savefig("panels.svg")                            # vector format
print(len(fig.axes), "axes")

# OUTPUT:
# 2 axes

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: verbose for complex charts, dated default look, two APIs (pyplot state machine vs object-oriented) cause confusion, and no built-in interactivity in static output.
codeExamples:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.plot([1, 2, 3])        # pyplot: implicit "current" axes - hidden global state
plt.title("A")
plt.figure()               # silently starts a new figure; later calls go there
plt.title("B")
print(len(plt.get_fignums()), "figures alive")   # easy to leak figures

# OUTPUT:
# 2 figures alive

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: slow with millions of points, limited web interactivity (use Plotly/Bokeh), and 3-D support is basic.
codeExamples:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

# Plot 1 million points: works but renders slowly - downsample or use datashader
x = np.arange(1_000_000)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(x[::1000], np.sin(x[::1000] / 1e4))   # decimate to 1000 points
plt.close(fig)                                # free memory
print(len(x[::1000]))

# OUTPUT:
# 1000

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use the object-oriented API (fig, ax) in libraries and services so state never leaks, and pick the Agg backend on servers. Matplotlib suits static, publication-grade output; choose Plotly/Altair/Bokeh for interactive dashboards and datashader for very large point clouds. Always close figures in long-running processes.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Plotly builds interactive charts (hover, zoom, pan, legend toggle) that render in the browser via plotly.js. plotly.express creates a full figure from a DataFrame in one call.
codeExamples:
import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px

df = pd.DataFrame({"day": [1, 2, 3, 4], "visits": [120, 150, 90, 200]})
fig = px.line(df, x="day", y="visits", title="Daily visits", markers=True)
print(type(fig).__name__, fig.data[0].type, fig.layout.title.text)

# OUTPUT:
# Figure scatter Daily visits

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Stakeholders explore data themselves: they hover for exact values, zoom into a spike and filter series. Static PNGs cannot do that, and web dashboards need a browser-native format.
codeExamples:
import plotly.express as px

fig = px.bar(x=["A", "B", "C"], y=[3, 7, 5])
fig.update_traces(hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y} units")   # custom tooltip text
print(fig.data[0].type, list(fig.data[0].y))

# OUTPUT:
# bar [3, 7, 5]

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Business dashboards (with Dash or Streamlit), notebook exploration, geographic maps, financial candlestick charts, and shareable single-file HTML reports.
codeExamples:
import plotly.express as px, pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3, 4], "y": [2, 3, 5, 9], "kind": ["a", "a", "b", "b"]})
fig = px.scatter(df, x="x", y="y", color="kind", size="y")   # color/size mapping
fig.write_html("report.html", include_plotlyjs="cdn")        # one shareable file
print(len(fig.data), "traces")                               # one trace per color

# OUTPUT:
# 2 traces

beginner.content:
Diagram

   DataFrame --> plotly.express / graph_objects --> Figure (JSON spec)
                                                       |
                         +-----------------------------+----------------+
                         v                             v                v
                  Notebook / Dash app           write_html()      write_image()
                  (plotly.js in browser)        (shareable file)  (needs kaleido)
                  hover - zoom - filter

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: interactivity out of the box, concise express API, 40+ chart types including 3-D and maps, exports to HTML/JSON, and integrates with Dash.
codeExamples:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=["Q1", "Q2"], y=[10, 14], name="Sales"))
